THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty the Qneen, Prince Albert, and the Royal guests at the Palace, visited Hyde Park yesterday morning as early as nine o'clock. They remained for more than an hour, and were principally engaged in examining the objects on the north side of the nave in the British division, espe- cially the "leather," "paper," and mineral manufactures, / sections, and the Fine Arts Court. Again during yesterday a large accession was made to the funds of the Commission, amounting altogether to upwards of 2500/. To-morrow the building will remain open till seven o'clock, and that arrangement will be continued, and probably extended if such is found desirable. The frequent visits of her Majesty and the Royal Family have added considerably to the popularity of the Exhibition —all minds are occupied with it, and all tongues are loud in praises; one of its peculiarities is its vast extent, which can- ' not be fully comprehended on the first visit, and it is only when an attempt is made to methodise and arrange the process of investigation and inspection, that the stupendous scale upon which the whole has been planned can be fully comprehended. The efforts of a long day sink into insignificance when a trial is made to explore the illimitable mazes opal and lime stone of Porto Santo, and the lignite of Madeira ; while a curious specimen of the porous stone peculiar to the Island of Terceira, formed into a large cauldron-shaped cistern, and practically exemplifying its filtering properti. s in a vessel below, is an interesting object in the centre of the area. The vegetable kingdom of Madeira, singularly prolific in all useful growths, is well illustrated in the specimens which are here provided, one of the most prominent features being a tableau of ferns verypicturesquely arranged under a glass frame. The manufacture, consist of linens and shawls, mingled with such light arts as hair and flower workings, small cabinet toys, and a series of wax models delineating the flowers and ' fruits indigenous to the island. ' Among the many curious and valuable specimens exhibited by Mr. Tennant is the large emerald, the property of his Grace the Duke of Devonshire, and which is said to be the third most valuable jewel in this country; the Koh-i-Noor being the first, Mr. Hope's great diamond the second, and the duke's large emerald the third. The story rues that when his grace was examining Mr. Tennant's collection of gems, he said, " I suppose you would like to have my emerald to exhibit 1" Mr. Tennant replied that he would be delighted to have an opportunity of doing so, but he was afraid of the risk. " Then," said his grace, " I shall take the risk ;" and the emerald was sent to Mr. Tennant. As the hour of closing approaches, the great bell sounds forth its note of preparation, and then the bulk of the visitors commence pouring out of the aisles and compartments, scampering down the staircases, and collecting in the transept and eastern and western entrances. Carriages are called up in rapid succession, and meantime the exhibitors commence the work of cleaning and making snug for the night ; feather brooms and brushes are called into requisition, and a prodigious dust is soon kicked up, which hastens the departure of these who have not yet drunk in their fill of the marvels of the Exhibition. Linen and calico cases and sheets are laid over the more precious articles, and the scantilyattired Venuses, Junos, and Ilebes, who have all day unblushingly braved the gaze of the many thousand connoisseurs and critics, are clothed in night-gowns or eaemises, while Power's Greek slave girl, who has been performing a/ fresco pirouettes all day to a crowd of admirers on her revolving pedestal, blushes to the ancles in a full suit of crimson drapery. The organs peal forth a final voluntary, although they are chary enough of their music throughout the day, and other indications of the shutting up of the great heeler are shown in the appearance on the scene of watchmen, firemen, watermen, and lamplighters; in addition to this numerous and efficient band of organised assistants, the opening of the water mains throughout the building are exposed, from whence start up huge brass-nozzled tubes, surrounded by buckets of water, leaving the spectator of these numerous precautions to infer that the whole building was as safe from fire as if it were enveloped in a wet blanket. A general scrutiny of the whole establishment succeeds—as the shades of night begin to fall, the great eastern star, the diamond mountain, sinks into its impenetrable safe, "the watch is set," and the frail crystalline fabric is as eafe from intrusion as if it were encompassed by walls of adamant. It having been determined that on and af:er the 26th of this month the charge for admission into the Exhibition shall be reduced to Is. for four days in the week, her Majesty's Commissioners have again had under their consideration the question of making arrangements for the accommodation of the working classes who may be expected to arrive from the country for the purpose of visiting it. This subject has engaged the attention of the commission from a very early period; and when, in July last, Mr. Alexander Redgrave, of the Home Office, was appointed for the special purpose of co operating with Colonel Reid in obtaining such information and making such arrangements as might facilitate the visits of the labouring population to the Exhibition, he particularly desired to consider the advisability of instituting a register of lodging and lodging-houses, for the information of visitors arriving from the country. The general result of the inquiries which the commissioners have made is, thatvit will be better for them to leave this matter to the exertions of visitors themselves, and to abstain from attempting to organise a system for their accommodation, as it appears that by doing so they would interfere with many praiseworthy undertakings of private individuals, by means of which it is now probable that their object will be more fully accomplished than it could be by any system of centralisation. The commissioners have learnt with much satisfaction, that in many cases very liberal arrangements have been made for the reception of persons coming from particular districts. Where this is not the case, they recom',lend that mechanic , , about to visit the Exhibition should endeavour, by mutual co-operation, and by arrangements made before leaving their homes, to obviate the inconvenience which might arise from their coming together in large numbers without previously preparing for their accommodation. The following letter has been addressed to a morning contemporary : Sir,- -Yon have given the world the advantage of a considerable and judicious body of criticism on many of the works of art no iv to be seen in the Great Exhibition. Will you permit me to draw the attention of the public to one particular object, which I do not remember to have seen noticed in your reviews—l mean the Bible! To a man capable of serious reflection there is probably no work in that vast and astonishing magazine of human genius and skill which appears more carious and remarkable than the Bible exhibited by the British and Foreign Bible Society, and primed in no less than 130 different languages, now spoken by the various tribes of the human race. Such a work is without previous example. No other book was ever printed in one-fourth part of such a number of tongues. As a specimen of industry, consecrated and glorified by religion, it is well worthy of a place in a building which was inaugurated by prayer, and by the noblest chorus of thanksgiving to Ciod which the genius of man ever immortalised in music. Asa representative and type of the missionary spirit of the nation, these 130 copies of the Bible are a subject of profound interest, no less than of just pride, to every Protestant Englishman. But, I grieve to say it, these considerations appear to have been but lightly regarded by the subordinate, though really acting, managers of the committee of the Great Exhibition. When the agents of the Bible Society first applied for permission to exhibit their extraordinary work, they were met with a flat refusal. Subsequently, when it was found impessible altogether to reject so just a claim, a place was allotted for the work; but the place was a bad one, and the space was not one-third part as large as was required. But, even this place was subsequently usurped for the purpose of occupying it with a staircase. Room was, however, afterwards given to the Bible; but, by way of compensation, I suppose, it was thrust into a bypassage, where one can hardly discover it. It is at the back of the room which contains the Prince of Wales's cradle. Finally, in order that there should be no mistake about the spirit in which the Bible was treated, the number in the catalogue which ought to have contained an account of this wonderful national work (for it is a national work) was printed blank. I cannot help contrasting the very different treatment which Mr. Pugin and other exhibitors who profess the Roman Catholic faith have received. They have had their specimens of mediaeval rat set off to the best advantage. I don't complain of this. I don't begrudge to any exhibitor, whatever his creed may be, the most advantageous room for his works. I ask for no favour. I ask only for justice and impartiality. I say it is a national disgrace; I had almost said it is a national sin, that the Bible should be so treated.— I am, Sir, your obedient servant, May 13. A PROTESTANT CLERGYMAN. THE PRIMATE'S PRAYER. TO THE EDITOR OP THE ST. JAMES'S CHRONICLE. SlR,—Should you have received no previous communication in reference to a letter which appeared in your columns, signed a" Lay Christian," criticising the form of prayer used at the opening of the Great Exhibition, will you give insertion, if you think desirable, to the following. The complaint is that the Redeemer's name is not rendered more prominent; but this criticism, whatever it is worth, must apply equally to all our Church prayers; nor can it attach in any case (as I believe) where prayer is offered through the mediation of Christ, as expressed at the conclusion, such a termination having the effect of signatures to any public documents, i. e., bearing a reflex and diffusive force through all the previous clauses. Thus much I felt bound to say, being so far at the antipodes of a " Lay Christian" in the matter, that I could not forbear taking the form of prayer into the pulpit, that the poor of my flock might be partakers of its edification and my thankfulness; and I will further take the liberty of adding, that I do not think it a greater matter for thankfulness that prayer should have been used on the occasion than that the prayer should have been this—so suitable, so Scriptural, so excellent, so much, in a word, in accordance with the tone and spirit of our incomparable liturgy.—l beg to remain, yours obediently and truly, CALEB WHITEFOORD, Rector of Burford, Salop. Whitton Rectory, May 12, 1851.

CARPETS FOR THE GREAT EXHIBITION.—The local exhibition of articles intended for the World's Fair, in Hyde Park, was held in Messrs. Henderson's new carpet. weaving shed, Back-lane. The appearance of this noble edifice attracted general attention, not only on account of its great extent, but from the admirable lightness and beauty of its proportions. It. is said to be the largest structure devoted to the specific purpose of carpet-weaving to be met with in England. and Is, we understand, but one of a series which this enterprising firm contemplate erecting for the purplse of carrying on their large and widely-extended trade. The present building, which has just been completed, was designed by P. C. Hardwicke, Esq., the architect of the New Hall, and , seems in every respect admirably adapted for the object in view. The room is 164 feet long, by 76 broad, and is about 30 feet high.. It has two roofs with lanterns, which give it an extremely light and elegant appearance. A•VASE OF SHELLFLOWERS FOR THE EXHIBITION.— A. very large and splendid vase of shell flowers, destined for the Great. Exhibition, has been on view at Manchester. The story of its extremely ingenious and tasteful fabricator is interesting. She is a poor woman, upwards of 40 years of age, and formerly laboured for years far below ground, in a coal-pit. She had the misfortune to fall down the shaft, a great depth, and sustained severe and lasting injury. Subsequently, she married a poor fisherman of Southport, and is the mother of eleven children, eight of whom are still living and around her. With such a family; andher husband's small earnings, life must have been a long continuous struggle. But it is said necessity is the mother of invention, and taste, like poetry, is often' inborn. Her first attempt to contribute to the support of the family was, by making little models of cottages, churches, &c., and adorning them with sand and shells gummed upon the surface. With the money thus earned, she tried to form bhel I • fio wers, but only in a small way, and with limited means, and by no means good materials ; till one day her husband came home after a severe storm, and mentioned that he had found and left on the beach a branch of a true covered with what he called barnacles adhering to it. She requested him to bring it home, as she thought she could make something of it. She found the shells to be of a kind offering excellent material for the construction of flowers. Each pair (bi-valve) consists of two large and two smaller overlapping plates, and one long taper proboscis-like filament of shell. These her husband procures for her in large quantities ; and, having cleansed them and made them beautifully white, this ingenious and wholly self-taught artist proceeds to construct flowers from natural models, with a taste and judgment which would be rich gifts in any station of life, but which, under the circumstances, are most extraordinary in a poor fisherman's wife. In a rich and elegant porcelain vase, are grouped together, with exquisite taste, both as to elegance of forms and harmony of colours, a large collection of exotic and other choice flowers, mingled with wild flowers, and the blossoms of some of our flowering plants, trees, and hedges. We do not profess to be able to name all ; but amongst them are admirable specimens of the passion-flower, the large white and the yellow water-lily, the chrysanthemum, dahlia, ranunculus, anemone, moss and other roses, all arranged with great taste, and interwoven with many of the more graceful pensile blossoms, as the fuchsia, labor num, sweet pea, and even the hawthorn blossom, and the foliage and cones of the fir. The foot of the vase is , encircled with a simply elegant wreath of the hedge or briar rose. The stems and leaves are procured from the makers of artificial flowers in London ; and the artist has also procured thence the pigments with which she tints the flowers with so much delicacy , and -accuracy as to make them closely resemble nature: COUR7'.AND FASHION. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. BARER v. Fox AND HENDERSON.—At the Brompton County Court, on Thursday, the plaintiff, a journeyman painter, sued the defendants, Messrs. Fox and Henderson, the eontraetiirs for the erection of the Great Exhibition, Hyde-park, for the sum of £7 lie, balance of wages alleged to be due. Although the sum sued for was small in amount, the proc?edings were instituted on principle, involving nearly eighty similar claims, the claimants wishing to understand whether a fair day's work was not equivalent to a fair day's wages. — The cashier to the defendants, admitted that the plaintiff had been employed in the building of the Exhibition, but not by the defendants. There had been 2,600 workmen at the building, in each department of which sub-contractors had been deputed, the painting being allotted to a Mr. Robson, who, if anybody, was liable for the demand now set forth. He had understood that all the painters were engaged at the fixed wages of 4s per day.—The plaintiff, however, asserted that Mr. Robson agreed to give sixpence an hour for ten hours' work daily, and that he entered into a contract with Mr. Robson only as foreman, in which light he was looked upon, and as such was paid by the defendants, from whom he received a certain weekly salary as their servant. He told him at the time of being employed that the defendants were to be his paymasters. Mr. Robson was not present.—His Honour observed that the question was of the greatest importance to masters and workmen, and required thorough investigation. In the construction of railroads subcontractors employed the workmen, but still it did not follow that the same plan was to be adopted at the Crystal Palace. He, could not go further into the case without examining Mr. Robson, for whose attendance he should adjourn the hearing till the next court day.—Adjourned accordingly.

As things stand at pre- sent, even the men who are on duty in the Crystal Palace itself have seen nothing beyond the limited district ap- portioned to each individual. MR. PAXTON'S PLAN rOR A WINTER GARDEN. Mr. Paxton has just issued a pamphlet, on the subject of the retention of the Crystal Palace, and the purposes to which it is applicable. He proposes to turn it into a Winter Park and Garden, in which the trees and plants might be so arranged as to give great- diversity of views and picturesque effect. Spaces might be set apart for equestrian exercise, and for carriage drives; but the main body of the building should be arranged with the view of giving great extent and variety for those who promenade on foot. Fountains, statuary, and every de- scription of park and garden ornament, would greatly heighten the effect and beauty of the scene. " Beautiful creeping plants might be planted against the columns, and trailed along the girders, so as to give shade in summer, while the effect they would produo, by festooning in every diversity of form over the build- ing, would give the whole a most enchanting and gorge- ous finish. " Besides these there might be introduced a collection of living birds from all temperate climates, and the science of geology, so closely connected with the study of plants, might be illustrated on a large and natural scale, thus making practical botany, ornithology, and geology familiar to every visitor. " The alterations necessary to the building itself, to produce the effects I have suggested, would not be many, or cost much money. Shortly will be published, by me, a view showing how the whole may be finished so as to do away with all idea of smoke, chimneys, o: other kind of nuisance. The details of the alterations neces- saryl, do not propose to treat of now; but I mav men- tion, for the information of those who live opposite the Crystal Palace, that I should recommend the wood board- ing round the bottom tier of the building to be removed, and replaced with glass; the present appearance of it is heavy, and gives anything but the idea indicated by its name. When glass is sbjected for wood, the appearance will be marvellously changed; these who drive and ride in the park will, even in winter, see the objects within as they pass by, and the whole wili have a light aerial ap- pearance, totally unlike what it has at present. In sum- mer I should recommend the whole lower glass tier to be entirely removed, so as to give, from the park and the houses opposite the palace, an appearance of continuous park and garden. Here I must state what I believe will be the position of those who live opposite the Crystal Palace. I fully admit they have had just cause of complaint, by having all the turmoil of so vast an undertaking as the Great Exhibition developed ut-. der their eyes and ears, with all its attendant incpnve. niences; but if the building is allowed to stand,. and be adapted as I propose, the advantages derivable to them will compensate for all the evil they may have sustained in that respect. The boarding being all removed and glass substituted, they will have, within a few minutes' walk, a beautiful park, decorated with the beauties of nature and art, under a sky-roof, having a climate warmed and ventilated for the purpose of health alone, furnishing close to their own firesides, a promenade unequalled in the world, for the six winter months, a temperature analogous to that of southern Italy. Although placed in inch immediate proximity to this country, and with such daily and hourly means of communication, our Dutch neighbours appear to have been somewhat slow to avail themselves of the opportunity afforded them of displaying their peculiar manufactures and inventions to the rest of the world. The compartment appropriated to the productions of Holland is small, and by no means over-crowded. The most striking and attractive display is In front of the compartment. It Is • corsage of diamonds and pearls to be worn in the stomacher, by Remain of Rotterdam. The central ornament is a medallion portrait of her Majesty, which may be removed and another ornament substituted. The pearls and diamonds composing this costly piece of workmanship are of large size and are arranged to form wreaths of flowers and leaves on elastic sterns. Van Kempen, of Utrecht, exhibits specimens in silver of the Gothic, Renaissance, Louis XIV., and Louis XV. style., and there is a very well-exeeuted silver beaker formed from a single piece, which displays the art of embossing as practised in Holland. A silver kettle on • stand is another highly ornamental specimen of embossing; the figures forming the stem, handles, and lid are appropriate and well executed. There are some flower' and butterflies sculptured in Carrara marble, which have all the delicacy of wax, and some cameos in Imitation of the antique. Several candelabra of large size are exhibited, In which an attempt is made to Introduce crystal stems as an accessory to the ornsmentation. Having seen what has been almompliahed in this way by Osier, of Birmingham, and some of our other English manufacturers, we must set down these specimens of Dutch art manufacture as primitive and unsatisfactory. The glass has neither the transparency nor the high polish of the English " metal," although the design as a whole is well conceived and striking, and the gilt caryatides at the base • novel effect. The Dutch have been long proverbial for the flue.. seas and beauty of their linens and damasks, although the spedmens here exhibited me not very numerous. There are some cloths for communion-tables richly damasked, and specimens exhibiting the arms and peealiar weapons of Holland and Warts.- burgh, and a manufacture in gold cloth and silver damask, which is extremely rich and beautiful. The millet& laneous articles include toys, basket-work, clocks, in which the Americans have DOW left them far behind; screens in lacquer, and piano -fortes in purple and satin flower-tables and baskets, and vases, in wood and twisted reed, which have a good effect, and are evidently manufactured ,at a small price. The cotton and woollen goods are peculiar, the blankets, of Dutch wool, hare the solidity of broad cloth, and appear made to last for ever—there are specimens exhibited for the different foreign markets which they supply, but they have the lightness nor the fineness of Koglish manufacture. Among the agricultural implements and machinery are earth-borers, a percussion-cap making machine, in which the copper, in stripes of ribbon, is rapidly and by an ingenious process brought into , shape, and the caps loaded. Some agricultural and improved 1 engineering articles we shall have a word to say upon at another time. In the gallery above there are some well-exouted models of crane and swing bridges for railways. The crane-bridge has been constructed by Cott rad chief-engineer of-ti,, Botch ?Away, over seer mad I. iighli and easily managed. A model of • roiling-bridge, by the same engineer, over the old Rhine, below Leyde, is not apparently so satisfactory in its working, although it exhibits some novelty and ingenuity. For a country which keeps its head above water mainly by the counteracting influence of the wind—the whole of Holland being continually under the action of windmills, whit& carry the surplus water out of the dykes into the sea —we are surprised to find only one specimen of a water-mill In the entire collection. The mill has two screws, and is calculated to lift a large quantity of water. An improved break for railway carriages is rather a clumsy-looking affair. A sugar.. cane mill is remarkable for the great power exhibited in a paratively small space, and appears to be an effective arrangement. The lady visitors will admire some cloaks, muffs, do., made of the feathers of the crested pigeon, embroidery, and bronzes for flower vases, dic. As nrght be anticipated, the bells by which the chimes or car& ions are rung in the churches and cathedrals are a prominent , 1 feature in the display of that country in which ills said they were originally Invented; they are brought to great perfection in point of tone and tune, the former arising from the quantity of silver added to the inferior metal, and the latter from the pains taken to render them really effective as musical instruments. At a meeting of the Royal Commission held on Tuesday in the Crystal Palace, His Royal Highness Prince Albert announced that Her Majesty had determined to open the Exhibition on the Ist of May in state. The details of the pageant have not yet been arranged. The whole of the jurors for the different classes of articles were elected on Tuesday. Among the jurors will be found the names of the most eminent scientific men in the country, as well as those of the highest standing in the various branches of mechanical and manufacturing skill and industry, and who, from their high position and known integrity, will not fail to ensure respect for their decisions. In strict accordance with the comprehensive spirit and character of the undertaking, it is proposed to call into requisition the refined taste and discriminating judgment of a a committee of ladies,uponwhomwill devolve the duty and the honour of deciding upon the merits of those peculiar branches of industry which fall more appropriately within the sphere of their observation, such as fancy and industrial needlework, Her Grace the Duchess of Sutherland has already kindly consented to act, as well as a number of other ladies of distinguished rank, and of intimate acquaintance with the subjects on which they will be called upon to adjudicate. THE PROTECTION OF INVENTIONS ACT.—The new act, which received the royal assent on Friday, to extend the provisions of the Designs Act of 1850, and to give protection from piracy to persons exhibiting new inventions in the Exhibition of the Works of Industry of all Nations has Just been printed. It contains ten short clauses, and came into force on the 11th instant. It is provided that the proprietors of new inventions are to be allowed to exhibit them without prejudice to letters patent to be thereafter granted. The inventors before public exhibition are to be provisionally registered, and not to be used before the granting of letters patent. The public trial of agricultural or horticultural implements, under the direction of the commissioners of the Exhibition, is not to prejudice the validity of any letters patent. Certificates of invention are to be granted for provisional registration by the Attorney- General, or such other person as he may appoint. Such certificates are to be registered. In the latter branch of industry their superiority will not be grudged, and they really owe society some act of reparation Tor having introduced among us Colt's revolvers. The artificial leg patented by Mr. Palmer, is, in its way, a most admirable, ingenious, and philanthropic contrivance, and its invention is so remarkably characteristic of the country from whence it comes, that we cannot resist the temptation of inviting attention to it. The patentee in some way or other lost his leg, and, having tried the best substitutes hitherto devised for such a case, like a true American, he set himself to think whether he could not improve upon them. His study of the subject was crowned with the most striking success, and he exemplifies that success in his own person by walking about almost without any perceptible lameness, and with an apparent ease and comfort which are truly surprising. He publishes annually at Philadelphia a journal, which he calls Palmer s Patent Artificial Leg Reporter and Surgical Adjuvant. This curiously entitled periodical accompanied a specimen of the leg to the Exhibition, and the Ist chapter of vol. 3, No. 1, we find commenced by this heading, "Fugitive thoughts on amputation." From another chapter, entitled " Synopsis of the in• vention," we gather that it is distinguished by its perfect combination of lightness with strength, and by the extraordinary fidelity with which it imitates nature. Having closely examined it we can testify to its merits on all the leading points specified, nor have we any reason to doubt that the enamelled surface of this leg, as stated, "is rivalled only by the mechanism of nature, and that a lady may wear silk hose and slippers without betraying the loss she has sustained." Mr. Palmer has received extensive orders for his patent in this country, and the public may soon expect to see timber-toed veterans no more stumping about Greenwich or Chelsea. A Prottrlinp Coat fur the Submarine Telegraph. —Among the home contributions is an invention of unpretending appearance but of excellent promise for real value, Mr. Dick, of Ayr; numbered 431 in Class X. It is protective casing for the wires of the electric telegraph, especially meeting and obviating the mischief which the wires are liable from the beating of the chafing sea on a rocky shore. It will be recollected that the telegraphic communication opened last year as an experiment between Dover and Calais was interrupted, a few hours after it was made, the cutting in two of the telegraphic cord, on the rocks forming the French shore : the rolling sea chafed it asunder in more than one place, on the sharp edges of the stone. A cheap and effective protection of the rope has been a desideratum for which inventors have much cudgelled their brains. Two very opposite qualities must be combinedextreme hardness, with perfect flexibility. In the invention of Mr Dick these two qualities are completely "blended. The material is cast-iron—at least hard enough; and the form adopted to secure flexibility is that which nature has selected for protecting the most delicate and powerful telegraphic apparatus yet known to man—the cord of nerves which radiates from the brain to the extremities of the higher animals, through their spine or vertebral column. The backbone of a man, or that of a more flexible creature, the snake or eel, might have been taken as a pattern ; but in that case there would have teen a complication of “processes” and interlocking projections to imitate : Mr. Dick has taken simpler form, and has thus unconsciously hit on the fonn selected by Nature for the backbone of the shark, —an apparatus at once powerful and more almost than any other flexible. A large bead of iron is threaded on the cord of electric wires, (which is previously encased, as at present, in a thick tube of gutta percha), then a perforated cylinder, like a “ bugle,” is threaded on to the string next to the ball; then another ball is threaded, and then another cylinder, and so on. The two ends of each cylinder are made concave, so as to receive the convex surface of the two balls on each side of it. Thus the whole string of iron beads aud bugles ” makes an iron tube, which protects the electric cord on which they are threaded, and is at the same time so flexible that a rope of it massive enough to weigh thirty or forty pounds to the lineal yard, (without the telegraphic cord,) will double up in loop that will lie round the rim of your hat. The merits of the contrivance is its perfect simplicity and effectiveness : it consists but of balls and cylinders, the chief cost of which must he only that of their cheap material, cast-iron. With such a protection, one would think that the wires of the submarine telegraph would safe against the beating of any sea, on any coast.

Some of our " Liberal" contemporaries are extremely indignant at the proposed arrangements for opening the Exhibition by the queen on the Ist of May. The Daily New s remarks " We understand, that at a solemn meeting of the Commissioners of the Great Exhibition, it has been determined that the Crystal Palace is to be opened in state by the Queen on the let of May; and that the only persons to be admitted to this ceremony are the Royal Commissioners, the diplomatic body, the members ef the government, and of the household. A more impolitic, a more absurd, or a more ludicrous resolution the Commissioners could not have come to. That a mere knot of individuals, about whom, with the exception of the Queen, the Prince, and one or two ministers, the people of England care not one farthing, should thus, like maggots in a huge Cheshire cheese, enjoy the opening of a vast national exhibition, which in itself, and in its inauguration, is not only a national but a European fete, is monstrous. That these gentlemen should enjoy the honours and privileges of a private and premature view is all very well. They may enjoy it in secret and in quiet on the last day of April, and the public will not inquire: But that upon the day which has been already announced for the first day of opening, not only the public, but even that elite of society, which could afford, and which has paid, its three guineas for season tickets—that they should be excluded, is really impertinence, to use the least offensive word." The Times says:— Her Majesty's intention of opening the Great Exhibition in persoa on the let of May has already been made known to the public. It may not, however, be as generally known that all visitors —even the exhibitors, as we understand the matter—are to be excluded from the building while the Queen, attended by a score or so of Lords and Ladies in Waiting, shall have celebrated the opening mysteries. The resolution of the Commissions, which embodies their determination of excluding the public, is now lying before us, and we here copy it verbatim, lest we should be suspected of an attempt to practise upon the credulity of our readers. It runs as followst—' Her Majesty having been pleased to signify her intention of visiting the Exhibition on the occasion of its opening, on the Ist of May, the doors of the building will not be opened to the public on that day till one o'clock, at which hour the holders of season tickets will be admitted.' "Now, what does this mean? The only possible suggestion which can occur to the mind is that some doubt may exist in the mind of her Majesty's advisers as to her safety, in case she should enter a building in which so thousands of persons are t o b e co ll ecte d together. But where does the real danger lie? Is it within or without the building, even admitting the preposterous idea that there is any danger at all Is it not just as complete an affair of police regulation to take proper steps for her Majesty's security within as wi s hout the Crystal Palace 1 It is of course not withoutgreat repugnance that we bring ourselves even to mention a question of this kind, but it is impossible to offer a satisfactory comment upon the resolution of the Commissioners without adverting to the probable motive upon which that resolution has been founded. If it be as we suppose, her Majesty's advisers are leading their Royal Mistress to a course which will be profoundly unpopular, and without an adequate motive. Queen Victoria receives every day sufficient evidence of the loyalty and affection of her subjects without attempting to banish them from her presence upon so interesting and so:emn an occasion as the opening of the Great Exhibition. As far as regards any isolated attempt at violence which might occnr to the febrile imagination of a 7rench or G;ermars Socialist, surely it is not necessary that a Person with such intention should gain access to the body of the building in order to carry out his purpose. Her Majesty would not be otherwise in danger in the Crystal Palace on the Ist of May than she yesterday, or will he to-morrow, whilst she drives out for an airing in the public stre:ts. What an unworthy part would these nervous advisers cause the Queen of England to play ! Surely Queen Victoria is not Tiberius or Louis XI., that she should be smuggled out of a great glass carriage into a great glass building under cover of the truncheons of the police and broadswords of the Life Guards ? Where most Englishmen are gathered together there the Queen of England is most secure ! "Let all reasonable and proper precautions: be taken for her Majesty's safety, just as when see opens parliament in person. That is as it should be. But have the Commissioners reflected upon the menner in which they are depriving the Queen of all enjoyment in the spectacle by banishing her subjects from the building ? What satisfaction can it afford her Majesty to be introduced into a monster upholstery warehouse, or engine-house, attended only by a few , gold sticks and silver sticks? One thinks! involuntarily of Wordsworth' famous description of A party i n a parlour, All silent, and all damned!' But what is the silence of a parlour to the silence of the Great Exhibition, when not a sound, save perhaps a faint murmur of discontent, shall be heard from the thousands of excluded ticket -holders who are flattening their noses against the outside wainscotting or panes? No reasonable person would ask more than that the 6000 or 7000 holders of season -tickets should be admitted to the whilst her Majesty is opening the Exhibition i building n person. Th e pr i ce of the ticket affords something hike a guarantee that the mob would be of a select character—sufficiently so for the purpose in view. Besides, there is no reason to doubt that, in numerous instances, the season-tickets were purchased on the faith that their holders would be admitted T.o a sight of the opening pageant. What does the number of 6000 or 7000 persons signify within the area of this vast building, which wo u ld contain 40,000? They would scarcely be sufficient to give her Majesty a hear ty cheer worthy of th e C rystal Palace and the occasion. We tru st mos t sincerel y , on all accounts, that her Majesty's advisers will re-consider this resolution. i Better, far better would t be, to forego any publi c ceremon i a l whatsoever, than to carry it out in a form so offensive t o the feelings of every E ng lishman. This is to turn Queen Victoria into another Lady Godiva; and doubtless the modern will be attended with as much success as the legendary experiment. Friday the 27th ult. was a half-crown day, but notwith. standing the increased charge of admission, and the heat of the weather, 2,9691. 6s. were taken at the doors, and 29,033 people entered the building. The oppressive heat on Saturday proved too great even for the attractions of the Crystal Palace, and since it was opened there has scarcely been so small an attendance. The sum taken at the doors was 15901. 16s., and the number of persons visiting the building, 11,501. Tn vain did ladies appear in the thinnest muslin dresses, and gentlemen walk about with- out hats. The wind would not blow in such a direction as to secure a thorough draught, and in the desperate effort to find relief from their sufferings, some clustered round the fountains, others saturated themselves with filtered water, and many spent the greater part of the afternoon in eating ices and drinking lemonade and soda water. On Monday there was a very considerable falling off in the numbers that visited the building, the police returns giving 52,879 as the total, while the receipts at the doors amounted to 2,4691. 16s. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. TUESDAY. Teere were on Tuesday striking evidences of "the beginning of the end." One of the most attractive and beautiful objects in the centre of the building, Oster's crystal fountain, was gone, and over the brickwork foundationwas placed a spacious platform, which occupied the whole of the centre of the transept, and upon which the ceremony of closing the exhibition on the following day was to be gone through. All the statuary near the centre of the transept had been huddled into a corner of the refreshment court, to make room for rows of benches. Nearly all the machinery had ceased working, and the artisans and smiths were here and there making the preliminary preparations for taking to pieces those splendid specimens of the industrial progress of the country and of the scientific ingenuity of our engineers and mechaniciane. The gilded cage of the Koh i-floor, now shorn of its great attraction, re.enained merely to point a moral, but. a rival celebrity took post beside it, and the ' diamond was forgotten in " the old woman from Cornwall," in her slouched hat, who had a crowd about her all day more compact and more curious than were Been congregated about the jewele of the Q leen of Fspain. Tae Queen and his Royal Highness Prince Albert, accompanied by the Princess Royal and the Princess Alice, visited the building again on Tuesday, for the purpose of making a final inspection of its contents. The Royal family arrived from Windsor shortly before ten o'clock, and were received at the private entrance by Mr. Dilke and other officers of the establishment. The route taken by her Majesty included the circuit of the whole of the central foreign galleries. Herr Sommers was here staticreci with his sommerophone ' and if he did not delight he must have at least astonished the Royal party by the immense volume of sound with which he filled the entire building. The Queen then made the circuit of the British galleries, through long avenues of silks, ribbons, and lace sparkling ranges of gold and silver plate, and cases and caskets of glittering gems, any of them fit to grace a regal diadem. Passing through the horological department, the Reyal party reeched the extreme west of the buddies, and here her Majesty paused a moment to look down the long and splendid pageant, extending nearly half a mile before her, and revealing almost at a glance an amount and variety of industrial riches and treasures of art such as was never before collected under one roof. The work of demolition and disruption which had already commenced was in itself suggestive of the vanity and perishaLleness of all earthly things; and withent pretending with the author of" The Lily and the Bee" to be acquainted with what was passing in her Majesty's mind, the scene was calculated to inspire reflections upon the evanescent nature of all the highest and most glorious productions of industry and creations of art. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The most remarkable circumstance to be noted in the record of Tuesday's proceedings at the Crystal Palace was the enormous number of visitors who attended during the day, considerably above 74,000 having pessed the barriers between 10 o'clock in the morning and 6 in the evening. There was at one period 61,000 persons within the building, equal to the population of a large continental city or a fourth or fifth-rate town in our own country. This extraordinary influx mey be attributed partly to the great attraction of the Exhibition itself, but an accidental circumstance contributed to swell the numbers beyond what would probably have otherwise betel their amount. There were great numbers of farmers tending from all parts of the country to the Windsor Cattle Snow, and they no doubt took London in their way, in order to have a peep at the wonders in Hyde Park. As Tuesday's numbers may probably not again be equalled, it will be worth while to note the rate at which the visitors poured in. 11 o'clock, 22,068; 12 o'clock, 21,711; one o'clock, 14,713; two o'clock, 16102; three o'clock, 4679; rive o'clock, 1427; six o'clock, Such an extraordinary assemblage could not, of course, be collected in one soot without producing a perceptible increase of excitement in the vicinity. Daring the morning the footpaths on both sides of the road presented one continued stream of pedestrians, and the carriage-way from Hyde Park-corner down to the Exhibition was a dense mass of omnibuses, cabs, vans, and other vehicles of all sorts and sizes. Her Majesty arrived shortly after nine o'clock, accompanied by Prince Albert, and inspected the Austrian toys and glass. The Queen afterwards examined the Austrian and Lyons silk, and devoted some time to the inspection of the beautiful printed muslins in the Mulhausen gallery. A large party of boys and girls from the Foundling Hospital Scieaol arrived during her Majesty's visit, and they were graciously permitted to form in line, and make their obeisances to their sovereign. There were one or two large attachments from the great towns in the north, and a band of 150 workmen from Carshalton, franked by their employer, Mr. Muggridge. These men marched up to the entrance with a band of music at their head, and enjoyed themselves exceedingly. Several small schools also came in, but the vast majority of the visitors were countryfolk, with a considerable sprinkling of foreigners. These last were principally Uermans. The Hull police authorities sent up 20 of their men, being a second detachment, and we were glad to receive an intimation that the hints we recently gave to the Metro. politan Commissioners are likely to be acted on. It is understood that after the Ist of next month, when the men will be changed according to custom, each constable will have a day given him, without deduction of pay, in order that he may see the Exhibition. The arrangements for the Parisian festivities are in active progress. They are to consist of a ball at the Hotel de Ville, for which 4000 tickets will be issued, and a dinner for a more select few with covers for 200, with other attractions which are not as yet definitively arranged. It is hoped that the time will be so fixed, as to make one of the three days which the visitors will spend in France, the Ist of August, so as to enable them to see the annual play of the great fountains at Versailles. The party from the Exhibition will number about 800. The temperature of the interior was quite comfortable during Tuesday, the breeze being allowed full play across the transept through the openings recently made. The following are the official returns of the receipts of Tuesday : Season tickets £ 7 7 0 At the doors... 3502 1 0 Total receipts £3509 8 0 Police numbers 74,122 Yesterday the attendance, although many thousands below the monster gathering of the ,preceding day, was yet considerably beyond the number of previous Wednesdays: 58,000 persons were admitted on Wednesday week, while yesterday the numbers considerably exceeded 61,000. Her Majesty was, as usual, one of the earliest visitors, and proceeded to inspect the various articles displayed outside the west end of the building. Rogers' large anchor was first examined, the inventor being in attendance to explain its advantages. The Queen then examined the various large specimens of coal, among others the immense block, weighing 24 tons, from Stavely works, Chesterfield, which was raised from a abaft 459 feet deep, and the Earl Fitzwilliam's pillar, exhibiting a complete section of the Barnsley thick bed of coal from the Elsicot colliery. The Royal party then re-entered the building, and proceeded to the Indian department, where Dr. Royle was in attendance, and explained the nature of the mineral and vegetable products, and the Indian mode of manufacturing cotton and of preparing opium. The sugar specimens, and the mode of preparation, were also explained to her Majesty. The Queen then retired to her carriage, passing through a double line of the visitors to the door specially reserved for the royal exit. The temperature of the building was exceedingly pleasant, and there was not the slightest crowding or inconvenience throughout the day. The visitors were of an exceedingly mixed character, but the provincial physiognomy was not quite so conspicuous as on former occasions. There was a great muster of schools both public and private, the latter taking advantage of the halfholiday for their visit. Among the public schools were the Greenwich Union, the boys of which after their inspection drew up in the transept and sang "God save the Queen," but the mode of execution was not such as to provoke any very violent call fcr an encore. There was also the Aldersgate school, 114; the Seven Oaks, 25; and the Farnham; the latter, along with about 40 labourers and their families being treated by the Lord Bishop of Winchester. There was a body of workmen from Mr. Kingham's floorcloth manufactory. and the scholars from a school at Carshalton. The most conspicuous of the public schools, both in numbers and appearance, was the Licensed Victuallers, the boys and girls of which were sent in by Sir Henry Meux, and regaled, also at his expense, with a sub- I stantial cold dinner in Mr. Younghusband's dining-rooml for exhibitors. The respectable appearance of these children, so different from the pupils of other public institutions, was the subject of general praise and observation. A considerable quantity of new and remarkable goods has been added to various departments in the foreign nave. The Austrian stand yesterday exhibited some beautiful vases and goblets in Bohemian coloured glass, which had on one of the previous days been inspected and much praised by her Majesty. They are carved in deep intaglio, in the most skilful and elaborate manner, and have all the appearance of high relief. In the Dresden room fifteen cases of beautiful chin s were opened yesterday, and served completely to fill the large alcove which has lately been denuded of its contents to ornament the nave. They are principally table porcelain, but exhibit a great variety and novelty of pattern. The Italian court also exhibited, for the first time, some specimens of Roman art, which will no doubt be sources of great attraction to the virtuosi. They consist of models in beautiful Sienna marble of the ruins in the Roman forum, and, although not more than four feet in height, are perfect masterpieces in their way. It is intended to arrange them in positions similar to those in which the originals are placed, and there is no doubt but that they will become cne of the most prominent attractions of the court. There is also a splendid table inlaid in various oriental marbles, and a model of a bath in lapis lazuli, cut out of one of the largest blocks of the material that has yet been obtained. The last of the new importations is a small bust, an admirable likeness of Prince Albert, in antique marble, dug from the ruins of the Colliseum. This article was respectfully tendered to his , Royal Highness by Signor Carlo Trebbi, the Italian commissioner, but graciously declined, his Royal Highness, while warmly praising the workmanship, stating that his invariaMe rule was not to receive gifts from any of the exhibitors. The magnificent tams in Egyptian alabaster in this collection has been purchased by the Marquis of Westminster for 900/. Some few facts connected with the vehicular statistics of the Exhibition may not be uninteresting. It appears that 270 new omnibuses have been put on the line, in addition to about 100 regular stagers. Their average receipts are 10s. each journey, and they make eight journeys in the day. This would give a total of 1480/. per diem for omnibuses alone; but, in addition, the cabs must be taken into account, the receipts of which are of course inscrutable mysteries, except to the drivers and the fares; bat an approximate calculation taken by competent persons, gives the total sum paid for town travelling, as connected with the Exhibition, at 3500/. a day. ARRIVAL OF THE PETERHOFF STEAM YACHT.— This fine vessel, built by Mr. Mare, at Blackwell, and fitted with engines by Messrs. George and Sir John Rennie, to serve as an Imperial yacht to the Emperor of Russia, and which went, when on her passage to St. Petersburgh, on the racks off the Island of Oessel, in October last, has been recovered, and is now in the Import-dock of the East India Company at Blackwell, apparently in as good a state as before the accident, with the exception of the wood paneling of the cabins, which has yielded to the ill-treatment received and long immersio n u n d er w ate r ; but the hull and engines are as good as ever. The following details may prove interesting :—Various attempts were made by the captain and crew of the vessel to get her off, assisted by some officers and men sent by the Russian government, but without success. The vessel stuck fast on the ridge of rocks with a hole in her bottom, and being constructed of iron, she was abandoned by the Russian authorities to the agent of the company in London who had insured her, and the company sent out an able officer—Captain Fell—who after great exertions succeeded in getting her off the rocks. He I let the water into every part of her, and allowed her to remain I full all the winter. This bold experiment had the effect of preserving her from being battered by the winter storms, and in the spring the vessel was raised, and a f t er bein g partially repaired, he floated her to Riga, where she underwent a more thorough repair. He then tried the engines and found that they worked well, and ou trying the speed of the vessel at the measured mile, near Riga, the result was ascertained to be 16 knots an hour. From Riga Captain Fell proceeded with the vessel to Elsinore, and from Elsinore to Flamburgh, where he lay for a short time, and then left for England, and although he had to contend against a strong head wind reached the East India Docks, at Blackwell, on Sunday night last in 36 hours, being a distance of about 500 miles, showing the a,yerage speed of the vessel during. the voyage to be at the rate of upwards of knots per hour.

Among the curiosities of typo- graphy exhibited are specimens of different languages, printed on folio sheets. These commence with the Ger- man language of the present day; then follow the letters used for printing during the middle ages, the forms of which are represented by moveable types to the sixth century. A folio pagve of the Gutenburg Bible, in a frame, has been imitated with types which bear a most deceptive resemblance to the original, so that the original can scarcely be distinguished from the copy. Fron the oldest specimen of printing of the Gutenburg Bible we arrive at the depart- ment of wood-cut-printing, otherwise called Xylography. The most ancient woodcuts occupy the first place, and lead us to the different coats of arms, to Albrecht Direr's triumphal gate, the cuts of which have been collected, with the exception of a very few, by the Imperial Library. The woodcutting department of the establishment has un- dertaken to complete these woodcuts, in order to have them in readiness if a reprint of them should ever be re- quired. A number of initial letters and whole alphabets of the seventeeth century, also a number of seals, are here arranged. On Thursday, the influx of visitors to the Exhibition was greater than ever, and the sum taken at the doors could not have been much short of 12,000. This is, of course, entirely the proceeds of the 5s. entrance fee, and does not include the large amount still accruing from the sale of season tickets. All connected with the under- taklog are very naturally overjoyed at the success in a financial point of view which thus attends it, and which is manifested more and more decisively every day. The im- provement in the weather has acted with magical effect upon the flow of visitors, and brought out the beauty and fashion of London into Hyde-park, just as sunshine de- velopes butterflies. They take possession of the crystal palace in a manner which must make the royal commis- sion have sundry misgivings about their power to keep it in their own hands now, or to have it removed a few months hence. A man may be coerced, but how are la- dies to be dealt with should they take it into their heads to keep the building as a promenade, for which it really seems to be well adapted, when the exigencies of our most fickle and variable climate are remembered ? Other cities, under more genial skies, have their places of fashionable resort where friends meet and chat and part without the bother of a formal call. Here, unhappily, the weather destroys one-half our opportunities to learn cheerfulness, and our stiffness of character does the rest. One would think, from present appearances, that the Crystal Palace is likely to be seized upon by the public as supplying a great want in this respect. Of course at present, and while thronged with thousands of spectators, it is not a place of rendezvous. Friouds may he there and on the look-out for each other for hours together without meeting. In fact, this is generally the case, but as the first excitement wears off simple arrangements might be made for obviating inconveniences of this kind arising out of the size of the building. One particular central spot might be selected where mressages might be left that you had stepped into Tunis or China, or gone to Egypt or Italy, or started on a trip to America. Every one might be thus forthcoming to his friends at once, or if lie wished to avoid them, as is sometimes unfortunately the case, the Crystal Palace with its endless courts and avenues, with its secluded nooks for raw pro- duce and paper-hangings, is just the place for that pur- pose. Even now, when from 20,000 to 30,000 of the most inquisitive and adventurous people on the face of the earth are busily engaged in rum- maging its multifarious contents, it is quite possible to creep away into solitudes uninvaded by the bus- tling Babel elsewhere. Such is the size of the building, no part of which is overcrowded, while some still remain unvisited. Everybody whein he enters it has an intense desire to walk from end to end, to examine first one com- partment and then another, and to test his absorbing powers in the way of sight-seeing for one day. Under the influence of strong curiosity feats of pedestrianism are performed, the results of which are curiously mani- fested as the hour for closing approaches. Ladies are then seen anxiously casting about for seats in the already overcrowded benches with which the nave and transept are furnished. An army of exhausted finery reposes un- der the grateful shade of elms and palm trees singularly blended in the same scene. There they rest themselves after the fatigues of their progress through the industries of nations and continents, reluctant to quit a spectacle where their admiration has been so strongly aroused, and quietly watching the play of the great crystal fountain before them, the stream of gay company passing to and fro, the variegated effects of light shot through the Eglit- tering canopy over head, and ail the endless colours and forms of a perspective into which art has gathered her choicest trophies. What if this vast collection was destroyed by fire? Many cities might be burnt to the ground without causing such a sensation as that would. Yet, to that risk, the Crystal Palace was, for a moment, exposed yesterday morning. The flue attached to a gas stove in one of the ofices of the contractors became heated, and ignited a piece of wood with bunting which rested upon or touched it. A piece of the burning cloth fell into a small open cask of Indian corn, which stood, as tihe Irish say, "convenient." All this mischief was brewing in secret, in the southern part of the colonial collection, oi the east side. The drapery of the counter concealed what had happened, and it was only when the smioke began to break forth that aii alar u was raised. Fortunately, such casualties have been foreseen, and amply provided for. There are no less than a dozen large file-engines within the building, besides an amiple supply of water easily ob- tamable, and a thoroughly organized force ready to act at a moment's notice. Th'e fire of Sunday was extin- guished before it had time to lo more than slightly char one plank of wood, and nO anxiety need lie caused by an occurrence so trifling. It will, however, we trust, warn all parties connected with time building to be on the alert, and to trust nothing to chance. We have much pleasure in directing the attention of our readers to the following account of several ingenious productions about to be exhibited amidst the other attractions of the crystal palace. They are the invention of Mr. William Dyne, an employi of the London and South Coast Company, at their London station. Mr. Dyne is, we understand, the first person in the kingdom who applied gutta percha in the construction of life-boats, rafts, &c., he having taken out a patent for that purpose in 1847. A highly favourable opinion of these boats was expressed by Captain Austin, and but for an accidental delay some of them would have been taken out by the gallant Captain, on his recent Expedition in search of Sir John Franklin. The following description will convey to the reader some idea of the inventions, and of the extreme ingenuity their construction has called forth:- 1. THE ECLIPSE, OR STANDARD LIFE BOAT, possessing the following recommendations, which no other boat in its present construction can ever attain. It is economically constructed, possessing in its formation great strength and durability. It is very buoyant, frees itself instantly of all water shipped, will keep its upright position in the heaviest sea, is difficult to be turned over, and if upset will right itself immediately; impossible to be injured by hard collision, and is provided with a couch whereon to lay those suffering from immersion. It is formed of diagonal battens laid similar to that of lattice work, and its outer sheathing is formed of gutta percha; its buoyancy is 350 cubic feet of air, capable of sustaining upwards of 9i tons. It has in its bottom 3,600 holes half an inch in diameter to allow all water shipped to pass off; it has a convexed bottom, 30 feet long, 2 feet wide, and 18 inches deep, in which are placed three perforated fins for the purpose of steadying and keeping the boat in an upright position ; acting when the boat lurches from either beam similar to a paddle-wheel ; a re-action taking place through the perforated parts; which will be seen to multiply its weight of water to four times its amount; in this convexed part and between the fins is contained two tons of weight of water, which must be displaced therefrom before the boat can turn over, but such will be almost impossible, it being more than half the weight of the boat; bat as a provision against such a lamentable disaster, she turns over on her, quarter sixteen cwt. of water, which rights her again. It may be remarked that the two tons and sixteen cwt. of water referred to is not one ounce weight to the boat when in her upright position—thus, it will be seen that Nature is its servant as also its own master. At the stem and stern, and on each beam and quarter, is run a bow, to which is connected galvanized springs which will not corrode, and will be found of the greatest utility in the event of collision, which act similar to that of railway buffers; in fact, at the very glance of the model, will be seen great strength combined with lightness, and that its construction is so compact that it gains the admiration of all that see it. This model is submitted for the approval of his Grace the Duke of Northumberland for the prize of a hundred guineas, and bids fair to be the successful one, having all the qualities his Grace desires. 2. A GUTTA PERCHA LLFE BOOM, for the rescue of individuals from drowning, or to enable a stranded vessel to communicate with the shore. It is intended to be placed at the stern of the ship, so that on an alarm being given (a man overboard) the person at the helm can dislodge it instantly, and as it falls into the sea a fuzee becomes ignited, which burns with a brilliant light, guiding the sinking man to it; should it occur at night, four uprights are placed upon it, containing rockets, blue, and other li4sts, which ignite on being drawn out, thus acting as a beacon to the crew. 3. AN EMIGRATION LIFE RAFT, intended for a first• class vessel, of the following dimensions:-20 feet long by 14 feet wide; it is firmly united by strong bolts, and is very portable from the mode of its construction, which allows it to be folded up in the compass of 20 feet long by 2 feet 6 inches wide. On occasion of shipwreck it is capable of supporting 100 persons, as well as provisions for seven days, allowing to each individual two and a half pounds of food and one pint of water per day, in addition to which it may be made available for a portion of the cargo, and can be put in requisition in a few minutes. It will be found very useful in many cases of engineering, and may be used as pontoons, which they greatly surpass in buoyancy and portability, being easily carried by two or three persons, while the others require a waggon and two horses to convey them from place to place. 4. A LIFE LAUNCH on an entirely new principle: is rendered buoyant by inflated cushions placed under the gunnel, which protects it from injury when coming in contact with rocks or the sides of a ship, in being lowered for use. Let it be here remarked that the life boats now in use are almost invariably crushed and rendered useless in the event of a wreck, by concussion against the side of a ship. A boat constructed on this principle, from 25 to 30 feet in length, contains upwards of a thousand gallons of air, and would support six hundred persons, were it possible for so many to attach themselves to it. The tedious and incessant labour in baling, so necessary with all other life-boats is, by this invention, entirely superseded, being provided with a false bottom perf,mated with holes, through which the water passes off, leaving a dry surface. The boat is also furnished with a tank of fresh water, and the gunnels with lockers, containing water-proof bags of gutta percha, for the reception of provisions; a water-proof awning of gutta percha lies rolled up on the gunnel, which can be raised so as to form a complete protection from the inclemency of the weather, over which a lamp or other signal of distress is placed. Everybody waspreparedfor a great accession of numbers to the usual average of shilling visitors, but the most extravagant expectations could hardly have anticipated anything so remarkable as the actual realitv. On Monday 107,815 people entered.the building, and the sum of 51751. 16s. was taken at the doors. The dreaded limit of 100,000 spectators has been exceeded, and without any extra- ordinary inconvenience. In the Crystal Palace, as elsewhere, the people are their own best police, and from hour to hour crowds leave to make room for the gathering tide that enters. On Monday they began to ooze away as early as eleven o'clock; and so well balanced were the departures and arrivals that until the doors closed, it was possible, without much effort, to make a systematic and effectual survey of all the principal objects and departments. That nearly 108, 000 visitors should within one day, and under one roof, have enjoyed the grandest spectacle the world has ever witnessed, is of itself a sufficient marvel. When the crowd assembled within the building was at its culminating point, too, it was suddenly discovered that the Duke of Wellington was present. Instantly the manifes- tations of public admiration arose. Hats were taken off, and loud cheers burst forth, which were prolonged with immense energy. Those who were at a distance, surprised by an un- wonted agitation which they could not understand, fancied that there was something wrong, and rushed towaids the doors. The Duke also felt the awkwardness of his position, and beat a retreat. It appears that the visit of the Duke was not the least hazardous exploit of his Grace's long and brilliant career. The anxiety of the crowd to see and cheer the hero of a hundred fights was so great that a considerable smash took place amongst the French porcelain, and the exertions of the police were required to get his Grace safely out of the building. A constable supported him under each arm, and six men behind, under the direction of Mr. Pearce, kept the crowd by main force until at last exit was obtained at the south transept. Hbis Grace was exceedingly discomposed by the tussle. and seemed to think that even popularity and public gratitude might run into excess. The number of visitors on Tuesday rose to 109,915, while the sum of 52811 l0s. was taken in shillings at the door. Even the Bank has felt the flow of silver to its coffers from the glutted exchequer of the Royal Commissioners. It was found necessary to have two cabs to convey to Threadneedle-street the accumulation of the previous day, and the weight of specie am ounted to no less than 15 cwt. The truth is that the people had become the Exhibition, and that in the presence of such enormous masses as were on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednes- day, congregated together, the display of industrial products was no longer the chief attraction. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The list of applications for space at next year's Exhibition closed yesterday, and we shall soon know what to expect in this congress of nations. Till the lists are all published it will perhaps be premature to apprehend any serious omissions in the show. When all the world is invited to produce what it pleases, it is every body's fault, if every body is not quite satisfied. Every body is to do what he can, and, should the result in any respect fall short of expectation, the only infer- ence will be that time has not yet produced that which we desire, and that our imagination is running in advance of our age. We will, then, content ourselves with simply express- ing a hope that the Exhibition will take a useful and practical turn. We know not whether it is chiefly designed to bring out the inventive faculties, or whether it ia to encourage that mixture of industry and skill that leads to the production of the most perfect article in manufacturing competition. In either case an immense public service will be done. Look- ing, however, to the wants of Englishmen, and indeed of the whole world, we trust that when all nations are comparing their works side by side tbe circle of English ideas will be somewhat enlarged. There are many desiderata in our social and domestic economies which bold invention or foreign suggestion only can supply. If the Exhibition does not leave us much more comfortable than it finds us it will be a great opportunity sadly neglected. In every part of our houses there is room for improvement. We want walls combining warmth, cheapness, durability, and strength, faced with a material that shall imbibe neither the damp nor the smoke, and which an occasional ablution will make as good as new. We want a substitute for the everlasting paintpot, for scaffolds, and stench. Cannot this be effected by the use of bricks, hollowed, hardened, glazed, coloured, and moulded, as the case may require ? We want fireproof constructions for our floors and our partitions, not too heavy to be carried by ordinary walls. We may learn much from the French and Germans in their windows and the fastenings thereof. The English sash, with its ropes, pulleys, and weights, must be superseded at last. Ihe Crystal Palace will itself suggest the use of glass for our roofs, and, as the year of the Exhibition is, we trust, to be appropriately chosen for the repeal of the odious window tax, there is no reason why every house of any pretensions built henceforth in this country should not have a transparent roof, and be thereby enabled to utilize the space between it and the attics. The ventilation and warming of our houses demand a reform. At present we are exposed to the tortures which Milton assigns to some classes of the damned — we are suspended between a furnace and a draught, sitting before blazing fires knee-deep in streams of cold air. We want plans for diffusing a temperate atmosphere through all the rooms of a house, without a fire in every one of them, which few can afford, and which is far from advisable. The Eng- lish might learn a good deal from the stoves in use through the continent, especially those of Russia and Sweden. We want also a mild substitute for tiie feather bed and triple blanket, in which so many of our countrymen are still nightly stewed from November to May. Among other desiderata may be enumerated a more economical and effective kitchen apparatus, especially one that shall consume its own smell, or otherwise dispose of it ;— a mode of internal communica- tion which shdl dispense with tbe bell, and, if possible, also with the journey of tiie servant to ask wbat ia wanted ; window blinds that shall answer their various purposes better than either hollaod, or wire-gauze, or Venetian blinds, inside or out; plates and dishes that shall not break quite so fast ; furniture that shall not compel careful housekeepers to shut out the sun ; and decorations that will stand the air of London more than three or four yeara. AU these instances are from one department, and they serve to illustrate the scope that there is for enterprising inventors and exhibitors. Our other illustrations shall be more mis- cellaneous. The national style of dress is neither sightly nor convenient. Every article of it, from the hat above to tbe Wellington boot below, is open to serious objections. A looser style would answer its purpose better both in winter and in summer, indoor and outdoor, moving or sitting still. As we write we yearn for the philanthropist who will deliver us from penknives and inkglasses, by giving us a point that neither blunts nor runs dry. Oh, for a street pavement that shall be durable, noiseless, and smooth ! If that cannot be found we must be driven to railways on our principal thoroughfares, which at present are intolerable. Were there not a dead lock almost every half-hour we should soon lose our hearing. Taking a wide leap into another department, we beg to instance mass as a subject in which a reform is mnch needed. There is wanted a new style of engraving them, which seall exhibit with more distinctness and promi- nence the natural features, the cities, and the roads of tbe country ; in fact, one that shall give the traveller or the student a little more of that information which he learns from the handbook. Last, but not least, a great reform is wanted even in so humble an affair as children's toys.
