A Fortunate Emigrant.— Among the passengers on board the Indus, which arrived at Southampton with the India mail, was Mr. James Malcolm, a native of Caithness. 22 yeara ago he landed as a young emigrant at Van Die- men's Land with 50 shillings in his pocket; 15 years ago he crossed over to Port Philip, when there were only two huts in that now flourishing colony, and there he haa re- mained ever since. He is the largest individual sheep fenner in the colony, being the owner of 30,000 sheep, and land sufficient, reckoning, as he does, an acre to a sheep, to feed 60,000. He is now worth £3,000 a-year. Hia visit to England is to see the old country once more, after which he purposes- to pass the remainder ot hia life in South Australia.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. WVe have, upon several occasions, called attention to the urgent necessity which exists for exhibitors of machinery to send in the articles which they intend to exhibit at as early a period as possible, in order that this important section may be duly and properly arranged and placed in working order previous to the opening of the Exhibition. The Commissioners stand pledged to open the Exhibition on the 1st of May, and it is most important that at that period it shou!d be as perfect and as complete as possible. Not only is it important in a public point of view that exhibitors should have the whole of their productions pro- perly arranged, and that the Exhibition should be as perfect and complete as possible at the time of its opening, but the interests of the exhibitors themselves will be most materially affected by any neglect or delay on their part. The decisions of the juries upon the awarding of the prizes will have to be given previous to the opening of the Exhibition, and it is scarcely necessary to point out the mode in which the interests of exhibitors will be affected who have not the articles or machinery in the building upon which the juries are to form their opinion. A second point in which the interests of the exhibitors will be affected will be, that, as the catalogue must of necessity be printed by the opening of the Exhibition, and as a quarter of a million of copies of the first edition will be struck off, they will not, Of course, contain any notice of those articles which exhibitors have failed to send in previous to the time of going to press, and they will therefore lose the benefit of the publicity which would otherwise be given to their productions. It is most important that heavy machinery, and other articles which can with difficulty be moved about, should be sent in as soon as possible; and when required to be shown in motion, it is obvious that considerable time must be taken up in its arrangement, and placing it in working order. The flooring of a large portion of the building must also remain in an unfinished state until the whole of the machinery is fixed. The whole of the boarding which divides the various counters and classes from each other must, of necessity, be thrown down and removed at least a week previous to the opening on the 1st of May. The lighter and more portable articles of manufacture or other- wise intended for exhibition may be brought in and placed in their position in a very short time, after the necessary accommodation of counters, glass cases, &c., has been provided. This is not the case, however, with the more cumbrous articles to Shich we have referred. The, materials for the construction of the engine- house-which will be outside, upon the north-western side of the building,,and will furnish steam to the extent of 100 horse power-have already arrived, and will be in course of erection in a few days. ADMISSION TO THE EXHIBtTIoN.-Numerous ap- plications have already been made for season tickets of admission to the Exhibition. The executive are not yet prepared to issue the, tickets; they are, however, in course of preparation, and as soon as completed due notice will be given of the places at which they can be obtained. We believe that it is in contemplation to authorize the sale of the tickets at one or more central offices, to be sanctioned by the executive. Anything like traffic in the sale of the tickets will be strictly prohibited, and no discount or profit whatever will be allo=ed upon their sale. No " Free List" whatever will be allowed, except to servants or attendants employed in the building. The Commissioners, in addition to the valuable services which they have hitherto rendered, will be required to show their interest in the undertaking, by the purchase of tickets of ad- mission, in the same manner and at the same price as other visitors. Persons will not acquire the right to free admission on the ground of their being exhibitors, but will be entitled, upon application, to " free passes" for their servants, who may be required to be in attend- ance to explain or keep in order the articles exhibited. All visitors, therefore, with respect to the right of ad- mission, will be placed upon the same footing, and the executive will be spared the odium which attaches to selection, and the dissatisfaction which would attend the refusal tiO grant privileges to applicants, on the ground of real or supposed services rendered by them to the Exhi- bition. This piece is of the highest artistic merit. The most refined delicacy of female feature is ecuibined in the face of the Amazon with a magnificentintensity of masculine energyandfell purpose. the tiger is remorseless, and you writhe with sympath for the horse, whose attitude pictures at once his death. agony and his unsabdued spirit superior to death; but you draw your breath deeply with relief as you feel that the Amazon's spear will in an instant transfix the tigers heart and hurl him dead to the ground. The balance of the female figure on the horse is exquisite: the right leg drawn up from the tiger, gives that side of the body a contraction that will steady the hold of the rider on her horse and give irresistible rapidity and force to her blow: while the extended leg on the other side conveys with marvellous skill the idea of security due to the equipoise and symmetrical power of the whole igure. There is no other sculpture, foreign or English, to compare with this work of Herr Kiss. It is cast in zinc, and has been bronzed in the new mode invented by Geiss. The Crystal Palace continues to be a daily-increasing source of attraction to the Londoners ; for it must be borne in mind that as yet there are scarcely any foreign arrivals of visitors, and very few from the provinces. -On the average, there are 8000 or 10,000 fresh visitors every day; and if to these be added about 2S,000 season-ticket holders, the capacity of the building may be readily estimated, because up to the present time there has been nothing like a crowd in any part, unless where the envelope-making machine, or the ' mountain of light," or tile French displays of gemis, or the Italian court of statuary, form estuaries, around which the living tide rolls and surges in its onward course. A gloomy overoast sky acts upon the exchequer of the )oyal Commission as sinister rumours, however groundless. do upon 'Change. Thursday tie 8th was bright and cloudless, and the receipts from Bs. visitors rose to upwards of 20001. On Friday the sun did not deign to shine, and the money taken fell to between 17001. and 18001. This is quite independent of the sale of season tickets, which still goes on prosperously. Saturday is proverbially the fashionable day in London; and the appearance of the Crystal Palace in the morning in- dicated that it wvas the great centre of attraction for that numerous class, the principal business of whose life appears to be amusement and excitemnent. For nearly two hours after the doors were opened there wvas a line of private carriages extending some distance beyond the building setting down visitors, and of these at least one-half were new arrivals, as they passed through the pay-doors instead of the season-ticket entrances. As a pecuniary speculation, the success of the Great Exhibition has now been fully established. On Saturday morning the Queen and Prince Albert, accom- panied by their Royal guests, visited the Exhibition, and re- m.ained for nearly two hours. The illustrious party examined carefully the jewels belonging to the Queen of Spain, exhibited on the south side of the nave, in the French division. They also inspected the Swiss collection, and admired the fine dis- play of artificial flowers contributed by Constantin. They paid a visit to the Sheffield Court, and minutely inspected Hoole's and Stewart and Smith's grates. In the section of woollen fabrics their attention was attracted to the specimens shewn there of Huddersfield. Bradford, and Leeds umanufac- tures. The collection of cottons and linens was also examined, and the Royal party took particular notice of Mercer's new patent method for increasing the brilliancy of colours, of Lvdiarud's chintzes, and of the contributions of Black, of Glasgow. During their stay they passed through the agri- cultural implement department, in which her Majesty seemed to be most interested by the display of churns and beehives. the ?? party appeared highly delighted with their visit. At twelve oclock the public were admitted to the building and flowed in w'tb such eagerness that in the course of the afternoon more than 1SO01. was taken at the doors. Amron, the early arrivals was his Grace the Duke of Wellington, Iho is a frequent visitor. He passed through the British depart- ment of the building, stopping occasionally to have a lonk at some of the curiosities displayed around him, or to note the progress of the unfinished portions. Although recognised by numbers who bowed to him as he passed, there -was no at- tempt to crowd upon or inconvenience him, and he was left free to follow the bent of his inclinations. On arriving at the Indian collection he made a pause, and, influenced probably by old reminiscences, suddenly turned into the department and took a survey of the Exhibition, which is still very iu- complete, the greater portion of the packages from India having only arrived on Friday. On reaching the transept the Duke again paused, apparently undecided whether he should retire or proceed further. After a moment's deliberation he resumed his peculiar gait and crossed over to the foreign side, where his appearance created a much greater sensation, the exhibitors pouring out from the different compartments as he passed, and all saluting him, and, except the Queen herself, no Royal personage could be treated with more distinction. He remained for upwards of an hour in the building. On Monday morning the Queen, accompanied by Prince Albert, again visited the Exhibition. During the time the Royal party spent in the building the weather was fine, and the number of visitors verygreat: but in the afternoon heavy rains fell. article_text: THE GREAT EXHIBITION. There are several changes in the interior, completed or contemplated, which deserve notice. The first of these is that the gigantic American eagle which overshadowed with its wings the east entrance of the building has been entirely eclipsed by Messrs. Gray and Davidson's organ, which has been recently removed there. The king of birds, after a vain effort to cover the emptiness of the Yankee compartment, appears to be shrinking abashed behind the melodious shelter afforded to it, and our cousins really have reason to congratulate themselves that their eagle at last shews some traces of modesty and diffidence. Anotherpoint of interest relates to the Koh-i-noor. After all the work which has been made about that celebrated diamond our readers will be rather surprised to hear that many people find a difficulty in bringing themselves to believe, from its external appearance, that it is anything but a piece of common glass. Amid all the adventures that have befallen it, there is, perhaps, none more odd than that its genuineness should now be doubted. Yet so it is. The fact is, that the " Mountain of Light" has been shockingly ill-used in the cutting, And that when placed in the open light of day, without any arrang ements to draw forth its brilliancy, it does not sparkle an d gleam like other jewels of the kind. To obviate this disadvantage, and demonstrate to the world that the Koh-i-Noor is a veritable diamond, it is to be surrounded with a canopy or tent, the interior of which is to be lighted with gas, and the idea is that this will develope its beauties as a gem of the purest water, with a certainty and splendour which undoubtedly are not attained at present. A remarkable feature of Thursday s experience in the interior of the Exhibition was the appearalce there, at an early hour, of nearly 800 agricultural labourers and country folk, from the neighbourhood of Godstone, in Surrey, headed by the clergymen of the parishes to which they respectively belonged, and organised for the occasion into companies like a regiment of militia. They paid ls. 6d. each towards the expenses of the trip, the rest bring defrayed by the gentry of the neighbourhood ; and, notwithstanding the state of the weather, they were conveyed to the Exhibition and back again to their own homes in a very expeditious manner, and with the utmost :are for their comfort. The railway station was reached by waggons, and from London-bridge terminus to Westminster they were brought up by steamer. Thence, after seeing Westminster-hall, they proceeded on foot and in marching order to the Crystal Palace, and, having spent several hours there in exploring the wonders of art and industry, at four o'clock they took their departure, returning as they came. The men wore their smartest smockfrocks, the women their best Sunday dresses, and more perfect specimens of rustic attire, rustic faces, and rustic manners, could hardly be produced from any part of England. The town portion of the assemblage gathered round them as they mustered before departing in the transept, with looks full of curiosity, not unmingled with a species of half pitying interest ; and many were the questions put to them as to what they thought of the Exhibition ? what they were most struck by ? whether they understood what they had seen ? and if they would like to come again ? After some little marshalling they left the Exhibition in close order, moving three abreast—an affecting array of young and old, male and female, in which each observer might read with his own eyes the evidences of a laborious life, little relieved by intelligence or education, but simple, unpretending, and not unaccompanied by domestic virtue and happiness. On Friday the price of admission was half-a-crown, and £2,206 ss. was the amount taken at the doors, the number of visitors being 24,520. The Duke of Devonshire has sent to the Crystal Palace a very remarkable contribution in the shape of a hawk, which is executed with great spirit, and studded all over with precious stones. This object will no doubt attract great attention, and will probably be placed in the nave, near the department of Holland. His Grace has also forwarded a magnificent snake-chain of silver filligree work, the design of which is singularly chaste and beautiful. We understand that measures are to be at once adopted for allowing the humbler classes easy access to the model cottages of the Prince Consort. The narrowness of the staircase renders it necessary to limit the number of visitors at a time, but no great practical difficulty is likely to arise from this. The ex-Queen of the French, accompanied by the Duchess of Orleans and several other members of the late King's family, visited the Exhibition on Friday, and were chiefly occupied in examining the industrial products of the country which they so lately ruled. It was an affecting sight to withess the respectful sympathy of manner with which they were received. M. Salandrouze, with head uncovered, conducted them through the collection, and the Frenchmen present paid all suitable homage to the illustrious visitors. Our countrymen and women were hardly so polite, their curiosity collecting them in a dense mass round the strangers. On Saturday morning the Queen and Prince Albert resumed their examination of the interior and their personal interviews with exhibitors. Their first visit was paid to the Koh-i-noor, which is now surrounded within a tent, lighted in a particular manner by gas. It was confidently expected that this experiment to develope the lustre of the diatr4ond would be attended with complete success, but the result still remains unsatisfactory. The Norwich shawls, lace, and poplins, which are arranged in the south galleries of the transept, next attracted the attention of the Royal party, and Her Majesty was pleased to make several purchases here. Business in London is still at a stand-still. During Whitsun-week even the streets were not more crowded than usual, nor was attendance at the Crystal Palace larger than it was previously. The theatres and other places of public amusement say they never saw so dull a season. Batty, who must have been at enormous expense in the erection and fitting up of his Hippodrome at Kensington, is said to be losing some two or three hundred pounds a week. Lord Stanley, at the annual dinner of the Merchant Tailors' Company, London, on Wednesday last, in a brilliant speech, testified to the success of the Great Exhibition. Up to . the present time there are among 'the articles found in the Exhibition and deposited with the police, 75 parasols and 175 silk handkerchiefs, which have not been claimed. A silver watch and two or three purses, with money enclosed therein, are also included in the unclaimed list. . Mr. Ruskin, in one of the appendices to his recently. published " Stories of Venice," thus justly criticises and condemns the Great Glass Building in Hyde Park : " All art which is worth its room in this world, all art which is not a piece of blundering refuse, is art which proceeds from an individual mind, working through instruments which assist, but do not supersede the muscular action of the human hand, upon the materials which most tenderly receive, and most securely retain, the impressions of such human labour. And the value of every work of art is exactly in the ratio of the quantity of humanity which has been put into it, and legibly expressed upon it for ever :—First, of thought and moral purpose; secondly, of technical skill ; thirdly, of bodily industry. The quantity of bodily industry which the Crystal Palace expresses is very great. So far it is good. The quantity of thought it expresses is, I suppose, a single thought of Mr. Paxton's, probably not a bit brighter than thousands of thoughts which pass through his active and intelligent brain every hour—that it was possible to build a greenhouse larger than any greenhouse was built before. This thought and some very ordinary algebra, are as much as all that glass can represent of human intellect. But one poor half-pennyworth of bread to all this intolerable deal of sack.' Alas I The earth bath bubbles as the water hath : And this is of them.' "

GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday the receipts at the doors of the building rose to £2,933 10s. 63., and 60,497 persons visited the interior. By the sale of season-tickets Li 10s. was realised. On Tuesday the sum of £3,008 9s. was taken in shillings at the doors, and £1 for the sale of a season-ticket. The number of visitors, according to the police returns, was 62,622. On Wednesday the receipts amounted to £2,537 is., the number of visitors, according to the police returns, being 52,757. On Thursday the police numbers were 58,600, and the receipts £2,810 is. 6d. The Californian gold plate, exhibited in the nave, on the north side of the United States department, is an object of much attraction. The set consists of four gold pieces—a tea-kettle, a coffee-pot, sugar-bowl, and cream-jug; and of one silver piece—a salver of hammered work with gold edges. The value of the gold before it was manufactured was £750. The price paid by the citizens of New York was £l,OOO. The salver bears the following inscription : " This service of plate is presented by the citizens of New York to Edward K. Collins, in testimony of the public sense of the great honour and advantage which have been conferred on the city and whole country through his energy and perseverance in the successful establishment of an American line of Transatlantic steamers. Aug. 1851." A short time since we stated that Her Majesty had been pleased to express her approbation of the good conduct of Superintendent Pearce upon the occasions of her frequent visits to the Exhibition, by directing that a silver teapot should be presented to him. Her Majesty's commands have, within the last few days, been carried into effect. The teapot, which was made by Messrs. Garrard, is of a very elegant design and shape, and richly chased, and the handle is of ivory. It bears the following inscription:— Presented to Superintendent Pearce, by command of the Queen, as a mark of Her Majesty's approbation of the constant zeal, intelligence, and discretion shown by him when in attendance upon Her Majesty, on the occasion of her frequent visits to the Great Exhibition." The Executive Committee on Wednesday decided upon stopping the further sale of season tickets. This step may be viewed as an additional proof, if any such were necessary, that it is not intended to close the Exhibition with any public ceremonial similar to that which took place at its opening. The whole question was, as we stated some weeks since, fully discussed by the Commissioners, and the conclusions at which they arrived upon that occasion were then made public. It may be remembered that we stated that the Commissioners intended to hold a meeting in the building on Wednesday, the 15th of October, for the purpose of receiving the reports of several juries, and of taking leave of the foreign Commissioners: and that the exhibitors, the jurors, the foreign and local Commissioners, and the secretaries and members of the local committees were to be invited to attend upon that occasion. There were various considerations — and, among others, the uncertainty of the state of the weather, and the probability of the building being overcrowded—which influenced the Commissioners in deciding upon not closing the Exhibition with any such ceremony as that which so appropriately marked its opening; and there is no reason whatever to believe that any deviation from the course then laid down will take place. With respect to the often discirssed question of the appropriation of the surplus, we need scarcely say that any decision Upon the subject would be at present premature, and that the Enal solution of the difficulties may well be postponed until it shall be known who are the parties that will have the right of disposing of it. Of one thing we feel certain—that it is not necessary to remind the Commissioners of facts with which all the world are acquainted, in order to insure a due recognition on their part of the value of services voluntarily tendered for the purpose of aiding and carrying out this great and successful undertaking. Some weeks since we took occasion to refer to the fact that many of the persons employed had voluntarily tendered their services gratuitously —that others had been but insufficiently remunerated—and we added that the claims of these persons would no doubt receive due consideration when the question of the disposal of the surplus funds was discussed. Since the period of our making those remarks, the whole question of the salaries and services of the persons employed has been fully gone into, and a report upon the subject will be laid before the Commissioners at their next meeting. COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ABERDARE.—The coroner's Jury returned the following verdict in the case of this lamentable occurrence, by which fourteen lives were lost: " Accidental death, caused by the breaking of the iron rods Which connected the cross and the bucket. But the jury cannot separate without expressing their disapproval of the present system of letting workmen go down to their work in the same way as materials are got up; and they recommend that drifts should be made in all similar works, so as to enable their workmen to go to work without any thger." The work of demolition and clearance fairly cOm- titmesced yesterday, and the long and countless arn.av 1° ?? b,;ad omnibuses which, but a fevy days be- I e fore, wiere busy in conveying hopeful and expect.ut exhibitors and visitors, is now succeeded by a more sober and business-like class of vehicles. Carts, waggous, and trucks were employed yester- s day by hundreds in removing the contents of the wondrous palace of glass. Nearly the whole of the jewellery ani works in precious metals have X been cleared away, 350 exhibitors in this class alone 5 having removed their things in the course of the day, and it is probable that within a week scarcely a light or conveniently portable article will be left in the building. The foreign department is now placed in the hands of the Customs, and barriers have been erected down each side of the nave and between the respective foreign countries. We understand that Prince Albert yesterday addressed autograph letters to each qf the Special Commissioners, Colo- rnel Lloyd and Dr. Playfair, and to the members and secretary of the Executive Committee, acknow- ledging the value of the services which they have rendered in connection with the origination and successful prosecution of this great undertaking. The awards of the jurors appear, we regret to say, to have given very general dissatisfaction. ?? uncalled for restriction of the number of the higher class medals, and the withdrawal altogether of the thiud or lower class, has most undoubtedly led to the rewarding with the "prize" medals such a vast number of miscellaneous articles of varied degrees of value and merit, as to deprive them of much, if not all, value to the possessors. Thus Mrs. Haight, the fortunate exhibitor of a well-made shirt from the United States, or an exhibitor of " lambs' tails nil," a " clay tobacco pipe," a " wedding cake," a " box of sweatmeats," a " walking-stick," a " pail," or a " broom," receives a medal of equal value with that awarded for the crystal fountain of Messrs. Osler, the beautiful pianofortes of Messrs. X Broadwood and Messrs. Collard, the effective rail- way break of Mir. Lee, the porcelain and statuary of Messrs. Copeland and Messrs. Rose, Ericsson's new motive power and his other highly valuable and philosophical inventions, and the nationally im- portapt and commercially valuable inventions of the Chevalier Claussen. It was perfectly right, no doubt, to reward excellence in whatever class it might be found; but to place articles like those above men- tioned upon the same footing, and to reward the one equally with the other, can be considered only as a wanton perversion or gross disregard, to say the least of it, of the decisions of the Commissioners. The reports of the jurors will no doubt throw some light upon the course which they have pursued; but at present we confess ourselves utterly incapable of discovering anything like a principle to guide us in our examination of theawardswhich havebeen made; and we think that the exhibitors and the public have some cause to complain that more effective means were not devised by the Commissioners for the performance of that duty with which they were entrusted by the Crown, viz., " the determination of the nature of the prizes, and the means of securing the most impartial distribution of them." SIR,—I take a considerable degree of interest in watching the working progress of the Mercantile Marine Act, because, first, it is a measure professing to benefit parties who from its first introduction in Parliament to the present moment have utterly repudiated it. Next, because it has been made so mucn or at an aaa ½ er Board of Trade, and intended to lull discontent on the part of the shipping interest, as a something to qualify a worse measure, the repeal of the navigation laws; and lastly, because that without any testimonials or evidence to the fact, the right honourable gentleman told the House of Commons on the 21st of July last, "He believed it was working satisfactorily to all classes." True, the right honourable gentleman has tried to reconcile "all classes." But has he succeeded so as to justify a public expression of "belief" that he has done so; and my object shall be again, as in my former letter on the same subject, to also w that lie has not done so, by the facts ot renewed hostility from all parties against it. Do shipowners complain of the act as a most unnecessary and vexatious interference, they are told it is to protect them from the evils of desertion, and enable them to maintain a better state of discipline. Do the seamen complain, as in the spring of the year they did in the north, Captain Beechey is sent down to tell them that the object of the act is that of protecting them from imposition on the part of shipowners (highly complimentary, no doubt, to the latter). Are either of these parties yet reconciled to the act, which has now been in operation nine months? I answer no, as the following facts must determine. In the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette of the 6th inst. is reported a vast meeting of seamen at Newcastle, attended by those also from the ports of Hartlepool, Shields, &c. Was it to pass a vote of thanks to the government for this act, or coneratulations on the benefit arising from the repeal of the navigation laws? Quite the contrary. It was to petition parliament to do away with the registry-tickets--the unconditional repeal of the Mercantile Marine Act, and the amendment of the present navigation laws. Is there nothing momentous in the display of the English and American flags in juxtaposition with the motto, " Which will you choose 1" as addressed to British seamen under excitement frcin injuries (even supposed ones). But have they not injuries to complain of? Is the destruction of their carrying trade no injury? Is it no injury to see the daily increase of foreign tonnage superseding our own at home and abroad? Is it, in other words, and from a higher authority, right "to take the children's bread, and give it to strangers?" THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty, Prince Albert, the King of the Belgians, with the two young princes, and their respective suites, visited the Exhibition on Saturday morning at half-past nine o'clock. Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Kent was also present in the early part of the day in another part of the building, as well as the Duke and Dachese de Nemours, and other distinguished personages. The Royal party visited the French department, bestowing much attention upon the very magnificent collection of bronzes. They afterwards visited the French furniture reoms, and then crossed the nave to Tunis, stopping to admire the very beautiful mosaic painting which has just been put up in a conspicuous place opposite the Italian compartment. The picture is the work of Rinaldi, of Florence, and has all the richness and finish of an oil painting, with the softness and delicacy of a porcelain picture. Its composition can only be discovered by the most minute inspection. We may observe that there are man' equally beautiful specimens of mosaic painting in the Roman collection. After going through the very beautiful collection of gold and silver embroidered muslins and other delicate tissues displayed in the African bazaar, the Royal party proceeded to the western, or British side of the transept, and traversed the south central gallery, in which some of the most exquisite and valuable of the British productions are displayed—namely, the gold and silver plate, jewellery, bijouterie, and lace. The illustrious visitors left snortly after eleven o'clock. Mr. Hope's blue diamond, which is now covered with a hood of red cl ot h, lik e th e Kohnoor, was much au mired. It may be as well here to correct an error which has crept into all the accounts respecting this diamond. It has been generally believed to be 177 ' carats weight, which would make its value somewhat enormous, but its real weight is 177 grains, or carats. The , wonderful fur cloak, in the Russian department, has also been erroneously described as belonging to the Emperor of Russia, but this is not the case; it is a lady's cloak, and belongs to the furrier by whom it is exhibited. Its value is stated to he upwards of 3000 guineas, being formed of the best portion of black fox skins—one of our eminent manufacturers has, however, offered to produce one equally good, of the same skin, for 1000 guineas. Beside this cloak is a lady's cloak of the silver fox, which is also extremely valuable. The black diamond from Bahia, recently exhibited by Mayer, of Liverpool, was also examined by her Majesty. It is a shapeless, rough-looking stone, with something of the brown semi-transparent tinge of flint, to which it bears a great resemblance; it weighs 350 carats, and its hardness is such that it is said it cannot be cut or polished. We are glad to observe that many of the most valuable articles of silver plate and jewellery exhibited by Messrs. Hancock, Hunt and Roskeil, Garrard, &c., are marked as "sold." Among the purchasers, whose names are attached to many of these beautiful productions, are Prince Henry of the Netherlands, Prince Serge Kolchoubey, Prince Demidoff, the Earl of Eliesniere, Earl Craven, &c. In the Portuguese department a very magnificent state sword, mounted with brilliants, and enclosed in a richly chased and massive gold scabbard, which was presented by the officers of the Portuguese army serving in the Peninsula to l their General, Field Marshal Lord Beresford, has just been displayed. The scabbard contains, in a number of compartments, in relief, devices illustrative of the various actions and sieges in which the army took part. It is valued at 1200 guineas. Up to four or five o'clock on Saturday there were not more than 7000 or 8000 persons present in the building, which gave it an air of great coolness and repose, strongly I contrasting with the dust, and noise, and excitement of the early part of the week. It consists chiefly of three splendid folio volumes of the Oriental Collection, and the most cursory inspection of these exquisite works of art cannot fail to impress the beholder with a high idea of the talent with which the large scope for illustration, afforded by the nature of these works, has been made available by the artists employed in their production. The first of the three is the first volume of a translation of the "Book of Kings," by Aboulkasim-14 irdousi, with commentaries, published by M. Jules Mohl, member of the Institute of France. The second is a translation into French of a portion of a work, written in Persian by Raschid . Eldin, its title being the " History of the Moguls of Persia," by M. Eugene Burnouf, member of the Institute of France. The paper works upon a reel, and is continuous,like the telegraphic coil. The paper passes over the type on a cylinder, and when one side is worked the paper is reversed, and the other side printed with c most perfect register, and the sheets are clipped apart, as they come from the press, by an ingenious contrivance. There is no limit hardly to the speed at which the press will work; itsCiactness is beyond anything known in this line of machinery; and what is better than all, the largest size press can be put up at a cost of not more than 500 dollars. ' ADVERTISITIG.—Nothing is more clearly settled, or more universally admitted, than that the best money spent by a business man is that paid for advertising. The fact has been demonstrated throughout the world. Men will pay enough for a handsome sign to embellish their stores, for elegant windows, and oysters, drinks, cigars, confectionery, and knick-knacks, to pay half a dozen years, advertising bills, and all without any benefit to their business or themselves. Hundreds ought to be paid for advertising, where tens are now, if merchants Would thrive and make money. It does not answer to dabble lightly in the matter. A man may as well expect to wash his hands by dipping a finger's tip into the water, as to give his business a sensible; clean lift by a little advertising. The true way, and the profitable one, is to pay for liberal advertising, and then use it. Keep the mill wheel turning all the while. Depend upon it, half the business men who "burst up" might avoid the painful and disastrous event by resorting to the printer's Instead of the shaver's aid to hold them up. Half the sum paid for shaving and other follies would make the foolish men who pay for these luxuries rich and comfortable. Try it, and see. Every dollar paid tor advertising in country newspapers will pay back twentyfold.—Albany Evening Journal. A MORMON LEADING ARTICLE.—The following is "the leading article" in a late number of the Deseret News:—" We feel thankful to our Heavenly Father; that is inspiring the hearts of the farmers more and more, to bring in their butter,"eggs, cheese, &a., to strengthen the hands on the public works: who also feel thankful and praise God for the same, and pray for their brethren more abundantly. Formerly, at this season of the year, putter was being packed away to sell to emigrants; now it is brought forward to help to build a temple. Formerly, some of the brethren buried their faith with their butter, and their hearts were cold enough, in the absence of ice, to preserve their butter until they could make sale at an enormous price, and would let the public works stand still, their brethren and sisters and little ones, who.tlid not make of their own, eat bread and water, rather than sell them an ounce at a reasonable price; and their hearts were so cold it did not seem to trouble them, and they did not appear to know but they had done right, and they knew not joy or happiness; now they sell freely to those who have none, at reasonable prices, and their hearts are so warm that butter will not keep on their farms; and they are so full of joy and happiness they have to come and bring a pail of butter to the tithing office, and tell how they rejoice, and how much better they feel than they did last year and the year before; and God is blessing them in basket and in store, in flocks and in herds, in fields and in gardens, and they are getting rich a hundred fold faster than they were formerly, and they are not afraid to see a good brother from the city, lest be should ask them if they could sell him a pound of butter or cheese, and they should have to tell a lie to keep it for the emigrants. No! they have done with such foolish things. My Father, continue to bless them in the name of Jesus. Amen."

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The notices that have appeared in some of our contemporaries on the subject of the plating of metals by means of electricity having attracted a good deal of discussion and remark in consequence of the imperfect and occasionally erroneous manner in which the original discovery has been referred to and the various processes described, we propose to-day to enter at some length into the subject, and to furnish our readers with a variety of curious and interesting facts, which, we believe, will be found to be tolerably accurate, and which will give the public some idea of the extraordinary agency by which this very beautiful and ingenious manufacture is accomplished. In describing the art of depositing metals by the agency of electricity, or electroplating as it is termed, it is difficult to avoid the use of scientific terms and reference to chemical processes, for the understanding of which some previous knowledge of the science is required. Hence the art of electro-plating is imperfectly understood by that portion of the public to whom such phrases as "positive" and "negative poles" convey no more definite meaning than if they were algebraic signs. As one of the objects of the Exhibition is to reveal the recondite mysteries of science and their application to the every-day purposes of life, we shall endeavour to give the crowds who gaze upon the wonderful creations of metallic art contained in the bronze stall and electro plate cases a familiar, if somewhat superficial, idea of the process by which these works of art are produced. In no departinent of the Exhibition are the advantages which science confers on art more clearly illustrated than in electro-metallurgy, wherein the agency of the subtle fluid, which, directed by the cunning hand of man, shivers into fragments the sunken rock, also gilds the wing of the butterfly so delicately that the exquisite framework is not hidden by the golden filial. Messrs. Elkington and Mason are the discoverers of the process, and hold the valuable I patent. Other manufacturers who plate by the same process are licensees. The patent was perfected in 1840, and notwithstanding that, in common with nearly every discovery which revolutionises existing practices, it encountered much opposition, it has already become an important branch of industry, and by the facilities it affords for the production of the finest forms and most ornate compositions, it is now, and will still mo re l arge ly b ecome, an i mportant ad- Linnet to art education. The advantages which plating by the agency of electricity possesses over the older process will be readily understood whea it is stated, that until this discovery, raised surfaces, and especially high relief, which are cast, could not be produced on articles of plate in other metal than pure silver. Hence plating was confined to articles having a plain surface, or when applied to ornamental designs, such as a salver, or dish with a raised border, the relieved portion was formed of a thin stamped surface of silver, filled with base metal, and attached to the body of the article. It is evident that a process so limited in its application to ornamental manufacture could never have popularised the use of compositions having any preten' sioa to art beyond beauty of outline. The costliness of silver is necessarily a hindrance to the production, as it is to the use of elaborate works in th it metal. The proce,s of electro gilding, by its comparative inexpensiveness and un- I • limited application to all purposes to which silver is applicable, is designed to be, as it has to a considerable extent already become, a school of art at the table of every man of even a moderate income. If our readers will glance at any of the centre-pieces in the cases of the Messrs. Elkington, in the south-west gallery, for example, the " crown imperial," or the figures and festoons on the Exhibition vase, they will perceive at once that the truth of the forms and the spirit of the compositions depend upon the relief of the parts, and consequently that there is much of whet is called " under-cutting. ' The floral wreaths on the vase referred to, or the curl of the leaf of the crown imperial, may be taken as familiar illustrations of the term. Such articles could not be produced by the old process; but by the electro system the subtlety of the agent employed in plating carries the particles of decomposed metal to every crevice of the composition, and hence no elaboration of ornament, height of relief, or complication of design presents the slightest difficulty to the electro-plater. Another important advantage is, that, uulike the old process, the electro-plater is not restricted to the use of soft solder, composed principally of lead, which melts at a low temperature, and forms an insufficient joint. The articles made by Messrs. Elkington are soldered with hard silver solder, not affected by any ordiaary degree of heat, and forming a joint as strong as the metal itself. The base, or body upon which the pure silver is deposited, is a white metal approximating to silver in colour and density of structure. These preliminaries being understood, the reader will easily comprehend the process of plating. The troughs in which this goes noiselessly forward are three parts full cf solution consisting of dissolved or decomposed silver, and an alkali called cyanide of potassurn. This forms the plating solution. In connection with the solvent, it is a singular fact, that, notwithstanding the numerous attempts made to discover a more suitable oxide, no change has been made during the eleven years the system has been in operation. About twenty patents in connection with the process have been obtained, all of which are held by Messrs. Elkington; but none of the discoveries have effected any material alteration in the composition of the solution. The articles to be plat, d are suspended in the solution by wires in contact with rods connected with the electrical current. Until about twelve months ago the source of electricity was the galvanic battery. The defects of this medium, its unequal power, and the slowness of the process of deposition, were early discovered; and about seven years since a patent was obtained by Mr.Woolryche,of Birmingham, for the substitution ofa permanent magnet as the source of electricity. The patent was purchased by Messrs. Elkington, and the plan tried; but from a defect in the construction of the magnet, or in the mode of its application, the current it gave out was deficient both in quality and intensity, and for a time it was abandoned. The megnitude of the operations of the manufacturers, and the ditEculty experienced in getting a sufficient amount of power from the battery, again tempted to further experiments with the magnet; and the result is that the batteries have been superseded, and a steady, inexpensive, and never-failing current of electricity is evolved from the machine. The importance of uniformity cannot be overrated, as it enables the operator to calculate with precision the quantity of metal deposited in a given time. Of scarcely less importance, where the operations are so extensive as in these works, is the rapidity of the deposition. By the galvanic battery the process of plating occupied about eight hours—the same effect can now be produced by the magnet in two, with this additional advantage—that the more rapid the deposition, the more hard and firmly is the silver deposited. The machine of Messrs. Elkington has eight series of steel plates, and is driven by a steam-engine. Thus, then, we are in possession of a correct though non-scientific knowledge of the plating and the depositing ! agent. Now, the article to be plated having been suspended in the liquid, the magnetic current is passed through it, and the result of the action is, that the solution is decomposed, the metal separated from the potash and gradually deposited on the surface of th e article,—the potash, of the coating being determined by the duration of the immersion, the quality of the solution, and the strergth of the current. In the process of plating the solution of course becomes exhausted of the metal. To keep up the supply plates of pure silver are suspended in the liquid, and the silver dissolves as rapidly as the deposition on the articles takes place, atom for atom. For several years the metal so precipitated hid a dead or frosted appearance, such as that in the figures of the centre-piece called the National Uames," and other figures in these cases, and was subsequently burnished; but by the use of a little bi-sulphuret of carbon in the solution, the after labour is avoided, for the article now leaves the trough with a high degree Of polish. Like many other important discoveries this was the result of accident. The bi-sulplairet of carbon was used for giving elasticity to vulcanised India rubber moulds, and a particle of the substance having mixed with the plating solution, it was observed that the deposit of metal assumed a bright appearance. Hence the important improvement. Such is the process of electro-plating, the gilding being almost similar, with this difference, that order to expedite the operation, the solution is heated. It is at once evident that such is the command of the operator over the thickness of the coating that the quality of the plated article depends altogether upon the character of the manufacturer, and upon that also depends the permanency of the plating. In the hands of a skilful operator the covering adheres so firmly as to become one body with the metal upon which it is deposited. In the manufactory of Messrs. Elkington, we are informed, the quality of the work is submitted to two or three convincing tests. The frosted figures are annealed after being plated, as in articles made of pure silver, and the plain surface goods, such as salvers, side and vegetable dishes, (Sec., are submitted to the action of the hammer, 20 men being engaged in the manufactory in the work of hammering alone if, therefore, there ever is in any electro-plated articles a tendency to skin or peel off, the fault arises from the bad quality of the metal employed, or from the careles,ness or incompetence of the operator, not from any defect in the system. The artistic uses as well as the economical value of this application of science to manufactures is well illustrated by the contributions to the Cyrstal Palace. The efforts of the patentees seem to have resulted in a union of science, fine art, and manufacture, the velne of which who can estimate 1 As showing the spirit and enterprise of these gentlemen it may be stated that with few exceptions all the articles in their cases are, understand, expressly designed, modelled, and, of course, made, for the Exhibition. The four figures round the base, war, rebellion, hatred, and revenge, disarmed and chained, show the influencs of peaceful pursuits; and the figure of Prince Albert on the apex, awarding the honours to successful inditdtry, gives time and locality to the millenial era. SUNDAY PERFORMANCES OF THE EXECUTITE COMMITTEE OF THE EXHIBITION.—Signor Monti, a wellknown Italian sculptor, resident in London, was one of those who contributed some groups of statuary to the great bazaar in Hyde -park, among which may be remarked two girls fishing—the daughters of an English gentleman— and the statue of a veiled nymph. The other day, on entering Mr. Hennenian's establishment, in Regent -street, Signor Monti discovered a photograph of one of these statues, which had been taken entirely without his knowledge or permission ; and he was still more surprised on learning that the counterproof had been carried off to Paris, where, by this time, his statues may be already pirated in clay or porcelain by some of those persons who are to be distinguished from artists as "art-manufacturers." Last Friday week Mr. Tudor purchased the veiled nymph, then apparently perfect and intact. On the Monday following, however, three of the fingers of the nymph were found broken off; and Signor Monti, on inquiring among the police, learned that friends of the Executive Committee, who are, it appears, admitted gratis on Sunday in considerable numbers, had removed the statue from its place on that day for the purpose of taking a photograph of it, without Signor Monti's knowledge or permission; and it was during this operation that the fingers were broken off or separated from the statue, which has thus led to an exposure. Mr. Tudor has now refused to take the statue. It is asserted that the fingers had been already broken off and repaired ; but that does not in the least affect the question at issue, which is, " whether the Executive Committee is to be allowed the special privilege of pirating the works of exhibitors without their express permission ?" On Monday a parliamentary paper was printed, containing a copy of the Royal warrant to enter on the ground in Hyde-park for the Great Exhibition, and a copy of the deed of covenant from the Commissioners to her Majesty, by which they undertake that the said Exhibition " shall be closed or concluded on or before the Ist of November, 1851." All things are to be removed and carried away at the expense of the Commissioners by the Ist of June, 1852. SERIOUS ACCIDENT.—On Friday a serious accident occurred at the railway station, Kendal. The ornnibusses were in attendance for the arrival of the train due from the south at noon, and the drivers were busily engaged in portering for their passengers, when the horses belonging to the King's Arms conveyance, frightened by the starting of the engine, set off, and before the men were able to lay hold of them, got into full speed, and not succeeding in turning the corner, ran diagonally across the road directly into the window of one of the cottages opposite the railway inn. The window was dashed to pieces, and one of the animals, a valuable one, received a deep wound in the head, which caused its almost immediate death. The pole of the omnibus was broken, but the vehicle sustained no further damage. The other omnibus started off just after, the horses thinking " all right," and dashed through a bed of lime, used in the buildings connected with the railway inn, no w i n t h e course o f erect i on; b ut h app il y succeeded in the turn, and the vehicle was soon arrested in its career. Two children were run over, but we are happy to le.rn that the injuries they sustained were slight. With whom the fault chiefly lies has not yet been determined. If the railway Company employed a larger and a competent number of porters, the men belonging to the omnibusses would not be called upon to assist in that capacity, which is certainly not a part of their duty; but, at all events, the horses, however ac customed they may be to waiting, ought not be left so much to themselves.—Kendal Mercury.

ENVELOPE FOLDING eMACHsNES AT THE GREAT ExHe. ?? of the working mechanisms attract so much attention as the envelope folding machine of Messrs. De la Rue and Co., which occupies a conspicuous place in the main avenue. At that distance from the source of steam-power, in the north portion of the building, it is most convenient to work the machine by hand, the operator, however, being concealed from view. A boy feeds the instrument with the papers to be folded, which are previously cut and stamped, and placed in a heap by his side. A piece of paper having been laid on a metal cell the size of the envelope, a plunger instantly advances and thrusts it in, by which means the shape is given and the corners are turned up. As the plunger is withdrawn, two triangular pieces of metal close over the paper and fold down the ends- a steel arm, having at its end a piece of sponge or brush charged with gum, rapidly gums the edges; the top end bottom ere pressed down by other triangular pieces of metal, and the envelope being then folded, it is removed from the cell by a steel hand that takes hold of it in each end. and places it on an endless band, which is kept slowly in motion. and carries the envelopes under a roller to be pressed. Those last made push forward those before them, and the collection of envelopes is piled up in a perpendicular heap. When the machine is set in motion by steam-power, the only manual operation consists in feeding the instrument, and the envelopes are thus made, with the assistance of a boy, at a rate of sixty per minute. In the machinery department there is another envelope folding ma- chine, invented by Mr. Remond, of Birmingham. It is in many respects the same as that of Messrs. De. la Rue, though apparently more self-acting, for it feeds itself, and stamps an impression on the paper as well as gums the edges. The feed. lug part of the operation is very curious. The end of the arm that lifts eacii piece of paper into its place on the top of the metal cell is hollowed, and is connected by a tube with a small instrument like a pair of bellows, which produces a partial vacuum, and causes the paper to adhere to the end of the arm by the pressure of the atmosphere. The reversal of the action deposits the paper in the position to receive the blow from the pluoger, which brings down at the same time the die to stamp the impression. When the plunger is removed, the bottom of the cell falls down, and delivers the envelope into an inclined trough, whenceait falls into a box The envelopes then require to be gathered by a boy, and pressed. This machine does not appear to act so rapidly as Messrs. De la Rue's, though it is worked by steam power. The number made per minute is stated to be about forty. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. (From the Times of Thursday.) The Great Exhibition has killed everything else. The Court, the two Houses of Parliament, the nobility, the gentry, the commonalty, the army, the police, carriages, cabs, and omnibuses, are all dancing attendance upon it The shops are unfrequented. The places of public amusement are comparatively deserted. Even the railways lose their summer excursionists. Hampton Court and Greenwich exhibit in vain their horse chestnuts in bloom and their whitebait in season. We question whether even the great Derby-day will attract so large a fraction of a million as it has usually done. The tall plant in Hyde Park has smothered everything in its neighbourhood. The Exhibition is London ; the Exhibition is the Parliament; it is the British empire; it is house and home; it is drawing. room and study; it is parterre, conservatory, and promenade; it is park and club; it is shed and bazaar, theatre, picture-gallery, panorama,—everything in a word, which a man or a woman wants in this metropolis. The possessor of a season ticket, with a small surplus for cabs, or, in default thereof, a good pair of legs, is set up for the season. In a palace large enoogh to be a glass-case for Versailles or Windsor Castle, filled with all that is ingenious, precious, beautiful, curious, or rare, he walks at large, monarch of all he surveys. From the regalia of Indian dynasties to the last invention of European science—from the rude manufactures of people who dwell by the desert, or under the Mountains of the Moon, to the patent for separating the long and short fibres of wool, which is to found a new family of millionaires, everything that the eye can gaze on or the mind can apprehend, invites admiration. There is no door to be opened—no wants intimated—no importunity to be repelled,—no purchases expected. To all appearance some twenty or thirty thousand of this metropolis have resolved to enjoy themselves in this palace till they are compebed to be content with two days in the week, or to be lost in a crowd still larger than themselves. But such days and such insatiable wanderings are very exhaustive. Even two or three hours amid the "hum of nations" is enough to knock up a strong man, and we question whether, since the war, there ever was such an amount of physical and mental fatigue as there has been in this metropolis every evening since the first of this month. Parliament cannot continue to sit with any effect in the face of so powerful a rival, and with so great a drain on the strength of legislators as well as of all other classes. June and July, too, have other attractions, which will begin to hold up their heads and exert their influence should the novelty of the Exhibition wear off. The season will probably be one of more than usual hospitality; for there is hardly a family of any position or means in the country that will not find its w 4 to town. With so much to distract, and so much to fatigue, it is I useless to say that members of parliament ought to be at their posts to make a house when wanted, to support their party, and do other political drudgery. They ought perhaps, but nevertheless they will not. The session will be I the struggle of a sleepy man under a long and heavy sermon. He may open his eyes, shake himself and pinch but all to no purpose. After a hundred convulsive efforts at attention, he will be utterly unable to state either the text or the subject of the discourse. He will have lost an hour, and gained nothing but the discredit of an involuntary inattention. Perhaps the House of Commons ought to do more this session; but, in matter of fact, it will do no more. It will only waste its time and injure its character by an obstinate and slovenly perseverance in its duties, when it has neither the heart nor the strength for them. Under such circumstances, the sooner it shuts up shop the better for itself, and the better eventually for the business of the country.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Two hundred thousand visitors to the Crystal Palace in the first four days of the present week attest the ceaseless attractions which are contained therein. Of this number, vast as is its ma gn it u d e , pe r haps 19 out of every 20 are natives of the provinces and foreignees, and the remaining unit a Londoner. By far the larger proportion of country folks . are able to set apart but one day for the inspection of these accumulated treasures of nations, !ind let them be as industrious as they may it l a Physically impossible to do more than take the merest cursory glance at the whole. Here are 50,000 people con- Fentrated in a given space, and an endless variety of objects before them, ranging through avenues many miles in extent. instead of moving always in one direction, the living curare constantly running counter to each other, and the !abour of walking, with the thermometer at 75 or 80, is of itself sefficient to tire a strong man ere half the day is Thus, limited by time, and their own physical I nabi4:tty to thread the ever opening and almost interminable Wiedinge which meet them in all directions, and pressed on every side by momentarily increasing crowds, the great bulk of the people who frequent the Exiiibition are compelled to "Try over the various departments as expeditiously as they can, " Move on," says the policeman—" move on" is echoed 'by the eager sight -seers from behind, struggling successfully or unsuccessfully, as it happens, to reach the var.. And so t hey "keep moving on" hide to the advantage of the artisan or mechanic, who had hoped by his trip to town to acquired information which would turn out to be useful to him in his trade. Such is the state of things on the crowded "shilling days"—not so on Fridays and Saturdays, and these are th e d a y s w h en , if at all, a visit to the Exhibition will repay that class of persons, and those days we would emphatically recommend them to prefer. Even on the shilling days, however, no one who has visited the building can quit it without carrying with him many im- Pressions of an agreeable character. The outline of the Palace itself—the swarms of his fellow-men whom he has met there—the crystal fountain—the colossal figures and group s in sculpture which adorn the nave—the equestrian statue of her Maiesty, and the revolving lighthouse; will be indelibly engraven on all memories, when everything else has faded away, or is remembered only as a beautiful dream. ,And this we apprehend will, in most instances, be the chief "compensation" received by those who have come from a ,distance by cheap excursion trains for all the trouble, labour, anxiety, expense, and loss of time which they have incurred. The attendance of visitors at the Exhibition yesterday was about the same, in point of numbers, as on the previous Friday, and mrso composed of the same mixed class of persons. The temperature of the building beivg high, there was an extraordinary demand for ices and other refreshments of a cooling nature, and a good stroke of business must have been done in this department. M. le Ministre,-The undersigned are anxious to take the earliest opportunity on their return to England, after the brilliant and memorable fetes at which they have had the honour of being present as guests on the invitation of the City of Paris, to express, both in their own name and in that of other visitors on that occasion, their sense of the facilities afforded them by the government of France in dispensing with the formalities usually requisite on entering a foreign country. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Friday the 20th being a half-crown day the admissions fell to 31,8634. The difference caused by a rise of price throws a curious light upon the consideration in which the public held eighteen-pence, but the Royal Commission do not, in the aggregate, lose much by a dimunition of the crowd of visitors, for on Friday they took 2,8191. 4s. 6d., their receipts on Thursday being about 1601. more. The sale of season tickets realized during the day 361. 15s., which is more than it has done for some time. Her Majesty and Prince Albert, with the Princess Alice, visited the Exhibition at half-past nine, accompanied by the King of the Belgians, the Duke of Bra- bant, the Count of Flanders, and the Princess Royal of Bel- gium. An interesting experiment with fire-engines took place, in the presence of the jurors, on the north side of the building, close to the Serpentine, during the day. The object was to test the respective merits of each, and, for this purpose, parties of the Foot Guards, in fatigue dress, were set to work them. In discharging a column of water perpendicularly the fire- engine from Canada appeared to have a decided advantage, but, when the pipes were held horizontally, its superiority over its English competitors was not sustained. The receipts on Saturday from Us. visitors amounted to 1,6741. lOs., and according to the police returns 12,732 persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and the Prince resumed their inspection of the interior and their personal interviews with exhibitors during the forenoon and before the admission of the public. They examined the sections of furs and skins, of carriages and textile fabrics, and were attended during their stay by the acting members of the Executive Committee, Mr. Cole, Mr. Dilke, and Col. Reid. On Monday 67,555 persons visited the Building, and 3,0161. ies. was the amount taken at the doors. Two new and remarkable contributions have just been made to the collection ; one of these is a magnificent dressing-case from Buckingham Palace; the other is an immense black diamond, in the rough state, from Bahia, contributed by Mr. Joseph Mayer, of Liverpool, so hard that it has hitherto defied the lapidaries to polish it, and weighing 350 carats. "Next to the state opening,'5 says the Times, "the most im- pressive sight, perhaps, that the building has yet presented, was on Tuesday morning. Thousands of shilling visitors had entered during the first hour, when, without a note of pre- paration, by the good management of about a dozen police- men, an avenue was formed down the nave, and the Queen, who had, as usual, come early, was, on leaving, enabled to pass along between living walls of her people as quietly as if she was in her own drawing room. Hitherto her Majesty has usually taken her departure by one of the side passages, but on this occasion she veryunnexpectedly put her shilling-paying subjects on their trial for respectful and courteous behaviour towards her. Leaving the north half of the Indian depart- ment, and preceded only by Mr. Mayne and Mr. Belshaw, she proceeded, leaning on the King of the Belgians' arm, to Osler's fountain, which for a short time arrested her attention. The effect at this point produced by the thousands of excited spectators was exceedingly fine, and all kept their places with an admirable and praiseworthy sense of propriety. Every- body seemed to feel the novelty of the situation, and to desire that justice might be done it. It was, in point of fact, the first extempore wialk of the Sovereign in the presence of her people without other guards than themselves. The gratifi- cation caused by the event was visible in every face, and the occurrence seemed greatly to surprise and please the many foreigners who happened to be present. Here and there cheers were raised when the loyalty displayed rose to its highest point, but the spectators generally appeared to sup- press their feelings, as if they doubted the good taste of ex- pressing them on such an occasion. The Royal party was attended by Mr. Cubitt, Sir Stafford Northcote, Colonel Reid, Mr. Cole, and Mr. Dilke, Dr. Plavfair, and Mr. Bowring; they commenced their tour by examining the fixed machinery and receiving the explanations of Mr. Hensman and the the exhibitors present as to their respective contributions. After admiring the marine engines, locomotives, and other interesting objects which this department contains, they minutely inspected Cox and Company's new soda water machine, and not far off from this their attention was directed to the remarkable collection of the sacred volume produced by the British and Foreign Bible Society. Her Majesty during her stay for the first time saw the splendid ivory throne, studded with jewels, presented to her by the Maha- rajah of Travancore, with the extraordinary magnificence of which she appeared greatly astonished and pleased. It is to be hoped that the respectful conduct of the people on Tuesday may lead to a repetition of such acts of condescension as we have just recorded, and that the thousands of country folk who now daily flock to the Metropolis to see there, once for all, an epitome of worldly magnificence, may occasionally be able to carry back with them to their homely firesides the simple story of the Queen walking among them, and graciously receiving their una3ffected homage. The receipts at the doors amounted during the day to 31861. 12s. ; and, according to the police return, 68,394 persons entered the building Among the visitors were 445 agricultural labourers from the estate of MSr. Pusey, whose expenses were kindly and liberally defrayed by that gentleman. Some remarkable experiments were made on Tuesday in the presence of the jurors, with Henley's snagneto-electric telegraph. Two lengths of gutta percha covered wire having been laid across the Serpentine and con- nected to the instrument, each length had a portion of the gutta percha cut away and the wire well scraped to a bright surface. Not withstanding this, however, the telegraph worked well. One length of wire was then cut in two, and a long piece of uncovered bright -wire was inserted between, yet the result was again satisfactory, the water failing to deviate the course of the electric current. The third experiment made consisted in cutting asunder the wire and letting the ends fall into the water at some distance apart from each other. Even through this defective insulation the instrument worked well, and continued to do so after a still greater quantity of the gutta pereha coating had beer. removed. These results place in a remarkable point of view the merits of this in- vention, whereby the inconvenient and expensive use of a galvanic battery to the present electric telegraph is entirely superseded." The number of visitors on Wednesday was less by about 10,000 people than on the previous day, being 58,445, and the receipts at the doors in consequence fell to 2,6951. 1 Ss. Of late a feature of great interest has been added to the many others which the interior presents, in the gradually increasing influx of the children supported by our numerous charitable institutions. On Wednesday the boys of Christ's Hospital, to the number of 800 or 900, visited the Building, and there were other charities among them-the Jews' Orphan Asylum, and the children of Miss Burdett Coutts' school, whonm that benevolent ladv accompanied during their stay. On Thursday the receipts and the number of visitors again suffered a slight decline, the former being 2,7221. 10s., and the latter 57,781. 'T'he Queen and the Royal party at the Palace were again in the building, and commenced their survey by an examination of the Milan gallery. From this they proceeded to our own sculpture court, after which they went into the Indian collection, and then, ascending to the sections of glass and pottery, they were advantageously seen by the crowds who had by that time assembled. Some new arrivals of an interesting character were received on Thursday. They consist of contributions of various kinds, including arms, dresses, trappings, and ivory from Abyssinia, and a large round table from the Sandwich Islands; these contributions, which are presents to her Majesty, also include two silver coronets. It appears from an official return that the total number of persons who have entered the building from the opening day to Saturday last, was upwards of a million and a half.

Cheap Lodgings : Beware. —The Scotsman says,—“ A gentleman in Edinburgh, induced by an advertisement of a tempting kind, relative to cheap lodgings,’ applied a few days ago to the proprietor of lodging-house at a short distance from the Crystal Palace, as to tenns for a residence of fourteen days for himself and lady. The reply is quite a curiosity : For a bed-room and sitting-room, for a fortnight from the Ist of May, the charge will be i?3l 10s.; bonus to be paid in hand to secure the rooms, £5 55.; service, 2s.; —total, 15s.’ Thirty-eight pounds fifteen shillings for mere lodging for fourteen days—all payments for food to be over and above! venture to say that nothing more monstrous is to be found the whole annals of extortion. The rooms in question, judging from the inspection of the friend who made the inquiry, were such as in usual times are hired for two guineas week ! It is very desirable that the authorities connected with the Exhition should publicly announce the whereabouts of the lodgings that are offered on reasonable’ charges to visitors. It is entitled A Bill to regulate the Mode of administering the Oath of Abjuration to persons professing the Jewish Religion,” and runs as follows : Whereas her Majesty’s subjects professing the Jewish religion are law capable of being elected to sene as members of the House of Commons, anil of holding divers offices in respect of which they are or may be required take the oath of abjuration ; and it is expedient to direct in what manner that oath should in all cases administered to persons professing the said religion ; He it therefore enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons in this present Parliament assembled, and the authority of the same, that whenever any of Her Majesty's subjects professing the Jewish religion shall present himself to take the said oath of abjuration, the words, Upon the trae faith of a Christian,' shall omitted out of the said oath in ministering the same to such person; and the taking of the said oath by such person professing the Jewish religion, without the words aforesaid, in like manner Jews are admitted to be sworn to give evidence in courts of justice, shall be deemed to be sufficient taking of the oath of abjuration.” Public Income and Expenditure. —A valuable parliamentary paper, obtained by Mr. Cardwell, has been published by order of the House of Commons. It contains an account of the public income and expenditure for each year since 1822, showing the amount received into the Exchequer, the expenditure under its several heads, the surplus or deficiency of income ; the amount of taxes repealed, reduced, or imposed, distinguishing the principal items; the total capital of debt funded or unfunded ; and the balances in the Exchequer at the close of the year. Since 1822, taxes have been repealed or reduced to the amount of .£36,918,503. and taxes have been imposed to the amount of £9,861,756, leaving a balance of taxes reduced or repealed to the amount of 27,083,747. Between 1822 and 1830 the net reductions amounted to £17,078,409; between 1830 and 1840, to £5,258,608; and between 1840 to £7,746,738. The total revenue for the year 1822 was £54,135,743; and for 1850,52,810,680. From a statement of the value of our imports and exports during the same years, it appears that in 1822 the value of imports into the United Kingdom, calculated at the official rates of valuation, was £30,520,663; and of exports, £53,464,123. In 1849 the value of the imports was £105,874,607 ; and that of the exports, £190,101,394. Defrauding the Queen. —Mr. John Marchant, a coal merchant in the Strand, has been summoned to answer the charge of sending in coals of deficient weight to Buckingham Palace, and also for using a defective weighing machine. It appeared that on the 4th inst, the defendant received an order to deliver 20 tons of coals at Buckingham Palace. The coals were loaded at the wharf, and there was in all five waggons, containing 160 sacks. It was found when the coals were discharged at the Palace that there was a deficiency in weight to the following extent—in the first waggon, 12 cwt. 18 lbs., in the second, 13 cwt. 10 lbs., in the third, cwt. 73 lbs., and in the fourth, 9 cwt. 35 lbs., whilst to the fifth waggon an itn perfect weighing machine was attached. The coals having been weighed in a machine kept at the Palace, the discovery of the false weight was made known to the Master of her Majesty’s Household, and the result was that the present summons was taken out with a view to deter others from rendering themselves liable to a similar charge. Mr. Huddlestone appeared for the defendant. The prisoner alleged that he was 78 years old, and entrusted his business to the management of other parties, by whom, without his knowledge, the fraud had been committed. The price of the coals sent in was 255. 6d. per ton, —rather above the average value, but the defendant alleged that he had to give from six to nine months’ credit at the Palace. After hearing the evidence, the magistrate said it was clear a gross imposition had been practised, and as it was obvious that defendant’s servants had no interest whatever in the deficient weight, he was bound to consider it was done for the benefit of, and with the permission of the defendant himself. He should not, however, inflict the full penalty, which would amount, at £5 for each sack short weight, to between j£Boo and j£9oo. But he would inflict penalty of £o for five sacks in each waggon, making £lOO, with £5 besides for the defective weighing machine. This, he thought, might meet the justice of the case, especially as defendant would lose the valuable custom of Her Majesty. Marchant has regularly supplied the Palace with coals for a period of 17 years.
