THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Thursday, according to the police returns, 54,669 persons visited the Crystal Palace. The sum taken in shillings at the doors was 2,379/. 7s. There were therefore 47,587 people who paid for entering, and 7,C80 season-ticket holders. The class who now come to the Exhibition remain a shorter time than their more fashionable predecessors. They generally arrive at an early hour, and begin to leave between 1 and 2 o'clock. Notwithstanding the immense numbers the utmost order and propriety of conduct prevailed. The Queen and her illustrious guests came to the Building at their usual early hour, and remained for some time, as on a former occasion, watching with curiosity and interest the influx of people when the doors were opened. Among the vast assemblage rnieit be observed numbers of workmen from Mr. Cubites and other large establishments. On Friday the price of admission, as settled by the Royal Commission, WAS half-a crown. It was not anticipated that the number of visiters would be great, nor was it so, but the result exceeded the calculations made, and the receipts at the doors were 2 839/. 83. The police returns represent that 30,345 'persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and the Royal family continued their inspection, the people inside conducting themselves with marked propriety. During her last two visits the Queen had taken particular notice of several branches of national industry, the contributors to which will feel flattered by such attention. She examined closely the specimens of Paisley shawls, and the needlework of the Scotch and Irish peasantry. Some embroidered vests from Belfast, exhibited by Mr. M‘Gee, especially attracted her; and the collection of embroideries by Salomons and Sons was also much admired by her. Her Majesty looked over with great care and interest the display of Lyons silks, and the muslins and printed fabrics of Mulhausen. On Friday an unexpected rise took place in the sale of season tickets, and the receipts from this source amounted to fill. 10q. It is now quite clear that from that quarter the finances of the Commission can hence. forth derive no material aid, unless the present scale of prices is low3red. In imitation of the style of decoration adopted in the eastern division of the building, it is, we hear, proposed that the flags of our principal manufacturing towns should be displayed over their respective allotments in the western nave. Leeds has already set the example in this respect. On Saturday the charge for admission to the building was ss. Owing to the attractions of the drawing room, of a review at Woolwich, and of the other festivities connected with the celebration of Her Majesty's birthday, there was a smaller attendance of visiters than usual, the number being only between 15,000 and 16,000, and the receipts being 1,771/. 12s. 61. The Queen, for the first time, to-day meets the exhibitors, a portion of whom are requested by circular to be in attendance, in case explanations should be required of them. On Saturday, a considerable sensation was created in the building by the appearance among the visiters of a Spanish family, dressed in their picturesque national costume. They were accompanied round the interior by Lord Ranelagb, and were stared at and crowded round with a perseverance and impudence which, considering the charge for admission, and the presumed presence in consequence of a rather select assemblage, said very little for its good breeding. Greeks, Persians, Egyptians, Indians, Turks, and Armenians, have all been allowed to exhibit their finery since the Exhibition opened without let or hindrance, but the appearance of a Spanish senora in the dress of her country offered too great an attraction to be resisted in deference to the ordinary rules of politeness. —Times.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION_ The unceasing labour of the workmen, the exhibitors, and their assistants, during the last few days, has greatly simplified our duey of noticing the more prominent features of the British side of the exhibition. The piles of packing cases and rubbish by which the main avenue was encumbered have been nearly all cleared away—most of the bulky and unwieldy articles are in their places—the hoardings which separated the different compartments and countries have been taken down—and the eye, ranging over the ample expanse and still more formidable length of the building, is able to form a better e3timate of the present arrangements and prospective effect of the whole. Proceeding from the western entrance—on the outside of which something like order is beginning to be observable among the gigantic masses of coal, ironstone, and huge blocks of granite here deposited—the whole range of British art and industry is before us; objects of peculiar novelty, or striking interest, or whose vast proportions exclude them from the compartments, are ranged above the central avenue, leaving abundant space on either side to facilitate the largest amount of "circulation" that can be anticipated. On the stalls and counters on either hand of this main artery, whatever is most costly, or beautiful, or ingenious in the productions of this country, are now being arranged with such ornamental and decorative aids as the rules of the executive committee will permit; and such attention to harmonious and artistic grouping and display as the taste of each exhibitor can command. Behind these lines the articles of larger size and coarser material, although probably not less valuable and practical in their uses, will be placed ; and at the sides of the building, machinery in motion and at rest—the basis of the commerce and manufacturing greatness of this country —will be displayed on the right hand, and agricultural implements, furniture, and other ornamental and useful articles on the left. Such is the general character of the arrangements; but the prescribed order is interfered with in exceptional cases here and there. As we have already said, the central avenue on the British side of the building is overcrowded, as compared with the foreign nave; and this considerably mars the general effect, and interferes with the isolation and display so essential to the just appreciation of works of art. This is another reason why we must regret that the parties entrusted with the supervision of the arrangements, should have sanctioned the introduction on this prominent space of articles not fairly entitled to so distinguished a position. It woild be at present, and before the final arrangements are completed, invidious to particularise the objects to which we take exception—the public will, next week, have an opportunity of exercising their own judgment upon this point; but the mixed and somewhat incongruous character of the whole, although it indicates the extent and variety of the industrial and artistic contributions of the country, exhibits a want of classification and coherence, and such startling contrasts, as seriously impair the general effect. At the western extremity of the nave the beautiful model of the town and docks of Liverpool, the arrangement of which has occupied a large number of hands for many weeks, will form an object of much interest to our continental visitors, le ho by means of it can form some estimate of the gigantic scale upon which the trading and commercial operations of that port are conducted. It is constructed upon a scale of eight feet to the mile, and every building will occupy its exact locality and proportionate size. Models of railway and other tubular bridges will fitly illustrate the stupendous scale upon which our engineering achievements in this improved mode of intercommunication have been executed. The light and graceful character of the lofty bronze dome erected by the Colebrook Dale Company, will exhibit the progress we are making in the adaptation of metals to ornamentation—the dome is surmounted by an eagle, and will have placed in its interior the celebrated German statue of the eagle slayer, with a lamb at his feet, which his rifle has compelled the wounded robber of the fold to let fall. A clock of large dimensions and peculiar construction by Dent is another appropriate exemplification of our unrivalled chronometrical excellence. A large model of Lever Bridge Church, Bolton, Lancashire, in Ladyshore terracotta, will introduce many of the visitors to a new style of decorative building. Thomas's large fountain, surmounted and surrounded by groups of figures embodying the story of Acis and Galatea, holds also a prominent place in the nave; and near it is a refracting telescape, 13 feet long—one of the largest instruments of the kind ever constructed in this country, placed upon an equatorial stand. In addition to the figures and groups which we enumerated a few days since, we observe a large group in plaster of a dead warrior, the broken battle-axe falling from his hand, and his faithful steed and a female figure bending over the prostrate hero. Another well-executed group is the liberated captive—a kneeling Christian knight, indicated by his cross-handled sword, is severing the chains of a venerable figure. A cast from the original statue of the Apollo Belvedere, is an extremely successful attempt to imitate a peculiar grain and semi-transparency of marble. A bronze group of the horse and:dragon in mortal combat, complete the list of works of art placed in the western nave. In the transept, several additiona have been recently made to the hall of statues—at the northern extremity we find two wellexecuted equestrian statues of the Queen and Prince Albert —a quiet and graceful group of Milton and his Daughtersan Ancient Briton—the Triumph of Sin, represented by Eve and the Serpent—the Chained Captive, a vulture with outstretched beak and wings peering into the I eyes of the prostrate and helpless figure, from Milan, is a spirited production—statues of Wellesley, Wellington, Peel, and several other distinguished personages have also been added to the long - 11,!t of work of art collected in this part of the building. The works of arranging and displaying the goods is now in full activity in every part of the extensive pile—some thousands of hands are rapidly reducing the accumulated heaps of industrial or artistic treasures poured in from all parts of the world to order and system, while the active and intelligent body of engineers exercise a general superintendence over the labours of the exhibitors, and jealously guard against the slightest infringement upon the space marked out for the public avenues and passages. It is not surprising that the anxiety of individual contributors to exhibit their own goods or manufactures, although possessing no peculiar claims to novelty or excellence, has led in many instances to the introduction of articles which might well have been spared. On the other hand, we miss the contributions of some of our most eminent manufacturers in the optical, astronomical, scientific, and other departments, men whose world-wide reputation leaves them nothing to expect from a rivalry of this sort, but the want of whose productions detracts from the completeness of the display as an exposition of British industry. The great defect of the British department generally is the overcrowding of articles from a somewhat pardonable anxiety to make the most of the space at their disposal. Report, as well as the occasional glimpses caught through the surrounding canvas, speaks highly of a wedimval court, furnished with the most costly and elaborate models of the ornaments and furniture of the olden time, by Pugin. The agricultural implements occupy a very extensive tract on the south side, and are striking and impressive evidences of the ingenious contrivances and progressive improvements that have taken place within the last few years in this most important, but hardly-used branch of our national industry; and the number and variety, the superior finish, the massive character, scientific combinations, and engineering skill displayed in the machinery employed in the development and multiplication of our various textile fabrics, indicates the sources and the secret of our manufacturing excellence and superiority. The progress made within the last few days in the fitting up of the foreign side of the building is remarkable; but whether more space has been allotted to our continental neighbours than they are able to occupy, or whether further arrivals at this, the eleventh hour, are still looked for, we know not; but we find extensive tracts in the eastern galleries entirely deserted up to the present time. A transfer of some of the redundant wealth of the British end would, at the sacrifice of some little consistency as regards classification, be extremely desirable. What our beighbours have already exhibited gives abundant promise that their contributions will exhibit striking evidence of well-directed industry, combined with correct taste, and an amount of artistic education in the citizens of other countries that we have not yet attained to. The refreshment courts are still in a very unfinished state; and it is in this quarter of the building that the largest number of workmen are at present employed. The exigencies of the executive committee have compelled them to put up this service to public tender; and the large sum lend by the Messrs. Schweppe for the privilege of supplying the visitors, and the effect of again subletting the contract to other parties, will, we fear, operate injuriously upon the public as regards the prices to be paid for refreshments. The exhibitors are at present supplied with cold luncheon, and the artisans With dinner, by Younghusband and Sons, of Gerard's Hall, in a suite of large rooms set apart for their accommodation on the north side of the building. The greater part of the glass roof is now covered with canvas; nevertheless, in middle of the day s when tht beats strongly upon the large surface of glass, the heat is rather uncomfortable. Here and there a painter may be detected lurking in some obscure corner, and finishing off some forgotten portion of the work. Double seats, each capable of containing about twenty persons, mounted upon a light iron frame-work, are being placed along the nave, and dwarf iron posts connected by a thick crimson rope will surround the counters and compartments to keep off the pressure of the crowd. The walls are now displaying a variety of tapestry, earpetting, paper-hangings, and mural decorations, in encaustic, distemper, and oils. In the galleries considerable additions have been recently made to the display of stained and decorated glass; and lace and embroidery, bi j auterie, and other costly and perishable articles, protected by glass cases or covers, are giving an air of elegance and approaching completeness to the scene. Down the long avenues and vistas which the removal of hoardings and packing-cases has opened up, numberless busy hands are at work, and glimpses of treasures whose full-blown beauties and perfections are yet unrevealed, may be caught occasionally by the passing visitor. The announcement of her Majesty's intention to open the Exhibition in state has given a new stimulus to the energies of all parties employed in the decoration of the building or the final arrangement of the goods. We trust that the additional labour which this will entail upon the executive committee may not have the effect of retarding the main business in hand—namely, progress of such works as are more immediately connected with the opening of the Exhibition to the public. Now that it is understood that holders of season tickets will be admitted to witness the interesting ceremonial, we would impress upon the contractors and the committee the necessity of making in time such arrangements as, while keeping carefully in view the comfort and convenience of her Majesty and her illustrious visitors, will afford sufficient accommodation to the many thousand persons who will be present. For this purpose much is yet wanting, within and without the building. Facilities of ingress at all the entrances, which will necessitate the clearing away of a vast deal of rubbish and obstruction outside, and such accommodation within, by the placing of seats along either side of the nave and in the galleries, as the time at their disposal will permit of. The price of the season tickets was yesterday raisedthe gentlemen's to four guineas and the ladies' to three guineas; and should the demand of the next day or two continue, either the price will be again raised or the sale will be suspended until after the state opening, as the. executive committee are naturally unwilling to undertake the responsibility of introducing more than a certain number of thousands. We can assure them that such an arrangement will be far more judicious than the indiscriminate admission of a fashionable mob, whom it will be impossible to restrain and keep in order if facilities be not afforded them of witnessing the state procession through the building.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Thursday. — The receipts amounted to £2,72b 145., the number of visitors being 57,161. . •*- , - Friday.— The receipts at the doors amounted to £2 415 15e., th 2 number of visitors being 23,014. In another fortnight tbe Great Exhibition close?, the Crystal Palace will have fulfilled its purpose, and Oose vast as- semblages of spectators which for months past have mado pilgrimages from every eonier ofthe globe to the shrine of industry will be deprived of the centre round whicb their curiosity attracted them. When that event happens the grindeur of the demonstration which has taken place in favour of the peaceful arts will be more distinctly appre- ciated, and the results, beneficial or otherwise, which tbe display leaves behind it, will be calmly ascertained and realized. A melancholy occurrence took place about three o'clock in tfie afternoon in the western refreshment- room. An elderly gentleman suddenly dropped down, and to the horror of the bystanders expired instantaneously. Saturday. — £l,Bs2 2s. 6d. was taken at the doors of the building, the number of visitors being 20,236. During the afternoon an extraordinary specimen of gold ore from California was placed in the American portion of the nave, which, from its size and evident richness, attracted an im- mense amount of attention. In appearance it is a huge block of quartz rock, impregnated in every part with the precious metal, and the value of it may be estimated from the fact that the fortunate owner refuses to part with it for £3,250. He has arrived in England with this specimen for the purpose of buying machinery to work the vein in which it was discovered, and he is himself as curious and interesting an object as his contribution, being fresh from the diggings, and wearing a gold watch chain of the most preposterous dimensions. The recently discovered gold mines in Australia are also now represented in the Crystal Palace at No. 51, class 23. We hear that his Royal High- ness Prince Albert has purchased the magnificent vase with oxidized silver handles exhibited by Messrs. Minton and Co., their stall, No. 1 , in the Ceramic department. The price is said to be 200 guineas. On Friday, Pursuant to the terms of their agreements with the Woods nnd Forests, and with the contracters, the Royal Commission gave legal notice to Messrs. Fox and Henderson of their intention to remove the building. By a curious coincidence this formal art took place on the anniversary of placing the first column of the Crystal Palace, and this fact will probably long be re- membered as one of the most striking illustrations of the rapid execution which has characterised the whole un- dertaking. Of course the giving notice cannot be regarded as finally conclusive of the fate of the Building, for the resolution of the House of Commons, and the still unascer- tained pleasure of the Crown upon the subject, will keep the matter in suspense at least until Parliamentreassembles. At present, however, everything tends to the conviction that the removal from Hyde Park will take place as originally intended. Monday. — The approaching close ofthe Exhibition now begins to be felt unmistakeably. To-day £3,295 15s. was taken at the doors, and there were 68,542 visitors. Among them came Mary Kerlynack, the Cornish octoge- narian. We have been requested (says the Times) to say that certain announcements of jury awards recently made by a morning contemporary are entirely inaccurate, the names of three jurors in one case being given as the win- ners of great medals, and in another section tbat of one juror. Third-class medals are also spoken of, though no such distinction exists or is contemplated. Premature and incorrect 'announcements of this kind inflict a large amount of practical injustice, and the authorities ofthe Exhibition charged with the management of that department are naturally indignant at the attempts made to forestall their own labours, wbich will be continued up to the last mo- ment, so that publicity, when it is invited and desirable, will have the advantage of truth in its favour. The pro- gramme of the closing is so far settled, and circulars are about to be issued to exhibitors informing them that the building will be closed to the public on Saturday the llth of October ; that on th * 13th and 14th they will have the privilege of going there with two friends, and that on the 15th they are invited to be present at 12 o'clock at the meeting of the Royal Commissioners. By this arrange- ment the exhibitors will have tbe farewell view of the Crystal Palace, and a deference is thus shown to their labours and their sacrifices on its behalf, which we are sure they will not be slow to appreciate. With a view to render- ing the ceremony of the 15th as imposing as the circum- stances will permit, Mr. Fox, the eminent contractor, has addressed a letter to the Executive Committee, offering the services of the Sacred Harmonic Society in assembling 1,500 performers on the occasion, tbe whole to be con- ducted by Mr. Costa. As the period for the closing ap- proaches, the propriety of some respectful observances of form to accompany it appears to be more deeply felt, but the Royal Commission make no sign upon the subject. What was undertaken with the highest sanction of the State and with the solemnities of religion should obviously not be allowed to expire without some expression of grati- tude for success, however simple and unpretending. There are, undoubtedly, difficulties presented by the season of the year and by other causes ; but we cannot think that with so many ingenious minds ready to devise a suitable method of showing public thankfulness, the practical realization of that sentiment should be withheld. If the commission and the Prince have not the spirit to undertake it, the people will probably do it after their own* fashion ; and, though a spontaneous effort of this kind is open to many disadvantages and drawbacks, its genuine character cannot be doubted, and the impression which it produces, if successful, is superior to the most premeditated and skilful arrangements for display. Bloomerism at the Crystal Palace. — On Thurs- day afternoon the visitors to the Great National Exhibition in Hyde Park had an opportunity of judging of the style of the new American costume, of which Mrs. Bloomer is the reputed inventor. Shortly before two o'clock three ladies attired according to tbe Bloomer fashion, and accompanied by two gentlemen wearing the habiliments of the new sect made their appearance in the large open space to tbe left of the Crystal Palace. They appeared to be persons of bigh station in society, and bore witb con- siderable good humour the taunts which were freely directed against them. Tbey walked round tbe building followed by a large number of persons, wbo had been attracted towards them by the novelty of their dress, but did not enter the Exhibition. They carried with them a quantity of printed bills, announcing a lecture by one of their order in Fiusbury, on Monday evening next, and these they politely distributed amongst persons as willing to accept them. Bloomerism in Lonuon. — On Monday evening an immense number of people assembled at the Royal British Institution, Cowper Street, City Read, London, to hear a lecture announced by the " apostle of Bloomerism," Mrs. C. H. Dexter. Every door of the building was regularly besieged, and two or three times stormed by the advancing party, who, regardless of the entreaties of the doorkeeper, would come in and see the fun. By eight o'clock every nook and corner of the large school-room was completely filled, the ledges of the wall, and even the rafters, being turned into the " perch" of some adventurous spirits. When this in-flowing had been accomplished to the full capacity of the building, those within set their backs against the doors, and successfully resisted the further influx of the sightseeing mob, of whom, by the by, the greater part were males. Half-past eight arrived (as was shown by a tell tale clock in the room), but no Mrs. Dexter. Those who had paid their money naturally waxed impatient, and began to indulge themselves in a few noises and other popular amusements so thoroughly congenial to the tastes of a large set of enlightened waiting Englishmen. But time wore on, and at last some one in authority (one of the committee, we believe), announced that Mrs Dexter would appear as soon as the audience conducted themselves properly. This, perhaps, was not the most judicious way of securing silence. By and by, Mr. Dexter appeared in the nondescript dress of his order, and said that his lady would appear so soon as the police could clear a way for her outside ; and a few minutes afterwards announced that she was in the building, and only waited till silence could be commanded to come forward. This alternate speechify- ing of Mr. Dexter and the committee-man continued till nearly 10 o'clock, not one word out of a dozen being heard on account of the cries for order and facetious observations ofthe visitors. The Perth Courier states that Lord Willoughby d'Eresby has, with his usual liberality, hired, at his own expense, a house in London for the accommodation of such of the tenants on his extensive estates as may wish to visit the Great Exhibition. The general principle on which the arrangement of the goods in the Exhibition will be carried out, viz., that foreign countries will occupy the eastern. and Great Britatn and her colonies the western portion of the building, has been already stated. The produce of foreign countries will be arranged in nations, placed, us far as practicable, according to their respee- tive latitude, and the productions of England and the colonies in thirty separate sections. The position in the building which will be occupied by each of these sections has now been fully determined upon. Of the four main divisions into which it will be divided, it has been decided that machinery shall occupy the north side, raw materials and produce the south side, and that the centre shall be reserved for manufactures and the fine arts. Along the central passage to the west of the transept, a front- age upon each side of seven bays, or 168 feet, will be occupied by the productions of the colonies. Adjoining the colounes, and upon the north side of the passage, will be placed articles included in the section of paper, printing, and book-binding. By the side of these will be placed furniture and upholstery decorations, paper-hangings, and papler machi. Manufactures in mineral substances, used for building or decorations, as In marble, slate, porphyries, cements, artificial stones, &c., are placed next in order. Manufactures in leather. skins, furs, and hair occupy the next position; and adjoining to them are the cotton manufactures; and to printed, dyed, woven, and felted fabrics is allotted the space next to that of cotton. Crossing the western extremity, and retracing his steps upon the south side of the central passage, the visitor will arrive at the place allotted to mixed fabrics, and pass on to that assigned to wool- len and worsted manufactures-next to the space occupied by flax and hemp and the linen manufactures,,ybich will be im- mediately opposite toJhose of cotton. Adjoining the linen manufactures will be articles of cutlery, edge tools, and surgical Instranments,together with locksnsdgrates; and bythe sideof the latter will be displayed glass, china, pottery, and ceramic goods, with the colonial products adjoining. Mining, quarrying, metallurgy, and mineral products will be placed along the southern passage, and the space between them and manufac- tures will be occupied to a great extent by agricultural imple- ments. Jewellery. and the greater proportion of silks and velvets, with lace, embroidery, and other light and fancy wares, will be placed, as far as praoticable, in the galleries. Such are the general features of the arrangements. Some matters of detail in connexion with the allocation of the space yet remain to be carried gut. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The returns of visitors to the building yesterday again show a decrease, the numbers being 51,069, and the amount taken at the doors 2,491. 10s. The interior was exceedingly cool and agreeable during the day, and there would no doubt have been a larger attendance but for the showers that fell during the morning and the afternoon. We would strongly recommend all who come as strangers to the Exhibition, on entering, to examine carefully the large plan which is displayed at th? south side of the transept, from the information contained in which they will be enabled to find their way much more easily to the points which most engage their curiosity. This plan has been chiefly prepared by Corporals Baker and Mack, of the Sappers , and is a most creditable performance. Indeed, that body have rendered invaluable services, not only in the general arrangements of the interior, but more especially in making those nice measurements which were essential with reference to the question of space. The training which, under Sir C. Pasley's system, they undergo admirably prepares them for this description of work, and they have brought to it the practical e xperience acquired during the Irish, Scotch, and English surveys, which it will be recollected they were employed upon in compliance with a most valuable suggestion to that effect made by Colonel Reid. The plan to which we allude is a highly creditable specimen of the skill which the Sappers have attained to in the art of surveying. A curious accident occurred yesterday near the east entrance of the building. The heavy rain which fell in the morning caused a branch of one of the large trees there to give way, and descending upon a boy who had taken refuge beneath it for shelter, it killed him on the spot. Two men were apprehended in the afternoon by the police picking pockets. FINE ARTS.—Messrs. THE GREAT EXHIBITION FETE IN PARIS. PROGRESS FROM LONDON TO PARIS. We have the following letters ftom our correspondents describing the progress of the English visitors towards Paris : BOULOGNE, FRIDAY AFTERNOON. At eight o'clock this morning the London-bridge station was occupied by a large number of the guests, and the crowd increased every minute. By half-past eight o'clock the platform was crowded by aldermen, sheriffs, deputies, and corporation dignitaries, mixed up with M.P.'s, savaes, Royal Commissioners, Americans, and other foreigners. For a time all went smoothly pleasant, chatty groups were formed, and friends discussed the prospects of the day. It soon, however, became evident that something more than usual was engaging the attentention of the porters and railway officials. The crowd thickened, and as visitors looked around and recognised acquaintance after acquaintance, suspicion arose that London was on the move, and that the Saturday's fashionable swarm at the Crystal Palace was en route for Paris. A rush was made at the barriers, and a close column of porters' trucks formed before it, like a train of artillery, while on either side a forlorn hope made desperate efforts to get through the gaps, which were sternly guarded by picked members of the railway staff and police. Some dignitaries had left their blue-bordered tickets behind; others found that their tickets of invitation to ball and concert did not pass wives and daughters through the railway barriers. Anxious consultations were held, detachments were sent to the pay places to secure whatever tickets could be got, and the company reaped a .rich harvest from the assembled multitude. Ladies got through the barriers as they best could, and occupied seats. Slowly and gradually the majority of the attendant crowd oozed through the narrow strait; but now new difficulties were to be encountered. Parties of two or three wished to go together, and anxiously looked about for convenient places. From carriage to carriage they peered about, daintily rejecting the odd seats, and hoping for better luck further on. Soon it became apparent that even odd seats were scarce; husbands vainly searched for wives and daughters—ladies wandered about, looking for their partners. Groups were formed round carriage -doors, .discussing claims which were put in for seats that had been retained, or for compartments taken; and plaintive voices urged how hard it was to separate husband and wife. American ladies asserted their claims as only American ladies can to the " cars" of which they had assumed the temporary ownership, and strenuously assailed as cowardly and ungentlemanly any attempt to occupy the vacant seats. The foreign visitors wandered about, hopelessly resigned to their fate, almost in despair of ever getting through. What became of the luggage is not known; but strong hopes ore entertained that it will all be found at Paris. The last bell rang, the guards became importunate to close the doors, and the storm of the barriers was renewed. Mr. Paxton made his way through with beaming face, and, it is to bo presumed, as the hero of the dey, obtained a seat; but it was reported that a strong detachment of the corporation of the city of London was left behind. Several stout gentlemen were seen standing guard over bags swollen with scarlet robes and uniforms, and cases with cocked hats and deputy-lieutenants' swords. The Lord Mayor's fat footmen were in the rear, whether in charge of the state coach is not known. The superintendent with great difficulty got the doors of the carriages closed, though ladies made stern efforts to signal their absent lords and set their protest against divorce and separate maintenance. By the kindness of the authorities we got packed in a carriage after some fruitless efforts, but the great mass were not so fortunate, and we saw as we left a large assemblage awaiting the next train. The railway authorities did the best they could under the circumstances, and provided a monster train for the Royal Commissioners and their friends, but so profuse has been the hospitality of the French Government and city of Paris municipality, that no single train could convey the assembled multitude. By great exertions, an enormous number was carried off by the first train, and we passed on the line numerous strings of empty carriages, drafted by telegraph from all parts to the scene of action, so that all will be got off this morning, and it is intimated a fleet of steamers has been assembled at Folkstone. The weather was brilliant in the morning, and gave good augury of a happy commencement to the festivities. The train started punctually at nine, and in forty minutes got to the Reigate junction, and made a halt for water. Here some hapless visitors were assembled, in hopes to catch the train en route, but such good fortune as a vacant seat in the closely packed train was hopeless. By a very good arrangement, with the view to save trouble, the " blue bordered" or privileged passes, and the purchased tickets were all made through to Paris. Besides Reigate a stoppage was only made at Tunbridge, and the train got into Folkstone at twenty minutes past eleven. FO LKSTON E. The train got into the station as first said, and we found a large party of the inhabitants assembled to witness the proceedings. In the harbour great excitement prevailed, and the shipping were dressed with all their colours, presenting a very gay appearance. In about ten minutes the train got to the harbour, and the sea was as smooth as a mill-pond.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. There was, as might be anticipated, a considerable falling off in the number of visitors on Friday, and a large proportion of those present were season-ticket holders. The transept was again fitted with seats and the flowers and trees which have been for the last few days drooping have all been renovated and refreshed. A large and very beautiful model of the Queen, first-rate man-of-war, sent by the Admiralty, has just been put up in the centre of the transept, the site selected being very appropriately that on which her Majesty's chair of state was placed on the opening day. We were somewhat surprised to hear that this elegant and very characteristic emblem of the national power and greatness of England was refused a place in the first instance, as being too large, while there are hundreds, nay thousands, of articles exhibited ten times its dimensions. The whole rigging is not yet completed, but with all paraphernalia of miniature blocks, sheets, guns, Re., and the Royal Standard flying at the main, it is one of the most interesting and attractive ornaments of the transept. Another of the novelties which has just made its appearance is an iron cage in front of the Dutch compartment, modelled somewhat after the Koh-i-Noor cage, and containing a number of extraordinary , gems belonging to Mr. Rope. Among them is a large pearl, the largest it is said ever yet found, weighing I.„800 gfains. It is shaped somewhat like a closed hand, and is surmounted by a miniature crown emblazoned in brilliants. The colour is not quite perfect, but it is the most wonderful specimen ever exhibited in this country. There is also a large crystal, with • drop of water or some other fluid in the centre. Our philosophers will be puzzled to account for its Imprisonment. The largest cat's-eye (quartz) known is also among the collection, and a specimen of a very rare description of this stone called gold-coloured cat'seye. A very perfect specimen of the fire opal and another of the pearly opal, about two inches long and an inch across, are also to be seen. They are from Mexico, and are both of great transparency, showing in every direction beautiful iris colours, the red and green heing particularly vivid. There is also • large crystal of the precious beryl from Siberia; emerakhi, some in the matrix, jacinths, a cluster of amethysts, uncut shells, with the pearls embedded in them, and a number of other valuable gems. The Russian collection, from which the public are still excluded, is fast approaching completion. We yesterday visited the model houses for four families erected at the Cavalry Barracks, Knightsbridge, on the south side of the Crystal Palace, by his Royal Highness Prince Albert, in connection with the Exposition of the Works of Industry of all Nations. His Royal Highness has had this building raised on his own account, with a desire of conveybig practical information calculated to promote the muchneeded improvement of the dwellings of the working classes, and also of stimulating visitors to the Exhibition, whose position and circumstances may enable them to carry out similar undertakings, and thus without pecuniary sacrifice permanently to benefit those who are greatly dependent on others for their home and family comforts. In its general arrangement the building is adapted for the occupation of four families cf the class of manufacturing and mechanical operatives, who usually reside in towns, or in their immediate vicinity; and as the value of land, which leads to the economising of space, by the placing of more than one family under the same roof, in some cases renders the addition of a third, and even of a fourth story desirable, the plan has been suited to such an arrangement, without any other alteration than the requisite increase in the strength of the walls. The most prominent peculiarity of the design is that of the receding and protected central open staircase, with the connecting gallery on the first floor, formed of slate, and sheltered from the weather by the continuation of the main roof, which also screens the entrances to the dwellings. The four tenements are arranged on precisely the same plan, two on each floor. The entrance is through a small lobby, lighted from . the upper part of the door. The living room has a superficial area of about 150 feet, with a closet on one side of the fireplace, to which warm air may be introduced from the back of the range; over the fireplace is an iron rod for hanging pictures; and on the opposite side of the room a shelf is carried above the doors, with a rail fixed between them. The scullery is fitted up with a sink, beneath which is a coal-bin of slate; a plate-rack at one end, drained by a slate slab into the sink, covers the entrance to the dust-shaft, which is enclosed by a balanced self-acting iron door. The dust-shaft leads into a closed depository under the stairs, and has a ventilating flue, carried up above the roof. The meat safe is ventilated through the hollow brickwork, aiad shelves are fixed over the doors. A dresser flap may be fixed against the partition. The sleeping apartments, being three in number, provide for that separation which, with a family, is so essential to morality and decency. Each has its distinct access, and a window into the open air; two have fireplaces. The children's bed-rooms contain 50 feet superficial each, and, opening out of the living room, an opportunity is afforded for the exercise of parental watchfulness, without the unwholesome crowding of the living room by its use as a sleeping apartment. The parents' bed-room, with a superficial area of about 100 feet, is entered through the scullery— an arrangement in many respects preferable to a direct approach from the living room, particularly in case of sickness. The recess in this room provides a closet for linen; and a shelf is carried over the door, with a rail fixed beneath it—a provision which is made in each of the other bedrooms. The water-closet is fitted up with a Staffordshire glazed basin, which is complete without any wood fittings, and supplied with water from a slate cistern in common of 160 gallons, placed on the roof over the party and staircase walls. The same pipes which carry away the rain water from the roof serve for the use of the closets. The peculiarities of the building as regards constructive arrangement, are, the exclusive use of hollow bricks for the walls and partitions (excepting the foundations, which are of ordinary brickwork), and the entire absence of timber in the floors and roof, which are formed with flat arches of hollow brickwork, rising from eight to nine inches, set in cement, and tied in by wrought-iron rods connected with cast-iron springers, which rest on the external walls, and bind the whole structure together; the building is thus rendered fireproof, and much less liable to decay than those of ordinary construction. The roof arching, which is levelled with concrete, and covered with patent metallic lava, secures the upper rooms from the liability to changes of temperature to which apartments next the roof are generally subject, and the transmission of sound, as well as the percolation of moisture, so common through ordinary floors, is effectually , impeded by the hollow brick arched floors. The external and main internal walls are of patent bonded ' brickwork, which has the important advantages of securing dryness and warmth, with economy of construction; another gteat benefit arising from the use of hollow bricks is, that where they are laid double, in parallel courses, without headers, as in the p a t en t bonded brickwork, the internal face of the wall is sufficiently smooth to render plastering unnecessary. In the present instance, where plastering has been resorted to, it is confined to . one Bide of a thin partition, or to partitions formed with bricks not intended for the situation in which they are used. In regard to some other parts of the brickwork it should also be observed that, owing to the erection of the building having been determined on late in the winter, many difficulties had to be contended with in obtaining a sufficient supply of hollow brick, and from accidental circumstances diappointments were experienced in reference to a coneicierable number; on which account the structure should be regarded rather as the pledge of future excellence in hollow-brick construction than as its full accomplishment. The glazed surface of the bricks used in the two upper floor living. rooms, and at the foot of the staircase, may be referred to as a specimen of what can be accomplished by the skilful adaptation of fitting materials, and as highly creditable to their maker. Specimens of glazed bricks of clay from the north of Devon are also exkibited. The advautages afforded by the use of hollow bricks in securing an effective system of insensible ventilation deserves particular notice. Fresh air is admitted from any suitable point of the exterior of the building to a chamber at the back of the living-room fireplace,. where being warmed it may be conducted to any convenient place of exit above the level at which the fresh air is admitted. Vitiated air may be conveyed either into the chimney flue or to any other suitable place of exit through the upper wall courses, perforated for this purpose, beneath the springing of the arch, or through the arch bricks themselves. Suitable air bricks and ventilators have been prepared with these express objects in view. Internally French plaster has been used as arying quicker, and having a harder surface than ordinary plaster. The floors, where cot of Portland cement, are aid with Staffordshire tiles, excepting to the right hand room first floor, which is of lava. The coping is in Portland cement. The external string courses and internal cornices are patent bonded bricks set in Portland cement with the splayed side outwards. The mode of fire-proof construction, and the general arrangement of the fittings, are such as have been used in the model houses built by the Society for Improving the Condition of the Labouring Classes, to which the architect of this building, Henry Roberts, Esq., F.S.A., also acted as honorary architect. In most parts of England the cost of four houses built on the plan of this model structure, with ordinary materials, and finished similar to the ground floor apartments, may be stated at 440/. to 480/., or from 110/. to 1 1201. for each tenement, contingent on the facilities for obtaining materials and the value of labour. Such dwellings, let at 3s. 6d. to 4s. a week would, after deducting ground. rent and taxes, afford a return of 7 per cent . , on the amount of outlay. Where hollow bricks are obtainable at a fair price their use ought to effect a reduction of about 25 per cent. on the cost of the brickwork, or equal on these four houses to about 40/. On Thursday a private view of this most interesting work of art was given to the press previous to the opening to the public. A globe having a surface of 10,000 feet is a novelty in geographical science, and the mere mechanical compos;.- tion of so gigantic a structure might have been expected to , place innumerable diffitulties in the way. Indeed, we learn from Mr. Wyld himself, that it is only after many failures that he has succeeded completely; and the Great. Model Globe will, probably, take its place in the public . estimation as one cf cur greatest national works of art. Mr. Wyld's globe differs from an ordinary' globe in one or two respects. It is not merely a spherical map, it is a model. The diversities of the earth's surface are modelled with the most minute accuracy, the scale being one incn to a mile vertically, and one inch to ten miles horizontally, the diameter being 60 feet. The spectator is supposed to be in the interior of the earth, and to look up to its concave nurface. The different countries are tinted, so as to represent the truth of nature as nearly as possible, and no writing or inscription of any kind disfigures the general appearance of the gigantic model. The visitor enters the model through the South Pacific Ocean, and the southern extremity of Africa is the firet land of which he gets a view. Four galleries, one above the other, enable the visitor to examine closely every portion of the model. It is intended to supply the visitors with a kind of index to the model, by arranging index maps in the different galleries. At present the shape and relation of the different parts of model alone explain the identity of the different countries. Ss exact and minutely accurate, however, is the delineation, that the visitor, moderately educated in geographical science, can see at once the places for which he is in search. To quote Mr. Wyld's interesting description : "By vareing the scale, in a due proportion, the elevated portions of the globe are made apparent to the eye, and heights and lowlands of our little island are shown, down to+ the smallest hills and the narrowest marshes. Wherever it , was practicable the hills have been modelled from the latest surreys. In our own country, the Ordnance Survey has been , followed. The northern hemisphere being well known, is very fully modelled. Amongst other portions, England, - Ireland, and eiwitzerland may be especially referred to, for ' the elaborate minuteness with which they are detailed. The knots and chains of hills in the Alps, and the springs of the Danube, the Rhine, and the Po, will also be found worthy of minute investigation, as exhibiting the wondrous works of the Almighty. Indeed, wherever the eye rest; something will ba found to awaken the interest and to raise the feelings of even the most thoughtless. "That nothing may tend to divert the attention teom the natural appearances which the earth's surface presentee there is no writing upon the Model. The sea is coloured blue, and the land of as natural a tint as possible. The great Mcetel teaches what no map can teach—the earth's form as a whole, its general aspect, the relative quantities and Positions of its several parts, the bearings of its hills, the flow of its great; waters, and the seats of its rich dales and its barren wastes.. Here the intending emigrant may trace out his path over thee great deep, and find out the spot on which his kinsmen have settled themselves on the shores of New England, or amidst the goldbearing mountains of California, the wilderness of South Africa, or the great plains of Australia. "The top of the globe is made the north pole, and the bottom the south pole, without regard being paid to what ie known as the inclination of the ecliptic." Wyld's work is something more than a mere exhibition for amusement. It is probably the most useful of all the metropolitan exhibitions. The mere mechanical skill which could build out of thousands of plaster blocks a complete arid accurate model of the earth's surface, is no ordinary , ' triumph; but no dencription can convey an adequate idea of the Effect to the spectator of Mr. Wyld's model. No exhibition in London will secure more numerous nor, we venture to predict, more int eres t e d v i s it ors than dr. Wyld's , magnificent model. THE NAVY.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Each succeeding week attests the popularity of the Great Exhibition. With few and rare Sibthorpian exceptions, the words of Mr. Cobden are receiving the fullest verification; The Great Exhibition satisfies the expectations of everyone.” It is no nine days’ wonder ; it is no mere fashionable lounge ; but really and truly a great national gathering, and jubilee of the industry of the world. On Thursday, according to the police returns, 54,669 persons visited the Crystal Palace. The sum taken in shillings at the doors was £2379 7s. There were there 47,587 people who paid for entering, season ticket holders. The shilling visitors for the most part remain a much shorter time in the building than their fashionable predecessors. No doubt this is to be attributed to the pressure of domestic duties upon the women, and the demands of their daily toil upon the men, rendering very considerable numbers of this class unable to command the whole day for the purposes of sight-seeing. To a considerable extent, therefore, there is a constant efflux as well as influx, thus relieving the interior of the building from much of the greater pressure due to the augmented numbers. Still the numbers simultaneously in the building on Thursday were, toward noon particularly, very great. The class who now come to see the Exhibition remain a shorter time, notwithstanding which the utmost order and propriety of conduct prevailed, nor was it necessary for the police to interfere, except at one or two of the more attractive points, in preventing an undue accumulation of visitors. The Queen and her illustrious guests came to the building at their usual early hour, and remained for some time, as on a former occasion, watching with curiosity and interest the influx of people when the doors were opened. Among the vast assemblage of Thursday might be observed numbers of workmen from Mr. Cubitt’s and other large establishments of the metropolis. In most of these, arrangements have very thoughtfully and properly been made for allowing the men to see the wonders of the Crystal Palace. Friday last was the first half-crown day. It was not anticipated that the number of visitors would be great, nor was it so, but the result exceeded the calculations made, and the receipts at the doors were £2,839 Bs. The police returns represent that 30,345 persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and the royal family continued their inspection in the morning, the people inside conducting themselves with marked propriety. During her last two visits, the Queen has taken particular notice of several branches of national industry, the contributors to which wrill feel flattered by such attention. She examined closely the specimens of Paisley shawls, and the needlework of the Scotch and Irish peasantry. Some embroidered vests from Belfast, exhibited by Mr. M’Gee, especially attracted her; and the collection of embroideries by Salomons and Sons was also much admired by her. Her Majesty looked over with great care and interest the display of Lyons silks, and the muslins and printed fabrics of Mulhausen. Friday was remarkable for an unexpected rise in the sale of season tickets; the receipts from this source amounted to 19s. The Times observes, “It is now quite clear that from that quarter the finance of the Commission can henceforth derive no material aid unless the present scale of prices is lowered. Whether it is desirable that a reduction should take place must depend on a variety of contingencies which the Commission are alone able to estimate properly: but if there be valid impediment to a new issue of season tickets at a smaller charge, we do not see why such boon to the public, and such a source of revenue, should any longer be withheld.” Saturday last was the first five-shilling day at the Exhibition since the reduction of prices. Many persons, considering that on the previous Saturday more than 20,000 persons had been eager to visit the Crystal Palace upon the same terms, had looked for a large attendance on that day. But never since the Ist of May have so few persons entered the building as on Saturday last. Immediately after the opening of the doors at 12 o’clock, great number of season ticket holders entered the building, soon to be lost in its vast avenues and compartments innumerable, and these were followed by 7,086 visitors paying the admission fee of the day. The paucity of attendance by the upper classes on a day which would be naturally attractive to them, is explained by the fact that her Majesty’s birth-day was being kept, and that in commemoration of the event various special fetes and festivals were announced. The Queen’s drawing-room drew out large numbers of the fashionable visitors to the Crystal Palace : then again, there was a magnificent Floral Display, and also a Grand Review at Woolwich. At four o’clock on Saturday afternoon, Mr. Best repeated, on Willis’s Great Organ, his performance of selections from Mendelssohn, Handel, and Bach. The highly agreeable effect produced in the French department of the Exhibition by the suspension of flags from the gal - leries facing the main avenue, has suggested to the royal commissioners the propriety of a similar decoration on the British side. It proposed that each corporate town exhibiting should send a banner bearing its anns, not too costly, yet sufficiently handsome to be worth preserving in its town hall or other public place as a memorial of the great industrial event. Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Bradford, and Huddersfield, have ordered their several flags, which are to be of silk, the arms painted on both sides, feet three inches long, by 4 feet inches wide, attached to a blue staff', with gilt spear head. On Monday Her Majesty and the Royal visitors went to the Crystal Palace at 9 o’clock, some 400 or 500 exhibitors having been formally requested to be present. The portion of the Exhibition marked out for inspection was the south gallery on the west side of the transept. Hitherto the Royal visit’s have been made in a very private manner, and, although the principal contributors were made aware that the Queen was coming, no official announcement of the fact was made to them as body. But as Her Majesty now wished to bestow a more distinctive mark of honour upon the Exhibitors, a formal command was issued for their attendance. To nearly all, it was an extraordinary event to brought face to face with the Royalty of England. Lips and tongues, that before ordinary mortals ’•'"’.ld run freely on in the labours of explanation, become confused and falter when the Queen asks what they have to show. There were many manifestations of that kind on Monday, and according to the Times, one distinguished contributor, a manufacturer of warlike weapons, too, fainted under the excitement. Her Majesty began with the chymicals, in which department she especially admired the contributions of Pontifex and Wood. Her attention was also drawn to the display of preserved meats, and particularly what related to the supply of the navy. She made particular inquiries into the regulations adopted for ascertaining that this supply was good and proper for the use of the sailors. The most important feature of this survey, was the illustration of his ingenious process in the conversion of flax fibre into a substitute for cotton by the Chevalier Claussen. Her Majesty’s attention was particularly drawn to the process for the solidification of milk, and to the display of preserved fruits by Fortnum and Mason. She remained for two hours in the building, and during her stay conversed in the most affable manner with a great number of the exhibitors. The return of Skeggs and Burchmore to St. Albans, from which owing to their visit to Boulogne, they had been absent since April last, when they absconded from the Parliamentary Committee, has created some little sensation in that locality. It appears that after being discharged from the Mansionhouse they repaired to _the Great Northern Railway, and arrived in St. Albans the same evening, where they took up their quarters at the George Hotel. It is said they feign forgetfulness on all matters connected with local and electioneering affairs, and appear to prefer answering all questions and kind inquiries in French, with their proficiency in which they edify their fellow-townsmen. It has been ascertained with considerable certainty that Waggett has emigrated to New York, one of the local police at Dieppe having informed Forester that he saw him embark on board for that purpose. Hayward is still understood to be in France, and Edwards, who it will be remembered was committed to the custody of the Sergeant-at-Arms, on being liberated from New• gate on the day of the prorogation of Parliament, returned to his family at St. Albans, after a period of four months' confinement. Being committed for a misdemeanour of what, - 'in prison parlance, is called a misdemeanour of the first class, he was allowed in Newgate to have what he liked, and looked none the worse on the day of his discharge when the formal authority of the Speaker was issued for the purpose. It is said that, although the proclamation for the apprehension of these men became a dead letter on the adjournment of the House of Commons, whose power over the delinquents also expired, that the House of Lords, whose constitutional powers do not decline with the close of the session, have the power, the St. Albans Bribery Commission Bill having been, before them, to detain and commit the parties for contempt and absconding. Though the proclamation of reward for the capture of the absent witnesses is alleged only to run during the period of the session, the proclamation itself makes no mention of this, however that might, so to speak, be the reasonable intendment. By some it is thought that the reward is legally recoverable, but if so, as the proclamation was royal, and as a subject cannot bring an action against the Queen, the question would have to be raised by what is called a petition of right. The entire transaction since April last has been most cleverly " clandestined " by the secret agencies behind the scenes, and the cost is supposed to have been considerable. THE SLAVES OF ROME. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The building of the Exhibition may now be considered as completed, and the work of decoration and fitting up is being carried on with vigour. A very large number of exhibitors attend daily at the offices of the contractors to give their orders for the counters and glass cases which they may require. It has been estimated that the cost of counters and fittings for the whole building will not be less than £60.000. The task of pleasing the tastes an fancies of every exhibitor, and of completing the enormous amount of work required, is one which would overwhelm many persons and would alone be sufficient to prevent the opening of the Exhibition at the appointed time. The same energy and enterprise, however, which hasraised the building for the Exhibition in so incredibly a short space of time will, we are confident, complete by the required time the minor details of the work. During the last week the laying down of the mains and water-pipes in the building has been completed. They are always charged with water, and evtry possible precaution has been taken to prevent any accident from fire. The decoration of the transept is completed, and now thtt the greater part of the scaffolding is removed, the effect of the system of colour adopted may be seen to advantage.

Tin FIRST CONTRIBUTION.—In the midst of all these preparations, and with the actual realization of the Exhibition so close at hand, the public will be interested to know what enterprising person has been first upon the boards of the Crystal Palace in the character of contributor. All of a sudden the glazing of about 1,000 square feet gave way, but not in the usual way when glass is blown in, for it rather seemed to be the effect of an eddy than of a direct current of air. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. COMPREHENSIVE VIEW OF THE CONTENTS OF THE CRYSTAL PALACE. A comprehensive view of the vast collection of objects in Hyde-park is what the public stand most in need of. When they have thoroughly mastered the disposition and arrangement of the building, when they know in which direction to go in search of Austrian or American products, and where the different branches of our native industry are represented, they will still find themselves at sea in endeavouring to form a just conception of the whole display, in distinguishing the characteristic features of each part, and storing their minds with definite ideas of the industrial attributes developed at this gathering of nations. When a man is introduced to a number of strangers, his first instinctive tendency, after examining their respective appearances so as to distinguish them again, is to ask himself and study attentively what tendencies of the intellect or what traits of the heart he can gather from the expression of each countenance. Now, this process is exactly what the public are at present endeavouring to go through within the transparent walls of the building in Hyde-park. They have been presented there to the industries of all nations. They find each country preserving the individuality of her own collection. They can go to one portion of the building and see France, to another and see Germany, and so on round this family s eirele of the globe for the first time in man's history formed. Well, then, the question arises, what are they all like? In no fairer or truer mirror can national characters be represented than in their industrial products. Other pictures may deceive, but this must tell the truth. The course of events, guided as it is by a higher power than man's, does not always illustrate the moral and social attributes of communities. Not so the fruits of labour—the quality and description of material which engross the toil, supply the demand, and engage the tastes and predilections of a people. These tell their story as faithfully as the actions or the physiognomy of an individual indicate his nature, and by them, thus considered, we hope to help the public by a new path and under a fresh light through the marvels of the Great Exhibition. THE BIIITISIT SIDE. Let us commence at home, and see what appearance this island of ours puts on at the peaceful reunion of nations. Is it Britannia, with her trident and plumed helmet and the lion recumbent at her feet, or John Bull's portly form, carrying weight in every limb, and determination, not unmingled with prejudice, from the crown of his broad-brimmed hat to the soles of his top-boots? Far otherwise. Some traces of those popular types of our nationality may indeed be traced, but England has greatly changed. Her genius is mechanism, her master spirit the civil engineer, her tendencies to relieve labour from its drudgery, and delegate to iron, to steam, and to the other powers of the inanimate world, as much as possible of the burden of toil. If you doubt this, go and look at the great department of machinery in the Crystal Palace; watch that vast collection of interesting objects, every portion of which lightens immeasurably the burden of life and releases hundreds of hands from the most irksome forms of industry. You will there see how mechanism is extending her dominion over the whole empire of labour; how she rises in textile fabrics to the manufacture of the most delicate and intricate lace; how from wood she aspires to fashion iron into the most exact proportions; how, with steam as her handmaid, she works the printing press and navigates the ocean, and outruns the swiftest animal in her course. Turn into the agricultural implement department, and you will find everything now done by machinery. By it the farmer not only sows and reaps ' but he manures and. hoes. By it he thrashes out and grinds his corn and prepares the food for his cattle. He can even drain by machinery, and it is difficult now to find a branch of his business into which it does not largely enter. In our manufactures tho mechanical genius of the country reigns supreme. These beautiful fabrics are nearly all the evidences of its power. Soft goods and hardware are equally indebted to it, and in its presence the unaided efforts of handicraftsmen appear small and insignificant indeed. It travels everywhere and invades every compartment, even that of the fine arts, in the court dedicated to which some of the most conspicuous contributions are specimens of printing in oil, and attempts to reproduce by mechanical means the sentiment and inspiration of the painter. Yet we are not altogether abandoned to this power—this Frankenstein which we have created, and which is dragging us we know not whither. The mediteval court and its crowds of visitors, and its gaudy embellishments, still draw us back to days when ornament was not inseparably wedded to usefulness, or when at least, if that pact was completed, she was not acknowledged to be the "weaker vessel.' We have some specimens of sculpture, such as those from the hands of Gibson, APDowall, and others, not unworthy of" art." The two colossal statues of the Scots have about them a certain solemn and massive grandeur which some minds will not unnaturally associate with the characteristics of the national intellect. These and other points will press upon the mind of an attentive observer; yet our main hope for the creation of the beautiful rests still in the adaptability of that power by which as a nation we labour and produce. Through multiplied evidences of neglected taste, and violations of harmony in colour and design that must shock many of our visitors, the traces a better and purer style of national industry begin to be discernible. Even our mechanical tendencies are yielding to the higher inspirations of the fancy, or perhaps we should say, are subjecting the admiration to their stupendous efforts. Witness, in illustration of this, the great interior of the Crystal Palace itself, that surprising and splendid piece of mechanism, wherein the civil engineer has displaced the architect and iron and glass been substituted for bricks and mortar. Of our colonial possessions visitors will gather at tho Exhibition an interesting but imperfect impression. They will see in that preponderance of raw produce the evidences of infant societies still struggling forward to a larger industrial development. The philosophic mind will be attracted by the advantages which the rising communities that have swarmed from our shores to settle in distant scenes possess—how science and education help them to investigate the natural resources of the new regions which they occupy—how, having tilled the virgin soils of Australia or Canada with the agncultural knowledge of the mother country, they at length send home the fruits of their labour to be absorbed by our markets. We enter the Indian collection, and examine thoughtfully the products of our empire in the East. What do they tell us? Those jewels, that rich display of mineral and vegetable produce, those shawls and carpets in which the harmony of colours is so admirably represented; filigree work in silver and gold, brocaded stuffs, curiously executed carvings, rude models of machinery, musical instruments, arms, elephant naval architecture —how suggestive the y trappings, and what stories they tell. H ere are ey a ll are, gathered together the trophies of ancient civilization and arts, marvellously rried down to our own time. H ero may b e studied the industrial habits of nations preserved through centuries without cha or mogress, yet still wonderful an d magnificent in the eyes of modern labour. Look at those alabastar chai rs , how r e gal they appear, how fitly they represent a country wher e :any dynasties conquered and flourished and wore overcome before the British sway was established over its dusky populations. Nearly every thing in that collecti on w hi ch is the work of man's bands indicates a vast expenditure of time for its production and a great display of taste. Yet it is nearly all ornamental, rather than useful, in its character. Whenever the really useful arts appear, rudeness of material and design are visible. The following are some of the most recent additions to the Exhibition :—Three enormous elephant tusks, considered by scientific men to be the finest specimens of the kind ever seen in this country. They are the property of an English gentleman who resided in Southern Africa for a number of years, and are justly denominated the Mammoth tusks—their dimensions being 8 feet 6 inches each in length, and 22 inches in circumference, and their weight 164 lbs. each. They arrived the other day by the Bosphorus steamer from the Cape of Good Hope, and were obtained in the immediate vicinity of the great lake lately discovered in Southern Africa. To the Indian department has just been added a magnificent oil painting, 6 feet long by 4 feet, in a massive gold frame. The subject is the Grand Mosque at Beejapoore ; Ibrahim Adleshan, the fifth King of Beejapoore, and his attendants, forming a group of 600 persons, are seen in their ornamental costumes, proceeding to morning prayers. In front of the mosque is depicted a large tank, containing a water fountain, at which the Mahometans are seen performing their ablutions previous to entering the mosque. In the avenue (not far from the crystal fountain) is added a large glass case, containing a piece of marble sculptured by an his]; lady, the subject of which is "A Scene at a Northern Irish Fair." It pourtrays thirty-one characters of the various classes who attend such places, from the rollicking Irish boy, to his grandmother, Mrs. Biddy Brallagan, all dancing to the violin of Mr. Murphy, who is seen perched up in the corner on an Irish cask of poteen, which has been done due honour to on this eventful fair day. From the satisfaction evinced by all visitors on viewing this ingenious specimen, we can only regret that it was not sent in at a much earlier period. To the Irish Society of Dublin the public are indebted for this importation. Two splendid specimens of lead-ore from Western Australia, weighing three cwt. each, are well worthy of inspection by those interested in such matters. We may also allude to an extraordinary lock, the workmanship of a poor blacksmith, and of which he affirms that it is impossible to pick it or to model the key. Not being in a position to stake any money against Mr. Hobbs, he merely wishes that that gentleman should be permitted by the Executive Committee to execute his ingenuity in picking the said lock, which may be seen in class 22. The key forms a square cross, containing eight secret wards. The lock has been inspected by competent judges, and has received their approval. WHIT -MONDAY AT THE EXHIBITION.—A cloudy morning; symptomatic of rain, ushered in the great holiday, Whit-Monday ; but it could not damp or depress, in the minds of the people, the pleasure-seeking spirit of the day. great western road gave signs from an early hour that the Crystal Palace had a rival in the one at Hampton, for huge and well-filled vans were seen proceeding to the latter, early in the day. The happy-looking persons who Were seated in the said vans had each subscribed, we understand, 2d., or some such small sum weekly, for some weeks back, in order to enjoy the pleasure of a trip to Hampton- Court; and throughout the season, we learn, every Monday exhibits a similar series of those vehicles carrying those subscribers whose "turn" it is for that day to take advan tage of the" People's Hampton Court Mutual Conveyance Company." From a people so prudent and innocent in their pursuit of pleasure no evil could be apprehended, even no Whit-Monday, on account of their admission to the Crystal Palace. On Friday a very crowded meeting of the inhabitants of St. Margaret's and St. John's, Westminster, was held in the vestry-room for the purpose of making a poor-rate for the ensuing year. Mr. Burridge was in the chair. The chairman stated that a sum of about £28,490 would be required for the purpose, and that a rate of 2s. in. the pound would leave a surplus of about £3OO. Mr. Sherlock wished to know if the amount asked for included any rating of the Crystal Palace. Mr. Rogers, the vestry clerk, replied that it did not. Mr. Bigg, one of the overseers, said the matter was attended with a great deal of difficulty. They had seen the commissioners on the subject, and had been received most courteously, but they could obtain no definite answer. They had, however, subsequently had a letter from Mr. Maule, the solicitor to the Treasury, stating, in effect, that the Exhibition was not rateable to the poor-rate, and that the commissioners could not be held responsible for it. The overseers had had counsel's opinion, and that was that the Exhibition was not liable to the poor-rate. Mr. Clark wished to know if the parties who sold refreshments were not rateable? The vestry clerk said unquestionably they were, if it could be pros ed theirs was a beneficial occupation, by deriving profit from what they sold—a very difficult thing to establish. He was satisfied that, if the Crystal Palace was rated, they should get into litigation, in which half the rate would be expended, even if they succeeded, but they might get nothing. Mr. Bigg observed there was another element in the matter, which ought not to be overlooked. It would bring great obloquy on the parish if this rate were persisted in, more especially on the officers who enforced it. It would, besides, lead to enormous law costs. Standing still in the gallery, a little close observation will satisfy the curious that the flooring upon which he stands vibrates under his feet, that the solid iron pillar which he grasps trembles in its firmlyrooted base—that the long range of cases and counters are all in motion, the groups of statuary, the massive iron and bronze candelabra, and the ponderous trophies of timber or metal, as well as the lighter structures of silk or damask, or lace, placed on the flooring, or suerended from the girders, 'are kept in agitation by some hidden but powerful agency.
