Dr. Cox preached an eloquent and impressive sermon to Young Men, in connexion with the Young Men's Baptist Missionary Association, at the close of which he gave his hearers the following pract!cal can. tions:— " Here I should close the present discourse, were it not for the remarkable character of this day, which seems to require at least a passing notice. Such a building as the Crystal Palace has never before been erected in this country, opened to-day with so much pomp, and collecting together, as by an irresistible attraction, specimens unrivalled, if not unnumbered, of the industry, ingenuity, and commercial zeal of the nations, and the living representatives almost of the whole earth's motley population. " If, since the world was created, any period deserved to be called age of progression, it is surely the present. Not that other times have not been distinguished by events or movements that have conduced to the improvement of mankind,—not that the moral and politica; heavens have never before been brilliant with the productions of genius, or the devices of benevolence. Looking along the surface of history, we find Hesiod, Homer, and Virgil, at once stimulating and gratifying the imagination of man by the beauty and the power of immortal verse,'—the writers of Greece and Rome generally pouring the tide of civilization into the barbaric regions of the earth,—au Archimedes penetrating with the keenest intelligence the recesses of unexplored knowledge, and giving an impulse to the researches of then unborn generations,—a Galileo, a Kepler, and a Newton, treading the high paths of science, and beckoning the nations to contemplate the wonders of God's creation, and pay their devout homage to the All-wise in his glorious temple, —a Luther rescuing essential truth from its deep interment in the accumulated superstitions of centuries, and proclaiming a Reformation of religion to the world,—a Howard illuminating the darkness and cheering the solitude of dungeons, and performing, with untiring zeal and self-denial, the circumnavigation of charity ;'- -these, and a thousand others, in different spheres of action and at different times, have contributed to advance the interests and elevate the character of the human race. But their efforts have been comparatively unsustained and uncombined ; they have affected only small portions of the society in which they lived, while the mass remained inert, ignorant, and unconcerned about progress. Their influence was not diffusive or extensive. They did not quicken into life and activity the sleepy age. Others did not move on with them, nor were aroused to inquiry, emulation, and moral daring. They mostly shone as solitary stars while they lived, and, when they died, were left alone in their glory.' Whenever there was progress, it was progress in one direction only, and the progress of a few. There was little or no general impulse. The stream of existence flowed on, and they resembled sparkles on its surface, that reflected beau- I tiful colours for a moment, arid then vanished away. " It is observable, in tracing the history of human development, that eminently important discoveries or projects have originated in individual minds, and in those minds, perhaps, in an accidental or momentary thought. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The value of the industrial, scientific, and artistic operations is in no branch of manufacture so marked in regard to the material to be acted upon as in that of porcelain. The recent introduction of what is termed Parian china has effected almost a revolution in the manufacture, and it is mainly due to the skill and enterprise of two firms, Messrs. Copeland, and Minton and Co. We understand that the former firm was the first to solve the problem of its applicability under judicious treatment; not that in this respect Messrs. Minton's claim is one whit the less for the skill, talent, and enterprise with which, from the beginning, they entered into the race for excellence; and in all the examples shown by these two houses we have the result of the great amount of experience, artistic knowledge, and manufacturing tact which their great past experience has given them. In Messrs. Minton's display of Parian there is little left for the most fastidious to wish; and, in spite of our desire to see the application of it kept within those legitimate bounds as to size and use, to which its character best fits it, we are compelled to admire the beauty of the renaissance chimneypiece, because the design has been so thoroughly adapted in all its parts to the requirements of the material. The caryatides are spirited and expressive, the ornaments appropriate and graceful, and the whole well fitted together. The painted porcelain panels, too, add to the effect in no mean degree. On the shelf of this chimney-piece are three novelties in statuettes. The Flora is rather overstrained in pose, though there are excellent points; and of the pair of the zon and the Warrior, we are inclined somewhat to question the taste of the former, though the execution and spirit are very admirable. In both there is an enormous amount of energy and power. A wine-cooler, decorated with cleverly designed incidents of the chase in which the animals are modelled with great accuracy, the figures of the controlling sportsmen, or boys en costume, being very spirited, is an excellent example. The vine, as festooned around the whole, is charmingly treated, and the crowning group of figures, with an emblematic barrel of Bacchanalian dimensions, is original and pleasing. The heads of the boar and fox are very finely executed. There is a second example of this piece in which gilding is used as a means of decorating certain salient points, but to our mind the Parian in all its integrity is the best. Another work in Parian is a centre-piece, with fine emblematic figures of the seasons, very beautifully treated, the figures being well designed and modelled, the pose of the " Winter" being very grand, and the treatment broad. Ia colour, the light blue, gold, and Parian produce a most harmonious result. In statuettes, the reduced copy of Power's " Greek Slave" deserves marked attention for the excellent manner in which the expression and sentiment of the original has been preserved. This, however, is only one out of many which either have been or are destined to be very popular. "The Babes in the Wood," after John Bell, and a statuette of the late Sir Robert Peel, possess excellent points, though widely differing; and a group of cupids with a goat, or rather two treatments of the same subject, forming a pair, are remarkable for excellence of drawing, modelling, and the florid character of the treatment. In short, nearly all the chefs d'ouvre of our ancient and modern sculptors have been reproduced in the most successful manner. When the difficulties of the process are considered, the skill by which portraits and likeness are preserved appears almost marvellous. The Parian cast, although a perfect Inc simile on a reduced scale of the original watue, a group, when placed in the furnace shrinks considerably, and sometimes very unequally, so that many of the casts are destroyed, being perfectly useless. In Messrs. Copeland's collection, the Parian statuette of "Sappho," from the original by Theed, in the possession of his Royal Highness Prince Albert, strikes from itssize, being probably the largest figure yet produced in the material: but for that very reason we think it is not so covetable as many of the higher class statuettes, out of the forty examples exhibited by this house. The hands and feet seem out of proportion to the head. This may be a fault of the original, but it is quite as likely to arise from, or be exaggerated by, unequal tiring, which we think a fatal objection to attempting large works of this kind. Under any circumstances, the shrinkage of a material so variable in this respect as Parian, is likely to be more regular in a statuette of sixteen inches high, than in one of thirty-five inches; for when it is remembered that this shrinkage invariably reaches one-sixth, the calculation of the proportion to fairly accomplish a thoroughly good work, even when small, is no indifferent item in the skill employed in producing the result. The " Ino and Bacchus" of Foley has been admirably reduced, and, with an appropriate pedestal, stands out with peculiar grace and fitness. This is a beautiful subject for the crowning ornament of a decorated clock, and, with suitable bronze adjuncts, would look even better than it does as a single work. The '• Dancing Girl reposing," by Marshall, is very ch4rMin:g; and the head of a young fawn, draining the "Last Drop"- - - the title of the work—from. v, dri-Ai ng vessel, is admirable. The extremities of the figure, however, have a "wooden" look. Durham's elegant bust of "Jenny bind" is, to our minds, the best in Pariau yet published. Many of the other examples are tolerably well known to our readers, by occasional illustrations either from the originals or from the Parian reductions. Probably the greatest novelty, certainly in the Parian, is the " Tripod Flowerstand." The design is classic and appropriate; it is beautifully modelled, and the difficulty of uniting the parts has been well got over. The example in terracotta is also very meritorious. The collection in the north-west gallery is so extensive that it would be utterly impossible to notice a tithe of them, but we cannot conclude our notice of the contributions from the Staffordshire potteries without calling attention to the very admirable di , play of door furniture in china, by Mr. W. S. Kennedy, of Burslem. Thus we have finger-plates, door-handles, paterx for bell-pulls, &e., many of them very excellent in design and execution, and of all styles and colours. Nor should a cleverly reduced model of the chaste bust usually known as " Clytia," exectsted in terracotta, and exnibited by James Marsh, of Longport, be overlooked, and still less the wineecooler, also in terracotta, by the same youth, who is, we understand, a pupil of the Hanley School of Design, in which these works were executed. The latter example is clever in design, and the chimer are spiritedly modelled. We were somewhat surprised to find, in an obscure corner of the agricultural department, a machine which has certainly little in common with the rougher operations of husbandry. It is a jacquard loom, fitted up by Messrs. Campbell, Harrison, and Lloyd, of Spitalfields, showing the method of weaving brocaded silk ; and in the loom is a specimen of black brocade of a very elegant pattern, similar to that exhibited in another part of the building by Messrs. Lewis and Allenby, of Regent-street. The niacniue is of the most complicated appearance, requiring 23,880 cards to complete the pattern, and no less than 80 or 90 shuttles are employed in the weaving. It is worked by two silk weavers, and would probably attract as much attention as Atkinson's poplin machine, if its whereabouts was better known to the visitors. One of the curiosities of weaving, as exhibiting, by contrast, the great improvement that has taken place in this department of manufacture, will be found on the stall of one of the Irish linen manufacturers, whose name we cannot call to mind. It is a Royal table-cloth, 135 years old, manufactured at Waringetown, cour.ty Down, Ireland. It is the coronation cloth made for George L, and contains portraits of the bishops, officers of state, dukes, barons, collate. &c., who officiated at the ceremonial. The King himself is represented in his coronation robes, seated on his throne; and notwithstanding the long period that has elapsed since it was made, the fibre of the cloth is still strong, and the damasking fairly executed. DISASTROUS ACCIDENT AT KENSINGTON.—On Saturday morning an accident of a very lamentable nature took place at Kensington, which has already resulted in the death of one man, while two others and three lads have been seriously injured. The accident occurred at some new buildings in that part of Kensington known ae the " New Town,' on the south side of the great western road, and close to the turnpike grate. About eighteen months since the old Kensington workhouse, which stood on the eastaide of the Gloucester-road, leading to the old Brompton-road, was vacated by the inmates, who were removed to the new workhouse, and a lease of the ground was taken by Mr. Inderwick, of Leicester-square, who immediately proceeded to pull down the old building, and laid one a square of firstclass houses upon the site. One side of this new square is already finished, although not yet inhabited, and the carcases of the houses on the opposite side are built up to the height of four stones above the basement, and roofed. It was on this side of the square, formed of six houses joined together, and two larger projecting ones at eith er end, that the accident occurred. A number of plasterers were employed in putting up a massive projecting cornice between the third and fourth stories of the central houses, and commenced their work on Saturday morning at the usual hour, when everything appeared to be in the same state of security as it was left on the previous evening. The men continued working on the top tier of the scaffolding, a height of between forty and fitly feet from the ground, till about twenty minutes to eight o'clock, when suddenly the whole of the cornice work of four of the houses gave way, and falling upon the scaffolding with great force, precipitated the whole to the ground, with the persons at work thereon. The loud crash was heard at a great distance. All the men employed upon the works immediately hastened to the "ambitonce of the unfortunate suffer, re, who were buried under the broken scaffolding and portions of the parapet wall, which had also given way. The centre of the cornice was composed of large fiat stones, one end of which was built into the front wall, and all these had broken short off, and come down. Three men and three stout lads, who were serving the plasterers with cement, were found partly co• vend by the stones and rubbish, five of whom were promptly extricated, and conveyed in cabs to St. George's Hospital. The sixth sufferer, who when carried out rip , peared to be in a lifeless state, was attended by Mr. Abraham, a surgeon residing close to the spot, and who had hastened there on hearing the crash, but he was found to be quite dead, the lower limbs being broken, and there being also a serious fracture of the skull. The body was shortly afterwards conveyed to the dead house of the New Kensington Workhouse, where it awaits the coroner's inquest. On inspecting the buildings from which the cornice has fallen, the remaining portions of the flat stones were found to be still embedded in the wall, the exterior portion, being much the greater part, and which supported the whole weight of the cement, having broken off close to the wall. The scaffolding, which has apparently fallen outwards, still remains supported by the firmly bound cords, although some of the upright poles base been snapped asunder at different lengths. The names of the sufferers are :—Robert WoodWg, about 25 years of age (killed) ; Dennis Hurley, 28 • Daniel Delany, 28 ; Dennis Earley, 15; John Calaghan;l4 ; and Michael Gorman, 14. On inquiring at the hospital on Saturday we were informed that all the injured persons were progressing favourably. One of the men has had the breast-bone broken, and one of the lads has had his back severely strained ; the other injuries are principally severe contusions. Many rumours are afloat in the neighbourhood as to the cause of the accident, which of course must be strictly investigated at the inquest. Ilad the accident occurred only 20 minutes later in the day, there would have been no serious result, as the men would have left for breakfast.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. An cutline of the proceedings at the cose of the Exhibition was given in our last by telegraph, but the following further details will be read with interest:-The reserved seats were occupied by a numerous and distinguished company, among whom, and close to the platform, were Lord John Russell, Sir Charles Wood. the Earl of Carlisle, Sir George Grey, Mr La- bouchere, the Right Ron. Fox Maule, and other members of the Government. Several of the diplomatic corps were also present, and among them the American, Prussian, and Bel- gi:n Ministers. Beyond the limits of the transept, the nave cast and west for a considerable way was crowded with spec- tators, and the galleries commanding a view of the central point almost as far as the eye could reach. About 25,000 in all were present. Precisely at twelve o'elock the Royal Commission, headed by the Executive Committee, moved in a species of procession from their apartments to the platform. They were accom- panied by the Bishop of London in his robes, and on their appearance the immense assembly rose and welcomed them with loud cheers, while the choir performed the first verse of the National Anthem. Having taken their seats, Viscount Canning, on behalf of the juries, rose and read the following report of their proceedings:- "Having had the honour of acting as President of the Coun- cil of Chairmen of the Juries, it falls to me to lay before your Royal Highness and Her Msjiesty's Commissioners the reports of the several juries upon the subjects submitted to them for examination, and the names of the exhibitors whom they have judged entitled to rewards. "In doing so, it will be convenient that I should state brief- ly the principle upon which, by the authority of lier MUajesty's Commissioners, the juries wkereconstituted " The various subjects included in the Exhibition -were di- vided, in the first instance, into thirty classes. Of these, two were subsequently found to embrace fields of action too large for single juries, and were therefore divided into sub-juries. This increased the number of acting juries to thirty-four. "Each of these :34 juries consisted of an equal number of British subjects and of foreigners. The British jurors were se- lected by "Her Majesty's Comlmissioners from lists furnished by the local committees of various towns, each town being invited to recommend persons of sklill and information in the manufac- tures or produce for which it is remarkable. The foreign jurors were appointed by authorities in their own countries, in such relative proportion amongst themselves as was agreed upon by the Foreign Commissioners sent here to represent their respec- tive Governments. "In the event of the jury finding themselves deficient in technical knowledge of any article submitted to them, they were empowered to call in the aid of associates. These associ- ates, who acted as advisers only, without a vote, but whose services were of the greatest value. were selected either from the jurymen of other classes, or from the lists of persons who had been recommended as jurors, but who had not been per- manently appointed to any jury. " Each jury was superintended by a chairman, chosen from its numbers bv Her Majesty's Commissioners. The deputy- chairman and the reporter were elected by the jurors them- selves. "'Such was the constitution of the thirty-four juries taken sinaly. They did not. however, act independently of each otlhr, inasmuch as they were associated into six groups, each group consisting of such juries as had to deal with subjects in somne degree of kindred nature ; and before any decision of a jury could be considered as final it was required that it should be brought before the assembled group of which that jury formed a part, and that it should be approved by them. The chief object of this provision was, that none of the many foreign nations taking part in the Exhibition should in- cur the risk of seeing its interests overlooked or neglected from the accident (an unavoidable one in many instances) of its being unrepresented in any particular jury. Each group of juries received the assistance of a deputy- comnmissioner and of a special commissioner, appointed by Her Majesty's Commisaioners, to record its proceedings. to fmrnish information respecting the arrangements of the Exhibition, and otherwise to titcilisato the labours of the juries composing the group. "1 It was further determined by Her 'Majesty's Commission- ers that the chairmen of the juries, consisting of British sub- jects and of foreigners in equal numbers, should be formed in- to a council, and that the duties of the council should be to de- termine the conditions upon which, in accordance with certain general principles previously laid down by Her Majesty's Commissioners, the different prizes should be awarded; to frame rules to guide the working of the juries; and to se- cure, as far as possible, uniformity in the result of their pro- ceedtugs. These ure the most important features of the system upots wVhich the jurors foLund themselves organized. ITvill nowv refer briefly to their course of action. 'i The Council of Chairmen, in proceeding to the discharge of their duties, were met at the outset by a serious difficulty. Her Mejesty's Commissioners had expressed themselves de- sirous that mierit should be rewarded wherever it presented itself, but anxious at the same time to avoid the recognition of competition between individual exhibitors. They had also decided that the prizes should consist in three medals of dif- ferent sizes; and that these should be awarded, not as first, second, and third in degree for the same class of subjects and merit, but as marking merit of different kinds and charac- ter. " The Council of Chairmen found,to their regret, that it would be impossible to laydown any rules forthe awarding of the three medals, by which the appearance, at least, of denoting diffir- ent degrees of success amiong exhibitors in the same branch of production could be avoided. Accordingly. after fully explain- ing their difficulty to Her Majesty's Commissioners, they re- quested, as a course by which it might be materially diminish- ed, that one of the medals might be withdrawn. Its application, however, was not without difficulties, especially as regarded the foreign jurors. Many of these had taken part in the national exhibi- tions of France and Germany; and to them the distinctive cla- racter of the two medals, and the avoidance of all recognition of degrees of merit between the recipients of prizes were novel principles, and at variance iwith their experience; inasmuch as one of the chief purposes of the national exhibitions of the Continent has been to distinguish the various degrees of suc- cess attained by rival exhibitors. " It was to be expected, therefore, that cases would arise in which the council medal, as the higher reward, would be asked for exhibitors whose claims were only somewhat stronger in degree, without differing in kind, from those of others to whom the prize medal had been awarded. On the other hand, some instances have occurred in which they have felt themselves called. upon to confirm the claim to a council medal where the object for which it was claimed showed, in itself; less merit of execution or manufacture than others of its class. It follows, therefore, that the award of a council medal does not necessarily stamp its recipient as a better manufacturer or producer than others who have received the prize medal. It is rather a mark of such invention, ingenuity, or originality, as may be expected to exercise an influence upon industry more extended, and more important, than could be produced by mere excellence of manufacture. "This is to be borne in mind in considering the list of awards which I have the honour to lay before your Royal Highness; and I trust that it will be found that the juries have succeeded in doingjustice to the exhibitors of every na- tion and class, and that they have not departed in any im- portant degree from the purpose of Her MIajesty's Commission- ers. " One of the first instructions addressed to the juries by the Council of Chairmen was to the effect that the prizes should be awarded without reference to the country of the exhibitors, the Exhibition being considered in this respect as recognising no distinction of nation. It is not too much to hope that the happy influence of this intercourse may extend and endure far beyond the pre- sent occasion. "1 It is not necessary that I should detainyourRoyalHighness and Her Majesty's Commissioners with a recital of the other instructions framed by the Council of Chairmen for the guid- ance of the juries, or with a detailed account of their proceed- ings in the discharge of their own functions. CURIOSITIES OF THE OLD CHURCH a&NONS.—TII the Gentleman's Magazine we meet with the following illustrations of one of the customs of our ancestors : " We learn from the Council of Waterford (about 1158, x. p. 1183), that the English were in the habit of selling their children as slaves to the Irish, and this not from the pressure of extreme want, but from sheer cupidity. The Council directed that all the English slaves throughout the country should be forthwith emancipated, in order to avert the expected manifestation of Divine wrath. The Council of Armagh (1171), which by some writer is supposed to be the same as the last mentioned, published a similar •decree, and, moreover, acknowledged the political subordination of Ireland to England. In fact, in days of old, England seems to have been been the hot-bed of Slavery. Nowhere did that atrocious vice flourish with greater luxuriance. The Council of Eanhatn (Ensham, Oxon), held about 1009, forbade the selling of Christians into a foreign land ; the Council of Westminster denounced those who sell men like beasts, " as had hitherto been done in England ;" and the Council of Haban anathematizes all such as were guilty of so grievous a sin. Pursuing the same policy, the Council of Valladolid excommunicated those who sold men and bartered them away as slaves to the Saracens. These enactments all bespeak the frequency of the practices against which they were directed, and the impossibility of restraining them by the provisions of mere temporal legislation." COWPER'S OAK, IN YARDLEY CHASE, NEAR WEsTox. —ln the opening of the forest you see the remains of very ancient oaks standing here and there. You feel that you are on a spot that has maintained its connexion with the world of a thousand years ago ; and amid the venerable trees you soon see the one which, by its bulk, its hollow trunk, and its lopped and dilapi_ dated crown, needs not to be pointed out as the Yardley oak. Here Cowper was fond of coming, and sitting within the hollow boll for hours ; around him stretching the old woods, with their solitudes and the cries of woodland birds. The fame which lie has conferred on this tree has nearly proved its destruction. Whole arms and great pieces of its trunk have been cut away with knife, axe, and saw, to prepare different articles from. The Marquis of Northampton,. to whom the chase belongs, has had multitudes of nails driven in to stop the progress of this destruction, bur, findi ng that not sufficient, has affixed a board bearing this inscription :—" Out of respect to the memory of the poet Cowper, the Marquis of Northampton is particularly desirous of preserving this oak.—Notice is hereby given, that any persouidefacing or otherwise injuring if will be prosecuted according to law." In stepping round the Yardley oak it appeared to me to be, at the foot, about thirteen yards in circumference.— Ty . Howitt's Homes and Haunts of British Poets.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday, to the astonishment of almost everybody, notwithstanding the fall of price to is., the interior of the Crystal Palace was not so much crowded as usual. A great crush was anticipated, and the consequence was that a comparatively small number came. Up to five o'clock only 21,258 persons entered the building, and the receipts at the doors fell to .£920. This, with the sale of season tickets, made a total of £96o—an immense decline from the amount collected on Saturday. The visitors appeared chiefly to belong to the middle class of society, and few fustian jackets were observed among them. They did not confine themselves to the nave, but were well spread over the interior, and all seemed intent on making good use of their time, and studying carefully the departments which most interested them. By a judicious arrangement the seats which had previously been distributed in the nave and transept were removed to the more retired and less attractive parts. The only other novelty connected with Monday's experience at the Exhibition worth mentioning is the capture of three pickpockets—two women and one man—who made a sad mistake in going there to exercise their vocation. The women were detected by two Belgian policemen, and, from their dialect, were evidently provincial thieves. One stated that she was from Edinburgh, and spoke undoubted broad Scotch. The other said she came from Cork, but her accent is not Hibernian. The male thief is a Frenchman, and has been "in trouble" before. He was admirably got up for the occasion, with a new hat and coat, an unexceptionable white wa i s tcoat, and patent leather boots, very smartly made. The uninitiated would have set him down as a fashionable foreigner come to look at the mob in a philosophic spirit of ob-ervation ; but a detective, with an unfortunately tenacious memory for faces, recognised him as he passed through the entrance, and he was followed, observed actively engaged in the mysteries of his profession, and at once removed from the scene of temptation into which he had intruded. "What time did the magistrate give you before," said Superintendent Pearce to him at the station. "Six weeks," was the reply of the swell-!nobsman, who appeared to consider himself the most injured and unlucky of mortals. On Tuesday the receipts rose from £920 to £1,347. The increase no doubt will be gradual from day to day, until it at last culminates to a point equal, if not superior, to the most sanguine anticipations. This must be regarded as a happy and fortunate feature in the history of the Exhibition ; for time is thus afforded to make all necessary and suitable arrangements, and the people, accustomed to selfgovernment, will become in the Crystal Palace, as elsewhere, their own police. Her Majesty, Prince Albert, and the Royal party at the Palace visited the Exhibition at their usual early hour, and inspected carefully, among other departments, that of Sheffield hardware, in which section they took particular notice of Messrs. Rogers' Cutlery Trophy, placed in the nave. They remained for some time after the is. visitors began to arrive, and Her Majesty from the corner of the north gallery, look into the transept, watched with great interest the influx of the crowd. On Wednesday the total number of persons present was estimated at 40,000; and the amount received at the doors was £1,859, to which is to be added £l3 13s. for season tickets. This would give about 37,190 persons who paid during the day; and as the number of season ticket holders admitted could only be estimated at some 4,000 or 5,000, it seems certain that there were upwards of 40,000 present in the course of the day, and about the middle of the day more than 30,000. Thursday was the fourth shilling-day at the Cyrstal Palace, and the assemblage proved that the anticipated gradual increase in the number, and the continued decorum in the conduct of the visitors, was fairly made.' The attendance has not at any time been inconveniently crowded, arising, in a great measure, from the fact that those who attend on those days are content with an inspection of four or five hours at most, and that whilst it is convenient for many to be at the Exhibition in the morning, others take the after part of the day, and thus a continued stream to and fro is maintained. The visitors are much more equally spread over the interior than was the case during the fiveshilling days. There were a number of private schools of both sexes in the building—some in the machinery department, but mostly in the British and the Colonies. The general appearance of those present was of the middling and lower classes, with here and there a few holders of season tickets. The question as to what is to be done with the Crystal Palace is thus referred to in last Saturday's Athenown. It is to be hoped the idea will not be thrown away. Our contemporary says :—" We will take for granted, at the moment, that the Royal Commissioners before laying down the temporary offices which they were appointed by the Queen to discharge, will purchase the Crystal Palace in the name of the English people. Should it then be announced to all the present exhibitors in the first instance that such of them as have fitted up stalls or obtained spaces may retain them for, say a year, on the condition of keeping them filled with their present, or other contributions of the same high class of excellence—we think it probable that a great majority of the most useful and beautiful articles would be left on such terms. The workers in silk, wool, worsted, gold, silver, iron, and copper, mahogany and other woods —the makers ofmusical and scientific instruments, watches, chronometers, carriages, agricultural machines and fountains—the producers of flowers and plants—decorators and stained-glass makers—sculptors and carvers in wood and ivory—printers and hard-workers of most kinds would, in all probability, be glad to have such a universal and permanent exhibition-room for their wares, works, and discoveries. Many things of mere curiosity and rarity would no doubt be removed; but the absence of the Koh-i-noor, the Spanish jewels, the Indian diamonds, and similar articles if it should be proved to lessen the mere splendour of the Exhibition, would not materially detract either from its moral interest or its practical usefulness. The earnest seeker after knowledge is more attracted by a collection of minerals and metallic ores than by the Russian or the Portuguese diamond valued at millions. " Specimens of the jewellery, which borrow their highest value from the genius of the artist, would propably be left as examples and advertisements. We do not doubt that it would be worth the while of our most eminent goldsmiths to maintain a showroom in the Great Exhibition to be from time to time supplied with whatever is new and excellent in their current manufactures. The same may be surmised of our great drapery and silk mercers. What artist would not be glad to have a space assigned to him on the walls of the National Gallery on the easy condition of always having a picture hung there ? In the Crystal Palace the artist and the artisan in silk, cotton, wool, metal, and so forth, might, under some such arrangement as we are proposing, obtain their National Gallery and academy. Even in the series of costly and complicated machines in motion, we imagine that not a few of the most beautiful and interesting would be willingly allowed to remain. Most of these machines, we believe, are made in model. They cannot be sold or used in actual factories. If taken away, they will either be broken up or buried in local museums. Their proprietors would naturally preferthat they should remain as their advertisements and representatives in the great centre of observation. There is plenty of room, besides, for a winter garden. Indeed, the place is a garden even now; and its beauties in that respect would increase with every year. The contributions of industry leave plenty of space for trees and shrubs and flowers, The elm and the palm tree here grow side by aide ; and there will be room abundant for exotic plants and indigenous parterre. The works of mind and the work of nature already blend here with a harmony of tints and tones beyond the power of imagination to have conceived. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Every week is now a busy one with the officials in the Glass Palace. They have but little more than two months left for the reception and arrangement of all the goods to displayed, and they seem by their activity to be quite alive to the necessity for full exertion. More than thousand packages have been received during the last six days, of which more than threefourths are from abroad. The foreigners are first in the field ; those at home must at once bestir themselves, for he who is late sins not only against his own interests, but adds to the labours of those who have worked so long and heavily to secure the punctual completion of the great show. During the past week considerable progress has been made in the erection of counters and fittings in the spaces marked out for the goods of foreign countries. The counters already completed are of a plain and substantial character, but it will of course be competent to the various foreign commissions to consult their peculiar tastes in cases where fittings of an ornamental nature may he required for the display of goods exhibited. Large arrivals have already taken place of the productions of France, the Zollverein, Mexico, Prussia, Canada, Italy, and other places. Amongst the Canadian products are some very beautiful specimens the skins of wild animals—an elaborately ornamented canoe, and samples of the most durable and beautiful kinds of timber furnished by the extensive forests of that country. No arrangement of the goods thus forwarded has been yet attempted, nor can any such be commenced for some davs to come. As each van-load of cases arrives in the building, it is immediately consigned to the surveillance of the custom -house authorities on the spot. The pile of cases having been transferred to the floor of the building they are roughly examined, numbered, and registered by the officers, and conveyed to their appropriate hoardings. The packing-cases are subsequently broken open, and, when time serves, an examination of their contents is made. Packages, however, containing glass and other fragile materials, are exempted from this latter process, and they will not be disturbed until the fittings for the reception of their contents are completed. The marking out of the spaces for the various classes of British and colonial products is proceeding in the most satisfactory and systematic manner. The particular spots which are to be occupied by cotton machinery in motion, are all indicated, and include stations for every kind of machine used in the preparation and manufacture of cotton. The compartments in which are to be arrangad flax, linen, and woollen manufactures are also defined. Progress is also making in the mapping of the spaces for furniture contributed by the provincial towns, and in various parts of the galleries the places chosen by some of the most eminent firms in the kingdom, for the exhibition of the articles produced in their factories, arc exactly delineated. Maps have also been prepared of the various sections, on which the space assigned to each exhibitor is indicated with the utmost exactness, and a power of direction for the proper disposal of the goods is thus obtained, w’hich will doubtless greatly facilitate their arrangement when the fittings are completed for their reception. The town to which the honour is due of being the first to complete its fittings is the comparatively insignificant one of Dunfermline, and there is little doubt that as time advances strenuous efforts will be made in all quarters to escape the unenviable notoriety which will inevitably attach to the locality which may happen to be latest in making its arrangements. A considerable portion of the decorative painting in the south-west galleries is finished, and the flooring of the central avenue is laid down at different points, where it will not interfere with the transit of goods through the building. No heavy machinery has been yet forwarded, and any prolonged delay in the transmission of the articles belonging to this class will necessarily be regarded with much anxiety. —Exhibition Express. GREAT EXHIBITION. .-•-•- While, by a slow but satisfactory process, the public are gradually adapting their examination of the interior to its arrangement and sectional importance, the Executive Committee are still anxiously considering the educational uses to which the occasion can be turned. They appear to feel the impossibility of establishing any organisation for regular instruction among their adult visitors, but they entertain hopes that the great metropolitan schools will avail themselves of this opportunity for a systematic and careful study of the Exhibition. To such institutions they would be prepared, we understand, to grant every possible facility ; and, when the aptitude of youth to catch instruction at the eye is considered, it would be a thousand pities if such a chance were neglected. From a well-regulated survey of the products of the world's industry, boys will be enabled to form a clear conception, not only of the starting points whence they each stretch forward on their respective careers, but of the line they should take, and of the departments in which their tastes and habits of mind qualify them to excel. There is another consideration also, which should not be lost sight of. Hitherto, in our schools, the bias of education has run so strongly in favour of what are called by a natural partiality of expression, "the liberal professions," that they have been overstocked, while trades and manufactures have been treated with unwarrantable disfavour. Our industrial classes have risen to importance unaided by the taste and refinement which instruction imparts, and at this moment there is no greater want felt among us than that which arises from our deficiency in designs. The productive energy is strong, but the power which rests in the imagination—which gives grace to form, and purity and harmony to colour, is too often wanting. Whence does this arise? and would h be so much the case if our great metropolitan schools had an opportunity afforded them of seeing the grandeur of the peaceful arts, of estimating material industry by a correct standard, and of observing how in each department human ingenuity had pushed its way, little aided by learning, and owing its chief impulses to the strong action of necessity and the sterling qualities of the national intellect? There is an ample supply of able and competent men available for the insti uctional purposes now contemplated, and the idlest schoolboy in London would jump eagerly at the prospect of an introduction to the Crystal Palace and its varied wonders. If our great seminaries have any real zeal in the cause of education, they will not heaitate at once to organise the means for turning this opportunity to profitable account, and, from all we can learn, we believe that they will find every disposition among those placed in authority to aid them in their efforts. It is not consistent with our character as a people that this Exhibition of the world's industry should degenerate into an empty show to gratify idle curiosity, and to stimulate the jaded appetite of the public for excitement. On the cover is a group representing the sport of hawking, and around the body in high relief are two hunting subjects—the Boar hunt, from the famous picture by Rubens and Snyders, in the collection of the Earl of Derby, who is one of the stewards of the race, and the Stag.hunt, from another picture in the same collection. The handles, which imitate oak branches, are made to spring from the laudscapes . of these alti-relievi, and the stem of the cup is decorated with implements of the chase. Around the foot are three racing grouts in the costume of the last century, the subjects of which are the jockey mounting his horse, pr . eparTg to weigh, and being led to the course. The whole is sdesigned by Mr. A. Brown, and it certainly reflects credit on his taste and invention. The cup stands at least three feet high.

OPPOSITION TO THE RETENTION OF THE CRYSTAL PMACE FOR A WINrTE GARDEN.-On Saturday at a meeting of the vestry of St Marylehone, held at the Court House, Marylebone-lane, the Rev. Dr. Spry, rector in the chair, a communication was received from the Marylebone Committee for the Exhibition of Works of Industry of AU Nations, requesting permission of the vestry to place a petition for signature at the Court House, in favour of of the non-removal of the Exhibition building, it being the opinion of the committee that the greatest advantages would result to the public from the continuance of the building as a winter garden. Sir Peter Laurie and several other gentlemen opposed the project; and, so strong was the feeling against it, that the vestry even rejected the application for permission to allow petitions to lie at the Court House in favour of its continuance. The arguments were that the Great Exhibition had proved most preju- dicial to every branch of trade, and was calculated to produce a still greater extent were it perpetuated. The application was rejected accordingly.

Mr. Ripley's collection is classified into no less than six different heads—viz., teas from the Fokien Hills, Nukoi teas, Canton made teas, Nankin teas, Present teas, and Physic teas, a large proportion of the specimens included in which are, strange to say, unknown to the English markets. The teas from the Fokien Hills are—Congou, Souchong, Pouchong, Golong, at 21s. per lb.; black leaf Pekoe Ning Yong or Koken, and Flowery Pekoe, at 40s. and 50s. per lb. Of Nukoi teas two varieties are shown—the plain Caper and the plain orange Pekoe, The Canton made teas include the scented Caper, which is scented at great expense with flowers; the scented orange Pekoe, each leaf of which is so twisted that it looks like wire, a small quantity being sufficient to flavour many pounds of any other tea. You,no; Hyson, small leaf Hyson, Imperial and Gunpowder, all very curious, and of very superior quality. The Nankin teas comprehend specimens of Twankey, Hyson, Hyson skin, young Hyson, Imperial, and Gunpowder, all of which ar© the produce of one plant, and are said to he'dtied, not on copper, according to the general belief respecting green tees, butt on iron. Under the class of Nankin teas are alio exhibited spurious scented Caper an spurious Gunpowder made in Canton from tea dust and rice water without a leaf of the plant in them, and appropriately called by the Celestials " lie teas." The present teas include a box of Cumshau, nude up in the shape of balls, faggots, and cigars, The examples shown are seldom to be met with, and are said to be grown by the priests on the different hills in the tea district. Of the Physic teas the following amusing account is given by Mr. Ripley : " No. 1 is made from the common description of black teas, and is adulterated with herbs; it is used as a universal madicine. The cakes are made on the fifth day of the fifth month, or Dragon's Feast,' at noon, and come from tht! province of Fokien. " No. .2 is said to dissolve a glutinous spittle, to dispel h riskiness, to quiet troubled feelings, to clear the mind, to brighten the vision, to engender a wholesome moisture in the mouth s to moisten the lungs; its odour is fragrant, its taste savoury. This cake is much used by persons when travelling. " No. 3 is called Suun-Kok, and is considered useful in curing a variety of complaints; but fevers and rheumatic attacks are principally mentioned on the card. No. 4 A. tea from the ridge or back of a hill in the province of Kwangse, called the Dragon's Cavern, whence the tea is called Dragon's Black Tea.' It is effectual in quieting troubled feelings, in assuaging thirst, removing undigested food, dissolving phlegm, and enlivoning the spirits. " No. 5 is a specimen of the 800 •Uria-tes, from the department of that name, in the province of Yunnan, and is used to prevent indigestion. " No. 6 is another specimen from the province of Yunnan; it is said to be unadulterated with herbs, and is used for the slims purpose as. No. 5. " No. 7—Sung-Lo cake. Sang•Lo is in the province of Ganhway, near Nankin. The virtues of the tea have been doubled by its being done up into this cake. It is particularly powerful in removing all kinds of inflammatory diseases, as also those ariaing from the impeded circulation of the fluids. " No. B—Same as No. 6, only smaller. "No. 9 Is a round cake, also from the province of Yunnan; used for assisting indigestion. A cup of this tea is found very beneficial in removing repletion. " No. 10 is called Eleong-Pien, and is used as a drink on hot days; it is supposed to cool the bbod. "No. 11—Chin-Chew, basket tea called Lek•Oan, This tea is exported largely to Batavia. " No. 12—Cakes olcoarso tea, said to be used after too large an allowance of Sam-Shoo. One cap is supposed to be sufficient to remove any ill eff,c:s of the previous night's debauch. Looking at this singular specification, which is said to be translated from the Chinese Chops, the public will be reminded of that favourite quotation of teetotalism—" the cup which cheers but not inebriates." When the Royal Commission recently visited Liverpool they inspected among the other sights of that great seaport the new Albert Dock, and there, in one warehouse, they saw 20,000 chests of tea, which they were assured supplied only one week's consumption for the whole country. This gave an immense idea of the tea-drinking :powers of our population. Let any one, however, go with the facts which we have just mentioned into a small space in the very heart of the Chinese collection, and he will there see, within a few glass cases, about forty different specimens of the plant, a large proportion of which have hitherto been unknown even to our most enthusiastic teetotallers. The Great Exhibition among its other strange revelations, discloses many new varieties of a favourite, and shows how, in the Celestial Empire, an excessive allowance of " Sam Shoo," or the effects of a night's debauch, may be cured, how " troubled feelings," thirst and indigestion may be relieved, how the blood may be cooled, " the impeded circulation of the fluids " restored, and the traveller sent on his way rejoicing. Looking at the information which Mr. Ripley's collection conveys, who can doubt that the qualities of the tea plant are still very imperfectly appreciated among the barbarians of western Europe? Indeed the road from the Crystal Palace, though no longer inconveniently thronged with omnibuses, cabs, carriages, and every sort of two and four-wheeled vehicle under the sun, was still a moving mass of vehicles, owing to the number required to convey away the costly and bulky productions of the exhibitors. The United States have commenced packing, but nothing as yet has been cleared away. Brother Jonathan, we calculate, will not have a very heavy, or a very anxious, task in this respect. In the Russian department the silver articles and precious stones are removed; the malachite doors, as well as the large vases, are still in the Exhibition, but packed up ready for extradition. The Koh-i-Noor, the misnamed "Mountain of Light," is reported to be still in its original cage, but guarded carefully as a prize of such fabled value ought to be. The statues remain pretty nearly as they were. The colonial department resembles a large wholesale grocer's warehouse, from the number of casks and bales which are strewn about. The Custom-house officers are keeping strict guard over articles liable to duty. The western department has suffered the least; the large organ remains in solitary and silent grandeur, but the other musical instruments have vanished. In the carriage department, the prize carriage has gone, others are ready to follow. In the machinery department, great progress has been made, but in consequence of the ponderous character of many of the steam and other engines, the entire clearance will be a work of time. We may say, generally, that nearly all the other departments are in a state of forwardness as far as removal is concerned, but two days of heavy labour have hardly made any sensible impressionon the vast accumulation of productions It is calculated that some weeks of continued labour must elapse before the Crystal Palace will have nothing to boast of but its own transparent walls. The invited guests found their way down to Liverpool as best they could, the foreigners getting passes and the natives paying their fares as usual. At ten o'clock they all assembled at St. George's Dock landing-wharf, where they embarked on board a river boat, and, under the guidance of" Mr. Brown, who received them there, proceeded to view the steam-ship America, then with her steam up and waiting for the mail-bags to start for New York. The spacious quarter-deck, the cabin accommodation, the machinery, and the stores, of this fine vessel were all attentively examined. The Alderney cow to supply milk, the poultry, the joints of meat for roasting, enveloped in masses of ice —these, and a hundred other objects, were carefully noticed. At length the mail-bags were all received, the noble ship started on her way, and, with a parting salute and cheer, Mr. Brown and his friends left her to pursue her voyage. The strangers then betook themselves to the Birkenhead side of the river, where they landed and strolled about for some time, viewing with interest that remarkable example of over-building, and those indications of future greatness and prosperity with which. Birkenhead abounds. From this place Mr. Brown conducted his guests to the Atlantic steamer, which . was found to be fitted up with a splendour truly astonishing: one felt quite at a loss whether inest to admire the great sweep of her quarter-deck, the magnificence with which her state-rooms and berths are equipped, or the cyclopean dimensions of her engines. After completing their survey of her, the company returned to the Liverpool side of the river, and, led by Lord Granville and Mr. Greville, made their way to the new Albert Dock, the various striking improvements in the construction of which were fully explained to them. The most remarkable is the application of the hydraulic press power by Armstrong's patent in such a manner as to secure the complete action of cranes, ascending platforms, and such-like, machinery used in docks, at any point, however distant from the press, and by means so simple that the strength of a child can completely control them. The extent and contents of /he bonded warehouses seemed particularly to astonish the foreigners, who, on entering one room filled with nothing but tea boxes, and on asking a few very simple questions, were told that the number of boxes was 20,000, the quantity less than usual, and about a week's consumption for the whole country. They also appeared a good deal surprised at a range of warehouses filled witb raw cotton, and considerably longer than the Crystal Palaoe. One other point now only remained, in order that the strangers might have as complete a view SS circumstances admitted of the mercantile marine of Liverpool. The Custom-house accordingly underwent a rapid survey. On Monday there were 62,694 visitors, and £2,957 was received. THE PROPOSED VISIT Or THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS TO NOTTINGIIA.3I.—The Nottingham Mercury says:— "Every preliminary arrangement having been made, Mr. Felkin, our respected chief magistrate, has conveyed to the Prince Consort, and his colleague, the Royal Commissioners, an invitation to visit this town early in August, when an entertainment will be provided worthy of the guests and of the vast industries which employ the people of Nottingham and the midland counties. A variety of suggestions have been made to give eclat to the proceedings, but at present it would be difficult to say what programme will be adopted. The invitation in the first instance is the Mayer's, for the purpose of reciprocating the hospitality he and his brother commissioners have received; but the corporation, merchants, manufacturers, and other principal residents, anxious to do every honour to the occasion, have requested that they may be allowed to contribute their co-operation, so as to render the entertainment as general and magnificent as possible. So universal is the desire to make the visit every way auspicious and interesting, that the committee scarcely have had to look about them for means to entertain their highly intellectual guests. Mr. North, the proprietor of the 13abbington and Cinderhill collieries, is desirous that in approaching the town the distinguished visitors should inspect his extensive works, superintended by Mr. J. T. Woodhouse, C.E., and perhaps the most complete works of the kind in the kingdom. These colleries have twenty miles of tramway running through and connecting them, which would facilitate a rapid inspection, and then, after luncheon, the party could be conveyed along this line to Radford. When in Nottingham the number of objects to be visited is great, but not greater than can be well inspected in one day by judicious selection and arrangement. The proprietors of the great cotton-doubling mills would throw open their establishments, and have everything ready for examination without delay; the same with the leading factories, hosiers, lace dressers, lace warehouses, dyers, fancy paper makers and printers, &c.. But the great object to be attained by this visit is to . inaugurate the splendid Arboretum, just formed, occupying the same area as the Exhibition of All Nations, to lay the foundation-stone of refreshment-rooms and a winter garden therein, to be built partly after the plan of the Crystal Palace, to open new pleasure-walks, streets, &c., many miles in extent, and of great beauty with regard to richness and variety of scenery. This the good people of Nottingham are desirous of doing in the memorable year 1851, in the presence of the representatives of all nations, when every department of the local manufactures are being placed upon a differeat footing by inventions of machinery and improvements in taste, and when much of their future success depends upon the degree of cheerfulness, energy, confidence, with which they embark upon a new career of :world-wide competition. Lest the weather might net be suitable for dining in the Arboretum, it is proposed that the company adjourn thence to the Exchange Rooms, there to spend the remai n d er of ' the evening. The day, it is anticipated, will be kept as a general holiday, and the Mayor, Town-clFrk, and corporate officers, will lead the severaltprocessions in their civic robes and uniforms. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Next to the state opening, the most impressive sight, perhaps, that the building has yet presented was on Tuesday morning. Thousands of shilling visitors had entered during the first dour, when, without a nate of preparation, by the good management of about a dozen policemen, an avenue was formed down the nave, and the Queen, who had, as usual, come early, was, on leaving, enabled to pass along between living walls of her people as quietly as if she was in her own drawing-room. Hitherto her Majesty has usually taken her departure by one of the side passages, but on this occasion she very unexpectedly put her shilling paying subjects on their trial for respectful and courteous behaviour I towards her. Leaving the north half of the Indian department, and preceded only by Mr. Mayne and Mr. Belshaw, she proceeded, leaning on the King of the Belgians' arm, to Osier's fountain, which for a short time arrested her attention. The effect at this time produced by the thousands of excited spectators was exceedingly fine, and all kept their Places with admirable and praiseworthy sense of propriety. Everybody seemed to feel the novelty of the situation, and to desire that justice might be done it. It was, in point of fact, the first extempore walk of the Sovereign in the presence of her people without other guards than themselves. The gratification caused by the event was visible in every face, and the occurrence seemed greatly to surprise and please the many foreigners who happened to be present. Here and there cheers were raised when the loyalty displayed rose to its highest point, but the spectators generally appeared to suppress their feelings, as if they doubted the good taste of expressing them on such an occasion. The Royal party was attended by Mr. Cubitt, Sir Stafford Northcote, Colonel Reid, Mr. Cole, and Mr. Dilke, Dr. Playfair, and Mr. Bowring; they commenced their tour by examining the fixed machinery and receiving the explanations of Mr. Henstnan and the exhibitors present as to their respective contributions. After admiring the fine display of marine engines, of locomotives, and other interesting objects which this department contains, they minutely inspected Cox and Company's new soda-water machine, and not far off from this their attention was directed to the remarkable collection of the sacred volume produced by the British and Foreign Bible Society. Her Majesty during her stay for the first time saw the splendid ivory throne studded with jewels, presented to her by the Maha rajah of Travancore, with the extraordinary magnificence of which she appeared greatly astonished and pleased. It is to be hoped that the respectful conduct of the people on Tuesday may lead to a repetition of such acts of condescension as we have just recorded, and that the thousands of country folk who now daily flock to the metropolis to see there, once for all, an epitome of wordly magnificence, may occasionally be able to carry back with them to their homely firesides the simple story of the Queen walking among them, and graciously receiving their unaffected homage. Seguier, Mr. Colladon, and Mr. Denison vcere appointed by that jury to act as a sub-committee, with Mr. Lawrence as an " associate ;" and that the duty of this sub-committee was to make a report to the jury as the basis for them to adjudicate upon; but that, somehow or other, I contrived togive JuryX. the go-by, erected my subscommittee into an independentjury,with myself as chairman, transformed 31r.Lawrence outofan associate without a vote into ajuryman with one, and then, by the help of this vote, and my own casting vote as chairman, I drove my two foreign colleagues off the field, and carried triumphantly a great medal for my intimate friend 3lr.Dent; leaving to Baron Seguier asd Mr. Colladou no other resource but that of protesting against the anard and publicly disclaiming all responsibility for it. And perhaps the following facts will be found to present a still more serious obstacle to the credibility of this history of injustice. I was requested several times before the Exhibition opened to act as a juror for horology, and I as often refused; first, because, I disapproved of the medals altoge. ther; and secondly, because it was no secret that I had given. Mr. Dent the design for this great clock, and therefore 1 knew that any award which might be made in his favour would be accused of partiality, even if I did not vote for it. X. colnd pjusibly have appointed aqy sub-committee on horology or anything else. One would have thought that decorative ingenuity had been exhausted in making the Crystal Palace the great centre of metropolitan attraction, but so did not think Mr. Ferguson, florist, of Aylesbury, who, having come up to town betimes on Saturday morning, laden with the fragrant treasures of his rose gardens, proceeded to " gild refined gold," by setting the great fountain in a deep border of verdant moss, studded with roses of all tints and odoura, and tastefully arranged into the expansively philanthropic motto, "God bless all uatiens. ' The effect of this novelty on entering the transept was peculiarly te4easant and refreshing. The cool green of the moss . eorsned a tittirg resting place for the eye, dazzled by the glare of the surrounding objects, and the sweet perfume of the fresh-gathered flowers rising pleasantly, as it were, on the moist spray of the fountain, diffused a luxurious attuos-I:lltere, which delighted the fair visitors by whom this favoured locality was surrounded during the day. As is the custom on Saturdays, the general public were not admitted eintil 12 o'clock. the morning being reserved for her Majesty's undisturbed inspection of the contents of the Exhibitiou. The Royal route was on this occasion somewhat varied from that of previous visits, her Majesty driving in the first instance to Prince Albert's model cottage, which she minutely inspected, the benevolent Earl of Shaftesbury being in attendance to receive her, and thence walking across the road to the Crystal Palace, leaning on the arm of his Royal Highness. The Queen immediately noticed the floral decorations of tire fountain, and walking leisurely roniel,to read the inscription, smiled with an air of surprise at its comprehensive benediction. Thu royal party then proceeded up the nave to the Spitalfields gallery, in which the satins, silks, velvets, end other costly fabrics are exhibited. All the exhibitors had been previously warned of the intended honour, and were present to afford any explanations that might be required. Mr. J. Lavanchy had the honour of submitting to her Majesty and the Prince specimens 01 Spitalfields silks made upwards of one hundred Years ago, in the year 1745. The silk was manufactuted by James Leraun, of the city of London, and designed by John Van :Sommer, a Dutch artist. Amongst the specimens were a Pattern of the silk made for 'Queen Caroline, wife of George 11., and some for court dresses, worked in gold and silver, the whole of which are of the most perfect make, of beautiful colour, and elegant designs. The Royal vi s it ors - then passed on to the lace department, examining the peculiarities of the licuiton, point, and other hand-made laces, And also the machine-made lace of bobbin net, the coarser 'descriptions of which are now manufactured so cheaply as lo be extel eively used for window certains and hangings. 'The mode of manufacture was explained to her Majesty by the Mayor of Nottingham and other exhibitors present. The Queen then passed through the jewellery and gold and silver Plate department, all the exhibitors being here also in attendance. The extensive purchases recently made in gold and elver plate by Prince Henry of the Netherlands, Prince Demidoff, the Paths of Egypt, and other distinguished Personages, were pointed out to the Queen, who has been a - very extensive purchaser herself in various parts of the Exhibition since its opening. Some jealousy, however, having been created by the ticketing of articles marked as sold to her Majesty the executive committee have directed the removal of all the labels. Her Majesty having concluded her inspection went out for the first time at the south transept entrance and graciously bowed from her carriage to the group s o f fashionables who were waiting there for 'admission, and who, of course, tendered their respectful homage. Much amusement was created here by a little child, hardly three years old, who, running to the edge f the steps, kissed its hand with tremendous vigour to the Royal party. GREAT EXHIBITION. .-•-•- While, by a slow but satisfactory process, the public are gradually adapting their examination of the interior to its arrangement and sectional importance, the Executive Committee are still anxiously considering the educational uses to which the occasion can be turned. They appear to feel the impossibility of establishing any organisation for regular instruction among their adult visitors, but they entertain hopes that the great metropolitan schools will avail themselves of this opportunity for a systematic and careful study of the Exhibition. To such institutions they would be prepared, we understand, to grant every possible facility ; and, when the aptitude of youth to catch instruction at the eye is considered, it would be a thousand pities if such a chance were neglected. From a well-regulated survey of the products of the world's industry, boys will be enabled to form a clear conception, not only of the starting points whence they each stretch forward on their respective careers, but of the line they should take, and of the departments in which their tastes and habits of mind qualify them to excel. There is another consideration also, which should not be lost sight of. Hitherto, in our schools, the bias of education has run so strongly in favour of what are called by a natural partiality of expression, "the liberal professions," that they have been overstocked, while trades and manufactures have been treated with unwarrantable disfavour. Our industrial classes have risen to importance unaided by the taste and refinement which instruction imparts, and at this moment there is no greater want felt among us than that which arises from our deficiency in designs. The productive energy is strong, but the power which rests in the imagination—which gives grace to form, and purity and harmony to colour, is too often wanting. Whence does this arise? and would h be so much the case if our great metropolitan schools had an opportunity afforded them of seeing the grandeur of the peaceful arts, of estimating material industry by a correct standard, and of observing how in each department human ingenuity had pushed its way, little aided by learning, and owing its chief impulses to the strong action of necessity and the sterling qualities of the national intellect? There is an ample supply of able and competent men available for the insti uctional purposes now contemplated, and the idlest schoolboy in London would jump eagerly at the prospect of an introduction to the Crystal Palace and its varied wonders. If our great seminaries have any real zeal in the cause of education, they will not heaitate at once to organise the means for turning this opportunity to profitable account, and, from all we can learn, we believe that they will find every disposition among those placed in authority to aid them in their efforts. It is not consistent with our character as a people that this Exhibition of the world's industry should degenerate into an empty show to gratify idle curiosity, and to stimulate the jaded appetite of the public for excitement. The attendance of visitors at the Exhibition when the doors were opened on Saturday morning was by no means so numerous as on the preceding day. This fact was partly to be accounted for by the cold and unpropitious state of the weather, and in part by Saturday being the day of the first show of flowers at Chiswick Gardens. The issue of the day tickets oh Saturday amounted to about 500. From about one o'clock the i numbers began rapidly to increase, and a long string of carriages, extending from Hydepark Corner to the building continued to pour in a constant stream of visitors until nearly five o'clock. Her Majesty arrived shortly hefts; e ten o'clock, acccompanied by his Royal Highness Prince Albert, Prince Alfred, the Princess Alice, the Prince and Princess of Prussia, and Prince Frederick William of Prussia. Her Majesty and her royal guests remained for more than an hour walking through the various parts of the building, examining the principal objects ot interest. A considerable time was devotE dby Her Majesty to the examination of the department in the gallery in which articles of British plate are exhibited. During the whole of Sunday, though the weather was extimely cold, with showers of hail and rain at intervals, the vicinage of the Exhibition presented an animated scene. Thither, from all parts of the metropolis, and its most remote suxburbs, a great concourse of persons, chiefly artisans and shopmen of every class, had collected, whose occupations preclude them from visiting the site of the Exhibition on any other day of the week But a few were seamen of different nations, who had come from the docks and "below bridge," and who wandered about in groups. On Monday, the price of admission fell from £1 to 55.; and in consequence the receipts at the doors rose from £5OO to about £1,500 or £1,600. The sale of season tickets also " continues active," and the total receipts of the commission during the day considerably exceeded £2,000. The financial success of the Exhibition, therefore, promises to be as great as its warmest supporters could desire. Still the southern galleries of the foreign half of the building are filled with carpenters and packing-cases ; and even on the basement the French and other parts are far from a state of readiness. An official order was posted throughout the building, to the effect that exhibitors would be allowed to complete their fi tings during the day; but that any workman who was found not doing his work in the building, would be at once expelled. Some decisive step is obsiously necessary to counteract the listlessness of the foreign workmen. ALARM or FlRE.—About two o'clock on Thursday one of the police on duty at the southern entrance of the Crystal Palace observed some smoke to issue from the southwestern angle of the ground floor, where the officers of the contractors, Messrs. Fox and Henderson, adjoin the section of the building assigned to Canadian produce. On closer observation, it became apparent, from what ever cause, that the bottom of a chest, containing some specimens of straw and other cereal produce, from Canada, had become ignited. By the prompt application, however, of one of the engines belonging to the Palace, the fire (if so it can with propriety be called) was extinguished, and without the slightest damage either to any portion of the building or its valuable contents. SPECIAL RELIGIOUS SERVICES.—A full cathedral service was celebrated on Sunday at St. Paul's Cathedral, and an eloquent discourse was delivered by the Bishop of London, from "Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." At Westminster Abbey full cathedral service was also celebrated, and appropriate discourses were delivered by the Bishop of Oxford in the morning, and the Rev. Lord John Thynne in the evening. Special services were also commenced in the large room at Exeter-hall, which was crowded to excess. In the morning the Rev. B. Noel preached from John iv. 10. In the evening, Mr. Binney delivered a very appropriate discourse from Daniel v. 30, which was listened to with great attention. SOYER'S SYMPOSIUM.—Within two hundred yards of the Crystal Palace is an establishment which will certainly prove an additional attraction and a great accommodation to sight-seers. It is Gore House—once the residence of Wilberforce, more lately of the Countess of Blessingtonnow in the possession of the famous Alexis Soyer, and fitted up by him for the entertainment of visitors of all ranks and in any number. To begin at the basement—there is a wonderful array of culinary machinery. It contains a water-mark portrait of the Queen, con- trived, not as the ordinary water-mark in mere outline hitherto used in bank-note and other paper, but so as to give the gradation of light and shade of an Indian-ink drawing, such as is seen in the porcelain pictures intro- duced from Germany. Here is a man, calling himself an agent and accountant, doing the business of a solicitor for a bankrupt, a publisher and bookseller of some position, and sending in a biU for letters, attendances, .te- as formal and lawyer _ ke as ever issued from an attorney's office.
