What was accomplished by accident was further perfected by stratagem. A descendant of one of these Lorraines proceeded to Germany as a musician and found means to get into some of the strictly' watched manufactories, and obtained a knowledge of the method of making German spread glass for windows. Suspicions, however, were excited. He was seized, tried, and ordered to be executed, but was fortunate enough to make his escape, and on his return here his services were publicly acknowledged in the Gazelle, and a grant of fifty pounds (!) voted to him by the existing government. Since then the manufacture of this description of glass has been carried out to an enormous extent, and it is now exported to all parts of the world. The first blown glass was made in this country in 1673, at Lambeth, by Venetian artists, who were brought over under the patronage of the Duke of Buckingham. Colbert was the introducer of blown mirror glass into France, and nobles only were at first allowed to be masters of the glass-Works. We may close these introductory remarks upon the early stages of glass manufacture by, a more authentic account of the real excellence and Value of the Venetian glass. Nearly 200 years ago, Maximilian Misson, a Frenchman, who visited Murano, said that Venetian crystal, formerly held to be the finest l in Europe, no longer merited that title, and the master of one of the glass-houses offered 100 1 000 francs to any one 1 who would teach him the secret of making glass as white as that of a cup brought from Paris. Mr. Pellatt says the finest ancient Venetian glass was celebrated rather for its lightness than its crystalline beauty, but that it is inferior to modern English crystal in pellucid refractibility. It would thus appear that our energy, our capital, and the discoveries of chemical science, have enabled us to transcend without an effort the most surprising wonders of ancient art, and to place within the reach of the middle classes what was formerly esteemed among the most costly treasures of the most lutturious Roman Emperors, or the princely rulers of the Italian states.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Friday, July 11.— Her Majesty and Prince Albert, accompanied by their Royal Highnesses the Princesses Alice and Helena, and attended by the Hon. Lucy Kerr, Lord Charles Fitzroy, and Lieutenant-Colonel Francis Hugh Seymour, visited the Exhibition to-day at the usual hour. Her Majesty first proceeded to inspect the Italian and Spanish departments, and the various articles of sculpture in the transept. The model of the machine for making the famous Tournay carpets was also minutely examined. The royal visitors then ascended the galleries and examined the china and porcelain, aud subsequently proceeded to the studio of M. Seloux, in the stained glass gallery, for the purpose of inspecting the grand painting of the inauguration of the Exhibition, which is now in course of execution. Her Majesty expressed herself exceedingly gratified at the progress made by the artist Her Majesty, having inspected the progress of this beautiful work of art, descended by the Belgian staircase, and left the build- ing at her usual place of exit. The number of visitors, Friday being a half-crown day, did not exceed 30,067. The amount received was, for season tickets, £17 175. ; at the doors, £3,145 17s. 6d.; total receipts, £3,163 14s. 6d. Saturday, July 12.— The Queen, instead of going direct to the Exhibition building, stopped to inspect the model houses for families, near the Knightsbridge Bar- racks. She was there received, at about nine o'clock, by Mr. Dilke. The Queen appeared much gratified, and expressed her approbation of the veiy comfortable arrangements therein made for the poorer classes. After half an hour's stay, her Majesty walked across to one of the small exit doors on the foreign side of the building, up the nave to the staircase in the Canadian department. At the bottom, Mr. Dilke called his Royal Highness Prince Albert's attention to a small marble bust of himself, carved at Rome, in 1850, by Barbato Cipriani, with which he appeared somewhat amused. After a short inspection of the Spitalfields silks, her Majesty's attention was next chiefly attracted to the five great Coventiy ribands,— three of which, it is stated, she herself intends to purchase, and the cheap ribands, manu- factured by steam. In passing through the part of the gallery devoted to the Exhibition of Nottingham lace, her Majesty was received by the exhibitors, headed by the mayor. In the section of precious metals her Majesty did not remain long, all the articles having been in- spected by her on two previous occasions, still she graciously acknowledged the merit of the articles pre- sented to her passing notice by the exhibitors. The bronzes and electrotyping in gold and silver of Messrs. Elkington and Co. retained' the royal party for some time. In its small unpretending casket they inspected Mr. Hope's blue diamond, considered unique from its sapphire colour and large size. Mr. Hope was himself present as the exhibitor, and took the beautiful bril- liant from its case, that her Majesty might handle it. The black diamond, belonging to Mr. Joseph Mayer, of Liverpool, was next shown. Her Majesty left the building at eleven o'clock, by the entrance in the south transept. The receipts during the day amounted to £1,589 15s. ; and the police returns gave 11,181 per- sons as the number who visited the building. Monday, July 14. — To-day the weather was exceedingly fine, and the visitors to the Exhibition were, as usual, very numerous, amounting in number to 62,694. Among them were 332 boys, with a baud, belonging to the Duke of York's School. The baud of the school played the National Anthem, the Duke of York's, and several other marches, and their excellent appearance attracted considerable notice. The amount of money received was — season tickets, £33 s.; at the doors, £2,960: total receipts, £2963 3s. Tuesday, July 15. — T0-day the unprecedentedly large number of 74,122 persons visited the Crystal Palace, and £3,509 Bs. was taken in shillings at the doors. Notwithstanding this immense influx, conse quent probably upon the combined attractions of the Exhibition and the cattle show at Windsor, which have brought swarms of people up from the country to " kill two birds with one stone," the utmost good humour prevailed, and less inconvenience from over- crowding was experienced than might have been anti- cipated. The Queen aud Prince Albert again visited the building eariy in the morning. They examined the Austrian toys and glass, the Lyon's silks and Mulhausen prints, and the Prince during his stay took especial notice of a new painting of the opening ceremony by Mr. Nash, forming one of the series of sketches of that remarkable event which he is preparing under the royal patronage. Wednesday, July 16. — The attendance to-day, al- though many thousands below the monster gathering of the preceding day, was yet considerably beyond the number of previous Wednesdays : 58,000 persons were admitted on Wednesday week, while to-day the numbers considerably exceeded 61,000. Her Majesty was, as usual, one of the earliest visitors, and proceeded to in- spect the various articles displayed outside the west end of the building. Rogers' large anchor was first exa- mined, the inventor being in attendance to explain its advantages. The Queen then examined the various large specimens of coal, among others the immense block, weighing 24 tons, from Stavely works, Chester- field, whicli was raised from a shaft 459 feet deep, and the Earl Fitzwilliam's pillar, exhibiting a com- plete section of the Barnsley thick bed of coal from the Elsicot colliery. The royal party then re-entered the building, and proceeded to the Indian depart- ment, where Dr. Royle was in attendance, and explained the nature of the mineral and vegetable products, and the Indian mode of manufacturing cotton and of pre- paring opium. The sugar specimens, and the mode of preparation, were also explained to her Majesty. It. appears that 270 new omnibusses have been put on the line, in addition to about 100 regular stagers. Their average receipts are 10s. each journey, and they make eight journeys in the day. This would give a total of £1,480 per diem for omnibusses alone ; but, in addition, the cabs must be taken into account, the receipts of which are of course inscrutable mysteries, except to the drivers and the fares ; but an approximate calcula- tion taken by competent persons, gives the total sum paid for town travelling, as connected with the Exhibi- tion, at £3,500 a-day. The police numbers for the day were 60,626 ; and the receipts, including season tickets, £2,913 7s. Entertainment of the Royal Commissioners in Paris. — The Times says that the rumoured fete to the Royal Commission by the city of Paris is now so far settled to take place that the programme is in process of arrangement. The invitations will probably embrace all connected with the Exhibition whose services entitle them to be present, and the festivities will, it is said, consist of a grand ball at the Hotel de Ville, and a dinner to a select party of our countrymen and the foreign Commissioners. It is likely that the event will come off soon, and a Friday is spoken of as the proper day for starting, Saturday for the joyous celebrations at the Hotel de Ville, Sunday for the waterworks at Versailles, Monday for sight-seeing in Paris, and Tues- day for the return home. Highway Robberies near Carlisle. — On Saturday morning some daring highway robberies were perpetrated in broad daylight in the immediate neighbourhood of Car- lisle by a man who was armed with a six-barrel revolver pistol, and wore a crape mask. The persons robbed were two farmers, named Bawman and Gibson, and Mr. Myers, a commercial traveller. From the latter two sovereigns were obtained, and from the former a silver watch and a few shillings. The first Locomotive on the Semmerisg. — The first ascent of a locomotive up a gradient of 1.40 was made on the Bth inst, by the engine Save, on the new Austrian railway which passes over the Semmering Mountain. The engine was ofthe eight-wheeled description, used on the South Austrian Railway. The engine drew up an eight- wheeled loaded truck at the rate of 14 English miles an hour, and was stopped several times, resuming its journey at the will of the driver — Daily News. The Stepney Abduction Case. — lt will be remem- bered that at the May session ofthe Central Criminal Court, a young man, named William Day, was convicted, under the Bishop of Oxford's Act, of the abduction of a young woman, named Harriet Newman, whose statement was a very extraordinary one. He was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour ; but since the conviction took place a statement of facts has been laid before Sir George Grey, through the exertions of Mr. Field, of the Society for the Protection of Young Females, and the right hon. baronet, after taking them into consideration, advised her Majesty to grant the prisoner a free pardon. He is now at liberty. Daring Leap of a Burglar from a Railway Train. — A very powerful man, named George Fisher, who was until recently a member of the Cardiff police force, from which he was discharged for misconduct, made his escape on Monday from a carriage on the Birmingham and Bristol Railway, by leaping from it while the train was in motion, and where he was in the custody of an officer upon a charge, or rather several charges, of burglary. Mr. Superinten- dent Stockdale, of the Cardiff police force, in whose custody the prisoner was at the time, although at the imminent risk of his life, instantly jumped out after him, but falling on the rail he severely bruised his shoulder, and was unable to pursue Fisher, who having run through the engine-house of the Great Western works, succeeded in climbing the bank, and escaping iutp the wood at the No. 1, or Brisling- ton Tunnel The police of Bristol, kc were immediately sent in search, but without success. The prisoner was last seen lying in a dry ditch, as if exhausted (with the hand- cuff on), between Bristol and Bath. — Moi ning Chronicle. Fire at Nutsford Vale, near Manchester.— Nutsford Nale, situated between the villages of Gorton aud Longsight, was, on Monday, the scene of a destructive fire, which broke out about nine o'clock in the morning on the premises of Mr. John Scott, and destroyed a considerable portion of the buildiugs before it could be extinguished. The business carried on at these premises comprised silk- printing and rope-making. 'Ihe materials in the building where the fire broke out burnt with inconceivable fury, aud the heat was so intense that the iron wheels of the machinery were fused and run together in masses. It was one o'clock before the flames could be got under, and at this time only a small portion of the walls of the building in which the fire commence! was left standing. The flames had swept off tho roofs of the engine-house, tar-house, dressing-rooms (destroying in the latter also the dressing- frames and a considerable quantity of hemp), and leaving only the cottages, silk-mill, and stabling, untouched. Some valuable blocks for printing silk handkerchiefs, which were in the dressing-room, wore saved. The worm is destroyed, and though the still, on being gauged after the fire, was found to contain about 100 gallons of oil unconsumed, it is believed to have been fractured inside the brickwork with the great heat to which it was subjected. The promises were not insured.

We proceed to call the atteution of our readers to that portion of the western nave on the . south side of which toe tissues of woollen and worsted, with their processes of manufacture,, are displayed. It will be necessary, however, previously to explain the promi- nent distinction between these two classes of goods, so frequently considered by most persons as absolutely identical. Wool is distinguished by the length of its fibres, the longer kinds being spun and woven in a similar manner to cotton, while the shorter undergo a further process, called fulling or milling, by which a close texture and smooth surface are produced. These two manu- factures are perfectly distinct, and are for the most part carried on in separate localities. Among the pro- ducts of the former are moreens, camlets, shalloons, tabinets, &c, while the woollen articles include all the varieties of cloth. Having premised thus much, we shall proceed to offer a few remarks upon the different qualities of wool, numerous specimens of which are contained in the cases in this department. The most interesting of these assortments is that of Messrs. Cheesebrough, of Brad ford ; it consists of a specimen from each of the forty counties' of England, one sample from Wales, from Scotland, and fi-om Ireland. An unpractised eye or hand would, detect no sensible difference between them, though they might, if indiscriminately mixed, be readily classified by an experienced sorter on account of their very different properties. The most casual observer, however, will not fail to perceive the marked distinc- tion subsisting between the short downy fleece of the mountain sheep of Wales and the long coarse locks from the lowland pastures of Lincolnshire. In like manner he will be able, upon minute scrutiny, to detect all the intermediate gradations of fineness. An adjoining show-case, Messrs. Milligan's, encloses beautiful alpaca fleeces from Pern in the crude state in which they are imported, as also five different qualities after having been cleaned and dressed. With these there appear, moreover, samples of mohair or goat's wool from the dominions of the Sultan, together with the peculiar long-toothed combs used in the first preparatory process. The effect of that process is ap- parent enough, for by the side of the combs are "slivers" of the long silky mohair perfectly disentangled and freed from extraneous substances, the steel teeth of the comb retaining the " noil," or portion they have severed after the sliver has been removed. Six slivers of differ- ent hue are then shown side by side, together with the result of their union, when all drawn to one sliver. The " stubbing" drawn from the six " slivers" appears next, together with other intermediate processes, until at last the finished alpaca coatings and mixtures are laid before us in the state fit for use. Messrs. Whitmore, of Leicester, have fitted up a case containing no less than 126 different qualities of yarn, severally intended for common hosiery, fleecy hosiery, embroidery, and soft knitting. Messrs. Brewin, of the same town, have a veiy interesting display of worsted yarns for hand knitting, &c. Some of sober shades for the German market, in 60 varieties; others still more sombre in colour for the American, while a further parcel, exceedingly brilliant in hue, is intended for fancy hosiery and embroidery ; together with merino yarns for knitting, &c. Messrs. Burgess, of Leicester, provide the student in the textile art with samples of wool in various states, prepared both for spinning worsted and woollen yarns. On one side we have the unprepared wool, while under the centre of the glass there are fleecy yarns, Berliri wool yams, others fbr woollen gloves, carpets, plaids, &c, altogether 107 varieties selected from English, Australian, German, Egyptian, mohair, and alpaca. It will be well now to proceed to another part of the same department which Messrs. Brookes, of Honley, near Huddei-sfield, have appropriately adorned with a cabinet of specimens of the more advanced stages of the art ; first we have assorted Silesian wool ; .then the same scoured, woaded, dyed, teazed, scribbled, carded, Ac., until we finally find it in the form of warp ready for the loom. Then we have the raw and the scoured thread, tbe balk or milled cloth, the cloth razed, crop- ped ready for boiling, boiled, tentered, and finished. — -Messrs. TownencL of Cullingyorth, have stocked another case (171) with raw material from Peru, from Northumberland, and Lincoln. It contains poplin yarn, mohair poplin, worsted genappe cord, two-fold mohair yam in a great number of varieties. But perhaps one of the finest cases is that of Messrs. Sugden, wherein are collected no less than 700 speci- mens of genappe and heald worsted yarns in two com- partments, as well as some beautiful varieties of me- rinos of every hue and degree of brilliancy. Few among our readers probably would have ima- gined that the qualities of the wool of different coun- tries were so totally distinct. English fleeces are now little used except for blankets, coarse cloths, stuffs, and "worsteds." Not long ago the Spanish wool obtained the highest price in the market, but wool from the Spanish breed of sheep introduced into Saxony is far superior to the former article. Australian wool has also for some years past been largely consumed in our manufacturing districts ; that from Germany beino- principally reserved for the finest cloths. The latter fleeces weigh ordinarily from two to two and a half pounds ; those of our own country generally averaging seven pounds. The first operation the shorn wool undergoes is that of "sorting." The wool from dif- ferent parts of the same fleece is of various qualities. Yet so sensitive, by use, do the fingers of the expe- rienced workman become that it is with surprising rapidity that he separates the masses before him into ten, twelve, or more kinds, taking due cognisance of the strength, cleanliness, regularity, colour, and soft- ness of each. The parcels thus formed are partially scoured with hot ley, and then dyed, if the goods to be produced from them are to be " wool-dyed," and not " piece-dyed." An instrument styled a willy is used to disentangle the locks. To facilitate this process oil is continually sprinkled over the wool, which now becomes fit for " scribbling," " carding," and " stubbing." It is unneces- sary to describe these technical terms, as in another de- partment of the Exhibition the three operations they in- dicate may be actually inspected. From the scribbling machine the wool falls in thin downy translucent layers; by the carding machine a delicate band is detached, rolled into the form of a slender rod the fibres being spread, not longitudinally, but nearly at right angles to the piece. The " slubbing-billy" unites these rods or cardings end to end, reducing then- thick- ness and of course elongating them, one ounce of slub- bing usually measuring about 150 yards. The wool, after all this previous manipulation, is now ready to be spun into yarn for the weaver by the agency of the mule spinning machines. By them the slubbing process is carried a step further. The wool is now drawn still finer, and again slightly twisted, when it is denominated spun-yarn. The " warp," or long threads, being spun in one way, the " weft," or cross yarns in another. The yarn, for either purpose, is immersed in size to facilitate its working, then follow the processes of "winding," "warping," "beaming," " drawing-in," &c, by which the warp is attached to the loom, and the weft to the shuttle. In the new and beautiful looms exhibited in the Crystal Palace the weavers are daily seen plying their busy trade, while the produce of their labour may be simultaneously inspected, as it slowly issues completed from their hands. Yet though completed so far, it is far from being "finished." It must now be cleansed from the oil adhering to it, and be milled or felted, that is, beaten incessantly for 40 or 50 hours, until the fibres become so interlocked that they entirely conceal the threads beneath. If, for obvious reasons, the latter processes be not demonstrated on the present occasion, there is no lack of samples to display their efficacy. When all that we have thus briefly described has been done, the nap of the new cloth has still to be " raised" and " cut," to reduce it to a smooth and uniform surface. A lustre is then imparted to it by " boiling." Little knots or extraneous matters are removed by "burling" or picking, when folding, pressing, and steaming, close the protracted labours. We may now take a rapid glance at the means by which worsted goods are produced. Of their increasing importance in a national view, nothing need further be said than that the exports in the year 1841 more than doubled, while those of 1850 nearly quadrupled, the exports of 1821. Bradford may be assumed as the centre of the worsted trade in England. A circuit of a few miles round that town comprises Leeds, Huddersfield, Dewsbury, Wake- field, Halifax, and Keighley, all admirably represented at the Exhibition, fancy goods chiefly predominating among their contributions. If the elementary cases in this department be ex- amined, it will at once be seen that the wool herein employed is much longer and coarser than that woven into felted cloths. After having been well scoured and dried, \t is passed through a "plucker," or machine consisting of spiked rollers, made to revolve so as to cleanse and straighten the fibres. It is now prepared for " caixhng,"or " combing," the latter when performed by hand being a very laborious and disagreeable opera- tion. The succeeding process, whereby the woollen fibres are wrought into worsted yarn, is analogous both to the preparation of woollen and of cotton goods, and the spinning resembles that in other branches of textile art. It may be likewise seen in the room where other similar operations are conducted. One. of the most curious of these machines is the Jacquard, producing its effect by means of a vast num- ber of perforated cards. For the execution of any parr ticular pattern, as many cards are required as there are weft threads in the design. But the holes in each of these vary greatly ; in some there may be thirty, some fifty or sixty. It would be needless to describe here the modus operandi ; suffice it to say, that the disposi- tion of the holes in each card depends chiefly on the nature and size of the pattern in the direction of the weft, and the number of cards on the pattern in the direction of the warp, each set of cards being only available for a single pattern ; ninety-thousand having been consumed in giving effect to the design displayed upon a cotton table cover representing the Great Exhibition Building. Of late years it has become the practice to inter- mingle much cotton with certain stuffs — such as Para- matta and Orleans, wherein the warp is cotton, the weft only of worsted. But if we advert to an admix- ture, in which a desire for cheapness has been the pre- vailing motive, what will our readers say to certain shawls manufactured (by Messrs. Bliss, of Chipping Norton) of the soft down of the beaver. Their appear- ance is at once novel and unique ; and if the cost do not deter purchasers, we may confidently predict a great run for these goods. In softness and silkiness of texture, they exceed the richest velvet, while for warmth and lightness they stand unequalled. The same manufactur ers have sent in what are termed royal angola, alpacas vicaua, and royal shawls, all admirable of their kind, but none approaching in dehcacy to the first named beaver. . But the case before which the greatest number of admiring visitors are usually congregated is that of Messrs. Gott and Sons, of Leeds (No. 73). Here may be seen in wonderful perfection and beauty the end and aim of all the processes hourly going on in the building around, not to mention many others of the same kind that could not be exhibited. The fine cloths here tastefully grouped according to their destiny, quality, and hue, are respectively intended for the home, the Russian, the Chinese, and the American markets. Here too, as in contemplating the cottons it is curious and not uninstructive to observe the eagerness with which some nations select the gaudiest, and others the soberest apparel. -♦ The .Irish Confederates in Australia. — The Irish Exile states that Messrs. The Volume opens with a rich and elaborate Article on the subject of Cotton, in which it is stated, that the average imports have been ascertaiaed at about 550 millions of pounds weight, exclusive of deductions for exports. Of this quantity, 500 million pounds are employed in manufactures, the annual value of raw material thus employed being about ten millions sterling, from which it will be seen, that England is a considerable customer to the United States, and that the close of the English Markets to the American Continent would go a great way to extinguish the trade. The total annual value of manufactured material has been approximately represented at about thirty-six millions sterling. The effect on the population of the manufacturing districts is not less surprising. These few figures give some idea of the importance of this one branch of British Commerce. This is followed by paper . printing, and bookbinding, forming, undoubtedly, one of the most interesting portions of this splendid volume. Arts. XXN, 4lcpr 617 much in this section we would like to quote, but we must refer our readers to the volume. The statistics which are here given are strikingly illustrative of the progress of England; the printing resources of London are stupendous beyond credibility. In one of the greatest establishments of the Metropolis, twenty machines are constantly occupied, each of which is capable of throwing off from 3,000 to 4,000 impressions per hour, and, in addition, a large number of printing machines for fine work are employed. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Friday the 25th ult. being a half-crown day, the sum of 2,9841. was taken at the doors, and 26,882 persons entered the Building. The number of visitors on Thursday was, by mistake, understated to the extent of about 4,000. On Saturday the sum taken at the doors amounted to 1,4781., and the number of visitors was 10,399. From the opening up to this day, no less than 2,929,778 visits have been paid to the Building; the sum of 66,6381. 5s. has been received from the sale of season tickets, and the amount taken in payments at the doors has been 181,0111. Os. With subscriptions, therefore, the total incomings of the Royal Commission considerably exceed 300,0001. On Monday the sum of 3,194?. l3s. was taken at the doors, and 67,170 persons entered the Building. Of these a very large party came from the town and neighbourhood of Reading. They came by the South-Western Railway, and marched in procession from the Waterloo station to Hyde Park, headed by a band of music, and rendered conspicuous by a profusion of banners. On Tuesday 68,496 persons visited the Building, and 32811. 10s. was the amount of money taken at the doors, and for season tickets 61. 6s. On Wednesday the receipts at the doors amounted to 2,8351. 6s., and the number of visitors was 58,382. On Thursday the number of persons who entered the Building was 57,849, and the receipts at the doors amounted to 2800Z. 16s. The price of season tickets is now reduced from 31. and 21. to 30s. and 11., and the Commission have come to a reso- lution by which the sale of those tickets ceases on the 31st of August. The 5s. entrance fee on Saturdays is to be re- duced immediately after the prorogation of Parliament to 2s. 6d., but the immense crowds that still flock to the Exhi- bition on the shilling days render it in the meantime imprac- ticable, in the view of the Commission, to adopt measures for admitting a larger proportion of the humbler classes than now find their way into the Crystal Palace. Two accidents happened in the Building on Tuesday. On entering the British nave in the morning, Thomas's large fountain was seen to be in ruins, the group of Acis and Gala- tea, at the top, having tumbled down, and crushed in their fall two or three of the syrens who had been so faithfully sup- plying them with water. The other accident happened in the medicevalcourt,inwhich the habtitue mightbave observed arow of five or six silver candelabra suspended from a gilt cornice, and filled with candles, after the manner of Roman Catholic churches; the rope which supported the cornice suddenly gave way, the silver lamps tumbled down, and were much damaged by the fall, and the candles were strewed all over the court. The damage has been estimated at some hundreds of pounds, and the court is temporarily closed during repairs. An interesting event, which would have rendered the Great Exhibition the birthplace of a youthful visitor, had nearly taken place one day last week. A young lady, accompanied by her husband and two female friends, who had been waiting for some time at the south entrance in the vain hope of ob- taining a conveyance, was suddenly seized with symptoms which indicated that she was on the point of becoming a mother. With the aid of Mr. Duncombe, the assistant-secre- tary, and several other of the officials, the lady was conveyed to the commissioners' room, and laid on the sofa. After the lapse of upwards of an hour she was placed in a cab, and shortly afterwards gave birth to her first child, a fine boy. We understand that both mother and child are progressing as favourably as might be expected under the peculiar circum- stances of the case. OPINIONS OF THE PUBLIC PRESS. (From the Times.) The Crystal Palace was on Tuesday night weighed in the balance of the State, and while Mr. Labouchere and the Chancellor of the Exchequer held aloof, and Inglis and Goulburn threw in their hostile opinions, it seemed for a time on the verge of its doom. Happily it is now respited, at least to the anniversary of its opening. A majority of 75 to 47 voted its preservation to the 1st of next May, by which day there will be time to collect opinions, to receive estimates, and to acquire some experience as to the winter capabilities of the structure. The objection most urged on Tuesday, and, indeed, the only objection that could reasonably be urged, against taking time for consideration, was a supposed pledge on the part of the Government that the Building should come down as soon as it had answered its immediate purpose. Indeed, as if delay were likely to be dangerous, a singular anxiety has been displayed to settle the question at once on the ground of public faith. To all intreaties for time, the standing answer has been, "I cannot find it in the bond." The sworn enemies of Troy were not more anxious to envelope its very origin with the charge of perjury and deceit than the Kensington chiefs are to attach the blot of broken faith to the structure before their eyes. A voice of indignation and despair seems to rise from the midst of the hostile camp,- " Nescis heu, perdita, needum Laomedontiadwe sentis peijuria gentis ?" Now, though it might be exceedingly proper for Lord Seymour, Sir Charles Wood, and Lord John Russell, to admit a solemn pledge, and to shew that the Building would never have been placed where it was but for the express un- derstanding that it would he removed, there nevertheless remains the question, who were the parties in this compact ? On this point we must hold with Mr. Wakley that the compact was made by the public with the public. Whatever Ministers may have promised or said, the thing was actually done by Parliament. The House of Commons, by a vote, from which we dissented at the time, placed the Building where it is. The House of Commons made no engagement with anybody besides itself. This was, then, a public reso- lution made by the State in its most popular assembly-an inward resolution in the mind of the Legislature. The House of Commons was acting with no party or interest, but with itself. It made up its mind to build a temporary palace for the Exhibition in IHyde Park, just as a man might resolve to erect a tent, or a temporary bridge, or a Chinese pagoda, or a maypole. In such a case a man might, perhaps, be charged with inconsistency or folly if be perpetuated the decorations of affte, but certainly not with breach of faith. An engagement may always be dissolved by the party with whom it is made; but when a State has only made an Lengagement with itself, it requires no consent but its own to . the determination of that engagement. It is true that there were certain parties which violently objected to the site chosen for the Exhibition, and it is true that some of those parties object as violently to the maintenance of the Building . on that site; but the engagement to remove it was not made bwith them. They were really not consulted in the affair at all. Their consent was neither asked nor given. In spite of 3the temporary character intended for the edifice, they never lfor a moment relaxed their hostility to it. How, then, can they now plead an engagement? What have they to do with the Building in Hyde Park, except that they do not like it, and never did like it ? In several respects, of course it would be desirable that another site could be found for the Building. Even as regards those parts of the metropolis which are out of its disturbing influences, it is rather too far for their convenience. The r truth is that a site was required that should be both far and near; near enough for access, and far enough not to occupy one's space or circumscribe one's view. What the Commis- . sioner's wanted was an Aladdin's lamp, that should light them to an endless succession of magnificent haIls, situated nowhere, cumbering no ground, monopolising no acres, cutting off no view. But where wras such a place to be found? If anybody fwill look at the map of London he will see that the Crystal Palace could not be stowed in a corner. If it is to be any- where, it must occupy space, and there is hardly such a thing as eighteen acres of clear, dry, level space near the metro- t polis. he appropriation of the present site is certainly to I be regretted, not merely because it happens to interfere with r the view from a few windows, the owners of which had no legal right to the view of the Park, but because those eighteen acres are taken away from the turf, and the air set apart for the public. But, now that the Building is there, and now that it presents the opportunity of the finest winter garden in the world, and promises to supply the greatest want of this metropols, we should very much deplore its destruction. The myriads of foreigners who, most of them for the first time, lhave come to visit this metropolis, and who must notice, in I some respects, the nakedness of the land, will think us down. Eright mad if we demolish one of the very few things that ?? has to be proud of. Excepting our Parks, which ireally are not to be surpassed in Europe, we have nothing to shew that is not more than matched in much smaller capitals. In churches, museums, picture galleries, antiquities, and na- tional monuments, we have little to boast of, while the dingi- ness of our buildings and the opaqueness of our atmosphere shew what we have to the very worst advantage. In the Crystal Palace we really have something colossal, unique, handsome, if not quite picturesque; and we have no doubt I well adapted to many purposes of recreation, instruction, and I health. The mad painter who turned his figures into skele- 3 tons, if his pictures were allowed to remain within his reach, . could not do a more absurd thing than we should be guilty of, I if we condemned this wonderful structure, scarcely yet finished, still less fully enjoyed, to wanton annihilation.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Prince Albert has addressed autograph letters of thanks to all the Foreign Commissioners, His Royal Highness has also written to the Council of the Society of Arts, and, after making a due acknowledgment of the services of the Society in the course of the Exhibition, suggests for the consideration of the Council the expediency of having the beneficial results of the display just terminated discussed in a series of lectures, to be delivered weekly during the forthcoming session of the Society, by persons the most eminent in their respective departments. The letter of His Royal Highness was laid before the Council on Monday, and they have, we understand, cordially entered into the proposal. Her Majesty has transmitted to Mrs. Dilke, for her acceptance, a handsome bracelet in token of the attention which she has received from Mr. Dilke during her frequent visits to the Exhibition, and, in the same amiable and considerate spirit, the portraits of the Royal children have been forwarded to Mr. Dilke himself. Loan BROUGHAM—AS for Lord Brougham's "es centricity," to the vulgar eye it stands confessed a fact. In the vulgar acceptation of the word, Lord Brougham is daringly eccentric. In free countries it is not permitted to men to differ from their neighbours, except in very slight and imperceptibie shades. Custom ont- 1 tyrannises absolutienr, In France or in Germany one may do as one likes, because society is ground dowaby a ruthless despotism; but in England, do as you like, ' ifyou dare! Lord Brougham, it seems, chooses to do as he likes. After a long day of arduous labour he prefers a walk to a ride, and if his blood, wants circalating, he walks fast. When he speaks bespeaks aloud, havingbeen used to so as a matter of business all his life. If his hands be cold lie puts them in his pockets; though fashions change for the benefit of tailors, Lord Brougham sticks (as many a north countryman has done before him) to the check or the plaid; not being particular about hats, be does not wear his stuck horizontally on the , top of his bead, an inverted chimneypot, bet lets it go aslant on the beek, a practice less painful to the forehead; being naturally of an ardentl and excitable temperament, he uses much gesticulation in talking—about as much as a Frenchman would require in order to tell you it is a fine day; in short,lord Brougham commits , divers offences against the leaden sovereignty oFoustons, all which are peculiarly shocking in a Peer. Being, too, naturally of an affable and sociable disposition, he fraternises quickly with those for whom betakes a liking, and spouts out his thoughts and , feelings, instead of flittering them, as your grave ones do. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Tun OPPICIkt CATlLOGlTlM—Preptirations on a large scale have been made by the contractors for printing the various catalogues of the Great Exhibition. The first step toward the accomplishment of this vast undertaking was the creation of the type necessary to print four editions —and Messrs. Clowes and Son, being type-founders as well as printers, came to the resolution of having the" whole of the type cast specially for the purpose. Their first effort was directed to produce the type for the small English, French and German catalogues; the quantity east for the purpose was 16,000 lbs. For the large and illustrated edition they have, in addition to their own foundries, employed those of Messrs. Figgins, Messrs. Bexley and Co., and Mr. Caslon, of London, und Messrs. Miller and Richards, of Edinburgh. The joint exertions of these firms have added 25,000 lbs. more to the general stock set apart for this vast undertaking; making a total of 41,000 lbs.—a weight sufficient to set up 48 Times newspapers. The casting of this large quantity of type gave employment to 250 persons for ten weeks. The number of separate pieces in 20 tons of type amounts to upwards of 26 millions, and each type or piece of metal passes through the hands of five persons in the process of manufacture. THE BUILDING.—On Tuesday some further experiments were made for the purpose of testing the strength of the galleries of the building of the Exhibition. A short time suice experiments were made for the purpose of testing to what extent oscillation could be conveyed to the gallery by the regular and irregular motion of a living load, and also to ascertain whether the provisions whkh had been made to meet such such contingencies were sufficient. The mode adopted was to construct a perfect bay of gallerr, with its floors, bi n d ers , g i r d ers , and connecting pieces, in every respect tomplete and similar to the actual gallery, supported on four points bedded on temporary foundations. Rows of planks, the full width of the platform, led up to it on the one side, and down from it on the other, so that a row of men as wide as the gallery were able to march up, across, and down in close column. Three hundred workmen were assembled and allowed to cover the platform and planks connected with it, and they were also crowded together into the smallest space on the gallery in which they could stand, The men then continued to jump simultaneously for several minutes, and finally the whole of the men of the Sappers and Miners employed at the Exhibition were marched over and around the bays, and. were made to mark time in the most trying manner. With the result of the various tests thus employed, the eminent scientific men present, including Mr. W. Cubitt, Mr. I. K. Brunel, and Mr. Locke, 3 1 . P., exp r e sse d th emse l ves perfectly- satisfied. It is difficult, however, to satisfy everybody ; indeed, it would appear that nothing but the realisation of the oft-repeated predictions that the whole structure would one day tumble about the ears of visitors," will over satisfy some persons. By some members of this class of objectors, it was urged that the trial ought not to be considered a satisfactory one, inasmuch as the planks leading up to the gallery served as buttresses to it, and prevented that vibration and oscillation which would have been felt had the test been applied continuously to a further extent of gallery. On the part of those, on the contrary ' who considered the test as sati s fact or y, it was contended that the load which was borne on the planks leading to and from the gallery represented the amount of pressure which would be produced by the crowding of adjacent bays in the gallery. Practically to settle the question as to the effect, of the vibration of a moving weight along the gallery WAS the object of the experiment made on Tuesday. For this purpose a square frame, containing 36 compartments, was placed upon the ground, and a 68 pounder shot was placed in each of the divisions, the shot resting upon the floor of the gallery. Upon the top of this frame were placed six ethers of a similar construction, in each of which was placed a similar number of the shot, making the total number 252, the weight of which was 17,1361b5, or rather more than seven-and-half. tons. The shot thus placed was drawn, by mean ni of pulleys and levers, along the centre of a large portion of the gallery, and notwithstanding this very severe test, which we have no doubt will be considered satisfactory, no sensible deflection or vibration was produced. It is intended to apply the test to the whole of the building, and we have no doubt but that the results will be perfectly satisfactory. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Saturday £1852, 2s. 6d. was taken at the doors of the building, the number of visitors being 20,236. With but two exceptions — viz. Tuesday the 15th of July, when the number of visitors was 74,122, and Monday, the 21st of July, when there were 70,640 — Monday was the most numerously attended day since the opening of the Exhibition. The number returned by the police was 68,542, the amount received being £3295 15s. Immense as the concourse of visitors was on Monday, it was exceeded on Tuesday, 69,346 persons having entered the building, and the sum of £3303 4s. being tak<>n at the doors. Notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather, the receipts at the doors, on Wednesday, amounted to £2830 lis., the number of visitors being 59,050. The total amount of monies in the hands of the Great Exhibition treasury, up to Saturday last, was £473,028. The Close of the Exhibition. — We understand it has been decided that the two days which will remain between the close of the Exhibition to the public, on Saturday the 11th, and the meeting of the commifi- sioners on Wednesday the 15th of October, will be devoted exclusively to exhibitors and their friends. It is intended to send to each exhibitor a ticket, which will admit himself and two friends upon Monday the* 13th, and Tuesday the 14 th, without any payment for admission ; and the ticket will also admit the exhibitor alone upon the 15th, to the ceremony of receiving the reports of the jurors, and other business connected with the proceedings of the day. — Morning Chronicle. Great Foot Race. — The great foot race between Heyes and Tetlow, for £100 a side, came off on Monday, at Aintree. Heyes was at one time 100 yards a head, and Tetlow, after a vigorous effort, succeeded in reducing that distance, but when near home he fell, and Heyes, of course, won easily. The Alleged Murder of a Policeman at Green- wich. — The man William Cressy, charged with the wilful murder of police-constable James Hastie, in Tinderbox- alley, Deptford, on the night of the 20th of February, 1846, was brought up on remand before Mr. Traill, at the Green- wich Police-court, on Saturday, but in consequence of it being found absolutely necessary that the investigation should still be followed up, some fresh and important evidence was not gone into, and the prisoner was again remanded. Monument to Wordsworth. — A monument to the memory of the poet Wordsworth has been erected in Grasmere Church, and it bears the following inscription : — "To the memory of William Wordsworth, a true philoso- pher and poet, who by the special gift and calling of Almighty God, whether he discoursed on man or nature, failed not to lift up the heart to holy things. Tired not of maintaining the cause of the poor and simple ; and so, in perilous times, was raised up to be a chief minister, not only of noblest poesy, but of high and sacred truth. The memorial is placed here by his friends and neighbours, in testimony of respect, affection, and gratitude." — Carlisle Journal. Election of Lord Mator of London. — AJ Common Hall was held on Monday, for the purpose of electing a Lord Mayor for the ensuing year, when the Court of Alder- men recommended Alderman Hunter, the senior alderman, to the office for the year ensuing, which was confirmed by the Livery, and agreed to unanimously. On the evening of the same day, the Lord Mayor entertained the Lord Mayor Elect and the members of the Court of Aldermen at dinner. Covers were laid for 70 in the long parlour, and there were also present the Recorder, the chairmen of the several cor- porations of the city, the sheriffs, their chaplains, the city officers, and several private friends of the Lord Mayor. Return of Sir John Ross. — Rear-Admiral Sir John Ross arrived at the Admiralty on Saturday, having reached Stranraer in the Felix the day before. The Mary tender is left in Barrow's Straits. We understand that the gallant admiral, for want ot any further or more exciting intelli- gence to communicate, brings home the old defunct story of the murder in Baffin's Bay — the invention of his own Esquimaux interpreter last year, and proved to be a fiction to the satisfaction of the whole squadron. Sir John can add absolutely nothing to the authentic tacts brought home by Captain Penny — having, as wo understand, parted company with Captain Austin on the same day on which the latter left Captain Penny off Cornwallis Islands. — Morning Chronicle. Suspected Murder of a Wife. — A man named Joseph Parker, of middle age, was charged at the Worship-street police-office, on Monday, with killing his wife on the pre- vious Saturday evening. Both the prisoner and the deceased were, it appeared, confirmed drunkards, and had been taken to their house by the neighbours in a state of intoxication two or three hours before the latter was found in bed insensible, and bleeding from a wound in the forehead. The husband would give no expla- nation of the injury, and the unfortunate woman was removed by the ponce to St. Bartholomew's Hospital, where she died in a few hours. The prisoner had been seen to beat her during the afternoon, but there appeared to be no direct evidence of his having inflicted upon her the fatal injury. He was remanded for a week, saying in his defence that the deceased had injured herself by falling out of bed. No weapon with which the wound could have been inflicted was found in the room. Dreadful Murder in Somersetshire. — A murder of the most shocking description has been perpetrated near Frome, in the county of Somerset. The victim is a young girl, only 15 years of age, named Sarah Watts, who resided with her father and mother at a small farm in the West Woodlands, three miles from that town. It appears that the parents left her at home about nine in the morning on Wednesday, and proceeded to Frome market with butter, but on their return, at three o'clock in the afternoon, they were horror-stricken by discovering that during their absence the poor girl had been murdered, and her lifeless body lay prostrate on the floor of the dairy. The wounds on the body and head of the deceased appeared to have been inflicted by some blunt instrument ; her dress was very much torn, and the marks of bloody fingers were visible on the wall of the dairy. The property taken from the house by the murderer consisted of a black coat and waistcoat, a drab spotted shawl, and a small quantity of butter and cheese.— Morning Chronicle.

The upper part of ihe ridge plates has a cast iron ornament running along which gives a pleasing finish to tbe roof. A ventilating shaft rises from the centre of the roof, furnished with a flap valve for the emission of heated air. The room is lighted by four windows at the front and four at the back, all of which open as French easements. THE GREAT EXHIBITION The great building in Hyrle Park is now a splendid ruin, and, with some trifling exceptions, oue half of it may be said to be a desert. The British exhibitors having been originally limited to tbe 31st of October for clearing out their goods, anil having had some previous experience of the peremptory cha- racter ofthe executive, set about the removal with such good will that little remains to do in tbe ensuing week. An exten- sion of time, however, has been granted to Nov. 22, ns some of the larger and more unwieldy tuasse3 of Machinery will require some time for their taking asunder and packing up. Colonel, now Sir Wm. Reid, the chairman of the executive committee, paid his last visit to the building on Friday, previously to his departure to assume his new duties as Governor of Malta. Many of the gentlemen who had been his colleagues and fellow labourers during the last twelve months assembled to bid him farewell, and express their wishes for his prosperity. With tlie exception of Wyatt's equestrian statues of the Queen and Prince Albert, which still keep possession of the transept, the loug array of sculptured forms that surrounded this central part of the building has vanished. At the remote north end, however, whether by accident or design, with her back against the Colebrook Dale gates, stands Mr. Forrester's statue oi " The Forsaken," her eyes turned up to the glass roof, and looking the very iinpersonitication of despair as she draws a scanty robe over her shoulder. The attitude and character ofthe figure accord well with the locality, which is now com- pletely deserted and stripped of its former brilliant ilei-orations. In the English nave the two colossal statues of SirWm. Follett and the Duke of Rutland stare curiously at one another from opposite sides, now that they have nothing else to look at, for the whole of the compartments, down to the Mediaeval Court, have been completely cleared out. and even from this most of the valuable articles have been removed. Farther on, the bronze statue of Andromeda, which has been purchased by her Majesty, elevated on a wheeled truck, stands patiently awaiting her further progress down the nave, with her hands chained behind her. We then come to a wide and extensive waste, above which towers the large stone cross, still untouched. Still nearer the western entrance the Colebrook Dale dome is rapidly falling to pieces, while Shakspeare looks calmly on at the work of destruction ; and then we enter upon the region of bales, boxes, packing-cases, and hampers, which cover a vast extent of flooring up to the very door through which they are being carried out in rapid succession. Of the varied contents of die two large carriage departments nothing remains but " the Vic- toria omnibus," which is probably destined to carry out the last exhibitor; the agricultural implements are gone, and all the nulway and locomotive carriages but one. The machinery department shows tbe most striking murks of havoc — wide rents aud chasms in the flooring, massive brick foundations, and pools of water, indicating the position of some of the com- plicated and ingenious machinery which was here collected. Indeed so rapid has been the work of removal in the English and colonial side that we could almost enumerate all the articles that remain. The galleries, both of the English and foreign sides, are completely stripped, and as it was here the most valuable and perishable goods were displayed, the whole of the canvas covering has been removed from the roof, no further damage being to be apprehended from leakage. As we ap- proach the foreign side the idea of a gigantic barricade natural! v presents itself, the pile of packing-owes and boxes at tlie en- trance covering almost an acre of ground. Threading our way through this immense mass, indications of activity in striking contrast to the descried aspect of the English side meet us in every quarter. All the statuary has been removed with the exception of Godfrey de Bouillon and the Mdzeppa group: some carefully wrapped up in paper, and laid at length iv carriages and boxes for the convenience of transport; others hedged in with all manner of wooden bars and braces, which have not in all cases been sufficient to protect the fragile material from injury. To become the personal chattels of kings was ignominious enough for mankind; to sink into a drove of cattle was a still more ignoble lot. Men will overlook anything but a paltry attempt to cheat them on the part of monarchs—an outrage on their feelings as well as an insult to their understanding—despicable in a king, in a pope unpardonable. The speaker proceeded to trace this systematic habit of deception (the resource of timid and imbecile minds) in the earliest acts of his pontificate, and in the wording of his various encyclical and political manifestoes, whether in the full noon of his popularity, or in the disastrous eclipse of Gaeta: he never could be got to look a plain question in the face, his object being constantly to mystify and delude. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Yesterday 2,4651. 10s. was the sum taken at the doors of the building, the number of visitors being 50,233. Singularly enough, the sale of season tickets still continues, and in the diurnal bulletin of receipts 81. 103. figures as realised from that source. The expediency of a reduction in the charges of admission is now attracting much attention, end it becomes obvious that one half-crown day in the week would be sufficient. Some of the authorities still hesitate about the propriety of bringing the price down lower than a shilling under any circumstances ; but when it is considered that a large proportion of the labouring classes in the metropolis have not yet visited the spectacle which their industry has largely helped to create, it is to be hoped that some arrangements may be made for enabling them to gratify their curiosity in this matter. If the workman could be expected to go alone to the Crystal Palace, the present charge would raise no serious obstacle ; but he naturally wishes to bring his family along with him, that they may share in his delight; and why should he not be indulged in that laudable desire ? At least the experiment might be tried, and if it does not answer it will be easy to return to the old system. Notwithstanding the short remaining space of time during which the great display is to remain open to the public, additional contributions of great interest and value continue to arrive from abroad. A ship's load from Sweden has just been announced, and will be added to the department of that country in a day or two. Several chef-d'seuvres of art, also, have recently been received, and among them one of surpassing merit by the celebrated Dutch sculptor, Van der Yen, representing the Temptation of Eve. It is placed in the nave, and attracts an immense amount of attention. The treatment of the subject is bold and original, the form of the first woman being developed with a freedom, grace, and life-like effect which cannot be too highly praised. It is rarely that so wonderful a specimen of the plastic art is to be seen in this country, and one of its chief excellences is that in its composition there is no trace of that disposition to borrow from the classic styles of antiquity, instead of relying upon nature, which so often detracts from the merit of modern sculpture. Mr. Spense, an English artist at Rem; has also lately contributed a statue of Burns' " Highland Mary," which is much and justly admired. The Executive Committee still continue to receive numerous applications for admission into the British department of the Exhibition, which, however, they always reject. These are made chiefly with the object of obtaining the advantages of patent right secured to exhibitors fora year. Yesterday morning an interesting series of experiments took place at the west:end of the building for the purpose of determining the relative merits of Porter's and Rogers' anchors. The trials made were conducted in the presence of Mr. Lindsay, the well-known shipowner, but no satisfactory conclusion was arrived at, and it was armnged that the Admiralty should be invited to examine and decide upon a question in which the whsle marine of this country is so largely interested.. Both the anchors thus brought into . competition appear to have a decided superiority over that of Sir William Parker, which is the one chiefly used in the navy. They differ, however, materially from each other in the principles of their construction, the patent of Lieutenant Rogers having its arms and flakes of a wedge-like shape, while in Porter's patent the arms move upon a pivot in such a way that while one holds on the ground the fluke of the other presses upon the shank, thus increasing the power of resistance. SHIPSTON.ONSTOUR.-It is not a little remarkable that a second crop of wheat, which is now in flower, has sprung up in those fields that were either much injured or entirely destroyed, by the late terrible hail-storm. And even in those fields which were mown after the storm, a second crop has sprung up, and appears likely to be ready for the sickle by the letter end of September. In those cases where the first crop was left standing it is considerable, and the farmers are much puzzled in deciding whether the first crop should be sacrificed to secure the second, or the second to secure the first, as both cannot be secured. It unfortunately happens, in several cases, after the wheat was mown, either the ground was ploughed, or cattle were turned upon it to eat the springing blade. This was done, of course, in ignorance of the extraordinary compensating power of nature in the vegetable world, in the case of injury, or apparent destruction.— Oxford Chronicle. Another of thaw terrible accidents which, from time to time, occur in the working of coal mines, took place this morning at the Malays Vale works, in the parish of Bedminster, near this city, and has lost to society, and to those more immediately dependent on them, five valuable lives. Intelligence of the catastrophe first reached Bristol as early as six o'clock in the morning, and upon my proceeding to the spot I found the colliery surrounded by a large crowd men and women, chiefly fathers and mothers, wives, brother, sisters, or children, of the colliers who were known to be . down the pit, all of them influenced by the most feelings of suspense and alarm, and some of them Tent to their feelings in cries and supplications, and lye in imprecations on the parties connected with the executive department of the works, which it was truly heartrending to hear. A little alter three o'clock, one of the working parties having come out of the pit, ten others entered the bucket or cart, and were lowered down the shaft, which is upwards ate 240 fathoms in depth, to replace them. The work of lowering proceeded without the occurrence of anything unusual until the cart had reached to within a very few feet of the bottom. Upon its reaching to the depth of the first vein, somewhere about 200 fathoms, five of the men got out of it. and proceeded to their work in that part of the colliery, and the cart, with four men end a lad, was then lowered towards the bottom vein, and had, as before remarked, de-elided to within a few feet of the bottom, when the rope, 011 its passing over the second wheel immediately above the mouth of the shaft, suddenly parted, and in the fare of the terrified vanger, the mass, which with the cart arid bonnet must have weighed three or four tons, was precipitated to the bottom. Those in charge of the works sought to give temporary comfort to the afflicted by suggesting that as the cart was su close to the bottom when the rope broke, the inmates might have escaped without considerable injury ; hut to those censer- mint with the matter it became at once evident that their lives were sacrificed. The iron bonnet which was suspended above their heads by the tension of the rope, must upon the parting have fallen upou thin, as likewise the rope itself ; hut besides these there was depth of several feet of water at the foot of the shaft unprotected by any stage or covering into which they would have been precipitated. At length, after the down mail had passed, they went on towards Bristol, passed through Bath, taking in water there, and steamed on very slowly so far as Fox's Wood just before the entrance of the No. 3 llrislington tunnel, where, either through the want of coke, or some mishap the engine, the train broke down and came a standstill: It must unfortunately happened that there was a return engine and tender coming from ' Bath, and after the train had been standing for about ten minutes, this engine, which was seen approaching by some of the passengers, ran into it from behind. Among some eighteen or twenty more or less injured were several respectable tradesmen of Bristol, but it is gratifying to believe that there were no bones broken, and that as all the parties were able on reaching the terminus to proceed to their homes no serious consequences will result. The Marquis of Anglesey will hear with a feeling of satisfaction that if our cousins beat us in yacht-building, they are equally pre-eminent in the manufacture of artificial legs. In the latter branch of industry their superiority will not be grudged, and they really owe society some act of reparation for having introduced among us Colt's revolvers. The artificial leg patented by Mr. Palmer, is, in its way, a most admirable, ingenious, and philanthropic contrivance, and its invention is so remarkably characteristic of the country from whence it comes, that we cannot resist the temptation of inviting attention to it. The patentee in some way or other lost his leg, and, having tried the best substitutes hitherto devised for such a case, like a true American, he set himself to think whether he could not improve upon them. His study of the subject was crowned with the most striking success, and he exemplifies that success in his own person by walking about almost without any perceptible lameness, and with an apparent ease and comfort which are truly surprising. He publishes annually at Philadelphia a journal, which he calls Palmer's Patent Artificial Leg Reporter and Surgical Adjuvant. This curiously entitled periodical accompanied a specimen of the leg to the Exhibition, and the Ist chapter of vol. 3, No. 1, we find commenced by this heading, "Fugitive thoughts on amputation." From another chapter, entitled " Synopsis of the invention," we gather that it is distinguished by its perfect combination of lightness with strength, and by the extraordinary fidelity with which it imitates nature. Having closely examined it we can testify to its merits on all the leading points specified, nor have we any reason to doubt that the enamelled surface of this leg, as stated, " is rivalled only by the mechanism of nature, and that a lady may wear silk hose and slippers without betraying the loss she has sus. t ained." Mr. Palmer has received extensive orders for his patent in this country, and the public may soon . expect t o see t i m b er -t oe d veterans no more stumping about Greenwich or Chelsea. The dentist who fills the beauty's mouth with a set of pearly teeth, and the artist who dyes the grey or red head, and covers baldness with an artificial profusion of locks, have now added to their amiable deceptions those of the American artificial leg, which may occasionally lead to awkward mistakes, but cannot fail to be regarded as a great boon to suffering humanity. The number of persons employed at present in the building is 2,000, and under the impelling force of this array of labourers every department of the works is advancing towards completion with marvellous rapidity. More than one-half of the glazing of the transept is now finished. Oc- cational suspension of the roof glaxing here is unavoidable, in consequence of the diffleulty experienced by the con- tractors in obtaining a continuous and sufficient supply of glass of the requisite shape and dimensions. Two days were thus lost in the course of last week. The quantity of glazing yet unfinished in other parts of the building is comparatively inconsiderable. The face boarding by which the lower portion of the structure is surrounded, and which will furnish the greater part of the wall space available for exhibitors is almost entirely completed, Since onr last report large addi- tions have been made to the quantity of flooring laid down both on the ground and gallery tiers, and the erection of the simple but elegant tailing, by which the galleries are to be fenced, is being natively proceeded with. The paint- ing of that part of the roof of the transept where the glezing ha been finished was commenced yesterday. The colours used on the ribs are blue, yellow, and red, the blue predo- minating. Temporary rough boardings are being constructed to indicate the spaces in which it is proposed to separate the productions of the various exhibiting nations one from the other. It has been determined that the half of the building westward of the transept is to be devoted to the recep- tion of the productions of the United Kisgdom and the Colonies. In the eastern aisles and galleries will be grouped the materials and manufactures contributed by foreign countries. In determining the positions assigned to them on what may be termed the map of the Exhibi. tion, the executive committee have been guided chiefly by the latitude of the places, but as various causer of alteration may arise previous to their final adjust- ment, any statement of the order in which it is at present proposed to arrange them would be premature. There is no doubt, however, but that there will be " ample room and verge enough for all." Permission has at length been obtained from the Commissioners of Woods and Forests to remove one of the trees near the grand entrance, the preservation of which was owing to the persevering exertions of Colonel Sibthorp. Yesterday the Duchess of Cambridge, the Duke of Cam- bridge, the Grand Duke and Duchess of Mecklenburg, and the Princess Mary visited the building. DEATH CAUSED BY JUMPING FROM A RAILWAY TRAIN.—A melancholy accident occurred on Thursday morning at the Wingfield station, on the Midland Railway, which resulted in the death of one young man and the serious injury of another. Richard Griffith, who keeps the Post-office at Higham, near Alfreton, and a companion named Mosley had been to Derby, where they remained all night at the house of a relative of the former—Mr. Hudson, ticket collector at the Derby station. Mosley having to b e at home to his employment the first thing on Thursday morning, Griffiths agreed to accompany him, though his time was by no means so pressing. An excursion train from London to Leeds was upon the point of leaving the station about six o'clock, and whether they considered this the ordinary six o'clock train, or whether they believed it would stop at Wingfield station, is not known, but in this train they seated themselves. Finding, on their arrival at Wingfield that the train would not stop, they unfortunately jumped out. Mosley sprang upon the platform, and, rebounding, fell underneath the carriages and was killed on the spot. His companion was more fortunate, but whether he will ultimately survive the shock we of course cannot say. When a sufficient quantity of the material was obtained, it was sent to Mr. .Pollock, of Leeds, for the purpose of manufacture. The Cashmere wool in its raw state is peculiar -in its character, being composed of two distinct I materials-one being of a very fine, soft, and pliable quality, and the other very hard, stiff, Iand coarse. The former is rich and beautiful .to the touch, and equal, perhaps superior, to the finest continental lambs' wool. This constitutes the wool, properly so called. The other por- tion is known as "kemp," and is a rough, coarse-looking hair, very irregular in its staple, and constantly avoided by the manufacturer, since the admixture of even a small quantity deteriorates the appearance of the manufactured fabric. To separate these two very distinct quali- ties of wool from each other is an operation of no small difficulty, since, when the fleece is shorn from the goat, they are indiscriminately in- termingled; and consequently the operation has to be effected by hand, no known machinery being capable of doing it properly. The manufacturers were, therefore, in this instance, compelled to have E recourse to the assistance of all who, from public- spirited motives, were inclined to aid them in pro- . moting the experiment of the Prince; and it is a re- markable fact that for several months the assorting of the wool and " kemp" of which the fabrics now Iexhibited are composed occupied more than 1,000 persons during their leisure hours. Many mem- bers of some of the most respectable families of the West Riding undertook this "labour of love;" and they have received as an acknowledgment a tastefully designed certificate, headed with an engraving of the Crystal Palace, setting forth that they had been so employed, being desirous to pro- ,mote the full realisation of the wishes of the Prince in the manufacture of his Cashmere goats' wool. Of course, the quantity produced was small, and scarcely adequate even to the manufacture of the shawls and dress goods here displayed. The kemp," or refuse, was, however, used for the Imanufacture of the coarse woollen cloths already alluded to, and by this means every portion of the material was worked up. How far the re- sult may be of value in a commercial point of view is doubtful; but any attempt of this kind is praiseworthy, and though, under ordinary cir- cumstances, the experiment would have been a very costly one, yet it is impossible to say whether more extended attention to the growth and prepara- tion of the material may not be of more value t han at first sight appears. After being open for five months and 11 days and concentrating in that time a larger amount of admiration than has probably ever been given within the same period to the works of man, the pageant terminates, the doors of the Crystal Palace no longer yield to the open sesame of a money, and in a few days hence thousands of hands will be busily engaged in removing all those triumphs of human skill, and those evidences of natural wealth which the - world was assembled to behold. As the day wore on, a remarkable concentra. tion of people in the nave began to be discernible. The people seemed to be taking up, their position there, and the galleries, as far as the eye could reach, were occupied by spectators, who, as they gazed on the vast assemblage beneath, evidently a ppeared to expect that some public demonstration was about to be made. As it drew near 5 o'clock, the vast multitude had become stationary, and were evidently awaiting, in silent but intense excitement, the last act of a great event, im- mortal in the annals of the 19th century. It was a most solemn and affecting scene such as has rarely been witness- ed, and for which an opportunity cannot soon again arise. Not only the days but the minutes of the Great Exhibi- tion were numbered, and the first sign of its dissolution was given by Osler's crystal fountain. Just before five o'clock struck the feathery jet of water from its sum mit suddenly ceased, and the silence of the vast assemblage became deeper and more intense. The moment at last came. Her Majesty and Prince Akbert, accompanied by the Prince of Wales and several members of the Royal janily, paid an early visit to the Exhibition on Tuesday morning. They inspected the different parts of the building, and watched withinterest the process of exarsin- ing the different packages by the custem-housa officers. Her Majesty has probably never been so near an eye- witness of the machinery which contributes so largely to the public revenue. The mode in which the work is conducted has its peculiar interest, like everything else connected with this great undertaking. As tile waggons containing the packages arrive within the building, they axe driven to the centre of the transept, and there un- loaded and marked by a custom-house officer. From the transept, relays of sappers convey the packages in trucks to the compartment of the foreign country whence they come. Deposited in this compartment another band of custom house officers are there to receive them, and a fresh party of suppers with chisels and other implements rapidly break open lids or other coverings, and with mili- tary deteroination sweep everything before them until the goods lie revealed. On Tuesday the Zollverein cora. partment was the principal one to which goods were consigned, though arrivals also took place for the Swiss and Canadian collections. Entering within the hoarding, where sapperg were vigorously engaged in breaking open great boxes, one might have almost fancied that some scene of plunder was in pro- gress. The variety of articles that the different packages presented was also carious, and even the Custom-house people themselves, hardened as they must be against that species of excitement, appeared interested in the miscellaneous character of their occupation. One box contained a set of trays, another earthenware images, another silk handkerchiefs or gloves, another parasol handles, another a machine for knitting, articles of gene- ral merchandise alternated with works of art and speci. mens of skilful handicraft. And we may observe that even at this early stage in the arrival of foreign goods, there are signs that thepalm of cheap production, and the merit of ant industrial system founded on the principle of utility, are not to be resigned to us without a contest by the States of the Zoliverein. Within the space allotted for native contributions few arrivals have taken place, and beyond the apportionment of ground hardly anything has as yet been done. The flooring is marked off with red paint or chalk, and one sees scrolled on the boards the familiar names of our different manufacturing communi- ties. In the division of machinery, Oldham has taken the lead by commencing the foundations of the complicated and splendid display of cotton machines which are to be exhibited from there. Other places would do well to fol- low this example, and not to lose a day in forwarding the arrangement of a department on which more than any other probably our industrial reputation depends. It is singular that, as a milliner v*a the first contributor to the stock of the Exhibition, the small Scotch town of Dunfermeline should have its stall soonest completed.
