On Tuesday morning, a little before eleven o'clock, a highly intererting experimnent was made at the building with a view to ascertain ptactically the strength of the gallerils, both under the condition of supporting what is technically called a dead load, and alo a rolling or moving one. A few simple figures will pretty clearly explain the basis of calculation upon which the dimen- sions of the several parts composing the galleries have been determined. The points of support on plan or- curring at the angles of squares of 24 feet, the area of each bay of gallery is equal to 576 square feet. From various experiments which have been made by Mr. Brunel, and by other engineers, it has been tound that the average weight of a number of persons standing together in a confined space rarely exceeds 501b. per square foot; that by packing men as closely together as possible it might be brought up to 701b. or 801b. and that, not even by picking out the heavy men and ga- thering them into the smallest compass, could an average of one cwt. per square foot be obtained. One cwt. wae therefore assumed as an amount certain to cover any unforeseen combination of circumstances. On this assumption no bay of gallery 24 feet square could pos- sibly be called upon to carry a lead equal to 30 tons. As it was ingeniously contrived by the arrangement of the flooring that the weight should be distributed over four girders, and every girder had been submitted on the ground to a pressure of 15 tons (that being only half the ?? weight that each was capable of supporting) applied exartly at the points upon which the floor would have to beat; bo, it will bo mmsifeat SLot %,very lr0g margin had been left to provide for contingencies arising from any motion which it was possible might be com- municated to such a load. The iimmediate object of the experiment tried on Toes day was to assure, by various tests of the severest cha- racter, to what extent oscillations could be conveyed to the gallery by the regular motion of a living load, and to ascertain whether the provision which had been made to meet such contingencies was sufficient. The preparations made for the experiment consisted of the construction of a perfect bay of gallery, :with its floor, binders, girders, and connecting pieces, in every respect complete and similar to the actual gallery, sup. ported on four points bedded ontemnporary foundations; rows of planks, the full width of the platform, led up tea it and dow n from it, so that a rowv of mess, as wide as the gallery, might be able to march up and down in close column. Three hundred workmen were first as- sembled by the contractors, and allowed to cover the platform and the planks connected with it. They swere then compressed into the smallest space upon which they could stand. The load borne on the planks repre. sented the share of pressure which would be produced by the crowding of adjacent bays of gallery. The amount of deflection produced by this load was inap- preciable. The men then walked regularly and irregu- larly, and ran over it. The elasticity of the floor- allowing play to the timbers and the wrought iron work -was admirably developed by this test, and it became apparent that this qualityof elasticity was ofthe greatest value in protecting the cast irou girders from sudden shock. Thus, in the seveiest test which could possibly be applied-when the man, standing closely packed to- gether, continued jumping simultaneously far several minutes, although in the regular vibrations of the lo6or the binders played up and down-the extreme deflection of any of the girders that could be ascertained at any moment did not exceed one-quarter of an inch. As the contractora' men were unable to keep military time in their step, and it was considered desirable to ascertain the effect of perfectly regular oscillations, the whole of the sappers and miners on the ground, in close columns, were marched over and over and round and round, and were finally made to mark time in the most ?? manner. With the result of this last test the eminent scientific men present expressed themselves highly gratified, observing, that while at the climax of vibration the motion did not exceed that common in ordinary London houses at evening parties. Having now enumerated the majority of those artists whose works we consider-either for their i merits, or for their exhibiting defects mixed with beauties-to be worthy of comment, we shall con- clude our notice of English sculpture by alluding to the works of one who, though not of us, is with 1 us, and whose advent to this country we cannot but hail with pleasure and satisfaction. The Baron Marochetti has already acquired a European repu- tation. His grand statue at Turin would have alone sufficed to make good his claim to be considered one of the most daring and excellent sculptors of the I present age. That reputation he has not forfeited i in his great work which is placed outside the build- ing. His "Richard Coeur do Lion" is. a noble figure; the head is exceedingly fine, and we cannot but concur in the view that the artist has taken of the character of the lion-hearted monarch in endowing him with the attributes at once of colossal strength and powerful intellect. We have been, perhaps, too apt to fancy him a regal athlete, forgetting his varied accomplishments, and the energy and decision of his character. In the horse, Marochetti has not been in all respects so successful as in the rider, the hind quarters appearing pecu- liarly deficient; and, if in the criticism of a work of art we may use so technical an expression, they are remarkably " cat-hammed." In completing our observations on the English school of sculpture, as represented in the Great Exhibition, we must once again express our con- viction of the generally satisfactory nature of that display. We believe that, viewed impartially, object for object, with any foreign school, our own would be found to possess most of the leading qualities which constitute beauty in art, in a higher degree than any other. It is in the combination of ob- jects-that is, in dramatic action and epic character -that the English school exhibits its most remark- able deficiency. In turning to the districts of the Zollverein, the case is very different. There, as a general rule, we find the wsthetic tendencies dominant. Even in the smallest object, the philosophy of life furnishes the moral to the artist's composition. His figures all tend either to the enunciation of some truth, or to the illustration of some phase of nature bearing upon the abstract qualities of man. There is a silver vase executed by Wagner, of Berlin, which, within the compass of a very few cubic feet, reveals more lofty thought than we can perhaps trace in the whole English collection. The greatest work that has been transmitted to us from any German ateier is, without doubt, the colossal group of "The Amazon," by Kiss. Its faults are many, and manifest to the most superficial observation. Its noble qualities are equally nume- rous, and equally apparent. There is about it afire and energy which arrests the attention and compels admiration, and, so long as that impression lasts, blinds the spectator to the discovery of its defects. I The Amazon is, as she should be, the noblest of the I three figures. In her the courage is greatest, for she feels and overcomes the sense of danger. In the animals, courage is instinct; in her it is intrepid resolution. The failing seat betrays the shrinking of the woman from danger, and the uplifted arm the nobler spirit overcoming the meaner resolve. We have heard that the Goldsmiths' Company are about to lay out a large sum of money in the pur-1 chase of works of art, and that the corporation of London have adopted a similar resolution. If either of these bodies would wish to do good to English art, let them purchase, and place iu the most con- spicuous situation they can obtain, this noble statue. When it is remembered that out of the whole community of this country, not less than two millions are con- tinually occupied in the preliminary processes neces- sary for the manufacture of clothing of all kinds, little more need be added to induce our readers to ponder for a while upon the marvel- lous results of so vast a mass of industry. By fhe labour of their lives it is, that the flocculent masses of cotton, the slender filaments of silk, of flax, and of wool, are wrought into those indispensable integuments intended to moderate the severity an4 alternations of the seasons. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Monday was certainly one of the most crowded days at the Crystal Palace since the opening. The visitors were nearly all of the working class, and exhibited a greater number of agricultural labourers and their families than have been observed, even on a Monday. The separate parties from large farms were beyond counting, and whole districts poured forth their organised and banded inhabitants to swell the Monday's reckoning. No less than 3,000 persons of this descrip- tion arrived in town from Devonshire on Saturday evening. A great novelty was exhibited in the American section, the conductors of which, following the example of Sweden, seem determined to make up at the close of the Exhibition their remissness in sending goods at the beginning. In the front of the counter upon which stands Mr Hobbs's wonderful lock, there appeared on Monday for the first time a large glass case, containing a magnificent tea service of gold plate, a testimonial from the citizens of New York to Mr Collins, the founder of the American steam-packet line. The service, which is stated to be of pure gold, without alloy, consists of a large tea-kettle, tea pot, cream ewer, and sugar basin, all arranged on a large salver of the same precious metal. The whole service is made of Californian gold, 23 carats fine, and contains no admixture Rf any other metal. This, which is the most singular fact of the description, is accounted for by the fact that Californian gold, 'besides being finer, is more malleable than gold from any other of the auriferous regions of the earth, and therefore has to be worked without any admixture of silver or copper. Reid, IK.C.B., chairman of the Executive Coumittee, yesterday paid his last visit to the 5ene of his arduous labours in connection with the xhibitiOll, previous to leaving this country to dim- charge his houourable and important duties as Governor of Malta. Sir W. Reid's connection with the Exhibition was of a more recent date than that of some of his colleagues, he having succeeded Mr. Robert Stephenson in the office of Chairman of the Executive Committee. The nature of the engagements of Mr. Stephenson, particularly those in connection with the completion% the great Tabular Bridge, rendered it impossible for him to devote that time and attention to the affairs of the Exhibition which their importance demanded, 3nd he consequently resigned. It was at this junc- ture that Sir William Reid, at the desire of his Royal Highness Prince Albert, was requested by pearl Granville to occupy the post. The precise and business-like habits acquired by Sir William Reid ,in long professional and official career, and the latured and valuable experience which he brought to bear upon all matters with which he had to deal, were of the utmost value to the committee. One of the most difficult questions which the executive bad to decide-viz., that of the arrangement of the goods in the building-owed its solution entirely to the suggestion of Sir William Reid. Apparently unconscious of the magnitude of the task, it was proposed to arrange in a philosophical manner the whole of the articles to be ex- hibited. To have done this, however, completely, to have assigned separate localities to each de- scription of article of textile or other manufactures, shawls, teapots, and the thousands of varied kinds of articles exhibited, in the brief period which could be allowed for the purpose, would have been a work beyond human power. In addition to all this, the Commissioners would have had endless difficulties in assigning the position to each respec- tive article, and the wishes of the exhibitors, anxious to prevent as little subdivision of their goods as possible, would have been completely set at defiance. As a means of obviating the diffi- culty, and at the same time of preventing any reasonable cause of ill-feeling on the part of exhibitors, Sir William Reid suggested that geographical arrangement of the building which has afforded so much satisfaction to both visitors and exhibitors. The transept was to be considered the equator, and the foreign countries and colo- nies were to be placed respectively east and west of it, according to their tropical position. Throughout his entire connection with the Exhi- bition it has been his constant endeavour to make it practically instructive to all classes of visitors. The system of giving lectures on different branches of industry and science, and the establishment of guides, were results of his constant endeavours to this end. Of his kind and courteous readiness at all times to afford information, few persons have had more frequent opportunities of judging than our- selves, and the numbers who attended yester- day to take a final leave of him bore testimony to the respect and esteem in which he was held. His disinterestedness has been shown in his refusal to receive any pecuniary recomp ense for his ser- vices in connection with the Exhibition. In the profession to which he is an honour, his brother officers proved the respect which they entertained for him by their attempt-successful, we are happy to suc-to dissuade him from retiring into private life; and there is not a sapper in the corps who does not acknowledge his ceaseless exertions to im- prove their social and intellectual position. Among the subordinate officers and crnploydes in the Ex- hibition, Sir W. Reid is highly esteemed, and to his generous forbearance not a few of them have been deeply iniebted. Few persons have more worthily deserved, or obtained by more honourable means, the esteem of au extensive circle of friends; and most cordially do we trust that his high honour and independence, his great experience, and his ardent desire to promote the comforts and best interests of all classes will be duly appreciated in Malta. Wyatt's work, with the intention of presenting themn, when complete, to some of the native princes of India, as a proof that their exquisite contributions, though unre- warded by the jurors, have not escaped the atten- tiou of persons capable of appreciating real excel- lence and beauty of design. The following extract from the text of the work, on the specimens of Indian embroidery from Dacca, will be read with juterest:- The system of the division of labour, which modern political economists have demonstrated to be the only mode of successful production in the countries of Europe, has in India been known and practised from a very remote period. There can be little doubt that, while the institution of austes in that country originally sprang from political and social considerations, whoever framed the laws which regu- late those minute distinctions in society must have had some perception of the effect which such a grouping of the various classes of the population would necessarily produce upon the arts of the country. All those admirable results which the guilds and corporations of the mlidle ages produced upon specific arts and manufactures are constantly effected in the present day in the productions of India by the distinctions of caste in that interesting country. The man who from his birth is destined to be a shawl-maker, a goldsmith, or a muislin-weaver, has, from his earliest years, every faculty of his mind and every physical quality of his constitution con- centrated upon the one pursuit, excellence in which is to be at once the standard of his social position, and his security for obtaining the necessaries and comforts of life. " Thus it is that the hands of the Hlindoos have acquired that marvellous sensibility of touch which alone enables thread of a teauity scarcely equalled by that of Lisle, Brussels, or meclhlin, to be spin by their delicate fingers. Thus it is that the designers of shawls and embroidery have learnt, fronm their earliest infancy, the forms and tints of those patterns which have descended fronm generation to generation in the families of their caste. This peculiar social combination necessarily affords them an opportunity for re- fining on the works of their predecessors; and to the exercise of a consequent power of minute criticism we may readily trace that extraordinary elegance, and perfect balance of forms and hues, which, to the civilised nations of Europe, appear altogether incompatible with the works of a people reared in a condition which is commonly regarded as ap- proxiniating to barbarism. " The enrichment by embroidery of these plain stuffs- Ivwiichl are generally of a rich red, blue, green, or black Colour-is extensively carried on both in Delhi and in Daoea; and gives employment to a great number of skilful work. Men. There is a marked difference between the embroidery of these two cities, both in tile quality of the silk thread and in tile length of the stitches. In that of Delhi the stitches are short and cleanly worked, in a style somewhat resembling tile Chinese embroidery, the silk thread being closely and nleatly spun. In that of Dacca, on the contrary, the stitches are long, and tile silk employed is of a more flossy character, excepting in those instances in which a special commission effects an alteration in the general character of the work. As may naturally be in- ferred' the embroideries of Delhi are more highly esteemed by the natives, and are consequently more expensive, than those of Dacca. The latter city is, however, famous for its embroideries of net and muslin, which are, perhaps, better known to Europeans than any other variety of Indian ?? in this department of industry; and in the 'pecimen which forms the subject of our illustration, the native workman hias executed, in gold thread and flattened wire, upon a piece of fine Cashmere stuff, a very elaborate pattern, the design of which must be gratifying to all who cats appreciate the ingenuity of the artist in adjusting so skilfully the relative quantities of pattern and ground, and the harmonious combination of the various lines and orna- ments. " The manufacture of the gold thread, in which this spe- cies of embroidery is executed, is largely carried on at Boor- hanapore. A deseription of the process employed in that district has been furnished to the ' Illustrated Catalogue' of the GreatExhibition, by R. N. Hamilton, Esq,, the British resident at Indore; and the scattered notices in Mr. Mont- gomery Martin's ' Eastern India' give us reason to believe that the samee process is adopted throughout that portion of the peninsula, The operation is described as ?? common bricks are laid on an earthen floor, and a, layer of charcoal is placed at the bottom. Upon these aclay crucible containing a quantity of silver is deposited, and being covered over entirely with ignited charcoal, the fire is fanned by a hand-punkah (a piece of matting about four inches by nine) to increase the heat, additional charcoal being occa- sionally added in small quantities. In somewhat less than an hour the silver melts, and is run into moulds, by meals of which it takes the form of small rods. A sheet'of gold is then well washed, and boiled in fresh lime juice and water. Whilst it is still warm, it is rolled completely round the rods we have described ; and the process of plating the silver with gold is thus completed. The next operation is that of drawing the rods through perforated steel plates, in a manner similar to that practised in English wire-drawing - and thus gradually lengthening them until they have ob- tained the requisite tenuity of wire. To receive still further compression, they are passed between aniiall rollers, and flattened en an apvil by the blows of a hammer, until -at length they assume the form of exceedingly minute ribbons. A thread of silk is then suspended with a spindle at the end, a corresponding spindle is attached to one of these golden ribbons, and the spinner who sets both in motion so regu- lates the contact of one with the other as to cause the gold to completely cover the whole of the silk thread. Thus pre- pared, it is done up in skeins, and sold to-the embroiderer"."

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The rush of visitors yesterday was, if possible, still greater than on Monday, and vehicles of all descriptions were put in requisition to accommodate the crowds, who, starting from various parts of the metropolis, poured along the western road in a continuous stream from the time the doors were opened till past twelve o'clock. Before eleven the whole line from Hyde Park-corner to the narrow straits of the Knightsbridge road was completely blocked up, and the omnibus and cab men, who knew that their future sources of profit were still in the rear, encouraged the delusion that it was impossible to get forward, and got rid of their fares a full half mile from the building, and then wheeled about to practise fresh frands upon the newer arrivals. We saw no cabs during the first hour with less than fonr, and the average was six, passengers to each. More fines could have been levied upon the omnibus men for the dozens they carried over the legitimate two-and-twenty than would have yaid for the Crystal Palace. The new patent omnibus had not only every compartment filled, but at least a dozen ladies extra were afforded the opportunity of displaying their dresses and figures in the surrounding balcony, while the pyramidal-shaped locomotive was crowned by a thickly set group of outsiders, all parties, except the horses, appearing to enjoy the fun amazingly. There were a large number of vans freighted heavily from the railways and the rural districts about London, which were amongst the earliest arrivals. Workmen were employed upon the roof of the transept, from an early hour, repairing the damage that was occasioned by the passage of the balloon on Monday afternoon; had the grappling-iron caught in the trusses, or semi-circular iron ribs spanning the transept, it is impossible to estimate either the amount of mischief that might have ensued, or the still more disastrous results from the alum that would have been created in so dense a mass of people. We never remember to have seen the building fill so rapidly as yesterday, and before one o'clock many places were quite impassable. It is evident, from the experience of yesterday and the previous day, that 60,000 is as many as can be comfortably ac • commodated. The fame of the Koh-i-noor, enhanced as it has been by the recent experiments, has revived all its original attractions, ad the numbers who crowded about , the narrow opening during the early part of the day were so great that the circulation became quite obstructed at this point. The policemen worked their hardest, but before one , o'clock they were fairly exhausted with their exertions•, flesh and blood could stand it no longer, and the covering,gas lights, mirrors, and all " the properties" attached to the display were removed, and the diamond exposed in all its original simplicity and beauty. We were sorry to observe that the " Youthful Athlete" and another piece of sculpture in the nave bore marks of the overcrowding, the foot and a portion of the drapery being broken off. The arrangement of the Indian presents to the Queen still goes forward—a large wooden frame is being constructed on which to display the , gorgeous elephant trappings, and the massive-looking case ' in which the ivory throne of state is deposited is in itself a curiosity. It is formed of solid teak wood, bound with brass, and with massive brass handles and hinges. The case is . inlaid with ivory ornaments, and an ivory tablet inserted on ; the side indicates that it is sent "to her Most Excellent Majesty the Queen of England from his Highness the Maharajah of Travencore." The new body of guides and interpreters entered upon their duties yesterday for the first time. It is impossible yet to calculate either the numbers who may be disposed to avail themselves of their services or the amount of assistance that may be thus obtained. Unless the charges be moderate few during the first four days of the week will be disposed to avail themselves of their services. A great deal of practical information is evidently being acquired by the intelligent and inquisitive class of visitors who now throng the building. Comparisons of value and workmanship are being instituted in every direction, and it is much to be regretted that the decision of the Royal commissioners was against the affixing the prices to articles at least of ordinary manufacture. What information, we should be glad to learn, can the public derive from comparing a piece of Lyons silk with a piece of Spitalfields of equal excellence of texture and manufacture, without a comparison of the price of each? What advantage will our Birmingham and Sheffield manufacturers or workmen obtain from finding that the German States, or Belgium, or France, is able to produce articles of steel, iron, and brass, ' of a similar quality to them now, if they do not know something of their market value? And the absurdity and inconvenience is carried a step further when we find some ; specimen of manufacture in metals or textile fabrics marked up, as exhibited for its superior quality, and the low price at which it can be produced, when we know nothing about the price. We hear something of an exhibitors' priced catalogue that is about to appear. It would be much better if the commissioners would at once give all parties who chose to avail themselves of it permission to 'label their goods. Sales and orders to an enormous amount have already taken place in every department of the Exhibition. You cannot look at an article of superior beauty or elegance but you find it marked as sold or disposed of. These sales might be carried still further if the goods were marked, for we frequently meet visitors unable to find the parties in charge of the compertments, and who are thus unable to effect purchase. It was understood before the opening of the ' Exhibition that no sales would be allowed to take place until it had terminated; bur as the thing is now matter of public notoriety, end of daily and hourly occurrence, the practical value of the collection would be much enhanced if the cost could be ascertained in all cases where a near approach was made by one couu'ry to another ha the quality of the article. The Queen did nt visit the build ing yesterday, but two of the youthful princes were present for about an hour. Some of the fashionable world are still daring enough to mix with the °vet flowing multitudes who now swarm through every part of the building ; but their number is becoming daily fewer, and they will be by degrees elbowed out by the shilling visitors, and compelled to restrict themselves to the Fridays and S tturdays in each week. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty visited the Exhibition again on Saturday morning, arriving at the building precisely at half-past nine. She was accompanied by his Royal Highness Prince Albert, the Prince of Wales, and Prince Alfred. The Royal party entered at the private door at the back of the Belgian compartment, and proceeded straight to the western division of the machinery in motion, the exhibitors in which had received notice to be in attendance, to offer any explanations that might be required. The Royal party were attended by the chairman and members of the executive committee, and several of the Royal commissioners, including Earl Granville, Mr. Cubitt, Mr. Begley, of Manchester, Mr. Fox, Professor Cowper, Mr. Hensman, director of the section of machinery; and Mr. Belsbaw. The Royal children were not taken into the machinery department, being placed in charge of Mr. Cole, who,in the varied collection in other parts of the building, found ample means of amusing and instructing them. Her Majesty spent nearly two hours in examining the machinery connected with the manufacture of flax and cotton, commencing with the opening, cleaning, carding, &c. The action of the self-acting mules was explained, and some of the Jacquard looms were inspected, as well as the steam-engines by which the machinery is driven. The Queen made numerous inquiries as to the details of the manufacture of cotton and other fabrics, which evinced an intimate acquaintance with the subject. About one-half of the machinery was examined, and the R )yal party then left the department at about half-past eleven o'clock—the Queen intimating her intention to return and complete the interesting survey at a future day. The Royal party then proceeded to the refreshment rooms which adjoin the machinery in motion, where they were received by Messrs. Schweppe, Welch, and Masters, the contractors for supplying the refreshments. Her Majesty and the Royal party partook of some refreshment, and also of some cream ices, produced by the ingenious machinery of Mr. Masters for freezing by artificial means, and which on this occasion was put in action by steam power. The singular powers of this machine were explained to the Royal party by the inventor in person, - The Queen, who wee accompanied by her Royal Highness the Duchess of Saxe Coburg Gotha and his Royal Highness Duke Ernest of Wartemburg, left before the public were admitted. It is not known how the accident occurred, but the general impression is that some person either wantonly or inadvertently pushed down the spring on the top, by which the contents are exploded. The Russian compartment, although not entirely arranged, was thrown open to the public, under the impression that her Majesty would pay it a visit. The great feature at present is the display of large vases, tazzas, tables, chairs, and smaller ornaments in malachite, beautiful ly ornamented with ormolu. There are also some very splendid jasper vases of large size and rich veining. There is also a very rich and costly display of gems by a St. Petersburgh jeweller. A tiara of large pear-shaped emeralds, of a very fine colour, set au jour, and surrounded by large brilliants, a very magnificent necklace of diamonds and rubies, and a superb bouquet or stomacher of diamonds and pearls, are amoag the collection. We must protest, however, against a newly-introduced watering-can, which is called into requisition, for the last day or two, just when the crowd is at its height. It throws the water in a thin spray in all directions, and, as no notice is given of its approach by the attendants, the ladies' dresses are saturated with water almost before they are aware of it. On Saturday, more especially, this annoyance might be got over before the doors are opened. In the collection of Mr. Hope's jewels, placed in the nave, we observe a very large specimen of the precious beryl,forming the handle of Murat' s state sword. Near these, Herr Krupp, an iron manufacturer of Essen, in Prussia, has a piece of ordnance, a long 18-pounder, finished in the most perfect and workmanlike manner. Every part of it is as brilliant as silver, and it would seem almost a pity to soil it with gunpowder. He has also some light steel cuirasses, only 101 b. and 121 b. weight, which he warrants to resist a musket ball fired at twenty paces' distance, and a mass of the finest tempered cast steel, weighing nearly 40001 b., a rare specimen of the fine quality of the Prussian metal and of superior manufacture. The Koh-i-noor diamond is now tabooed, a stout railing being placed all round it at a distance of about two feet from the cage. The plea for this additional isolation is, that ladies, in their anxiety to see the diamond, got their clothes frequently torn in ascending the narrow platform. The valuable collection of jaws's of Messrs. Hunt and Roskell also gives indication of the anticipated pressure of the Whitsuntide holidays. In addition to the stout iron railing surroundiug the case, a wooden framework, throwing the spectators still further back, has been added. The display is certainly one of the largest and finest in the Exhibition, and since it was placed in the gallery has been all day long and every day surrounded by crowds of eager and excited visitors. In the centre of the case is a magnificent diamond bouquet, the flowers composing which are the anemone, rose, carnation, lily, &c.—all of them modelled from nature. The ornament is divided into seven different sprigs, on elastic stems, each perfect in design, and the complicated flowers can be separated by a mechanical contrivance. It contains nearly GOOO diamonds, the large ones weighing 10 carats; and it would require 1000 of the smaller to weigh one carat. Above this is a large enamelled portrait of her Majesty, in gold, by Haslem, after Winterhalter. The portrait is surrounded with a wreath of oak, enamelled in pure gold, set with pearls and diamonds. Near this is a novel and beautiful ornament for the head, composed of branch coral connected by leaves of enamel and gold, enriched with brilliants. Several brooches and bracelets in enamelled gold, set with diamonds to represent flowers, and an enamelled portrait of the Queen in gold, set in a bracelet with carbuncles and diamonds, are of the most gorgeous character, and display great skill and taste in the arrangement. Ear-rings of emeralds, diamonds, and carbuncles, after the marbles from N ineveh, indicate the introdnetion of a new style of ornamentation. Portraits of Shakspeare, the late Sir Robert Peel, and other distinguished pessonages, set in rings, and surrounded with diamonds and a variety of other costly ornaments, to display peculiarities of workmanship in diamonds, are also exhibited. In the same case is a large number of diamonds and other precious stones, from the collection of the late Henry Philip Hope, Esq. A Golconda brilliant of oblong shape, and crystalline water, is evidently of iminenFe value—it weighs 57 grains. Pink, apricot, and lemoncoloured brilliants are also to be found here, of smaller size; another, table-shaped, is of the very purest water, and varieties of the same gem in chrysolite, green, and cymophane, which are exceedingly rare and almost priceless. One diamond set in a gold ring presents an engraved portrait of the Emperor Leopold IL, in whose possession it formerly was. The engraving is highly polished in all its parts, and those who know anything of the cutting of diamonds will understand the difficulties the artist had to contend with. Heavy weights are required to press down the gem upon the turning mill for the purpose of polishing—the engraver uses long thin steel tools with a thin edge—these tools run in a lathe and frequently get broken, and are continually blunted from the extreme hardness of the gem—physical power, therefore, cannot be employed, and it is only by the most persevering assiduity and patience that he can succeed. Another curiosity is a portrait in relief of Louis XVI., composed of small rose diamonds. Two circumstances in connection with this , beautiful piece of workmanship are deserving of notice—first the diminutive size of the diamonds, which are all regularly cut into facets, some being so small that it would require 2000 to weigh a carat; and, secondly, the skill of the artist, who has with them represented a cameo portrait, and inserted the diamonds so admirably, that they represented a uniformly even surface, scarcely showing the silver in which they are set. The collection of Oriental rubies is large, and some of them of great size. One of an oval shape, is engraved in intaglio. It represents the figure of Minerva, i preceded by two serpents with twisted tails, and s the work of some ingenious artist of the 15th century. The specimens of sapphire are the largest exhibited in the Exhibition; one of them, of a light blue steel colour and of g . ree.t lustre, weighs 180 grains; and another, of a beautiful indigo hue, 118 grains. Many of the sapphires are set in gold swivel rings. An engraved Oriental topaz is evidently a specimen . of early antique cutting. It represents a hull in intaglto, with a Greek vase and some Greek letters. This is . also . set in a gold swivel ring. A specimen of Nine:panne Is, we understand, the largest in the world; it weighs nearly six ounces, is of a beautiful sea-green . colour, and extremely well cut, with seven rows of facets in front. Many of these stones of a smaller size are curiously engrayed, and there are also numerous specimens of jargoons, hyacinths, chrysolites, oriental garnets, topaz, toiirrealine, Mexican and Hangarian opals, and other gems, which indicate the vast ex tent of the collection, and the enormous sums that have been expended in bringing it . together. the whole is rendered complete by the exhibition of oyster-shells containing the pearls, rough diamonds from . the Brazils, resembling bits of dirty glass, and similar specimens from the mines of Golconda and Berne°. CONVENTION OF FREE NEGROES IN INDIANA.—A conventic-n of free people of colour is now in session at Indianapolis, and is occupied in deliberating upon various matters relating to the interests of its constituents as a class. There is said to exist among its members a strong inclination to remove out of the state of Indiana to sonic othercountry, where they hope to enjoy greater social advantages. After much debate a resolution was adopted, by a large majority, providing that should the laws of the state become so oppressive as to be intolerable, they would recommend their people to emigrate to Canada, Jamaica, or elsewhere, in preference to Liberia, against which there appears to be a violent prejudice in the convention. Among the countries spoken of for the purpose of emigration, besides those mentioned, are Mexico, New Granada, and Central America; but Canada is generally regarded as most eligible, on account of its accessibility. At last accounts the convention had under discussion a resolution somewhat contradictory to that which had just been passed, as mentioned above. It asserts, in substance, that the free negroes have a right to remain, if they choose, in the United Mates, the land of their nativity, and it accordingly recommends them to stay here, and strive for their moral, social, political, and intellectual elevation. Peto and Betts have contracted to excavate a new channel from West Lynn into the wash of Lincoln, for a distance of four miles. The terms of the contract are for the first two miles through the land, 143,0001. ; and for the two through the sand, :40,000/. The average depth of the excavation fir the first two miles will be 30 feet ; the width at the bottom, 265 feet ; and at the top, 518 feet. At the extreme end of the land cutting, the width will be 280 feet. This part of the excavation commences at West Lynn, near Fisher-street, and is continued in a straight line across North Lynn St. Edmund, as far as the dry land extends. The excavation will be further continued for two miles through the sands of the Wash, and thence it is expected that the new direction of the ebb and flow of a vast body of water will force a straight channel for many miles through the wash to the sea. The old circuitous channel, full of shifting sands, will be closed up, and thousands of acres will be laid dry, and be made available for agricultural purposes. Since December last about 1,200 men have been employed in the excavation work ; and more than a million and a half of cubic yards of earth have been removed. The soil is clay at the top, and below silth and strong loam ; so that the cutting through and removing such a vast quantity will require an enormous amount of labour. It is, however, expected that the first two miles of the new channel will be completed within a year, and then large vessels may be brought into this port. Whatever may be the benefit accruing to the trade of this town, there can be no question as to the advantage of reclaiming 30,000 acres of land ; adding in fact, so much to the territorial extent of the country ; and from this beginning we may anticipate that in time a large part of the land now under the waters of the Wash will be gradually laid dry. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Two hundred thousand visitors to the Crystal Palace in I the first four days of the present week attest the ceaseless attractions which are contained therein. Of this number, vast as is its magnitude, perhaps 19 out of every 20 are natives of the provinces and foreigners, and the remaining unit a Londoner. By far the larger proportion of country folks are able to set apart but one day for the inspection of these accumulated treasures of natione, and let them be as industrious as they may it is physically impossible to do more than take the merest cursory glance at the whole. Here are 50,000 people concentrated in a given space, and an endless variety of objects before them, ranging through avenues many miles in extent. Instead of moving always in one direction, the living currents are constantly running counter to each other, and the labour of walking, with the thermometer at 75 or 80, is of itself sufficient to tire a strong man ere half the day is expired. Thus, limited by time, and their own physical inability to thread the ever opening and almost interminable windings which meet them in all directions, and pressed on every side by momentarily increasing crowds, the great bulk of the people who frequent the Exhibition are compelled to hurry over the various departments as expeditiously as they can. "Move on," says the policeman—" move on" is echoed by the eager sight-seers from behind, struggling successfully or unsuccessfully, as it happens, to reach the var.. And so they " keep moving on" little to the advantage of the artisan or mechanic, who had hoped by his trip to town to have acquired information which would turn out to be useful to him in his trade. Such is the state of things on the crowded " shilling days"—not so on Fridays and Saturdays, and these are the days when, if at all, a visit to the Exhibition will repay that class of persons, and those days we would emphatically recommend them to prefer. Even on the shilling days, however, no one who has visited the building can quit it without carrying with him many impressions of an agreeable character. The online of the palace itself—the swarms of his fellow-men whom he has met there—the crystal fountain—the colossal figures and groups in sculpture which adorn the nave—the equestrian statue of her Majesty, and the revolving lighthouses, will be indelibly engraven on all memories, when everything else has faded away, or is remembered only as a beautiful dream. And this we apprehend will, in most instances, be the chief "compensation" received by those who have come from a distance by cheap excursion trains for all the trouble, labour, anxiety, expense, and loss of time which they have incurred. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. So far as the world at large is concerned the Great Exhibition is at an end. Its doors are closed to the general public, and it is now left for the pen of the historian to convey to future generations an adequate idea of its magnitude, its grandeur, and its success:. Yhilosophers and politicians will trace its influences upon the civilized portion of the human race; and as hitherto monuments have been left upon the battlefield to commemorate the physical triumphs of man, so, hereafter, some pillar will be set up to mark the spot where the arts of peace were shown to be more glorious than those of war. Long has Hyde-park displayed a memorial to the prowess of the sword, and at length the period is arriving when a similar tribute may be erected, to remind the world of the time and place when and where the nations of the earth struggled to show their superiority in the peaceful arts. Hitherto the doors on Saturday have nut been thrown open until twelve, but on this occasion the public were admitted as early as nine o'clock. From the latter hour until the approach of evening a continued stream of visitors flowed into the building, almost without interruption. Of course, the price of admission being half-a-crown debarred the humbler classes of society from taking a last farewell of the gorgeous spectacle ; but, although generally speaking the visitors were of the higher order, a few smock frocks were here and there visible. The season tickets, naturally enough, mustered in great force. Inside, every. thing went on as smoothly as heretofore, and with the exception of the notices that the Exhibition would close that day, there was nothing to be seen or heard that would have induced a stranger to believe that in a few days the vast and valuable collection of arts and manufactures before him wore to be again distributed over the world. True, in some few places symptoms of packing up were visible, but the casual observer could detect nothing in the shape of preparations for a removal. The sculpture rooms appeared to be the chief centre of attraction, particularly the one in the Austrian Department, where Monti's exquisite figure of the •" Veiled Vestal" as usual came in fur a considerable share of admiration. The sculpture, indeed, seemed to engage general attention, kut every part of the building bad its multitudes of visitors, and as each object was examined and admired, a feeling of disappointment or rather regret was audibly expressed that the hour had come when the enchanting scene must close for ever. The numbers returned by the police were as follow: Ten o'clock ... 4,790 Eleven 10,707 Twelve ... ... 19,207 One 27,311 Two ... 34,841 Three ... ... 42,870 Four ... 49,731 At five o'clock on Saturday the transept and surrounding galleries were densely crowded, and the heat and pressure extremely groat, but as it was understood that there would be some demonstration at the close, the fair visitors endured without wincing the inconveniences of their position. At length the National Anthem was played by the organs, the choristers and visitors and Herr Sommer joining in with a zeal and enthusiasm that have seldom been equalled. Right royal and hearty English cheers repeated three times three, and each time with increased vehemence, followed, and this scene was repeated at either end of the building by the persons assembled there. A second attempt to get up the National Anthem was put a stop to by the bells and gongs commencing to ring out the visitors. It was 20 minutes past five when the bells began to ring, to warn the company it was time to depart. From this moment a most extraordinary scene ensued. There was continual cheering from every quarter for Prince Albert, for Lord Granville, for Mr. Yemen, for the Royal Commissioners, &e. At a quarter to six the bell was again rung, but still nobody appeared to take any notice of it. The police now began to endeavour to induce the visitors to leave the building, which they were only at last enabled to effect by forming themselves, in conjunction with the Sappers and Miners, into parties, and, blocking up certain portions, gradually moving every person towards the egress doors, from which they were not allowed to return. Thus the Exhibition was at last closed, though it was not until long past seven that the whole of the lingering company was got out of the building. The private carriages continued taking up till past eight o'clock. According to the official returns furnished by the police, no less than six millions two hundred thousand persons visited the building while it remained open. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. DAILY MEMORANDA On Thursday, although a wet day, the receipts are re- ported to have been ±2,566..17. From Uie sale of season tickets £\S.. 18 was received, and Uie police returns state tbat 65,059 persons entered the building. On Fbiday the price of admission was 2s. 6d.„ and the wea- ther, though on the whole fine, looked for some time uncertain and threatening; but, notwithstanding these rather adverse in- fluences, £2,558.. 11 was taken at the doors, and, according to Uie police returns, 26,134 persons entered the building. On Satubday her Majesty the Queen, accompanied by Prince Albert and tbe Royal guests at the Palace, resumed their sur- vey of the Crystal Palace and tbeir personal interviews with exhibitors. The portion of tbe building which they examined was tbe western half of the space devoted to machinery in mo- tion, and as this is, perhaps, the most wonderful and important part of the whole collection, Uie attention bestowed upon it was commensurately great. The illustrious party were attended by Mr. Cubitt, President of the Institution of Civil Engineers, and by Mr. Hensmau, who has conducted with so much ability the management of this great department. Mr. Dilke and Colonel Reid also accompanied the Royal visitors, while Mr. Cole took the young Princesses by a different route through the interior. Her Majesty examined with great care and inte- rest the varied display of beautiful machines for the manufac- ture of cotton and wool, listening most patientiy to Uie expla- nations given of each, aud receiving exhibitors with a conde- scension which must have gratified tbem immensely. She ap- peared particularly struck at the outset of her inspection with the display made by Messrs. Hibbert and Piatt, of Oldham, the excellence of whose workmanship is beyond all praise. The succession of curious processes by which the raw material is wrought up into a manufactured shape was explained, aud Royalty probably never before had so good an opportunity of appreciating the patient industry, the mechanical genius, and and tbe enormons capital, which the inhabitants of the north of England have embarked in this branch of enterprise. From tile cleansing and carding machines, with the curious doffing apparatus attached, the Queen passed to those for winding and spinning, to tbe wonderful performance of Uie throstie, the bobbing frame, and the mule, with its innumerable whirling spindles; thence to the warping aud dressing machines, and, finally, completed her survey in the section of cotton by a care- ful examination of the numerous improved powerlooms, with their fast-flying shuttles. The Jacquaid and other looms ex- hibited attracted particular attention, aid also the machinery for the preparatiou and manufacture of wool, especially Don- nisthorpe's circular wool comb, an iuvertiou not less remarka- ble in the profitable results which it yields by the separation of the long wool from the short than in the means by which those results are accomplished, and which cause its action to resemble that of human labour rather than that of a mere piece of mechanism. The Royal party, after examining Masters' process for generating artificial ice, and partaking of refresh- ments, concluded their survey by a minute inspection of Mr. Whitworth's (of Manchester) extraordinary apparatus for mea- suring the millionth part of an inch, and even smaller quanti- ties. Both the Queen and Prince Albert inspected for some time tbis invention, wbich illustrates in a higher degree, per- haps, than any other object in Uie Exhibition Uie extraordinary progress we have made in mechanism. Just as they were about to depart, M. Sallandrouze de Lamornaix, accompanied by M. C. Dupin, and several of Uie most distinguished Frenchmen in London, met Uie Royal party, and the President of the National Assembly was presented to her Majesty. At twelve o'clock the public were admitted, but from the attractions of the Chiswick flower show, or tbe doubtful appearance of the weather, or from some other cause, there was au unusually small influx of visit- ors. The numbers were only 12,980, and the receipts, not- withstanding the ss. admission tharge, fell to i.'1,560..10. Nothing of any interest occurred during the day, except the accidental explosion of one of Phillips's patent fire anuihi- lators in the Eastern division of the building. How it went off no one can tell ; but had it taken place on a crowded day great alarm and even serious consequjnees might have resulted, for from the immense mass of vapour evolved everybody would conclude that a fire had broken out As it was, beyond the first start no harm was done. It is conjectured that some per- son set the machine off, either accidentally or by design, while examining it, for it is constructed in such a way that it could not explode spontaneously. Monday, the first day of Whitsuntide, passed without any unusual crush, and in a manner most satisfactory. Whether fear held people back or the inauspicious character of the wea- ther, or some other influence equally potent but less under- stood, it is impossible to say, but, nevertheless, it is a remark- able fact that Uie numbers who visited the Exhibition ou Monday were not so great as they have been on more than one former occasion, that no inconvenieuce was felt, and that it was not even found necessary to alter the usual arrangements tor a free and uninterrupted circulation of spectators. At nine o'clock, or thereabouts, omnibuses, cabs, ar.d caravans filled widi happy holiday folk, might be seen passing in dense columns along ail the leading thoroughfares towards Hyde Park; the streets gave indications of an immense influx of visitors, and even the precarious elevation of the " knife boards" was fully occupied. Between the hours of ten and eleven o'clock 21,52b" persons were admitted, and appearances promised a day of unusual bustle and excit ;nient. From one of the galleries of the transept Mr. Mayue, the Commissioner of Police, might have been observed watching with anxiety the seemingly inex- haustible tide of restless humanity poured into the interior. The task of counting so enormous an influx became one of great difficulty, and already an assemblage unprecedented in num- ber was anticipated. Raiu began to fall, and all the indications of a damp disagreeable day were realized. Along the approaches to the building bands of sturdy pedestrians might, nevertheless, be seen pressing forward, sometimes seekiug shelter and then starting afresh. Another hour passed away, and it became evident that the rush of visitors was checked. From 11 to 12 o'clock the numbers admitted fell to 12,785, from 12 to 1 they were 8,064, from 1 to 2 o'clock 4,832, from 2 to 3 o'clock 3,312, from 3 to 4 o'clock 1,666, and the total according to the police returns up to the hour of closing was 54,194. At the doors A 2.436..4 was taken, and we find this amount increased by the sums of two guineas for the sale of a lady's season ticket. With vast energy (observes the Times) thelabours of inspection were pursued as the hours crept onward, and when the num- ber of viators reached the highest point, it was a curious aud a touching sight which Uie interior of that great store house of human industry presented. There were collected thousands of the labouring classes eagerly admiring the triumphs of their own handiwork, and appreciating most fully the effects which skilful combination produces. Nothing could be more orderly and decorous than their conduct, and still their arose from them that peculiar hum of satisfaction which forms so remark- able a feature of vast assemblages while their iuterest is excited and their tastes gratified. GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday last, the number of persons who were admitted far exceeded any former day. The :accommodation of 60,000 visitors in a single day at the Crystal Palace is no longer a problem, the enormous number of 60,241 having passed the barriers at four o'clock on Monday. The throng was in no way remarkable at the first opening, but it kept gradually increasing until mid-day, when the inward stream became incessant, and so continued. All the roads leading to the building were like a fair; indeed one could hardly suppose there were so many cabs and omnibuses in London as were continually occupied in conveying ; the sight seekers. We have said that the admissions had turned 60,000 at four o'clock, but that is by no means to be taken as an aggregate. The private equipages then began to set down, and the ticket holders to pour in, so that the grand total of the day did not fall far short of 6.5,000, being doubtless the greatest number ever congregated within the Crystal Palace, or under one roof either in ancient or modern times. The cash account for Monday stood thus : £ s. d. Season tickets At the doors 2,854 19 0 Total £2,866 10 0 Her Majesty and Prince Albert resumed their inspection of the machinery department and their personal interviews with exhibitors on Monday morning. They were attended, as usual, by the acting members of the executive committee and by Mr. Cubitt and Mr. Hensman. The first class of objects which attracted their attention were the machines for the manufacture of wood, and under this bead the models of the apparatus for cutting curved timber, the sash bar machinery used in the progress of the building, and the morticing machines of Furness were particularly noticed. On Tuesday the weather was as fine as it had been on Monday, and the concourse of visitors to the Crystal Palace was far greater. More than one excursion train sent their thousands, and some large schools their hundreds. From the London Orphan Asylum, at Clapton, 250 boys and 150 girls were brought. Three hundred more of the Scots Fusilier Guards, who are commanded by Prince Albert (at whose wish the men enjoy this privilege), were marched in—the same number as on Monday—leaving 600 more to follow. These were among the most interesting arrivals. The numbers, it will be seen, were much above any ever before known. In the first two hours forty thousand persons poured into the building; and the total number during the day was tint far short of seventy thousand. The'building was not at any time inconveniently crowded. The majority of the visitors were of the middle, though there were a great number of the humbler classes—many evidently rustic. The amount received during the day was— £ s. d. For season tickets ll 11 0 At the doors £3,202 13 0 At ten o'clock Professor Tennant lectured upon the subject of the species of stone employed in the outward construction of buildings.—At one o'clock Dr. Lemerier gave a most interesting lecture (in continuation of the series upon which he is engaged, on human and comparative physiology) on the stomach and the organs of digestion. These lectures are illustrated by Dr. Azoux's admirable and useful elastic models, in which all the parts and organs of the body are separately modelled, and then put together in their proper positions—so that they can be taken off one by one, and the entire figure, in fact, taken to pieces like a puzzle, and each portion distinctly examined. By means of these models the lecturer explained the processes of digestion in a manner perfectly plain and intelligible, and so as to convey a great deal of practically valuable information.—At four o'clock Professor Ansted lectured upon copper, silver, and other metals. The packages which had recently arrived at Liverpool from Rome were on Tuesday unpacked, and their valuable contents were disclosed, consisting chiefly of bronze statuary and mosians. The following are the principle articles :—A tazza c,f nero antico (a beautiful black marble found on the site of ancient Rome), very elegantly embellished, especially on the under side • another tazza of verdi ' antico—an elegant light green marble with blackish spots or streaks; two tazze and two vases, of the Egyptian Oriental alabaster of which there is a most magnificent specimen (a large tazza) opposite Tuscany, and which Professor Ansted eulogised the other day, when lecturing on ornamental marbles as one of the finest ever seen in this country. There are also a model in bronze (beautifully executed by Bernini) of a fountain at Rome; a model in bronze of the equestrian statue of Marcus-Aurelius at Rome; two models of fawns, one from Naples, the other from Rome; a very lovely piece of marble sculpture—a kneeling child, not unlike the two beautiful works of Belzoni, already exhibited; another piece of marble sculpture (by Bienanie) —" Love triumphant," represented by a cupid seated on a lion. There is likewise a series of tables exquisitely executed in mosaic, with various subjects—some flowers, others birds—and. with margins of marked beauty. We regret to hear that one of these was broken. There is, lastly, a series of pictures in mosia.c—wonderful imitations of oil painting. The subjects are two copies from Carlo Dolce—our Lord and the Madonna; views of St. Peter's, of the Coliseum, of the Parthenon., of a temple at Tivoli, and of various is ndscape scenes in and about Rome. Altogether these new objects from a very elegant addition to the contents of the Roman compartment, and well fill up the side-tables and walls of the front part of it. They are mostly of small size—both those in mosaic and those in statuary. - - Wednesday was another great day at the Crystal Palace. Notwithstanding the fluctuating character of the weather, the visitors began to pour in at an early hour, so that at two o'clock the interior might literally be called the World's Fair. The great increase of country visitors is now becomiyig quite noticeable, and the foreigners, who now form a large ingredient in the company, are no longer exclusively of the stronger sex. French and German may be heard r esounding through the building with a volubility which bearded lips would in vain strive to arrive at. Supposing the visiter to stand in the central or main avenue, opposite this compartment, he will see, at each of the four pillars which it comprises, a colossal candelabrum of gilt bronze, rising nearly to the gallery. The one at the left hand (or western end) of the compart ment has a base of black marble which has three concave sides, about a yard in breadth, and two feet in height. From these sides rises, at each of the three corners, a scrolled supporter, arching upwards towards the centre column which they seem to sustain—having each a small pedestal, on which is placed an armed warrior, his helmet and armour being allowed to stand out in the original dark hue of bronze. From between these figures rises a continuation of the central slender column, which sends forth four wide-spread branches, each bearing a lamp, and above these is another and smaller cluster of branches with similar lamps. The next two are somewhat similar in size and general effect, but different in style. The fourth is still more different in character, and even surpasses the others in size, as it varies from them in material. Each side of the base (which is, like the bulk of the rest of the candelabrum, of bronze gilt) is about four feet wide, and nearly five feet high; and round the top of each side is a space filled with flowers, from among which rises the body of the candelabrum, also of bronze gilt, richly decorated, and about the middle seeming to spread forth so as to embrace a large china vase. THE GREAT EXHIBITION On a first visit to the Exhibition (remarks the Times, in one of its admirable articles upon the subject,) little ornothing can be seen in detail of its marvellous contents. The mind and the eye have both enough to do in comprehending the general design and in becoming familiar with the coup danl of the in- terior. The truth is that the attractiveness of the display is only now beginning to tell upon the mass of the community, who were slow to believe the astonishing features of the collec- tion thrown open to their curiosity and admiration. At the opening several foreign compartments were still unfinished ; and though the Exhibition, as a whole, was in a very satisfac- tory state of forwardness, its completion in every respect ob- viously involved a considerable amount of time and labour. We may now regard the display as fully arranged, for the In- dian contributions are all in their places; Turkey has at length thrown open her industrial products; France is placing her last specimens in their appointed receptacles ; and Russia is rapidly receiving and adjusting the illustrations of her material resources. » • » Still it is extraordinary how little im- pressed the majority appear to be with the vast stores of valu- able information placed within their reach. There are crowds round every splendid object that can contribute to show or ornament, but the useful products, and those which illustrate the every-day wants of life, seem to be sadly neglected. Pro- fessor Anstead's minerals are visited at rare intervals, and coal and iron, and such like vulgar elements of national wealth, stand no chance with a brocaded elephant-cloth or a tea-service of porcelain, or even a Tunisaian packsaddle. The stalls in which our textile fabrics are displayed do not attract half so much attention as the performances of tiie little boy who pre- sides over the envelope-folder in the nave. Down the agricul- tural implement department, gaitered legs and broad brimmed hats and extensive " corporations " may occasionally be seen to pass with half-disdainful and haif-curious looks directed on either side ; but the influences of the Crystal Palace do not run in favour of rural pursuits, and ploughs, barrows, scarifiers, thrashing machines, and steam-engines show their attractions vainly to that fastidious and polished assembly. For machin- ery ft might be expected that great consideration would be shown, and, in part, it is so, but less than would be imagined. The rushing sound of wheels, and the impressive and almost so lemn effect upon the mind of so many iron frameworks, instinct with superhuman energy and power, produce a certain effect. The iapid clank of tbe power-loom, the stately movement of the long " mules" as they sway backwards and forwards, the whirl of roving machines, the hydraulic wonders of the centri- fugal pump, and the no less remarkable action of the vertical printing press, are marvels of mechanism that touch the most ob- tuse intellect, and cannot fail to attract notice ; yet they do not draw such crowds to tbe department in which tbey are exhibited as might have been expected, and, were it not tbat they are seen in operation, the space in which they stand would be well nigh deserted. Go into the hardware department, or into the carriage or railway sections, or mount to the galleries, and visit the clocks, or the pianos, or the pottery, and it is still the same. You will find people there pondering over particular articles of which they are probably in want, and enlarging their -ideas by the experience of the Exhibition; but there are no crowds of visitors like that in tiie Austrian furniture-courts, or that before the Queen of Spain's jewels, or that before the stuffed animals from Wurtemberg. So far India and tbe foreign ex- hibitors have carried off the lion's share of public admirution. The tide of spectators sets eastward with a far stronger cur- rent than towards the west. On our side tbe Fine Arts court, Pugin's court, aud the sculpture-room draw well ; and the gal lery for plate and jewellery is crowded. Our friends from abroad whose contributions seem to be most attractive are tbe Tunissiuns for their brocaded custumes and bazaar-like fit tings; the Turks for their embroideries and brocades, for their Damascus scarfs, their carpets, their tobacco pipes, and jewelled umber mouthpieces; the French for their tapestry and Sevres china, their jewellery, their artificial flowers, their furniture, and their Lyons manufacture; the Austrians for their furnished apartments, and the Milan sculpture-gallery; the Germans for the stuffed animals from Wurtemburg, and the octagonal hall decorated with porcelain. Other countries come iv for a fair share of attention, with two exceptions. Switzerland is lesa visited than she deserves to be, and the Americans, uninviting as their collection is, have many things to exhibit infinitely more worthy of notice than that rotatory Greek slave which they have had the bad taste to stick up in the centre of then- space. They don't " whip all nature hollow," but they have several very interesting machines, and the useful character of their display as a whole forms a really striking contrast to the showy attributes of the national industries developed around them. Of course we have drawn general conclusions only, for while the mass have been amusing themselves merely, in any have gone to the Crystal Palace for the purpose of study aud instruction. Among the latter, the most remarkable example has been set by her Majesty the Queen, who, at an hour when many of her fashionable subjects are still in bed, has day after day visited Hyde Park and gone patiently and carefully over the different sections and compartments.' Such perseverance and considerate study are beyond all praise, and ought to be more largely imitated. All matters that could stand over, such as the fate of the building, and the appropriation of the surplus funds, are still in reserve; but the following is a summary of the points finally settled:— The Royal Commissioners have fixed Saturday, the 11th of October, as the day for closing the Exhibition to the public. It is their intention to a meeting in the building on Wednesday, the 15th of October, at 12 o'clock, to receive the reports of the several juries, and to take leave of the Foreign Commissioners. On this occasion they intend to request the presence of the exhibitors, the jurors, the foreign and local C immissioners, and the members of the local Committees. Immediately after the close of their proceedings, permission will be given to the exhibitors to remove their goods, subject to such retilations as may be made by the Executive Committee. It is the desire of the Royal Commissioners not only to present medals to the individuals to whom the juries may have awarded them, but to mark their sense of the great exertions of all the exhibitors, and also of the jurors, the foreign and local Commissioners, the chairmen, treasurers, and secretaries of local Committees, and other persons who have rendered services in promoting the Exhibition, and to present them with n permanent memorial of the undertaking, by distributing medals to each, accompanied by a certificate and a copy of the reports of the juries. The three medals, of which the designs were originally approved, are intended to be applied as follows : —That by Mr. Leonard Wyon will be distributed to the prizemen selected by the juries, that by M. Bonnardel will be given in certain cases recommended by the Council of Chairmen, not as a mark of excellence in degree on the part of those who receive it, but for reasons which the Council of Chairmen have been requested to state specially in their reports. The medal designed by Mr. Adams will be given to the jurors. In addition to these medals the Commissioners propose to cause two other medals to be struck, which will be presented respectively to the Exhibitors, and to those who have rendered other services to the Exhibition. The great number of the medals, books, and certificates, which will thus be presented, obviously renders the distribution of them on a single occasion a physical On the other hand, the Commissioners feel that it would be invidious to select any persons to receive their medals at one time, and to omit others. Aud further, it is clearly desirable that the medals, the certificates, and the reports should be presented, simultaneously, and the length of time which must necessarily elapse before the whole of them can be makes it difficult to fix any precise day on which distribution could be effected. Under these circumstances the Royal Commissioners have come to the conclusion, that it will be most desirable to fix a s t a t e d p er i o d which eacn individual may make such arrangements for receiving medals, books, and certificates from the Commission as may best suit his personal convenience. Due notice will be given on this point as soon as the Commissioners are able to fix a time for the distribution to commence. INTERIOR ECONOMY OF THE EXHIBITION —The number of persons that are daily in attendance in the body of the building, augmenting the stream of its contents, is more considerable, perhaps, than the public in general are aware of. In addition to the regular police force and the sappers and miners, there are upwards of three hundred persons in the pay of the Commissioners, and two tholvand exhibitors and exhibitors' assistants, in daily attendance. With such a multitude of people engaged in the interior, and the infinite variety of risks which may arise from carelessness, and a thousand other causes, the reader may be curious to learn what precautions are taken to provide against accidents. Like everything else connected with this great work, they are extremely simple. In the first place, every exhibitor is left to take care of his own goods in the best way he can, which undoubtedly affords the best guarantee for the general security. The most complete protection against fire is organized all over the interior, consisting of sixteen hydrants, several fire-engines, and a large supply of fire-buckets and iron reservoirs, all of whi c h can be brought into Play at a few moments' notice. The instant the necessary labours are over (and as little as possible is done after dark), all lights are put out, and the protection of the building for the night is consigned to fifty policemen, twenty-four sappers and miners, and six firemen, who sleep upon the premises. But how is this extensive area kept in repair, dusted, and cleaned? BY a systematic) arrangement, equally simple and effective. Six hours, from four in the morning till ten, are dedicated to these purposes, and are found amply sufficient. The murmurs of dissatisfaction, which were becoming louder, at the proposed opening of the Exhibition by her Majesty in private, have been happily put an end to by the official announcement of the.order of proceeding, which we give below. The TiMes observed, a few days since, that " The Great Exhibition had killed everything else;" and added, "the Court, the two Houses of Parliament, the nobility, the gentry. the commonalty, the army, the police, carriages, cabs, and omnibuses, are all dancing attendance upon it." Without following the argument of which the above lines wvere the text, we may safely confirm the fact set forth in theem, and the following statistics afford sufficient proof of the hold on the public mind which the Exhibition has ob- tained. Writing at the hour we do, we cannot give the entire receipts since last Friday, but it appears certain that the sums which will be taken on each of the two last davs of this week will greatly exceed the receipts of any preceding one. The popularity of the Exhibition involves its severest trial, and the immense influx which is expected creates a difficulty that has not as yet been got over by the Royal Commission. We learn from the Times that " They are unwilling to question the capability of their great edifice for accommodating all who may present themselves for admission, and they therefore claim the first day of one shilling prices for experi- mental purposes. Barriers are to be erected at the en- trances to prevent any sudden rush, but otherwise no limit has been fixed to the numbers they are pre pared to receive, nor has it been deemed advisable to provide for the claims of visitors from the country." The Times comments upon this arrangement as followss: " How this will answer remains to be seen, but in the mean- time some points are obvious : first, that the interior can- not comfortably accommodate more than 60,000 people; secondly, that there are about 30,000 season ticket-hold- ers, many of whom will undoubtedly exercise their privi- lege of entry, the masses notwithstanding ; thirdly, that the attractiveness of the display has hitherto far exceeded the most sanguine expectations; fourthly, that the great majority of the inhabitants of London are waiting for the reduction of the entrance fee to is. in order to gratify their curiosity; fifthly, that they will probably completely block up the place both against foreigners and people from the country until their own curiosity is gratified. Rules have, wve hear, been laid down for the orderly cir- culation of visitors in the interior, but in practice these will be found extremely difficult of observance, for people won't be much disposed to move to the left when an object attracts them on the right-and in sight-seeing the privilege of going wherever one pleases is almost a necessary condition of enjoyment. We trust that if the building is found ina- dequate to accommodate the numbers pressing for admis- sion, the claims of visitors from the country will not be lost sight of or sacrificed, and the more especially as it would be very easy to come to some arrangement with the railway companies by which justice may be done to all classes." This problem will, however, be speedily solved, and though anxious on the subject, we are without misgiving. Every- thing connected with the Exhibition has been so well done hitherto, that it is only a reasonable expectation to suppose success to the end. As none have taken more interest in the progress of the Exhibition since Prince Albert first con- ceived the great idea than her Majesty and her Royal con- sort, so none have been more frequent in attendance at the Crystal Palace since the building was inaugurated. During the present week the Queen and all her Royal relatives and guests have been daily visitors; even on Thursday, the day on which the Court left town for Osborne.-Mr Paxton ob- served the other day at the Richmond dinner (of which we have given a report below) that he had entertained but one apprehension,-respecting the mode of keeping the building clean; our apprehension arose from a doubt as to whether an important compartment of the Palace would be adequately filled,-the void under the head of " RussiA " being so great, but wye are glad to learn that the Neptune steamer has arrived safely from St Petersburg, with 113 packages on board for the Exhibition. The first or great medals will be given only for articles of a very high order, and in no case will the medals be so awarded as to operate as inducements to a merely individual competition. According to the announcement of the Royal Com- missioners, made at a very early period of the progress of the Ex- hibition, all articles will be rewarded which may appear to competent judges to possess any decided superiority, of whatever nature it might be. According to this arrangement, increased usefulness, im- proved forms in articles of utility, superior quality or skill in work- manship, the use of new materials, new uses or new combinations of known materials, beauty of design form, or colour, and cheapness relatively to excellence of production, will, each and all, form fitting subjects for reward.
