THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The opening of the great industrial entertainment, to which we have invited the people of all nations, having been appropriately and happily consummated by the Sovereign, surrounded by all the insignia of her pomp and power (her Majesty having in the name of the people of this country welcomed the myriad strangers from all climes who are now daily arriving on our shores), the most serious of the many difficulties which beset the labours of the Royal Commissioners having been overcome, and the whole world at liberty, we wish we could say "free," to wander through its vast expanse, and gaze upon the many marvels it contains, we propose proceeding upon a more systematic and detailed plan than we have hitherto adopted in our cursory glances over the general arrangements, and, by a reference to the most striking and important objects in the Exhibition of each country, point out the novelties, the contrasts, the improvements, or the defects which appear to us most obvious, and by this means render it to the people of this country, what his Roy al Highness expressed a hope it might prove, "a true test and living picture of the point of development at which the whole of mankind has arrived in the great task, and a new starting point from which all nations will be able to direct their further exertions." Our examination will be therefore mainly directed to pointing out the progresei made by the industry and the intellect of man in rendering subservient, and moulding and fashioning to his use, the raw material which the various departments of nature offer to him, and to trace the gradual improvements and developments which the lights of science, the aids of a higher and more cultivated taste, and a nicer appreciation of the beautiful in form, have effected within the last few years. The various contributions of the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral kingdom which are here exhibited, both in the state of raw material and in the matured productions of human thought and ingenuity, have been comprehended under a general arrangement, which, commencing with the the five great sections of raw materials and processesmachinery—manufactures, and fine arts are afterwards subdivided into 30 classes. This arrangement has been carried out as far as practicable in the British, the colonial, and the foreign departments of the Exhibition, and although, for all scientific and really practical purposes, this is the proper and legitimate division, the general visitor, while keeping this classification in view, will be able much more satisfactorily to make a survey of the contents of the Crystal Palace, and avoid much of its perplexities and intricacies, by examining the productions of each country separately. We propose in our present and succeeding notices to assist him in this plan by glancing at the productions of each in the order in which they are arranged in the Exhibition. The greater state of forwardness and more numerous and varied display of the western or British end of the Exhibition has rendered it, up to this time, the leading point of attraction; but if the show made by our foreign friends and rivals is not:so great, there are many points of excellence and many valuable suggestions which, we trust, will not be thrown away upon the artisans and manufacturers of this country. With the view of making the Exhibition in this way practically useful, and as a compliment to which the foreign contributors are fairly entitled, we shall commence with the extreme eastern point of the building, and proceed gradually down the nave to the other extremity, making occasional discursive visits to the cross-avenues and galleries, and in this way place our readers in a position to comprehend the general plan and features and the leading characteristics of each department. The United States department, which occupies the extreme east section of the Crystal Palace, challenges, when compared with others,; but little opportunity for remark. All those products of a high state of civilisation which we find in most of the European divisions are absent here, and the American exhibition, in this respect, fails to command that attention which is elicited in the more immediate neighbourhoods of France, Belgium, and Austria. The only two works belonging absolutely to the domains of fine art are Power's statue of the Greek slave, and Stephenson's statue of the wounded Indian. The former is well known in this country, where it has for a long time time been located in a private collection. The latter possesses a vast deal of merit, going far to prove that America will not long remain behind-hand in these msthetic efforts which betray more than anything else the influence of education, the progress of taste, and the refinements that flow from the intercoune with Europe. The expression of agony depicted in the face of the dying Indian is admirably conveyed, and the whole composition is fraught with character and intelligence. Situated also in the nave, and in close proximity to the two figures to which we have alluded, is a huge railway bridge, the specialty of which we cannot at present determine, for as yet it is many removes from corapletion. the north side of the nave, the chambers in the occupation of the United States are principally devoted to machinery and agricultural implements, the latter predominating. We have ploughs, grindstones, oil-cake-breakers, barrows, and the like, intermingled with tools of various kinds used for gardening and domestic purposes, none of them inviting any particular notice on the score of originality, though all exhibiting excellent and superior workmanship the mechanical details. On this side a large variety of stoves, ranges, and other apparatus of the same household class is alas to be seen, among which a calorie engine of a peculiar construction for heating and cooling air is one of the most prominent objects. A set of punching machines also attract the observation of the spectator, which, furnished with rolling or knuckle joints, the long levers of which pass through a space of many feet, and move over not more than half an inch, concentrate a large amount of power. Some safes of professedly equal security to those of Chubb's, and several other iron works, both cast and wrought, for cognate purposes, are placed in this department; and though of little interest in themselves, are undoubted attestations that all conveniences of this kind are manufactured with equal skill on the other side af the Atlantic as here. The illustrations of the India-rubber manufacture are numerous, including a life-boat, which, although 6 feet long and 3 feet wide, can be put into a person's pocket. Maps printed on calico, artificial legs and other specimens of mechanical surgery, paper-hangings, and various specimens of block printing as diverse in design as in colour, make up the remaining contents of leading prominence on the northern aide of this section ; though we must not forget to mention the show of carriages, and other vehicles of the same sort, which exhibit abundant ingenuity in the application of the mechanical principles the best sailed to ensure locomotive case, and the least possible expenditure of wear and tear. Crossing the nave and entering the southern division a vast profusion of daguerreotypes and calotypes arc to be seen These are of varices degrees if merits. Some ot them ale effective, but in no instance no tie observe anything superior. to what we are in the habit of witnessing daily at home. Some portraits executed by Bredy of New York are remarkable for their increased superficies in comparison with those to which we are accustomed, but the reflctant quality of the polished metal is necessarily augmented, and hence no advantage is gained. This gallery of daguerreotypes is chiefly curious on account of its portraiture of the most illustrious men of the United Stated. Calhoun and others are here in al their reality of aspect, and the spectator acquires an idea of the lineamente of many an individual distinguished for his talents and inflnence, for his power as an orator or his wisdom as a legislator, which it is clear any of the ordinary modes of limning fail to supply. Some of the talbotypes are bold and effective; and in this department of the photogenic art the Americans may be said to have surpassed us. There is a large asssrtment of popular optical instruments, including some'clever hyalotypes, or positive pictures on glass plates, adapted for magic lantern slides. The lithographs, which are exhibited in tolerable numbers, do not evince any gret proficiency in this branch of artistic manipulation. The drawing is, in most cmcs, poor, mechanical, and spiritless, and the lithographic texture coarse and woolly. Several of the portraits which we observe in the gallery of daguerrotypes are re-produced on stone; but, for the reasons we have stated, demand but little admiration. Pirsson, of New York, furnishes a pianoforte, adjusted for two performers, one at each end, which cupplies a want that has occasionally been felt ; at the same tone an economy of space, is secured worthy of consideration. The shape of the instrument is a parallelogram—in fact that of two grand pianofortes placed, invertedly, side by side; the actions being totally distinct. This, as well as a patent square pianoforte, are contained in finely embossed rosewood cases, and are very beautiful pieces of furniture. 01 the tone it is impossible to speak, for in such an area as that of the Crystal Palace any musical sound generated by a process so delicate must inevitably be shorn of any resonance :and beauty which it may possess. Another pianoforte, from the factory of Meyer, of Philadelphia, is constructed almost wholly of iron frames, in which respect it bears some affinity to the euphonicon, which, a year or two ago, was patented in this country by the eminent firm of Beale and Co., the only difference being in the shape. Other musical instruments figure in pro' fusion, but they are simply the contents of an ordinary music-shop. At the extreme east of this side there is a large display of glass-rare, as well a fine model of a glass factory and all that appertains to it. The textile fabrics of the United States are exhibited in an imposing manner. The printed cottons from New York and Massachusetts evidence the growing skill of the Americans, not only in the conception of pattern, but in the superiority of manufacture and the flannels, blankets, and cassimeres, &c., from the same districts, here displayed, are, in short, most favourable examples of American industry, and, as such, merit examination. The furrier trade is also well exemplified; so likewise boot and shoe-making, book-binding, and divers other handicrafts. Scientific instruments are to be found in great abundance, besides entire chemical laboratories. Several specimens of oil-cloth also appear on this side of the nave, whose brilliancy and decision of colour at once strike and gratify the eye. But it is in the raw materials of the country that the chief interest of the American exhibition mainly rests. There is a large collection of woods and vegetable substances from Maryland, arranged in a spacious cabinet. It will easily be supposed that metallic ores are no less plentiful. Ohio sends a large assortment of geological specimens, and it has been well and truthfully remarked, that, on looking at them, "No one can avoid the thought that the district producing such minerals must possess a most valuable mine upon which industry has only to exercise her skill." The specimens of vegetable produce include tobacco, Genessee flour, Indian corn, and malt prepared from it, maple sugar, mustard, oil of peppermint, and the like, to which we can only incidentally refer, but which will repay examination. The gallery in the occupation of our Transatlantic brethren is at present but scantily filled, the chief tenant being a perfumer from Philadelphia, who seems to pride himself upon his fancy soaps, some of which he has moulded into busts and other configurations. Such are the principal contents of the space allotted to the United States. At the first glance, the objects, we repeat, are not so striking as those of a showier and more ornamental kind, but still there is much that is worthy of scrutiny, much to amuse, much to instruct. The want of a catalogue by which the various articles may be identified, and their points of interest elucidated, is at present sorely felt, for though the sixpenny synopsis which is officially published gives a pleasant insight into the class of things to be observed, it does not contain a syllable of detail. This, it is to be hoped, will be remedied in a few days, when the doors of the Palace are shut against further contributions, and the Exhibition is pronounced complete. Russia, to whom a very extensive hay or compartment has beea allotted in the north of the nave, and a smaller one in the south, comes next in point of locality, and we are sorry to find that her real geographical position has been the means of leaving the greater part of the space allotted to her by the Royal Commissioners up to the present time a waste as barren and deserted as one of her own steppes. The vessel freighted to convey the great bulls of her goods to the Exhibition was for several weeks frozen up in the ice, and it will, we understand, be some weeks yet before the goods will all be landed and fully displayed. There are a few very beautiful articles displayed, which make us only the more anxious to see the industrial resources of this vast empire fully developed. In front of the compartment are two massive richly chased and gilt candelabra, about ten feet high, standing on triangular pedestals of black marble; they are very fine examples of parqueterie, and the finish and proaortions are faultless. Some jasper eases, well finished and highly polished, exhibit novelty of design, and there are two very large porcelain vases enriched with raised vine leaves and stems in dead gold. The enamel paintings on these vases are very delicately executed. A circular table in metal, with the painting on the slab annealed, has no pretensions to artistic merit. There are a Large number of electrotype and plastic medallions and casts, bat the most striking and elaborate contribution at present displayed is a cabinet in tulip wood, ornamented with bronze and porcelain. The medallions on the panels are very fine specimens of painting, and the whole is extremely creditable to the St. Petersburgh manufacturer. Two grand pianos in rosewood are plain substantial looking instraments, possessing little of the finish or decoration of the French or English workshops. A table inlaid with various stones in Florentine mosaic, and mounted on an elaborately carved bronze gilt pillar, and some specimens of coloured inlaid floors, comprise nearly all the articles in the northern compartment, and the southern portion is still less furnished. One of the curiosities exhibited is a miniature likeness of the to represent a fine steel engraving, which turns out to be executed in black needlework upon a white ground. In the centre of the compartment of Sweden and Norway is a marble statue of a shepherd's boy, executed at Rome by M. Moline, a Swedish sculptor, possessing considerable merit. As might naturally be anticipated, these countries are rich in illustrations of the manufacture of metal. There are various specimens of ore from the mines of Bofors and Dannemora, and a large number of tubes, iron plates, files, cutlery, inlaid with gold and silver, sabres and daggers, if they do not present the same finish as our own articles, show the high temper and superior character of the Swedish steel. Cotton and woollen goods, of coarse bat substantial texture, produced in the hand looms of the peasantry, and Swedish silks and satins, moire faconnee, and a portrait of King Oscar, woven in silk by the Jacquard loom, are among the textile fabrics exhibited. There are also specimens of cobalt and nickel from the Norwegian mines. The whole of this little collection is extremely interesting. Danmark stands next in geographical position, and shows many curious mechanical contrivancss, which display a good dell of ingenuity. There is a modification of the machine, introduced some years ago in this c ,untry, for composing and adjusting types, which it is said obviates many of the objections of the original. A pump, which can be converted into a steam-gauges, astronomical clocks, self-registering thermometers,ezimuths,&c. There arc a large number of contributions from the Royal porcelain manufactory at Copenhagen, which are very delicately executed. Much of the business of this establishment of late years has been devoted to producing reduced copies of the works of the celebrated sculptor Thorswaldsen, in bisque china, and most of them are here, as well as has reliefs in biscuit, of sacred, allegoricel, and mythological subjects. HIGHLAND JEWELLERY.-ThIe seasons 1849 and 1S50 were remarkable to the seekers of precious stones in the Cairomorm range of mountains, for the abundance with which the genius of the hills gave up his treasures. It was supposed, and possibly with truth, that the unusual plenty of the beautiful crystals was attributable to the unprecedented character of the floods which marked tihe opening of the first named of those years-sweeping clown, as the angry waters did, vast quantities of earth and rock from the higher and less accessible parts of the mountains, and clear- ing out many a spot where the stones had been hidden for scores of years. The search, as we mentioned some time ego, was resumed this season with some little spirit, though the number of searchers was not so great as in the two preceding summers; but, so far as we can learn, no great good fortuio has attended the season hunting. Few might have been the crystals brought into the town for sale-we might rather say none; and fortunate it was for the jewellers that the stocks they laid in during the preceding plenty, were large enough to carry them through the scarcity now experienced. The popularity of Cairn- germ bijouterie seems to be much on the increase, and certainly the beauty and variety of the ornaments in which it is used with effect, and the really lovely shades of some of the crystals, are good reasons why they should come Into general favour. The other day we were shown a brooch, the stone of which, and a large one it was, might almost have passed for a monster ruby, so brilliant and so ruddy were its sparkling hues. Most of the claims on the funds at our disposal, however, are already discharged, and after all shall have been satisfied, a consi- derable surplus will remain, the precise amount of which cannot be ascertained until the accounts are finally wound up, when they will be duly laid before your Majesty, but which surplus we have reason to believe will not be less than 150,0001. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. We give to-day a tenth notice of the Ecclesi- astical department of the Exhibition, selecting for the subject of our remarks those'specimens of em- broidery and textile fabrics which, from the nature of their material or of their ornament, are. adapted for ecclesiastical purposes. ECCLESIASTICAL DEPART.MENT OF THE EXIIIBITION.-No. X.> EMBROIDERY, TEXTILE FABRICS, &C. Those who are not acquainted with any ancient specimens of the best sort of needlework and em- broidery can form little or no idea of the degree of perfection to which the art was brought in the middleages. Berlin patterns-even the showy cheval screens of the present day -form no data from which one can theorize as to the nature and merit of that opns Anglicanurn, as it was called, which so charmed Pope Innocent IV as to make him exclaim, as Matthew Paris reports, " Truly Eng- land is our garden of delight, in sooth it is a well inenhaustible; and where there is great abundance, from thence much may be extracted." It is sur- prising how few remains of ancient needlework and embroidery exist. The Bayeux tapestry, indeed, is a specimen now more easily accessible than for- merly ; but even this can give little idea of embroi- dery proper, such as may be seen in the famous " Dalmatica di San Leone," preserved at St. Peter's, in Rome, and so eloquently described, both as to its design and execution, and as to its his- torical associations, by Lord Lindsay, in his work on Christian Art. There are a few other known examples ; for instance, a vestment kept in the sacristy of Bamberg, and a Clwr- gowanal, as it is called-probably erroneously- in a parish church at Mayence ; and, in our own country, either in private hands or in various museums, may be found several medimeval vest- ments of extraordinary beauty and magnificence, not to speak here of many fragmentary pieces of ancient embroidery scattered throughout England in our parish churches-either thrown on one side, or serving as hangings for pulpit or altar. But lone of these can be seen without some degree of trouble and expense ; and in consequence, church embroidery had become, like so many other things, an extinct art, and in general people did not ?? what its real capabilities were, or what cause they had for regret. Unfortunately, this department of ecclesiastical art is most inadequately represented in the Exhibi- tion-a circumstance not surprising, perhaps, when it is rmiembered that its revival has been mainly due to the skill and taste of a few individual ladies, but not the less to be regretted. All who are ac- quainted with some of the more remarkable works of church building, or church restoration, of late years, will remember how great a progress has been made in reproducing the kind and excellence of embroidery for which our fair country- vronleu v were of old so distinguished ; and many modern altar-hangings could be pointed out which reproduce with great success the richness, and brilliance, and harmony, and high artistic merit of ancient needlework. It is to be lauented that some of these specimens have not been contributed, if only as samples, to the Exhi- bition. As it is, we have to content ourselves with noticing a generally lower class of embroidery, ex- hibitetl, with very few exceptions, by professional producers, not by amateurs. Still there are some hopeful signs to be observed in the specimens dispersed through the Exhibition building, although the degraded Renaissance style appears, particularly in the works of foreign coi- tributors, to maintain a more uninterrupted sway in the department of needlework and embroidery than in other branches of ecclesiastical art. Mlr. Pughn, in the Medireval Court, exhibits two cases of vestments and hangings. We need not say that in shape, quality of material, and method of workmanship, his Speci eiss are most cornimendable. But we look in vain for any high merit in design or execution. The embroidery of figures-of course the highest application of this art-is scarcely attempted ; only indeed, and that on a small scale, in the hoods of two processional copes. In one of these there is embroidered the full face of a bishop wearing a mitre ; the subject of the other is the coronation of the Blessed Virgin. In both, the style is too archaic ; there is no force in the drawing; and the general re- stilt, from the absence of strong black lines, and other like expedients of the old artists, is far less effective than ancient embroidery. On the other hand the fabrics out of which Mr. Pugin's vestments are made are generally admirable; and he has attained great success in weaving, for orphreys and the like, a number of laces of ecclesi- astical pattern, instead of producing these orna- ments by hand embroidery. How far this is de- sirable-how far it is advantageous to produce cheap ornament of this kind, at the risk of being nauseated by its continual repetition, and offended by its improper use, we need not here inquire. Messrs. Newton, Jones, and Willis, of Birming- ham, have made a far better display of ecclesiastical embroidery and needlework, intended for the use of the Church of England. To exhibit their skill, they have chosen, besides a variety of altar-haugings for different seasons, several specimens also of the ancient vestments still retained, not merely in the letter of a rubric, but in actual use in the English Church, on occasion of the coronation of our sovereigns. For example, Messrs. Newton and Co. have prepared a " dalmatic"-a robe worn by the Queen at her coronation. This is a beautiful speci- men; it is of the richest white silk, with exquisitely embroidered borders, or orphreys, in coloured silks, all done by hand. The letters "V. R." are combined in a sort of monogram, for the appropriate orna- nientation of the laticlave of this judiciously-chosen vestment. There are also two copes, one intended for the archbishop, the other for an attendant bishop, at a coronation. Both robes are charmingly designed, as to the contrast and harmony of colours, and the workmanship is exceedingly good. But here, as in Mr. Pugin's embroidery, the highest art-the representation of figure-subjects-has not, we are surprised to see, been attempted. In passing, we must remark that we have had au opportunity of learning that Messrs. Newton, Jones, and Willis had the wisdom to ob- tain the professional aid of an architect (Mr Street) in directing their various efforts to reproduce a more appropriate style of ecclesiastical furniture. This is as it ought to be. It is next to impossible that capitalists, or men of business, en- gaged in the actual production of such fabrics, or in the sale of them, should themselves have skill, or taste, or experience enough to design them ; and we owe much of the present degradation of art of this sort to the disuse, by the manufacturers, of the practised knowledge of the professional designer. We do not doubt that Messrs. Newton, Jones, and Willis will benefit by their judgment and spirit in thus seeking the best artistic guidance. Certainly they owe to it their unquestioued superiority to any of their rivals in the present Exhibition. We must now say a word of the altar-hangings exhibited by this enterprising Birmingham firm. There is one of white silk, striped with diagonal bands of gold embroidery, of flowers and the sacred monogram, with a fringe of white silk over gold. This is for high festivals, such as Christmas and Easter. There is another frontal, for Lent, of violet, em- broidered in silks with monograms and fowers, and having an upper hanging, or superfrontal, of red, with red and white fringes. This we think a fairly successful solution of a rather difficult problem of coloration. Two other frontals, for ordinary use, are of green-one in silk, one in velvet-with varied and beautiful flowers, and superfrontals of red. Some of the patterns are copies from well-known ancient examples, and are most beautifully worked, all by hand; and there are several examples of borders, or orphreys, of good design, also worked by hand, I and contrasting advantageously with Mr. Pugin'| woven laces. Messrs. Newton and Co., whose display is more than usually extensive, exhibit also specimens of ecclesiastical carpets, of stuffs for wall-hangings, &c., of various degrees of riehness, and of linen for church purposes. Ia all we observed, with much satisfaction, a careful attention to the pro- prieties of ecclesiastical character, in general style as well as in the most minute detail. As pro- duoers of ecclesiastical furnitures, this firm have no rivals in the Exhibition. Mr. French, of Bolton, is in most respects a * Previous notiles upon this department of the Exhibition appeared on the 16tb of MIay, 7th and 20th of June, 2d and 2ad of July, 6th, l1th, and 16th of August, and 6th of Sep- tercbar. igreat contrast to the last-mentioned manufac- turers. He has evidently omitted to avail himself of professional guidance in his various works, which accordingly, even when well meant, are seldom above mediocrity. This gentleman exhibits three altars, complete,with their hangings-a piece of questionable taste considering the nature of the 'Exhibition, and from which a more reverential feeling has restrained all the contributors, with the exception of himself, Mr. Harrison, and Mr. Pugin. But this might be more easily pardoned than the indifferentism in art to which we must ewe the juxta-position of three different types of altar, to meet respectively the presumed tastes of the supposed middle and two extreme schools of theology in the English Church. Of these we will only say this much-that the one approaching more nearly to the standard of ecclesi- astical propriety appeared to us to be but ill-pro- portioned, while its ornamentation is coarse and commonplace. Mr. French has, however, succeeded far better in various wall-hangings, and carpets, and other ecclesiastical materials. He exhibits also some good, because unpretending, damasks, &c.,for sacred purposes. A more ambitious one-the pat- tern of which is made up of various sym- bols and two attitudinizing angels-is by no means an improvement on the more sim- ple designs. We regret that Mr. French's evident zeal and enterprise have not led him to distrust more his own guidance, and to obtain the aid of a better artist ; and this is the more to be wondered at since he has earned, by several bro- chures, a well-deserved reputation in connection with subsidiary questions of art connected with his business. Mr. Jaucovwski, of York, exhibits, in Class XIX., some rich but tasteless embroidery of a modern sort. Mrs. Cornelia Mee shows, in various speci- mens of secular design, much vigour and boldness. We regret that she has furnished no ecclesiastical work. Mrs. A. E. Roome, of Lincoln, has wasted both time and manifest skill in imitating line engraving, by her embroidery of a south-west view of York Minster in black silk upon a white ground. Miss King has very accurately reproduced the old kind of embroidery, on a small scale, in a figure of St. John. She has, however, made the drawing ill- proportioned and grotesque, and the work might have been more delicate. A very fair funeral pall, of black cloth, with a large red and yellow cross upon it, and appropriate legends along the borders, and an Agnus Dei in the middle, is contributed by Mr. M'Carten, of Bir- mingham. The design is, perhaps, too rigid for needlework. Mr. Helbronner, of Regent-street, deserves credit for boldness of effect in some stoles, but he has kept to no particular style. Mr. Harrison, of Brownlow-street, has an altar, all but complete, with hangings of red and a border of flowers, with stars and monograms in diaper, of indifferent design, but well worked. There are cushions on the top, and the set of plate, manufac- tured by Messrs. Widdowson and Veale, which we described in a former paper. Messrs. Lambert, Brown, and Patrick, of Regent-street, have a speci- men of the right kind of church embroidery, but of inferior design, in a frontal, which is ornamented with a plain cross, a crown of thorns, and a " glory." Some Masonic badges are also shown by them, fairly embroidered, and a rich copy of the embroi- dered cover of the Bible used by Charles I. on the scaffold. We noticed, with especial satisfaction, several examples of much improved design in silks and brocades, intended primarily (we imagine) for church purposes. In particular, Mr. I. Boyd, of Spital-square, has several silks of pure design ; and we must mention also the name of Messrs. Houlds- worth and Co., of Manchester, for their pattern called " the Melanthus," and some other specimens. Among the works exhibited by Messrs. Laugher, Dwyer, and Co., are some excellent floral patterns in ribbons, manufactured by Cope, Hammerton, and Co., of Coventry, which it is hard to be- lieve are produced by machinery. A brocade, of which the pattern represents the Works of Mercy, by the same exhibitors, is successful only in aim and intention. Here we may call attention to some excellent works, particularly to an imitation of Spanish point-lace, produced by the Irish Work Society. This lace is most suitable for altars. Turning now to the foreign part of the Exhibi- tion, we may notice first an altar-cloth by M. Som- merfeld, of Berlin. It is of blue velvet, embroi- dered in gold. It is meant to cover only the top 3 and the front of the altar, and is for the use of the Lutheran commuuion. On the depending part there is a chalice embroidered, with legends, in ( German, round it. At the lower angles are devices of crosses and flowers. The style of em- broidery is rather coarse. In the Russian department there are some ex- ceedingly good gold brocades, which, from their design being diapered in crosses of ornate forms, are, we should suppose, intended for ecclesiastical uses. There are also several frontals, very like those exhibited by Messrs. Newton, Jones, and Willis; but they are a little more free in general design, and deal much more in flowing, as opposed to geometrical, lines. No shading is admitted in these beautiful specimens of embroidery; they are more tame, owing to the absence of strong black lines and other contrasts, than our own works. It I is not a little curious to remark that the Exhibi-E tion contains specimens of Russian, Anglican, and Lutheran frontals; while the Roman altars, exhi- bited as altars in the Medheval Court, are not pro- vided with those appendages, though ordered by the canonical regulations of the Latin Church. M. Krickl, of Vienna, exhibits some Church vestments, in most incorrect shapes, and with much ?? architectural ornament, em- broidered in the modern fashion. MM. Fries and Zeppezaner, of the same city, display several eccle- siastical stuffs, exceedingly vulgar in idea and colour and design. Their diapers are generally of the most extreme rococo style; as also are those of MM. Lehmann and Son, also of Vienna. It is impossible to describe the va)garity of the em- blems used on these really rich, and, so far as tex-l ture is concerned, sometimes beautiful fabrics. Skulls, winged hour-glasses, church fapades, an- chors, and chalices are common, among ether more appropriate devices ; and the worst imaginable i form of each emblem is sure to be used. With the exception of one beautiful, because plain, cloth of silver, by Lehmann and Son, we noticed no single example of an improved taste in the Austrian col- lection. Equally unfavourable is the criticism we must pass on the specimens shown by the firm of Le- mire, pare et fils, of Lyons. These vestments are of corrupt shapes and of most debased ornament, with sham jewels plentifully displayed. We could see in them many signs of manual skill, but no improvement of style and character. However, we must say that M. Van Halle's three dressed ecclesiastical figures, in the north-east gallery, in the Belgian department, which have changed their names since the opening of the Ex- hibition, surpass, in absurdity and vulgarity, any- thing we have ever seen. It is altogether unneces-. sary to point out, much less to enlarge upon, the ri- diculous anachronism, the tawdriness, the degraded l taste, and the corrupt forms, combined in these ludicrous effigies. They are useful in showing from what depth of debasement mr. Pugin had to begin his retorm. Another Belgian artist, M. Paternostre, of Lou- vain, while not free from the worst faults of the modern school of Church embroidery, has clearly aimed at something better. There is an Annun- ciation on one of his vestments, coarsely enough executed ; but some smaller specimens show better workmanship. We noticed a frowning figure of St. Paul, after Vandyke, worked on the back of one of his chasubles, of a debased Renaissance style. MM. Cuylits, Simond, and Co., have some specimens which, for coarseness of conception and workman- ship, for tawdriness of ornament, and inappropriate- ness in the use of symbols and devices, are as bad asl any in the whole range of the Exhibition. We cannot leave this subject without briefly con- trasting with the last-mentioned works the chas- tened taste, exquisite coloration, and even purity of design to be observed in the Indian, Turkish, and Moorish embroidery. In the department of Turkey i especially, there are specimens of needlework-for table covers, for example-which are faultless in colour and design, and which approach in general . conventional treatment, and especially in the avoid- ance of shadows, to the style and character of the purest mediaeval work. There is also some Persian needlework, with bands of ooloured patterns, ex- quisitely treated. In carpets, always excepting those from Turkey, and the ecclesiastical opecimena we have noticed, there appears to be no visible improvement in design. And we looked in vain for indications of better taste among the velvets of Genoa. Upon the whole, we fear that, in the class of subjects treated I in our present paper, there is less evidence of a revived feeling for propriety and purity of design than in any other department of art. THE HUINDRED AND TWENTY-SIXTH DAY. Yesterday placards were posted up, by order of the Com- mittee, announcing that the Exhibition will close on Satur- day, the 11th of October-that the building will be open upon that day at nine instead of twelve o'clock, as upon other Saturdays-and that no Bath chairs will be admitted. This announcement will of course set at rest any doubts which may have existed on the subject of the final closing of the Exhibition upon the 11th of October. It has been difficult to make many of the foreigners believe that it was really intended to close the Exhibition upon the day originally named, and it was not till they saw the fact actually posted up in black and white that they appeared to be convinced of it. Indeed, to such an extent has this misapprehension prevailed, that advices were received only yesterday to the effect that a large quantity of goods bad just been shipped from the States of the Zollverein for the Exbibition; the owners, mistaking the purport of the address of the House of Commons on the subject of the retention of the building, conceived that that body had ordered the Exhibition to re- main open till the 1st of next May. With respect to the closing ceremony on the 15th of Oc- tober, we have no reason for believing that any deviation will take place from the plan already decided upon. The details of the arrangement are not yet finally completed, but it is probable that seats will be provided, upon a raised stage in the centre of the transept, for the accommodation of Prince Albert and the other Royal Commissioners, and in the immediate neighbourhood for those invited to be preo sent. The principal portion of the business transacted will consist in one of the members of the Council of Chairmen- probably the chairmarn, Viscount Canning-announcing to the Commissioners the awards of the prizes which the jurors have made, and stating the grounds upon which they have been given. Prince Albert, as President of the Com- mission, will then, in all probability, on behalf of the Royal Commissioners, thank the jurors for the attention which they have bestowed upon the subject; and he will, no doubt, take that opportunity of alluding to the great success of the undertaking-the assistance which itl has received from all classes of the community-the benefits to art, mann. factures, and commerce, which may be expected to fiowfrom the lessons which it has taught-and the services of the foreign, metropolitan, and local commissioners and commit- tees ; and last, but not least, the cordial support and as- sistance rendered by the exhibitors will be duly ac- Iknowledged. It is not intended to admit the public upon this occasion, as accommodation for witnessing the ceremony andI hearing the addresses, could not be provided for a greater number of persons than the exhibitors, jurors, foreign and local commissioners, and members of local committees whose presence it is intended to request. The holders of season tickets will not, of course, possess any right to be pre- sent by virtue of their holding tickets, as the Exhibition will have closed to the public on the previous Saturday. The distribution of the medals will be a matter of after con- 6ideration,as comparatively few of those requiring the names of the owners to be stamped upon them will be ready for delivery by the 15th of October. A curious Swiss muff was yesterday shown by Mr. Hill- man, the agent for the Swiss goods, to the Executive Com- mittee and some other officers connected with the Exhibi- tion. The article is said to have been made upwards of 200 years. It is composed of cocks' feathers, stained a bright red colour, and, notwithstanding the length of time which had elapsed since it was made, the colours were remarkably brilliant. Tire whole, as made up, presents a singularly beau- tiful appearance. In consequence of its late arrival, arid its not being an article of recent manufacture, it is not publicly shown in the Exhibition. The Crystal Palace, it appears, is to remain standing during the winter, and without coming to any definite arrangement as to its final destination, it may be as well to test the effects of the storms and rain and snow which it will have to endure before the first year of its existence has expired. Should the result be satisfactory, we have no doubt the idea which has been suggested in so many quarters, of converting it into a public promenade and winter garden, will be ultimately carried out; and if so, the residents of the neighbourhood, who have been the most determined in their opposition to the building remaining as a permanent structure, will be the parties most likely to be benefited. It is evident that persons living any distance from Hyde Park will rarely have the opportunity of entering the building, unless on the occasion of public fees, entertainments, or flower shows, after its present contents have been dispersed. With regard to the funds for maintaining the building as a permanent structure, the continued daily receipt of from 2000/. to 3000/. must set all doubts on that point at rest. A contemporary, who is probably more in the secrets of the Royal Commissioners than we can pretend to, throws out a suggestion that the surplus ought to be devoted to making some compensation to the exhibitors who have spent much time, labour, aud money in producing articles for exhibition, and who cannot be considered adequately rewarded by the presentation of a bronze medal. Considering that the commissioners have throughout refused to these exhibitors the trifling bonus of a season ticket, the suggestion, so far as it may be of any practical value, is not a very happy one, unless the Royal authorities have tardily repented of their very shabby treatment of the men who have made the Exhibition what it is. We believe the refusal to admit the exhibitors has thrown a good deal of public odium upon the whole affair; and the exhibitors themselves are so indignant at the treatment they have received that, indepennently of the almost certain refusal of thess gentlemen to contribute to any future exhibition, they would in all probability now refuse to accept any such favour from the Royal Commissioners. The glass-making of Bohemia, at which we now propose to glance, has naturally operated very powerfully, in addition to the recent freedom from excise restrictions, in stimulating and advancing the glass manufactures of this country. It has supplied us with the models for imitation in colour, form, and beauty of adaptati m and ornamentation. Without any wish to echo the cry of superiority of the German artists, it must be acknowledged that these primitive Bohemian workmen are yet our teachers. Their trade is carried on in small companies, called a " fabrique," of about 25 men each, and the glass villages are scattered through the mountainous districts in the heart of immense forests, the proximity of which furnishes the fuel upon which it is asserted by many the excellence of the manufacture depends. The Bohemian workmen employed in this country insist upon it that if they could be supplied with the timber of the Black Forest, they would undertake to make the true Bohemian glass here. It is certain that the component parts of the metal, and the various oxides employed, are precisely the same, and the management of the heat may, therefore, have more to do with the matter than is generally supposed. The glass is merely moulded into form in the " fabriques;" the work of engraving, colouring, and vitrifying is cerried on in the lit , le cottages which surround the glass-house, where each workman has his little muffle fitted up. The engraving involves a large amount of skill, and a familiarity with artistic forms generally. The operation may be described as the cutting away by abrasion or grinding of certain portions of the surface in intaglio. This is effected by small copper wheels, turned with great rapidity by a lathe, the wheels being touched with emery to improve their cutting powers. The more minute the details of the design the smaller the wheel, and in some cases it does not exceed the size of a pin's head. The Bohemians are hereditary glass-makers, and this is one of the secrets of the lealiiliC of the workmen. Whole families are brought up from childhood in painting and drawing upon glass, and boys of thirteen and upwards are employed in this delicate department. The engraver lives in a blockhouse of two apartments. One is his workshop, with space enough to hold three or four little lathes for engraving glass, and here he and his sons, from 12 to 16 or 18, work. The faithfulness and spirit of the productions speak for themselves. Most of these men are familiar with the best specimens of ancient and modern art, and many of them are naturalists, by which they gain that minute acquaintance with the forms of natural objects observable in their works. Taere is thus no royal road to excellence, and these details may convince our English workmen of the necessity oi education and study. With these superadded to their admitted mechanical superiority they would soon excel every other country. The Bohemian contributions to the Exhibition are pregnant with lessons to our manufacturers. Notwithstanding the great improvements in brilliancy of colour and elegance of form we are yet inferior. The rich ruby observable in their specimens has never yet been fully achieved by us, although some of our manufacturers make creditable approaches in brightness and depth of colour. The display of Count Harrach is wonderful in the variety and beauty of the forms and decorations. Flanking the stalls, and facing the nave, are four candelabra in ruby glass, about ten feet high, richly decorated with gold. The brackets are of dead crystal, and the forms symmetrical. Their price must be enormous; as the Bohemian ruby, from the difficulty of the manufacture, and the large quantity of gold that enters into its composition, is very coetly. The transparent drops certainly not equal to the diamond-like purity of the English crystal. Two massive pedestals and vases, in semitransparent white glass, with foliated mouldings and ornaments of green, will win admiration for the exquisite beauty of their proportions, the purity of the material, and the harmonious contrast of colour. We are glad to perceive that Lloyd and Summerfield have very successfully reproduced this peculiar green colour. Some crystal cups, apparently as thin as tissue paper, and covered with lines of ruby glass, are marvellous specimens of delicate manipulation. Drinking cups of a fine rich green, covered externally with minute ornaments in silver, and with liqueur bottles to match, are superior in design and beauty of execution to anything we have seen, even in a collection of such extent and magnificence as the present. It would be utterly impossible to describe all the wonders here displayed, nor could any mere description convey an adequate idea of their beauty. The peculiar German beer glass has net been omitted, and musi, feel somewhat astonished at the fine clothes and fine company it is in. Count Schaffgotsch, of Warinbrunn, in Silesia, sends some elegant and novel designs from his glass works at Josephinenhutte. They include enamel vases, aqua-marine enamelled vases, and cups with gilt ornaments, chalice glasses with carved arabesques and handles. Tacchis of Frankfort has a very beautifully modelled alabaster fountain in the centre of the compartment; and Vogelsang some pink-coloured glasses, plated with layers of alabaster, &lased and gilt—hock bottles and glasses cut in the ruby Gothic pattern, and spiral engravings, and other varieties of enamelling and tracing, all of which are unique of their kind. Beyond the comparison this display affords to the English manufacturers, no information is derivable as to the peculiarities of manufacture that give Germany the pre-eminence. Whether the depth and brilliancy of colour be due to the oxides employed, to the fusing heat, or to both, is a problem to be solved only by further experiments. We are evidently on the right road to the solution, and the spirit, perseverance, taste, and ingenuity our manufacturers have recently displayed, is a guarantee that it will be satisfactory. In our rambles on the north-east gallet 5 , we lighted upon a case of very superior bows of English and Spanish yew, manufactured by Messrs. Ainge and Aldred, of Oxfordstreet. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The controul of the "Crystal Palace" having passed to the , commissioners the Executive Committee decided on closing the admission of visitors to the building, to prevent the confusion that would arise consequent on any interruption during the arrangement of the articles intended for Exhibition. This arrangement, which was to have taken place on Monday, was, however, considered inopportune, and it was urged that in consequence of the opening of Parliament, it might be considered as an attempt to prevent members of both or either House of Parliament from inquiring into or examining the structure, the Executive Committee therefore resolved upon leaving the building open for a further period of days, for the admission of members of Parliament exclusively, to each of whom an invitation was forwarded. The invitations attracted a considerable number of the members of both Houses of Parliament, including the Duke of Wellington, who was loudly eheared by the crowds outside the building, both upon his arrival and departure. On Monday a report was very generally circulated that her Majesty intended to visit the building, and as much preparations as could hastily be made for her reception were adopted. Twelve o'clock was the hour named, and Mr. and the members of the Executive Committee were in attendance to receive her Majesty upon her arrival. The time, however, wore on, and numbers of the visitors continued patiently to occupy their seats or positions in the galleries from which a good view could be obtained, until nearly five o'clock, when it became evident that the pleasure which they had anticipated would not be afforded them. The amount taken for admission at the doors, on Saturday and Monday, considerably exceeded £5OO. The Board of Trade have to Bristol the privilege of an extra first class eataraination for masters and mates.

I| We understand that the period for closing the Exhi- bition to the public has been fixed somewhere about the middle of October, and in all probability Saturday the 11th of Outober will be the day. There will be a public ceremonial, at which her Majesty and Prince Albert will assist on this interesting occasion; but, as none of the arrangements have yet been finally determined upon, it would be premature to anticipate. The principal prizes will be given to the fortunate candidates either by her Majesty in person, or the Prince as her representative. The work of clearing out the building will follow imme- diately after the distribution of prizes, and will occupy, it is calculated, three or four months. The general impres- sion is that the greater part of the foreign goods will, after paying the duty, be sold in this country; and the French have already named the Lord Mayor (Musgrove) as the person to dispose of their extensive and varied collection by auction. The recent visit of the civic functionary to Paris has secured him the business of his numerous admirers there, and the mingling of profit with pleasure is a stroke of business befitting the commercial character of the country which he represented at the Hotel de Ville.-Observer. Yesterday week the number of persons who visited the Exhibition was 20,859; the amount of cash received was £2,160. INDIANS AT THE ExruaBIToN.-Among the visitors yesterday week came a party of four Iroquois Indians, who, besides inspecting the interior of the building, had a " palaver" with the executive committee, and were less reserved and more sensible than from American romance might have been expected. They expressed great astonishment, not at the Koh-i-noor itself, but at its value; and the whoop which they raised when Mr.' Catlin, their guide, told them this for a moment suggested mis- givings for the safety of the policeman who guards the treasure. The machinery in motion also produced a strong impression upon these wild men of the woods, and when one of the self-acting " mules" was suddenly arrested in Its course, "the maniton" or "great spirit" was the cause. Their "palaver" with the executive related, we hear, to some things which they had brought over, with them from the other side of the Salt Lake, and which they wished admitted into the Exhibition.-Times. AIvritoinmArioTN OF THE FUNDS.-The gossip of the transept to-day ran upon a rumour which will probably take the public by surprise. The calculation at present is that the receipts of the Exhibition by the time it closes will amount to about £400,000. Of this immense sum, one-half, it is calculated, will defray all the charges connected with the building, and the government say to this sum only have the commissioners any claim, and that the surplus belongs to them. The precedent of Mr. Pitt, who, when hard pressed during the war, appropriated without ceremony some £80,000 subscribed by the customhouse and excise clerks for a superannuation fumid, has, it is said, been brought forward in support of this arrangement, which it is urged will have the advan- tage of setting at rest the vexed question of what is to be done with the surplus? THE GREAT EXHIBITION. A new subject has been added to the collection of statuary and sculpture in the foreign nave. It is by Hanel and Lanchammer, of Prussia, and represeets a full-sized female tiger, modelled from the one in the Zeological Garden, the Reg-nt's Park. The peculiar crouching and stealthy gait ' of the animal, the wild glare ef the eye, and the powerful muscular development of the frame, are truthfully modellee; and although the subject is somewhat repulsive, the details, even to the erect and excited appearance of the furry coat of the treacherous looking animal, who appears in the act of springing upon her prey, are rendered with muck artistic skill and effect. The transparent soap manufacturer from the United States, who like one of his own hardy pioneers in the march of civilisation ventured into the" far east" of the American gallery, and was for a long time monarch of the wide waste around him, has now the comfort of seeing himself surrounded by a crowd of active and thriving competitors in different departments of art and manufactures. Many of the French and German exhibitors, who came late into the field, not finding space on the ground floor, have located themselves in these distant regions, and the odds and ends of various states and countries now find here a local habitation, relieve the gallery of its former barrenness, and add to the completeness of the Exhibition. We are glad to find that the suggestion we threw out some time since, for throwing open the Exhibition free t 4 the public for a limited period, has been taken up by some of our contemporaries, with the difference that they stipulate for a small payment of 31. a head. Even this sum, however, would be considered by many thousands a burdenseme tax, especially where there are whole families whose means are only one degree removed from pauperism. It would absorb the whole means of support of the family for the day; and if the act of liberality we have suggested is to be carried out, let it be done wholly and ungrudgingly, and without the little threepenny sting in the tail, which would deprive it of all its grace. If the two first days in each week in the month of August were made free, it would give at lea.t half a million of the poorest of the metropolitan population an opportunity of viewing the wonders of the Crystal Palace, who will otherwise never obtain a sight of the interior, and the money would never be missed from the overflowing coffers of the Royal commissioners, who, if the rumours we have heard be tine, are actually Mousing under a veritable embarras vie rich,esses. The crowd of visitors still continues pouring in—there is generally a slackening observable towards the midile of the week; but of late, during the first four daye, there are points at which the main avenues, wide as their space is, are quite impassable. Defame's envelope folding machine is one of the great sources of attraction to the country visitors. The French organ, which is constantly in requisition, is another great leading point; and India with its treasures swarms from noon till closing time. For those who are in search of a cool and quiet retreat we recommend the extensive and well-arranged compartments which are devoted to the display of our woollen manufactures, and cottons, calicos, and muslins. Much as there is here to excite admiration, as to the extent, and beauty, and finish of these fabrics, they possess no peculiar or striking novelties to attract the croud, and hence, when there are 60,000 visitors swarming up and down the naves, transept, and galleries, there are here long vistas tastefully hung with drapery of every variety of colour and texture, without a single person in sight. Although many portions of the building are very indifferently watched, the number of petty thefts has been most satisfactorily small, and are far more than counterbalanced by the number of lost articles picked up and handed over to the police. In this respect the Exhibition, through which two or three millions of persons must have passed, is extremely creditable to our national character; and seeing that the foreign detectives and policeofficers who were sent over at the opening of the Crystal Palace, from all parts of the Continent, have had a complete sinecure since their arrival, and that officers have been taking each other into custody for want of other and worse sujels, we must suppose one of two things, either that the foreign visitors, as a body, are as well conducted and as honest as ourselves, or that the visitation we have referred to had more covert and less creditable motives. If the surveillance of the foreign exiles was the obj?.ct, we sincerely trust it was without the countenance or sanction of our government, which has been at all times ready to afford an honourable and perfectly secure esylum to political exiles, while it has beets equally capable of taking care, without foreign interference, that the sanctity of its protection should not be violated by any secret organisations or conspiracies. The production of the Zaubeviote is another welcome addition to the richly-stocked repertoire of the Royal Italian Opera. Frequently as it has been performed in this country, it has probably never been given under such attractive circumstances as now, for, although chefs-d'ceuvre of the German school are not those best adapted for the practical uses of a company more or less Italian in its habits and predilections, the melodious flaw of this charming work and the acquaintance operatic singers have with it, give it superior chances of complete and able development. We are all well acquainted with the circumstances under which it was composed, and the generous sympathy of Mozart with the ungrateful Schickaneder is a tale which enriches the pleasure attached to its production, whenever that fortunate event occurs. Added to whieh it was, observes Mr. Holmes," during the composition of the Zauberflote that the eruption of those symptoms which portend decay of vital powers, and a general breaking up of the constitution, first appeared. As usual, Mozart grew interested in his work, and wrote day and night; but not as formerly, with impunity. He sunk over this composition into frequent swoons, in which he remained for several minutes before consciousness returned." A series of circumstances, therefore, conspire to enhance the interest in this great masterpiece, which musicians unite to a man in declaring to be of matchless and imperishable worth. We know of no opera, simply because no opera exists, which recommends itself so immediately to the common auditor, who listens to its endless stream of melody with a delight gentrated at the moment, and without the remotest sensation of satiety. Mozart, so says the gossip connected with Zauberflote, " commenced this opera with a vow, that while he would do nothing derogatory to his artistical dignity, its airs should be whistled, sung, and thrummed about the streets of Vienna." That he accomplished this and more need not be told, for there is scarcely a piece in this fascinating work which is unknown to the world at large. Titles need not be cited, but several of the melodies will recur to the mind as familiarly as" household words"—melodies in which amateurs have long had a direct and enduring property. But while the miscellaneous public is thus delighted, the taste, the erudition, and the ingenuity of the musician are also appealed to. The score of the Zaubeillote abounds in some of the finest disclosures of science—science that is not set forth with the slightest leaven of pretence or affectation; but still how grand, how learned, how felicitous are the devices of harmony which meet tLe student at ev3ry bar ! Pity is it that all this supreme musical excellence is wedded to such lan infirm and unnatural libretto. Had it been otherwise the ZauberflotO would have been met with upon the stage as frequently as the Naaze di Figaro or the Don Juan, but the trials of Pamina and Tamino, the simplicities of Papageno and Papagena, the anxieties of the Queen of Night, and the admonitions of the hierophant, awaken no human sympathy whatever, and the dramatic interest, which has never at any period been raised to even an ordinary point, wanes finally into rciserable ar.d contemptuous indifference. The mad and unmeaning jargon of Schickaneder has been patiently borne for the sake of the music; and this is no weak and unsuggestive testimony to the preciousness and rarities of its merit. The libretto of the Zaubollote, in a word, is without exception the poorest and the most unintelligible of anything of the kind that literary silliness ever conceived; and it has often been a source of regret that some groundwork of an analogous sentiment has not been devised, with a view to the transference of the music, and a more rational process of enjoyment. The execution last night was not so smooth and perfect as it will be when the forces have gone through a little more discipline. The Royal "command" occasioned a certain degree of haste that in some cases was fatal to the closeness and beauty of ensemble; both the delivery, on the whole, was creditable, and unfolded the treasures of the opera in a very striking and picturesque manner. No musical work that we are acquainted with requires such a large amount of superior vocal force. There are "three attendants" on the Queen of Night, and three " benificent genii," upon whom devolve some of the loveliest strains to be found in the score; and it has always been a matter of difficulty to get a group of soprano artists only moderately qualified to undertake these apparently subordinate responsibilities. The provision made by Mr. Costa was no better than what has been made before, and the music in which these individuals are concerned suffered accordingly—that of the "attendants" being, it is but right to add, particularly inexact and offensive. The Queen of Night was embodied by Madame Ana Zerr, a vocalist who, fresh from the Italian Opera of Vienna, has recently sung at several of the metropolitan concerts. The two great airs belonging to this part have been her principal achievements upon these occasions. Pos,esi,ing a thin and flexible voice, and a species of vocal daring which never within our experience has failed of its mark, her execution of the declamatory music associated with this character is at least a source of wonder. The extravagance of deportment which she has manifested in the concert-room was materially abated on the stage, and her delivery of the airs alluded to may be placed among the most remarkable triumphs of last night. Tha delicious music of Pamina was admirably sung by Grisi, whose lustrous voice and equally lustrous execution afforded infinite delight throughout. The pathetic song in G minor, in the second act, the lovely " Ah, lo so," never met with a more passionate exponent, and the effect was beautiful in the extreme. Mario was a worthy Tamino for such a Pamiraa. He rendered the celebrated "0 care imagine," and the " Quel . suono," with unrivalled taste and purity; while his energy in the scene of the ordeal was unexceptionable. A nobler Sarastro than Formes we have never had. We could, however, have preferred a little more delicacy in the delivery of the " Qui sdegno," which in other respects was a fine piece of vocalisation. His previous execution of the authoritative passage in the finale to the first act was grave, weighty, and portentous, though this too would have benefited by a little more attention to light and shade. The fantastic pair, Papageno and Papagena, were fantastically personated by Ronconi and Vierdot —the former readily apprehending the comic features of the part, and portraying them with industrious minuteness and animation. His humour at times touched on the domain of the buffoon, but it was nevertheless excessively diverting. Papagena has so little to do that it may be inferred Viardot simply lent her name to strengthen the aspect of the cast on a particular and interesting occasion. The orchestra acquitted itself with its usual skill, and the matchless accompaniments were detailed with superb and bewitching finish. THE GREAT EXHIBITION Proposed Dinner to the Foreign Exhibitors in the Crystal Palace.— We understand that the British exhibitors have it in contemplation to give the foreign ex- hibitors an entertainment in the nave of the building on some day to be set apart for the purpose, and of which due notice will be given. The Exhibition will, of course, be closed to the public in such case, and ladies only will be permitted to be present in the galleries. The idea of fraternising in this truly English manner with their foreign neighbours and friendly rivals is a happy one, and we trust it may be carried out in the spirit of cordiality and good feeling in which it has been suggested. The consent of the royal commissioners must, however, be obtained in the first instance. — Morning Herald. Model or the Koh-i-soor. — Commencing with the brilliant display of glass at the head of the gallery, the Queen examined with some interest the model of the Koh- i-noor, with its two attendant satellites, which has just been placed in front of Mr. Apsley Pellatt.B collection. The velvet cushion, the gold stems and wires on which the diamond is supported, the glass shade, and a miniature iron gilt cage, surmounted by a crown, have all been success- fully imitated ; and we believe many persons, after looking at the original aud the copy, would be puzzled to tell which is the great Indian diamond, valued at £2,000,000 sterling, and which the piece of British crystal glass, value — say one shilling. The glass is of the purest colourless crystal, and the size, shape, cutting of the facets, &c., have all been most accurately reproduced. — Morning Herald. Diamonds. — The presence of so many rare and valuable diamonds in the Great Exhibition has directed consider- able curiosity towards the history and origin of these most precious stones, none of which so puzzled chemists and philosophers generally, as the large black diamond exhibit ed by Mr. Mayer, of Liverpool. This extraordinary stone was found about four years ago, in the new diamond mines discovered in the debris of a mountain range, about 300 miles from the port of Bahia, in Brazils. It is of the great weight of full 300 carats, and is as yet uncut, presenting, in fact, the same appearances as it did when first discovered. It appears to have been once attached to another piece, which, to carry out the usual form of diamonds, would make it nearly twice its present size. This black diamond has baffled the skill of the lapidary, as from its extreme hardness it cannot be cut by the usual process adopted in transparent specimens, but hopes are stdl entertained of polishing it. Its appearance is very singular, showing evident marks of having passed through some great heat, somewhat similar to the scoria formed on the sides of Mount .-r-.tnu during an eruption. So great is the interest excited by this diamond that Mr. Mayer has been requested to exhibit it to the French Academy of Sciences in Paris, where some light will perhaps be thrown upon its formation. Many fine diamonds of great size and value, are now found in Rajah Brooke's territory of Sarawak, in Borneo. On Tuesday, tbe Queen visited the Exhibition, and re- mained till half-past ten o'clock. THE GREAT EXHIBITION FETE IN PARIS. PROGRESS FROM LONDON TO PARIS. We have the following letters from our correspondents describing the progress of the English visitors towards Paris : BOULOGNE, FRIDAY AFTERNOON. At eight o'clock this morning the London-bridge station was occupied by a large number of the guests, and the crowd increased every minute. By half-past eight o'clock the platform was crowded by aldermen, sheriffs, deputies, and corporation dignitaries, mixed up with M.P.'s, savans, Royal Commissioners, Americans, and other foreigners. For a time all went smoothly pleasant, chatty groups were formed, and friends discussed the prospects of the day. It soon, however, became evident that something more than usual was engaging the attentention of the porters and railway officials. The crowd thickened, and as visitors looked around and recognised acquaintance after acquaintance, suspicion arose that Loudon was on the move, and that the Saturday's fashionable swarm at the Crystal Palace was en route for Paris. A rush was mad at th e b arr i ers, and a close column of porters' trucks formed before it, like a train of artillery, while on either side a forlorn hope made desperate efforts to get through the gaps, which were sternly guarded by picked members of the railway staff and police. Some dignitaries had left their blue•bordered tickets behind; others found that their tickets of invit..ition to ball and concert did not pass wives and daughters through the railway barriers. Anxious consultations were held, detachments were sent to the pay places to secure whatever tickets could bo got, and the company reaped a .rich harvest from the assembled multitude. Ladies got through the barriers as they best could, and occupied seats. Slowly and gradually the majority of the attendant crowd oozed through the narrow strait; but now new difficulties were to be encountered. Parties of two or three wished to go together, and anxiously looked about for convenient places. From carriage to carriage they peered about, daintily rejecting the odd seats, and hoping for better luck further on. Soon it became apparent that even odd seats were scarce; husbands vainly searched for wives and daughters—ladies wandered about, looking for their partners. Groups were formed round carriage -doors, discussing claims which were put in for seats that had been retained, or for compartments taken; and plaintive voices urged how hard it was to separate husband and wife. American ladies asserted their claims as only American ladies can t the " cars" of which they had assumed the temporary ownership, and strenuously assailed as cowardly and ungdrukuaanly any attempt to occupy the vacant seats. The foreign visitors wandered about, hopelessly resigned to their tate, almost in despair of ever getting through. What became of the luggage is not known; but strong hopes are entertained that it will all be found at Paris. The last bell rang, the guards became importunate to close the doors, and the storm of the barriers was re- nerved. Mr. Paxton made his way through with beaming. face, and, it is to be presumed, as the hero of the day, obtained a seat; but it was reported that a strong detachment of the corporation of the city of London was left behind. Several stout gentlemen were seen standing guard over bags swollen with scarlet robes and uniforms, and cases with cocked hats and deputy-lieutenants' swords. The Lord Mayor's fat footmen were in the rear, whether in charge of the state coach is not known. The superintendent with great difficulty got the doors of the carriages closed, though ladies made stern efforts to signal their absent lords and set their protest against divorce and separate maintenance. By the kindness of the authorities we got packed in a carriage after some fruitless efforts, but the great mass were not so fortunate, and we saw as we left a large assemblage awaiting the next train. The railway authorities did the best they could ueder the circumstances, and provided a monster train for the Royal Commissioners and their friends, but so profuse has been the hospitality of the French Government and city of Paris municipality, that no single train could convey the assembled multitude. By great exertions, an enormous number was carried off by the first train, and we passed on the line nume rous strings of empty carriages, drafted by telegraph from all parts to the scene of action, so that all will be got off this morning, and it is intimated a fleet of steamers has been assembled at Folkstone. The weather was brilliant in theporning, and gave good augury of a happy commencement to the festivities. The train sterted punctually at nine, and in forty minutes got to the Reigate junction, and made a halt for water. Here some hapless visitors were assembled, in hopes to catch the train en route, but such good fortune as a vacant seat in the closely packed train was hopeless. By a very good arrangement, with the view to save trouble, the " blue bordered" or privileged passes, and the purchased tickets wero all made through to Paris. Besides Reigate a stoppage was only made at Tunbridge, and the train got into Folkstone at twenty minutes past eleven.
