THE GREAT EXHIBITION. . _ Monday was one of 'the most remarkable days in the annals of the. Exhibition since its opening. For days before the public had been pouring in their 5s. for ad- rMission, a general opinion prevailing that when the shilling days came the building would 'be so crowded as to prevent any one viewing the contents. This feeling appears to have produced quite an opposite result, and the consequence was that Monday was one of the most comfortable days in the Exbibition. The loungers about one or two particular spots hac4 gone-very few holders of season tickets presented themselves-under 22,000 people visited the Exhibition, and these were so dis- tributed in the various sections that, looking down the naves or main thoroughfares, the building appeared com- paratively empty. With regard to dress, one could scarcely distinguish the majority of the visitors of Mon- day from their more fashionable predecessors of the previous week, but that they were of a different class was evident from the care and attention various articles :were examined and descanted upon by different groups, who evidently understood their manufacture from ex- perience and practice. On Tuesday morning our daily contemporaries enter- tained their readers with various learned arguments to prove, thateitherthepeople would not cometothe Exhibi- tion because it was cheap, or, knowing that they had plenty of time before them, they were in no hurry to go; but the latter part of the day told for itself what was the reason why the attendance was so slack on Monday, the visitors amounting to upwards of 30,000, all fear of overcrowding having passed away. On this day, too, her Majesty showed that she could be equally at home amongst her subjects who have but 1s. to spare, as those who have 5s.; and having visited the Exhibition at her usual hourofoine o'clock, remainedin it until considerably after eleven, some time after the general company was admitted, her Majesty having watched their fast ad- mission from the North Gallery; and here we rejoice to record the fact that, though it was known her Ma- jesty was in the building, she was less annoyed or 'inter- fered with than she was upon the more aristocratic days. There were also more season tickets presented at the doors, but it was remarked that they were nearly all held by gentlemen. On Wednesday, the progress of the revolution in the opinions of the people, as to the effects of the shilling days, was even more strongly marked than on Tuesday, an additional 10,000 paid for admission at the doors, the 'season tickets again came freely in, and the duchess, the Ilaundress, or the milliner, moved as freely about the .Exhibition as though they were all on an ?? one objecting to mix with the people, and the people themselves being too busily engaged in admiring the wonders of nature and art by which they were surrounded to notice the difference between the brocaded satin or the .humble Manchester print. On Thursday the number. of visitors was still in- creasing, those present amounting to nearly 55,000, of whom upwards of 47,000 paid for admission, the re- mainder consisting of holders of season tickets. Her Majesty, with the Prince and other members of her family, was again at the Exhibition, and, as on Tuesday, spent a considerable time, after having gone over a large portion of. the building, in watching visitors entering at the various doors on their being opened. And here we may be allowed to add that her Majesty, learning that the Executive Committee had declined to accede to a request made to them to admit the children of the Royal 'Asylum of St. Ann's Society to the Exhibition free, at some time when it was not open to the public, has graciously ordered that the expense of their admission shall be paid from her privy purse. It is gratifying to know also that these are not the only children educated in .our public schools who are to be allowed to enjoy a day in the Exhibition, as we find, by our report of the proceedings at the dinner of the Royal Freemasons' School. for. Female Children, that a number of ladies present at the festival entered into a subscription to defray their expenses to, from, and in the Exhibition- an example which we trust, and no doubt will be ex- tensively followed by other parties connected with the various orphan and other schools in the metropolis. Friday and yesterday were high priced days, re- spectively 2s. 6d. and 6e., when the season-ticket holders came out in full force, and the carriages at the gates were as numerous as ever. Taken as a whole, we look upon the success of the arrangements as complete, and weI doubt not that. next week's receipts will show a considerable increase on those of this week, which have added something like 12,000 or 14,000 to the funds at the disposal.of.the Committee. As regards the Exhibition itself but very little altera- tion has taken place since last week, though in the Russian division they are remarkably busy in preparing to show their productions, which arrived by the Neptune yesterday week, and will doubtless be ready for exhi- bition before we next address our readers. Having made these few general observations, we will now resume our Walks in the Exhibition, but before doing so we feel ourselves bound in justice to notice a letter which we have received relative to our article last week. We then said, speaking of Wilkins's lighthouse, " This lighthouse, we are informed, is attended by a person to explain its design and principle, visitors not being allowed to enter it, but somehow or other, though we, like you, kind reader, have been there some dozen, or perhaps more times, 'have never been able to meet with him." We have since received a letter from a friend of the party in charge of the lighthouse, assuring us that he has made every inquiry, and finds the man is more regular and constant in the discharge of his duties than almost any other person in the building, hardly ever leaving it to get refreshment, and generally taking his meals at his post, " sitting down on one or other of the numerous seats close by." If this is the case, andi we have no reason to suppose that the writer of the letter would tell us anything that he did not believe to be so, we have been most unfortunate, as we assure him that we did more than once make some inquiries relative to the lighthouse,, and can only suppose that we have not found the right party to obtain it from owing to his "sitting down'? on one or other of the seats, and his not wearing anything to distinguish him from the general company. At the same time we beg to assure him that we bad no intention of casting a "stain on his character," or singling him out for our " animadversions," and that no one can more sincerely regret it than we do if we have given him pain by an observation which was written as much in badinage as in earnest. We may also mention that we are informed by friends' of ouys-who have had the advantage of his expla- pations that the party to whom we alluded is a very intelligent and. courteous individual. We will now, reader, if you please, take A Walk in, India. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Vn baturday, the 21st, the receipts amounted to 1,6741. los., and according to the police returns, 12,732 persons entered the building during the day. On Monday commenced the fifth shilling week at the Crystal Palace. and from an early hour the aspect of the western part of the metropolis indicated an undiminished concourse of people. From every part of town, from' every suburb, from every line of road, and from every railway terminus, ouni- busses and cabs, loaded inside and out, were proceeding rapidly towards the great western road, which passes the Exhibition; and for more than a mile that road presented one mass of moving vehicles, including many large vans filled with labourers or other rural folk, and ornamented with ever- greens, favours, and banners. Soon after nine o'clock groups of visitors, eager to be early, gathered round the chief eu- trances; and by ten o'clock these groups bad 'clustered into crowds, each numbering hundreds, and almost sufficient of themselves to fill any building of less colossal capacity than the Crystal Palace. When the doors were opened, every avenue to the pay-stands was at once blocked up; Sand people pressed in as rapidly as their shillings could be put down,.and their bodies squeezed through the narrow openings. Thus, at the principal entrances, there were some sixparallel columns of visitors pressing in as fast as possible-it has been estimated at the rate of one for, every two or three seconds, or at least twenty per minute. The reader will therefore not be sur- prised to learn that, in the first hour, nearly 23,000 persons had poured into the building, and by one o'eloek niore than 50,000; and by two o'clock nearly 60,000 had entered. Its style sis transitional from the gothicto the renaissance, and Xof course, is sprinled with fleu--de-lis and other his- torical allusions to the sway of the elder Bourbon branch. II one of the side pa- nels, and in close connexion with Spanish diamonds of the first water, have been gathered paste dupli- cates of the sword, sceptre, and other emblems of Haitian sovereignty. The crown of the Queen is conspicuous on a velvet cushion, but that of the King having proved a comparative failure, has been ignominiously placed into a drawer beneath; Those who have sufficiently taxed the powers of their eyesight seek relief in indulging other senses, and are especially attracted by She fragrant perfume emitted by the jet of eau de cologne, which plays by intermittent fits in the rooms fitted up with the rcostly and splendid furniture from Vienna. The names of those great Viennese upholsterers,C. Leistler and Son, and that of their architect, Mr. - Bernardo Xde Bernardis, are not more generally unknown to most people than the style adopted in their decoration of the furniture, or the wood employed in its manufacture. This wood is that of the locust tree, a species of acacia, which is imported from l Brazil, which has been for the first time turned to its present account; and as far as outward appearances go, the result seems most favourable. In its solid yet slightly ponderous character one is unconsciously reminded of the contents of old English mansions, though the rich stuffs whi ch used formerly to aid in the embellishment of large rooms, have been almost entirely dispensed with, so as not to distract the eye in any way fiom the lavish expenditure of carving throughout ; and by that, means, thatwhich might have seemed oppressive with minutenessis rendered remarkablysober. The tester of the large bedstead is even covered with a dark brown velvet, made almost to match the colour of the wood. Its general arrangement, as we have said, is a plea- sant departure'from any given, style; and we may fancy the puzzled air of an antiquarian compelled to give an opinion oa the subject a century or two hence. small pillars clustered round a spiral column of equally diminutive proportions, form the fore-posts, in the spaces between which are carved Adam and Eve, the four ages of man, &c. In another apart- ment is a Gothic oak bookease, sent as a present to the Queen by the Emperor of Austria; and which contained some books carved and embossed, which would make even "' Luke Liinnor" stand aghast. They are full of original designs in water-colours by German artists. Amid this wondrous work there is one ornamental contrivance which has puzzled most people by its novelty, being more like a coat and umbrella stand than anything hitherto known or seen. Its four panels, jutting out from their central shaft, which turns on a pivot, however, proclaim its destination as a receptacle for family portraits. There is some- thing out of the common if this fanciful idea, of thus collecting family portraits round a common centre. The artist seems to have selected lighter toned woods, according to the humour or destination of his per- formance. In this respect the Hungarian ash seems admirably suited to the sportive character of the cupids dancing together perched on their bracket- stands. As for the chairs and sofas, the keeper will have to expend a vast amount of logic before he can persuade people that they have no right to sit down in them, so inviting are their airs of repose. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. - r nRE IN THIE CRYSTAL PALACE. Yesterday (Thursday) the influx of visitors to the Ex hibition was gteater than ever, and the sum taken at the doors could not have been much less than 2,0001. This is of course entirely the proceeds of the 5s. entrance fee, and does not include the large amount still accruing from the sale of season tickets. The improvement in the weather has acted with magical effect upon the flow of visitors, and brought out the beauty and fashion of Lon- don into Hyde-park just as sunshine developes butter- flies. They take possession of the Crystal Palace in a manner which must make the royal commission have sundry misgivings about their power to keep it in their own hands now, or to have it removed a few months hence. A man may be coerced, but how are ladies to he dce!t with should they take it into their heads to keep the building for a promenade, or whirls it really seems to be well adapted, when the exigencies of our variable climate are remembered ? Even now, when from 20,000 to 30,000 ofthe most inquisitive and adventurous people on the face of the earth are busily engaged in rummnag- ing its multifarious contents, it is quite possible to creep away into solitudes uninvaded by the bustling Babel elsewhere. Such is the size of the building, no part o I which is overcrowded, while some still remain unvisited. What if this vast collection was destroyed by fire'? Many cities might be burnt to the ground without caus- ingesuch a sensation as that would. Yet to that risk the Crystal Palace was for a moment exposed yesterday morning. The flue attached to a gas stovein one of the offices of the contractors became heated, and ignited a piece of wood with bunting which rested upon or touched it. A piece of the burning cloth fell into a small open-cask of Indian corn, which stood, as the Irish say, " convenient." All this mischief was brewing in secret in the southern part of the colonial collection on the east side. The drapery of the counter concealed what had happened, and it was only when the smoke began to break forth that an alarm was raised. Fortu- nately such casualties have been foreseen and amply provided for. There are; no less than a dozen large fine.engines within the building, besides an ample supply of water easily obtainable, and a thoroughly organized force ready to act at a moment's notice. The fire of yesterday was extinguished before it had time to do more than slightly char one plank of wood, and no anxiety need be caused by an oc- currence so trifling. It will, however, we trust warn all parties-connected with the beilding to be on the alert, and to trust nothing to chance. The executive com- mittee continue to receive all kiads of applications from the country with reference to the terms of admission when the low prices commence. Among others several clergymen have weritten to them etfering to bring up with them all theit parishioners in a body. Fox and Hender- son are contemplating a grand entertainment of roast beef and pli pudding to be given by thseir foremen and chief workmen to the ws rkmeo from foreign countries in the building. At present there are selling about 10,000 copies of the small catalogue per day-an enormous number when the bulk of the volume is remembered. Ads yet only one portion of the larger work has appeared, e nd both from unavoidable causes have many deficiencies. With reference to the countries overtaken in their pre- parations by the opening; and compelled now to confu- sion and labour while others ate exhibiting their contri- butions, France is thee most conspicuous instance of that tardiness. The Tok is proverbially slow, the Russian is frozen up in the Baltic, ?? East India Company have half the world to cross and the Cape of Good Hops to double before they can bring the produce of theii vast empire to swell the wonders of the Crystal Palace but the French have only a small gut separating theib shore from ours, and we are told by one of their favouritt writers that 'their motto is '1toujours prdts." Franc waited tilt the liast moment, but she has not gone ahead In our own division of the building a few things an creeping into spots left unoccupied, or which at the las moment it was found impossible to complete in rims Among these was brought in and placed in the nave yes terday, a beautiful model, executed bv Mr. Deighton, o Great College-street, Westminster, of the interior of he Majesty's Theatre. The decorations are all carefull: represented, and to the multitudes who throng the centr of the Crystal Palace this work will convey a very accu rate sand pleasing idea of the extremely light and elegar yet rich style in which " Her Majesty's" is fitted up.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Thubsd ay.— Notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather, 61,492 persons visited tbe Crystal Palace, and tbe large amount of £"2,958 wm taken at the doors. Fbiday.— Her Majesty, the Prince, and the members of tbe Royal family, visited tbe Exhibition again, and spent some time in tbe French and Italian compartments. They afterwards passed throngb the central refreshment court, but tbe hour of tbeir visit wm too early to partake of any refresh menu. Crossing the transept, the Royal visitors entered tbe EMt Indian compartment, and examined with some attention the gorgeous display of gold, jewellery, ivory, silks, and other tissues therein displayed. Messrs. Jackson and Graham's silk loom wm also visited, and Ha peculiar action explained, and after viewing Mr. H. C. Selous' large picture of the inauguration of the Exhibition, in which portraits of most ofthe distinguished persons who assisted are introduced, the Queen proceeded to the north foreign gallery, where the stained and painted glass is dis- played, aad passed down its entire length. Her Majesty left the building about half-past ten o'clock. The heavy rain of Thursday penetrated through the roof in various places, and did some damage to the goods here aod there. Workmen were to-day employed upon tbe outside in repair- ing the damage, which is generally occasioned by the canvas covering becoming loosened by tbe wind — the flapping of the loose portion breaks the glass, and the defect is not discovered till a sudden shower givw moat unpleasant inti- mation to the exhibitors below. This is one of tbe defects which, owing to tbe peculiar construction of tbe building, it will be impossible entirely to obviate. A new aad very comprehensive chart of the building has just been published oy Herr Heine, in German, French, and English. The principal objects of interest in the different compartmente are indicated, and tbe whole building appears to nave been carefully gone over by the publisher and his assistants, who, we understand, were four weeks constantly engaged in the preparation of the map! Saturday. — To-day the Queen instead of going direct to the Exhibition Building, stopped to inspect the model houses for families near the Knightsbridge- barracks. She wm there received, at about 9 o'clock, by Mr. Dilke. The Earl of Shaftesbury, Mr. Roberto, and Mr. Chad wick were also present and conducted Her Majesty through the rooms. The Queen appeared much gratified, and expressed her approbation of the rery comfortable arrangements there- in made for the poorer classes. After half an hour's ?? Her Majesty walked across to one of the small exit doors on the foreign side of the building, up the nave to the stair- case in the Canadian department. At the bottom Mr. Dilke called his Royal Highness Prince Albert's attention to a small marble bust of himself, carved at Rome in 1850, by Barbato Cipriani, with which he appeared somewhat amused. After a short inspection ofthe Spitalfields silks, Mr. Dilke showed to Her Majesty the beautiful designs which we cannot describe better than by quoting the letter sent with them :— " Mr. John R. Laranchy hM the honour of submitting to Her Majesty and bis Royal Highness Prince Albert specimens of Spitalfields silks made in the early part of 1745, and manufactured by James Leman, of the City of London, and designed by J. V. Sommer, amongst which the pattern of silk made for the Queen Caroline, wife of George 11. , and some for court dresses worked with gold and silver, the whole of wbich are of tbe most perfect make and of beautiful colouring and splendid designs." In the case of Messrs. Campbell Harrison, and Lloyd was shown a piece of the same gold brocade as wm worn by bis Royal Highness Prince Albert at the fancy ball at the Palace. Her Majesty's attention wm next chiefly attracted to the five great Coventry ribands, three of which, we believe, she herself intends to purchase, and the cheap ribands manufactured by steam. In passing through the part of the gallery devoted to the exhibition of Nottingham lace, Her Majesty wm received by the exhi- bitors, headed by the Mayor, whose services in the cause of the Exhibition have been very numerous. In the section of precious metals Her Majesty did not remain long, all the articles having been inspected by her on two previous occasions, still sbe graciously acknowledged the merit of the articles presented to her passing notice by the exhibitors. The bronzes and electro-typing in gold and silver of Messrs Elkington and Co., retained the Royal party for some time. In ite small unpretending casket they inspected Mr. Hope's blue diamond, considered unique from iv sapphire colour and large size. Mr. Hope wm himself present as the exhibitor, and took tbe beautiful brilliant from ite case tbat Her Majesty might handle it. The black diamond belong- ing to Mr. Joseph Mayer, of Liverpool, wm next shown ; of this diamond we can say nothing but that it wm found in the Bahia mines, and that it has successfully resisted polishing. Her Majesty left the building at 11 o'clock by the entrance in the sonth transept creating no incon- siderable commotion among the numerous Bathcbairs collected round the gate. The receipts during the day amounted to 1 589/. 155., and the police returns gave 11,181 persons as the number who visited the building. The above is taken from the Times. The Morning Chronicle gives further particulars, m follows: — " Her Majesty much admired the articles in shawls and scarfs exhibited by Messrs. Ball and Dunnicliff, of Nottingham, and two shawls have been sent from this case to Bucking- ham Palace for inspection. [They were purchased by Her Majesty.] The exhibitors explained the process of manu- facure, amongst the rest, the Mayor, Mr. Felkin, whose services in promoting the Exhibition, and in arranging the Nottingham portion of it are highly appreciated." Monday.— This day 2,957/. Bs. wm received at the doors of the Crystal Palace, which wm visited by 62,694 persons. Tubsoat.— The unprecedentedlylargenumber of 74,122 penr-ynm visited the Crystal Palace, and £3,509 Bs. wm mense influx, consequent probably upon the combined at- tractions of the Exhibition and the cattle-show at Windsor, which have brought swarms of people up from the country to " kill two birds with one stone," the utmost good humour prevailed, and less inconvenience from overcrowding wm experienced than might have been anticipated. The Queen and Prince Albert again visited the building. They ex- amined the Austrian toys and glass, the Lyons silks and Mulhausen prints, and the Prince during his ?? took especial notice of a new painting of the opening ceremony by Mr. Nash, forming one of the series of sketches of that remarkable event which he is preparing under the royal patronage. The production in question is even more suc- cessful than his first, and depicte the spectacle which the interior presented when the Queen, after visiting the foreign division of the building, wm returning past the Amazon group towards ber throne under the transept. In point of colouring, and in the truthfulness with which the scene is reproduced, this sketch is a very happy effort of the artist. The rumoured fete to the Royal Commission by the city of Paris is now so far settled to Uke place that the pro- gramme is in process of arrangement The invitations will probably embrace all connected with the Exhibition whose services entitle them to be present, and the festivities will, it is said, consist of a grand ball at the Hotel de Ville, and a dinner to a select party of our countrymen and the foreign Commissioners. It is likely that the event will come off soon, and a Friday is spoken ef as the proper day for start- ing, Saturday for the joyous celebrations at the Hotel de Vtlle, Sunday for the waterworks at Versailles, Monday for sight-seeing in Paris, and Tuesday for tbe return home.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The first day of the last week of the Exhibition has passed off in a manner at once gratifying and surprising. Everybody was prepared for a great accession of numbers to the usual average of shilling 'visitors, but the most extravagant expectations could hardly have anticipated anything so remarkable as the actual reality. On Monday 108,813 people entered the building, and the sum of £5,175 16s. was taken at the doors. Pacts so astounding speak for themselves, and derive no additional force from expatiating upon them. Were it not so, we should despair of describing the scene which the interior presented. The dreadful limit of 100,000 spectators has now been exceeded, and without any extraordinary inconvenience. That nearly 108,000 people should within one day and under one roof have enjoyed the grandest spectacle that the world has over witnessed is of itself a sufficient marvel, but that they should have done so without a single known casualty to life or property is almost incredible. So, however, it is, and we leave to revolutionary and discontended minds the stately of facts which place in so clear and unquestionable a light the love of order and the general kindliness of spirit which pervade all classes of our population. Yet, while we dwell with a natural complacency on those evidences of a happy and prosperous people, circumstances are constantly occurring to warn us of possible disaster. Such an event took place on Monday. When the crowd assembled within the building was at its culminating point, it was suddenly discovered that the Duke of Wellington was present. Instantly the manifestation of public admiration arose. Hats were taken off and loud cheers burst forth, which were prolonged with immense energy. Those who were at a distance, surprised by an unwonted agitation which they could not understand, fancied that there was something wrong, and rushed towards the doors. The Duke also felt the awkwardness of his position, and beat a retreat. His great age does not now permit him to execute such movements with the precision and firmness which in former days were his characteristics, but he made his way nevertheless to the south entrance of the transept with surprising alacrity, followed as he went by the most vigorous demonstrations of popular regard. Superintendent Pearce, with great tact, stopped the rush towards the places of exit, and by his judicious management the fears of the most timid spectators were in a few minutes effectually quieted. —Times.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. {From the Alhenaum.) The enthusiasm which hailed the opening of the Palace of Glass, instead of falling off, as many feared it would, like the sparkle of yesterday's champagne, has settled into a powerful and well-sustained movement. Like an ocean following in the wake of the first wave of a returning tide, public interest has set broadly in the direction of the first day's flow. The eye never wearies with the beauty— the mind never feels satiated with the knowledge to be harvested there at every turn. There is enough and to spare for all tastes and appetites. The senses, the imagination, and the intellect, all find food in over-abund- ance. Beauty is here reproduced in forms yet undreamed of, — and he who offered a reward for a new sensation should have lived till now. The artist and the artisan, each quitting for a day the narrow circle of bis own professional ideas, learns to compare aud comprehend the whole range of works on which the genius of labour is employed, and his relation to them. Self-knowledge speaks from every corner, and every species of mirror reflects sound wholesome truth. Individual coxcom- bries perish at once in this marvellous atmosphere, and na- tions become individuals in presence of a world. As commu- nities learn here their weakness, so also they learn their strength ; and the rebuke administered to the one chastens, and so dignifies, the pride due to the other. Presiding at a banquet such as no country every spread before, England is sober and serene. All the morals of the magnificent scene are souud, chastening, and corrective. Meanwhile, the E xecutive Committee, anxious to bring out all the powers of the exhibition — to make it more than a mere self- eloquent spectacle— are considering how its educational capa- bilities may be turned to the most profitable account. At this point a new and vast field of thought opens before us : and we perceive how full of oracles not foreseen is the temple whicli we have reared to Wisdom. The great thing is to let the people hear them speak — not to suffer an occasion such as the world never had before to pass away without yielding the lessons with which it overflows. When was an Encyclopaedia of Knowledge like this ever edited by any land before ? Here, for the first time, is a Library, to which all the world has contributed its living books. With or without aid and countenance from the Commission, au uninterrupted process of education will go on within these walls of glass, of whicli the fruits will be seen in years to come ; but it does not seem to us that it would be difficult to devise a means whereby that process might be most materially quickened and enlarged. Every one who bus seen much of the scientific aud the operative minds of England, has found more or less occasion to regret that the two orders of men dwelt so far apart — that no readier and more open channel of commnnication existed between tbem, so that the information acquired or the principles established by the one class could be instantly made available to the other. As it is, the knowledge which in practical hands might be made pro- ductive of comfort and advantage to the world, is sometimes locked up for a time in coteries and classes. A new vegetable substance— gutta percha, for instance— is discovered and sent over to England. Learned meu iv blue spectacles, and learned ladies in blue stockings, pore over it, and wonder what the curiosity is good for ; but so soon as a practical worker looked at the substance, it becomes at once an article of daily use, administering to the comfort and ornament of life in a variety of different ways. Now, Nature is uot exhausted. Within her fertile bosom there may be thousands of substances yet unknown as precious as the only r'eceutly-found gutta per- cha. To doubt this would be to repudiate the most logical inference afforded by the whole history of the earth. Com and the grape excepted, nearly all our staples in vegetable food are of comparatively modern discovery. Society had a long existence without tea, coffee, cotton, cocoa, sugar, and potatoes. Who shall say there is uot a more nutritious plant than the sugar- cane—a finer root than the potato— a more useful tree than the cotton ? Buried wealth lies everywhere in the bowels of the earth, which needs but the true divining rod for its discovery. The system of discoveries by which the unknown wealth of Nature is laid open to the notice of civilized men is in action — continual but incidental and unregulated action — at present; but it seems not impossible that some methods might be adopt- ed for organizing these discoveries so as to render them more promptly available. What is chiefly required is, the meaus of bringing the scientific and practical intellects ot the country together; and this maybe achieved, to some extent at least, in the Crystal Palace. Why not institute in that grand and neutral arena public lectures in each department of the exhibi lion ? Why not set all the masters to teach, and all the pupils to learn, in this true university ? Here are all the sciences in their relations and their results. The Sussex fanner will be able to judge for himself of the value of Yorkshire carts and Pennsylvania ploughs ; but he might glean a great deal of novel and useful information from a scientific botanist in a well-arranged lecture on foreign seeds, roots, fruits, trees, and so forth. On dyes and colours the chemist would be able to communicate uumerous hints to the practical dyer and colour- ist A well-versed mineralogist could in like manner instruct the practical miner in various things whicli it behoves him to know— the science of his art, the modes and practices of foreign countries, the history and the peculiar incidents of his business. So throughout. The Oxford mau would do well to come out of his cloister into thisgraud college, and see how full the world is of things not whispered beneath the tower of Cbristchurch. The Palace of Glass contains the complete and practical logic of the earth. DAILY MEMORANDA On Saturday morning the Queen and Prince Albert, accom- panied by their Royal guests, visited the exhibition, and remained for nearly two hours. The illustrious party exam- ined carefully the jewels belonging to the Queen of Spain, exhibited on the south side of the nave, iv the French division. They also inspected the Swiss collection, and admired the fine display of artificial flowers contributed by Coustantin. They paid a visit to the Sheffield Court, and minutely inspected Hoole's and Stewart and Smith's grates. Iv the section of woollen fabrics tlieir attention was attracted to the specimens shown there of Huddersfield, Bradford, and Leeds manufac- tures. The collection of cottons and linens was also examined, and the jlloyal party took particular notice of Mercer's new patent method for increasing the brilliancy of colours, of Ly- diard's chintzes, and of the contributions of Black, of Glasgow. The Royal party appeared highly delighted with their visit. At 12 o'clock the public were admitted to the building, and flowed in with such eagerness that iv the course of the after- noon more than 421,800 was taken at the doors. The Duke of Wellington is a frequent visitor at the exhibition. He was there ou Saturday, and with Mrs. Fox, the wife of the contractor, on his arm, examined several of the departments. However crowded the spot may be where his Grace makes his appear- ance, a space is immediately cleared for him, and, except the Queen herself, no Royal personage could be treated with more distinction. Her Majesty paid another visit to the Crystal Palace on* Monday, and remained a considerable time examining the agricultural implements aud machinery, and the collection of ores and minerals. The number of visitors was not quite so large as on Saturday, tbe afternoon having turned out unfa- vourable, but the dimiuution could only be perceived by those who are in the habit of frequenting the building daily, and, indeed, the weather has little effect upon the cluss of visitors to whom it is as yet confined, and who are to some extent independent of atmospheric inconveniences. Tbe average daily receipts since the opening have been little short of £2,000, and if the income continues to maintain the same high figure the whole expenses of the building will have b^eu paid off before the price falls to a shilling and the general public are admitted. The frequent visits of her Majesty and the Royal Family have added considerably to the popularity of the Exhibition— all minds are occupied with it, and all tongues ore loud iv praises; one of its peculiarities is its vast extent, which cannot be fully comprehended on the first visit, and it ts only when an attempt is made to methodise and arrange the process of investigation aud inspection, that tbe stupendous scale upon which the whole hus been planned can be fully comprehended. The efforts of ja long day sink into insignificance when a trial is made to explore the illimitable mazes of the aisles and ave- nues vanishing in the remote perspective, or the sweepiugexteut of the galleries, to traverse which alone would be considered a reasonable promenade for a day. The pedestrian feats wliich delicate ladies^ accomplish within the building are marvelous, and it is only 'the sustaining power of continued excitement and novelty, the desire to pass from one object of interest to another, the swallowingof everything with the eyes and retaining little in the mind, the anxiety to see everything at once, aud the utter impossibility of seeing anything well, that carries them through a radier fatiguing movement of four or five hours employed in advancing, turning back, stooping, straining, dart- ing into this compartment, aud gliding out of that, crawling slowly up staircases and skipping lightly down ; and thus the movements of the visitors themselves are among the most curious aud interesting features of the Exhibition. Certainly oue of its many characteristics— apart from the aichitectural beauty of the lofly trausept, the grand sweep of the naves, and the interminable looking aisles and passages, in which the allusion of remoteness and distance is still further heightened by the airiness and transparency of the encasing material, aud the presence of the majestic mouarchs of the park, that spread their branches overhead— is the fact that there is no one indi- vidual article, nor no particular collection, that monopolises attention to the comparative neglect of others. Apart from the attractions of the Kohi-Noor— which, although oue of the first objects sought for, never receives a second look, the feeling of most of the visitors being that of disappointment at its com- paratively small size and want of that peculiar brilliancy which is conventionally attached to the diamoud-the crystal fountain, which is continually receiving fresh accessions of admirers, and the costly display of gems belonging to the Queen of Spain- setting these aside, which always captivate the attention of iresn arrivals, the four great classes into which the Exhibition is divided appear to have equal attractions for all. Those, however who wish to obtain a fair idea of the contents of the Crystal 1 alace, will do well to take each country iv detail, aud then, having gone through the foreign departments, with their corresponding galleries, proceed in like manner through the western portion of ihe building. Every piece has been produced with equal care and liberal expenditure. A theatre conducted on these principles, with the well-assorted available talent included in the company, must succeed, and will advance in public estimation with certain progress. There are yet assisting influences proceeding from high quarters which might be brought in, to aid still further the cause of the legitimate drama, and which might elevate its moral and political influence far beyond what can be effected by managerial tact and acting ability. Of this we shall treat hereafter, when we have more time and space to enter on what we consider a very important, and in many respects a national consideration. A genuine English tragedy, such as the Gamester, essentially sound, and universally applicable, so finely acted as it was last night in the two principal characters, and so received by such an audience, is not an occurrence of common place interest, or confined in its effects to the individual locality or single occasion. It bears a reflected influence on the stage as an instrument of utility as well as entertainment, and becomes an era of some importance as regards the advancement of the drama. It is a public lesson for the use of all students in a refined, ennobling art—a moral lecture in a captivating form, delivered in a school of acknowledged superiority. If we search the modern stage for a specimen of living talent, less open to criticism or objection than any other, we may select the Beverley and Mrs. Beverley of Mr. and Mrs. Kean, and rest satisfied that we have seen two very forcible dramatic conceptions embodied throughout with a truth, a power, and a distinctness which can only be mastered by comprehensive genius, joined to long experience. Mrs. Beverley is drawn by the author as a natural, unaffected personage, as far as possible removed from a heroine, invested with no regal loftiness of position to give solemnity to grief, thrown into no extravagant dangers, and encircled by no mantle of romance. Her sorrows are purely domestic, such as the humblest can understand and feel the reality of, and which may happen to any one at any time. They arise from the fatal propensity of her husband for one overwhelming vice, his only failing. She still fondly loves and trusts him in spite of his follies and infatuation. The very simpleness and familiar tone of the character render it difficult for stage embodiment. It requires the consummate ability of a great actress to preserve the dignity and impressive effect of tragedy under circumstances of every day's occurrence, in the ordinary rank of educated life. Mrs. Kean manages all this with surpassing skill and delicacy. She can have derived scarcely any hints or assistance Irons her predecessors who had nearly all the stage before her career commenced. She could have known little of them beyond traditionary description and vague reminiscences. Her idea of the character is entirely her own, and in several points strikingly original. We may select her scene with Beverely in the second act, where she surrenders her jewels on the first hint that he requires them, and her interview with Stukely when het ventures to lay bare his infamous designs. Her answer to his assertion that the jewels have been given to a mistress, not believe it," produced a sensation in the house which told that genuine nature was there and recognised unanimously. It was one of those master touches never to be forgotten : the refined pencilling of genius which marks the wide distinction between the simple painter and the firstrate artist. Mr. Kean's Beverley is deserving of equal praise. Of the two the part is the more telling, as abounding in superior bursts of passim and greater variety of emotions: alternately swayed by excitement and repentance, spurred on by hope, exasperated to frenzy, or sunk down to the lowest depths of despair. His third act scene with Stukely, when driven frantic by his losses, and his concluding act in the prison, after swallowing the poison, are fearfully contrasted, and arrest the audience in a manner we never saw surpassed. The men held their breath in rivetted attention, and women sobbed with uncontrollable agony. If effect be a just test of the actor's merits, as it unquestionably is, here is an instance in which triumphantly exemplified. An individual spectator it is m r may t object to a particular reading or passage, or a second may differ altogether from the conception of the actor. Either may be right or wrong; but the collective audience is the safest tribunal. The object is to produce effect; and he who can produce the strongest effect in the right place is certain to be the most popular actor, and is in all probability the best. It rarely happens that the majority are wrong, or that thousands can be wrought up to simultaneous approbation unless the spark of genius has been kindled to inflame them. Mr. and Mrs. Kean should always be seen together in the same play to be fully appreciated. Their styles assimilate either by natural sympathy or long practice. Their powers are doubled by actiug in unison. Either deprived of the other would be like a general without his right arm, or a ship divested of rudder and compass. GREAT EXHIBITION. Monday was decidedly one of the great days at the Crystal Palace. Great in the number of visitors, great in their infinite variety of countenance and of costume, great in the heat of the interior. The numbers were 70,640; total receipts, £3,344 13s. 6d. On Tuesday the receipts at the doors amounted to £3,236 25.; and the number of visitors was, by the police returns, 68,161. _ _ _ The unfavourable state of the weather on Wednesday sent the receipts at the doors of the Crystal Palace down to £2,438 145., the number of visitors being only 50,599. Owing to the very unfavourable state of the weather on Thursday, the number of visitors, as might have been expected, was not so great as upon the previous days. It amounted to 44,458. The amount received during the day was £2,286 is. On Friday the numbers were 26,348. An interesting event was well•nigh taking place on Wednesday which would have rendered the Great Exhibition the birth-place of a youthful visitor. A young lady, accompanied by her husband and two female friends, who had been waiting for some time at the south entrance, in the vain hope of obtaining a conveyance, was suddenly seized with symptoms which indicated that she was on the point of becoming a mother. With the aid of Mr. Duncombe, the assistant-secretary, and several other of the officials, the lady was conveyed to the Commissioners' room, and laid on a sofa. After the lapse of upwards of an hour, she was placed in a cab, and shortly afterwards gave birth to her first child, a fine boy. We understand that both mother and child are progressing as favourably as might be expected under the peculiar circumstances of the case.

The attendence at the Crystal Palace once more appears to be on the increase, and yesterday the receipts at the doors rose to 2,767/. 175.; the number of visitors according to the police returns was 56,852. For this increase several reasons may be assigned, among which may be mentioned the gradual diminution of harvest labour and the approaching close of the Exhibition. Another feature now becomes prominent. The working classes appear upon the scene in great force, and seem determined to witness the spectacle while it is still in their power to do so. We do not remember to have seen so many artisans and mechanics present in the interior as there were yesterday. During the whole of the forenoon they might be observed in continuous streams from every avenue of approach flowing towards the centre of attraction, and their attention was principally occupied by the machinery in motion, which during the day was almost blocked up with visitors. A curious fact was mentioned to us as illustrative of the anxiety still felt in the provincial towns to inspect the wonders of the Exhibition. On Saturday night, before the departure of the excursion train to London, one pawnbroker in Leeds had received on deposit no less than a bushel and a half of watches ; and this sudden and extraordinary accession of business he attributes entirely to the desire which those who are little able to afford the treat have to visit the Crystal Palace. The building in Hyde-park is at last drawing towards it the humbler classes of the population. They find that a reduction of the existing admission fee is now hopeless, and they make up their minds to gratify a long pent up curiosity at all hazards and regardless of expense. 'The unpacking of the recently arrived contributions from Sweden still continues, and is superintended by the commissioner from that country, M. Hjertsberg. Though late in the day, these exertions to make a worthy display in the great industrial gathering of all nations will no doubt be fairly appreciated by the public. It may be satisfactory to the shopkeepers and trade of Landon generally to know that the Royal Coin- ' mission are fully determined to adhere strictly to their early pledges, and that they will not lend themselves, under the most pressing circumstances, to any sales which might interfere with the ordinary course of business, and would certainly be foreign to the main objects of the Exhibition. Strong representations have been made to them on this point by contributors from abroad, and especially from those whose Governments have come forward most liberally in helping to defray their expenses. This is another example, if illustrations of the point were wanted, of the advantages of a self-relying spirit, and of the evils consequent upon state support used to bolster up private enterprise. There is every reason to believe that France will benefit largely by the share which her manufacturers have taken in the Exhibition; extensive purchases have been made of the goods displayed in that d. pertinent; and we observe that M. Lacrosse, the president of the permanent committee, at a recent meeting of that body in Paris announced that two of the principal branches of French manufactures (jewellery and c abinet-making), which it was feared would be without employment during the winter, would be able to furnish work to their numerous hands by means of the large orders which they bad received in consequence of the Exhibition. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Friday the receipts from half-crowns amounted to £2051 7s. and the number of visi- tors was 20,859. The principal objects of interest added to the Exhibition on Saturday, were a number of idols from China, contributed by Major Edy, the gro- tesqueness of which appeared to afford much amusement to ordinary observers, whilst a still greater attraction for the philosophic visitor was to be found in their symbolism of the worship of Fo, supposed to be the Buddha of the Hindoos. These divinities seem to have been surrendered hy their priesthood with great facility ; they were brought without difficulty from a temple at the mouth of the Yang-tse-Kiang, or Blue River— the " consideration" on which the idolaters gave them up being simply a supply of opium, whilst the worldly prudence of the lukewarm worship- pers was exhibited in their retention of the pre- cious stones with which the images were adorned. The number of visitors was 16,741 ; the amount received, including £'29 for season tickets, was £1621 7s. 6d. On Monday, the Exhibition was opened at nine o'clock and closed at six, instead of opening at ten and closing at seven, as on previous days — the gradual shortening ofthe days having led to this alteration. Owing, probably, to the change not being very generally known, the number who availed themselves of the earlier hour for visiting the Exhibition was comparatively small; the to- tal number arriving up to ten o'clock being not more than 3478. Within the next hour upwards of 11,000 arrived; at twelve o'clock the total number admitted was 30,589 ; at one, the num- bers reached to 41,017 ; and at two, to 45,513. The amount received was £2511 165., of which sum £5 was the produce of the sale of season tic- kets. During the day many of the visitors were surprised by seeing, towering high over the di- minutive throng, what was at first considered to be a colossal statue ; but, upon closer investiga- tion, proved to be the famous giantess from Lap- land, who is upwards of seven feet in height. She is handsome and well-proportioned, and, as might be expected, attracted considerable notice. She was accompanied by a female attendant in the costume of a Laplander, who, although of fair average height, appeared by her side a per- fect dwarf. An important meeting of the Royal Commission, which was very fully attended, took place in the Ciystal Palace, and was presided over by Prince Albert, who was naturally anxious to see certain ques- tions satisfactorily solved which pressed for a de- cision before his departure to the Highland? . All matters that could stand over, such as the fate of the building, and the appropriation of the surplus funds, are still in reserve ; but the following is a summary of the points finally settled: — The Royal Commissioners have fixed Saturday, the 11th of October, as the day for closing the Exhi: bition to the public. It is their intention to hold a meeting in the building on Wednesday, the 15th of October, at 12 o'clock, to receive the re- ports of the several juries and to take leave of the foreign commissioners. On this occasion they intend to request the presence of Ac exhi- bitors, the jurors, the foreign and local commis- sioners, and the members of the local committees. Immediately after the close of their proceedings permission will be given to the exhibitors to re- move tbeir goods, subject to such regulations as may be made by the executive committee. The reports of the juries and the names of the persons to whom prizes shall have been awarded will af- terwards be published in the London Gazette. It is the desire of the Royal Commissioners not only to present medals to the individuals to whom the juries may have awarded them, but to mark their sense of the great exertions of all the exhibitors, and also of the jurors, the foreign and local com- missioners, the chairmen, treasurers, and secre- taries of local committees, and other persons who have rendered services in promoting the Exhibi- tion, and to present them with a permanent me- morial ofthe undertaking by distributing medals to each, accompanied by n certificate and a copy of the reports of the juries. From this it will be seen that it is not at present contemplated, to close the Exhibition with any pomp or ceremony; thatthe Commission desire, as far as medals, cer- tificates, and jurors' reports can do so, to please everybody ; that they canuot render the closing and the distribution of rewards and honours as they ought to be simultaneous acts ; that the offi- cial announcements of prises will be postponed, and other steps taken to avoid as far as possible individual jealousies and " make things plea- sant." Interior Economy op the Exhibition. — The number of persons that are daily in attendance in the body of the building, augmenting the stream of its contents, is more considerable, per- haps, than the public in general are aware. In addition' to the regular police force and the sap- pers and miners, there are upwards of three hun- dred persons in the pay of the commissioners, and two thousand exhibitors and exhibitors' assistants in daily attendance. With such a multitude of people engaged in the interior, and the infinite variety of risks which may arise froni careless ■ ness and a thousand other causes, the reader may he curious to learn what precautions are taken to provide against accidents. Like every- thing else connected with this great work, they are extremely simple. In the first place, evipry exhibitor is left to take care of his own goods in the best way he can ; which undoubtedly affords the best guarantee for the general security. The m st complete protection against fire is organized all over the interior, consisting of sixteen hy- drants, several fire-engines, and a large supply of fire-buckets and iron reservoirs, all of which can be brought into play at a few moments' notice. The instant the necessary labours are over (and as little es possible is done after dark), all lights are put out, and the protection of the building for the night is consigned to fifty policemen, twenty -four sappers and miners, and six firemen, who sleep upon the premises. But how is this extensive area kept in repair, dusted,and cleaned? By a systematic arrangement, equally simple and effective. Six hours, from four o'clock in the morning till ten, are dedicated to these purposes, and are found amply sufficient. It is, perhaps, the only instance on record of a great pnblic ex- hibition which has received troops of visitors for a period of three months without having been closed up for a single day to be repaired or re- freshed. This Exhibition is independent of such necessities, for which it is partly indebted to its structure being a self-acting duster and cleaner in its floors and roof. — Frazer's Magazine.

The following letter has been addressed to the Royal Commissioners by the Commissioner from the Netherlands: " Gentlemen-When already so many voices have ex- pressed ao eloquently their admiration of the great work which has so brillantly and successfully terminated, it would almost seem presumption in me to add my feeble praise. " But now, on the eve of my return to my country, I would rather leave myself open to the charge of presump- , tion than ingratitude, for not to express my deep sense of the many kindnesses received, the flattering reception I met with during my stay in England, slid the great indulgence shown me by the Royal Commission and Executive Com- mittee, would indeed be ingratitude. " It here becomes my painful duty to refer to the la- mented death of my predecessor, Mr. Camp. Permit rae, gentlemen, to remind you, but for that melancholy event, which deprived me of a valued friend, he would have ful- filled the task much better that now devolves upon me ; for if I have at all deserved the too flattering praise that the august President of your Commission has addressed to me, it is because my young friend had made the preliminary a?- rangerments belonging to my department in ?? a manner an at once to ensure the successful discharge thereof. " After this act of justice rendered to his memory, allow me, gentlemen, to express loyally and sincerely my deep gratitude, and to assure you that it can only be equalled by my admiration of the measures the Royal Commission took to secure the complete success of this grand enterprise. I have also infinite pleasure in acknowledging the aid afforded me by the Executive Committee, by the superintendents of thevarious departments, and by all those Who, during so long a time, contributed to render easy the task so difficult, and without that almost impossible to him who has the honour to be, with the profoundest respect, your most obedient ser- vant, " G. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. In a few short weeks a collection of industrial l products more complete than the world has ever before seen will be resolved into its original ele- ments, and the contents of the Crystal Palace will be re dispersed to every corner of the earth. How- ever stroun our conviction that the main purpose of l their conjoint exposition will have been at- E tained, it would be irrational to deny that the time allowed for their examination has been ex- 'c tremely limited, considering the extent and variety s of the subjects courting and deserving the most s minute inspection. It is, therefore, with much I pleasure that we learn that the Imperial Aus- t trian Commission has proposed that the rich col- lection of minerals at present in their department c shall remain in this country-we giving in ex- c change such of our minerals, especially our carboniferous products, as are of no value to us, though of much interest to them. Nor f can we see why this interchange should stop here. On the contrary, we trust that the principle of reciprocity will be extended to all samples in every branch of art and manufacture included in the Ex- hibition. We consider the suggestion so valuable, that we feel assured of its meeting the full support of those with whom it lies to give it effect. We give to-day zt fourth notice of the specimens and apparatus exhibited illustrative of the process of manufacture of the principal produce of our sugar growing colonies, the cultivation and prepara- tion of which are well deserving the attention of all who are interested in the continued prosperity of l our colonial possessions. SUGAR.-No. IV.Y Having desv iibed the various apparatus employed in the evaporation of sugar, we have now to direct the attention of visitor-.s to the Exhibition to an ex- ceedingly curious and weil-represented collection of apparatus for effecting the separation of molasses, or uncrystallised matter, from crystallised sugar, by the l agency of rotatory force. This is altogether a novel means of effecting the desired effect-the first application of the principle dating scarcely so far back as six years; and the machines by which the principle is applied still undergo alterations so frequent and so numerous that the rotatory drainage of sugar may be said at l this time to be in a state of transition.I Before proceeding to a specific description of these machines, their construction, and their mode of action, it will be necessary to advert to the condi- tion of sugar after its crystallisation and before its drainage. We have already pointed out the de- structive effects of heat on sugar solutions, and have shown that, even underthe ameliorative operation of the vacuum pan, these destructive agencies cannot be entirely overcome. It follows then that, even if the vacuum pan has been employed as the evapo- I rative apparatus, and supposing a pure white so- lution of sugar and water to have been the material on which evaporation has been performed-still the result of this evaporation will not be pure white crystallised sugar, but a mass of small crystals, varying in their shade from yellow to brown, and mixed with a semi-fluid, yellowish brown, uncrystal- lised mass, to which we may apply the general term inolasses. Ulnless this condition of sugar subsequent to the evaporative process be well realised, it is impossible that the functions of the various kinds of centri- fugal apparatus to which we purpose to draw attention can be understood. We will, therefore, desire the reader to figure to himself a loaf of white sugar steeped in treacle until every 1 part of its crystalline structure has been equally saturated. This was almost precisely the original I condition of the loaf after it had been filled into the mould and allowed to cool; this was the condition, more or less marked as to degree, of all sugar loaves, from whatever source obtained; and the last pro- cess of sugar purification consists in effecting the I removal of this impurity. It will considerably facilitate the comprehension of the means employed to effect this separation, if the reader assume white sand to take the place of sugar in the preceding case. If a mixure of white sand and treacle were poured into a sugar-loaf mould, of the ordinary kind, and if a person unac- quaiuted with the manipulation of sugar were de- sired to separate the treacle and leave the sand, he could scarcely fail to see that such separation might easily be effected by washing. IHe would 1 open the small aperture in the apex of the mould, place the mould on a convenient stand, and pour water ol its base. The result of this would evi- dently be a total removal of the treacle, which eventually would leak away. Now this is precisely analogous to the desidera- tum of the sugar manufacture at the present stage; the treacle or molasses is required to be washed away from the sugar, which it contaminates. It will scarcely fail to be perceived that, in the case of sugar, our conditions are different from the case of sand-inasmuch as water, being a solvent for sugar, could only be employed as a washing agent at a considerable expense. Not only would it wash away the contaminating treacle, but also a considerable amount of sugar. Supposing, there- fore, water to be the agent employed, some peculiar means of using it must be devised-means having for their object the limitation of the quantity of water used, so that the minimum of crystallized matter may be dissolved. The best practical me- thod of accomplishing this consists in mixing the 1 water with clay into a paste; which paste, being superimposed on the base of the loaf, is evolved so I slowly that the minimum of crystalline sugar is I liquified. In this operation consists what is termed the process of claying-universally em- ploved not many years ago in refineries, and still very generally used in Cuba, Brazil, and some 1 other foreign colonies. In India, where alcohol is very cheap, this liquid l r is occasionally used as a washing agent, and it pre- sents the advantage of dissolving a very inconsi- derable amount of sugar. A far better plan, however, consists ill using as the washing agent a pure and concentrated solu- , tioD of sugar and water. This is the plan which is now, under the den omi- nation of liquoring, almost universally employed in refineries; and which, anterior to the introduction of , the rotatory machines as sugar-purifying-agents, . was appliedwithout any other adjunct in aid of drain- age than the natural force of gravitation. Hence i it was that the time occupied in liquoring a sugar. loaf, and in allowing it to acquire a sufficient amount of dryness to be stoved, was scarcely less 3 than a week; thus rendering it exceedingly desirable - that some means could be devised for hastening the operation. Moreover-anterior to the application of the ro- tatory principle to the sugar manufacture-it was impossible to submit to the operation of liquoring, or washing, sugar in any other condition than that ! of loaf. Indeed, this fact affords an explanation of 3 the existence of sugar loaves-no other mechanical 3 form beintg so favourable to drainage. The rotatory - principle of drainage was no sooner applied, how- ever, than it became far easier to purify sugar in the condition of disintegrated crystals than in loaves, although the latter desideratum has been accomplished by the genius of M. Van Goethem, of Lembecq, near Brussels, whose centrifugal loaf- machine will presently come under our notice. The facility with which a large mass of wet cloth is dried when exposed to violent rotatory. ' action was first taken advantage of by Mr. Seyrig, I who devised a machine for accomplishing that end. | Some years ago a machine of this kind was ren- i dered familiar to the visitors of the Polytechnic o Institution, and a specimen of it, No. 405, Class 6,1 e may now be seen in the Exhibition. It was manu- 8 factured by Messrs. Manlove and Alliott, and is o exhibited by Messrs. Rotch and Finzel. It would be a task no less difficult than invidious I to specify the first person who applied this rotatory 6 cloth-drying machine to effect the purposes of sugar drainage. In the case of this, as of most 1 other inventions of importance, the varying claims of rival inventors were the cause of long-protracted t and ruinous litigation, until the idea occurred to Athea of consolidating their interests, and trading * Former notiesa5 this subject appeared on the 9th and 16th of June, ond the d q( July, in common. Accordingly, no fewer than seventeen patentees have now combined, and delegated the supervision and general management of their inte- rests to Messrs. Rotch and Finzel, whose namles will be seen attached, in the Exhibition, to certain i rotatory machines as applied to sugar, although the names of others are attached to the same descriptionI of machines in connection with cloth. I That the first application of these machines was attended with difficulties, is no more than might have been expected; but judging from the progres- sive series of them now to be seen in the Exhi- bition, it can scarcely be doubted that the diffi- culties will in time be removed. The advantages of the rotatory principle of l sugar parification naturally flow from the vast l saving of time which it effects in completing the processes of draining and washing. The disadvan- tages may be reduced to the following:- I 1. The small amount of sugar (about 56Ibs.) to which the rotatory agency is, under common cir- cumstances, limited. 2. The great vibration, and extreme wear and tear, to which these machines, owing to their very rapid velocity (from 800 to 1,400 revolutions per minute), are subject. 3. The necessity of stopping the action of the machines, for the purpose of charging and discharging them. The first disadvantage-namely, the small amount of sugar capable of being rotated at one time- seems to be a necessary concomitant of these ma- chines; excepting, indeed, those made for the pur- pose of exposing sugar loaves to centrifugal agency, of which we shall presently treat. The objections and difficulties relative to the friction attendant ol such high velocities as those of these rotatory engines must always be considerable, notwithstand- ing the ingenious methods of weights and springs which have been applied by way of corrective. But the third difficulty has probably been overcome by the inventions of Messrs. Napier and Bessemer. . In all these machines, however they may be varied by secondary modifications, the main con- Fstruction is the same ; they are composed of a cup- like form, placed horizontally on a pivot or axis, having sides of wire gauze or finely perforated metal plate, and supplied by some means with the neces- I sary rotative velocity. With the view of overcoming the necessity of stopping the engine for the purpose of charging and discharging, Mr. Napier has supplied the in- side of the revolving cup with a curved ledge, which is intended to discharge the sugar regularly andcontinuously. We, however, neversawthisvar iety of machine at work, aud therefore can offer no prac. tical opinion on its value. More hopeful, we think, is the modification of Mr. Bessemer, also to he seen in the Exhibition, No. 400, Class 6. This gentleman, with the double object of diminishing friction and of enabling the rotatory portion of the l machine to be removed at pleasure, altogether dis- penses with anyextraneous motive power, and makes the machine self-motive by a very simple application of direct steam. Most of our readers arefaniliar with the pyrotechnic contrivance termed the Catherine- wheel. Mr. Bessemer's rotatory apparatus is a Cathe- rine-wheel worked by steam, instead of gunpowder; playing horizontally, and carrying ol its surface the rotating disc, with iron gauze sides, into which the mass of damp and impure sugar is put. The result of this arrangement is, that-instead of scooping out the sugar when purified by sufficient rotation- the sugar rotator and its contents are removed, and another rotator, already charged, being simply de- I posited on the steam Catherine-wheel, the operation goes on as before. The great clearing power of these rotatory or centrifugal engines-touerbincs as the French call them-can only be appreciated by those who have seen them at work. That they are destined to effect great changes in the system of sugar ma- nufacture cannot be doubted, but considerable difference of opinion exists as to the stages of the manufacture in which their maximum benefit will be - felt. We apprehend that they will eventually be found of the greatest benefit in the colonies; indeed, we believe that, were colonial sugar-growers in a position to adopt the chemical and mechanical im- provements in the sugar manufacture which are now developed, white sugar might be made from 1 the juice direct, so largely, easily, and systemati- cally, that European refineries, except for beet- root sugar, would in the natural course of events disappear. To what extent the rotatory machines are now employed in the maiafacture may be in- ferred from the circumstance that the three Euro- pean nations which are farthest advanced in manu- facturing art exhibit three instruments under various modifications of original form; and Mr. Van Goethem, the philosophic beet-root sugar inanufac- turer of Liembecq, exhibits a specific modification of this machine, adapted for the purpose of making not sugar in disintegrated crystals-techiiically called in England crushed lump-but sugar in the form of loaves. I Whatever may be the differences of opinion as to 1 the personal merit of inventing other forms of sugar centrifugal engines, we believe there can be no doubt that Mr. Van Goethem is the inventor of the one now under discussion. We are particular in mentioning this, because the appa- ratus could only have been the result of a combina- tion of qualities which one individual does not frequently possess-fertility in conception, patience in working out details, mechanical address in applying then, and a happy union of technical with general information. Whatever may be the objections raised against the expense in motive power of Mr. Van Goethem's loaf-making centri- fugal machine, or against its danger-and we con- sider it open to both-there can be no question as to the ingenuity displayed in the design of the ap- paratus itself, or as to its efficiency. . THE GREAT EXHIBITION. As the eye beccnies more accuctomed to the details of the great collection of objects and materials within the building, and as the feeling of novelty wears off, a more accurate judgment will be formed of the nature of its contents, and of the microcosm of human industry and ingenuity which it presents. Every succeeding visit more distinctly shows the impossibility of neaetering the whole of the details without devoting an anaceat of time which few can spare; and those, therefore, who wish to turn it to pracCcal account - ,vill do well to apply themselves to the careful study and analysis of those portions in which they are most interested. A six months' residence, an intelligent guide for every separate department, and a mind as fully stored with knowledge as an encyclopeedia, would alone suffice to comprehend tha whole. The attempt will, however, be made by few. Some will come in the spirit of true religion as wonder-stricken children to a vast temple, in which all the treasures of art and science, and all the marvels of industry and mechanical genius, are heaped up—admiring everything, comprehending nothing fully, and impressed with mingled feelinge of awe and reverence for the Great Being who has endowed his image with the wisdom and the power to produce such wondrous results, and so magnificent a crystalline cathedral for their display. Others will regard it as a means to an end—as the initiatory step in the union and fraternisation of the nations of the earthas the first indication of a return to the golden age of universal peace and brotherhood, and of the permanent advancement and improvement of human society. Others, again, will view it as a great scene of industrial rivalry and competition, and with this class the feelings of jealousy, of ambition, or of triumph will predominate, and the mental process of collating, comparing, and contrasting will take the place of higher and nobler emotions To many it will prove a great practical school of education in various departments of science, art, and industry, while some will look upon it as nothing more than a great bazaar for the exhibition of goods and a fashionable lounge for the display of fine dresses. It is this vast variety of aspects in which it may be viewed that renders the Exhibition so complete, so effective, and so comprehensive —many articles are in themselves plain, common-place, and inelegant; but it is the vast collection, as a whole, of the contributions of human industry in every degree of excellence that stamps it with its peculiar character, and renders it unlike anything that has ever yet been attempted in any country. The feeling of satiety is already manifesting itself with many of the habitua, who begin to turn their attention from the Exhibition to themselves and their neighbours—catalogues, which are never opened, supply the place of fans and parasols; pleasant little coteries are formed in the transept, the naves, and the refreshment salons, and picturesque groups lead animation and variety to a scene in which nature and art are combined in the most harmonious, and fascinating, and original manner. Nevertheless, although weariness may be observed here and there, the influx of visitors still continues; every day adds to the vast human tide that pours along the aisles and passages to look upon the records and monuments of the industrial history of all the nations of the earth. The work of decoration and display goes on but slowly. France is still considerably behind hand. Turkey and Persia are progreasing, but that is all; and India,whose collection is one of the most interesting and attractive of the whole, abotit which we shall have a few words to say on Monday, has nearly completed her arrangements. We are sorry to observe that some French plaster groups intended for the nave, and which have just been opened, have suffered severely in their transit to the Exhibition. One of them, which is shattered to pieces, is a wolf dog defending a child from the attack of a serpent : it is a spirited and well-arranged group, and we wish the artiet success in his efforte to restore the fragments to their original beauty. The east end of the building below and in the galleries still exhibits unfurnished pedestals, naked shelves, and unoccupied counters. We trust some means will be adopted to remedy this deficiency, and render the whole building more harmonious and symmetrical in its arrangement; and seeing the increasing crowds that are daily attracted to the Exhibition, we would suggest the necessity of additional precautions with regard to the safety of the property, and an increased number of police to maintain the circulation uninterrupted, before the floodgates are opened, and the vast multitudes whom the shilling admission will let loose upon Ory4tal Palace sweep away all hope of seeing the wonders .of the intefor wlth either safety or comfort.
