Further consignments from the same country have yet to arrive, FETES AT PARIS.—The following is a copy of the letter addressed by the Marquis of Normanby to Earl Granville, in reply to the request of his lordship, on behalf of the visitors to Paris, to express to the President of the Republic and the Prefect of the Seine the grateful acknowledgements of the kind and cordial reception which they had met at the hands of all classes in Paris : Paris, August 7. "My dear Granville,—Pray assure the gentlemen who have signed the letter which you have committed to my charge that I will take the earliest opportunity to communicate the sentiments expressed in that paper to the President of the Republic and the Prefect of the Seine. " It is my intention to write officially to the Minister for Foreign Affairs on the subject, and also to repeat verbally both to the President and the Prefect of the Seine these expressions of gratitude on the part of the Commissioners, jurors, and others connected with the Exhibition. "I am convinced that the Prince ' and all the members of his Government, will receive with much satisfaction the assurances that their cordial hospitality has been duly appreciated by those to whom it was freely offered; and it is a matter of gratification to me, as the representative of my Sovereign, to be the medium. of making known to the Government to which I am accredited such a declaration on the part of my countrymen. "Having, during the last five years of uninterrupted residence in this country, laboured incessantly, under varied circumstances, to promote a kindly feeling between these two great neighbouring people, I receive from you with peculiar pleasure this testimony of the first beneficial result of the Great Exhibition, in itself so well calculated to promote the development of mutual good-will amongst nations. _ . "The city of Paris on this occasion has displayed no idle or unmeaning hospitality, if from a survey of its municipal constitution we can gather a full impression of the necessity which exists for reforming that of London, and if from the examination of its magnificent public buildings and institutions, founded and liberally supported by Government for the free use of an intelligent people, we can borrow ideas to be realised hereafter, whereby our industrial energies may be directed by the rules of good taste, and a more artistic spirit be harmoniously combined with the strong utilitarian tendencies of our manufactures." PRINCE ALBERT AND THE GREAT EXHIBITION.--..M. Charles Dupin, President of the French Commission for the Universal Exhibition at London, wrote on the 27th ult., before quitting that city, to Prince Albert, complimenting his Royal Highness on his share in the Exhibition, expressing gratitude for the interest which Her Majesty and august family manifested in it, praising the Executive Committee, and making some general observations on the importance and object of the Exhibition. Prince Albert, by a letter dated Osborne, the 31st ult., replied as follows : Monsieur le President,—l have received with much satisfaction the letter of the 27th of this month, which you have addressed to me in my quality of President of the Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851, in the name of the French Commission, on the occasion of your return to France, after having terminated your labours relative to the juries. I fully appreciate, together with all the Commissioners of Her Majesty, the great devotedness displayed by you and by the commission over which you preside. I appreciate the incessant zeal and scrupulous attention with which, during three months, you have accomplished, together with a great number of the most eminent men of all countries, the extremely laborious and responsible duty of jurymen. The best recompense that you will have to receive will be given to you by the general approbation of the public, when the result of your labours shall be known. The Royal Commissioners are not insensible to the readiness with which the members of the French commission have conformed to the regulations imposed on the subject of the conditions on which the first medals were to be accorded, though your experience of French exhibitions caused you to consider those conditions as not necessary. It is scarcely necessary to say that the regulations in question were only laid down by ,Her. Majesty's Commissioners after the most complete consideration of the peculiar circumstances of the Universal Exhibition ; all their desires were to act in the way best calculated to obtain the success of the enterprise. I cannot let this occasion pass without expressing our sentiment of the great advantage we have derived from France having formed by her productions such an interesting and precious portion of the Exhibition; and at your Government having taken care to send so many chefs-d'oeuvres, the character of which will certainly exercise a happy influence on the sciences and arts of our own and other countries. I conclude by expressing to you, both in my own name and in that of the Royal Commissioners, our thanks for the part which you have personally taken in our labours, both as president of one of the groups of juries, and as vice-president of the superior Council of Presidents, as also for the impartiality and urbanity you have displayed on all occasions on which you have fulfilled those functions. The visits of the Royal Family have now become matter of regular occurrence, and have, no doubt, tended to make the Exhibition still more popular with the aristocracy and gentry, who appear never to grow tired of examining its wonders, and visiting over and over again the treasures it oontains. The Indian treasures have now been finally arranged, and have been visited by wondering crowds The ivory throne of state has been removed to the Indian compartment on the north side of the nave, and has at length found a resting-place in the centre of the toot, amidst congenial Oriental marvels. The carving is most elaborate and delicate; the front and arms of the throne are studded with precious stones, rubies, and emeralds; the cushions are of green velvet, embroidered in gold. Two steps covered over with green velvet form the approach, and the back is surmounted by the Royal arms, also exquisitely carved in solid ivory. The Koh-i-noor appears to get itself talked or writtea into notoriety. If the light from the jets was concealed, and the diamond made to revolve slowly on its axis its beauties and brilliancy would then be more fully displayed. Having given a slight sketch of the contents of the Fine Art Court, we shall now proceed to notice them more in detail. The collection of works assembled in this part of the Exhibition is rather miscellaneous but they are all more or less intimately connected with the arts of design and ornament. On entering the attention is first engaged by an assortment of colours exhibited by Mr. Miller of Loagacre. These are called "silica colours." They certainly have a very brilliant effect, set out as they are on paper or china palettes. But when practically applied, as is shown in two or three pictures executed with theni, we do not find that they possess any particular advantages. To our eye these pictures have no more force or brilliancy than water-colour drawings executed in the ordinary materials. Whether the colours possess any superiority lathe facility of manipulation or in durability we have no means ofjudging. In close proximity to these is placed a marine picture, by Mr. Concanen, executed in what is called the new style of aerial tinting. In this work, also, we fail to perceive the particular advantage of the process— Judging, of course, only by the results as they appear .to the eye. In this part of the Fine Art Court there is an assortment of the various implements of art, such as pencils, brushes, colours, oils, and varnishes exhibited by Messrs. Rowney & Co. and Messrs. Re: bertson & Co., which display the 6legree of Perfection . s- tition with — those produced by foreign manZfac - ture — r - s. Some specimens of crayon painting, executed with Kearney's Venetian pastils, are worth observing. This style of painting is impervious to damp, and, though too delicate for external, may be advantageously applied to internal decoration. This invention is also of some utility to oil painters from the readiness with which the material coalesces with oil colours. The students of the Government School of Design, both male and female, here exhibit many examples of their talent in designs for furniture and internal decoration. They show considerable taste and great variety in the patterns. Among them will be found designs for carpets, table-covers, floor-cloths, wall-papers, tea-services metal gates, chintzes, panels, &c. Near these is placed a table top of slate, painted in imitation of mosaic. The imitation is capital, and we think it would be difficult to detect the means by which it is effected were it properly polished; it is the work of a lady named Burrows. Another object of curiosity in this part of the court is a model in elder pith, by Mr. Cossens, representing a Turk smoking under a canopy. The model is cut with ingenuity ' and has a pretty effect; but the most remarkable work of this description is a design for a book cover, carved with a penknife in cardboard, by Walter Blacket. The neatness and delicacy of the cutting, and the tastefulness of the pattern render this specimen almost unique; it has the effect of fine ivory carving. The model of a Highland cottage, by Mr. Bond, of Edinburgh, is ingenious, and appears to realise the views of the designer, in combining simplicity of construction, comfort, warmth, ventilation, and economy. The design for a pediment, by Mr. C. Fox, which stands next to this object, is liable to one objection. As it contains two rows of figures, one in very high and the other in very low relief, the consequence would be that the first alone would be seen when viewed from the ground. The series of designs by Mr. M. D. Wyatt evinces taste and ingenuity in the collocation of the colours. These designs are adapted for different manufactures, for mosaics, encaustic paving, stained glass windows, and also for bookbinding. There is in this part of the court a very ingenious model of an easel for artists, the invention of Mr. F. Harvey. Its distinguishing feature is its containing in a moderate compass everything required by the artist in colours, pencils, brushes, he. For those who are in the habit of sketching out of doors, an easel of this kind must be very convenient. The specimens of anastatic printing, exhibited by Mr. Cowell, are curious and interesting. This is an invention but yet in its infancy, and its resources may be said to be scarcely developed. The operation is not very complex. But of all the products exhibited in the Russian compartment, those which, for the last few days, have attracted the greatest public attention are the productions in malachite. The majority of these works, from their colossal dimensions, the fine taste that has presided over the working a material so precious, and the exquisite finish of their execution, constitute a style of decoration entirely novel in the history of art and ornament. Malachite is a very rare mineral, consisting of carbonate of copper, and is of all known substances the very best for the execution of ornamental objects where it is wished to concentrate an impression of beauty and richness. Owing to its extreme density, and closeness of its grain, it is capable of the finest polish, while the marvellous' vivacity of its tints, and the infinite variety of natural designs which result from their combination, afford the designer resources of a unique description. These surprising effects, produced as they are by innumerable gradations of the same colour, impress upon' ' the objects manufactured from it a variety--a har-' mony--and a distinctness which calmot be attained with other minerals in use for decorative purposes,' in all of which it is to a certain degree impossible to avoid either monotony or a too great contrast. To these properties of malachite that of an excessive rarity may be added. This kind of mineral occursor at least traces of it are found—in the generality of copper mines. But in a whole century we can scarcely enumerate two or throe instances in which specimens have been found adapted for ornamentation. The indefatigable miners who are now exploring our South Australian possessions have but Just recently discovered some fragments in the Burra Burra Mine, which have afforded a fair prospect of successful working. It is well known that up to the present day Siberia alone has furnished this precious material in adequate quantity for the construction of articles of any considerable size. The first mine which supplied this mineral to the artists of England, France, and Italy was almost exhausted, and malachite was only to be met with in rare fragments, until the house of Demidoff furnished a block of it almost a hundred times larger than any that had yet been produced in Asia or America, and of a quality superior to any specimen previously known. It was from this block that the magnificent pillars of the Cathedral of St. Isaac at St. Petersburg were formed. The finest part of the block just noticed, and not employed in the decoration of that sumptuous building, was elaborated by a body of workmen, organised for the purpose in that city, into the form now so much admired in the Great Exhibition. The appearance of soeh an object of skill and an-evessaii arts, since it is the first time that it has been within the power of private individuals to view an article of such great estimation. A work of so unusual a description ' and which both in material and workmanship has absorbed so vast a sum, must be regarded as a homage rendered by Russia to the great idea in ' which England has taken the initiative. The exhaustion of the material in the first instance, and the impossibility of finding a purchaser for &II article the value of which is so considerable, will probably, for a long period, render the reproduction of such a work impracticable. Possibly, it is destined to become one of the most characteristic, as well as the most permanent monuments of the Great Assembly of all Nations. The malachite palatial gates are, as we have already stated, valued at £B,OOO, and some of the tables and vases are worth 1,000 guineas each. It is a matter of regret that the other great proprietors of mines in Russia have, by not taking measures to be represented in the Exhibition, left so large a haitus in this tableau of the resources of that powerful empire. We have remarked, however, with interest, the fine quality of the copper of the two houses of Pachkoff, in the government of Orenburg; the magnificent sheet iron from Madame Ponomareff, in the government of Viatka ; and lastly, the excellence of the steel and workmanship in cutlery exhibited by Madame C. Jacovleff, from the government of Rizan. These last are important, as showing that Russia is beginning to advance in industrial progress, and that she already manufactures successfully for her own consumption those fine kinds of iron which have hitherto found their only vent in the workshops of England. The Russian Government has sent over a curious variety of mineral products, provided for the most part from the Imperial mines, under the directions of the officers of the mining corps of the empire, and superintended by his Excellency General Foulon. Amongst other remarkable products of this section we have to point out the iron ores and cast iron from the districts of Olonetz, Kuchwa-Zlatowst, Kamensk, and Kamskovotkinsk. The last gives us a great idea of the degree of perfection to which Russia has arrived in the employment of the new process applicable to the fabrication of iron. We also direct attention to the fine quality of the copper from the works of Perm and Bogoslovsk, the cast and damasked steel, the fabrication of which has been introduced in the Ural and Altai by one of the most skilful officers of the mining corps, Gen. Anosoff. The scythes made after the Styrian method in the works at Avtinsk, are acknowledged to surpass in quality articles of the same kind from the works of Styria, Austria, the Tyrol, and Westphalia. This remarkable success of Russian industry is doubtless attributable in a great degree, to the excellent nature of the steel eutployed but it would be unjust not to give also the due merit to the pains-taking skill, the energy, and the ability of that scientific corps to whom has been confided the high mission of I propagating, step by step, a knowledge of the peso. tice of the arts of the west in the depths of the forests of the Ural and Altai. Amongst the manufactures forwarded from Russia are some rich specimens of brocade of excellent design and workmanship, which will well repay an attentive inspection. NATIONAL MONUMENT TO PnINCE ALBERT.- Mr. Bennett, C.E., of Westminster, proposes that a national monument to Prince Albert should be erected to com- memorate the Great Industrial Exhibition of 1851, and the chief events connected therewith- the latter to be effected by castings in relief, in bronze, and by emblema- tical sculpture, illustrative of the noble object his Royal Highness had in view as the originator of the enterprise. Besides indicating the fact that the Prince was the origi- nator of the Exhibition, the commemorative monument would indicate, in a very significant manner to foreigners, the affection with which the people of this country cling to each of the respective parts of the constitution. The design in question is square, the four sides being intended to obtain bronze reliefs, representing, first, the exterior of the building, secondly, the interior, thirdly, the inau- guration, and fourthly, the distribution of prizes to the exhibitors by her Majesty. It is proposed that each cast- ing should be twice the size of those affixed to the Nelson monument. On the other side of these bronzes it is pro- posed to have sculptured figures in niches, emblematic in their character, while above this base will be four other figures, representing Europe, Asia, Africa, and America; and again, above these, a granite semblance of the globe, surmounted by a statue of the Prince, enshrined in a metal gilt temple, dedicated to Fame and Prosperity, with the royal crown of England on the top. Flanking the whole structure, it is intended that there shall be four gi- gantic lions couchant and slumbering, as types of the in- ternational tranquillity to which the enterprise is attribut- able, and which it is, in like manner, eminently calculated to promote and perpetuate. A SERVANT GIRL'S VISIT TO Tar EXrHrBITIONa- Monday fortnight was the time fixed for a young woman to start from Bath to see the wonders at the world's fair, and the train selected, from motives of economy, was the "Parliamentary" one; but, as it happened, the train was either too early, or the young woman was too late. No- thing daunted, with a quarter's wages in her pocket and something more, she preferred the next train to the next day, and she soon found herself passing the engine which was to have conveyed her to London, and this in some degree satisfied her for the extra outlay, forgetting that her altered plans in Bath would also operate at the Lou- don terminus. Here she failed to meet her friends who had been appointed to conduct her safely to her destina- tion, and in her dilemma sought refuge in a cab, with a request to the driver to take her to a certain street in Kensington; but, after numerous fruitless inquiries, Ken- nington was found to be the desired haven, which, after much perplexity, was reached at the cost of 6s. cab fare. Happy in meeting her friends, the young woman found no further annoyance till she went to the Crystal Palace, when her gratification was alloyed by a tremendous shower on leaving the building, which rendered her Ex- hibition bonnet and dress useless for the future. The mishaps which attended her starting appeared to follow her, for on her return, wishing to call on a relative in Gloucestershire, she inquired for the railway which would take her to Strond, perhaps without designating the county. She was referred to the London Bridge termi- nus, and having procured a ticket a pleasant ride followed; but the sight of the sea gave her misgivings that she was w-ong, and finding her journey at an end, asked the guard if that was Stroud, in Gloucestershire, when, to her great dismay, she found herself at Stroud in Kent. Here, to the credit of the railway authorities, no advantage was taken of the error, and being satisfied with the truth of the servant's statement, they returned the fare and sent her back to London, and the girl sustained no other in- convenience than a return to Rennlington. She was more careful in her next exploit, and on Nfondy evening reached home, little the worse for her numerous calami- ties, but with the full conviction that she never wished again to see London. This is really a prodigious success, and astonishes even those who had made the most sanguine and extravagant calculations on the subject. The truth is, that the attractiveness of the display is only now beginning to tell upon the mass of the community, who were slow to believe the astonishing features of the collection thrown open to their curiosity and admiration. Notwithstanding the immense assemblage yesterday gathered within the building, it still remains as a whole by no moans overcrowded. The nave is well filled, but no inconvenience is experienced there in passing from point to point, and, though the more attractive objects have groups collected around them, it is quite possible, with a little patience, to see everything worth inspection comfortably and well. The more remote parts are visited, but not in large numbers, and there are some portions which, during the entire day. remain almost empty. Increased experience justifies, in a groat measure, the confidence in the capabilities of the vast edifice, which it is evident, from their arrangements, the executive committee entertain ; and, if the multitude do not present themselves in greater force than 50,000, or even 60,000, on Monday, little difficulty will be found in accommodaing them. It is useless speculating upon the probabilities of an event now so close at hand; but, if all goes on smoothly and well, it will be a grand sight to see the vast tide of humanity rolling along that sublime central avenue, and swelling through the courts and passages of the interior to its remotest boundaries. However true this may be with regard to poli ties and puddings, we will take upon us "to say, without much fear of contradiction from any housbeholder'ih Lbrdon or elsewhere, that the process of-removal is altogether a difficult, disagreeable, and dilatory affair. ACCIDENT TO THE MARCHIONESS OF LONDONDERRY,— An accident occurred to the Marquis and Marchioness of Londonderry last week, while driving in the vicinity of Garron Tower. The coachman had omitted to put on the drag, down a deep pitch on the road, and hence the carriage —an open one—was overturned on a small bridge and battlement, horses, carriage, and all, into a deep ravine, with a stream at the bottom. Fortunately, the vehicle was arrested by trunks of trees on the near appending bank, and the horses were stopped lower down, on the side of the bank. Workmen happily being at hand, Lady Londonderry was hauled out of the carriage, which it was necessary to cat into, the top and sides of the landau being undermost. Her ladyship was cruelly bruised, and very much alarmed. Lord Londonderry, who fell upon her ladyship, was in no degree hurt, and was safely pulled from the carriage. The horses were lacerated dreadfully, sad all the harness, carriage, &c., smashed; the coachman and servants, happily, escaped unhurt. Lady Londonderry w as th e greatest sufferer, and was brought home in a common car. Medical assistance was sent for from Ballymony and Crlenarn. We are happy to learn that, after some days' suffering, her ladyship is much better. DEATH OF MRS. SHERWOOD.—TtIe death of this well-known authoress took place rather suddenly, at her residence, Yelverton-place, Twickenham, on Monday, the 22d ult. This venerable lady was in the 77th year of her age. Mrs. Sher woed has, by her numerous writings for young people, done much to interest and improve the minds of her readers, and many will have a grateful recollection of the pleasant hours her works have afforded them. The religious sentiments expressed in her writings were fully carried out in private life; she was exemplary in every domestic relation; benevolence and charity were her principal characteristics, and all who have had the privilege of enjoying her society will ever regret the death of one whose cheerful manners and edifying conversation rendered her the valued companima of the young and the aged. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. BIKER v. Fox AND HENDEILSON.—At the Brompton County Court, on Thursday, the plaintiff, a journeyman painter, sued the defendants, Messrs. Fox and Henderson, the contractors for the erection of the Great Exhibition, Hyde-park, for the sum of £7 us, balance of wages alleged to be due. Although the sum sued for was small in amount, proceedings were instituted on principle, involving nearly eighty similar claims, the claimants wishing to understand whether a fair day's work was not equivalent to a fair day's wages.— The cashier to the defendants, admitted that the plaintiff had been employed in the building of the Exhibition, but not by the defendants. There had been workmen at the building, in each department of which sub-contractors had been deputed, the painting being allotted to a Mr. Robson, who, if anybody, was liable for the demand now set forth. He had understood that all the painters were engaged at the fixed wages of 4e per day.—The plaintiff, however, asserted that Mr. Robson agreed to give sixpence an hour for ten hours' work daily, and that he entered into a contract with Mr. Robson only as foreman, in which light he was looked upon, and as such was paid by the defendants, from whom he received a certain weekly salary as their servant. He told him at the time of being employed that the defendants were to be his paymasters. Mr. Robson was not pro. sent.—His Honour observed that the question was of the greatest importance to masters and workmen, and required thorough investigation. In the construction of railroads subcontractors employed the workmen, but still it did not follow that the same plan was to he adopted at the Crystal Palace. He could not go further into the case without examining Mr. Robson, for whose attendance he should adjourn the hearing till the next court day.—Adjourned accordingly.

PHOTOGRAPHY-CALOTYPES.* The results obtained by the photographic pro- cesses on paper are confined, with one or two trivial exceptions, to such as are produced by the calotype process of Mr. Fox Talbot. This process bears some relation to the daguerreotype, inasmuch as the sensitive surface in both instances is a compound of iodine and silver. In the calotype we have a true chemical combination effected between these substances, by washing the paper first with a solution of iodide of potassium, and then with one of nitrate of silver. In the daguerreo- type the surface is rendered sensitive by the action e Of iodine vapour upon a carefully prepared sheet of et silver. In both of these processes the image result- es ing from exposure to the solar radiations is dormant, and has to be evoked by a subsequent operation. Mercurial vapour is employed in one case, and a- gailic acid, which effects the decomposition of the id silver salt, in the other. In point of sensibility n- the advantage has hitherto been in favour of l-the metallic plate; the paper has, however, been rendered so exquisitively sensitive by a new mode of manipulation that it may soon be re- ld garded as equally susceptible of radiant influence with the daguerreotype plates. There is one essen.- tial difference between the daguerreotype and calo- type pictures; the former is produced at once, with lights and shadows correct as in nature-whereas id the latter has these in the reverse order, the high lights being represented by deep shadows, and the l contrary. Therefore, to produce a correct pic- e ture, it is necessary to take a copy from - the original, or negative photograph, which is n done by placing it, the face down, uponl another piece of prepared paper-when the solar ray, pass- ;e ing through the impressed to the plain paper, gives a picture possessing correct lights and shadows. There is this great advantage attending the calo- type process, that, one original being obtained, and a- rendered properly permanent, any number of copies can be produced from it. The largest exhibitors of pictures of this class are Messrs. Henneman and Malone, who are the principal agents for carrying out Mr. Talbot's patent in London. The process, as described in the patent of 1842, by which these pictures are taken, is the following:- " Take a sheet of the best writing paper, having ar a smooth surface and a close and even texture. The water mark, if any, should be cut off, lest it should injure the appearance of the picture. Dissolve 100 grains of crystallized nitrate of silver in six ounces of distilled water. Wash the paper with this solu- tion with a soft brush on one side, and put a mark on that side, whereby to know it again. Dry the paper cautiously at a distance from the fire, or else let it dry spontaneously in a dark room. When ie dry, or nearly so, slip it into a solution of iodide of potassium, containing 600 grains of that salt in Bt one pint of water, and let it stay two or three s- minutes in the solution. Then dip the paper into a vessel of water, dry it lightly with blotting paper, and finish drying it at a fire, which will not injure it even if held pretty near; or else it may be left to dry spontaneously. All this is best done in the evening by candlelight. The paper so far prepared is called iodized paper, because it has a uniform pale-yellow coating of iodide of silver. It is scarcely sensitive to light; but, nevertheless, it ought to be kept in a portfolio n or drawer until wanted for use. It may be kept for a- any length of time without spoiling, or undergoing d any change, if protected from sunshine. When the paper is required for use, take a sheet of it and wash it with a liquid prepared in the following 1i manner :-Dissolve 100 grains of crystallized nitrate r- of silver in two ounces of distilled water; add to 8 this solution one-sixth of its volume of strong acetic acid. Let this be called mixture A. Make a saturated solution of crystallized gallic acid in f. cold distilled water. The quantity dissolved is d very small. Call this solution B. Mix together a the liquids A and B in equal volumes, but only a small portion of them at a time, because the mix- ture does not keep long without spoiling. This mix- d ture is called the gallo-nitrate of silver. This solu- tion must be washed over the iodized paper on the n side marked, and being allowed to remain upon it for half a minute, it must be dipped into water, and " then lightly dried with blotting paper. This opera- i tion in particular requires the total exclusion of day- n light ; and although the paper thus prepared has e been found to keep for two or three months, it is a advisable to use it within a few hours, as it is often rendered useless byspoutaueous change in the dark."E 0 As in the daguerreotype, so in the calotype, the t adjustments of the camera and the character of the i lens determine the degree of perfection in the I picture. The | a recoil is well provided for by a sloping stage, while a bedu formed of the bark of the beech tree, possessing an elastic c character, prevents the shook which would otherwise be bE felt after firing. The fore part of the carriage is se- cured to the battery or fortress by an iron bolt, which acts as a pivot, and by means of which it can be pointed in any required direction by the action of a wheel, which | travels transversely at the hind part. The muzzle is de- pressed, or lowered, by means of a screw working under wedges. Two small cannons (six-pounders) are placed by the side of this monster piece of ordnance, one of them formed upon the Danish, and the other upon the Swedish model. The Swedish iron, on account of its extreme tough. ness, is the only iron adapted for casting pieces of ordnance, and instead of being cast in sand it is run upon clay moulds. Large quantities of iron cannon areconstantly cast in Sweden for use in foreign countries, and the proprietors of the large foundry in which these specimens were made have now orders to supply a large quantity for the Russian, Danish, and Sar- dinian Governments. Some fiery neat and well-finished models of guns and ammunition waggous, made to scale, have been sent over by the Swedish Government, and form part of thisinteresting collection. Instruments of warfare are not, however, the only contributions of that kingdom. Passing from these the eye is attracted by the colossal and elegantly shaped porphyry vase, and other specimens of work more in harmony with the character of the building in which they are shown. We notice also, in the Norway department, a very in- genious construction for window-eash fastenings, shown by l the exhibitor and inventor, Stadshauptmand (Major) C. G. Rosenkilde, from Christiansand, in Norway. While it is perfectly secure against the possibility of persons from without opening up the sash for the purpose of entering the house, it has also the additional advantage of presenting l an obstacle to children opening the window in the inside - at the same time, it is easily opened by grown per- sons. This simple invention consists of a spring, which is fitted into a recess made in the edge of the style of the sash ; the free end of the spring takes into a catch formed in. the window frame, by which the sash is im- movably fixed until the projecting piece is pressed or lifted out of the catch-for which purpose the end of the spring projects a small distance beyond the surface of the sash- frame, so that, by applying the finger to that projection, the sash-frame is moved either up or down, as the case may be. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. | TUESDAY.-The receipts at the doors of the Crystal Palace amounted to C2,415. 2c.; the number of visitors, according to the police returns, wits 53,371. Amid the swelling tide of s popularity which besets the Exhibition, its practical uses and the best 'means of turning them to account still continue a g subject of anxiousconsideration, atd undoubtedly form one of i immense importance. What, then, is to be done with the vast crowds of spectato rawho rush to tlis centre of attraction, eager Y to acquire from ai few- days inspection a comprehensive idea of its contents ? Are they to be left to themselves in 1 finding their inexperienced way through an assemblage of products illustrating every branch of industry and the t treasures of every country and climen? People who come s there for a specific purpose experience great difficulty in r discovering what they are in search of; and it is believed that a system by which spectators could be supplied with all necessary facilities for exploring the interior might be made self-supporting. Strangers, on entering a continental city, or in ascending to the top of a Welsh or Scotch mountain, do not hesitate to avail themselves of the services of experi- enced persons to direct their footsteps. It seems, therefore, only fairly probable that, within reasonable limits, they would be willing to pay for the advantage of having some one to help them in making a satisfactory survey of the Exhibition. Books for such a purpose are comparatively useless. The executivecomm itteeceannotwithproprietyorganise such abody of guides as would prove suitable under the circumstances, but if the matter was taken up by private parties in a proper manner, they would, we have no doubt, receive every assistance and co-operation from those in authority. In London there exists no class of men, like the conmiissiott- naites of foreign capitals, whosedaily avocations well qualify them for the duties now contemplated; but nevertheless we cannot think that much' difficulty would be found in the selection of persons sufliciently intelligent and acquainted with the Exhibition to help visitors to a good and satisfactory survey of its contents. Another and hardlyless important subject of consideration in the present state of the Crystal Palace, is the character of the arrangements between the industrial classes and their employers, for enabling the former to see the glories of the great temple which their labour has reared and furnished. Nearly all the great establishments, both in town and country, are preparing to give their men the opportunity of a visit to Hyde Park. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Friday the 4th inst. upwards of 26,000 people entered the building, and the receipts were 2,6141. 3s. 6d. The finances of the Commission are now in a most flourishing con. dition, for 196,2341. has been taken at the doors and by the sale of season tickets, which, added to the 77,7001. from sub- scriptions and contracts, makes a total of 273, 9341. On Saturday morning the Queen and Prince Albert re- sumed their inspection of the interior, and examined the two north galleries in the western half of the building. Nearly a thousand exhibitors whose contributions are placed there were assembled in their respective allotments to receive the Royal visitors. The receipts at the doors amounted to 1,5661. 15s., and the numbers entering the building were 11,747. On Monday the number of visitors rose to 61,670, and the receipts at the doors amounted to 2,8521. 2s. For the first time since the opening the sale of season tickets was a perfect blank. Among the crowds that thronged the interior were about 500 men and boys in the empioyof Messrs. Clowes, the extensive printers and part contractors for the official cata- logue. Mr. Gladstone treated 50 of his poor fellow pa- rishioners to a view of the interior, and accompanied them in their survev. On Tuesday the receipts at the doors rose to 3,1691. 5s., the largest amount, with two exceptions, that has yet been taken in shillings. On the 17th of June, 3,1911. 2s. was the sum taken, and on the 24th of June, 3,1861. 12s. According to the police returns, 65,962 persons entered the building. On Wednesday 58,055 persons entered the building, and 2,7701. 6s. was the amount taken at the doors. Her Majesty and Prince Albert visited the building at their usual early hour. They first went to the offices ofthe Electric Telegraph Company. Messrs. Clark and Watcher, the company's prin- cipal engineers, were in attendance to give explanations, and communications were opened with Birmingham, Manchester, Normanton, Newcastle, and Edinburgh. An order was sent to the last-mentioned place desiring that a message containing local news should be forwardea through the instrument. This was instantly done, with astonishing rapidity and success, and announced the arrival of the ?? family of France at Edinburgh on the previous evening. After having wit- nessed the sending of messages by the company's printing telegraph direct to Manchester, and the operation of the double needle, the Royal party left, expressing great satis- faction at what they had witnessed. They then proceeded to examie Mr. Cotton's ingenious and beautiful invention for the separation of heavy and light sovereigns. Here the Governor of the Bank of England (Mr. Thomson Hankey, jun.) was recognized by her Majesty and the Prince, who conversed with him for some time. From the survey of Mr. Cotton's machine, which is placed in the nave, they proceeded at once to the agricultural implement department, where a large party of exhibitors had assembled to receive them. Some displayed the action of their contributions, and the illustrious party saw mangold-wmuzel and straw cut, corn bruised, hollow bricks moulded, and butter churned with a facility which must have astonished them greatly. Mr. Allen Ransome was present, and explained the merits of his seed. dropping machine, and Mr. Fowler also drew the Prince's attention to his new construction of mole plough. On leaving the agricultural implement department, her Majesty and the Prince passed into the nave, which they traversed for some distance through a line of shilling visitors, drawn up in the most orderly manner for their reception. Nothing could ex- ceed the propriety and good behaviour of the crowds assem. bled. Mr. Pusey, M.P., Colonel Challoner, Mr. B. Gibbs, and other gentlemen connected with the Royal Agricultural Society, attended the Queen in her progress, and gave ex- planations of contributions wherever they were required. On Thursday, notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather, 61,492 persons visited the Building, and the sum of 2,958L. was taken at the doors. The prizes are not it is said, to be awarded until after the close of the Exhibition, the period for which was fixed, on Saturday, for about the middle of October. It is intended that arrangements shall be made for lighting up the building in the evening- At a meeting of the Derby Town Council on Saturday, a petition to the Queen was adopted, praying that the Crystal Palace may not be removed. it was resolved to send the petition to the Duke of Devonshire for presentation.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Yesterday the receipts at the Crystal Palace amounted to a higher sum than has yet been received. So great was the influx of visitors that 2,2001. was taken in money at the doors, and the sale of season tickets also rose so high that the funds of the Commission had during the day an accession altogether of at least 3,0001. The French exhibitors still continue their preparations, and the goods forwarded from Turkey are not yet arranged. Professors Royle and Soley are busily engaged in the distribution of the large and valuable additional consignment within the last few days received from India. Several of the most valuable articles have been placed in the stalls facing the nave, and ao great is their value esteemed, that they have been surrounded with a railing, as if they were State prisoners. We hardly think that this precaution was necessary, and it certainly is not ornamental. Our own jewellers have not considered it requisite to adopt any such measures of safety, and they ought to know something of the risks incurred. However, we do not cavil at the East India Company for what they have done, the more 'especially as their collection promises, when completed, to be one of extraordinary interest, splendour, and attractiveness. In addition to the Lahore jewels, they have now, in stalls facing the nave, the " Durria-i-Noor," or " Sea of Light,"—an immense diamond set as an armlet, with ten smaller stones around it; a necklace of 224 large pearls, and a shorter one of 104 smaller pearls; a necklace of four large rubies, a pair of emerald armlets, a carved emerald and diamond turban ornament, an emerald and diamond bridle and martingale, a gold mounted saddle, set with diamonds, emeralds, and rubies; a magnificent brocaded robe, richly decorated with pearls; and an emerald girdle, the stones in which are of immense size, and most of them of very fine quality. This list of jewellery will give the public some idea of the manner in which our Eastern empire is represented, and will recall some at least of those visions of fabulous wealth and splendour with which the name of India used in former times to be connected. Until the collection is completely arranged it would be premature to notice further the more prominent features of the fresh arrivals. The Royal Commission have again had under their consideration the propriety of making arrangements for the accommodation of the working classes who may be expected atter the 26:h to visit London in order to see the Exhibition. They have determined to abstain from organising any system with that object , a s their doing so would interfere with many praiseworthy undertakings of private individuals for the same purpose, but they recommend mechanics to co-operate, and to take such . steps before leaving home as may obviate the inconvemencies that would otner wise arise from large numbers coming together without any previous preparation. THE GREAT EXHIBITION, Fears have been entertained by exhibitors that it will not be possible to keep the building of the Exhibition water-tight, in consequence of its having been found that the rain comes through many parts of the roof. Such apprehension believed to be entirely without foundation ; the roof has been carefully gone over, the broken glass replaced, and deficiencies in the glazing work made good. This was being proceeded with rapidly previous to the commencement of the heavy rains, about fortnight since, when it was of necessity suspended. Those parts of the flooring upon which the wet falls have been carefully marked, so that no difficulty whatever will exist, upon the cessation of the rain, in discovering the faulty parts of the building. Upwards of 8,000 packages were sent in up to last week; and already, on the British side, the visitor may form a fair notion of the exceeding value and variety of the articles to be exhibited. The foreign countries still continue backward in their preparations, but the representatives of France and several other countries state that they are perfectly confident of being ready by the Ist of May. No intention whatever is entertained by the Commissioners of postponing the opening beyond the Ist of May, and notices have been posted up in various portions of the building, calling the attention of exhibitors to the decision of the Commissioiers that the Exhibition would open on that day. A meeting of American Contributors, Agents, and others, from the United States of America,” was held on Wednesday, at the Chapter Coffee-house, Paternoster row, in pursuance of an advertisement, in which it was stated that they were convened on important business connected with the Exhibition Mr. John, of New York, in the chair. Previous to the commencement of the business, an application was made by some reporters to he present A discussion arose as to the propriety of their admission, when a resolution was agreed to that they would be allowed in the room on condition that their report should be subject to revision. This was, of course, refused, upon which some of the representatives of the daily press went away. At a subsequent period another reporter entered the room, but he was not allowed to take notes. The Times, and other journals, are most indignant at the insult thus offered to the British press, and especially by Americans, who boast so loudly of their ” free institutions.” It appears that at this meeting the American contributors were anything but pleased with some of the regulations and arrangements. They strongly opposed the appointment the jurors to decide on the relative merits of the foreign contributions, also to the adjudication of the bronze medals as prizes by ihk royal commissioners, when awards of much greater value had. been promised, which they considered not keeping faith witn contributors; they also objected to the price of admission of three guineas for a season ticket. Strong observations were made in consequence of contributors being at the expense of erecting their own ” fittings.” It was stated that English contributors were at the expense; but, in answer, it was observed that the original understanding was that contributors should be at no expense. Another ground of complaint was in reference to the delay in affording protection to articles which required a patent, and upon this subject a resolution was agreed to, that a deputation be appointed to wait on Sir G. Grey, intimating to him that until some security be given to such contributions, no packages should be opened. At the close of the proceedings the reporter asked to look at the resolutions, but on show of hands this was refused. A Long Wire.—Amongst the most remarkable productions from Birmingham at the Great Exhibition, there will be a piece of iron wire, for the purposes of the electric telegraph, a mile long. This is the greatest length of wire that has ever been drawn; it is from the mill of Mr. John Cornforth. understand that at the meeting on Saturday Her Majesty’s Commissioners examined into the report of the leakage of the roof, and after hearing Mr. Stephenson and Mr. Cubitt on the subject, and communicating with Mr. Fox, the contractor, they were of opinion that the leaking had been greatly exaggerated, and Her Majesty's Commissioners requested Mr. Cubitt to prepare a report for the next meeting to be held by the Commissioners. In the meantime we may state that but little doubt is felt that a week's fine weather would enable the contractors to make the building perfectly water-tight. Messrs. Fox and Henderson have made a curious discovery recently, which solves a mystery that had for a long time puzzled them. Along a particular row of columns in the building there was observed to a constant leakage when rain fell, from some cause which could not be detected. At last they were induced to examine the line of drain pipes which runs from column to column, and there they discovered a nailbag securely wedged in by some mischievously disposed workman, and which by stopping the current of water of course caused the columns to overflow.— Times. Thomas Scott, murderous whitesmith in Leeds, fired a pistol at Mistress Widdop; the ball struck a bone in the stays of Mrs. Widdop, made her hiccough, gave her a stitch in her side, and then glancing off pursued it* cour*e no one knows whither Thomas Scott then fired another pistol into himself; and, for want of stays, lies badly wounded in the Infirmary. Nothing ever so clearly this proved the sanatory use of stays, or the evils to the human figure of not using them ; and as it is the only use of stays to a healthy person one ever heard of, one ought to the more struck with the force and value the proof. V IRESIsE MEs-rRimsai-Dr Herbert Mayo, in a supple- mentary chapter to the new edition of his interesting little work-, " On the Truths containedin Popular Superstitions," mentions that he has just discovered-the following Od proof of the reality of Mesmerism. It is one which any of our readers may try for himself. Take a gold ring-the more massive the better, but our wife'swedding-ring will do, if you are so lucky as to have one. Attach the ring to a silk thread about twelve inches long- fasten the other end of fhe thread ound the nail joint of your right fore-finger; and let the ring hang about half an inch above the surface of the table, on which you rest your elbow to steady your hand. Holdyour finger horizontal, with-the thumb thrown back as far as-possible from tle rest of the hand. If there be nothing on the table, the ring will -soon become sta- tionary. Then place some silver (say three half-crowns) immediately below it, when the ring will begin to oscillate backwards and forwards, to you and from you. Now bring your thumb into contact with your fore-finger, (or else sus- pend the ring firom your thumb,)wand the oscillations will become transvereeto their former swing. Or this may be eflected by making a lady take hold of your disengaged hand. When the transverse motion is fairly established, let a gentleman take hold of the lady's disengaged hand, and the ring will change back to its former course. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Thursday. — The receipts and the number of visitors again suffered a slight decline, the former being 2,722/. 10s- and the latter 57,781. The heat of the weather, great aa it was outside of the building, was still more oppressive within, and, in consequence of the inconvenience ex- perienced, we understand that it is determined to remove the inside glazing at the eastern snd western entrances, and to endeavour in this way to secure a refreshing thorough draught from end to end of the interior. This will be an immense relief to visitors if successfully carried out. The Queen and the Royal party at the Palace were again in the building this morning, and commenced their survey by an examination of the Milan gallery. From this they pro- ceeded to our own sculpture court, after which they went into the Indian collection, and then, ascending to the sec- tions of glass and pottery, they were advantageously seen by the crowds who had by that time assembled. Some new arrivals of an interesting character have been received. They consist of contributions of various kinds, including arms, dresses, trappings, and ivory from Abyssynia, and a large round table from the Sandwich Islan Is. Among the dresses are " three fine cotton cloths worn by Abyssynians of rank," and two sheepskins worn over the cloths, each the skin of one sheep. There are among the arms two double-edged sabres, with handles of Rhinoceros horn ; and the contributions, which are presents to Her Majesty' also include two silver coronets. The flag decoration in progress in the British half of the nave would be rendered much more effective if carried ont in the same manner as it has been by the different foreign countries. We hang out our banners at right angles," while their spear poihts are placed at an angle of 45 degrees. Shortly before 10 o'clock the King of the Belgians, attended by Mr. Dilke, his Excellency M. Vandeweyer, M. de la Pierre, M. The D uchess of Kent, the ?? of the French, the Duchess of Orleans, and the Prince of Wales were also present, at- tended by their respective suites, during the day. Saturday. — The oppressive heat proved too great even for the attractions of the Crystal Palace, and since it was opened we have hardly seen so small an attendance there. The Queen, Prince Albert, the King of the Belgians, and lhe younger members of their respective families, visited lhe building at an early hour, and remained for some time. The Royal party was attended by Baron Dupin, M Sa- landrouze, and many of the leading French exhibitors in their progress through the department of that country, with the varied features of which they seemed much gratified. In connexion with the Exhibition there is a subject to which every day more and more interest at- taches, and to which it is now necessary that public at- tention should be very seriously directed. For the last six weeks the jurors have been incessantly at work iv collecting tho materials for making their awards. Those duties now approach to a close, and we understand that nothing can exceed the labour and care which have been bestowed by them in the coarse of their investigations. Hitherto they have, it is said, worked very harmoniously, and it is not anticipated that in the distribution of second- class prizes much difficulty will arise. These prizes will be distributed iv sufficient numbers to cool down any undue amount of jealousy or heartburning among exhibi- tors, at the same lime that their value as honourable testimonials of merit will be preserved. With lhe first- class prizes, however, the case is very different, and in the award of them, from all that we hear, great and serious annoyances will arise unless the utmost caution and prudence are observed. As they are to be the rewards of only the very highest merit, the struggle for the pos session of them will be a fierce one, not only as between individuals, but also as between countries, and there is some reason to apprehend that in our anxiety to secure credit for impartiality we may fail to assert wiih proper firmness the just claims of native excellence. It is an important point that wherever doubts as to the real justice of an award arise, the benefit of them should be given to our friends from abroad ; but it is equally essential that all should be fairly judged by the same standards, and that where we have the balance in our favour, the su- periority established should be firmly maintained. The delicacy of our position necessarily places ns at a disad- vantage in this matter, and there are other circumstances which have come to our knowledge, but on whicb it would perhaps be improper at present to touch, which still fun her increase the chances of our rendering to others more than they may feel disposed to render to us in re turn. The British jurors and the Council of Chairmen will both remembei that they have to deal with the ques- tion of prizes on a footing just to themselves as well as to the rest of the world, and they must for the sake of all be prepared to resist any nndue desire to gratify the amour propre of any individual country. From what we can gather, it would seem a point of primary consequence so to abridge the number of first-class prizes that they might be confined entirely to cases of paramount and undoubted excellence, and leave the less scope either for national or personal jealousies. At present the number spoken of as likely to be awarded is 200; but il that is found an unmanageable quantity, leading to stormy discussions, which are sincerely to be deprecated, it seems an obvious mode of relieving the ship to throw half or even three-fourths of the freight which thus endangers it overboard. Ma. Nash's Drawings of the Crystal Palace, made for her Majesty the Queen. — " We have to acknowledge the courtesy of Messrs. Dickinson and Co., of New Bond Street, for an invitation to inspect four of the most exquisite and interesting drawings which we ever remember to have seen ; they represent four different por- tions of the opening of the Great Exhibition by Her Majesty. Those who were present at that memorable ceremony cannot fail to remember its unapproachable splendour, and the hopelessness with which they endea- voured to describe to others, or even to recall themselves, the wonderous pageant they beheld ; and with what regret they saw it terminate, as a thing, perhaps, never to be re- alised, or so much as attempted again ! To paint, or to pourtray it in any shape, seemed impossible. Tbe vast extent, the thousand groups, the combination of colours, the endless detail — all militated against tbe idea of its being approached with even tolerable success. The attempt has, however, not only been made, but success, perfect and absolute, has been achieved by Mr. Nash, in the drawings to which we allude. Undertaken at the Queen's command, honoured by Her most marked and unequivocal approba- tion, purchased by Her Majesty, and at her express desire now being multiplied in fac simile on stone for general circulation, Mr. Nash may well be proud of the distinction his drawings have obtained for him. We congratulate bim on his well-earned success ; and we are sure the public will feel gratified by having the duplicates placed within their reach. The value of the prints will, of course, de- pend on their fidelity to the originals. Ob that bead there is no ground for apprehension. Mr. Nash is himself at work upon the stones, and as the originals are, by Her Majesty's command, to be placed within the Crystal Palace for public inspection, the fidility of the copies is easily ascertainable. Our foreign friends will, we have no doubt, gladly carry back with them to their distant homes and friends copies of these beautiful productions of British art."— Morning Post. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On entering the building yesterday, it was satis- factory to find that the daily complaints of the public and the press on the subject of ventilationhadnot been left wholly unattended to. The whole of the glass in the east and west galleries has been removed, and such light airs as generally blow in that direction have free ingress and egress. A similar change is contemplated with respect to the north and south transepts, and that ones effected, the rest must be left to the pitying breezes. What has been done has made the place much cooler, and there is little doubt but that the completion of the alterations will make the temperature all that could be expected in the middle of one of the hottest summers we have had for some years. Among the crowds of country folk who availed them- selves of cheap trains to obtain a peep at the wonder. of the Crystal Palace was a detachment of 130 workmen from the extensive lime works near Rochester, all in holiday-trim, and decorated with blue rosettes in tbeir button-holes. These poor men were retiring after about two hours' be- wildered gazing in every direction, when, being met by a person more intimate with the contents of the building, and asked what they had seen, it came out that they had. really seen but few of the sights of the place. Some of them hav- ing wandered recklessly from the main body once or twice, had nearly lost their way, and this So alarmed the rest, that they prudently resolved to keep to the nave while they're- mained, and to get out of danger as soon as possible. How- ever, being provided with a volunteer guide, a large number gladly returned to view the treasures of the precious metals' gallery and other objects of interest. Such incidents as these are by no means of unfrequent occurrence, and they show that in the case of large parties of unsophisticated country people a leader of some acquaintance with the place would be absolutely necessary to enable them even partially to enjoy their treat. The jurors were actively employed all day examining and deliberating, and exhibitors were equally busy making speculations, sanguine in proportion to the number of times they hadbeenvisited. But all guesses thereorelsewhereare wholly useless. The strictest secrecy is observed, and any violation of it on the part of any person, however subordi- nate, will be punished with instant dismissal. Itis expected that the awards will be placed in the hands of the printer on the 16th of next month. The number of stray articles in the hands of the police is daily increasing. TH.E GREAT EXHIBITION. An interval of six weeks only remains for the completion of all the arrangements of the Exposition, if the promise of its opening on the Ist of May is literally kept. Considerable speculation is afloat as to the possibility of the enormous amount of necessary preparation being got through. Some time has, it is feared, been lost in arranging the different allotments of space to the representatives of some foreign countries; but those difficulties have now been disposed of, and all parties are now perfectly well pleased as regards the question of space; and it is sincerely to be hoped that no fresh disagreement will arise to destroy that spirit of combined And harmonious action, the establishment of which becomes every day of greater importance, especially as the arrangements of foreign contributors are still in a very backward state, and their best efforts must be used tohave everything in order by the Ist of May. The Executive Committee are evidently aware of the necessity of urgency in their dealings with contributors, and have issued notices which will tend to aced°. rate their movements, if they do not wish to hazard the chance of exclusion. One very important consideration, with reference to the observance of punctuality in the opening of the Exhibition, has lately arisen with reference to the building itself, and serious fears as to its perfection as regards the very essential point of its being "weather-proof." The ridge and valley roof during wet weather has always leaked a little different points, but it was believed that when the Paxton gutters had been well pitched, and the interior of the sashbars painted, no inconvenience on this score would be experienced. The late heavy rains have dissipated this idea, and water has penetrated in so many places that serious fears are entertained by some as to the practicability of securing that exemption from drip or damp which is indispensable in such a building. We believe that the desired object can still be accomplished by administering a thick coat of paint to the sash-bars on the outside; but this constitutes a formidable addition to the work which the contractors have now scarcely six weeks to finish. The chinks and crevices have been regularly and constantly stopped up with paint and putty, and it is hoped that when the calico covering has boon got up, the wind will be prevented from driving the rain with such force through any seam that may still remain open. A suggestion has been made by a correspondent of the Times that "the whole of the roof be covered, and that the material used should be rendered waterproof: this might be done at slight additional expense by saturating the material with linseed oil. A covering so prepared will not exclude the light, and, if carefully looked after, and kept in good order, will probably prove tho best protection against both sun and rain." It seems to be feared that the materials employed—iron. wood, glass, and putty—will scarcely bear the effects which are likely to be produced on them by the combined action of a hot sun and an occasional thunder-shower in the course of the summer. There can be no doubt that during the late heavy rains the building has " leaked " sufficiently to alarm those who are desirous of exhibiting costly and perishable articles. But it is, nevertheless, to be doubted whether the building, and its capabilities of resisting the weather, could have been put to a severer test than the last fortnight's continuous heavy rain, accompanied by high winds and hail. At least, this test will be so far well-timed that it has been applied at a period when no damage been done to any of the contributions of exhibitors; and if there be a deficiency in this very essential particular, there is yet an opportunity given for its remedy by the same skill and activity which projected, and has so nearly brought to completion, the most extraordinary, not to say wonderful, building in the world. THE SUBMARINE TELEGRAPH.-Yesterday week the great cable, for telegraphic communication between this country and the Continent, was at length completed by carrying it up one mile out of the sea to Sangatte, on the Calais coast. Telegraphic communication between Calais and the South Foreland-the latter about three miles from Dover -was practically effected between coast and coast. It is not yet known at what precise date the wires to connect the cable at the South Foreland with the telegraph-office of the South-Eastern Com- pany at Dover will be completed. The extension of the telegraphic wire to Marseilles is now looked upon in France as an indispensable adjunct to the completion of the submarine telegraph, since the rami. fication of the wires between Paris and that port would place the capitals of both countries in instantaneous communication with the Mediterranean. On the other hand, the telegraphic communication is now completed from Ostend to Trieste, giving a through stretch of telegraphic communication little short of 2,000 miles. Telegraphic extension is also progressing throughout the east of Europe. Three great routes are now being laid down through the interior of Hungary; and the Turkish Government have come to the determination of laying down the telegraph in Turkey.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The concourse of visitors at the Exhibition seems to be a steadily advancing tide. Now and then, as in the case of yesterday week, a billow of enormous dimensions rolls in its 74,000 spectators, and retires in the way of all billows. But it never recedes to its former boundaries. The maxi- mum number becomes a new standard, round which the subsequent admissions fluctuate, until another monster day gives a new starting point, a permanent increase being per- ceptible in all the future fluctuations. Thus the numbers admitted daily varied from 50,000 to 60,000, until one day the admissions reached 68,000. Then 60,000 became the standard, until a week since, when the numbers reached 74,000, and ever since 60,000 has been the minimum on shilling days, and will no doubt so continue until some great occasion, such as the contemplated visit of the teetotallers who promise a select party of 60,000, when 80,000 will probably be the day's admission, and continue the standard until the sub- ject of thousands of bets is decided by the admissions reaching 100,000. The number of visitors yesterday was close upon 70,000. They were badly distributed, and the consequence was a suffocating temperature in the more frequented portions of the building. So great was the heat that many hundreds were obliged to leave before half their inspection had been completed, and thus presented the novel feature of long streams of departing visitors so early as two and three o'clock. If something be not speedily done with the ventilation the heat will be too great for curiosity, and the interests of the Exhibition must suffer in the absence of necessary precautions. 4arious attempts have been made by the Executive Committee to procure an additional supply of fresh air. The two ends of thetransept have been almost entirely taken out, and the effect has been beneficial in as far as they are concerned, but the naves still remain close and sultry, and the police and others whose duty com- pels constant attendance in these tropical regions, complain of frequent headaches and other derangements of the sys- tem in consequence. The ventilation is here interrupted by the refreshment and machinery courts, and until these latter are thoroughly opened, especially on the north side, very little relief can be hoped for. The visitors still consist mainly of country people, and almost all from the agricul- tural districts. There were great numbers present yesterday from almost every county in England; and they might be seen leaving about three o'clock in long processions for the various railway sta- tions at which their excursion trains awaited to take them home. There were also some charity schools; , among others the Foundling Hospital, but except a general glance at the building the children could gain but little by their visit. Of these the most attractive are a looking- glass and a console table, each consisting of an extremely elegant device, which probably could not have been brought to the same statesof perfection by the use of any other material. THE BOILER EXPLOSION AT MANCmESTEs .-TAhe second adjournment of the inquest on the nine persons killed in Riga-street, Manchester, by a boiler explosion, being till Saturday afternoon, the proceedings were then resumed. The principal witness examined was Mr. W. Fairbairn, C.E., who gave the following report in evi- dence. He visited the scene of the explosion on the Thursday following the event. The boiler was cylindrical in form, 21 feet 6 inches long, 6 ft. 2 inches in diameter, and composed of plates 6-16ths of an inch thick. It had a flue of the same thickness of plates, 2 feet three inches in dia- meter, which passed through it from end to end. The flue was six inches clear at the bottom, and the boiler had two diagonal stays an inch and three-quarters square, flattened at the end and riveted to the bottom of the flue. The other extremities of the stays were attached to the flat ends, com- posed of three-eighths plates, which passed through two picees of angle iron by a round pin. The ends of the stays rivetted to the flue were flattened to receive the rivets, leaving a very small portion of metal between the edge of the rivet-holes and the ends of the stays, to resist any severe strain in the event of the accumulation of high pressure steam in the boiler. I have com- puted the bursting pressure, assuming the flue to be covered with. water. at 140lbs. to the square inch; and, providing the ends had been properly stayed, it would have sustained a pressure of 276 lbs. to the square inch. The accident did not, however, arise so much from defec- tive construction as from gross mismanagement and igno- rance of the inevitable consequences which must arise From the state of the boiler at the time of the explosion, as indi- cated by present appearances. On a careful examination of the flue and the lower parts of the boiler, there was every indication of a deficiency of water having existed, and that a considerable portion of the upper parts of the flue, and of the sides of the boiler, had been red hot during an hour or two previous to the explosion. The fire must have been under the boiler from the time the engine stopped until the explosion took place, there being no escape for the steam, excepting only a defective safety-valve. The result must have been a gradual increase of pressure, and that, probably, without exciting the most distant suspicion on the part of the engineer that the boiler was in a dan- gerous state. I fully believe that might have been the case,. from my experience of engine-tenters. I should call this reckless inattention on the part of the en- gineer, assuming he had knowledge of his business, but I know there are a vast number who have not. Taking all the circumstances into consideration, I have no doubt of the cause of this melancholy occurrence. I firmly believe the boiler was short of water, every outlet for the steam closed, the safety-valve probably-fast, the flue and upper sides of the boiler red-hot, highly elastic steam was generated until the balance of the resisting forces of the material was overcome, when an explosion must have ensued. If the stays had been better' arranged that might have pre- vented the accident had the engine started, because the boiler would have been relieved; but supposing the engine not to start, no amount of staying could have prevented ex- plosion ultimately. But that is supposing the plates of the boiler were not hot. The blue appearance spoken of by Reed confirms my opinion of the great elasticity at which the steam had arrived. Cross-examined by Mr. Bent, soli- citor for the ?? were only two stay-bands, and I think there should have been more. The occupation of the engineerin astate of excitementthroughbeing engaged in packing the cylinder might excuse neglect at that time, but not for four or five hours before. By the coroner-I do not think blame attaches to the engineer alone, but I think blame attaches to those who employ incapable engineers, and there is great blame to the engineer, who from recklessness neglects attending to the state of water in the boiler, and other ordinary precautions. Mr. John Higgins was the next witness called, but not making his appearance, the inquest was further adjourned to Wed- nesday next.
