THE GREAT EXHIBITION. COMPREHENSIVE _VIEW OF THE CONTENTS OF THE CRYSTAL PALACE. A comprehensive view of the vast collection of objects in Hyde-park is what the public stand most in need of. When' they have thoroughly mastered the disposition and arrangement of the building, when they know in which direction to go in search of Austrian or American products, and where the different branches of our native industry are represented, they will still find themselves at sea in endeavouring to form it just conception of the whole display, in distinguishing the characteristic features of each part, and storing their minds with definite ideas of the industrial attributes developed at this gathering of nations. When a man is introduced to a number of strangers, his first instinctive tendency, after examining their respective appearances so as to distinguish them again, is to ask himself and study attentively what tendencies of the intellect or what traits of the heart he can gather from the expression of each countenance. Now, this process is exactly what the public are at present endeavouring to go through within the transparent walls of the building in Hyde-park. They have been presented there to the industries of all nations. They find each country preserving the individuality of her own collection. They can go to one portion of the building and see France, to another and see Germany, and so on round this family circle of the globe for the first time in man's history formed. Well, then, the question arises, what are they all like? In no fairer or truer mirror can national characters be represented than in their industrial products. Other pictures may deceive, but this must tell the truth. The course of events, guided as it is by a higher power than man's, does not always illustrate the moral and social attributes of communities. Not so the fruits of labour—the quality and description of material which engross the toil, supply the demand, and engage the tastes and predilections of a people. These tell their story as faithfully as the actions or the physiognomy of an individual indicate his nature, and by them, thus considered, we hope to help the public by anew path and under a fresh light through the marvels of the Great Exhibition. BRITISH SIDE. • Let us commence at home, and see what appearance this island of ours puts on at the peaceful reunion of nations. Is it Britannia, with her trident and plumed helmet and the lion recumbent at her feet, or John Bull's portly form, carrying weight in every limb, and determination, not unmingled with prejudice, from the crown of his broad-brimmed hat to the soles of his top-boots? Far otherwise. Some traces of those popular types of our nationality may indeed be traced, but England has greatly changed. Her genius is mechanism, her master spirit the civil engineer, her tendencies to relieve labour from its drudgery, and delegate to iron, to steam, and to the other powers of the inanimate world, as much as of the burden of toil. If you doubt this, go and look at the great department of machinery in the Crystal Palace; watch that vast collection of interesting objects, every portion of which lightens immeasurably the burden of life and releases hundreds of hands from the most irksome forms of industry. You will there see how mechanism is extending her dominion over the whole empire of labour; how she rises in textile fabrics to the manufacture of the most delicate and intricate lace; how from wood she aspires to fashion iron into the most exact proportions; how, with steam as her handmaid, she works tho printing press and navigates the ocean, and outruns the swiftest animal in her course. Turn into the agricultural implement department, and you will find everything now done by machinery. By it the farmer not only sows and reap, but ho manures and hoes. By it he thrashes out and grinds his corn and prepares the food for his cattle. He can even drain by machinery, and it is difficult now to find a branch of his business into which it does not largely enter. In our manufactures the mechanical genius of the country reigns supreme. Those beautiful fabrics are nearly all the evidences of its power. Soft goods and hardware are equally indebted to it, and in its presence the unaided efforts of handicraftsmen appear small and insignificant indeed. It travels everywhere and invades every compartment, even that of the fine arts, in the court dedicated to which some of the most conspicuous contributions are specimens of printing in oil, and attempts to reproduce by mechanical means the sentiment and inspiration of the painter. Yet we are not altother abandoned to this power—this Frankenstein which we ravei created, and which s dragging us we know not whither. The mediaeval court and its crowds of visitors, and its gaudy embellishments, still draw us back to days when ornament was not inseparably wedded to usefulness, or when at least, if that pact was completed, she was not acknowledged to be the "weaker vessel." We have some specimens of sculpture, such as those from the hands of Gibson, M`Dowall, and others, not unworthy of "art." The two colossal statues of the Scots have about them a certain solemn and massive grandeur which some minds will not unnaturally associate with the characteristics of the national intellect. These and other points will press upon the mind of an attentive observer; yet our main hope for the creation of the beautiful rests still in the adaptability of that power by which as a nation we labour and produce. Through multiplied evidences of neglected taste, and violations of harmony in colour and design that must shock many of our visitors, tho traces of a better and purer style of national industry begin to be discernible. Even our mechanical tendencies are yielding to the higher inspirations of the fancy, or perhaps we should say, are subjecting the admiration to their stupendous efforts. 'Witness, in illustration of this, the great interior of tho Crystal Palace itself, that surprising and splendid piece of mechanism, wherein the civil engineer has displaced the architect and iron and glass been substituted for bricks and mortar. Of our colonial possessions visitors will gather at the Exhibition an interesting but imperfect impression. They will see in that preponderance of raw produce the evidences of infant societies still struggling forward to a larger industrial development. The philosophic mind will be attracted by the advantages which the rising communities that have swarmed from our shores to settle in distant scenes possess—how science and education help them to investigate the natural resources of the new regions which they occupy—how, having tilled the virgin soils of Australia or Canada with the agricultural knowledge of the mother country, they at length send home the fruits of their labour to be absorbed by our markets. We enter the Indian collection, and examine thoughtfully the products of our empire in the East. What do they tell us? Those jewels, that rich display of mineral and vegetable produce, those shawls an d carpets in which the harmony of colours is so admirably represented. filigree work in silver an d gold, brocaded stuffs, curiously executed carvings, rude models of machinery, musical instruments, arms, elephant naval architecture —how trapping s, suggestive they all are an d what stories they tell. H ere are gathered together the ' y trophies of ancient civilization an d arts, uaarvellousl carried down to our own time. Here may be studied the industrial habits of nations preserved through centuries without change or progress, yet still wonderful a n d magn i f i cent in tho eyes of modern labour. Look at those alabaster chairs, how regal they appear, how fitly they represe n t a country where many dynasties conquered and flourished and were overcome before th e British sway was established over its dusky populations. Nearly everything in that collection which is the work of man's hands indicates a vast expenditure of time for its and a great display of taste. Yet it is nearly all ornamental, rather than useful, in its character. Whenever the really useful arts appear, rudeness of material and design are visible. A warlike weapon will be finished off in the most elaborate style, yet a pair of scissors be manufactured in a manner worthy of the South Sea Islanders, The East India, Company begin their rule of India as if it were a now country. The evidences of barbaric pomp, the state umbrellas, the cloth of gold, and robes deorated with pearls and diamonds, concern not them. These belong to the natives to tho traditions of the past, and to industries which have been bequeathed from ago to ago as an heirloom, Our part of the collection is the raw produce—the mineral, vegetable, and Lui ma! treasures =disguised and unused till our COMMOTCO and the wants of our manufactures sought them out. Resting upon them, we strive to build on substantial and permanent foundations the structure of empire and government in India; at least, that is the lesson which the Exhibition seems to teach, and the question which each visitor asks himself as he surveys that most interesting collection is, "Shall we succeed in our attempt ? " Such is a brief outline of what we conceive to be the character and inward meaning of the vast mass of objects which have been collected within the British half of the Crystal Palace. Each reader will fill up the sketch according to his peculiar bent of mind, and from the ideas thus formed may be gathered a succinct conception of the whole, tending to relieve the mind from those vague, unsatisfactory, and distracting impressions of astonishment and admiration which, with the great majority of visitors, are, we doubt not, in the ascendant.

The council of chairmen have confirmed the recom- mendation of the jury on agricultural implements, and awarded a great medal tb Cyrus Hall M"Cormick, in the American department, for his reaping machine. This implement is now performing a highly successful experi- mental tour through the country. It commenced opera- tions at Tiptree Farm, and was next heard of at Far- ninglham, then its capabilities were displayed at Mr. Mangle's; and on Friday it was shown at work on the large farm attached to the Agricultural College at Cirencester. The season of the year and the eclat of the Great Exhibition present the inventor with unusual facilities for demonstrating practically the value of his machine. The public will not be surprised to bear that this implement is attracting an immense amount of at- tention and interest among farmers. On its first suc- cessful trial at Tiptree the agriculturists present raised a cheer. At Farninugham the enthusiasm manifested was still greater ; and on Friday. at Cirencester, there was no lack either of curiosity or approval among the crowds assembled. It was tried on barley, wheat and oats, and under circumstances fairly calculated to test its merits. To say that where corn is badly lodged or thin, or where the land is rough with stones, its success is only partial, is to state what everybody of sense would expect, for machines must have foar play shown them, and it is the duty of the farmer so to cultivate his soil that mechanical facilities can be brought to bear upon it with every rea- sonable advantage. Yet it is wonderful hor well, coming upon a system of agriculture totally unprepared for it, the American reaper does its work. A stubble longer and more irregularly cut will occasionally mark a spot |where the crop was so trampled or borne down that it could not be well got at; but wherever it stands at all well, it is removed with perfect precision and evenness, both on level land and on the most rapid declivities and curves. This was fallyshown on Friday, the fields where the experiments were made, presenting a very undulating surface. There cannot be a doubt that if the machine is taken up in this country, as it ought, it will speedily undergo extensive improvements. We see no reason, why it should not be made to deliver the crop after cut. ting it, thereby dispensing with the use of one man, whose sole occupation is to rake off the receiving board its ac- cumulations, and whose labours will be better estimated when it is remembered that the implement gets over 15 acres per day. With respect to cost also there appears room for a reduction of price which would render its adoption far more rapid and general than it can be if the present charge of £28 be maintained. There is nothing in the nature of the machine which should render it so expensive. The farmers of Cotteswold appeared greatly pleased with the experiments of Friday, and assembled to witness them in numbers which did credit to their en- terprise and their desire to go ahead. Among those who witnessed the operations of the reaping machine were Earl Bathurst and a party of friends, which: included the Duke and Dachess of Bedford.-Times. HORRIBLE MURDER AT FRoME, SOMERSET.-A murder of a horrible description was committed on Wednesday week, near Frome, the victim being a young girl 15 years of ag'e, named Sarah Watts. The deceased resided with her father and mother at a small farm in West Woodlands, about three miles from Frome, and it appears that the parents left home on n thdnesday serunigot for Frome market, and on their return ?? the afternoon found the lifeless body of their child lying on the floor of the daisy room. There were appearances of a dreadful struggle ?? ensued. Several basins were found broken, and a tub containing a quantity of whey was also upset. The wounds on the body and head of the deceased appeared to have been caused by a blunt instrument, and her dress was much torn. The marks of bloody fingers were also found on the dairy wall. It further appeared that the un- fortunate victim had been ravished before being murdered. The house was completely ransacked, and several articles carried away, but not of any great value. The diabolical perpetrator of this double crime has hitherto escaped detection. The shocking event has created the greatest excitement in the neighbourhood. The inquest was commenced on Friday, and resumed on Tuesday, when Mr. Francis Giles, surgeon, deposed that he had made a post iorteie examination. He found a large quantity of blood between the scalp and the bone on the fore part of the head towards the right side. On opening the skull, he found that the bone was not fractured; the brain was very much congested, but in other respects healthy. On the neck were two bruises beneath the skin, one in the middle line, just over the windpipe, the other two or three inches distant on the left side. The heart and lungs were verv much congested, but in other respects healthy. All the other viscera were healthy. (The post ms-tem examina- tion also proved that a rape had been committed.] He believed death to have been caused by strangulation. It was quite impossible the girl could have strangled herself. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty and the royal visitors came to the Crystal Palace on Monday morning at nine o'clock, and, as some 400 or 500 exhibitors had been formally requested to be present, more than usual interest attached to the occasion. The por- tion of the Exhibition marked out for inspection was the south gallery on the west side of the transept. Hitherto the royal visits have been made in a very private manner, and, although the principal contributors were made aware that the Queen was coming, no official announcement of the fact was made to them as a body. lIt will be remembered that the honour of a personal inspection was promised them about the time that the building was opened; and it was deemed proper in fulfilment of that promise to give to Her Majesty's gracious patronage of the Exhibition a more decided and positive character. Ac- cordingly, when the royal party presented themselves at the Crystal Palace on Monday some 300 exhibitors were in their places ready to receive them. The public, we fear, hardly do justice to the estreme sensibilities of this class; jealoas as they naturealy are, each in his own department, for the main- tenance of thesr several excellencies, it is an extraordinary event with them to be brought face toface with the royalty of England. Lips and tongues, that before ordinary mortals woold run freely on in the labours of explanation, be- come confused and falter when the Qeean asks what they have to show. There were many manifestations of that kind on Monday, and one distinguished contributor, a manufacturer of warlike weapons, too, fainted under the excitement. Her Majesty began with the chymicals, in which department she specially admired the contributions of Pontifex and Wood. Her attention was also drawn to the display of preserved meats, and particularly what related to the supply of the navy. She made particular inquiries into the regulations adopted for as- certaining that this supply was good and proper for the use of the sailors. In the survey of vegetable products, the fine spe- cimens of grain from the Home.Farm exhibited by Prince Al- bert did not escape attention. The most important feature of this survey, however, was the illustration of his ingenious pro- cess in the conversion of flax fibre into a substitute for cotton by the Chievalier Claussen. Her Majesti's attention was par- ticularly drawn to the process for the solidification of milk, and to the display of preserved fruits by Fortnam and Mason. She remained for two hours in the building, and during her stay conrersed in the most affable manner with a great num- ber of the exhibitors The receipts at the doors daily, amount to about t.2000, and the number of spectators varies from 45,000 to 50,000. The crowds who throng the Exhibition now approach nearer the ideal upon which the scale of shilling admissions was fixed than anything we have yet witnessed. The mass was well leavened with the numistakeable traces of a laboturing popula- tion; it was at once interesting and gratifying to observe how after a short time spent in simple wonder and astonishment, each seemed br a natural instinct to betake himself to those departments upon which he could bring his own practical knowledge most distinctly and intelligibly to bear. Every portion of the interior was well examined, and though crowds still collect round the more curious and attractive objects, there is evidently a singular instinct at work among the body of the community to which our upper classes were not subject. While they retained possession of the building, the eastern or foreign half, was more favoured and frequented. Now the western division comes in for the largest amount of admira- tion. Altogether, the conduct of the visitors to the Great Ex- hibition, now that the price of admission is lowered to Is., is beyond praise, and amply vindicates the confidence reposed in I their good behaviour.

SHIPBUILDING-YARD IN DUNDEE ON FIRE. -- On Monday evening, shortly after seven o'clock, the shipbuilding-yard of the Tay Company, situated between the south side of the Victoria Dock and the Marine-parade, and to the east of the powder magazine, was discovered to be on fire. The flames had attained such an ascendancy before the arrival of the engines, from the combustible nature of the materials, that the energies of the firemen were directed to the preservation of the property still untouched rather than the salvation of any of that on fire. A large vessel, in course of construction, was for a time in imminent danger. In less than an hour the fire had consumed the steaming-box, the shed and work-shop, and a saw-pit, with its contents. The endeavours of the firemen were thwarted by the water in the mains having been screwed off. The mastery was obtained over the devastating element at about half-past nine o'clock, when water was obtained, and at about ten o'clock the fire was wholly suppressed. A detachment of the 33d Regiment from the barracks were present. The damage has been estimated at 10001., but we believe the property is totally insured,

"I You cannot point to any period in the world's history, B. when those in authority over any people paid so much atten- a tion to the wants, desires, and comfort of the mass of their subjects, as you find embodied is all the arrangemeats and d regulations for the carrying out of this great undertaking. : In former times the paramount consideration was the luxury d ant enjoyment of the few; the present object is to promote is the instruction and happiness ot the "million." CITY OF LONDoN LIFE AssunANCE SOCIETY.- Yesterday the annual general meeting of proprietors was held at the offices, Royal Exchange-buildings; Dr. J. R. ?? in the chair. The minutes of the last meeting having been confirmed, the secretary read the report, in which the directors congratulated the proprietary on the satisfactory lbalance-sheet which they were enabled to submit to the meeting. The unexampled exemption of the society from claims during the first four years could not, of course, be expected to continue; and the claims of the past year, though not exceeding the aggregate amount calcu- lated on-being, in fact, 7,720K.-were considerably short of the ordinary income of the society. The sun assured by new- policies was 75,4331. 10s. 4d., which produced an additional annual income of 2,6041.19a. lid. The total sum now assured amounted to 265,8271., yielding an income of 9,235?. 29. lid. There were besides additional propositions under the consideration of the board, and which it was ant considered desirable to accept, to the Iamount of 24,5101. Since the close of the company's financial year a further sum of 4,420a. had been insured, and assurances amounting to 5,600?. werein course of completion. It was also stated in the report that the directors had under their consideration plans for extending the advan- tages of life assurance, and for enabling them to curtail their expenditure. Mr. Rainbow addressed the meeting at much length in dissent from some of the propositions embodied in Ithe report, and contended that if the business of the society .were properly stated on the balance sheet, it would appear that while they were liable for about 22,0001., their assets were only 1.5,0001. Mr. Lamb agreed with the objections put forward by Mr. Rainbow, and censured the expenditure of the company as unnecessarily high. Mr. Farrance (the actuary of the society), in reply, read a statement of the per centage expenses of five other first class life assurance offices, rom whica it appeared that the expenditure of the City of Lendon Society was considerably less than that of those offices, and he showed that as their operations extended, the expenses which now seemed heavy would then appear light. The principles upon which the business of the office was conducted had received the approval of the first authorities in the kingdom on such matters, and although Mr. Rainbow thought there had been a considerable loss on their transactions, he could assure him that the directors might, at the present moment, transfer the business of the ociety to another office, and have a surplus remaining of I,5001. He (ir, Farrance) undertook to demonstrate this fact to Mr. Rainbow, if he would investigate the affairs of the society. The Chairman and others of the directors made Statements showing that the income of the society had been steadily increasing, and expressed an unanimous desire that Mr. Rainbow would make any investigation he pleased of the accounts and business of the society, the result of which they were assured would convince him that his state.i ments were utterly without foundation. After a long dia- cuesion the report was unanimously received, and Mr. Rainbow, in conjunction with Mr. Farrance and a sub- committee of the directors, undertook to make an inquiry into the constitution and condition of the society, for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not his allegations were well founded. A resolution, declaring a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent. per annum, was carried-there being, how- ever, five dissentients. The proceedings terminatedwith votes of thanks to the chairman, board of directors, and the officers of the society. NEW RULE REILATING TO THE SITTINGS OF COUNTY CounTs.-In the recent rules issued for the regu- lation of County Courts, there is one declaring that " On or before the 1st of January, 1852, the judges shall appoint the days and hours for holding each of their courts during the months of January, February, and March in the said year, and on or before the first day of every month after the said month of Januacy the judges shall appoint the days and hours for holding each of their courts during the month next following the three months previously appointed, and a notice of such appointment shall forthwith be put up by the clerk in some conspicuous place in the court house, and in the office of the clerk; and whenever any day so ap- pointed for holding the court shall be altered, notice of such alteration and the time when itwill take effect shall be put up in some conspicuous place in the court house and clerk's office, provided that the judge may from time to time hold additional courts besides those hereinbefore required to be appointed. Two courts shall not be held before the same judge in one day." It is to be hoped that the time when the courts are to rise each day will be stated, which notice would benefit all parties and prevent late sittings. NATIONAL FREEHOLD LAND SOCIETY-This so- ciety is extending is operations in the southern counties. It has made anothe- valuable purchase, consisting of an , estate at Chichester, within three-quarters of a mile south- east of the city walls, on the Bognor-road. The estate is already laid out in a picturesque manner, and is intersected by a good road running from east to west, calledWickham- road. At a meeting of the society, held at Chichester, a few evenings ago, to celebrate this acquisition, the chair was occupied by the Rev. W. Malden, a clergyman of the place. Mr. Clarke, of Walthamstow, delivered an address, in which he pointed out the desirability of the industrious classes availing themselves of this excellent opportunity of obtaining the franchise by such a small outlay Mr. hit. tingham, the secretary of the society, detailed its operations from the commencement, showing that the scheme had flourished far beyond the most sanguine anticipations. He trusted that the advantages held out by their having ob- tained an estate in close proximity to the stronghold of pro- tection would not be lost sight of; at the same time he dis- claimed any political bias for the society, its object being to widen the franchise for the benefit of all parties. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. THE LAST WEEK. (From tlie Times.) On Thursday, notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather, 01,298 persons visited the building, and the re- ceipts amounted to JE3.080..12..0. On Fbiday the number of visitors was 31,951, and the re- ceipts iJ3.354..3. On Saturday there were 29.610 persons in the building during Uie day, and the sum of £2,882-14 was taken at the doors. Monday, the first day of the last week of the Exhibition, has passed off in a manner at once gratifying aud surprising. Everybody was prepared for a great accession of numbers to the usual average of shilling visitors, but.the most extravagant expectations could hardly have anticipated anything so remark- able as die actual reality. On Monday 107,815 persons entered tbe building, and tlie sum of £5,1 75. .16 was taken at the doors. Facts so astounding speak for themselves, aud derive no ad- ditional force from expatiating upon them. Were it not so, we should despair of describing the scene which the interior pre- sented. Popular demonstrations are always grand. Taking place in such an arena they exercise a transcendent and over- powering influence. In the presence of such an assemblage as was yesterday collected together the highest triumphs of in- dustry "and art are forgotten, and the mind has only time to think of that great mass of humanity tendering its homage at the shrine of labour, and vindicating the nobility of toil. If any lingering doubts have been entertained that the Crystal Palace has not been popular among the masses, its closing hours will set them completely at rest. Great as the influx of visitors was yesterday, it will most probably rise still higher to-day ; but it is satisfactory to think that however vast the numbers that present themselves the building will be found capable of accommodating them all. The dreaded limit of 100,000 spectators has now been exceeded, and without any extraordinary inconvenience. In the Crystal Palace, as else- where, tlie people are their own best police, and from hour to hour crowds leave to make room for tlie gathering tide that enters. Yesterday they began »o ooze away as early as eleven o'clock, aud so well balanced were the departures and arrivals that until the doors closed it was possible, without much effort, to make a systematic and effectual survey of all the principal objects and departments. We have no doubt that with con- siderably increased numbers this will continue to be the case, and a sanguine hope is entertained that no pressure will arise so great and inconvenient as to render it necessary to check the flow of visitors. That nearly 108,000 people should within one day and under one roof have enjoyed the grandest specta- cle the world ever witnessed is of itself a sufficient marvel, but that they should have done so without a single knowu casualty to life or property is almost incredible. So, however, it is, and we leave to revolutionary aud discontented minds the study of facts which place iv so clear and unquestionable a light the love of order and the genuine kindliness of spirit which per- vade all classes of our population. Yet, while we dwell with a natural complacency on those evidences of a happy and pros- perous people, circumstances are constantly occurring to warn us of possible disaster. Such an event took place to-day. When the crowd assembled within tbe building was at its cul- minating point, it was suddeuly discovered that the Duke of Wellington was present. Instantly tbe manifestations of pub- lic admirations arose. Hats were taken off and loud cheers burst forth, which were prolonged with immense energy. Those who were at a distance, surprised by an unwonted agi- tation which they could not understand," fancied there was something wrong, and rushed, towards the doors. The Duke also felt the awkwardness of his position, aud beat a retreat. His great age does not now permit him to execute such move- ments with the precision and firmness which in former days were his characteristics, but he made his way nevertheless to the south entrance of the transept with surprising alacrity, fol- lowed as he went by the most vigorous demonstrations of popular regard. Supt. Pearce, with great tact, stopped the rush towards the places of exit, and by liis judicious manage- ment the fears of the most timid spectators were in a few minutes effectually quieted. There are few things wbich to one weU acquainted with tbe collection of products in Hyde Park appear more striking than the remarkable aids which the. science of ?? It there seen lending to our manufactures. The Erocess of tbe Chevalier Claussen for converting flax fibre ito tt substitute for raw cotton has already attracted great public notice, and b likely to lead to most important prac- tical results. Mercer's discovery for improving the dyeing properties of cotton fabrics, and giving to their texture the closeness and fineness of linen, b another singular example of thb kind. It was in making some experiments on water that he accidentally hit upon the influence of soda on the great staple of our manufactures, and he patiently pur- sued bb investigations until they led him to the process which now bears hb name. We have to add to the list of chymical contributions to our natural industry developed in the Exhibition another striking and important discovery made by Mr. James Young, of Manchester; but in order to understand its character it b necessary to give some ex- planation. It may be recollected tbat some time ago a spring of mineral oil, like those in Persia and many other countries, was found in a mine in Derbyshire. On distilla- tion it was ascertained to be an oil of great value for the lubrication of machinery, and was much used for that pur- pose in Manchester, but the supply ceased. Mr. Young's attention was then directed to the subject. From ita con- nexion with the coal district he believed that it might be produced therefrom by chymical means. The naptha pro- duced by tbe distillation of coal differs entirely from that found in the natural spring referred to. Mr. Young, how- ever, bas discovered a process by which he entirely converts the volatile principle of coal into a liquid oik and into a substance called paraifine. Tbb substance had never pre- viously been produced from coal, though it had from tbe distillation of wood. If paraffine be heated, it is converted into defiant gas — the illuminating principle ofthe ordinary gas which lights our streets and houses. It may, therefore, be appropriately termed " solid gas." The oil. produced is also paraffine in a different condition, and thus Mr. Youog, by distilling coal at a low heat, has succeeded in producing solid and Uquid gas. The importance of thb discovery was pointed out by Baron Liebig in a recent work, wherein he describes the solidification of gas as one of the greatest wants of tbe age. Mr. Young has produced the desired result by a process preliminary in its stage to that hinted at by the great cbymist, and in weight the results obtained by him tally exactly with what they would be in tbe manu- facture of common gas. In practice nothing can be more simple than this discovery. The coal introduced at one end ofa retort b screwed out in the form of coke at tbe other, while the liquid and solid products of distillation come away from a separate opening. If successfully car- ried out on a large scale, Mr. Young's process will yield very important results, and among these may be specified the economical production of coke for our railways, in the manufacture of which vast quantities of gas are now en- tirely wasted. On Saturaay night, before the departure of the excursion train to London, one pawnbroker in Leeds had received on deposit no less than a bushel and a balf of watches ; and this sudden and extraordinary accession of business he attributes entirely to the desire which those who are little able to afford the treat have to visit the Crystal Palace. A French Murderess.— A woman, aged 40, named Anne Valby, was tried four days ago by the Court of Assizes of the Cote-dOr for the murder of her husband. In early life her conduct was most scandalous, and she had two illegitimate children. She was also suspected of having caused the death of one of them by plunging it when quite young in cold water. She was also suspected of having occasioned the death of her sister. In 1842 she married an old rmn named Faivelcy, of Comblar.chien, and he diod six weeks after with violent pains in hb bowels. Before his death she had criminal relations with more than one person. A little after she married another old man, named Guillaume, ofthe same place, and, though she had two children by bim, her conduct continued to be scandalously licentious. She had frequent quarrels with her husband, and used violent threats against him. In the night of the 28th of March last the neighbours heard them quarrelling and fighting, but paid no attention. Two days after tbe woman announced that her "old man" had disappeared, and that she did not know what had be- come of him. She, however, made no s.arch after him, and after a while went to an adjacent village to pay a visit. During her absence tke body was discovered in the well of her house. She returned just as the neighbours had, with some difficulty, succeoded in getting it up. She passed by it with unconcern, and, while it was being ex- amined, coolly sat down and paitook of food. Traces of blood were fouud on the bed, on the walls, and on an axe, and the woman was arrested. Her children, a boy of 13 aud a girl of seven, then stated that they had been awakened on the night of the 2Sth of March by the quarrel and fight of their father ar.d mother; that the latter had beat the old mini ou the head with an axe until he lell on the bed and died ; that she had then made the- boy assist her in dragging the body to a dark corner and in placing some furniture before it to prevent its being seen : lhat she had afterwards washed the blood out o°f the sheets, atrd made him and the girl sleep in the bed from which the corpse had been removed; that the next morning she h.ad kept them at home until all the neigh bours had gone into the fields, and had then made them assist her in tossing the body into the well. The principal witness against the woman was her own sou ; but, though his evidence caused a thrill of horror through the court, it produced no effect on her. The jury declared her Guilty, without extenuating circumstances, and the Court con- demned her to death. She displayed no emotion on hear- ing the sentence, and walked ay. ay with a firm step The next day she was head singing and dancing in hpr cell

Continuing our notice of the glass exhibited, we subjoin the following details, from a work by Mr. Apsley Pellatt, as to the peculiarities of its manufacture. Glass has the property of being indestructible, and maray curious specimens of ancient glass have been handed down to us in their original beauty and purity of colour. The translucency of glass is a property by which it is made not only greatly to conduce to the comfort and cobvenience of man, but extending his view to other worlds, enables him to form some conception of their multitude, and to trace the laws by which their motions are governed; whilst his view is enlarged to comprehend the mechanism of the most minute created object. What discoveries may be made in the science of electricity, we know not; but the value of a substance which can arrest the progress of this mighty and subtile fluid cannot be small. Glass has also the property of resisting the action of most acids and alkalis, rendering it an object of importance to the mauufaciurer and chemist. With the exception of the diamond, all the precious stones are similar in their composition to manufactured glass, being the coraboaation of silica with an alkaline earth, which substances can only combine under the influence of heat. Flint glass (being that quality of ,glass from which all articles of luxury are manufactured, and which is known on the Continent under the generic title of crystal), besides silica and alkali, contains a large proportion of oxide of lead, for the purpose of increasing its density and brilliancy, and ot adding to its ductility whilst in the semifluid state. Flint glass then is composed of silica, alkali, and lead in certain proportions, liquified by heat, and solidified by cooling. The superior quality of British flint glass is, in a great measure, due to the very careful manner in which the lead is prepared. All the oxides are used, but the preference is given to the peroxide. No good flint glass can be made without oxide of manganese, although the quantity used is very small. Were all the other materials chemically pure, the glass would not be colourless, but invariably of a green tint, resulting from deoxidation; the greater the degree of heat, the greater the amount of deoxidation, and consequently the deeper this tint. To prevent this, the oxide of manganese is used; it holds combined a large amount of oxygen, which it has the property of parting with very slowly; it. supplies to the other materials, during the fusion, sufficient oxygen to mrentain them in a certain state of oxygenation, in which state only a colourless glass can be obtained. If too much oxide of manganese be used, the glass is of a purple tint, and this is produced, not by the colouring property of the base, but by an excess of oxygen. This purple tint is replaced by the green upon the application of heat. The green tint may be made to give place to the purple when glass is slowly heated to redness in contact with the atmosphere as in the process of drop pinchipg; this chan ge i s i n all probebility due to the oxygen it takes up from the air. Nor is it necessary that heat be employed to effect this; exposure to the atmosphere for a long period equally effects a change of colour. Indeed the colour of all glass is changed sooner or later according to the base of the colouring matter. Flint glass, perhaps, from the quantity of lead entering into its composition, is less affected than other glasses; but plate and window glass are very susceptible. Colourless glass of this description, in which there is manganese, becomes purple; light tinted green glass is changed to straw or yellow; and, in fact, the whole art of producing colourless glass lies in the proper regulation of the quantity of oxide and manganese, a matter of extreme difficulty and nicety. To the nature of the fuel in this country is to be ascribed the superior quality of English glass of every description; the molecular structure of which is clo,er, because it contains a larger proportion of silica than the foreign. The materials, after having been carefully weighed, are intimately mixed, and upon this depends the homogeneity of the melted mass. The want of homogeneity in glass is its greatest defect. In the case of liquids of different specific gravities being mixed, and resuming their state of rest, it will be found that each liquid is arranged according to its gravity, and while this is taking place it will present the appearance of cloudiness. This is precisely what takes place in glass, the difference in specific gravity of the materials being very considerable. The cloudiness or want of homogeneity is termed striae. Another cause also exists to produce cloudiness or strips. The back of the crucible in the glass furnace is exposed to a greater degree of heat than the front and sides ; consequently a current of the melted glass is constantly passing from back to front of the crucible. It is the want of homogeneity that prevents the manufacture of large achromatic lenses, and although some attempts to overcome it have been made, they have not yet been entirely successful. For the very best glass, virgin materials only are used, as every remelting deteriorates the quality. Daring the melting, vehich occupies about 60 hours, the glass assumes different appearances. Alter the first ten or twelve hours it appears a honeycombed mass, very white, and perfectly opaque ; in a few more hours the opaque appearances yield to a transparent body, filled with thousands of air bubbles; the white colour now gives place to a light purple tint, produced by the oxygen given off from the oxide of manganese. As the melting continues, the purple tint gradually vanishes, the air-bubbles become fewer and larger, and at length quite disappear, when - the glass is fined and ready for manipulation. This is a curious and interesting process, differing from every other, inasmuch as a change in the organisation of the material takes place, and that so instantaneously as to appear the effect of magic. That wh.eh .1 ha meet tefo:e appeared an opaque, semi -fluid . end non-lucent body, w;thout form, and apparently of a bright yellow colcur, ie a moment assumes various opposite qualities. The opaque is now beautifully transparent; the semi -fluid, a colourless solid of the most perfect molecular structure; and whilst these changes take place, the utmost symmetry of form has been acquired. The manipulation depends upon certain general properties which glass possesses. At a red heat one piece of glass is welded to another by mere contact; at a lower temperature, in contact with a cold iron, glass is fractured evenly and perpendicularly, and may also be cut with scissors with nearly the same ease as cloth; and at a higher temperature may be elongated to any extent; in this respect being superior to the most ductile metal. It may be spun to the finest hair or blown to an almost imperceptible substance. Coloured glass is produced by adding to the ordinary glass mixtures the oxides or carbonates of certain metals, thereby causing such an atomic arrangement that one or more rays of a pencil of light are reflected. It is usual to ascribe one particular colour to a particular metal, say blue to cobalt, or green to copper; but Bontemps has shown that all the colours of the spectrum may be produced by any one of the ordinary metals, which he ascribed to the degree of heat to which the mixture or the colouring metal is subjected. In all instances of change of colour of glass, heat can only be the agent by which the change is effected, the colour depending upon the combination of the metallic base with oxygen or carbon, and upon the vertical e. molecular structure of the glass resulting therefrom. This composition, it will be remembered, was performed on the day of the auspicious inauguration, and it will be thought to have been equally, if not even more fittingly, chosen, as the concluding utterance of national sein- timent on the day of the triumphant close. The people of England will learn with satisfaction that the last formal and aggregate expression of feeling heard in the building, where, if anywhere, human vanity might, perhaps, have been pardoned some manifestation, was that of rejoicing but reverent acknowledgment of the King of Kings. The chorus being over, Prince Albert withdrew amid much acclamation, and was followed by the Royal and Foreign Comnmissioners, the latter being afterwards introduced to his Royal Highness in the Commissioners' Room, for the purpose of a final leave-taking. His Royal Highness soon afterwards took his departure. So ended a ceremony which, though it had as little that was imposing in it as could well be, was at all events a more decorous termination to the Great Exhibition than was the strange, ill- arranged proceeding of Saturday. It will, how- ever, be remembered that, after all, yesterday's cere- monial was a private one. The aristocracy and commonalty of England, and of the world, were invited to see the building inaugurated; but nearly the only persons admitted to witness its closing were those who happened to have contributed to furnish it. Without the slightest idea of disparag- ing for a moment the invaluable class who consti- tuted the audience yesterday, we may fairly assert that it was not the class which stood around the platform on the lst of May. The spectators on that day were the representa- tives of the nations of the earth; those of yes- terday were persons whose business happened to connect them with the Exhibition. Consequently, neither for England, nor for the nations whose Go- vernments have so frankly and nobly supported her in her novel and magnificent undertaking, has there been any formal close of the Great Exhibition. The world will learn that the place is closed, because, on applying at the doors, they will not be able to get in; but how far such a mode of signifying the fact is worthy of the Exhibition, or consistent with the proceedings of May-day, is, we ima- gine, a matter of which those in authority have hardly heard the last. We have not closed the Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations -we have simply " shut up shop." As a nation of shopkeepers, perhaps it was thought well we should know our place. It was, in many quarters, expected that the opportunity would have been selected for paying some marked honour to those who had designed and reared the building, and to those who had devoted so much of their valuable time and attention to the carrying out of the Great Exhibition. It may have been thought that some such honour as is con- ferred upon mayors and aldermen who happen to be in office at a lucky moment, would not have been too great for those who have done so much for the reputation of the country. A knighthood, for example, bestowed upon those persons within the walls of the Crystal Palace, would have been a graceful tribute-would have resembled the old chivalric knighthood conferred on the battle-field where it had been won. Although, however, no public recognition of these services took place, we understand that at a later period of the day a com- muuication was made by Lord John Russell to Mr. Fox, to the effect that her Majesty was graciously pleased to signify her intention of conferring the hoimour of knighthood upon him and Mr. William Cubitt, the commissioner who had superintended the erection, aud on Mr. Paxton, who had furnished the design of the building. The visitore, on Thursday were of the usual class, mostly agriculturists or mechanics, with here and there a long file of children, marched hurriedly through the building, without much opportunity of examining anything accurately or eatisfactorily. Nothing can he more interesting dierinf; the crowded parts of the day than to stand in ono ot the galleries near the transept, and watch thu hinnan tide as it pours along, swaying to and fre s and emptying itself into the great avenues here --1 there, or toiling, circling, and eddying round gone obstructions where any object of peculiar interest arrests the attention of the moving mass. The un • impeded circulation of some 50,000 or 60,000 personals certainly one of the wonders of this vast building, but its "pulse," the ceaseless throb that gives it lifelike character, has probably been less noticed. Standing Still in the gallery, a little close observation will the curious that the flooring upon which he stands vibrates under his feet, that the solid iron pillar which he grasps trembles in its firmly. rooted hate—that the long range of cases and counters are all in motion, the groups of statuary, the massive iron and bronze candelabra, and the ponderous trophies of timber or metal, as well as the lighter structures of silk or damask, or lace, placed on the flooring, or suspended from thsi girders, are kept in agitation by some hidden powerful agency. The organs vibrate before a chord to struck—the suspending chains of the clocks have a itotion independent of the pendulum, and even the massive-looking statue of the Queen, erected by the le:elle Montague Company, with a base like a pyramid, wears an air of unsteadiness, and in the midst of her loyal and living subjects the Sovereign of that throne whose foundations are laid the deepest and the most secure, nods and trembles. Higher up, those who have had th e privilege or the daring to ascend to the roof of the transept, may hear the vibration of a thousand harmoniously blended sounds in the ring and rattle of the immense sttrface of glass spread out and around, and which partakes of the throbbing peculiarity of the Whole structure. But there is nothing in all this to excite alarm—it tends rather to establish the elastic and well-knitted character of the frame-work, which yields and rebounds to every force applied, instead of exhibiting that rigid tension which the first sudden and undue pressure would rend asunder. The glass will probably want renewing now and then, and the iron-work tn Occasional coat of paint; but the building is liktly to survive as many summers and winters as if It had been constructed of the more cumbrous and expensiVe materials of brick or stone. The continued wet weather still keeps alive the fear that the ridge and valley roof of the Crystal Palace cannot be made watertight—at least, not in time for the opening on the Ist of May. Workmen are busily engaged upon it, and there is no doubt that many of the openings through which the rain penetrates aro broken panes of glass, which of course can be mended. The mischief, however, is not altogether of this description; and we observed that during the heavy showers yesterday morning the spots of wet caused on the floor by the drip from above followed very frequently the line of the gutters. The present state of the building is seized upon by all who are behindhand in their preparations as an apology for further delay, and native and foreign exhibitors who are not ready by the Ist of May will not be slow to throw all the blame upon the contractors and the Executive Committee. Immense exertions continue to be made in carrying forward the preliminary arrangements, but the nearer we approach the time fixed for opening, the more doubtful, or rather, we may say, impossible, does it seem that all will then bo in order and fit for publicinspection. Great, however, as the intervening difficulties may be, we still regard it as a matter of vital importance to the success of the Exhibition that the Commissioners should keep their plighted word. The first few days of the month of May will probably determine its character, and if during that critical period the preparations are still going forward, and chaos is not reduced to order, what will be thought of our punctuality? The Executive Committee seem determined to do all that in them lies to secure the derircd result, for they have issued a caution to exhibitors not to delay sending in their goods till the 2d of April; by doing so at the last moment they may be disappointed of the means of conveyance. Agricultural and horticultural implements and machines must be deposited in the building by the 29th inst. The select iein for tried will be made by the jury on the Ist of April, and the actual trials will commence on the 2d. The arrivals of packages, both from home and foreign contributors are daily and hourly increasing, and an immense number of hands arc incessantly employed in every part of the building. THE FIRST SHILLING DAY.—To those who anticipated a monster "crush" at the Crystal Palace on Monday, and depicted in their mind's eye scenes of con. gregated myriads battling at every door and inlet for admission long after the interior was crammed full as the Black Hole of Calcutta with dense masses of human beings, the reality must have fallen on them with all the stunning though cooling effects of an unexpected showerbath. It was the first day of the shilling admission to this eighth and crowning wonder of the world; and yet, where thousands were expected, only hundreds came. All the world expected a rush on the first day. Of our own knowledge we can °Large ourselves with the misdemeanour of advising some score of eager country friends to take patience for four-and-twenty hours, until they could go comfortably, with a chance of seeing something more than a huge sea of hats and bonnets, with their respective occupants fainting and exhausted with the beat and pressure of a hundred thousand cosmopolitans, packed into a building, which, capacious as it may be, was never calculated to hold more than fifty thousand, with ease to themselves and safety to the structure and its contents. Many acted on this view of the matter, and stayed away on the first day, the natural consequence being, that the dread ofthe evil proved a most effective preventive. The authorities, however, very ! wisely took every precaution to prevent the dangers which might arise from an over-great throng of visiters. At an early hour barriers were erected at every avenue. and a strong body of police was dispersed among all , the points at which crowding was feared. In addition, arrangements were made for ascertaining the number ,of persons who entered the building, and as soon as 60,000 had obtained admission, notices would have been put up, stating that the building was full, and no more would be admitted. In fact, every arrangement that prudence could dictate was very properly made. The doors were open at ten o'clock, when about 1,000 people presented themselves for entrance, who in a few moments were spread over the building without the slightest rush or inconvenience. The barriers erected at the different entrances being found inconvenient as well as useless, were speedily withdra en as unnecessary, and there was scarcely any perceptible difference from the former days. The stream confirmed to pour in, and as policemen had been stationed at each entrance to count the number of those persons in, it was found at eleven o'clock that 7,022 had entered the building in the first hour; from eleven to twelve 3,980 entered, and in the next half hour the number increased by 1,400, making in all 13,313, who entered the building during the first two hours and a half. During the remainder of the day this number was not materially augmented, and on the whole the:l3 was scarcely half the number of visiters that came on the Saturday, the last day of the five shilling charge.—Morning Advertiser. On Monday, to the astonishment of almost everybody, notwithstanding the fall of price to Is., the interior of the Crystal Palace was not so much crowded as usual. A great crush was anticipate!, and the consequence was that a comparatively small number came. Up to o'clock only 21,258 persons entered the building, and the receipts at the doors fell to 9201. This, with the sale of season-tickets, made a total of 9601., an immense decline from the amount collected on Saturday. The visiters appeared chiefly to belong to the middle class of society, and few fustian jackets were observed among them. It is not now probable that there will bs any very great rush of people to Hyde-park till the Ist of June, when the summer excursion trains begin to run. Three pickpockets were taken on Monday, two women and one man. The women were detected by two Belgian policemen. One stated that she was from Edinburgh, and spoke undoubted broad Scotch. The other i.said she came from Cork, but her accent is not Hibernian. The male thief is a Frenchman, and has been " in trouble" before. He was admirably got up for the occasion, with a new hat and coat, an unexceptionable white waistcoat, and patent leather boots, very smartly made; but a detective with an unfortunately tenacious memory for faces, recognised him as he passed through the entrance, and he was followed, observed actively engaged in the mysteries of his profession. and at once removed from the scene. We may mention—as a hint to those ladies and gentlemen who shrink from a too close contact with the people—the shilling people—that the Dutchess of Sutherland, with Lady Constance Gower, and -Lady Blantyre, passed a portion of the day in quietly con tinuing their inspection. Sixty thousand was the smallest number of visiters anticipated, and placards had been actually prepared announcing the closing of the doors on the admission of that number. Wooden barriers bed been prepared at the various entrances to prevent pressure, and two hundred additional policemen were called into requisition to preserve order. The whole of the road from Piccadilly to the entrance of the Palace was biscated by constables at stated distances, to regulate the vehicular ebb and flow, and mounted patrols rode up and down to see that " the rules of the road" were not infringed on. But, to the surprise of every one, the first shilling day was the most tranquil and orderly since the never.to-be-forgotten Ist of May. Instead of the slowly progressing procession of carriages ten abreast, which blocked up the road on Saturday, the ordinary omnibuses, and a solitary cab now and then, formed the entire of the morning carriage traffic, and the trottoirs exhibited no greater show of pedestrians than might be seen in the same quarter on any ordinary summer's day. At the usual period of opening, there were not more than &thousand persons about the doors. Those who did come, however, seemed highly delighted with their visit. They rushed about from wouder to wonder in a sort of perspiring bewilderment. There were general inquiries amongst the fair visiters for the fountain of golden water, to which so many handsome allusions have been made since the opening; but the purveyors, in despair of administering olfactory satisfaction to relays of 60,000 each, had ungraciously cut off the supply. We were extremely surprised to see a plan adopted,—and, as regarded the galleries, most rigidly and eauselessly enforced,-- which we bad thought had been completely abandoned,—viz., that of compelling the comparatively few visiters to pass in particular directions through the building, thereby converting into a mere spectacle that which was intended for the purpose of study and minute inspection. We trust that the Commissioners•will at once prevent that interference with the free movements of a more humble class of visiters which, except in particular instances, was not adopted towards the higher and more wealthy. The experience of the second shilling day (Tuesday) was such as to prove, in the most convincing manner, that the class of persons for whose benefit and instruction the Great Exhibition was mainly intended, know bow to - avail themselves of the advantages which it affords to them, by studying carefully its varied contents. The example which Her Majesty has set, in common with many members of the nobility, in visiting the Exhibition upon the days devoted to the more humble class of visiters, will be universally appreciated by public feeling, and is calculated to produce the happiest results. Her Majesty, Prince Albert, and the Royal party at the Palace, remained for some time after the is. visiters began to arrive, and Her Majesty, from the corner of the north gallery, looking into the transept, watched with great interest the influx of the crowd. About twelve o'clock the Duke of Wellington arrived, but discovered that he was too late to inspect the works of industry in his accustomed quiet manner. After passing a short way up the centre avenue he returned, and left the building, in which he had remained but ten minutes. During the day we observed the Earl of Glengall. the Earl of Carlisle, Earl Granville, Lord Broughton, Mr. Moffatt, M.P., and other Members of Parliament. One or two of the Bishops were likewise present. The police did not enforce the regulation about passing up and down in a particular direction, except itt one or two narrow and very crowded passages. The number of visiters on Tuesday paying the shilling admission w as cons i derably larger th a n upon the previous day. Although there was no rush or excitement, still there was, from the hour of opening, a steady influx of visiters, until the general appearance of the building approached to that which it presented lest week. The .centre and transept were not so crowded, and the vistters were more distributed and dispersed. The visiters were mostly of the class of those who paid to see the Exhibition, and really meant to see it, and who had no time to lose in useless promenading, but worked hard to do all they could in a day. The character of the multitude was exceedingly respectable. The total amount of money received at the doors was 1.347/. 17s. The produce of the sale of season-tickets was 19/. 19s. The number of visiters paying the shilling adtatssion was therefore about 27,000. The building was half cleared as early as five,—the obvious reason being, that people had come early, and had done a good day's work. Moreover, the price of admission being only a shilling, the pleasure could be renewed at a moderate cost. He said Having had the lionour of acting as President of the Council of Chair- men of the Juries, it falls to me to lay before your Royal Highness and her Majesty's Commissioners the reports of the several juries upon the subjects submitted to them for examination, and the names of the exhibitors whom they have judged entitled to rewards. In doing so, it will be convenient that I should state briefly the principle upon which, by the authority of her Majesty's Commissioners, the juries were constituted. The various subjects included in the Exhibition were divided, in the first instance, into thirty classes. Of these, two were subsequently found to embrace fields of action too large for single juries, and were therefore divided into sub juries. This increased the number of acting juries to thirty-four. Each of those thirty-four juries consisted of an equal number of British subjects and of foreigners. the British jurors were selected by her Majesty's Com- missioners from lists furnished by the Local Committees of various towns, each town being invited to recommend persons of skill and information in the manufactures or produce for which it is remarkable. The foreign jurors were appointed by authorities in their own countries, in such relative proportion amongst themselves as was agreed upon by the foreign com- missioners sent here to represent their respective governments. In the event of a jury finding themselves deficient in technical knowledge of any article submitted to tham, they were empowered to call in the aid of associates. These associates, who acted as advisers only, without a vote, hout whose services were of the greatest value, were selected either from the jurymen of other classes, or from the lists of persons who had been recommended as jurors, but who had not been permanently appointed to any jury. Each jury was superintended by a chairman, chosen from its number by her Majesty's Commissioners, The deputy-chairman and the reporter were elected by the jurors themselves. Such was the constitution ofthe thirty-four juries taken singly. They did not, however, act inde- pendently of each other, inasmuch as they were associated into sic groups, each group consisting of such juries as had to deal with subjects in some degree of kindred nature ; and before any decision of a jury could be con- sidered as final, it was required that it should be brought before the as- sembled group of whicls that jury formed a part, and that it should be ap- proved by them. The chief object of tlis provision was that none of the many foreign nations taking part in the Exhibition should incur the risk of seeing its interests overlooked or neglected, from the accident (an un- avoidable one in many instances) of its being unrepresented in any parti- cular jury. Each group of juries received the assistance of a deputy- comnsissioner and of a special commissioner, appointed by her Majesty's Comissieners to record its proceedings, to furnish information respecting the arrangements of the Exhibition, and otherwise to facilitate the labours of the juries composing the group. It was further determined byher Ma- jesty's Commissioners that the chairmen of the juries, consisting of British subjects and of foreigners in equal numbers, should be formed into a Coun- cil; and that the duties of the Council should be, to determine the condi- tions upon which, in accordance with certain general principles previously laid down by her Majesty's Commissioners, the different prizes should be awarded; to frame rules to guide the working of thejuries; and to secure, as far as possible, uniformity in the result of their proceedings. These are the most important features of the system upon which the jurors found themselves organised. I will now refer briefly to their course of action. The Council of Chairmen, in proceeding to the discharge of their duties, were met at the outset by a serious difficulty. Her Majesty's Commis. sioners had expressed themselves desirous that merit should be rewarded wherever it presented itself, but anxious at the same time to avoid the re- cognition of competition between individual exhibitors. They had also decided that the prizes should consist in three medals, of different sizes; and that these should be awarded, not as first, second, and third in the degree for the same class of subjects and merit, but as marking merit of different kinds and character. The Council of Chairmen found, to their regret, that it would be impossible to lay down any rules for the awarding of the three medals bv which the appearance at least of denoting different degrees of success anongst exhibitors in the same branch of production could be avoided. Accordingly, after fully explaining their difficulty to her Majesty's Commissioners, they requested, as a course by which it might he materially diminished, that one of the nsedals might be withdrawn. Of the remaining two, they suggested that one, the prize medal, should be conferred wherever a certain standard of excellence in production or work- manship had been attained-utility, beauty, cheapness, adaptation to parti- cular markets, and other elements of merit being taken into consideration according to the nature of the object; and they recommended that this medal should be awarded by the juries, subject to confirmation by the groups. In regard to the other and larger medal, they suggested that the conditions of its award should be some important novelty of invention or application, either in material, or processes of manufacture, or originality combined with great beauty of ddsign; but that it should not be conferred for excellence of production or workmanship alone, however eminent; and they further suggested that this medal should be awarded by the Council of Chairmen upon ohs recommendation of a jury, supported bv its group. The principle thus described met the views of her Majesty's Commissioners, and was subsequently further developed by them in a minute which they communicated to thse Coucil of Chairmen. Its application, however, was not without difficulties, especially as regarded the foreign jurors. Many of these had taken part in the national exhibitions of France atd Ger- many; and to them the distinctive character of the two medals, and the avoidance of all recognition of degrees of merit between the recipients of prizes, were novel principles, and at variance with their experience; inas- much as one of the chief purposes of the national exhibitions of the Conti- nent has been to distinguish the various degrees of success attained by rival exhibitors. It was to be expected, therefore, that cases would arise in which the Council medal, as the higher reward, would be asked for exhi- bitors whose claims were only somewhat stronger in degree, without dif- fering in kind from those of others to whom the prize medal had been awarded. In such cases it became the duty of the Council of Chairmen to refuse their sanction to the award of the Council medal; without, how- ever, necessarily impugning the alleged superiority of the article for which it was demanded. On the other hand, some instances have occurred in which they have felt themselves called upon to confirm the claim to a Council medal where the object for which it was claimed showed, in itself, less merit of execution or manufacture than others of its class. It follows, , therefore that the award of a Council medal does not necessarily stamp its recipient as a better manufacturer or producer than others who have received the prize usodal. It is rather a mark of such invention, ingenuity, or origieality as may be expected to exercise an influence upon industry m~r extended, and niece important, than could be produced by more ex- CcllOco of manufacture. This is to be borne in mind in considering the list of awards which I have the honour to lay before your Royal J-ighness; I trust that it will be found that the juries have succeeded in doing justice to the exhibitors of every nation and class, and that they have not departed, in aily important degree, from the purpose of her Majesty's Commission- Crs. One of the first instructions addressed to the juries by the Council of Chairmen was to the effect that the prizes should be awarded without re- feresce to the country of the exhibitors, the Exhibition being considered in tlis res~ect as recognising no distinction of nations. It is gratifying to add that the jurors of every country cordially acquiesced in this principle, and that notwithstanding unavoidable differences of opiniein, uninterrupted harinony prevailed amongst them throughout the whole course of their hours. Viscount Canning having resumed his seat, Prince Albert rose, and after the cheering which greeted him had subsided into silence, delivered the following address: MY LORD,-Tbe Royal Commissioners are much indebted to your lord- ship, and to the distinguished gentlemen of this and other nations, who have acted on the juries entrusted with the award of the prizes in the recent Exhibition, for the zeal with which they have undertaken, and the ability with which they have fulfilled, the task which has been allotted to them. The Commissioners are sensible that the services of these gentlemen have in many instances been rendered at great inconvenience to them- selves, and at the sacrifice of very valuable time, and of important avoca- tions. It is with pride and pleasure that they have noticed in the lists of those who have performed this service to tie Exhibition the names of men of every nation, of the most exalted rank, and of the most eminent repu- tations in statesmanship, in science, in literature, in manufactures, in com- merce, and in the fine arts; of men in every respect well calculated not only to form a correct technical judgment upon the merits of the articles submitted to their inspection, but also to maintain the high character which the Commissioners have uniformly striven to impart to the Exhibi- tion. In no department of the vast undertaking which has just been brought to a happy close were greater difficulties to have been apprehended than in that in which your lordship end your eminenteolleagues have given your assistance. On this, the first occasion on which the productions of the different nations of the globe have ever been brought together for the purpose of comparing their severaljmerits, not only were prejudices and jealousies to have been expected to interfere with the decisions, but the nature of the case presented many difficulties of a formidable character to the formation of a judgment which should appear satisfactory to ll. The names of the jurors, indeed, when once made known, were of them- selves a sufficient guarantee for that impartiality which was essential to the fulfilment of their task; and, from all that has come to the knowledge of the Royal Commissioners during the progress of their labours, they are fully satisfied that every award has been made with the most careful consideration, after the most <ample and laborious investigation, and upon grounds most strictly honourable, just, and candid. But although the high character of the jurors would have fully justified the Commissioners in entrusting them with the award of the prizes without fettering their discretion with any instructions what- ever, had nothing more than an impartial decision been required, there were difficulties of a very peculiar nature inherent to the task, which seemed to render necessary the adoption of some regulations that might, at first sight, appear to have been someiwhat arbitrary in their character. The differences in the wants of various nations having necessarily impres- sed their several manufactures with different characteristics, it would seem to be almost impossible for those who have been in the habit of judging the productions of their own country by one standard, to enter fully into merits which can only be properly appreciated by another standard, since the very points which in the one case appear to be excellencies, may in the other, not unnaturally, be taken as defects. This consideration, and a knowledge of the evils which were to be apprehended from any acci. dentally erroneous decision, in a matter so intimately connected with the commercial interests of every nation, induced the Royal Commissioners to lay doan, for the guidance of the juries, those principles to which your lordship has referred. It would perhaps have been more interesting to the public had the Commissioners instructed the juries to follow the prac- tice which has usually prevailed in the exhibitions of individual nations, and to grant medals of different degrees, to mark the gradations of excel- lence among the exhibitors; but they feel that they have adopted the safer course, and that which was upon the whole most in accordance with the feelings of the majority of the exhibitors, in directing that no distinc- tion should be made between their merits if their productions came up to the standard requisite to entitle them to a prize, but that all should without exception take the same rank and receive the same medal. The Commissioners, however, considered it right to place at the disposal of the Council of Chairmen a peculiar or " Council " medal in the cases to which your lordship has referred. Important discoveries in many branches of science and of manufactures have in this Exhibition been brought under the notice of the public; and it seems just that those who have rendered services of this kind to the world, should receive a special mark of acknowledgement on ain occasion which has rendered so conspicu- ous the advantages which the many have derived from the discoveries of the few. The grant of the Council medal for beauty of design, and for excellence in the fine arts, as applied to manufactures, though made upon a somewhat different principle, is also compatible with the views of the Commissioners, sinse in the cases in which it has been given it does not mark any greater comparative excellence of manufacture, or assign to one producer a higher place than is accorded to others, but is to be regarded as a testimony to the genius which can clothe the articles required for the use of daily life with beauty, that can please cite eye, and instruct and elevate the mind. Valuable as this Exhibition has proved in many respects, it appears to the Commissioners that there is no direction in which its effects will be more sensibly and immediately perceived than in the improvement which it may be expected to produce in taste, and the impulse it has given to the arts of design; and a special acknowledge- ment is justly due to those who have afforded the best examples of art, whether pure or applied, and led the way in this interesting career of im- provement.
