STATISTICS OF THE ExHIBrcoeN.-In looking back over the career of the vast enterprise which has thus auspiciously been terminated, the consideration which first and most strongly impresses itself on the mind is the unprecedented popularity which it has attracted. Of this we quote some striking facts as illustrations. In the month of May 734,782 visits were paid to the building; in June, 1,133,116; in July, 1,314,176; in August, 1,023,435; in September, 1,155,240; and in the first 11 days of October, 841,107. These figures give a total of 6.201,856 as the sum of visits to the Exhibition. Every one will calculate according to his particular fancy the proportion between visits and visitors, but at least it is obvious that several millions of people have spent a portion of their time in the Crystal Palace. The greatest number of people ascertained to have been in the building at any one time was at two o'clock on Tuesday week, when 92,000 persons were present. On the same day the number of visitors reached its maximuzm, and was 109,915. Between eleven and twelve o'clock on Monday week 28,853 persons entered the building in one hour. When it is remembered that these extraordinary figures, which can be thoroughly relied on for accuracy, illustrate popular move- ments that only a few years ago would have been pronounced on the highest authority most dangerous to the safety of the State, we have the more reason to wonder that they should have taken place not only without disorder, but also almost without crime. The total number of charges made at the police-station at the Prince of Wales' Gate relating to offences within the building is twenty-five, of which nine were for picking pockets, six for attempts to do so, and ten for petty larcenies at stalls. GREAT EXHIBITION. On entering the building on Monday, it was satisfactory to find that the daily complaints of the public and the Press on the subject of ventilation had not been left wholly unattended to. The whole of the glass in the east and west galleries has been removed, and such light airs as generally blow in that direction have free ingress and egress. A similar change is contemplated with respect to the north and south transepts, and that once effected, the rest must be left to the pitying breezes. What has been done has made the place much cooler, and there is little doubt but that the completion of the alterations will make the temperature all that could be expected in the middle of one of the hottest summers we have had for some years. Among the crowds of country folk who availed themselves of cheap trains to obtain a peep at the wonders of the Crystal Palace was a detachment of 130 workmen from the extensive lime works near Rochester, all in holiday trim, and decorated with blue rosettes in their button-holes. These poor men were retiring after about two hours' bewildered gazing in every direction, when, being met by a person more intimate with the contents of the building, and asked what they had seen, it came out that they had really seen but few of the sights of the place. Some of them having wandered recklessly from the main body once or twice, had nearly lost their way, and this so alarmed the rest, that they prudently resolved to keep to the nave while they remained, and to get out of danger as soon as possible. However, being provided with a volunteer guide, a large number gladly returned to view the treasures of the precious metals' gallery and other objects of interest. Such incidents as these are by no means of unfrequent occurrence, and they show that in the case of large parties of unsophisticated country people a leader of some acquaintance with the place would be absolutely necessary to enable them even partially to enjoy their treat.. The jurors were actively employed all day examining and deliberating, and exhibitors were equally busy making speculations, sanguine in proportion to the number of times they had been visited. THE GREAT EXHIBITION Saturday at the Crystal l'alucc preserves its select and exclusive character, although its five shilling admission fee has now become matter of history. The company on Saturday last were rather thinly scattered through the building, but the gaydresses and, generally speaking, superior appearance of the various groups made up a more pleasing although perhaps not so imposing a picture, as the surging multitudes on the shilling days. Such of the aristocracy as remain in town at this season of moors and watering places, continue to use their season tickets. The Duke of Devonshire was among the visitors on Saturday, as were also the Duke and Duchess of Norfolk accompanied by one of the Ladies Howard, and Prince Callimachi, the son of the Turkish Ambassador in France. A pleasing result of the comparatively thin attendance, was observable in the facility with which numerous invalids were wheeled about in their Bath chairs, stopping before every object of interest, and thus whiling away the pangs of illness by a participation in the enjoyments of the healthy. The public are also led away by an impression that by the de c:siou of the House of Commons, the building must in any case remain intact, until the first of May next. But they should be made aware that its duration until that time is only permissive, and that the commissioners are by no means prevented, should they think tit, taking it down in October. It is high time therefore that individuals in whom the people have faith, men uninfluenced by sordid views, by the whims of mushroom exclusions, or the crotchets of red tape precisions, should takethe matter manfully in band, collect into a focus that mass of public opinion, which undoubtedly permeates society in favour of the retention of the palais Paxton, and treat its distructivcs to such a demonstration as would put an eetinguisher once and for ever on their Vandalic intentions. The Swedish department was in full glory on Saturday. The red curtain had disappeared, the lately arrived articles might be seen tastefully arranged, and three or four polite and intelligent Scandanavians were in attendance to afford explanations to the company. Among the new goods is a chariot which certainly need not put Long-acre iu a fright from the beauty of its form or the costliness of its decorations, but which claims a novelty in principle in tho construction of its forewheels, enabling them to be turned to any extent without running under the body of the carriage, The machinery by which this result is obtained is rather complicated, but one great advantage is, that by the arrangement, the four wheels are permitted to be of equal size, to the great advantage of the draught, and cousequent ease of the horses. The springs, also, are novel in form, being spiral, and although by no means elegant in appearance, are said to be much easier and stronger than than previously in use. The learned in such matters may find it worth while to visit this department, and judge for thew selves. There are also in this section various models cannon, ornamented sword-blades, and other destrnetteu weapons, made from the famous Swedish iron, Rai indicating that the warlike propensities of ChUill Illottze are not yet quite extinct among his trymen. More homely, but intrinsically far valuable, there is a case of stearine candles, tiful in colour and quality, and which, by a I newly invented process, are made at a greatly reduced price. The inventor hu also found a use for the residuum of the composition of which they are made, and which has hitherto been thrown away. By hardening it he produces • material very much resembling alabaster, and admirably adapted for casts of medallions, &c. This material is worth examination, as it may possibly afford an additional aid to the manufacture of Varian. Some specimens of textiles and a few toys complete the collection. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. ADMISSION ON Hne FIRST OF MAY.-Her Majesty having signified her royal pleasure that arrangements should be made to enable her Majesty to gratify a wish very generally expressed on the part of the public to be present at a ceremony by which her Majesty should open the Exhibition of the Works of Industry of all Nations on the 1st of May, her Majesty's commissioners hereby give notice that the pro- gramme of this ceremony, and the regulations under which the holders of season tickets will be admitted, are as follows:-Exhibitors' at- tendants, who have been sanctioned by the Executive Committee, will be admitted between the hours of eight and nine o'clock, at doors specified on their cards, and will immediately take their places by the counters or objects exhibited by their employers. Holders of season tickets will be admitted at all doors on the east, south, and west of the building, between the hours of nine and half-past eleven o'clock, and will be allowed to take their places, subject to police regulations, in the lower part of the building, and in the galleries, except the parts railed off in the nave and transept. A platform will be raised to the north of the centre of the transept, on which a chair of state will be placed. Her Majesty's commissioners will assemble at half- past eleven o'clock, in the transept, opposite the platform, together with their Executive Committee and the Foreign Acting Commission- ers, in full dress. or in plain evening dress. His Grace the Areb- bishop of Canterbury, her Majesty's ministers, the great officers of state, and the foreign ambassadors and ministers will take their places on the platform, to the right and left of the chair of state, in full dress also, at half-past eleven o'clock. Her Majesty proceeding in state, with the royal family, foreign guests, &c., and her and their suites from Buckingham Palace, up Constitution hill and down, Rotten row, will enter the Exhibition Building by the north entrance precisely at twelve o'clock. She will ascend the platform and take her seat in the chair of state. On her Majesty's arrival a choir will sing ' God save the Queen." On the Queen taking her seat, his Royal HIighness Prince Albert will join the royal commissioners, and when the music has ceased, proceed at their head to the platform, and read to her Majesty a short report of the proceedings of the commission up to that time, which he will then deliver to her Majesty, together with the catalogue of the articles exhibited. Her Majesty will return a gracious answer, handed to her by the Secretary of State, after which his Royal Highness Prince Albert will take his place again by the side of her Majesty. The doyen of the corps diplomatique will read an address to her Majesty on behalf of the foreign nations who have contributed to the Exhibition, to which her Majesty will likewise return a gracious answer. His Grace the Archbishop of Canterbury will then say a prayer, invoking God's blessing upon the undertaking, followed by a short anthem sung by the choir. A royal procession will then be formed, preceded by the commissioners, which will turn to the right, move to the west end of the nave by its north side, return to the east end of the nave by its south side, including the south end of the transept, and come back to the centre along the north side of the nave ; thus enabling all those present, who will be expected to keep the places which have been assigned to them, to see her Majesty and the procession. During the procession, the organs appointedwill play marches, taking the music up at the Queen's approach. On her Majesty's return to the platform, the Queen will declare ' The Exhi- bition Opened !" which will be announced to the public by a flourish of trumpets, and the firing of a royal salute on the north of the Ser- pentine; whereupon the barriers, which had kept the nave clear, will be thrown open, and the public will be allowed to circulate. Her Majesty will then return to Buckingham Palaceby the route by which she came. All the doors, which will have been closed at half-past eleven o'clock, will, upon her Majesty's departure, be opened again. -By order of her Majesty's Commniesioners, EDGAR A. BowRING, Acting Secretary. Exhibition Building, Hyde park, 22nd April. 1851. In accordance with the powers vested in the Royal Commission, the price of the season-tickets was raised on Thursday to four guineas for a gentleman's and three guineas for a lady's ticket ; and such is the present rapid demand for the tickets that we apprehend, in the course of a day or two, a further increase in price will take place, for the purpose of limiting their sale. The progress made during the last few days in the completion of the arrangements of the Exhibi- tion have been such as to render it impossible in any single notice to convey to the reader any adequate idea of its extent. In whatever direction the eye turns, some newly-developed production of industry or something illustrative of the wealth of nations meets the gaze. The French department presented on Thursday a most extraordinary and exciting scene. Upwards of a thousand of the exhibitors of that country were present, for the purpose of unpacking and ar- ranging their goods. Though much remains to be done, there is no doubt that on the 1st of May the exposition of French industry will be one of the most perfect and complete in the Exhibition. From Rome several very fine groups of statuary have been unpacked, in- cluding, among others, " Rinaldo and Clorinda," by Rinaldi of Rome; Cupid and Psyche," " Fidelity," and " Gratitude;" two statues of "Nymphs," by the late R. T. Wyatt; and a statue by L. Macdonald. A sculpture court in the Austrian department, devoted to articles chiefly of Italian sculpture, is now exceedingly interesting. The Zollverein may be said to have almost completed the whole of its ar- rangemnents and fittings, and its various courts promise to be exceed- ingly interesting and attractive, from the great variety and value of the articles exhibited. An exceedingly rich display of gold and silver church plate was on Thursday added to the articles from the Zollverein. Holland has made a gorgeous display of carpets and candelabra; and a stomacher of brilliants, in the centre of which is a medallion of her Majesty, is of great beauty and value. Russia shovs some very fine specimens of inleidwood. Two porcelain vases, sent from the Imperial China Manufactory at St Petersburg, will, from the extreme richness of their colouring and the beauty of the designs, prove exceedingly attractive;, there are several exquisite paintings on china from the same manufactory, one of which, copied from Bergher, is a perfect gem. There are also two large jasper vases, ;otlargeia~ize and immense value, the polishing of which was effected ticles of malachite furniture. a ve~yieg~ siebord, ormd frm te tulip wood, has been sent, by eomm~4 hs Imeria Majsty.The United States make a very interesting and business-like show in the galleries, of calicoes, sheet- iDg. and printed fabrics, from the St Lawrence, and other manufac- tories in Massachusetts. On the British side the machinery is all in a remarkable state of forwardness, and awaits but the order to turn on the steam, to start at once into life and activity. One of the most ingeniously constructed machines, and one which, at the present mo- ment, is occupying a considerable degree of attention in the hosiery and woollen districts, is the circular loom of the Chevalier Claussen, which has been fixed in its place; a child may with ease make with it twenty pairs of stockings in a day. Any pattern may be intro- duced into the fabric, by an arrangement of the most simple nature, and one which supersedes to a great extent the use of the Jacquard loom. This small machine is the only machine worked by hand which is capable of producing a larger quantity of goods than any other single loom worked by steam.power. The number of " picks " which it can make per minute, when worked at ordinary speed, is not less than 700. In the weaving department, Messrs Kenworthy and Bulloughs, of Blackburn, also exhibit a very fine collection of their patent power-looms. The cotton machinery of Messrs Platt and Co. is probably unrivalled in the world. They have, we believe, expended upwards of 5,0001. in the getting up of the collection of cotton ma- chinery. The manufacturing tools and engines of Messrs Whitworth and Co., of Manchester, are of the highest possible character. Taken as a whole, we apprehend there is no country in the world which could produce such a room of machinery. In the department of locomotives and railway carriages, prominent above all other articles is the ?? Liverpool," upon Crampton's patent, sent in by the London and North-Western Company, the most powerful narrow-gauge engine ever constructed. There are a number of others-" Ariel's Girdle," a small four-wheel engine; " Little England," a small engine and tender joined together, upon six wheels; and a large one, sent lin by Stephenson, having twvo large driving wheels behind, and six smaller ones in the front of the engine. A considerable number of railway carriages, first, second, and third class, have been sent in, among which is a beautiful first-class carriage, formed of polished teak bodies, and made by Mr Williams, for the Great Northern Railway. Leaving the courts devoted to machinery, and entering, it will be found that in almost every department of manufacture British in- dustry will be well represented. Considerable advance has of late years been made in our glass and porcelain manufactures, and it is gratifying to know that the manufacturers of this particular descrip- tion of goods have exerted themselves in earnest to support the credit of the country. The principal exhibitors for Worcester are Messrs Chamberlain and Kerr, the specimens exhibited by whom are fully equal, if not superior, to any ever yet produced at the Worcester fac- tories. The most handsome and artistic are the sets of honeycomb china-a tea-table service with tray---and a communion service, the latter bearing beautiful paintings of scriptural subjects. A tea ser- vice of egg-shell china, recently ordered by Madame Celeste, will also form part of the display. Vases of various elegant kinds, and pictures in medallions, fruit and cake baskets, candelabra, Ac., will be shown by this firm. Messrs Grainger have concentrated their strength, almost exclusively, upon specimens of semi-porcelain- though they also send a few highly-finished articles in china. The semi-porcelain, from its superior strength and comparative cheapness, is likely to be generally used instead of the china, which it resembles in almost every respect, except its transparency. Amongst Messrs Grainger's contributions to the Exhibition are a ewer and basin of very elegant design; a d&jeuner service and tray of egg-sbape design, imitation honeycomb, traced in turquoise, with leaves and ears of wheat. The most remarkable part of Messrs Graingers exhibition, however, is a small model of a remarkable font at Brook, Norwich. THE GREAT EXHIBITION We give to-day a further notice of the articles exhibited in the chiss devoted to Furniture, Deco- rations, &o.-the specimells more particularly se- lected for remark being Parqueterie, Alarqueterie, and Buhl-work. FURNITURE, DECORATIONS, &-c.-No. VII.* | PAaQUET'ERIIE, MAUQULETEHI, BUHL WORK, &Cc. Although Furniture which may be considered as having a purely decorative character has already received some notice at our hands, we feel that Nwe ought not to dismiss this class of productions without devoting some attention to that particular branch of industry represented by Parqueterie, M arqueterie, and Buhi-work. In order that the reader may be enabled to distinguish between these different specimens of mechanical and artistic skill, we will state, as briefly as possible, the mode of production and the distinguishing features of each of these classes of objects. As on previous occa- sions, when attempting to convey an idea of mauu- facturing processes, we shall avoid all detail that is not absolutely necessary to our purpose, and all technicalities that would perplez the general reader. Parqneterie consists of ornamental forms, produced by combining, or inlaying, two or more different- coloured woods. The simplest illustration we can give is this-if we take two pieces of paper, one white and the other black, and lay the one upon the other, and on the upper piece outline a tulip and stem or other object-aud if then we apply a knife, and cut through the two pieces of paper, it is mani- fest we should obtain two tulips in outline, the one being black and the other white ; and if we then secure the black tulip iu the white paper, and the white tulip in the black paper, we have an exact representation of the process of the manufacture of Parqueterie. If we suppose the black paper to represent ebony, and the white paper holly, and, instead of the knife, a small saw made of watch spring, we have a perfect knowledge of all that is required for the production of Parqueterie. All that would then be necessary to make our tulip in Marqueterie is, that we should adopt other woods representing the natural colours of the flower, and shadow it, where shadow is required, with heated sand. Buhl-work consists in the production of ornamental forms by the same process in brass and tortoiseshell; but in the highest class of decorative furniture marqueterie is combined with buhl, by which means the general effect is much heightened, the artist's intention more fully developed, and much beauty given to the whole, by the introduction of ivory, pearl, tortoiseshell, and even precious stones. We have to regret that, in this class of objects, the most talented of our own countrymen are absent. To those who are familiar with this class of manu- facture, it is well known that there are works in the possession of some of the wealthier classes, which wouldjustify us in stating that we have amongst us those whose productions surpass anything that the public generally have any conception of, and which are as surprising for the correct taste, delicacy, and originality shown in design as for the fine and artistic feeling evidenced in the execution. We have felt it due to our countrymen to state thus much, because the workers in the highest class of marqueterie are few in number, and we lament that full justice should not be done to their high merits. Russia, Austria, and Belgium are the largest contributors of parqueterie, as applied to the deco- rating of flooring, for which purpose it is admirably adapted-stained woods not being required, and woods in their natural state being best suited for the covering of floors. A cursory examination is sufficient to assure us that this class of manufac- ture has received much attention, and is well understood in those countries. We have already mentioned the really beautiful, well- drawn, and harmoniously arranged specimens shown by Messrs. Leistler and Son, on the floors of the Austrian rooms, on the north walls adjoining these rooms, and, as applied to the purposes of the cabinetmaker, on the table in the library, where the well-arranged geometric forms are brought out with much skill, showing a judicious and effective arrangement of figures nicely adapted for the pur- poses of parqueterie ornament. Thevarious specimens shown in ?? Court, we observe, are by M. Miller, of St. Petersburg. Some of these are of well designed pattern, good in effect, and unexceptionable inexecutiou, showing that the manufacture is there well understood and is in a high state of perfection. We were much struck with one of the specimens exhibited, in which oak of the same colour as that which constitutes the ground-if so we may denominate it-of the pattern, is used for the pattern itself, producing a peculiar and damask-like effect, analogous to the appearance presented by the patterns produced in the loom on diaper damasks and table cloths. The drawing, however, of the pattern we have just mentioned is one of the least meritorious of the different speci- mens exhibited ; but each and all will rauk amongst the best specimens of parqueterie flooring, and must give a permanent celebrity to the manufactures'. In Belgium we have several fine specimens of parqueterie. Messrs. Couvert and Lucas, of Brus- sels (No. 404), are exhibitors of loors of this manu- facture, the general designs adopted being arrauge- ments of geometric forms-of which the example in the nave, with a well-drawn outer border of fret ornament is, perhaps, the finest. In this the woods combined to form the outlines and give effect to the pattern, are oak, rose- wood, satin-wood, and iron-wood, and the gene- ralappearance is harmonious and pleasing. The same firm are also the exhibitors of a loo-table-the top being parqueterie, combining satin-wood, rose- wood, and mahogany, in forms that are nicely arranged and balanced; and the stand of this table is highly enriched with much excellently-designed buhl ornament. The stand, however, is manifestly out of keeping with the top, and can never have been intended to accompany it, the ornaments being not only different in kind, bat evidently de- signed by a different hand. The Messrs. De Keyn Brothers (No. 406), are also exhibitors, in Belgium, of parqueterie flooring, and present us, in the nave, with what is pro. bably their finest example. This is one of those un- exceptionable compositions so admirably adapted for parqueterie ornament, and is of a highly classic character, with a mixture of complex geometric forms and guilloche ornament, well drawn and nicely balanced in the general design. The woods used are oak, satin-wood, mahogany, and rosewood, and the effect as a whole is light and elegant. Sardinia contributes somewhwat largely of deco- rative furniture of this class. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. A meeting of local contributors to the forthcoming Exhibition of the Works of Industry of all Nations was held on luesdav, at one o'clock, in the Council Chamber—the Lord Provost in the chair. The attendance was large. Mr. Johnson, the secretary, read a report by the deputation appointed at last meeting to proceed to London to make arrangements for the reception of articles intended for exhibition. With regard to extension of time, the deputation reported that all light articles—such as those which could be fixed in their places without much trouble—would be received up till the Ist of April next, or perhaps later; while all heavy articles— Inch as machinery in motion, the erection of which would occupy considerable time—must be forwarded to London before the 28th of February. The deputation recommended that the exhibitors of Lanarkshire should be divided Into classes, according to the kind of articles which each intended to exhibit; that a convener should be appointed In each class, and that sectional meetings should be held as soon as possible with the view of coming to a final decision as to the occupation, fitting up, and general arrangement of the space &Holed to Glasgow. Councillor Murray said they were much obliged to the deput . ition, who had spent six days in London endeavouring to make the best arrangement they could for the exhibitors of Lanarkshire. He was glad to bear that they bad secured a good position near Manchester and London; and all , they now required to do was to meet in different sections, and make arrangenients for the fitting up of the space which had been allocated to them. They must all feel highly pleased that the deputation had procured an extension of time for the reception of light goods; but, at the same time, the Executive Committe in London were anxious that the articits intended for exhibition should be for warded 110011 as possible. After a short convers ttion, in which the Lord Provost, Sir James Campbell, and others took part, the recommendation in the report was agreed to, and the Secretary was instructed to call a meeting of each class of exhibitors on an early day. This concluded the business of the general meeting; but in accordance with the foregoing resolution, a meeting of the exhibitors of cotton goods was held immediately afterwards, when the necessary arrangementa were completed.

'THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Saturday at the Crystal Palace preserves its select and exclusive charactei, although its five shilling admission fee has now become matter of history. There were young girls, struck down by premature disease, valetudinarians t who dared not face the slightest breath of the external at- e mosphere, and old men tottering on the very verge of human E ?? to compress 9 within an hour's promenade, the inspection of more objects I of interest than they had probably ever seen in the course I of their whole previous existence. THE-GREAT EXHIBITION. I'e give to-day a notice of the more important of the articles exhibited in Classes 1. and XXVII, adapted for Building purposes. BUILDING MATERIALS.* There are few sections of the Exhibition which are of more practical importance than that includ- 'D the specimens of natural or artificial materials which may be employed with advantage in the con- struction of buildings. The geological character of 3,y district must of necessity regulate to a great ex- tent the kind of material which is employed by its architects. The clay of the London basin may be re- garded as determining the brick character of this me- tropolis, in the same way as the granitic rock upon which Aberdeen and Peterhead are built has de- termined the use of this most durable of stones in those localities, or as the old and new red sand- stones of ?? lead to the peculiar charac- ter of the buildings in the midland counties. At the same time, though the stones which are raised il the neighbourhood will always be em- ployed when they are of a nature to admit of their use, it must often happen that the necessities of the inhabitants demand the use of materials which have to be brought from some considerable distance. For the bridges which span the Thames, the granite hills of Scotland, Devonshire, and Corn- wall have been laid under heavy contributions- the slate formations of Wales form a considerable portion of the metropolitan pavement; while forthe Houses of Parliament we have gone to the quarries of Yorkshire and Dorsetshire, and even to those of Caen in Normandy, and we are now macadamising our roads with porphyries which are brought from the far extremities of the island. A rather striking instance of the way in which the productions of one county are demanded by another is to be seen in the breakwater of Ply- mouth. A well-executed model of this great sea- wall is to be inspected in the main avenue, exe- cated in the material of which the original is con- stracted-the Oreston limestone. We cannot avoid incidentally remarking, in reference to this model, that there is a very unfortunate exaggeration in the relative levels of the sea within and without the breakwater; and it should be stated that the light- house, which is here most beautifully modelled in the same limestone, is in reality constructed of granite. The point, however, to which we have referred is the curious one that, between the points of high and low water, the limestone was being rapidly destroyed by the operations of marine ani- mals-certain species of torredos-which perforated the limesto e in every direction. Small as the operatitois of a little shell-fish may appear to be, certain it is that the destruction of the breakwater was threatened by it, and the remedy has been adopted of laying down granite over all those parts which were exposed to the action of the destructive ag-ents. The granites of the kingdom may be regarded as very fairly represented. The local comnmittees of Turo, and Falmouth, and Penryn have supplied specimells from most of the celebrated Cornish loca- lities: and the collection of the Messrs. Freeman ?? not only those granites of Cornwall and Devon which are brought into the London market, but those of Aberdeen and Peterhead, the Dalkey or V uleary granite from the county of Dublin, and specimens from other parts of Ireland, together with the Guernsey and Herm granites. The porphyries of Cornwall are also shown in the collection of building stones from the Truro and Falmouth committees, collected by Mr. Rorld, of Trebartha HIall, Mr. Whitley, and Mr. Hicks. Alany of these will be found upon inspection to be of a very beautiful character. The late Mr. Treffry, of Place, near Fowey, was one of the first to show the ornamental character of these stones ; and to the many beautiful specimens employed in the decoration of that gentleman's house, is chiefly due their introduction to the attention of his Royal Highness Prince Albert, and their use in Osborne. The ornamental character of the Cornish porphyries is best shown in the finished works of Mr. Pearse, exhibited in Class 27 ; and the slabs of black, red, and green porphyry, with the inlaid slab from Withiel, exhibited by Mr. Mere- dith, display several varieties. The collection of building stones from the Isle of Man, brought together by the exertions of the Rev. J. G. Cumming, and exhibited in his name, are of great importance. These consist of the Pogido- jija ,Sc/djst-black flagstone, from Poolvash, which is a most durable material, and which has been worked and exported from Castleton for near 200 years. Thesequarries furnished the stone steps of St. Paul's Cathedtal, which were a present from Bishop Thomas Wilson. Several kinds of marble are fur- nished froom the Isle of Mlan, consisting of the en- cirnitical limestone, and varieties of the carboni- ferous limestone. Flag-stones, the clay schist, and the old red sandstone front Peel, are exhibited ; and wve also find in the collection granites which are ex- ported from Douglas, Peel, and Castleton, and an exceedingly hard porphyritic greenstonefrorn Lang- ness. The Marquis of Breadalbane contributes granites and porphyries from Perthshire and Argyleshire. Granite from the Craignair Quarry, near Dalbeattie, Kirkcudbright, is sent by Mr. Maxwell; and Mr. Sirn is an exhibitor of granites from Loch Etive,- Mull, Inverary, and Bonan. We should occupy too large a space did we parti- cularize each variety of buildingf stone which is to be found in Class T. ; and any minute detail would necessarily prove"tiiinteresting, unless we could ex- tejid our description over a much wider field than is practicable. Every part of our island appears to have contributed something: \sandstone, inagne- sian limestone, carboniferous limestone, oolitic limestone, ashlar blocks for paving, freestone for building furnaces for glass houses, and a great va- riety of slates are exhibited. The several uses to which slate has been applied I are admirably illustrated by Mr. T. Stirling, jun. In his slate cabinet are to be found nearly all the varieties of slates produced in our islands. These are shown in the rough and manufactured state; and in connection with these, the very fine slabs from different localities which have been laid down at the entrances to the Exhibition building must be referred to as examples of this class of pro- ductions.t Turning our attention to the illustrations in I Class 27, we find the Devonshire marbles well dis- played in the madrepore marble columns in the west main avenue, exhibited by Mr. Champenowne, together with the other specimens exhibited by thurt gentleman, and also by Mr. J. Bovey among the mineral manufactures. These marbles are equally adapted for ordinary building purposes and for decorations. The Derbyshire, Irish, and other marbles, and the several varieties of granite, por- phyry, and serpentine, have been already referred to for their ornamental character. We have often regretted that, in the arrangement E of the building, the manufactured articles of Class 27 had not been immediately associated with the raw materials in Class I ; since then the study of this admiruble collection of our useful and orna- mental stones would have been far more easy than at present, and we believe more useful. A considerable variety of bricks is exhibited in Class 27. As a building material, burnt clay is more extensively employed throughout England than any other. In London the clay from which 'the bricks are made is usually that which is dug for the founda- tions of the houses built with them. This clay is obtained from the alluvial deposits which lie above * Forner notir upon the Min adapted for Building Purposes BPpae on te2fth of Myand 29th ot sept. the London clay. A cross section of the deposit shows three layers differing considerably in conipo- sition. The lowest consists of clay mixed with gravel and fragments of chalk ; the next, which is called malm, is mixed with mu ch sand, and finer particles of chalk; in the upper layer, the pure argillaceous matter preponderates-it contains but very little sand or gravel, and scarcely a trace of lime. This is formed into bricks by being worked up with the ashes, finely sifted, which are col- lected from the houses, and with sand. The middle Stratum requires no sand, and but a very small pro- portion of ashes. The first property of good bricks is, that they are sufficiently coherent to support the height of the wall which is to be piled upon them ; they must, therefore, resist a very consider- able crushing force, and they must not be liable to breakage in carriage. To withstand pressure the bricks must be perfectly flat, and not pre- sent any hollows; a straight and smooth surface is essential ; great weight is objectionable lightness combined with strength is important. Bricks must be capable of being dressed-they must be of such uniform structure as not to fall to pieces under the trowel. It is also important that the chemical composition of the brick should be attended to. If the clay contains organic matter, its -de- struction in the process of burning leaves hollows in the clay. If it is combined with chalk, this is in burning converted into quick lime; and if the brick is exposed to wet, the lime is slacked, and the brick rent to pieces in consequence. Iron pyrites, in the process of burning, is decomposed, and hollows are left ian the bricks made of clay which contains this compound (sulphuret of iron). In the manufacture of bricks there are many points of importance to be attended to; and although the process appears a very simple one, there are several manipulatory details, without attention to which a good building brick cannot be obtained. The RECOIL BBEARKWATER.-In the nave, close to the great model of the Liverpool Docks, stand a series of models and pictures representing the action of the recoil breakwater of Mr. William Henry Smith. The peculiarities of this in- vemieln deserve, and have met with, considerable attention from the scientific visitors to the Exhibition. Stone harbours, as is well known, take many years to execute; witness Plymouth, Cherbourg, and Kingstown, not yet finished. Moreover, they are liable to, and constantly suffer from the destructive effects of the sea, both during and after their construction They are always subject to silting or filling up, and to the engendering of bars and shoals. Howth, for instance, is completely destroyed; so are the old Cinque Ports. The ancient harbour of Claudius is now three miles inland. It is therefore clear that stone harboars are tedious and imperfect. They cost vast sums to execute and maintain, and in some cases, where most needed, they cannot; in their present condition, be made use of at all. Mr. Smith proposes to supply their deficiencies. For the explanation of his breakwater, there must be supposed the end view of a double triangular open framing, of solid timber. Of this the point goes down to the bed of the-sea, there to be secured by a link to the screw-pile, which can never be moved. Thus it is free to oscillate with the waves, as the top rises above the water. Attached to the top, at each side, are braces, which, running direct to the bed of the sea, are there weighted, and thence proceed outwards about an equal distance, there again to be secured by screw-piles. Thus the wave strikes the section and lifts the weights in a storm ; the section thus lifted drifts, and the wave becomes entangled as it were in the meshes of the framework, by which it is completely and speedily dispersed. Then, when-the-de- structive force of this rush of water is overcome, tbe recoil begins to act-thiesection is at oncebroughtback toits original position before the advent of the next wave-and this goes on, time after time, throughout the duration, of the storm. The wear of such a process is not excessive; the ex- pense of the breakwater is comparatively trifling ; anid the advantage is that small harbdurs could be formed around the coast in situations where they would be accessible at low as Iwell as at high water. Lighthouses, too, erected on this principle, nmay,~ like the breakwater, be laid down. in any depth of water ; and, to illustrate thle plan and its utility, Mr. Smith exhibits a large picture, representing a harbour near the Goodwin Sands-not on them, as has been proposed, as if to lure vessels to their destruction-but so approximating whilst. in deep water as to give warning of danger, without drawing the passing ships into too precarious a position. man Roe, of the Strand, shows a piece of -new pavement for nent way exhibited in the machinery department, Air. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. (From The Tines.) We have noticed at different times the dissatisfaction which has been expressed by the representatives of some foreign countries with reference to the amount of space allotted to their exhibitors. Except in the case of France, these differ- ences had almost entirely disappeared ; but the Commissioner of our continental neighbours continued still to struggle for increased accommodation. Happily the Executive Committee have been able to settle in an agreeable and friendly mamner their differences with this gentleman, who will now direct all his energy to the preparation and arrangement of the large area which his countrymen possessin the building. It appears that from two causes 12 bays have been placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee in the eastern or forcign half of the Exhibition. In the first place, Norway and Sweden and the States of Northern Germany had not supplied a sufficient quantity of articles to cover their allotments. They therefore willingly resigned their surplus space. America, again, wished to exchange a portion of the ground area assigned her for increased room in the galleries. Her agent has acted, we un- derstand, with great liberality in the course of these new arrangements, and has readily and cordially co-operated with the Executive Committee in securing a satisfactory settlement with our other visitors from abroad. Al1 parties are now, we hear, perfectly well pleased with reference to the point of space; and it is sincerely to be hoped that no fresh disagree- ment may arise to destroy that spirit of harmonious and com- bined action the establishment of which becomes every day of greater importance. France, Belgium, Austria, and the Zollverein have all been especially benefitted by the addi- tional accommodation placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee. A. splendid organ will be placed in the nave as one of the most striking articles in the French collection. This is the fourth organ we have heard of as intended for exhibition, and it is quite clear that the Crystal Palace may be made available for the pleasures of sound as well of sight, if the Royal Commissioners think fit that it should be so. Over that vast expanse the sublime music of The Creation may be made to circulate, and while thousands of spectators assemble to admire the chief wonders of human industry the swelling notes may be sounded in their ears which so fitly reed the greatness of that Power by whom are all things. The American contributions brought over by the frigate St. Lawrence are now rapidly arriving at the building, and although the quantity is not so great as was at one time ex- pected, the quality will, it is believed, be not unworthv of the great nation which acknowledges this to be its mother country. The collection includes splendid specimens of copper, iron, and zinc ore, to illustrate the mineral wealth of the United States; macsinery to shew the mechanical ingenuity of the people and -a most varied display of raw produce and manufactured articles, including an air-exhausted metal coffin in which a human body could, it is said, be preserved for ages without decay, and which contains, we hear, a bouquet of flowers as fresh as when it was first placed there. The Commissioner from Tunis has been the first foreign agent to unpack. Judg- ing from what we saw, this small section of the Exhibition will not be the least interesting portion of it; and the fair sex especially will flock to a compartment where they may have an opportunity of comparing their own style of apparel with that of the Moorish ladies. Among the entries in the catalogue of articles which the Bey has sent over is one which runs thus, "'The beauty's dress on leaving the bath." The display is rich in specimens of male attire, also in mule trap- pings, blankets, and stilettos. Turning to our own part of the Exhibition, there are several matters of importance to communicate since our last notice. With reference to the amount of work to be accomplished before the 1st of May, it now appears certain that the chief difficulty to be overcome lies in the completion of the building itself, The ridge and valley roof during wet weather has always leaked a little at different points, but it was believed that when the Paxton gutters had been -vell pitched, and the interior of the sash bars painted, no inconvenience on this score would be experienced. The late heavy rains have dissi- pated this idea, and ivater has penetrated in so many places that serious fears are entertained by some as to the practica- bility of securing that exemption from drip or damp which is indispensable in such a building. We believe that the desired object can still be accomplished by administering a thick coat of paint to the sash bars on the outside; but this constitutes a formidable addition to the work which the contractors have nowscarcelysixweekstofinish. Messrs. Fox and Henderson have done wonders, and we have no doubt will complete this great undertaking in a nmanner creditable to themselves, to their profession, and to their country. Their reputation is indissolubly bound up with the satisfactory manner in which the Crystal Palace fulfils the objects for which it has been created. If its gigantic roof cannot be made water-tight, Mr. Paxton's design, and their execution, will be equally condemned as failures. Not only so, but we should be ex- posed, as a people, to just complaint from the countries whose industrial products we have invited to an imperfect shelter from our damp and showery skies. The contractors and the Executive Committee are both fully alive to the necessity of curing this defect, and accordingly the glass roof of the build- ing has been in possession of gangs of painters and glaziers, who, carrying their scaffolding about with them, and ap- parently like flies, without specific gravity, crawl about in every direction, stopping up chinks and crevices with putty and paint, and repairing fractured panes of glass. W"hen in addition to this precaution the calico, covering has been got up, the wind will be prevented from driving the rain with such force through any seams that may still remain open. We are glad to find that the preparations in every part of the western half of the building are pushed on with untiring energy, and with every prospect that our native industry can by the 1st of May fearlessly invite the inspection of the whole world. The department of machinery still takes the lead, and many of the most interesting objects comprised in it are far advanced towards completion. Among other objects which will no doubt attract great attention, we hear of a model of Plymouth Breakwater, executed with surprising fidelity, and containing, among other things, the representation of a brig, two inches long-the complete epitome of a vessel-of-war. All the guns, masts, yards, rigging, &c., are given, and even the running-gear is rove and the deck planked. It is obvious that however great the progress hitherto made, and however certain the prospect of all being ready by the 1st of May, the time is now close at hand when the Executive Committee must begin to tighten the screw upon exhibitors, to gather up the ends of the great work intrusted to them, to get a stage clear of paint pots and men in paper caps before the curtain rises and the performance begins. The following are the resolutions which they have come to, in order that the opening may take place, as announced by the Commissioners: 1. On Wednesday evening, the 2d of April, the temporary entrance in the building for carts, wagons, and carriages of every description, will be closed, to enable the flooring of the building to be completed; and no articles wvill be admitted into the building which cannot be brought in by hand, and without the aid of machinery for lifting, fic. The interval which elapsed be- tween 1820 and 1830 constituted an important period in the progress of the pianoferte. About that time im. provements of the first order were patented, which, in their ultimate effects, produced a revolution in the instrument almost as signal and complete asthose which the discoveries and inventions of Watt produced in the steam engine-these improvements related as well to those parts of the mechanism on which the tone depend- ed as to those upon which the touch, and what may not improperly be designated bite articulation' depends. Before that time the framing by which the tension of the strings Was supported and resisted was formed of wood. Pins, inclined slightly in a direction contrary to that of the strings, were inserted in a plate of metal, and upon these pins the strings were looped at the eud. At The other end they were rolled round the iron pins, called technically ' rest puts.' These rest pins were themselves inserted in abed of timber, called the rest plank, which was connected with the plate, to which the other extremities of the strings were attached by a framing of carpentry, variously constructed by different makers, so as to resist as far as possible the tention of the striing. This principle of construction was radically defective. The timber framing not having adequate power of resistance, thie pianos not only did not retain their pitch and tune, but the makers were unable to introduce strings of that degree oi length and thickness which would have been necessary to give to the tone of the instrument all the beauty and roundness of which it was susceptible, Another system of framing was therefore necessary for the durability of the instru ment as then constructed, and still more so with a view to those improvements in its tone and power, of which it wasobviouslysusceptible,andwbichit has since received. An improved system of framing, which accomplished this was invented; it consisted of a series of metal bars, extending over and parallel to the strings so as to connect the bed of timber to which the strings at one end were looped with that in which the rest pins were inserted. By this expedient the strain of the strings was thrown upon those metal bars, being resisted by them in the direction of their length. The effilccy of this improvement was so obvious that it soon became generally adopted, and is now used in all pianofortes. This mode of framing eoon produced a rapid improve- ment in tone and power. Strings of increased length and thickness giving proportionately augmented poster and brilliancy were adopted. This mode of framing was also of great efficacy in pianos exposed to extreme vicissitudes ofclimate, as it was to a great extent inde- pendent of glue, which was often decomposed under the infuence of tropical climates. The length of the vibrating part of the string was limited by a timber bridge re- sembling the S-shaped curve forming the upper part of the harp. The strings, resting upon this bridge, were kept in their places and separated from each other by a series of inclined pins, The next improvement of con- struction was the substituting of a series of metallic studs for the bridge and pins. These studs were in- serted in the bed of timber which received the rest pins, and the tension of the strings was made to act upwards against them, instead of pressing downwards on the bridge as it had previously done. This gave further stability to the strings and firmness to the tone, and it has since been generally adopted by the piano- forte makers. Defective as the framing of the instru- ment was previous to 1824, the mechanism which mf- fected its articulation was still more so, and gave rise to the most urgent appeals from eminent performers to the makers to contrive some asieans by which the power of repetition, articulation; and expression could be im- proved One of the great objects to be aimed at in the mechanism of the touch is to give the performer that powerof expression so much admired in the harp. In that instrument the finger acts directl upon the string, and therefore the expression baa nso other limit thfa the SkilMi genius, and feeling of the player; but jie the case of the pianoforte the finger is se'parated from ae sitring by a distance more or less conssidetble, and aets upon it through the interven- tion of the mechanism of the key, the hammer, and their appendages. The makers were, therefore, called upon to contrive such a mechanism of the key as would enable the performer to act upon the string through its intervention with as much sensibility as if he touched it directly with the finger. In the piano- fortes constructed previously to 1823. this part of the mechanism was extremely defective. Not only was the touch heavy, the key responding with uncertainty to the finger, but a positive limit was imposed upon the executant which no skill or ?? finger could ex- Jeed. When the key was depressed, so as to strike the note, it was necessary before the same note coald be re- peated to allow it to rise to its position of rest. Now since the rapidity and promptitude of this aecent was not undet the controul of the performer, who, therefore, could not expedite it, and since it must be completed before the same note could be reproduced, it followed that the seime note could not be successively repeated at shorter intervals than those which vere compatible with the complete elevation of the key. Thus, whe ther the performer desired to play piano or forte, the hammer and key had each to be moved through the samns space, and, as the former must necessarily receive a certain momentum from the latter, and as this mo- mentum must be more or less regulated by the space through which it had to be propelled, the power of the performer was not only limited with respect to the pos- sible rapidity of repetition, but also with respect to the limit within which it was possible to vary the eiaun- sances of tone. These defects were severely felt by the eminent pianists of that day, and produced, on their part, urgent and rapid appeals to the makers. What was wanted was a greater power of repetition, united with increased power of varied expression. Both of these objects were attained with signal success by the mechanism patentei at the epoch already referred to, and which bas since been known in England as a, ' re- petition action,' and abroad as I double escapement.' This was accomplished by an ingenious combina- tion of levers and springs, interposed between the key and the hammer. It was so contrived that after the key had been depressed and the hammer driven against the string, the hammer was caught in its fall before descending. to its position of rest, so that, the hey being allowed to rise through little more than a quarter of its entire play, and being then again depressed, would cause the hammer to return upon the string and reproduce the note. The power of repetition by this expedient was increased in very nearly a fourfold proportiou, since the note could be reproduc- ed after the key hled risen through little more than one- fourth of its play, instead of its being obliged to wait for its elevation to its position of rest, as formerly. It was found that in strings of such length there was a con- stant liability of their striking each other, and jarring during their vibration, and this injured the effect of their tone. This detect is removed in the iaproved in- strument by making each hammer of the lowest octave act upon a single string, whose thickness is increased as well as its length. By this expedient, the jar which prevailed previuusly is ?? prevented, and force and fulness of tone are obtained, which exceed in a striking degree the effect of the ins-ruments of the old construction. Another novelty of construction in some of these in- struments, is an improved method of tuning them. Hi- therto the wvire has been wound round the rest pins, sometimes called tuning pins, placed at right angles to the direction of the string, and which is turned by the tuning key, so that it is rolled either on or off as it is desired to raise or lower the pitch. In the new system now exhibited, the rest pins are omitted, and replaced by a nut, to which the string is looped, and in which a fixed screw works. The taning key being applied to turn this fixed screw, the nut attached to the string is drawn or relaxed, according to the direction in which the key is turned, and thus raises or lowers the pitch. Another novelty which will prove a great conveni- ence and advantage to organists, is the addition of pedals to ties grand pianoforte corresponding with the pedals of the organ. By these means the performer plays with both hands and feet, exactly as in the case of then organ. All organe music, and the music of tile ancient composers, such as aishastian Bricb, the new compositions of endeissoho, Sctmoamann, and other modern masters, can be performed and practised on such an instrument. The effect is very remarkable, the notes produced by the feet having a power and qua- lity totally different from those which the same notes would have, if played by a second pair of hands upon the same instrument. In several of these improvements Messrs Broad-; wood have advanced pari possa with Erard; Thus they have also completely tramed the strings of their grand horizontal pianoforte in metal, the rest pins and studs being fixed in a metallic plate-extending across the entire scale. They have also, like Erard, en- larged the model of their grand pianoforte by increasing its length as well as the width of its narrow:end, and have produced like advantages in the length-and thickness and increased power of the strings of the lowest octave. Messrs Broadwood, however, have adhered to the systemi of double strings to that octave. In the American department is a double pianofortei made and exhibited by Pirson of Now York. The shape is rectangular, being ten feet two inches in length, and four feet seven inches in width. On a single sounding board it has two sets of strings, which are attached to a metallic framing, which completely surrounda the in- serument, having a diagonal plate upon which the ends of the strings most remote from the keys are attached. The performers sit face to race, and four can play simul- taneously upon it. Thie mechanism is so regulated that when a single performer plays, the same effect is pro- duced as if the second set of keys and strings were absent. In this pianoforte there is also a new me- chanism for tuning, someevhat analogous to but not identical with that of Erard, above described. At the extremity of each string a small toothed wheel, about half an inch in diamcter; is fixed, with its axis horizon- tal. Round the axis ties trieg is wound. Tie wheel is placed in conenexion with an endless screw or worm, cut upon a vertical pin fixed in the framing of tie instrument. By turning this pin with the tuning keey in one direction or tile other, one tooth of the wheel is advanced by the worm for each revolution made by the tuning key, and a corresponding portion of the string is turned on or off the axis of the wheel. This system is more complicated than that of Erard. In the system adapted by the latter maker the screw acts directly upon the string, drawing or relaxing it through a space equal to tie interval between its threads, by each revolution of the tuning key; whereas irn the System of Pirsou the same screw is used with the interposition of a toothed wheel and its axis, producing both complexity and espouse.

Her Majesty and the Prince Consort, accompanied by several of the Royal children, again paid a visit to the Crystal Pahee on Monday, and minutely inspected »e progress made in the preparations. The returns of goods received up to the close of last week are, 7,823 packages from foreign countries, 987 from our Colonial possessions, 27 from the Channel Islands, and 9,620 from home contributors. Robinson and Russell arc erecting an immense sugar-mill, the size of which will leave upon the mind an impression little short of that which the great hydraulic press already produces. National Antipathies. —There is one singular fact, which is worth being mentioned, with reference to the distribution of space to foreign countries. The original intention of the Royal Commissioners was to sink nationalities altogether, and have the whole Exhibition divided into sections, without reference to the part of world contributor came from. That idea was not acceptable abroad, and a geographical distribution was in consequence adopted. Even this arrangement, however, does not always please, and the representatives of Sardinia, Rome, and Tuscany are quarrelling because the idea of a common Italy has been realized to them within the Crystal Palace. Spain and Portugal, too, will not forego their distinctive nationalities, and insist upon defined boundary lines even in Hyde-park. But, strangest of all, a portion of Belgian territory stood in the way of France, and her indefatigable and diplomatic Commissioner did not rest until, rearrangement, satisfactory, of course, to all parties, he was enabled to absorb it. Among the articles in the Fine Arts department (Class 30, No. 296) is a painting illustrating the triangular and equidistant arrangement of the features, the work of an artist named ilopley. This singular production profesies to present a scalp of proportion borne out by the finest examples of art. Nine equal triangles, at equal distances from each other, and having one general base, are shown IA be an unnerring guide to pure facial proportions; under them, every important outline :of the features arranges itself, and the departure from this order produces the existing variations. Childhood, or the pre'symmetrical period, exhibits nine obtuse isoceles triangles; the post-symmetrical period, or maturity, develops nine acute isoceles triangles; it is only at the intermediate, the most beautiful, or symmetrical period, that these nine triangles are equilateraldemonstrating that when there is the greatest beauty there is the greatest symmetry. The artist or sculptor, observing through these fixed angles where features accord with or depart from this scale, will, it is said, be assisted to the speedy realisation of a correct outline; thus saving valuable time, and securing a better opportunity to study the mental characteristics of his sitter. The work has excited much curiosity amongst the artists who have visited the Exhibition, and, it is thought, will lead to results of a practically useful character. In about two months hence the Crystal Palace will bo left alone in its glory, and when the public arc once more admitted within its spacious precincts, and have time to admire in its unadorned grandeur the gigantic shell of the Great Exhibition, wo shall be surprised indeed if they allow it to be pulled down. CONFLAGRATION AT ENFIELD Yesterday ( Wednesd a y) f orenoon, about half past ten o clock, one of the most extensive fires that has occurred for some years past in the parish of Enfield broke out in the premises b e l ong i ng to Mr. A. Paris, known as Plumridge Farm, about four mites beyond the Barnet station of the Great Northern Railway. From inquiries made on the spot cur reporter gleaned the following particulars. Before, however, it is necessary, in order that the reader may correctly understand how it was that the fire made such fearful progress, to state that the farm-house stood in a direct line with the carriage road, whilst a number of brick and timber buildings used for dep os i t i ng corn, seeds, cattle, &c., ran in a kind of cir cu it ous form a consider a bl e di s t ance , and again approached t o within a short space o f th e first-named building. The space between the various erections was literally studded with wide and lofty stacks of corn, hay, and other farm-produce. Some of the ricks towered so high that there must have been between 200 and 300 loads of material in them. Between the ricks and the buildings a number of sheds stretched across. The fire commenced in a small shed, through the carelessness of one of the men employed on the estate beating a pot of tar. Whilst attending to the fire the contents of the vessel boiled over, and in an instant the combustible liquid became ignited, and ran like a sheet of flame over the floor of the building, so that in less than five minutes the flames rushed out of the property and seized upon everything near. The men employed on the farm, as well as many of the neighbours, hastened to the spot to render assistance, but in spite of their exertions the work of devastation continued with frightful rapidity. With as little delay as possible three engines of the parish went down, but by that period a large barn, between 80 and 100 feet long, and containing upwards of 150 quarters of corn, and a smaller one, about 40 feet long, and a number of sheds, were in flames. All chance of saving any portion of these premises appeared perfectly hopeless; every endeavour was therefore made to save the ricks of hay and wheat contiguous ; but so fiercely did the flames extend that very quickly a large wooden building nearly 70 feet long became fired, and but few minutes elapsed before the whole structure was enveloped in flames. The various persons at work at this conjun c t ure , on see i ng the Conflagration travelling so fearfully, were completely bewildered. A great many directed their services towards stopping the fire from reaching the stacks and ricks standing hard by, but even in that they wese to a certain extent disappointed, for rick after rick of corn and hay, to the number of eight, became ignited in rapid succession; and the flames being wafted by rather a stiffish breeze, extended their ravages to the stables and some carriage sheds. Nothing short of the complete destruction of the whole of Mr. Paris's property could now be expected, more especially as a lofty rick of hay or corn, containing nearly three hundred loads, was in flames. The men, however, in a most praiseworthy manner, resorted to various expedients to save from total destruction this stock, well knowing, if they could not, the bailiff's house and five other ricks must share the same fate as the others. Fortunately, by scattering the water and cutting the rick round they succeeded in saving the interior of the stack, and thereby cut off the the further spread of the flames in the direction of the bailiffs house and other valuable property. The fearful element continued to rage, and so threatening an appearance did it at length assume that it was deemed advisable to send a mounted policeman, and also to employ the electric telegraph to . give the ne cessary intelligence to the London fire stations, so that additional aid might be obtained. The moment the news was received in London, Scott, the head engineer of the Farringdon-street-station, started with one of the brigade engines and a powerful body of firemen. Mr. Connorton, the superintendent of the iVest of England fire brigade, followed soon after, and on their arrival they beheld a fearful scene ; for at the least computation they found property covering half an acre of land in a tremendous blaze. The brigade engine was forthwith taken to a pond of water, and its contents were pumped into the parish engines, for by that means alone could a continuous jet be thrown upon the fire. Fortunately, the firemen by eight o'clock succeeded in getting, as far as appearances went, command over the fire, that is, to stay its further extension, but at that hour the country fur miles round was most brilliantly illumined, and it was the opinion of the firemen present that they would be unable to get the fire completely extinguished before late this (Thursday) morning. To give anything like a correct estimate of the damage done would, at the present time, be impossible ; we can however state with certainty that up to eight o'clock last night the large barn, with 150 quarters of wheat, the smaller one 40 feet long, another building 60 feet long, a vast number of sheds, the stables, and eight stacks of corn and hay were completely destroyed, to say nothing of the damage done to the surrounding property. The increase in the receipts had not, however, kept pace with the increase in the number of passengers, which was to be ascribed to the merely nominal fares which they had charged during the late contest with the Edinburgh, Perth, and Dundee Company, for the traffic between Perth and Edinburgh. Her Majesty was one of the earliest visitors, and, attended by Messrs. Dilke, Cole, and Colonel Reid, proceeded at once to the electric telegraph office, and spent some minutes in watching the operations of this great scientific wonder of the country. Colonel Wylde, Mr. Peto, M,P., and two other directors of the telegraph company were in attendance, and explained the working of the machine to her Majesty. The answer, a paragraph of ten lines, came back before her Majesty left the building, and announced, curiously enough, the arrival of the Countess of Neuilly (ex-Queen of France) in the northern capital. The City of Paris has already sent 90 foremen and workmen to London to visit the Exhibition; and about 30 Chambers of Commerce of the chief manufacturing towns of France, and 20 Chambres Consultatives, have acceded to the wishes of the Government, and presented lists of first-rate workmen of all trades, amounting collectively to about 140, who are also to be sent to London; to them are to be added 12 foremen of the national manufactories of Beauvais, Sevres, and Gobelins, and of the professional schools of Chalons, Aix, and Angers. Dupin for his com- pliments in the name of the Commissioners, and concludes:- * iI cannot let this occasion pass without expressing our senti- ment of the great advantage we have derived from France having formed, by her productions, such an interesting and precious portion of the Exhibition; and at your Government having taken care to send so miany ckefs-d'ceusvres, the character of which will certainly exercise a happy influence on the sciences and arts of our own and other countries. I conclude in expressing to you, both in my own name and in that of the Royal Commis. sioners, our thanks for the part which you have personally taken in our labours, both as president of one of the groups of juries, and as vice-president of the superior council of presidents, as also for the impartiality and urbanity you have displayed on all occasions on which you have fulfilled those functions.- Accept, &c. " ALBERT "President of the Royal Commission of England."

With no foreign country are the English more familiar than China, not only from the numerous importations of its arts and manufactures, which have been made here for a long succession of years, but most particularly from the collection of the American merchant which for so many months occupied the pagoda-like building at Hyde Park Corner, and which is now revived at Knightsbridge, with but little diminution of its former splendour. The prescriptive exclusiveness of the Chinese has, however, limited the show of the natural produce more so than might have been expected or could have been wished. The Board of Trade and the East India Company send a few roots, some indigoes, dyes, hemp-seed, tobacco, foo.,but we have no specimens whatever of the miscellaneous plants, fruits, and vegetables which grow so profusely in the country; while the mineral kingdom is represented in an equally inferior manner, the coal and iron produce so plentiful in various parts, the gold of the royal mines, the marbles, jasper, and granite from the southern quarries, and the precious stones, by no means scarce, being wholly absent. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Friday, July 4.— Friday is now, perhaps, the most attractive day of the week at the Crystal Palace. The half-crown admission fee insures a certain degree of selectness on the one hand, while it prevents the inte- rior wearing a too deserted or exclusive look upon the other. The baskets filled with provisions for luncheon and the odours of gin and oranges are no longer per- ceptible ; nor does the visitor feel himself perplexed by the movements of a motley assemblage agitated like a bee-hive in summer, and from which a humming sound is ceaselessly ascending. He has leisure to observe everything without distraction, and when his curiosity about the inanimate objects around him is satisfied he can find relief in watching the company, in admiring the varied display of beauty, and even in enjoying the refreshing coolness of the air which by the system of ventilation adopted and the change in the weather has now been effectually secured. Upwards of 26,000 people entered the budding during the day, and the re- ceipts were £2,614 3s. 6<L The financies of the Com- mission are now in a most flourishing condition, for £196,234 has been taken at the doors and by the sale of season tickets, which added to the £77,700 from subscriptions and contracts makes a total of £273,934. With this vast run of fortune in its favour the Exhibition is freed from all pecuniary liabilities, and is hopefully entering upon the period when its surplus funds m^ be made available for those public purposes to which "Denarious" and Mr. Paxton have already invited attention. Monday, July 7.— To-day, by a sudden rebound the number of visitors to the Crystal Palace rose once more to 61,670, and the receipts at the doors amounted to £2,852 2s. For the first time since the opening the sale of season tickets presents a perfect blank. Among tbe crowds that thronged the interior were about 500 men and boys in the employ of Messrs. Clowes, the ex- tensive printers and part contractors for the official catalogue. Mr. Gladstone treated 50 of his poor fellpw- parishioners to a view of the interior, and, with a kind- ness which the public will appreciate, accompanied them in their survey. Tuesday, July B. — An almost unprecedented number of people visited the Crystal Palace to-day. The re- ceipts at the doors rose to £3,169 ss. — except on two days the largest amount that has yet been taken in shillings. On the 17th of June £3,191 2s. was the sura taken, and on the 24th of June £3,186 12s. According' to the police returns 65,962 persons entered the build- ing, and at two o'clock, when the interior was most crowded, the scene presented was certainly one of a most remarkable and interesting character. In the western nave, close to the crystal fountain, rises Messrs. Keith's Spitalfields trophy. From the top of it a very striking view is obtained of the central avenue, and at that elevation on Tuesday the building might be seen filled with a restless sea of human beings, agitated by the strong impulses of curiosity. The impression which so vast an assemblage produces seen at a glance, stretch- ing away into distance, and pervading the ground area and galleries of the great pillared edifice with all its industrial marvels, is inexpressibly grand, and must be experienced to be properly appreciated. There is a majesty about " the million " thus collected to survey their own peaceful triumphs, to which words cannot do justice. As the eye sweeps over them individualities arc forgotten, and " the People," in the full grandeur and significance of the term, is realised to the senses. They are moving in every direction, yet nothing seems to disturb the harmony of the general spectacle, and upon the ear rises a perpetual hum of busy and pre- occupied admiration. Wednesday, July 9.— The attendance to-day at the Crystal Palace, although not so great as on the previous day, was still greater than the Wednesday of the pre- vious week. Her Majesty was one of the earliest visi- tors, and, attended by Messrs. Dilke, Cole, and Colonel Reid, proceeded at once to the electric telegraph office, and spent some minutes in watching the operations of this great scientific wonder of the country. Colonel Wylde, Mr. Peto, M.P., and two other directors of the telegraph company were in attendance, and explained the working of the machine to her Majesty. As a test of the rapidity with which messages might be conveyed to and from distant points, her Majesty commanded that a message should be forwarded to Edinburgh for the latest paragraph of news in the Scotch papers. The answer, a paragraph of ten lines, came back before her Majesty left the building, and announced, curiously enough/the arrival of the Countess of Neuilly (ex-Queen of France) in the northern capital. After her inspection of the telegraph, her Majesty proceeded to the agri- cultural implement section, where Mr. Pusey, M.P., Colonel Challoner, and Mr. Brahdreth Gibbs, were in attendance, and -explained the working and uses of the different machines. The total number of visitors was 58,055. The receipts of the day were — from season tickets, £8 Bs. ; from shilling admissions, £2,710 65. ; total, £2,718 14s. Proposed Railways in Switzerland.— Tho Federal Council of Switzerland has drawn up a decree for the exe- cution of the railways proposed by Mr. Stephenson. One line is to traverse the country from the lake of Constance to Geneva, passing by Zurich. A branch line is to run from this trunk line to the Basle Railway, to unite with the German and French fines. Another line is to proceed from the lake of Constance to Coire, in the Grisons, to be prolonged afterwards across the Alps by Luckmanier into Lombardy. The total length of these lines is to be 650 kilometres (4055, English miles), and the expense 102,123,000 francs, or 157,112 francs per kilometre.
