Caution to Railway Servants. — Action for False Imprisonment. — At the Bolton County Court, on Friday last, an action was brought by a man named John Leather- barrow, against the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company, for an assault and false imprisonment. It ap I peared that the plaintiff, who is an overlooker in the cotton mill of Mr. Gidlow, of Ince, has been in the habit, for some time, of returning home to his parents at Westhoughton every Saturday night. On the evening of the 7th of June, he booked ?? as usual, as a third class passenger. A collier named Wain, who was going to Pendleton, got a third-clas3 ticket at the same time. The train was behind its time, and there was a great bustle. The third class carriages appeared to be all full, and they were going from one to another in search of seats, when the guard put them into a second-class carriage. When the plaintiff arrived at Westhoughton, James Mort, the station-master, demanded a penny, being the difference between a second and a third- class carriage. Leatherbarrow refused to pay the penny, was given into custody of Sergeant Ludlow, and was locked up from Saturday night till Monday at noon, when he was taken before the magistrates and the case was dismissed. These facts were supported by respectable testimony, and the Judge was of opinion that the man had been put into a second class oarriage; consequently the company had no demand upon him, and he therefore awarded the plaintiff the full amount of damage claimed— viz., £10 and costs.

TlE ERA. I I XowTOWN EDITION. SUNDAY, APRIL 27, 1851. ?? -- m I THE GREAT EXHIBITION. All ideas of roof and walls vanish upon entering the Great Exhibition. You are, as it were, in a novel little world, whose sky is glass, all shaped in parallelograms, and whose confines you know to be of a similar character. Everything is new. The order and seriousness that prevail denote the im- portance of what is going forward, and stalls unfold themselves as flowers do on a summer's day. Silently basy men (not only mechanics but a better sort) in shirt sleeves, incessantly npply themselves to their respective tasks, hammering, tacking, adjust- ing, arranging, and every hour produces a fresh object of interest in this place of surprising de- velopment. A walk through the principal thoroughfares in their present state, is enough to convince even the sceptic that the undertaking cannot prove a failure. He will acknowledge, before he has been there many minutes, that, independently of the structure itself-the latest wonder of the world - inde- pendently of the respective merits of the numeyous articles it will contain, an influence will be spread, and an example will be set, which shall immediately benefit the civilized globe, and this country in particular, and ripen into results that shall, in future, be important to the human race. This is our honest conviction. We are not about to anticipate what we shall hereafter have to describe in something like detail; we would merely prepare the mind of the reader for the extraorinamry impression which is to be soon made upon it, and relieve it of any doubts which exist there. It is only when you are inside the vast fabric of glass and iron, that you can comprehend its character. It is not enough to say so much of this, that, and the other has been expended. It is not sufficient to consider that contributors, from all corners of the earth, have sent their goods to be exhibited in this World's Fair, and millions of strangers will visit the metropolis to inspect the gigantic structure and its contents. Building materials to any extent and to any cost may be made to form but an unsightly and useless pile; articles of rarest manu- facture and extraordinary value may be collected to no beneficial end; and multitudes may assemble for no practical good. But the Great Exhibition is destined to fulfil the intentions of its promoters, and these, we presume, have been explained. There is little that man will not undertake, but he must be estimated by what he accomplishes. Here we have our national resources, our " means and appliances to boot" displayed in a manner calculated to make us proud of our country-for see how a fact is illustrated. It was decided that this Crystal Palace, so original and curious in its design, so light and so elegant in its construction, so capacious in its dimensions, and altogether so extra ordinary as to surpass what minds had previously imagined-it was decided, we say, that this mag- nificent and commodious mountain, this huge and transparent edifice should be thus raised and thus stored in a few brief months, and straight it teas done! What does this fact say for Great Britain? What does it say for the united efforts of her work- ing men ? No matter what has been the expense, what thelabourof heads and hands, what the influence used, the difficulties overcome, and the aid rendered; thereistheimmediateresult-thereis the present suc- cess, whatever the future consequences are destined to be! And it is the triumph which is most worthy remark, for every day the importance of this undertaking becomes more manifest. It is not a mere toy, a fair, a bazaar, but it forms, as it were, one immense advertisement for thousands of cam- petitors in the great World of Business. We were among the first to say,. "Now that this building is to be raised, let it be done in a manner worthy the nation, lest we be laughed at by the foreigner." Visitors from other shores will know little and care less about our social and political differences, judging us only by what is spread before them, andI to that we should look with an unanimous desire to leave nothing undone that can add to the general effect. But all this is growing out ot the mighty kernel that has been set, and the matter be- comes more and more serious. IrtercommunScation 'is aimed at as necessary for the destruction of igno- race and prejudice, the worst elements o0 Strife and the greatest bars to improvement. The circula- tion of truth is required for the mutual advantage it must brine about, and here we have it. What imuressions will a sight of the Crystal Palace make upon all beholders ? What intelligence will its wares convey to the deeply interested and the merely curious? Consider what we have to gain, and we have nothing to fear. Go to any stall and you will learn something. Notice, for instance, the beautiful marbles of Cornwall, the bleak and barren extreme West, celebrated only for its mines, and you will discover that Italy has nothing to surpass them, and thank the Exhibition. But, as we have said, we will not anticipate. It is sufficient to state that her Majesty has made gracious concession to the wishes of a loyal public, and the Exhibition will contain some thousands of her subjects when she opens it. The ceremony, too, will be worthy the occasion, and have all that royal state and solemn observance can bestow upon it. The Queen and her Ministers, and the other highest dignitaries of the land will be there, and the spectacle will be one for history to record. A sight more imposing and more suggestive can scarcely be inmagined. The formal ceremony, the pious invoca- tion, the organ's thrilling peals, the canuon s reports, the hum of many voices, the general excitement, the individual anxiety, the bustle and the crowd-these will help to make up such a first of May as few have ever seen, or seeing, cease to remember.

The second part of the official descriptive and illustrated Catalogue has just made its appearance, and will be welcomed by all who have been puzzled and perplexed by the meagre and unsatisfactory character of the official catalogue. It comprises the classes from five to ten, and in. eludes machines for direct use—such as carriages, railway and marine mechanism ; manufacturing machines and tools; engineering, architecture, and buildi ng contr i vances; naval and military architecture and weapons; agricultural and horticultural implements; and philosophical, musical, horological, and surgical instruments. It will be seen from the above summary that a very large and important section of the works displayed in the Great Exhibition are here included, and the illustrations and descriptions are sufficiently ample and intelligible to satisfy the requirements of all. Indeed, in so vast and varied a collection it is impossible to accomplish anything like a satisfactory inspection without some such guide, and our only regret is that circumstances have so long delayed its publication. We hope to find the remainder of this interesting and valuable record of the great industrial gathering of all nations follow at more brief intervals. Among the many inventions with which the Crystal Palace abounds there are few which, at this sultry season, will be regarded with more interest than the refrigerators and machines for making ice, of which there are numerous specimens exhibited. We have already referred to the large quantity of ices consumed in the building daily, and we may now stata that the luxury itself may be seen in process of manufacture in the western refreshment-room, where six of Masters' large freezing machines are kept in constant operation by the agency of steam,—one of the hottest substances we are acquainted with being thus made subservient to the production of the coldest and most refreshing. These machines, which are capable of making about 100 quarts of ice every quarter of an hour, can also be made to form solid cylinders of ice, in which leaves and flowers are introduced by way of ornament, and in which wine and other liquors may be placed to cool during dinner, while they impart an agreeable freshness to the atmosphere. On the counter is a small model of the freezing machine, which conveys a very clear idea of the whole process; and these machines, from their simplicity and economy, are now, we understand, very extensively used, and have tended considerably to extend the public taste for this grateful class of refreshments. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The accommodation of 60,000 visitors in a single day at the Crystal Palace is no longer a problem, no less than 65,000 having been admitted on Monday. The throng was in no way remarkable at the first opening, hut it kept gra- dually increasing until midday, when the inward stream became incessant, and so continued. All the roads leading to the building were like a fair; indeed, one could hardly suppose there were so many cabs and omnibuses in London as were continually occupied in conveying the sight-seekers. Nor was this all. The fineness of the day tempted whole troops of pedestrians, who crowded the road and the park. giving to all the vicinity the gay and animated appearance of some great festival. It would be a hard task to classify the enormous crowd which moved slowly backward and for- ward through the interior, seeing as much as they could, but greatly impeded in their object by their own immense accu- mulation. The contents of several excursion trains were there, among others the weekly Eastern Counties, and an extensive immigration from Berkshire, vid Great Western. The provincial aspect was frequently visible, bat by no means predominant, nor, judging by appearances, had our own ope- rative classes anything like a majority. The toilettes were, as a rule, gay and fashionable, and there was the same crowding round those objects which are supposed to interest the hiaher classes almost exclusively. The Queen of Spain's jewels awere regularly besieged, and the Koh i-noor knew no repose. The Dresden chamber was impassable, and in the Milan sculpture-room, the " pass on, ladies of the police- man was a never-ending ditty. But these symptoms of conjestion. vere only local, and such as may be witnessed even on high-priced days. The general circulation was tolerably free, notwithstanding the enormous crowd, suffi- ciently so to prove that the established maximum of the executive committee may be exceeded without any serious inconvenience. Her Majesty arrived for her daily visit at her usual hour, and devoted a considerable time to the in- spection of the machinery in motion, in which she appears to take a deep interest. The heat was very great towards the middle of the day, and in the nave and more crowded quarters excessive. Several cases of fainting occurred, among which were two or three from among the stronger sex, but the general aspect of the throng was pleasurable in the extreme, and they moved about as freely as could possibly be expected in so vast an assembly. On Tuesday the in- flux of visitors was even greater than on the day before, the grand total counted at six o'clock being 67,681. As might be expected with such numbers, the place was densely crowded indeed, between twelve and two o'clock, the period during which the greatest numbers sought admission, the transept and nave were almost impassable. Gradually, however, the vast crowds spread themselves through the courts and along the galleries, and more comfortable moving room was obtained. The only inconvenience that remained was a very high temperature, which required the services of all the watering-pots in the establishment, the thermometer giving seventy-five degrees in rather a shady corner of the nave. There were great numbers of country visitors; several van-loads having set down from the South-Eastern railway; and one of our charitable institutions, the London Orphan Asylum, treated its 500 little inmates to a visit. I The railways may now be expected to furnish an immense daily quota, one of them, the North-Western, being under contract to convey 1,000,000 persons to the Exhibition, the drafts to commence from the 1st of July, and to continue throughout the month. It is therefore not improbable that, before many weeks, there may be as many as 100,000 visi- tors to the Crystal Palace in a day. It is satisfactory to know that the balloon which paid such an unexpected visit to the roof of the transept on the previous day did no damage beyond carrying away a flagstaff. The Koh-i-noor, which had been surrounded by a crimson drapery and lit up with gas, is again restored to daylight and its gilt cage, the experiment not being considered satisfactory; in the first place, as not increasing the brilliancy of the gem; and, se- condly, as causing such a pressure in that particular quarter as greatly to increase the responsibilities of the police. The crowd on Tuesday was an exceedingly well-dressed one, and included many of our first fashionables, who bore the hust- ling with entire good hamour and patience. Some sensa- tion was caused about middav by the arrival of our old Chinese friend Keying in grand costume, with two attend- ants, having come to give a sitting to the artist who is pre- paring a picture of the grand opening. The illustrious stranger looked exceedingly well, and seemed wonderfully to enjoy the way in which he was run after by the country visitors. There was also a good sprinkling of the Scots Fusilier Guards, their colonel, Prince Albert, having pur- chased admissions for the whole regiment, to be sent in in drafts, as the exigencies of military duty might permit. Altogether the day was a feature in the history of the Crystal Palace. Wednesday was another great day at the Crystal Palace. Notwithstanding the fluctuating character of the weather, the visitors began to pour in at an early hour, so that at two o'clock the interior might be literally called the World's Fair The great increase of country visitors is now becoming quite noticeable, and the foreigners, who now form a large ingredient in the company, are no longer ex- clusively of the stronger sex. The beat of the weather, great as it was outside of the building, was still more oppressive within, and, in consequence of The inconvenience experienced, we understand that it is determined to remove the inside glazing at the eastern and western entrances, end to endeavour in this way to secure a refreshiag thorough draught from end to end of the interior. Friday was a half-crown day, but notwithstanding the increased charge of admission and the beat of the weather, 2,9691. 6s. was taken at the doors, and 29,033 people entered the building. The Crystal Palace presented on Saturday its usual appearance upon that, the chosen day of the select. The attendance WAS rather short of preceding Saturdays, and the temperature Was all the more pleasant in consequence. Her Majesty, Prince Albert, and the King of the Belgians, with the usual suite, arrived shortly after nine o'clock, and the Dutchess of Kent, and the Duke and Dutchess of Nemours, at a later hour. The attendance up to four o'clock was exceedingly slender, not exceeding 6,000 or 7,ooo—quite a solitude in such a vast building. From that hour the ticketholders began to pour in, and made up the numbers which will be found below. Even with such small numbers the want of ventilation was sadly felt, the temperature rising to 80 degrees in the 'main avenues, while it was 90 degrees in the galleries. The number of visiters, as taken by the police, was 11,371.

GREAT EXHIBITION. The funds of the Exhibition were increased on Saturday by the sum of £3,089 165., which was made up as follows . : —From season tickets, viz., 141 ladies and 83 gentlemen's admissions, £557 us. 6d. ; receipts at the doors, from 10,129 visitors at 55., £2,532 ss. The total receipts at the door last week were £13,406 10s., from 53,626 'visitors; 992 ladies' and 657 gentlemen's season tickets were sold during the same period. From the showery and uncertain character of the weather on Monday, the number of visitors showed a slight decline, but £2,345 was taken in ss. fees at the doors, and the sale of season tickets produced £4BB, so that the total receipts for the day amounted to £2,833. Her Majesty, with the Prince and the Royal party at the Palace, arrived at the building shortly after nine o'clock, and remained for about an hour. A morning clear, though cool, on Tuesday, gave pleasing proznise of a splendid day, and between nine and ten o'clock hundreds from all parts of the metropolis were wending their way to the Crystal Palace. Her Majesty arrived about halfpast nine, with the Prince Consort, accompanied by the Prince and Princess of Prussia. Of the royal children, the Princess Louisa alone was with the Queen, but the Prince of Wales was, we believe, with Mr. Birch, in another part of the building. Colonel Grey and Colonel Seymour, with Miss Stanley, were in the royal suite, and Colonel M a y ne was also in attendan-e. Mr. Dilke, as u•ual, received the royal party, and attended them throughout their visit; Her Majesty and the Prince referring frequently to him for information. After Her Majesty and Prince Albert retired, the Prince and Princess of Prussia remained, and walked about for some time. The visitors had by this period arrived in great numbers, and the animated aqpect of the edifice clearly indicated another good day for the Exhibition. We were struck by the very large number of clergymen present, who were to be seen on every side. Among the early visitors we noticed Mr. Macaulay and Mr. Evelyn Denison, with several other members of Parliament. The number of visitors was larger than upon any previous day—those paying the ss. admission money being 13,480, and the amount taken being £3,370. The number of season tickets sold was rather over 400. Such a result is truly surprising, and is probably attributable to the additional number of visitors brought up to town by the attractions of Derby-day. As the demand for season tickets at the present rate of charge is now visibly on the decline, it is a question whether the Commissioners ought not, by reducing the price, to try and open up a fresh demand. It is perfectly open for them to do so if they think proper, and, considering the size of the building, we cannot see any objection to such an arrangement. On Wednesday Her Majesty and the Prince Consort, with . the Prince and Princess of Prussia, the Prince of Wurtemberg, and the Duke of Saxe-Coburg, again visited the Exhibition. The Royal party examined the sections of Switzerland, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, and Persia. It the latter compartment they inspected the splendid Persian pavilion, just completed, which is exceedingly characteristic. The day was not particularly brilliant, and being moreover the Derby Day, one might have expected that there would be a much smaller number of visitors. Yet there seemed from the first no diminution; and although from three to five o'clock the arrivals were not ro rapid and incessant as usual, nor was there during the day such a crush of carriages, the entire number present was not less than usual. About half-past four the visitors began to depart as rapidly as they had arrived, having mostly been of the paying class who came early. Up to two o'clock, at one door alone, the money taken was £1,200 and upwards; and up to two o'clock the whole amount received was £2,676. Up to five o'clock, the amount received at the south entrance alone was £2,403 (the largest sum yet collected at one entrance), and the entire amount received, independent of the sale of season tickets, was £3,350. It thus appears that Wednesday, though a dull day and the Derby-day, was nearly equal, as regards the Exhibition, to the greatest of the preceding days since its opening. On Thursday Her Majesty left Buckingham Palace at a quarter past nine o'clock, and again visited the Exhibition. Her Majesty remained in the building for about an hour and a half, but Prince Albert, the Prince of Wales, and others of the party, remained considerably longer. The appearance of the outside of the Glass Palace is greatly improved. The hoarding which surrounded it, and which prevented a full view from being had, has been entirely removed, and its elegant proportions may now be viewed with great advantage. At the east end of the building an elegant tent has been erected, surrounded by railings of a very novel description, both bring intended to present an improved mode of constructing Indian encampments. At the west end, also, several improvements have taken place, and many objects of interest are exhibited which could not be seen before by the spectators outside. The works now exhibited at the west end are particularly worthy of notice. On Tuesday the Council and Chairman of the Metropolitan Local Commissioners gave a dinner to the Foreign Commissioners of the Exhibition, at the Castle, Richmond. rhe Council also got up a regetta on the river, giving prizes for a double sculler's race (with three heatsone at half-past four, one at a quarter to five, and one at five), and an outrigger race at half-past five, with a final heat of double sculls at a quarter to six. The beautiful grounds of the Castle-inn run down to the Thames, and thus such of the numerous guests (in all about 170) as arrived in time had the best possible opportunity of seeing the races. Many of the foreigners availed themselves of this opportunity, and the day being fine, :they saw this favourite place of resort, and this favourite English amusement under the most favourable circumstances, A capital brass band played, at intervals, stirring airs; many of the neighbouring gentry were gathered round; groups of ladies were scattered about, and the whole place had an exceedingly animated appearance. Nor was the town itself without demonstrations of a pleasing character. Banners of different nations were hung from all the inns (after the fashion of election-time), and crowds of ladies, posted at windows or other convenient positions, awaited the arrival of the guests, while at a central part of the town, near the Castle, a large mass of laurel branches, surmounted with flags, bearing the word " Welcome," attested the gratification of the townspeople at their delightful place of residence having been selected as the scene of the anticipated festivities. THE GREAT EXHIBITION ADMISSION FEES Mr. Paxton has addressed a letter to Lord John Russell, in which he suggests that, with the exception of the first fort- night of the Exhibition, and one day ineach week subsequently, the admission should be entirely free. He urges thin on tlie priuciple that, as we have invited tlie whole family of man to participate in the first banquet the world has ever dedicated to peaceful industry and intellectual triumphs, if a tax were laid upon those who rnnie to partake of it, the whole purpose of tbe Exhibition would forego v grace winch otherwise would endow it with a crowning lustre. Mr. Paxton admits that the Com- missioners bave contracted a large debt which must be defrayed, and thai tbougb the sums taken uuder his plan would be con- siderable, a large deficit would remain; but this he solicits his lordship to meet by a Parliamentary grant, beiug emboldened to do so by the fact that the Exhibition would cause a large addition to the revenue of the country, calculated upon trust- worthy authorities to be upwards of two millions, aud that the item required to throw open the doors of the building to the public would form but a trifling proportion of the amount. This proposal of Mr. Paxton elicits from the Times the fol- lowing prudential suggestions:— "We question whether the building, three-fifths ol it being filled with counters aud cases, and having from east to west only one grand promenade and two very narrow ones, will allow as many us fifty thousand persons to circulate freely about it. Witii that number we apprehend there will be here and there such an accumulation as to be inconvenient, even to a well disposed crowd, and such as may afford opportunities to the ill disposed to do various sorts of mischief which we need not particularize. Now, any Monday, we will not say also Tuesday, there are at least a quarter of a million men and boys idle in and about this me- tropolis—ihe greater part of them 'on the lark,' and just us ready, weather permitting, to stroll to Hyde Park as to the nearest public-house. Now. we are not going to speak harshly of a London mob. Everybody knows that when a mob does mischief, it not so much the mob as some very small but very active knot of men in it. In fact, there is a husk and a kernel in every such mob ; tlie stupid husk merely looking on, and the kernel acting uuder the cover of the husk. But who is to distinguish the kernel from the husk? Fifty thousand Mon- day idlers from the manufactories of Loudon, mixed with a few thousands who admit of no description, would be very awkward customers for the Exhibition, however numerous, knowing, and judicious the police. In point of fact, the place would be at their mercy, aud as the plunderers would operate in the heart of an innocent crowd, entangled in twenty miles of cross passages, and twenty acres of valuable commodities, we hardly see how any force, military or constabulary, could act well upon them. So loug as the circulation is free there will be no danger; but with a quarter of a million, or only a hundred thousand, besieging the place, pressing iv, accumu- lating, whether innocently or otherwise, the circulation would not always be free. Nor do we see how it could be kept free without continual orders to 'move on,' which would make it impossible to get more thau a cursory glance at the objects exhibited. Unquestionably there is some degree of risk iv tlie admission of a crowd under the most favourable circum- stances. Croakers have all sorts of misgivings, — robbery, in- sult, girders breaking, infection, and we know not what besides. Now, we think we could answer for any multitude likely to be in at onetime on payment of a shilling; for a perfectly free mob -we would radier not be bad." A meeting took place at the Vestry-hall, Church-street, Lambeth, on Tuesday, to consider the question of provid- ing lodgings for mechanics and others of that class of soci.Iy who may visit London during the period of the Great Exhibition, and to hear the suggestions of Mr. Sanmuel Sidney, who bad, at the request oR the royal corn- rnissioners, visited the various local committees in the West of England upon this subject. Mr. R. Taylor, churchwarden, in the chair. Mr. SlDN Y being called upon to detail the plan he had formed, stated that he appeared on the present occasion in his private capacity as a ratepayer. and although lie had had the honour of being employed by the royal corn- missioners, they were in no way parties to the scheme he had suggested. I-le need not dilate upon the fact that large crowvds of persons would visit London during the Exhibition, and therefore he would at once state, that the report which lie had made to the commissioners upon the subject had met their approval. He had discovered that clubs had been formed in various parts of England to bring the people to London in large masses ; but up to the present time no organized plan had been adopted with a view to supply these people with lodgings during their stay in the metropolis. The consequence would be, that the householders of London would not derive that benefit from the Exhibition which it ought to confer upon them ; and he had therefore turned his attention to a plan which lie thought would be the means of enabling persons who might have rootms unoccupied to make a profit by letting them. Lambeth being an extensive parish, containing a large number of persons in an humble position of life who had rooms to let, but with- out the means of advertising them, lie had thought it advisable to mention his views to the inhabitants of this district. His plan was, that the parish be divided into convenient districts, and that in each of these districts a register should be kept by a person, whose duty it would be, upon the receipt of a small fee, to register the accom- modation in his own locality. When they had filled up their registers they should give one regular return, and afterwards appoint a secretary to make a summary of the accommodation, and place himself in communication with the various travelling clubs. By such correspondence they would mutually ascertain what amount of accom- modation would be required by those who desired to obtain a temporary residence in the metropolis. He felt that if this system were properly organized it would be a source of comfort and gratification to the large numbers of persons who would visit London this year, and at the same time confer a great benefit upon the poorer classes of persons in this extensive parish. The CHAIRMAN said lie thouglit the present plan was well deserving their attention, and lie hoped it might receive the support of the parishioiiers. There were a large number of persons in the parish who had rooms to let at the rate of 5s. or 6s. a week, and it was with a view to benefit this class of people that the plan had been brought forward. He did not think they ought to think lightly upon a subject of this nature, but to do all in their power to ascertain whether the plan was feasible, and if feasible to support it. PRODUCTION FOR THE EXHIBITION Ingenious Work of Art. A space in the department of the Fine Arts has been allotted for the display of a most ingenious and tastefa work of art, constructed by Mr. Oscar Byrn, a gentle-, man who, although long known to the public as a professor of the terpsichorean art, to his private friends only has the knowledge of his more intellectual talents been hitherto confined. The specimen which is to be submitted for public approval was commenced upwards of twelve months since, and, like many others of a similar kind, includ- ing a noble model of a tomb at Verona, was intended by Mr. Byrn for the decoration of his own residence, but having come under the notice of Mr. Stanfield and other artists, at their suggestion it has become destined to take its place at the Crystal Palace. The subject is a sylvan landscape with figures connected with the sports of the period of Charles 11., and it is formed entirely of. cork, cut out with an ordinary penknife. The form is circular, and calculated for the frame of a drawing, painting, &c. On either side, meeting at the top, is a magnificent tree, the stem, branches, and foliage of which ale delineated with the greatest accuracy, taste, and minuteness. Above, in the centre, a hawk may be seen about striking a heron, and in the lower ground, on the right, stands a falconer, in the costume of the period, with a hawk on his right thumb, and his left arm leaning on a gate or stile. In the central fore ground may be observed two dead boars (as though recently killed), and which are watched by one of the dogs used in boar hunting. On the left lies a stag, which appears to have met with the same fate as the boars, and near reclines a peasant youth. The form of the stag and that of the other animals, as also the human figures, are most elaborately pourtrayed and delineated (particularly as regards the human feature) with a fidelity which is perfectly marvellous, while every due proportion and accurate perspective is preserved throughout. The latter is particularly apparent in the vistas between the trees. The whole is in bas relief, and, when the material of which it is composed and the mode of construction be considered, must excite the utmost admiration for the ingenuity anid indomitable perseverance that has brought to perfection so ingenious a work of art, and which at present has no rival among the contributions to the forthcoming Exhibition.

PAXTON'S ScutaEi FORt A WINTErC GARDEN.- We stated some weeks ago that Mr. Paxton, with the view of carrying out his original idea of devoting the Exhibition building to the purposes of a winter garden, had suggested various alterations in it, calculated not only to improve its external appearance, but also to afford facilities for the increase of ventilation which would be required. We have been favoured with an early proof of the lithograph prepared with reference to this object by Messrs. Day and Son, and which will be made public in a few days, in which the proposed alterations are shown. They would add considerably to the present attractions of this unique and wonderful structure. At the east and west ends, and upon each corner of the upper storey, it is proposed to place two square chimneys, having the appearance of towers, and of a construction similar to the other portions of the building. The chimneys con- sist of two tiers of arches similar in every respect to those in the exterior of the building, there being four arches upon each of their sides. At each corner of the second storey or tier of the building are represented towers of one tier in height, and formed of three arches upon each side. The effect of these towers is exceedingly pleasing, and they tend greatly to remove the monotonous and step-like appearance which the building in its actual state presents to viev. At each end of the lower or ground storey, a semicircular sweep of columns is added, for the purpose of affording greater scope for the artistic arrangement of the interior of the building. A grass plat, ornamented with statues, is shown at each end, with a broad gravel drive round the whole of the building. The whole forms an exceedingly effective design, and the alterations, if carried out, would render the Crystal Palace one of the finest ornaments of the metropolis.- Morning Chronicle. UNrPID ScnsCrPTIoNs.--It seems, from the state- ments published concerning the subscriptions to the Great Exhibition of industry in Hyde-park, that, of the sums subscribed, an amount of £10,000 remains unpaid. In this city, where a nice attention is paid to punctuality, a wihh is expressed that the names of the defaulters should be made public. We state this rather for the purpose of encouraging the parties in arrear to attend to their en- gagements, than for that of creating unnecessary annoy- ance. Some years ago, a baronet, in East Sussex, sub- scribed £500 towards the erection of an infirmary in the county. He had an electioneering object to answer, and his liberality, before his appearance at the hustings, was a subject of weekly eulogiurn in the local journals; but, having succeeded or failed, as the case may have been, we do not pretend to remember which, though our impression is that he failed, the £500 subscribed was never forth- coining, and the panegyrics bestowed in the first instance were reversed. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Tuesday the attendance was considerably larger than on the previous day. Her Majesty honoured the building with her presence in the morning, and during the day the Duke of Wellington, the Earl of Glengall, the Earl of Carlisle, Earl Granville, Lord Broughton, Mr. Moffatt, M.P., and other Members of Parliament, as well as one or two of the Bishops were likewise present. The total amount of money received at the doors was £1,347. 17s. The produce of the sale of season tickets was £19. 19s. The number vis'itors paying the shilling admission was therefore about 27,000. On Wednesday, the total number of persons present was estimated at 40,000; and the amount received at the doors was £1,869, to which is to be added £13. 13s. for season tickets. On Thursday there was a larger number of persons within the building than on any day since the opening- the nave and transept were at times blocked up, and even in the remote avenues and compartments crowds of eager and animated sight-seers kept pouring along throughout the day, and by six o'clock the police had counted nearly 55,000 persons. The total amount of money received for admission was £2,370. 7s.; the amount received for the sale of season tickets being £22. 10s.; making a total for the day's receipts of £2,401. 17s. Nothing could have been more quiet and orderly throughout the day than the conduct of the visitors, who belonged princi. pally to the better sort of the middle class, On Friday the price of admission, as settled by the Royal Commission, was half-a-crown. It was not anti-. cipated that the number of visitors would be great, nor was it so, but the result exceeded the calculations made, and the receipts at the doors were £2,839 8s. The police returns represent that 30,845 persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and h.te Royal family continued their inspectionthis morniing, the people inside conducting themselves with marked propriety. During her last two visits the Queen -has taken particular notice of several branches of national industry, the contributors to which will feel flattered by such attention. Her Majesty has purchased, at the Exposition, a tiara of sapphires of great lustre and size, and a brooch, consisting of two enormous rubies, set round with dia- monds, by Lemonniere, of Paris. On- Monday morning her Majesty and the Royal visitors came to the Crystal Palace at nine o'clock, and, as some 400 or 500 exhibitorshad been formally requested to be present, more than Issual interest attached to the occasion. The receipts at the doors amounted to £2,129, and the number of spectators who entered the building was from 45,000 to 50,000. The extreme beauty of the weather was in favour of a great concourse of people, and the evidences of an extensive importation from the country were more conspicuous than they have hitherto been. It was particularlyremarkable in the large number of Quakers present, probably attracted to town by the religious meetings of the season. It is rumoured that the Commissioners have it in contemplation to purchase or hire the articles exhibited and make the spectacle of Industry and Art perpetual. The total amount of receipts at the doors, from the 1st to the 31st of May, were £123,801. 1os. 6d.

The Royal and distinguished party remained for nearly two hours viewing the nave, transept, and galleries; and few of the early visitors were aware of their presence, while thosewho recognised them, with much good taste, permitted them to pass unnoticed. Police- constable Griffin, said he was stationed, with other con- stibles, in the carriage-road leading to the Exhibition, orders having been issued by the commissioners in writ- jng to allow no carriages in that road, but to oblige all vehicles to go up Rotten-row. About three o'clock that afternoon he saw the defendant driving a phaeton and a pair of horses up the road at a rapid pace. He was then 30 or 40 yards from the carriage, and he immediately sig. nalled to the defendant to go back by holding up his ainds. The defendant took no notice of the signal, and 'he called out to him there was no thoroughfare for car- riages up that road, and that the defendant must go up Rotten-row. The defendant whipped his horses, upon which witness caught hold of the reins, and then received a dozen blows from the whip in the defendant's hand over his head and shoulders. The defendant called out to him to let go the horses, to which he replied, " No; you cannot go up this road." Witness, however, did let go the reins, as he feared the carriage would upset, as it was almost on the bank, and then the defendant whipped his horses into a full gallop and tried to get away. blie de- fendant, however, was stopped by the horse patrol. Thie defendant in his flight dropped a horsecloth from the phaeton. The blows with the whip were given over the face and shoulders. Aboutfour lashes fell on his face, drawing blood ?? Defendant alleged he did not know the nature of the orders issued to the police. He had driven along the same road the previous day without in- terruption, and he was not aware lie could not do so that dlay. He denied his horses were going faster than a trot. The constable seized the reins and nearly threw one of the horses, a young horse, oh its haunches. Fearing the horse would kick, he desired the constable to let go. The con. stable would not, and he lost his temper and struck him. This useful invention is constructed in the shape of a box, ols the top of which the sheet is fixed by means of points. Three turns of a handle draws the paper through an aperture in the top, and immediately afterwards throws it out on the other side neatly folded. Three sheets may be put through the process at once ; for while the first and second sheets are being put into shape by folders inside the machine, a third can be placed upon the top and acted upon by the outside folder. The Queen paid another early visit to the Exhibition yesterday, and remained nearly two hours. Among the many cnriosities to which our attention has been directed is a patent Indian rubber air-gun. The invention, which presents a singular combination of the elastic powers of vulcanised India rubber and air, has been invented and patented by Mr. John Shaw, of Glossop, musical-instrument-maker. It will doubtless be gladly welcomed by the lovers of ball-shooting, as enabling them to enjoy their favourite diversion at a fractional part of its former cost. Without any previous pumping., the requisite pressure of air for one discharge is procured instantly at the pull of the trigger, by a single stroke of a condensing syringe, actuated by a previously-extended India-rubber spring. There is no separate pump, no reservoir of condensed air, nor valve of any kind. The whole apparatus is enclosed in a case, which, being stocked, has the appearance of a light and elegant fowling-piece without a lock. The invention possesses several advantages over the ordinary air-gun, one of which is its superior safety, owing to the absence of a large reservoir of highly-condensed air, and to the extreme simplicity of its mechanism. The air which expels the ball is Powerfully compressed, at the moment of discharge, by a piston acting within a cylinder, and moved with great force and rapidity by the sudden contraction of a spring composed of a number of vulcanised India rubber rings previously extended by band in a very simple and easy manner; and the ball is propelled with a force quite equal to that exerted in the common air-gun, and with this great advantage, too, in addition to those which we have already named, that the force exerted is always the same; whilst, in the common air-gun, it diminishes with every discharge from the reservoir, requiring the aim to be constantly varying. The invention is certainly a very ingenious adaptation of the great elastic force of vulcanired India rubber, of which so much use has been made of late. We yesterday visited the model houses for four families, ' erected at the Cavalry Barracks, Knightsbridge, on thesouth ' side of the Crystal Palace, by his Royal HighneFe Prince , Albert in connection with the Exposition of the Works of Industry of all Nations. His Royal Highness has had this building raised on his own a ccount, with a desire of conveybig practical information calculated to promote the muchneeded improvement of the dwellings of the working choses, and also of stimulating visitors to the Exhibition, whose position and circumstances may enable them to carry out similar undertakings, and thus without pecuniary sacrifice permanently to benefit those who are greatly dependent on others for their home and family comforts In its general arrangement the building is adapted for the occupation of four families of the class of manufacturing and mechanical operatives, who usually reside in towns, or in their immediate vicinity; and as the value of land, which leads to the economising of space, by the placing of more than one family under the same roof, in some cases renders the addition of a third, and even of a fourth story desirable, the plan has been suited to such an arrangement, without any other alteration than the requisite increase in the strength of the walls. The most prominent peculiarity of the design is that of the receding and protected central open staircase, with the connecting gallery on the first floor, formed of slate, and sheltered from the weather by the continuation of the main roof, which alto screens the entrances to the dwellings. Tiie four tenements are arranged on precisely the same plan, two on each floor. The entrance is through a small lobby, lighted from the upper part of the door. The living room has a superficial area of about 150 feet, with a closet on one side of the fireplace, to which warm air may be introduced from the back of the range; over the fireplace is an iron rod for hanging pictures; and on the opposite side of the room a shelf is carried above the doors, with a rail fixed between them. The scullery is fitted up with a sink, beneath which is a coal-bin of slate; a plate rack at one end, drained by a slate slab into the sink, covers the entrance to the dust-shaft, which is encloeed bye balanced self-acting iron door. The dust-shaft leads into a closed deposPory under the stairs, and has a ventilating flee, carried up above the roof. The meat safe is ventilated through the hollow brickwork, sad shelves are fixed over the doors. A dresser flep may be fixed against the partition. The sleeping apartment., being three in number, provide for that separation which, with a family, is so essential to morality and decency. Each has its distinct access, and a window into the open air; two have fire places. The children's bed-rooms contain 50 feet superficial each, and, opening out of the living room, an opportunity is afforded for the exercise of parental watchfulness, without the unwholesome crowding of tho living room by its use as a sleeping apartment. The parents' bed-room, with a superficial area of about 100 feet, is entered through the scullery— an arrangement in many respects preferable to a direct approach from the living room, particularly in case of sickness. The recess in this room provides a closet for linen; and a shelf is carried over the door, with a rail fixed bane ath it—a provision which is made in each of the other bed-rooms. The water-closet is fitted no with a Staffordshire glazed basin, which is complete without any wood fittings, and supplied with water from a slate cistern ! in common of 160 gallons, placed on the roof over the party and staircase walls. The same pipes which carry away the rain water from the roof serve for the use of the closets. The peculiarities of the building as regards constructive arrangement, are. the exclusive use of hollow bricks for the walls ' and partitions (excepting the foundations, which are of ordinary brickwork), and the entire absence of timber in the floors and roof, which are formed with flat arches of hollow brickwork, rising from eight to nine inchee. set in cement, and tied in by wrought-iron rods connected wito cast-iron springers, which rest on the external . walls, and bind the whole structure together; the building is thus rendered fireproof, and much less liable to decay, then those of ordinary construction. The roof arching, which is levelled with concrete, and covered with patent metallic lava, secures the upper rooms from the liability to changes of temperature to which apartments next the roof are generally subject, and the transmission of sound, as well as the perc o l a ti on o f moisture, so common through ordinary floors, is effectually impeded by the hollow brick arched floors. THE GREAT EXHIBITION, The Building.- The royal commissioners have re- solved to give up possession of the building to the con- tractors on the Ist of next month. As far as they are officially concerned, then, their power with respect to the preservation of the Crystal Palace will entirely cease at the end of this month ; and any further steps, if such should be deemed necessary, for its permanent existence, must be taken on the part of the government. We understand that the contractors have received altogether about £150,000, and that something like £50,000 more must be forthcoming if the building is to be preserved. — Daily News. The Crystal Palace. — Her Majesty and Prince Albert paid a short and somewhat unexpected visit to the Exhibition Building, on Tuesday, having come up from Windsor expressly for the purpose. The royal party arrived at the Crystal Palace shortly after twelve o'clock, and were received by Mr. Dilke and Mr. Cole, of the executive committee, who accompanied her Majesty and the Prince through the building. Her Majesty passed down the foreign nave, where the dis- persed workmen of Babel would seem to have reas- embled. In this once brilliant promenade there remains but little to engage the attention, and her Majesty gave but a cursory glance at the relics as she passed by. Her Majesty then ascended the southern gallery, and returned towards the British side, where still less remains than in the foreign section. What seemed to engage most of her Majesty's notice was the building itself, which she had now a better opportunity of ob- serving than on the occasion of former visits, when her atteution must have been unovoidably distracted by the gorgeous accessories displayed on every side, and the living panorama moving within. Her Majesty was evidently much struck with the view which the interior of the building even now presents, and was heard to express herself in warm terms of admiration. The royal party retired before one o'clock. The Sappers and Miners have been withdrawn from further duty in the Exhibition, with the exception of some twenty or thirty, who still remain to assist in the removal of the packages. The Tuscan goods have been removed, and the American are to follow in a few days.

A young lady, accompanied by her husband and two female friends, who had been waiting for some time at the south entrance in the vain hope of obtaining a conveyance, was suddenly seized with symptoms which indicated that she was on the point of becoming a mother. With the aid of Mr. Duncombe, the assistant secretary, and several other of the officials, the lady was conveyed to the Commissioners’ room, and laid on the sofa. After the lapse of upwards of an hour she was placed in a cab, and shortly afterwards gave birth to her first child, a fine boy. The Standard says that both mother and child are progressing as favourably as might be expected under the peculiar circumstances of the case. The youthful stranger has thus narrowly, and perhaps he will by and bye think, unfortunately, escaped incident which would have rendered him the “observed of all observers.’’ The Question of the Preservation of the Building. —The question, “ What is to become of the Crystal Palace!” begins to assume a different shape from what it did some days ago. It seems that the Royal Commission*are reluctant to mix themselves up with the scheme of a winter garden, and that though they do not disapprove of that idea, they feel that its adoption is not included in their powers and should not compromise their action. Under the circumstances, therefore, and looking to the advanced period of the session, an impression gains ground that the most prudent course to follow at present is to procure a vote of the House of Commons, whichmay save the building from falling into the destructive power of the Commissioners of Woods and Forests. If they once get hold of it they will pull it down without compunction. They have the legal right to do so, and no one can doubt that they will exercise it. The conversion into a winter garden may, it is thought, be safely left in the hands of the public, who will not think less of that plan from its being kept in abeyance for some time longer. If the Crystal Palace ought to be removed, at least, let it not be done in too great a hurry. Let the Royal Commission expire decently without having its end hastened, and its fairy house abruptly pulled down about its ears by Lord Seymour.— Times. Practical Results of the Exhibition. —lt is satisfactory to know that the Great Exhibition is producing results very gratifying to the spirited caterers of the feast. One of the exhibitors of chemical preparations, has received more orders, in consequence of the advertisement which the Exhibition has proved to his goods, than he can possibly execute. The same good fruits are being reaped in many of the English departments, and the French, while complaining that the attractions of London have made a thin season in Paris, at the same time admit that what they have lost in customers at present has been amply made up by the orders they have received from London since May Ist. Another instance nearer home is that of Pirn, Brothers, of Dublin, one of the exhibitors of Irish poplin. Previous to the opening of the Crystal Palace three looms supplied all their order for poplin, while now forty are barely sufficient, and the trade is still increasing. Historical Chess Table. —A very singular and beautiful chess table has recently been placed in the Crystal Palace, and is July 81. much and generally admired. It is the work of gentleman named Graydon, and, independently of its costly decorative beauty, displays in its design amount of antiquarian reading which would have delighted the great Wizard of the North* had he been alive to pore over its chivalric accessories. The pieces, by happy conception, represent the Saracens and Cmsaders ; every one, kings, queens, knights, bishops, and pawns, having pedigree showing his connexion with the Crusaders. They are all well carved, and have this recommendation, that they are made to be played with, without rough comers to knock each other down, and with such a correct centre of gravity as to stand upright except on very strong provocation. The chess-player will easily understand the value of this peculiarity. The squares represent the banners and devices of the holy war, and the sides are ornamented with friezes copied from the celebrated ones of Schwanthaler, at Munich. The table itself is Italian walnut, and is supported by saracenic pillars copied from the best authorities. The work has evidently been the result of curious reading, much patience and research, and high veneration for the “game of games,’’ and only wants, we feel sure, to be more generally known to become the cynosure of at least all chess-players’ eyes at the Exhibition. The Jurors. —Tlie juries have all completed their tasks, but the decisions will remain a sealed book until the close of the Exhibition. The finance committee sat on Saturday, and Prince Albert was expected up from Osborne to preside, but the Committee were obliged to dispense with the attendance of his royal highness. Bearing of the Exhibition on the Postal Question. —The Great Exhibition has shown how every nation—even the most backward, and whose government is the most unenlightened and arbitrary—feels interested in the arts of life, and how emulous it is of superiority over another. Governments and nations appear to be now sensible of the advantages that would be derived by intercourse with and assistance from the people of other countries, varying in genius and energy, and possessed of distinct advantages from themselves; and that they can obtain benefit, not only from the rich, but from the poor but ingenious artisan and mechanic. It is impossible, however, that any kind of international intercourse can take place to the extent desired or demanded in future, without the lowering of the prohibitory foreign postage tax. It will be impracticable, after the Exhibition is over, for nations to fag on after the old fashion, and for the Post Office to mulct a man of three or four shillings every time he wants to communicate with a person the other side of the British Channel. A poor journeyman mechanic, half of whose relatives perhaps are living in America, cannot much longer be compelled to pay a shilling for every letter he sends to them. Nor will a man, who can send a letter from the Land’s End to John O’Groat’s for a penny, submit to pay ten times that amount, if he merely requires to send message from Folkestone to Boulogne. —Daily News. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Saturday at the Crystal Palace preserves its select and exelusive character, although its five shilling admission fee has now become matter of history. The company on Saturday last w,re rather thinly scattered through the building, but the gay dresses and, generally speaking, superior appearance of the various groups made up a more pleasing, although perhaps not so imposing, a picture, as the surging multitudes on the shilling days. Such of the aristoeracty as remain in town at this sea Son of Moors and watering-places, continue to use their season tickets. The Duke of Devonshire was ainong the visitors on Saturday, as were also the Duke and Duchess of Norfolk accompanied by one of the Ladies Howard, and Prince Callimachi, the son of the Turkish Ambassador in France. A pleasing result of the eomparatively thin attendance, was observable in the facility with which numerous invalids were wheeled about in their 3ath chairs, stopping before every object of interest, and thus whiling away the pangs of illness by a participation in the enjoyments of the healthy. There were young girls, struck down by premature disease, valetudinarians who dared not face slightest breath of the external atmosphere, and old men tottering on the very verge of human life, who, favoured by the govius loci, were enabled to compress within an hour's promenade, the inspection of more objects of interest than they had probably ever seen in the course of their whole previous existence. Among them was a nonagenarian old Squire Warren, of Hampden House, Rumford, Essex, who, quietly wheeled about in his easy chair, enjoyed the magnificent collection with aft much gusto as the youngest of the visitors. From the commencement of the act, the First Commissioner of the Woods, &c., is to be the First Commissioner of the Public Works and Buildings, with a salary not exceeding 2000/. a year, and he may be a member of the House of Commons. The other corn missioners of the Woods and Forests are to continue to hold their offices, and their salaries are to be provided for by parliament, but they are not eligible to a seat in the House of Commons. The other officers to continue I in their situations. Officers may be appointed to assist in the Public Works and Buildings. The management of all the Royal parks is to vest in the Commissioner of Works, and not, as heretofore, in the Commissioners of the Woods and Forests. Parliament will also have to provide for the expenses relating to the department of the Public Works, as well as in the management of the Woods and Forests, which latter department was paid out of the revenues of the Crown possessions. After the commencement of the act the First Commissioner of Public Works is to be an enclosure commissioner, a commissioner of Greenwich Hospital, and a commissioner for carrying into execution the acts relating to Highland roads and bridges, a commissioner for building , new churches, and the president of the Board of Health. THE LORD WARDEN'S VISIT TO DOVER.—On' Friday the Lord Warden arrived from Walmer Castle at half-past 11 to hold an extra harbour session. As soon asi his grace's carriage came in sight the usual salute was fired.' and he was received at the Council House by a guard of honour and the band of the Rifle Brigade. The principal business of the present meeting was to legalise the alteration that has been found necessary to make in consequence of deepening the harbour of the tidal signals, which, being arranged by the officers of the board, a petition was read from Mr. Grant, distiller and wine-merchant, representing the danger likely to arise unless the prominent piece of cliff at the back of his premises in Snargate-street, amounting to many hundred tons, were removed, and which he prayed might be done by the harbour board. 'FILE IRON TRADE. —The position of this trade remains unchanged. The demand is scarcely so brisk, and though sufficient to prevent any accumulation of stocks under the present limited amount of employment, it is inadequate to warrant any extension of make or any expectation of early improvement in prices, these are still without upward tendency, unremuneraive. It is stated that the most expensive descriptions of Iron, for Birmingham orders, are being delivered here at 8/. per ton, and the lowest at about five guineas net. MELANCHOLY OCCURRENCE.—On the evening of Tuesday last a man nanied John Armstrong, while walking with his wife on the south bank of the Clyde, in the vicinity of Lanark, was seized with a suicidal frenzy, and immediately thereafter plunged into the river at a place known by the name of Mary Dick's Hole, which is here very deep. His poor wife, who was far advanced in a state of pregnancy, rushed into the water with the view of rescuing him, but both sank and were drowned. Armstrong had been for some time previously in a disordered and desponding state of mind. The tragedy did not end here. Among the crowd who had been collected to the scene of the catastrophe was a man nerved i Lochead, who fell down n a fit, and was carried home in a state of i nsens ibility, from which he never recovered, expiring the next morning. It is conjectured that Lochead'a sodden death is to be attributed to the high state of excitement into which he was thrown by the melancholy occurrence narrated above,

THE BURMESE BELL AT LIVERPOOL.—This gigantic bell, which was one of the spoils taken during the Burmese war, but which is new erected on the Liverpool Landingstage, for the purpose of giving warning during a fog, is found not to emit so loud a sound as was anticipated, and therefore proves to be comparatively useless. During the dense fog on Saturday night last, when the guns of the Canada were heard for some hours before her position was discovered, the Burmese bell was rung, but could scarcely be heard on the shore close to the landing-stage. The metal is so thick that an ordinary clapper is wholly ineffectual in bringing out the full tone of the bell, which requires a power equal to that of a steam-hammer to ring it effectually. In the endeavour to bring out the sound in all its power on Saturday night the tongue or clapper was several times unshipped, and fell upon the landing -stage, making indentations nearly an inch deep upon the oak floor, but providentially doing no other damage : Had this occ urre d d ur i ng th e day-time, in all probability loss of life would have been the consequence, from the number of people usually congregated on the spot above which it is erected. DESTRUCTION OF A PIRATE SETTLEMENT.—GREAT SLAUGHTER.—The Spaniards have carried into effect their threatened chastisement of the Sultan and people of Suloo, but it has been attended with a great sacrifice of human life, without compassing any ultimate object. The fire from the forts is said to have been incessant and tremendous, and the resistance offered extremely desperate ; every inch of ground was disputed, amidst cries of" Viva la Rebut," on the one hand, and the war yell on the other. All their hope of security lay in Fort Daniel ; here the fight was maintained, the slaughter fearful, each in succession possessing themselves of the place, but eventually the Suloos were expelled. The Spanish flag was hoisted on the fortress by Father Pascual Ibanez, a priest of the order of Recoletos, who paid for his daring by being slain. The assailants on the right had little to overcome; the Sultan's and other forts in that direction were abandoned. The Sultan, in escaping from his fort, accompanied by some of his Datoos and a large force of, Suloos, encountered the right division, which appears to have been panic-struck. At all events the officers and two colonels were immediately after the battle placed in arrest, and will be tried by a courtmartial for cowardice. Had these officers acted with decision the Sultan must have been either slain or made captive, and his escape vexed the intrepid Governor- General. The defenders of Fort Daniel fought till the last—every one of them perished. The whole of the forts and part of the town were destroyed on the same night ; the captured artillery, consisting of 130 pieces of ordnance and a quantity of ammunition, were embarked. The number of the defenders slain could not be ascertained, but must have been considerable. The expedition then sailed for Zamboanga, leaving the Spanish flag floating over the ruins of the deserted city of Suloo. Owing to the advanced period of the monsoon, and the difficulties of following the Sultan into the jungle fastnesses, the Governor-General did not carry out his promised extermination, but he will probably return to the work when the time is more favourable. Among the friends of this residuary band there are two parties—one wishing them to go on to America ; the other wishing them to stop for a limited time in England, in order that they may have a chance of returning to their native country. At a meeting, held on Wednesday, of the committee of management of the proposed entertainment to be given at Birmingham, to Prince Albert and the Royal Commissioners, the following letter; in answer to a request previously made, that a deputation might be permitted to wait upon the Prince on the subject, was read:- . Buckingham Palace, May 28, 1851. Sir,-I have had the honour of receiving, and of sub- mitting to his Royal Highness Prince Albert, your letter of the 24th instant, with the accompanying copy of resolutions passed at the meeting of Exhibitors, ho., held at Birmingham on the 21st instant. " No one can rejoice more sincerely than his Royal High- ness at the success which has so far attended the Exhibition, and he is much gratified by the kind mention made by you of the part taken by him in promoting that undertaking. 11 It is, therefore, with much regret that his Royal Highness finds himself unable to accept an invitation conveyed to him in so gratifying and flattering a manner. But the nature of his present engagements, and the answer which he has already given to other bodies who have proposed to confer upon him a similar mark of attention, make it impossible for his Royal Highness to avail himself of it. I Under these circumstances, his Royal Highness commands me to add, that he will not give the proposed deputation from Birmingham the trouble of leaving home, unless, indeed, they should wish to see him on any other subject, when his Royal Highness will be happy to receive them. "I have the honour to be, sir, " Your obedient servant, "Will'am Lucy, EBg." " C. GREY. Mr. Lucy (the mayor), who presided at the meeting, stated that he had waited upon several members of the Royal Com- mission and of the Executive Committee in London, and had eudeavoured to ascertain their sentiments as to the manner in which the town could best extend its hospitality to the foreigners who are now on a visit to this country. The feel- ing of those whom he consulted appeared to be that a studied and formal public dinner, at which 100 or 150 foreigners might sit for four or five hours listening to speeches of which they would be unable to understand a word, would be a very undesirable arrangement. Earl Granville suggested that the parties to whom it was intended to show a mark of respect would much prefer coming to Birmingham, and seeing some of the manufactories; and that they might be received at the Town-hall, where votes of thanks in acknowledgment of public services might be passed, and a hearty welcome be tendered to the foreign visitors. Refreshments, it was added, might be provided, and the Botanic Gardens visited by such as were so disposed, but no farther expense need be incurred. In pursuance of these suggested arrangements, should they be carried out, afate might be arranged to take place at the gardens, or, if the weather was untavourable, Bingley Hall would be available; and the entertainment might then be participated in, not only by the foreign visitors themselves, but by their wives or such other members of their families as they had brought over with them. A miscellaneous conversation ensued, and ultimately, on the motion of Mr. Blews, seconded by Mr. John Lows, a com- mittee was appointed to make the necessary arrangements;, and. in compliance with-a suggestion that the price of adaius- sion should be as low as possible, a subscription towards a guarantee fand was entered into. The Debats has the following on the late accounts from Algeria:-" Submissions have already been received by General St. Arnaud on the side of Djijelli, but the resistance offered to him was very determined; the column (from 5,000 to 6,000 strong) was scarcely strong enough to support the combat against the multitude of Kabyles, concealed in the woods and among the rocks, whose musketry harassed our soldiers on every side. A column compelled to carry with it its provisions and ammunition, and more particularly to con- vey its wounded, finds itself in Africa, embarrassed in its movements by a convoy, which requires a considerable de- tachment for its protection, and which is continually assailed by the skirmishers of the enemy. A letter from Djijeli states the logs at 600 put hors de combat, of whom twenty- seven are officers; the number of men killed is stated to be 300. These numbers appear to us to be exaggerated, particularly in that of the killed, the proportion being generally only one-third of the wounded. It appears that the greatest loss has fallen on two companies of the 10th regiment, who, being at some distance on one of the flanks of the columns, were decimated by falling into an ambush. These companies are said to have left 200 on the ground, including five officers. On the following day the heads of our unfortminte soldiers were seen stuck up on either side of the road through which the column was marching. After taking three days' rest at Djijlli, the column of General St. Arnaud again started on the 19th to attack the mountain tribes. The combat of the "2th was remark- able from the great force displayed by the Rabyles, and by the excellent military arrangements made by the general to cut off their retreat and drive them into a ravine, where several hundreds of them fell under the fire of our sol- diers. The Cherif Bargghela was not present at any of these engagements, but he was engaged in operating a well, combined diversion on another quarter. On the same day that General St. Arnaud left Milah for Djijelli, the cheriff made a descent on Bougia, situated twenty leagues to the westward, after having excited the Kabyles in those parts, who had hitherto remained quiet, to rise against us. As we have already stated, he was put to the rout by the garrison of that place. The cberiff retired about four leagues from the place, where he continued to preach a holy war, but, as has been already stated, he was driven away by the tribes, the principal chiefs of which had solicited pardon from the French. It is said that Genreal Bosquet is to be detached from the column of General St. Arnaud, in order to form a junction with General Camou, who has left Setif with some troops, in order to attack the cherif, andre-establish the communications between the two towns of Setif end Bougia."

Sir William Reid, the chairman of the Executive Committer, paid his last visit to the Crystal Palace yesterday, previous to the assumption of his new duties as Governor of Malta, for which destination he starts this day. It will be recollected that Sir William Reid wax nut the first chairman of the Executive Committee, he having succeeded Sir It. Stephenson, who found the duties connected with it to he incompatible with his other engagements. When Sir William Reid entered upon his anluous and responsible functions as chairman, it was a work of no ordinary labour to reduce to anything like regularity the chaotic mass of perplexed details with which the committee had to deal. It was at first proposed and intended that the articles of the various exhibitors should be classed acconling to their kind and cour.fry. This was au ilea which would naturally suggest itself to the mind, and there can be no doubt it would have beta highly aluable as a convenient and suggestive means of comparison. But, besides other weighty objections to the carrying out of such a plan, it was at once seen that it would have completely destroyed the brilliant variety which the interior of the Crystal Palace presented under the different arrangement which was carried out, and which we believe was first segg,sted by Sir W. Reid. It struck him that, as the Crystal l'alaco was to be a receptacle for the products of the globe, an ideal geographical. distribution would appropriately assign to each country its fitting place, and would remove all jealousy as to best :tad worst positions. For this purpose, the transept wax to be considered an equatorial line, and thence, in succession, the different countries were to be assigned their spaces in accordance wit!, their actual proximity to it ou the earth's surface. This idea once fixed upon, everything thenceforwanl went on with order and regularity, and every one of 5010,000 spectators will bear testimony tnat the result was must successful. Sir W. Reid was surrounded, on this occasion of his last visit, by several of his fellow-labourers, of whom he took a warm partiug, bat who still accompany him with wishes for his future welfare, and will long remember hint for his kind and unaffected demeanour.
