THE GREAT EXHIBITION The Crystal Palace continues to be a daily-increasing source of attraction to the Londoners; for it must be borne in mind that as yet we have scarcely any foreign arrivals of visitors, and very few from the provinces. On the average, there are 8000 or 10,000 fresh visitors everyday; and if to these be added the 25,000 season-ticket holders, the capacity of the building may be readily estimated, because up to the present time there has been nothing like a crowd in any part, unless where the envelope-making machine, or the "mountain of light," or the French displays of gems, or, most attractive of all, the Italian court of statuary, form estuaries, around which the living tide rolls and suril , es in its onward course. Saturday is proverbially the fashionable day in London; and the osppearance of the Crystal Palace in the morning indicated that it was the great centre of attraction for that numerous class, the principal business of whose life appears to be amusement and excitement. For nearly two hours after the doors were opened there WP,3 a line of private carriages extending some dist%nce beyond the building setting down visitors ; and of these at least one-half were new arrivt.ls, as they passed through the pay doors instead of the season-ticket entrances. As a pecuniary speculation the success of the Great Exhibition has now been fully established. Her Majesty paid another early visit on Saturday morning. She was accompanied by Prince Albert, the Prince and Princess and Prince Frederick William of Prussia, the Princess Royal, and the Princess Louisa. The Royal and distinguished party remained for nearly two hours viewing the nave, transept, and galleries; and few of the early visitors were aware of their presence, while those who recognised them, with much good taste, permitted them to pass unnoticed. This is an improvement which we feel much pleasure in recording. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, attended by Mr. Birch, also paid a visit to the Exhibition on Saturday forenoon. Among the early arrivals was his Grace the Duke of Wellington. He passed through the British departmeat of the building, stopping occasionally to have a look at some of the curiosities displayed around him, or to note the progress of the unfinished portions. Although recognised by numbers who bowed to him as he passed, there was no attempt to crowd upon or inconvenience him, and he was left free to follow the bent of his inclinations. On arriving at the Indian collection he made a pause, and, influenced probably by old reminiscences, suddenly turned into the department and took a survey of the exhibition, which is still very incomplete, the greater portion of the packages from India having only arrived on Friday. On reaching the transept tile duke again paused, apparently undecided whether he should retire or proceed further. After a moment's deliberation he resumed his peculiar gait and crossed over to the foreign side, where his appearance created a much greater sensation, the exhibitors pouring out from the different compartments as he passed, and all saluting him. He remained for upwards of an hour in the building. Yesterday morning the Queen, accompanied by Prince Albert, again visited the exhibition. During the time the royal party spent in the building the weather was fine, and the number of visitors very great; but in the afternoon heavy rains fell upon the great glass roof, and in some places penetrated it. So unfavourable, indeed, was the state of the weather that we expected to find the building half deserted. Public curiosity has, however, great perseverance when once fairly excited, and notwithstanding so formidable a drawback, 1600/. was taken in ss. payments at the door. The sale of season tickets also experienced a decline, but not so great as might have been expected, for nearly 750/. was collected in this way, the average having for some days past considerably exceeded 800/. The completion of various portions of the foreign department progresses but slowly. Persia represents, as yet, only sightless ranges of deal fittings and the back part of Turkey is not out of the hands of carpenters. The nave still continues to receive fresh accessions, among the latest of which is a lump of native silver, 1451b5. weight, from one ef the Chilian silver mines. Near M. Dueroquet's French organ, a handsome bronze fountain is being erected, and in front of the compartments of Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Russia, and the United States, are several large pedestals, which we anticipate are destined to receive some of the late arrivals. Power's Greek Slave Girl has been placed upon a revolving pedestal, so as to enable all the beauties of the figure to be fully seen. France is at length bestirring herself, and has at least fifty hands entirely employed in the work of decoration. The surplus of her exhibition, in metal bedsteads, billiard-tables, &c., has been transferred to a wing of the United States gallery, where they fill up one of the extensive gaps which the misunderstanding with the American exhibitors has left unoccupied. We cannot leave this remote and deserted district without bearing our testimony to the courage of an American fancy soap manufacturer, who has, Arab like, pitched his encampment in a waste remote from all human sympathy, and who proceeds in the work of decorating and arranging a very creditable display of his manufacture, in the vague hope that some stray visitor will find him out and admire his portraits of the Queen and other eminent persons "in soap," or his really handsome Gothic window, the stained glass panes being formed of transparent soap. Adverting again to the purely decorative portion of the contents of the Exhibition, we may remark that the main avenue is profusely decked with pieces of sculpture, both by British and foreign artists. In the eastern half the spectator will observe a fine statue of Dr. Goodall, Provost of Eton, by Weeks. The figure is represented sitting, and is dignified and grand in effect. Near this is placed a colessal statue in bronze of the late Marquis of Bute, by J. E. Thomas. A very prominent object of art in this portion of the building is a statue of her Majesty seated, elevated on a massive and highly-decorated pedestal, the whole cast in zinc, bronzed by the Vieille Montagne Zinc Mining Company. The face bears a strong resemblance to the Queen, but the head is rather too large, and the circlet by which it is surmounted is much too heavy. The sculptor who has executed this work is M. Denten. In close proximity to this imposing object are placed two beautiful female figures by R. J. Wyatt, to which no names or descriptions are affixed, and to which no clue can be found in the catalogue. Both fi e ures are represented standing, the one holding a wreath of flowers in her hand, and the other appearing as if just emerged from the bath. The forms of these figures are perfect, and the grace of their attitudes cannot well be excelled. A sitting statue of Dr. Jenner, by Marshall, is a work of art that commands attention; it is replete with the finest character. We observe by the label affixed to this figure that it is proposed to erect it by subscription gathered from all nations—a fitting tribute to the memory of a man who has conferred so much benefit on the whole human race. Next to this are placed two groups by Italian artists—one is a Cupid and Psyche, by Benzoni, and the other a group by Rinaldi, founded on an incident in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered." Tney are in:eresting groups, but not equal to some other pieces of sculpture by foreign artists which we shall have occasion to notice. Near the centre of the avenue are placed two large groups bearing no sculptor's name, and to which there is no reference in the catalogue. One appears to be intended to represent Charity, being a female figure, supporting an aged man and an emaciated youth. The other teems to represent Destitution, and consists of an old man, Ugolino-like, surrounded by dying children. The first of these groups is by far the finest, and few pieces of modern sculpture display a more perfect composition, or a figure more replete with dignity and expression than that of the female which forms its centre. At the base of this last-mentioned work are placed several has reliefs—one of which is a clever copy in bronze of the celebrated picture of the" Wreck of the Medusa;" and two youthful figures by Etex. In the immediate vicinity of these is a small bronze figure of Pandora bearing the Casket in her hand; a bronze group of Venus and Cupid, by a sculptor named Pradier; and also a very spiritedly designed and elastic figure in beonze of a Dancing Faun, by Lequesne. The next object which attracts attention is a fine heroic group, elevated on a pedestal of considerable height, by De Seigneur. The subject of this appears to be, for there is no reference to it in the catalogue, the Vanquishing of Satan, by the Archangel Michael, or it possibly may be an allegory to indicate Religion triumphing over Sin; the angelic figure has much dignity and grace. Near to this is placed a very spirited production in bronze, by Jean Debay ; the subject is a Stag Hunt. It is a fine group, full of energy and life-like movement, and we can hardly imagine that such a subject could have been more happily represented in sculpture. As the spectator advances towards the eastern termination of this avenue his eye encounters those pieces of sculpture which have been contributed by the artists of Prussia, Belgium, France, and other continental states. One of the striking of these occupies a central position; it is a colossal equestrian statue of Godfrey of Bouillon, by Eugene, a Belgian artist. We gather from the label affixed to it that a bronze cast of the same statue has been set up at Brussels. This piece of sculpture is so large in its dimensions that more space than even this enormous building affords is requisite to view it with proper effect. The same artist has also a statue of Truth in plaster, and two small statues, called the "Happy Child," amusing himself with flowers ' and the "Unhappy Child," lamenting over his dilapidated drum. Both possess nature and character. Near these is seen a recumbent statue of Psyche, by Fraikin, another Belgic artist, the action of which is rather extravagant; and another, more elegant, of Psyche running with a Cupid in her arms. The statue of Cain, by Jehotte, a Belgic sculptor, is natural in action and expression, though hardly elevated enough in form. The brand lies at his feet, and his face expresses a natural horror at the deed he is supposed just to have consummated. There is a group in plaster of " Cupid disarmed," by Jaiquet; a recumbent stag, in sine, by Schutz; and a group of the binding of Mazeppa to the wild horse by Pierotti, a spirited and clever production. Near these will be observed two sweetly-designed female figures, portraits of young ladies, by Monti; and a statue of Achilles receiving the mortal wound in his heel, by Fraccaroli. This statue has merit in the action, but the form is hardly heroic enough. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. We have noticed at different times the dissatisfaction which has been expressed by the representatives of some foreign countries with reference to the amount of space allotted to their exhibitors. Except in the case of France, these differences had almost entirely disappeared; but the commissioner of our continental neighbours—M. Salandrouxe de Lamornaix—continued still to struggle for increased accommodation. Happily the ExecutiveCommittea have been able to settle in an agreeable and friendly manner their differences with this gentleman, who will now direct all his energy to the preparation and arrangement of the large area which his countrymen possess in the building. It appears that from two causes 12 bays have been placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee in the eastern or foreign half of the Exhibition. In the first place Norway and Sweden and the States of Northern Germany had not supplied a sufficient quantity of articles to cover their allotments. They therefore willingly resigned their surplus space. America, again, wished to exchange a portion of the ground area assigned her for increased room in the galleries. Her agent has acted, we understand, with great liberality in the course of these new arrangements, and has mistily and cordially co-operated with the Executive Committee in securing a satisfactory settlement with our other visitors from abroad. All parties are now, we hear, perfectly well pleased with reference to the point of space; and it is sincerely to be hoped that no fresh disagreement may arise to destroy that spirit of harmonious and combined action the establishment of which becomes every day of greater importance. France,Belgium, Austria, and the Zollverein have all been especially benefited by the additional accommodation placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee, and we take it for granted that the difficulties arising from the disappointments of intending exhibitors whose contri• buttons, after inviting, we might be obliged to shut out, have now been overcome. We have again, however, to warn our friends fr.m abroad that their arrangements are still in a very backward state, and that they must without delay put forth their best efforts to have every thing in order by the let of May. Their things come in slowly, and the Custom-house examinations neces • sarily occupy a great deal of time. Besides M. du Seigneur's specimen of sculpture a splendid organ will be placed in the nave as ono of the most striking articles in the French collection. This is the fourth organ we have heard of as intended for exhibition, and it is quite clear that the Crystal Palace may be made available for the pleasures of sound as well of sight, if the Royal Commissieners think fit that it should be so. Over the vast expanse the sublime music of the Creation may be made to circulate, and while thousands of spectators assemble to admire the chief wonders of human industry the swelling notes may be sounded in their ears which so fitly recall the greatness of that Power by whom are all things. 'rho American contributions brought over by the packet St. Lawrence are now rapidly arriving at the buildieg, and although the quantity is not so great as was at one time expected, the quality will, it is believed, be not unworthy of the great nation which acknowledges this to be its mother country. The collection includes splendid specimens of copper, iron, and zinc ore, to illustrate the mineral wealth of the United States; machinery to show the mechanical ingenuity of the people; and a most varied display of raw produce and manufactured articles, including an air-exhausted metal coffin, in which a human body could, it is said, be preserved for ages without decay, and which contains, we hear, a bouquet of flowers as fresh as when it was first placed there. The Commissioner from Tunis has been the first foreign agent to unpack. Judging from what we saw, this small section of the Exhibition will not be the least interesting portion of it ; and the fair sex especially will flock to a compartment where they may have an opportunity of comparing their own style of apparel with that of the Moorish ladies. Among the entries in the catalogue of articles which the Boy has sent over is one which runs thus, " The beauty's dress on leaving the bath." The display is rich in specimens of male attire, also in mule trappings blankets, and stilettos. Turning to our own part of the Exhibition, there are several matters of importance to communicate since our last notice. With reference to the amount of work to he accomplished before the Ist of May, it now appears certain that the chief difficulty to be overcome lies in the completion of the building itself. As if the arrears of work already existing were not sufficient, new labours arise of a serious, but, we trust, not insurmountable character. The ridge and valley roof during wet weather has always leaked a little at different points, but it was believed that when the Paxton gutters bed been well pitched and the interior of the sash bars painted no inconvenience on this score could be experienced. The late heavy rains have dissipated this idea, and water has penetrated in so many places that serious fears are entertained by some as to the; practicabilty of securing that exemption from drip or damp which is indispensable in such a building. We believe that the desired object can still be accomplished by administering a thick coat of paint to the sash bars on the outside; but this ceisstitutes a formidable addition to the work which the contractors have now scarcely six weeks to finish. Messrs. Fox and Henderson have done wonders, and we have no doubt will complete this great undertaking in a manner creditable to themselves, to their profession, and to their country. Their reputation is indissolubly bound up with the satisfactory manner in which the Crystal Palace fulfils the objects fur which it has been created. If its gigantic roof cannot be made water-tight, Mr. Paxton's design, and their execution, will be equally condemned as failures. Not only so, but we should be exposed as a people, to just complaint from the countries whose industrial products we have invited to an imperfect shelter from our damp and showery skies. Fancy the exhibitor of costly brocaded silks from Lyons, or of rich velvets from Genoa, watching the effects of a summer storm of rain oozing through the great window frames above his head, and drop after drop irretrievably tarnishing the rarest products of his taste and skill. The contractors and the Executive Committee are both fully alive to the necessity of curing this defect, and accordingly during Friday and Saturday the glass roof of the building has been in possession of gangs of painters and glaziers, who, carrying their scaffolding about with them, and apparently like flies, without specific gravity, crawl about in every direction, stopping up chinks and crevices with putty and paint, and repairing fractured panes of glass, When in addition to this precaution the calico covering has been got up, the wind will be prevented from driving the rain with such force through any seams that may still remain open. We are glad to find that the preparations in every part of the western half of the building are pushed on with untiring energy, and with every prospect that our native industry can by the Ist of May fearlessly invite the inspection of the whole world. The department of machinery still takes the lead, and many of the most interesting objects comprised in it are far advanced towards completion. The public will regret to hear that in this part of the collection, closely identified as it is with the industrial reputation of the country, the Nasmyth hammer, one of our greatest mechanical wonders, is not to be included. The space requisite was allotted to Mr. Nasmyth for the purpose of showing his great invention, and everybody is quite at a loss to understand why at the last moment he declines coming forward; the expense of fitting up cannot be the obstacle. Among other objects which will no doubt attract great attention, we hear of a model of Plymouth Breakwater, executed with surprising fidelity, and containing, among other things, the representation of a brig, two inches long, —the complete epitome of a vessel-of war. All the guns, masts, yards, rigging, &c., are giving, and even the ruaning-gear is rove and the deck planked. There is only one other point which it is proper to touch upon in this part of the subject. It appears that the local committee of Sheffield, after attaining a pre•eminenco among all the towns in England fur the dilatory and unsatisfactory manner in which they conducted their preparations for the Exhibition, set the finishing stroke to their conduct by sending in for the approval of the Executive Committee a plan for the arrangement of their goods, which it was quite impossible to accede to. The proposal to select the principal firm in their own town to represent the section of cutlery by trophy in TUESDAY EVENING, the centre of the nave awakened among them all the fires of local jealousy. They had no objection to a London manufacturer, however small his business, occupying the pest of honour; but that Rodgers should have it was not to be endured. Fortunate it is for the Commissioners that they have deprecated so decisively the idea of arousing individual rivalries. It is obvious that however great the progress hitherto made, and however certain the prospect of all being ready by the Ist of May, the time is now close at hand when the Executive Committee must begin to tighten the screw upon exhibitors, to gather up the ends of the great work entrusted to them, to get a stage clear of paint pots and men in paper caps before the curtain rises and the performance begins. The following is the substance of some very important resolutions which they have come to in order that the opening may take place, as announced by the Commissioners. On the 2d of April the entrance into the building for carts and waggons is to be entirely closed, and the flooring still unlaid completed. No goods will be admitted after that date, except such as do not exceed six feet six inches in width. Between the 3d and the 10th of April everything brought into the building must be brought in unpacked; otherwise it will be put outside, and remain there till this condition is complied with. After the 10th, and from then till the 20th any goods that come in, without special leave for the delay (this special leave being granted only in rare cases), must pay a fine towards the funds of the Exhibition according to the following rates.—For every article weighing less than 281 b., 10s.; for every article weighing more, 11. per 281 b. After the 20th no goods can be received, except, perhaps, from foreign countries, under particular circumstances. These stringent regulations, if resolutely carried out, will do more than anything else to make exhibitors wind up their preparations in good time.— Times. BANK OF FRANCE. THE GREAT EXHIBITION The near approach of the closing day only increases the anxiety of the public to visit the Crystal Palace. Yesterday's was another enormous gathering, and would have been still greater but for the threatening aspect of the weather in the early part of the day. The great mass of the visitors aro }till country people, and the manner in which they crowd round the moat familiar objects proves them to be in the majority of cases visitors for the day only. The preparations for the final close go on with unabated vigour, and we believe that the ceremonial will take place in the quietest possible manner, without any musical " effects" vocal or instrumental, notwithstanding the strong hints daily thrown out by a morning contemporary. The public will and must take a final leave of the building on Saturday, the 11th of October, when, it will comfort our contemporary to know, any spontaneous burst of harmony will not be prohibited by the executive committee, but it must be provided by the public, and not by the royal commissioners. On the Wednesday following Prince Albert will attend, when the report of the jurors will be read by Lord Causing. To this his royal highness will respond in a short speech, and in 10 minutes after the workmen will be admitted, and commence the removal of the goods, and the preparations for the dismantling of the Palace. On this occasion the only persons admitted will be the exhibitors, and perhaps one or two friends each, by ticket, the public, ticket holders and all, being entirely excluded. This announcement we make on the highest authority. The suggestion for removing the Crystal Palace bodily to Battersea fields has created a good deal of amusement among the habitu.4, especially those who are at all acquainted with the winter aspect of thel locality in question. The Palace is already by no means impervious et top, and if it were placed in a situation where two or three feet of extra water might safely be calculated on at every spring tide during winter, its public utility in a sanitary point of view would become more than problematical. I THE GREAT EXHIBITION. I Her Majesty and his Royal Highness Prince Albert, accompanied by the Prince of Wales and several other members of the Royal family, paid an early visit to the Exhibition on Tuesday morning. They inspected the different parts of the building, and watched with interest the process of examining the different packages by the Custom house officers. Her Majesty has probably never before been so near an eyewitness of the machinery which contributes so largely to the public revenue. The mode in which the work is conducted has its peculiar interest, like everything else coniected with this great undertak- ing. As the waggons containing the packages arrive within the building they are driven to the centre of the transept, and there unloaded and marked by a Custom- house officer. Fronithe transeptrelaysof Sappers convey the packages in trucks to the compartment of the foreign country whence they come. Deposited in this compart- ment another band of Custom-house officers are there to receive them, and a fresh party of Sappers with chisels and other implements rapidly break open lids or other coverings, and with military determination sweep every- thing before them until the goods lie revealed. Tuesday the Zollverein compartment was the principal one to which goods were consigned, thbugh arrivals also took place for the Swiss and Canadian collections. Entering within the hoarding, where Sappers were vigorously engaged in breaking open great boxes, one might have almost fancied that some scene of plunder was in progress. The variety of articles that the different packages presented was also curious, and even the Custom-house people themselves, hardened as they must be against that species of excitement, appeared interested in the miscellaneous character of their occupation. One box contained a set of trays, another earthenware images, another silk hand- kerchiefs or gloves, another parasol handles, another a machine for knitting, articles of general merchandise alternated with works of art and specimens of skilful handicraft. And we may observe that even at this early stage in the arrival of foreign goods there are signs that the palm of cheap production, and the merit 'of an industrial system founded on the principle of utility, are not to be resigned to us without a contest by the States of the Zollverein. Within the space allotted for our native contributions few arrivals have taken place, and beyond the apportionment of ground hardly anything has as yet been done. On Tuesday morning, at a little before eleven o'clock, a highly interesting experiment was made at the building with a view to ascertain practically the strength of the galleries, both under the condition of supporting what is technically called a dead load, and also a rolling or moving one. A few simple figures will pretty clearly explain the basis of calculation upon which the dimensions of the several parts comiposing the galleries have been determined. The points of support on plan occurring at the angles of squares of twenty-fuur feet, the area of each bay of gallery is-equal to 576 square feet. From various experiments which have been made by Mr. Brunel, and by other engineers, it has been found that the average weight of a number of persons standing together in a confined space rarely exceeds 501b. per square foot ; that by pack- ing men as closely together as possible it might be brought up to 701b. or 801b.; and that, not even by picking out the heavy men and gathering them into the smallest com- pass, could an average of one cwt. per square foot be obtained. One cwt. was therefore assumeri as an amount certain to cover any unforeseen combination of circlin- stances. Oii this assumption no bay or gallery of twenty- four feet square could possibly be called upon to carry a load equal to thirty tons As it was ingeniously con- trived by the arrangement of the flooring that the weight should be distributed over four girders, and every girder had been submitted on the ground to a pressure of fifteen tons (that being only half the maximum weight that each was capable of supporting) applied exactly at the points upon which the floor would have to be borne, it will be manifest that a very large margin had been left to pro- vide for contingencies arising from any motion which it was possible might be communicated to such a load. The immediate object of the experiment tried on Tues- day was to assure by various tests of the severest character to what extent oscillation could be conveyed to the gal- lery by the regular motion of a living load, and to ascer- tain whether the provision which had been made to meet such contingencies was sufficient. The preparations made for the experiment consisted of the construction of a perfect bay of gallery with its floor, binders, girders, and connecting pieces, in every respect complete and similar to the actual gallery, supported upon four points bedded on temporary foundations; rows of planks, the full width of the platform, led up to it and down from it, so that a row of men as wide as the gallery, might be able to march up and down in close column. Three hundred workmen were first assembled by the contractors, and allowed to cover the platform and the planks connected with it. They were then compressed into the smallest space upon which they could stand. The load borne on the planks represented the share of pres- sure which would be produced by the crowding of ad- jacent bays of the gallery. The amount of deflection produced by this load was inappreciable. The men then walked regularly and irregularly, and ran over it. The elasticity of the floor-allowing play to the timbers and wrought iron work-was admirably developed by this test, and it becarue apparent that this quality of elasticity was of the greatest value in protecting the cast iron girders from sudden shock. Thus, in the severest test which could possibly be applied-when the men, standing closely packed together, continued jumping simul- taneously several minutes, although in regular vibrations of the floor the binders played up and down-the ex- treme deflection of any of the girders that could be ascertained at any moment did not exceed one-quarter of an inch. As the contractors' men were unable to keep military time in their step, and it was considered desirable to as. certain the effect of perfectly regular oscillations, the whole of the Sappers and Miners on the ground, in close columns, were marched over and over and round and round, and were finally made to mark time in the most trying manner. With the result of this last test the eminent scientific men present expressed themselves highly gratified, observing, that while at the climax of vibration the motion did not exceed that common in ordinary London houses at evening parties. A minute examination of the several parts of the con- struction likely to be affected by similar experiments, made immediately upon their completion, bore witness to the fact that no portion had suffered any injury what. ever from the strains to which it had been exposed. When it is remembered that the aarangements for the Exhibition in the galleries require passages only six feet wide on the sides of the gallery, counters for light goods occupying the central portion most liable to strain; and when it is borne in. mind that the galleries are of such extent as to render uniform vibration over any consi. derable portion of their whole area impossible, the results of the experiments we have described cannot but be regarded as calculated to relieve the apprehensions of the most timid. The committee appointed by the Bishop of London to take measures for affording the numerous visitors of the metropolis this year thle opportunity of attending public worship according to the ritual of the Church of England are proceeding in their inquiries and arrangements for that purpose. On Sunday, the 4th of May, a sermon will be preached by his Lordship, at St. Paul's Cathedral, on the occasion of the opening of the Exhibition. The incumbents of many parishes and ecclesiastical districts have informed the committee that they will be able to provide means of public worship for any probable influx of strangers acquainted with the English language. They will give additional facilities to strangers of attend- ing the ordinary services, and institute, if necessary, extra services in their churches, or open schoolrooms or hired buildings for divine worship. In some cases assistance towards meeting the expense will be required from the funds at the disposal of the committee. Offers of assistance have been received from thirty-three clergymen-either Frenchmen or Germans by birth, in English orders-or Englishmen well acquainted with the languages of the continent. It appears that in churches and consecrated chapels the liturgy can only by law be read in English; but seven unconsecrated or proprietary chapels have already been placed at the disposal of the committee for extra services in foreign languages. Brompton Chapel, Kensington, has been engaged for a French service, and St. Mary's, Park-street, Grosvenor- square, for German. The arrangements for other chapels lkave not yet been completed. As the attention of foreigners will be especially directed o our cathedral service, the authorities of St. Paul's and Westminster Abbey have it in contemplation to provide, if possible, additional means or opportunities of attending public worship in those magnificent edifices during the Exhibition. To assist foreigners in following the services of the church, the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge is printing editions of the Book of Common Prayer with English and French, or English, French, and German, in parallel columns. Copies of these useful works will be widely circulated by the committee. At the request of the committee the vicar and church- wardens of St. Martin-in-the-Fields have agreed to open St. Martin's Church for a course of evening lectures, to be delivered once a week during the Exhibition by some of our most eminent divines. The names of the preachers and the subjects of the lectures will be announced as soon as they are determined. For the benefit of strangers, a guide to places of public worship will be printed containing a list of all churches, chapels of ease, and proprietary chapels, with the hours of divine service in each. A number of tracts suitable to the approaching occa- sion have been prepared by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and effective measures will be employed to circulate them, and to offer Bibles and Prayer-hooks, both in English and foreign languages, at a cheap rate. A convenient depository will be formed at Knightsbridge for that purpose. To promote friendly intercourse with religious foreigners, it is proposed to hold a weekly meeting, and to open one or two reading-rooms, in which foreign pastors and other strangers. properly introduced, will have the opportunity of meeting the clergy, and in which a register of addresses will be kept. A reading-roonm has already been engaged in the parish of St Pancras. A special committee has been formed to make these arrange- ments. The above are some of the 'measures adopted by the Bishop and clergy of the metropolis to give foreign visitors a friendly reception, to provide them with the means of public worship, and to counteract, as far as possible, the moral and spiritual evils arising from a large and miscellaneous assemblage of strangers, including many of the worst and most dangerous characters, not only of other countries, but of our own. A CARRIAGE FOR TVIE E AqrfT..-Messrs. Meller and Turner, of 121, Long-acre, have prepared a chariot for the Exhibition, and a rare specimen of coach building it is. Our vehicles have no equal, and almost every foreign Prince rides in one. Naturally we shall have the French endeavouring to give us a wrinkle in this line, and they, in their turn, will regard with interest what we put forward as our best. We have gone on improving, decidedly amending as well as altering, our vehicles for centuries past, and this chariot is our latest invention. The makers have evidently aimed at the com- bination of lightness, strength, and elegance; indeed, these are the qualities which they must aim at uniting. Here we have lightness, consistent with durability, and the artisan has done his best. Cinderella never had a more beautiful coach. It is a credit to the trade, and the taste bestowed upon it is unquestionable. The inside is rose pink and silver-think of that, ladies ! The hammer cloth, white and silver. The body, black above, so glossy that the colour is lost in a mirror, and white, picked out with vermillion, below. The iron work all plated silver. It is suspended on snakes, and emblazoned in first-rate style. Thecharacterisdecidedly English-neat, compact, strong-and you behold perfection in its way. A French- man would bring art to his aid here, and garnish more elaborately; but no foreign hands could beat the work manship here exhibited. The vehicle suggests thoughts of marriage with an heiress :ike Miss Talbot, the luxury that might followv were the match what it ought to be, and such a pair of horses as one does not see out of England. BILLIARD TABLE FOR THE ExHIBITIoN.-Among the numerous articles about to be exhibited at the Crystal Palace, is a billiard table which we have been invited to inspect at the manufactory of Thurston and Co., Cathi- rine-street, Strand. This piece of workmanship, from the hands of the first billiard -table makers in the world, will naturally prove an object of curiosity. Messrs. Thurston have adhered rigidly to the character of the article, that of strength, solidity, uniformity. There are no vagaries in the produe tion. It is a massive and uni- form piece of workmanship, displaynig more handicraft than art. Tile legs are elaborately carved out of solid wood-mahogany-of which the frame consists, and not even a morsel of ivory mars the general and substantial effect. The cloth is, of course, laid on slate, reduced to a level so nice as mathematical precision and human skill can make it, and the eye and finger may search in vain for an inequality. Our foreign rivals may produce something more fanciful in design, but the superiority of this billiard-table-as a billiard-table-will be seen at a glance. COLOURED GLASS.-Mr. Hurwitz, house decorator, of Brydges-street, Covent-garden, is about to exhibit a curious- and remarkably beautiful specimen of glass embellishment, in the shape of an altar tablet, which is to retain its vivid hues and distinct figures for centuries. The process is simple. The artist engraves upon very thick glass the letters to be represented. These lie gilds or paints in choicest and brightest colours, and the gold or paint shows through the flat reverse. Over the side that is cut and coloured goes a thick coat of durable material, and this hardens, making all betwveen that and the glass air tight. You have then a glass face to most exquisitely formed and highly decorated letters or figures, detying even the weather. This is likely to lead to an improvement in altar pieces, tomb inacriptiona, namnes, and other wvritings in and outside houses, &c., &rc.,-&c., and we know not what else in connexion with decorative art. Mr. Hurwitz deserves much credit for lils pains and ingenuity. AN EXHIBITION GsEi.-SPLENDID TAPrSTRY.-We have been afforded a view, previous to its transmission to the Crystal Palace, of a most 'beautiful specimen of English industry and taste. This truly uniqoue and elegant piece of workmanship in tapestry has been pro- duced by Miss Flower, the well known embroideress of Duke.street, Grosvenor-square. The design is sin- gularly appropriate and elegant. The clever artiste, has brought together, worked on strong canvas, the flags of all nations. The distribution of the various standards, twenty - two in number, distinguishing the national emblazonments of the chief Powers of the world, at once strike the eye for truth, precision, and tasteful appor- tionmient. In the centre tue Star and Garter of England Msines (literally) magnificently conspicuous. The ma- terials which have been used to produce this gorgeous effect comprise beads of choice selection, cheville, beauti- fully interworked, and gold silk, thle ensemble of the con- gregated colours presenting a distinct appearance of a refined fresco. The happiness of the idea, as well as the beauty and fidelity of execution, can alone be appreciated by those who will bestow attention on the performance, which, we may mention, has elicited the warmest enco- miums from the elite of society; and we should say that the tasteful and graceful blending of the respective ban ners of the nations of the world with England's sove- reign emblem, cannot fail to secure the approbation of our foseign frieiids, while so happy an 'instance of English taste and English industry must infallibly gain the unqualified approval of the British public.. _ THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The experience of the second shilling day (Tuesday week) was such as to prove, in the most convincing manner, that the class of persons for whose benefit and instruction the Great Exhibition was mainly intended, know how to avail themselves of the advantages which it affords to them, by studying carefully its varied con tents. The example which Her Majesty has set, in common with many members of the nobility, in visiting the Exhibition upon the Oays devoted to the more humble class of visiters, will be universally appreciated by public feeling, and is calculated to produce the happiest results. Her Majesty, Prince Albert, and the Royal party at the Palace, remained for some time after the is. visiters began to arrive, and Her Majesty, fr om the corner of the north gallery, looking into the transept, watched with great interest the influx of the crowd. About twelve o'clock the Duke of Wellington arrived, but soon discovered that he was too late to inspect the works of industry in his accustomed quiet manner. After passing a short way up the centre avenue he returned, and left the building, in which he had remained but ten minutes. During the day we observed the Earl of Glengall, the Earl of Carlisle, Earl Granville, Lord Broughton, Mr. Moffatt, M.P., and other Members of Parliament. One or two of the Bishops were likewise present. The police did not enforce the regulation about passing up and down in a particular direction, except in one or two narrow and very crowded passages. The number of visiters on Tuesday paying the shilling admission was considerably larger than upon the previous day. Although there was no rush or excitement, still there was, from the hour of opening, a steady influx of visiters, until the general appearance of the building approached to that which it presented lest week. The centre and transept were not so crowded, and the visiters were more distributed and dispersed. The !miters were mostly of the class of those who paid to see the Exhibition, and really meant to see it, and who had no time to lose in useless promenading, but worked hard to do all they could in a day. The character of the multitude was exceedingly respectable. The total amount of money received at the doors was 1,3471. 17s. The produce of the sale of season-tickets 49 as 191.19 g. The number of visiters paying the shilling admission was therefore about 27,000. The building was half cleared as early as five,—the obvious reason being, that people had come early, and had done a good day's work. Moreover, the price of admission being only a shilling, the pleasure could be renewed at a moderate cost. A vast number of pocket handkerchiefs, umbrellas, small articles of jewellery, and similar things, left, or dropped by their owners, are in charge of the police. In the course of the day, two women were apprehended in the act of picking a lady's pocket, and, on being searched, a purse was found on one of them, the contents of which she was unacquainted with, neither could she give an account where she had obtained it. A magnificent day, added to the cheapness of admis sion, brought a great accession of visiters to the Crystal Palace yesterday. From some mistake the numbers who entered the building were not counted by the police, but the rise in the receipts from 1,347/. to 1,859/. 4s. shows distinctly enough the gradually increasing popularity of the display, and givespretty clear indications of the crowds that may by and by be expected. Season-ticket holders included, there must have been more than 40,000 visiters. The money taken proves that there were 37,186 shilling spectators, and mingling among these might be seen a very considerable proportion of that elegant and fashionable assemblage which has provided itself with a general right of admission. On Monday few season-ticket holders came, and they were chiefly gentlemen. On Tuesday the numbers increased, but not in a decided manner. Yesterday they flocked in without reserve, and it seems not at all improbable that they will continue to do so for some time at least. On Thursday, according to the police returns, 54,669 persons visited the Crystal Palace. The sum taken in shillings at the doors was 2,379/. 7s. There were therefore 47,587 people who paid for entering, and 7,C80 season-ticket holders. The class who now come to the Exhibition remain a shorter time than their more fashionable predecessors. They generally arrive at an early hour, and begin to leave between 1 and 2 o'clock. Notwithstanding the immense numbers the utmost order and propriety of conduct prevailed. The Queen and her illustrious guests came to the Building at their usual early hour, and remained for some time, as on a former occasion, watching with curiosity and interest the influx of people when the doors were opened. Arnong the vast assemblage might be observed numbers of workmen from Mr. Cubitt's and other large establishments. On Friday the price of admission, as settled by the Commission, was half-a crown. It was not anticipated that the number of visiters would be great, nor was it so, but the result exceeded the calculations made, and the receipts at the doors were 2,839/. 83. The police returns represent that 30,345 persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and the Royal family continued their inspection, the people inside conducting themselves with marked propriety. During her last two visits the Queen had taken particular notice of several branches of national industry, the contributors to which will feel, flattered by such attention. She examined closely the specimens of Paisley shawls, and the needlework of the Scotch and Irish peasantry. Some embroidered vests from Belfast, exhibited by Mr. M`Gee, especially attracted her; and the collection of embroideries by Salomons and Sons , was also much admired by her. Her Majesty locked over with great care and interest the display of Lyons silks, and the . ,,muslins and printed fabrics of Mulhausen. On Friday an unexpected rise took place in the sale of season-tickets, and the receipts front this source amounted to 61/. 19s. It is now quite clear that from that quarter the finances of the Commission, can henceforth derive no material aid, unless the present scale of prices is low!red. In imitation of the style of decoration adopted in the eastern division of the building, it is, we hear, proposed that the flags of our principal manufacturing towns should be displayed over their respective allotments in the western nave. Leeds has already set the example in this respect. On Saturday the charge for admission to the building was ss. Owing to the attractions of the drawing-room, of a review at Woolwich, and of the other festivities connected with the celebration of Her Majesty's birthday, there WR9 a smaller attendance of visiters than usual, the number being only between 15,000 and 16,000, and the receipts being 1,771/. 12s. 6d. The Queen, for the first time, to-day meets the exhibitors, a portion of whom are requested by circular to be in attendance, in case explanations should be required of them. On Saturday, a considerable sensation was created in the building by the appearance among the visiters of a Spanish family, dressed in their picturesque national costume. They were accompanied round the interior by Lord Ranelagh, and were stared at and crowded round with a perseverance and impudence which, considering the charge for admission, and the presumed presence in consequence of a rather select assemblage, said very little for its good breeding. Greeks, Persians, Egyptians, Indians, Turks, and Armenians, have all been allowed to exhibit their finery since the Exhibition opened without let or hindrance, but the appearance of a Spanish senora in the dress of her country offered too great an attraction to be resisted in deference to the ordinary rules of politeness..—Times. Some interesting and not altogether purposeless discussion has been raised concerning the ultimate destination of the Exhibition. That there will be a surplus even after buying the Building at 300,0001., cannot be doubted, and some have even dared to suggest that the contents might be purchased also ! Our cotemporary, the Alkenmunt, rapidly disposes of this dreamy suggestion. The lowest estimate of the value of the contents is twelve millions, and supposing the Commissioners were to receive 2,000/. clear profit daily, it would be twenty years before the necessary sum could be raised. The Athenceitm taking for granted that the Royal Commissioners will purchase the Crystal Palace in the name of the English people, thinks that if it be then announced to all the present exhibitors in the first instance that such of them as have fitted up stalls or obtained space may retain them for, say a year, on the condition of keeping them filled with their present or other contributions of the same high class of excellence, a great majority of the most useful and beautiful articles would be left. Last Monday was by far the greatest day in point of numbers which has yet been witnessed since the opening of the Crystal Palace. The number of persons who had entered by one o'clock was about 35,000, and before the hour of closing about 55,000 had entered the place. The receipts for season-tickets were 13/. 139., and at the doors 2,1201., making a total of 2,142/. 13s. The bustle, and excitement, and crowding in the neighbourhood, and especially at the principal entrance, baffle description, and yet we did not hear of any accident. Large numbers catne by the railways and steam-boats, and the appearance of the visiters was altogether more of the humbler classes of society than on any previous day. Her Majesty and Prince Albert, and the Duke of Wellington, paid their usual morning visit.

The half-yearly general meeting of the shareholders of this company took place in Paris on Thursday, M. de l'Espie, the president, iu the chair. Near him were seated the following directors :—Sir John Easthope, Mr. Reed, Mr. Geo. Lawrence, Mr. Blount, M. C. Laffitte, M. de Kersaint, M. Simons, and M. N. Duchdtel. The meeting being declared duly constituted, M. Tin- BIUDEAII, the secretary, preceeded to read the report: — This document commences by stating that the establishment-account, np to the 31st of December last, had amounted to 67,222,3921. 98c. Since then there has been expended a sum of 1,1261. 75e., and received from sale of ground, &e., 4,8831. 25c. ; so that, up to June 30, the whole amount is 67,218,631 f. 48c. The question of the indemnity for the devastations committed in February, 1848, has not yet been regulated. The committee appointed to estimate the amount of damage done, conceiving that it was called on to examine only what had occurred in the department of the Seine, and finding that part of the injury done to the railways had been inflicted in other depart. ments, had resolved that the documents relating to these matters should be transmitted to the Minister of Public Works. The Minister had, in his turn, referred the question to the central railway committee, which had just issued an opinion favourable to 'the claims preferred, and so the matter rested at present. The approbation of the Government had been at last obtained for the changes voted at the general meeting of Jan. 31, 1850, relative to the sinking-fund. In consequence of these modiffcations, the sum to be now set apart annually for the sinking-fund would amount to only 25,000 francs, in place of 360,000 francs as previously. Fifty shares were to be paid off every drawing, with a sum of 500 francs each, and in place cf each of these shares was to be given an action de jouissance, entitling the holder to a share of all dividend over 5 per cent., or 25 francs per share. The shares to be paid off wore to be drawn by lot, and the company had determined to adopt for the purpose the plan practised by the city of Paris, in designating such of its bonds as were to be reimbursed. The first drawing was to take place in presence cf the shareholders then assembled. The report next refers to the results of the working during the last six months. The receipts from January 1 to June 30, 1851, mounted to 4,053,2011. 65c. ; and the expenses to 2,862,4101. 6e. ; leaving a profit of 1,190,791 f. 590., which, after the payment of interest of the sum kept back for sinking-fand, foundation shares, &c., gave a dividend of 16f. per share. As the interest of 5 per cent. on each share would amount to 121. 50e. for the half-year, the dividend for each action de jouissance would amount to 31. 50e. Comparing the results of the working of the last six months with the corresponding period of 1850, the receipts of the half-year of 1851 show an augmentation of 120,1761. 20c., of which sum passengers give 80,1301. Sc., whilst the expenses of the half-year of 1851 show an augmentation of 123,726 f. 34e., of which sum the greatest portion is down for increased interest become due to the state. The report then remarks on the constantly increasing tendency of the working to lower the goods' tariffs, that course being necessitated by the competition arising both from other railways, and by the river navigation. The increased facilities of communication between Dieppe and Brighton, and Havre and Southampton, are next alluded to, and are stated to have been attended with such success, that from 30 passengers per day for the former line, the number had increased in June to 177, the goods' traffic having also augmented very considerably. The report remarks on the annoyance which passenger* meet with at the custom-houses of Southampton, and Newhaven, arid contrasts with the delays caused the infinitely greater liberality of the authorities in France. The plea.ure-trains had not succeeded in so marked a manner as in 1850, and the experience of June had induced the company to suppress the Wednesday trains, only one now leaving Paris on the Saturday. The lawsuit which had been pending for upwards of fire years between the Rouen company and the boatmen of the Seine has been lately decided by the Court of Appeal of Orleans in favour of the company. The circular railway round Paris, to connect the various lines together, had now been definitely decided on, and would be shortly commenced. Independent of the mania for locomotion which prevails in all quarters of the world, and 'covers the ocean with vessels bearing the anxious travellers to the Crystal Palace, the moment has now arrived when the fashionable watering places, with their sea-baths, are completing the migration of all that was left amongst us of elegant society. Boulogne, Dieppe, and Trouville, have the privilege of attracting the greater number of Parisiennes, who would unite, with the benefit of sea air and bathing, the charm of society and fashionable amusements. It is for these destinations that the present charming variety of elegant toilettes are being prepared. Morning negliges are composed of peignoirs with their vestes, or pelernies chales of jean, quilting, valencia of toile cashemire, in shades, grey, dustcoloured, and pale brown ; the greater part are trimmed with broad braids, and lined with pink or blue taffetas. A second slecAre is worn under the pagode of the redingotes of the same material, but tight, with a small turn-up cuff trimmed with braid ; the same trimming iu two or three rows forms a ruche round the throat ; a small plaid cravat, fixed with a large enamel or frosted silver brooch ; and an embroidered muslin cap, richly trimmed with strings of the same, or ribbon to match, the toques, which takes the place of the bandeaux until the hour of dressing. Capelines of taffetas, embroidered muslin, or coloured jaconot, with large curtain, protecting the face most successfully from the sun or wind, are much worn in morning promenades. Large scarf shawls of plain cashemire in blue, green, or grey, trimmed with a deep fringe, surmounted by a very broad velvet, with two or three rows of narrow on each side, either black or of the same colour as the shawl, but of a much deeper shade, completes this toilette. As it is often cold at the sea side, the mantelet scarfs are slightly wadded. At the hour of promenade the sea-side nearly resembles the grand walk of the Tuilleries, ladies and children displaying all the richness and grace of the Parisienne toilette. Robes of chine, pekin pompadour, taffetas d'ltalie, grenadine, or barege, have flounces printed in designs of wreaths of roses, honeysuckle, lilac—indeed, all kinds of graceful flowers, whose colours harmonise so well on grounds of grey, white, or sea-green. With this style of robe is worn the mantelet. Maintenon, with its triple garniture of black lace upon dark-coloured taffetas, or white lace upon lighter shades; the Mathilde mantelet, with its drawn ribbons mixed with guipure of the same shade as the mantelet, the cut of which so gracefully delineates the waist, that it appears an attribute of all young and elegant ladies. The mantelet Valerie of white taffetas, or gerenadine, with its beautiful embroideries in silk, or mixed soutaches, with deep headings which float as light as lace; or the mantille and a louse of black lace, with a wide trimming. This mantille, both for shape and elegant negligee ' is suitable for all toilettes. We must not forget the large square shawl of black lace, or rounded in front, forming a shawl behind and mantelet in front being Equally fashionable this season. MOst ofihedresses are now made with two bodies, in order to form double dresses, yet not to greatly increase the luggage. The low body has a berthe descending en cceur, the front trimmed with bows of ribbon, passementerie and bouillonnes, matching the trimming on the short sleeves and skirt. The high bodies are often made with basquines, cut in indentations • the sleeves match, and are sometimes upon the whole length of the arm, and fastened at intervals with bows of ribbon or buttons. This kind of Spanish sleeve is a very pretty novelty and an agreeable change to the unitbrenity of the pagodes, which, however, are still the fashion. When the btrquines bodies are open in front a small embroidered waistcoat is added, the buttons of which are of pearl, amethyst, turquoise, or emeralds. These waistcoats, which appeared at first rather venturesome, derive all their distinction from the happy manner in which they are combined. Their shades should never be striking, but soft, and harmonising with the dress. The most elegant are open en cceur, embroidered, with a double row of buttons on each side. This style, which is rather Oriental, has a good effect. A very clear muslin chemisette, or one composed entirely of lace, with large bouffantes under sleeves, with narrow wristbands, accompany this toilette. We must now speak of bonnets which have their importance at the seaside, being made for all circumstances, for heat, cold, wind, and sun. First, there are the coarse straws, the simplicity of which is relieved by the magnificent bows of plaid ribbons, double curtains, and broad strings, giving them the seal of distinction and fashion. Some are trimmed with dark blue or green velvet, mixed with open straw ribbon. The upper curtain is of velvet, the under one of straw. The strings are of broad velvet, and the inside is trimmed with toques to match the outside trimming, mixed with corn and straw foliage iu straw. Other bonnets, of coarse straw, are simply trimmed with a ribbon of straw ; curtain and inside alike ; the strings only being of taffetas, either white or straw coloured. This trimming has the advantage of withstanding the ill effects of rain or sun. For more recherche toilette, Leghorn and Swiss straws are worn. The manner alone of placing the straw curtain requires a talent which is confined to our great houses, and renders these bonnets quite a-lamode. The trimming is composed of a single bouquet of garden flowers, mixed with lighter flowers of the field, which fall gracefully on one side of the bonnet. The inside is trimmed to match. Some of the bouquets are of very dark poppies, mixed with ribbon grass ; others of rhododendrum placed on each side, and buds of the same flower inside ; or bouquets of roses, May jasmine, with a wreath to match inside. We have never observed the strings to bonnets worn as wide as they are at present. In order to render to render the light and drawn bonnets more serviceable in windy weather, a kind of lattice-work of fine whalebone covered with ribbon or taffetas is placed inside. The colour of these auxiliaries is the same as the tips of the ostrich feathers which trim the outside. We must now mention the cavalcador. Here is one of those sonorous words with which the Castilian language abounds. It is no longer the casaweck of the north, the English jacket, the juste. au• corps of Louis XIII., or the casaque dieppoise, that our fasbionables decide to wear with the waistcoat before mentioned ; for it is necessary to have some kind of pardessus with this novelty ; but this time the pattern has been sought in the sunny zone of Andalusia—it is borrowed from the graceful cavalieres of that poetic country, and produced under the name of cavalcadors, very open. on the uppgr part of the chest, and buttoned at the waist with three buttons only ; short sleeves a la Grecque, displaying the under sleeves, formed of three graduated puffs which reach the wrist, round which it is fastened. The cavalcador is generally of the same material as the dress. The buttons are small and banging, of steel or engraved or chased silver. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT THE DONCASTER RAILWAY STATION.--On Saturday last John Bishop, a guard in the employ of the Midland Company, while performing his duty, met with a severe accident at the Doncaster station. He was mounted on a carriage, and the train at the time having begun rapidly to move, it ran under the luggage gauge before he was prepared, bringing his face in contact with the cross beam with such violence as to throw him backwards. His nose was found to be cut in two, transversely, the lower hall being left attached merely by a little of the cuticle, and hanging over his mouth; the upper half was split open longitudinally; and there were other severe marks of the shock about the eyes, cheek, and upper lip. ELECTION OF LORD MAYOR. According to annual custom on Miche.elmas Day, the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, Aldermen, and other members of the City Corporation assembled yesterday at the Guildhall, for the pur pose of electing a Lord Mayor for the ensuing year. At 12 o'clock the corporation proceeded in state to the church of St. Lawrence Jewry, where a most suitable discourse was preached by the Rev. Doctor Vivian, chaplain to the Lord Mayor, and Rector of St. Peter-le-Poer, in Broad-street. The text was taken from Proverbs viii., 16: "By me princes rule, and nobles, even the judges of the earth." When the party proceeded to the church, the Lord Mayor and Sheriffs were attended by their respective chaplains; but as Mr. Swift, the new Sheriff, is a Roman Catholic ' he was attended by his chaplain, Father O'Connor, a Popish priest, who went no further than the church doors, and then retired. At a quarter past one, the corporation returned from church, and immediately assembled on the hustings in the Guildhall, when the usual forms were gone through, and Alderman Hunter ' of Coleman-street Ward, the senior Alderman who had not passed the chair, was elected Lord Mayor without opposition.

GREAT EXHIBITION. The number of visitors on Monday at the Exhibition was, according to the police returns, 61,670—the amount taken at the doors being £2,852. Among the more interesting incidents of the day we may mention the arrival of Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by fifty of the poor male parishioners of the parish in which he resides; the same number of female parishioners having, a few days ago, received a similar kindness from Mrs. Gladstone. Four hundred boys belonging to the Upper School at Greenwich also arrived during the day, their expenses having been paid by the Lords of the Admiralty. The question as to the propriety of admitting charity-schools to the Exhibition at reduced prices—a subject to which we have referred upon more than one occasion —was, we understand, under the consideration of the commissioners at their meeting on Saturday; but, although they were disposed to grant the boon, it was, we believe, considered advisable that free admission should not at present take place. As we stated a few days ago, it is not intended to award the prizes until after the close of the Exhibition—the period for which was fixed, at the meeting of the commissioners on Saturday, for about the middle of October. It is in contemplation, in order to admit of the Exhibition being closed at that time, to give increased facilities to visitors by lighting up the building in the evening. To persons occupied during the day this arrangement will be a great boon, and it will enable many thousands to visit the Exhibition who would otherwise be completely prevented from so doing. As the Exhibition would not continue open during many hours of the evening, it may be desirable that the rate of admission should be somewhat reduced. Among the more interesting of the additions which have recently been made to the Exhibition, are some pieces of sail-cloth placed near the model of the Queen ship of war, 110 guns, in the Transept, for the purpose of showing the effects of a hurricane upon that material. The manner in which they are torn and knotted is most surprising, and conveys a vivid idea of the terrible force exerted. The pieces exhibited were cut from the main-topsail of the ship Trafalgar, which experienced a severe hurricane off the Isle of France, on the 21st of March, 1851. She was hove to under close-reefed new fore and main-top sail; they were however torn into shreds, and knotted in the most extraordinary manner, by the force of the wind. Nothing could show in a more striking manner the great value and importance of attempts, similar to those made by Colonel Reid, to develop the law of storms, than this display of their terrific and destructive force; and if, by patient study and careful investigation, Colonel Reid should succeed in solving that mysterious problem, he will obtain for himself a reputation only to be equalled by that which he has won by his courteous and impartial conduct as chairman of the Executive Committee of the Great Exhibition, . • v ../••••••••VVvv ••••••• V.V./ An important addition was also made on Monday, in the shape of four pieces of cloth, dressed in various ways, by the Chevalier Claussen. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The near approach of the closing day only increases the anxiety of the public to visit the Crystal Palace. Yesterday's was another enormous gathering, and would have been still greater but for the threatening aspect of the weather in the early part of the day. The great mass of the visitors are still country people, and the manner in which they crowd round the most familiar objects proves them to be in the majority of cases visitors for the day only. The preparations for the final close go on with un- abated vigour, and we believe that the ceremonial will take place in the quietest possible manner, without any musical " effects" vocal or instrumental, notwithstanding the strong hints daily thrown out by a morning contemporary. The public will and must take a fanal leave of the building on Saturday, the 11th of October, when, it will comfort our contemporary to know, any spontaneous burst of harmony will not be pro- hibited by the executive committee, but it must be provided by the public, and not by the royal commissioners. On the Wednesday following Prince Albert will attend, when the report of the jurors will be read by Lord Canning. To this his royal highness will respond in a short speech, and in 10 minutes after the workmen will be admitted, and commence the removal of the goods, and the preparations for the dismantling of the Palace. On this occasion the only persons admitted will be the exhibitors, and perhaps one or two friends each, by ticket, the public, ticket holders and all, being entirely excluded. This announcement we make on the highest authority. The suggestion for removing the Crystal Palace bodily to Battersea fields has created a good deal of amusement among the lsnituds, especially those who are at all acquainted with the winter aspect of the locality in question. The Palace is already by no means impervious et top, and if it were placed in a situation where two or three feet of extra water might safely be calculated on at every spring tide during winter, its public utility in a sanitary point of view would become more than problematical. If it is to be taken down to be rebuilt elsewhere, and to be made a retreat for poor invalids, in whch they may take air and exercise, undeterred by the chilling blasts and damps of winter, some site must be chosen above, not below high- water mark. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty and Prince Albert paid a somewhat unexpected visit to the the Exhibition on Tuesday ; having, we believe, come up from Windsor expressly for the purpose. The royal party arrived at the Crystal Palace shortly after 12 o'clock, and were received by Mr Dilke and Mr Cole, of the executive committee, who accompanied her Majesty and the Prince through the building. Her Majesty passed down the foreign nave, where the dispersed workmen would seem to have reassembled. In this once brilliant promenade there remains but little to engage the attention, and her Majesty gave but a cursory glance, at the relics as she passed by. Her Majesty then ascended the southern gallery, and returned towards the British side, where still less remains than in the foreign section. What seemed to engage most of her Majesty’s notice, was the building itself, ‘which she had a better opportunity of observing than on the occasion of former visits, when her attention must have been unavoidably distracted by the gorgeous accessories displayed on every side, and the living panorama moving witiin. mentioned some time since, that the boarding which shut in the full view of the interier was being removed, the building was revealing itself a marvel of beauty. Her Majesty was evidently much struck with the view which the interior of the building even now presents, and was heard to express herself in warm terms of approbation at the prospect. When it is completely free of the rubbish which now partially disfigures it. it will present one of the finest architectural scenes of its kind in the world. The royal party retired before one o’clock. The sappers and miners have been withdrawn from further duty in the Exhibition, with the exception of some thirty or forty who still remain to assist in the removal of the packages. The Tuscan goods have been removed, and the American are to follow in few days.

Theexpediency of a reduction in the charges of admission is now attracting, consider- able attention, and it becomes obvious that one half. crown day in the week would be sufficient. Some of the authorities still hesitate about the propriety of bringing down the prices lower than a shilling under any circum- stances; but when it is considered that a large propor- tion of the labouring classes in the metropolis have not vet visited the spectacle which their industry has largely belped to create, it is to be hoped that some arrange- ments mnay be made for enabling them to gratify their curiosity in this matter. If the workman could be ex- pected to go alone to the Crystal Palace, the present charge would raise no serious obstacle, bat he naturally wishes to bring his family along with him, that they may share in his delight; and why should he not be indulged in that desire ? Se. veral c/ssf-d'rearres of art, also, have recently been re- ceived, and among them one of surpassing merit by the celebrated Dutch sculptor, Van dec Yen, representing the Temptation of Eve. It is placed in thne nave, and attracts an immense amount of attention. The treat- ment of the subject is bold and original, the form of the first woman being developed with a freedom, grace, and life-like effect, which cannot be too highly praised. It is rarely that so wonderful a specimen of the plastic art is to be seen in this country, and one of its chief excellen- cies is that in its composition there is no trace of the disposition to borrow from the classic styles of antiquity, instead of relying upon nature, which so often detracts from the merit of modern sculpture. Mr. Speose, an English artist at Rome, has also lately contributed a statue of Burns' "Highland Mary," which is much and justly admired. The executive committee still continue to receive numerous applications for admission into the British department of the Exhibition, which, however, they always reject. The colossal zinc statue of her Majesty, which fur- nished so conspicuous an object in the eastern nave, and which for soene days fast had been obscured from the public inspection, with the view of giving a bronze tint to both statue and pedestal, has been again exposed to the public gaze by the Vielle Montagne Company-its exhibitors. Those who have seen the statue in its zinc colouring would scarcely recognise it in its new dress. The dull and livid colouring of the zinc in its nataral state is the very reverse ofagood exponent of the human countenance, and, consequently, this colossal statue of the Queen, however prominent from its magnitude, was a very eyesore to the beholder. The substitution of bronze has completely removed this defect. The artist availed himself of the opportunity thus afforded to alter the bandeaux of the hair, with a view of rendering the statue a more faithful representation of her Majesty; and though he has, to some extent, succeeded, the original sin of heaviness and want of spirit has not been over- come. On Wednesday morning her Majesty and Prince Albert re- sumed their inspection of the Crystal Palace and their reception of the exhibitors. They then directed their steps to the section of machinery in motion, and proceeded with the inspection of a vast number of remarkable objects which they had not seen during their last vizit. Here they were again attended by Mr. Cubitt and Mr. Hensman, who, with the exhi- bitors themselves, explained to them the leading features of the different machines. Commencing with the tools exhibited by Whitworth, of Manchester, they spent some time in examining that really wonderful collection. They then passed in review the meritorious contributions of Sbarpe, the wire drawing process of Johnson, Hick's illustrations of the power obtainable by the hydraulic press-punch, the method of proving cast-iron beams exhibited by Cottam and Hallam, Ryder's remarkable machine for forging spindles, Holzapffel's ingenious specimens of turning In the lathe, Maudslay's now coining press, by which during their stay some medals were struck, the fine models of marine engines by the same maker, and the rope-making machine exhibited by Crawhall, of Newcastle, dispensing with the usual long gallery hitherto required in that manufacture. Undoubtedly, of late the popular element has been becoming more and more conspicuous among the throng of spectators, and there is no longer any difli- culty in finding among the vast concourse humble dresses and faces brown with exposure to the sun, and hands hardened by toil. The presence of mothers with their Infants, too, and luncheons emerging from homely-loolklng baskets during the intervals of rest-these and a hundred other signs indicate that the Is. does not operate as a barrier to the curiosity of the industrial classes; yet from some unexplained cause the masses have not yet presented themselves at the doors of the Crystal Palace, and the majority of those who go there still belong to the upper and middle ranks of life. It is almost incredible that the Whitsun holydays should have closed without the slightest detraction from the respectability of the Exhibition as a place of public resort, and that the actusl number of visitors during a period when labour is released from its toil should show a positive decrease.
