THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The popularity of the Crystal Palace is appareetly undiminished, and like a well-regulated piece of mechanism, the 1 falling-off occasioned by the unpropitious state of the weather ' on one day, is fully compensated by the re-action when the sun and the visitors come out in full force. Yesterday was an illustration of this; for, notwithstanding the increase in the price of admission, the building was almost as ' crowded as in the early part of the week. Either the 1 greater portion of those who attend are strangers, who visit I it for the first time, or the attraction of "the lions" in the naves and transept continues unabated for those who have seen them a score of times previously, the crowds assembled I round the statuary, jewels, &c., being so great as to render I access to them a matter of considerable difficulty. One of the great features of the past week has been the number of children visitors; but we question after all whether more is gained by the hurried manner in which the Exhibition is passed through than the gratification of that curiosity that appears to have seized upon all ranks and classes. Nineteen out of twenty of the objects around these children are quite beyond their comprehension, and there is neither time nor opportunity for leisurely examination, or the imparting of information by those in charge of juvenile sight-seers. They, however, enjoy,the fun and the crowd amazingly, and generally wind up with the National Anthem, after a fashion, which we have no doubt has had a I considerable effect in retarding the tuning of Willis's ; great organ. One of the most serious annoyances during the recent wet weather has been the prohibition to allow public vehicles to enter the park. Many ladies and children have got wet through, and ankle-deep in mud in making their way to the outer gates. We trust that there will be some relaxation of the rule in rainy weather, or that one of the ends of the building will be appropriated to the setting down and taking up of visitors in hired cabs. A new book on the Crystal Palace, iutitled " How to see the Great Exhibition in Four Visits," by W. B. Jerrold, has just made its appearance. It is written without any attempt at pretension, and is, so far as we have looked through it, a careful compilation of the various objects of interest in the different departments of the building. To those whose time is limited to three or four visits this little hand-book will be found extremely useful. Next to the valuable collection of gems and the costly and elaborate specimens of gold and silver plate, the collection of crystal in its pure and sparkling brilliancy, or enhanced by the applicatio n of the most beautiful prismatic colouring' may be fairly looked upon as among the most ornamental and attractive of the many treasures of the Crystal Palace. And yet, all the most valuable of the glittering collection displayed, all the symmetrical forms, all the lavish display of hig h artistic skill, and all the elaboration of colouring and design, in silvering, engraving, and staining, has been accomplished within the last few years. This is mainly owing to the removal of those fiscal regu- I lesions which paralysed the energies of our glass menu- I lecturers for so long a period. The trade since then has i advanced with giant strides, and a display which a few years I since would have excited only ridicule or contempt, now takes its position beside the finest productions of our Continental neighbours, as regards ornamental glass; while we are decidedly superior to them in the manufacture of the more useful kinds. The matchless specimens of crystal which cover the English stalls of the Exhibition indicate the perfection which freedom from legislative interference and control has enabled our manufacturers to accomplish but the building itself, covered by nearly a million of large ' squares of glass, enclosing more than 18 acres of ground, and weighing upwards of 400 tons, is one of the greatest triumphs of our national industry, and one of the most astonishing manufacturing marvels of the many which it encloses. Johnson, in his story of the Pecenician mariners, in the Ra , nbler, taking his account from Pliny, has thrown a poetic halo round the accidental discovery of this elegant art. The fire kindled by these castaways upon the seashore is said to have produced glass by the fusing of the sand with the alkaline substances around; but we believe in sober prose that Egypt, the cradle of art, I science, and civilisation, has a prior claim —witness the I fragments picked up among the ruins of Thebes, the indications of glass-making in the hieroglyphic paintings in her temples, and the fact that the sand near Alexandria is peculiarly fitted for the production of the finest glass. It is , evident, also, that they were acquainted with the colouring of glass by means of metallic oxides, another confirmation of the assertion of one of the philosophers of the day, that all our modern discoveries are but the revival of ancient art, and the specimens which have Come down to us, and which have been exhibited at the Society of Arts amongst their mediaeval collection, would indicate that they had attained to • no small degree of excellence in its manufacture. Greece , knew little of the art of glass-making, and China limited herself to the imitation of precious stones, whde the Romans obtained their most valuable specimens from Egypt. The value of the Koh- hnoor sinks into insignificance, compared with the sums paid by the Roman emperors to the Eeyptian princes for these costly vases. Hadrian had some which could only be used in the highest festivals and after peculiar ceremonies, and Nero paid 80,000/. of our money—an almost incredible suns in those days—for two Egyptian glass cups with handles. At a later period the art ef coating and cameo cutting was discovered; and the celebrated Barberini vase, which has so long delighted artists and puzzled the dilettanti, has turned out to be, not the work , of the potter, but of the glass blower and cutter. The Naples museum proves that the luxurious people who inhabited the cities overwhelmed by the eruptions of Vesuvius were well acquainted with the art; and among the Venetians the glassmaker held a dignified position—the island of Murano, in one of the lagoons, being celebrated for its productions. One of the properties said to be possessed by the Venetian . glass was that of flying to pieces when poison was introduced—a convenient myth which it was the interest of the nobles to impress upon the people. It is generelly supposed that glsws meking was introduced into Venice by the Crusaders in the beginning of the 13th century, and for a long period it formed a lucrative commercial monopoly. Its perfection, however, was more comparative than real. We have still numerous specimens of what was considered the finest Venetian glass, and some of our manufacturers have succeeded in re-producing the fragile and delicate cups and vases of frosted and gilt Venetian glass which was at one time considered almost priceless. Mr. Apsley Pellatt has been peculiarly successful in the imitation of this rare description, several specimens of which have been purchased by her Majesty. The Bohemians were the great rivals of the Venetians in variety of colouring and in the manufacture of cups, goblets, and vases, with this distinction, that the former have made wonderful improvements in the art, while the latter have retrograded. In England the invention was, it is said, kno,vn to the Druids, who made glass beads serve as amulets or charms; but the first English glasshouse was erected in the Savoy about the middle of the loth century, and was thence transferred by one of those accidents which are among the curiosities of its early history to the midland districts. The small band of Lorraines who were driven from their own country by civil dissensions and religious persecution to take refuge in England, like the stout Flemings, to whom we owe another branch of manufactures, not finding encouragement in London, settled near Stourbridge, having observed there evidences of the invaluable fire-clay, out of which the glass melting-pots are formed. With the exception of this and the coal, all the materials used even to the present day are procured at a distance, the sand being obtained either from the Norfolk coast or from Alum Bay, in the Isle of Wight. What was accomplished by accident was further perfected by stratagem. A descendant if one of these Lorraines proceeded to Germany as a musician and found means to get inte some of the strictly-watched naanufactoriet, and obtained a knowledge of the method of making German spread glass for windows. Suspicions, however, were excited. Ile was seized, tried, and ordered to be executed, lest was fortunate enough to make his escape, and on his return here his services were publicly acknowledged in the Gazette, and a grant of fifty pounds (!) voted to him by the existing government. Since then the menufacture of this description of glass has been carried out to an enormous extent, and it is now exported to all parts of the world. The first blown glass was made in this country in 1673, at Lambeth, by Venetian artists, who were brought over under the patronage of the Duke of Buckingham. Colbert was the introducer of blown mirror glass into France, and nobles only were at first allowed to be masters of the glass-works. We may close these introductory remarks upon the early stages of glass manufacture by a more authentic account of the real excellence and value of the Venetian glass. Nearly 20 0 years ago , Maximilian Nissen, a Frenchman, who visited Murano, said that Venetian crystal, formerly held to be the finest in Europe, no longer merited that title, and the master of one of the glass-houses offered 100,000 francs to any one who would teach him the secret of making glass as white as that of a cup brought from Paris. Mr. Pellatt says the finest ancient Venetian glass was celebrated rather for its lightness than its crystalline beauty, but that it is inferior to modern English crystal in pellucid refractibility. It would thus appear that our energy, our capital, and the discoveries of chemical science, have enabled us to transcend without an effort the most surprising wonders of ancient art, and to place within the reach of the middle classes what was formerly esteemed among the most costly treasures of the most luxurious Roman Emperors, or the princely rulers of the Italian states. _ _ The following is the official report of the receipts of the day : Season tickets X 6 6 0 At the doors 2984 0 0 Total receipts ... ... ... £2990 G 0 Police numbers 96,882 Tun COMING ECLIPSE.—Mr. Wyld, of Charingcross, has just published a map exhibiting the course which will be taken by the great eclipse of the sun on Monday next. DEATH OF ONE OF BURNS'S HEROINES.—A Glasgow contemporary records the death of one of the six " Mauchline belles," on whom Burns confers the fame of his verse. Mrs. Findlay, relict of Mr. Robert Findlay, of the Excise, Greenock, was one of the very few persons, surviving to our own times, who intimately knew the peasant bard in the first flush of his genius and manhood, and by whom her name and charms have been wedded to immortal verse. When we consider that sixty-five years have elapsed since Burns wrote the lines in which this lady is noticed, and that the six Mauchline belles were then in the pride of opening womanhood, it is surprising that two of them, who have often listened to the living accents of the inspired peasant, still survive. The fate in life of the six belles was as follows: Miss Helen Miller, the first-named, became the wife of B urns's friend, Dr. Mackenzie, a medical gentleman in Mauchline, latterly in Irvine ; Miss Markland we have already spoken of; itxiss Jean Smith was married to Mr. Candlish, a successful teacher in Edinburgh, and became the mother of the eminent divine; Miss Betty (Miller) became the wife of Mr. Templeton, in Mauchline ; and Miss Morton married Mr. Patterson, cloth-merchant, in the same village. Of the fate and history of " Bonnie Jean " (Armour) we need not speak. The survivors are Mrs. Patterson and Mrs. Candlish. — Scottish Press. The chair was occupied by Mr. Clowes. The Rev. H. H. Milman (the Dean of St. Paul's) stated that it was now four years since this design had been conceived by the admirers of the art of printing in the metropolis. The receipts, up to the present time, amounted to about 2451., and the expenses to 681., leaving a balance in hand of 1771. At the last meet. ing, held iJuly, 1849, the treasurer was authorised to incur expenses in collecting fresh subscriptions, but many circumstances had since transpired to prevent this and other steps from being taken. A substantive proposi- tion had, however, been received from the Coalbrookdale Iron Company with reference to the erection of the monu- ment, the nature of which would be stated by the secretary, Mr. Cole.-Mi. Cole said the proposition was this. The Coalbrookdale Company proposed to erect a figure seven feet high, on a pedestal, to make it suitable for a fountain, to supply the iron work, and to finish and deliver it in Lon- don for 5001. This company, as was well known, were exten- sive contributors to the Great Exhibition; and, finding that they had undertaken large works of statuary on specula- tion, he (Mr. Cole) had spoken to the manager, and asked him whether the company would be disposed to erect a -statue to Caxton. The answer was, they would undertake the risk,.on condition that they should be at liberty to erect similar statues in such other towns of the kingdom as might be willing to pay the cost. There were two questions for the meeting to consider-first, were they likely to col- lect 5001.; and secondly, were they justified in givig an order to the Coalbrookdale Company, on the data they had- now before them. His own opinion was, that if a creditable model could be shown, the whole of the 6001. would be forthcoming, for already they had 1701. in hands, and there were outstanding balances due to the amount of 1601. more. A long conversation ensued-some being of opinion that the money oughtto be returned to the subscribers, and others that it ought to be handed over to some Printers' Pension Society. Eventually, the secretary was requested to inquire of the Society of Arts, whether they would under- take to carry out the design in accordance with the propo- sal made by the Coalbrookdale Company, and, in the event of their assenting, the treasurer was authorised to pay over the 1701. to the Society of Arts. In the event of their refusing, then the secretary is to write to the subscribers and ascertain their wishes as to the final disposal of the money. The meeting, which was very thinly attended, separated, after having passed the customary compliment to the chairman. For an hour after the opening of the six-and- twenty door, by wbich visitor, are admitted the public docked in, and by two o'clock the interior of the building was one moving mass. At tbe close of tbe day £3073 bad been received at the doors, which, at 5s each person, gives 20,291 visitors, be- sides those who purchased season ticket., or already held them. The day was very hot, aud altogether such a one a. must realise or condemn the fears which have been so loudly expressed for the comfort of locomotion under a glass roof on a summer', day. But notwithstanding the great heat out of doors, the temperature in the building never rose above 65 deg, F. In order to give as much space as possible for tbe purposes of locomotion, the seats and benches, which on Friday nearly filled the transept, have been cleared away and placed in the central refreshment court and the large open saloon behind it, During the day the Russian goods, lately landed from the Neptune, were received into the building. The Twenty-second Day.— On Monday, to the astonish- ment of almost everybody, notwithstanding the fall of price to ls, tbe interior of the Crystal Palace was not so much crowded as usual. A great crush was anticipated, and the consequence was tbat a comparatively small number came. Up to flve o'clock only 21,258 persons entered the building, and the receipts at tbe doors fell to ?? Tbis, with the sale of season tickets, made a total of ?? an immense de- cline from the amount collected on Saturday. The visitors ap- peared chiefly to belong to tbe middle class of society, and few fustian jackets were observed among them. Tbey did not confine themselves to the nave, but tbey were well spread over the in- terior, and all seemed intent on making good use of their time, and studying carefully the departments which most interested them. The only other novelty connected with Monday's ex- perience at the Exhibition worth mentioning is the capture of three pickpockets, two women and one man, who made a sad mis take in coming there to exercise their vocation. The women were detected by two Belgian policemen, and from their dialect were evidently provincial thieves. One stated tbat she was from Edinburgh, and spoke undoubted broad Scotch. The other said she came from Cork, but ber accent is not Hibernian. The male thief is a Frenchman, and has been "in trouble" before. He was admirably got up for the occasion, with a new hat and coat, an unexceptionable white waistcoat, aud patent leather boots, very smartly made. The uninitiated would have set him down as a fashionable foreigner come to look at tbe mob in a philosophic spirit of observation, but a detective with an unfortunately tena- cious memory for faces recognised bim aa he passed through the entrance, and he was followed, observed actively engaged in tbe mysteries of his profession, and at once removed from tbe scene of temptation into which he bad intruded. " What time did tbe magistrate give you before ?" said Superintendent Pearce to him at tbe station. " Six weeks,'" was tbe reply of the swell mob's- man, who appeared to consider himself the most injured and un- lucky of mortals. The unfavourable state of tbe weather yester- day had, no donbt, some influence upon the influx of visitors, wbo for tbe most part must have gone to Hyde-park either in omnibus or on toot. There were very few season ticket-holders there during the day, and the thoroughfare from Piccadilly to Knights- bridge presented a remarkable contrast to the bustle and excite- ment of tbe last three weeks. The Twenty-third Day.— On Tuesday the aspect of affairs at the Exhibition was far different from what it had been tbe day before. Although there was no rush or excitement, still there was from the hour of opening a steady influx of visitors, until the general appearance of the building approached to that which it presented last week. There was this difference, however— that the centre and transept were not so crowded, and the visitors were more dispersed and distributed throughout the entire edi- fice. This may be partly owing to the fact that the Executive Committee have caused tbe seats to be removed from the centre of tbe building, and to be placed in outlying and comparatively unoccupied portions— so as at once to prevent crowding and to promote the free circulation of the multitude. But perhaps a more potent cause is to be found in the fact, tbat the visitors were mostly of the class of those who paid to see the Exhibition, and really meant to see it, and who bad no time to lose in useless promenading, but worked hard to do all they could in a day. Hence there were everywhere eager, observant, and intelligent groups. The character of tbe multitude was exceedingly re- spectable ; indeed, for the most part, it consisted of a far better class of persons than bad been expected, and they appeared per- fectly disposed to examine, appreciate, and enjoy. The usual place, of peculiar resort wereof course as crowded as usual; but there was a more even and equal degree of attention bestowed on the varied contents of the Exhibition. The useful as well as tbe ornamental had due consideration— the machinery, not less than the statuary— the raw material, along with the rich, the costly, and the rare productions of art, manufacture, or skill. Every- thing was more or less examined ; and nothing could exceed the admiration and delight unequivocally displayed at the vast, va- rious, and curious treasures of the Crystal Palace. Her Majesty and Prince Albert, with the Prince and Princess of Prussia, and several others of the Royal visitors, attended by the usual suite, arrived at the Exhibition shortly after nine o'clock, and carefully inspected the contents of the transept end of the north English gallery — chiefly the Staffordshire pottery. The Royal party remained in tbe gallery until uearly eleven, and consequently witnessed the arrival of the public. During tbe day we observed the Duke of Wellington, the Earl of Glengall, tbe Earl of Carlisle, Earl Granville, Lord Broughton, Mr. Moffatt, M.P., and other members of Parliament. One or two of he Bishops were likewise present. The police did not enforce the regulation about passing up and down in a particular direction, except in one or two narrow and very crowded passages. The consequence was, that throughout the day the utmost order and harmony appeared to prevail. The total amount of money received at tbe doors was -£1347 17s. Tbe produce of the sale of season tickets was £19 19s. The number of visitors paying the shilling admission was therefore about 27,000. At two o'clock, and for some time afterwards, the building was very full ; but after four o'clock the visitors began to depart, and the building was half cleared as early as five -the obvious reason being tbat people had come early, and bad done a good day's work. Moreover, the price of admission bein; only a shilling, the pleasure could be renewed at a moderate cost. A vast number of pocket handkerchiefs, umbrellas, small arti- cles of jewellery, and (similar things, left or dropped by their owners, are in charge of the police, to whom application should be made respecting them. The Twenty-foueth Day.— Magnificent weather on Wed- nesday, added to the cheapness of admission, brought a great ac- cession of visitors to the Crystal Palace. From some mistake the numbers who entered the building were not counted by the po- lice, but the rise in the receipts from ii 13+7 to _fc 1859 4s shows distinctly enough the gradually increasing popularity of the dis- play, and gives pretty clear indications of the crowds that may by and by be expected. Season-ticket holders included, there must have been more than 40,000 visitors. The money taken proves that there were 37,186 shilling spectators, and mingling among these might be seen a very considerable proportion of that elegant and fashionable assemblage wbich has provided itself i with a general right of admission. On Monday few season- ticket holders were present, and they were chiefly gentlemen. On Tuesday the numbers increased, but not in a decided manner. On Wednesday they flocked in without reserve, and it seems not at all improbable that they will continue to do so for some time at least. There ia something particularly gratify- ing in this fraternisation of the great and the bumble under cir- j cumstances so unusual, and we may add, so unexpected. No one anticipated that when tbe price of admission had fallen to its minimum that higb-born ladies would venture amidst the thronging masses, and intrust themselves to the politeness of the people. But see what one good example will effect. The Queen visited the building on Tuesday morning as usual, remaining till eleven o'clock. The most distinguished members of the nobility follow up those royal indications of confidence and affection to- wards the industrial classes of the community. This is aa it should be, and we thus finely illustrate to foreigners, who are curious about our manners and institutions, that one of the oldest and proudest aristocracies in the world can sustain its dignity and its respect without holding itself aloof from the body of the people. Twenty-fifth Day.— On Thursday, according to the police returns, 54.669 persons visited the Crystal Palace. The sum taken in shillings at the doors was ___379 7s. There were there- fore 47/587 people who paid for entering, and 7080 season ticket holders. The utmost order and propriety of conduct prevailed, nor was it necessary for the police to interfere except at one or two of the more attractive points, in preventing an undue accumulation of visitors. The Queen and ber illustrious guests came to the Building at their usual early hour, and remained for some time, as on a former occasion, watching with curiosity and interest the influx of people when the doors were opened. New Feature.— Sixteen London and provincial nnrserymen have been allowed to exhibit plants, and sell cut flowers to the visitors. This has added greatly to the attraction of the scene. Kossuth’s Address to the Republicans at Marseilles.— Louis Kossuth having been refused permission the Minister of Interior to proceed through France on his way to England. Addressed the following letter to the democrats of Marseilles, prior the sailing of the Mitsissipi on the Ist instant; M Citizens,—The Government of the French Republic having refused me permission to traverse France, the people of Marseilles, yielding to the impulse of one of those generous instincts of the French heart which are the inexhaustible source of the nobleness your nation, has honoured me manifestation of its Republican sentiments—a manifestation honourable for its motives, manlv for its resolution, peaceable in its ardour, and majestic its calmness, as nature, the grand image of God, before the tempest. 1 have heard ray name blended with the hymn of the Idaneilliiue, and with the ahouts of Vive la Repuhlique /—a cry which is the only legal one in France; the only one whose legitimacy has been won by the blood of the martyrs of liberty! It is light to suffer for it! It is almost less than a mere duty ; but there is, indeed, supreme glory in the thought of being identified with the principle of liberty in the mind of the French people. I have no desire for glory—but this glory accept, in order to merit it. I accept it as pledge of common interests {tolidarite), and I accept it as testimony of the fraternity of the French nation with all nations. I accept it as the sign of salvation for beloved country. To you, Frenchmen! Republicans! is the honour of that salvation ! To us, poor Hungarians, the duty of meriting it! We shall merit it! My nation will understand the Appeal of jour fraternity. It will be proud of, and bravely respond it, those ought to do who are honoured in being called brothers the French people. These are the only thanks worthy of the people of Marseilles; worthy of that manifestation with which they have honoured me—yet not me, but nation ! And, in my nation, the past less than the future! Permit me not to speak any more of the refusal of the Government of the French Republic to grant me a passage through its territory. I know that the French people are not responsible for, and are not identified with its acts. I know that neither M. L. N. Bonaparte, nor M. Faucher, are the French nation. I knew, and I know, that the Executive Power is delegated to them ; but that the honour of the French nation is not in their keeping. I shall no longer bear in mind their refusal, and I desire that bumauity shall not remember it, if any chance those who have been already in exile, and who, to all appearance, have forgotten it, should again be so. Last evening one of your brethren our brethren) —an operative of Marseilles—oh ! I know his name, and I shall not forget it, came, in spite of the cold, and swimming through the water, on board the American frigate, to press band. I pressed his hand with pity, with emotion, and gently reproached him for his temerity. Que vouUz vous answered, * I desired to touch your hand, I could not find a boat, I took to the water, and here I am. Are there any obstacles to him who wills ?’ I bowed to these noble words. The love of liberty, the sentiment of duty and fraternity, were mine before coming to Marseilles; but it is at Marseilles that I have found the motto. ‘There are no obstacles him who wills.’ That motto shall be mine. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The Derby-day had no effect whatever on the flow o visitors to the Crystal Palace. On the contrary, the numbers who flocked there on Wednesday were greater than ever, and L3512 were taken at the doors. The sale of season- tiekets amounted to L.279, and the total receipts were L.3790. Her Majesty and the Royal party at the Palace arrived at the building shortly after nine o'clock, and remained for neatly two bours, during which they examined the French, Spanish, Turkish, and Egyptian compartments. From all the accounts we receive of the success of the undertaking in a commercial point of view, and with reference to exhibitors, is likely to be quite as great as it is now certain to be finan- cially and with regard to the Royal Commission. Many of the most remarkable contributions have been bespoken for purchasers when tfe display terminates, and extensive orders have been given fotended an examples of excellence in the various manufactures produced.-Titees. Her Majesty and the Royal party at the Palace were. again on Thursday at their usual early hour, visitors at the Exhibi- tion, and examined during their stay the Indian collection. On Thursday L.379 7, lIs. were taken at the doors, besides L. 75, 7s. for season tickets, and the whole receipts were L.3972, l8s. On Friday the receipts at the doors from 5s. payments amounted to no less a sum than L.4o95, los. From the sale of season tickets L 134, Ss. was taken,so that the total sum added to the finances of the commission was L.4229, 18S. To-day (Monday) the price of admission is reduced from 5s. to is. Now, therefore, there is every reason to believe that the Crystal Palace will be the '" World's Fair" in earnest. The London and North-Western Railway Company calculate on bringing 1,600,oro people to see it, and other companies are no doubt makitng their arrangements for a proportionate num- ber. What the influx of foreigners, may be it is impossible to calculate, but they have yet to come, and we may now look forward to an influx of strangers unprecedented in the history of the metropolis. In the midst of this excitement the Royal Commissionseemat alos swbatsteps totake. Thev areunvwilling to question the capability of their great edifice for accommo- dating all who may present themselves for admission, and they therefore cla m the first day of is. prices for experiment- al purposes. Barriers are to be erected at the entrances, to prevent any sudden rush, but otherwise no limit has been fixed to the numbers they are prepared to receive, nor has it been deemed advisable to provide for the claims of visitors from the country. How this arrangement will answer remains to be been, but in the meantime some points are obvious; first, that the interior cannot comfortably accommodate more than 60,000 people; secondly, that there are about 30,000 season ticket holders, many of whom will undoubtedly exercise their privilege of entry, the messes notwithstanding; thirdly, that the attractiveness of the display has hitherto far exceeded the most sanguine expectations; fourthly, that the great majority of the inhabitants of London are waiting for the reducfion of the entrance fee to Is., in order to gratify their curiosity fifthly, that they will probahbv completely block up the place both against foreigners and people from the country until their own curiosity is gratified. Roles have, we bear, beenuaidx down for the orderly circulation of visitors in the interior, but in practice these will be found extremely difficult of obser- vance, for people wont be much disposed to move to the left when an object attracts them to the right-and in sightseeing the privilege of going wherever one pleases is almost a neces- sary condition of enjoyment. Although m compliance with the original design of its projectors, the Great Exhibition bas itself only in ephemeral existence, it is satisfactory to think that the most ample and complete records will be preserved of its character and details. Few events have attracted such an amount of contemporary publicity. The pen and the pencil have both been incessantly at work in perpetuating industrial triumphs, and when all the material vestiges of the display are removed from our eyes, it will still live in a form the most valuable and enduring. The reports of the juries in each class will obviously prove an important repertoire of facts and observations, and the information which has been collected in newspapers, in periodicals, and in other channels of instruction, may also be turned to excellent account, but it is to the Illustrated Catalogue that we must look as capable of being made the most complete and satisfactory work of reference hereafter on the great industrial pageant of 1851. That publication now approaches its completion, for three parts of it bave al- ready appeared, and the fourth will scon be ready. It is intended that it shall be issued in three volumes, the first two of which will be dedicated to the products of Great Britain and her colonies, while the last embraces the contributions of foreign countries. Of all literary labours, that of getting up books of reference is perhaps the most tedious and the most thankless. The bare name of a catalogue kills the interest of the most indefatigable bookworm, after the collection of objects to which it was intended as a guide has ceased to be accessible. The present, however, is an exceptional case, and we predict for the Illustrated Catalogue qf the Great Exhibition a standard reputation, and a large sh re of public patronage when the grass has once more grown over the site of the Crystal Palace, and the great event of this year bas become a thing of tbe past. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The receipts yesterday amounted to 2,537/. Is., the number of visitors, according to the police returns, being 52,757. Rather suddenly, during the course of the day, the sale of season tickets was finally closed, and from this step the conclusion is pretty generally drawn that a ceremonial of some kind or other is contemplated when the Exhibition terminates. In the month of October, the worst season in the year for any town demonstration, it would be vain to hope for a display such as that which signalised the opening of the Crystal Palace, but at least the decent observances of respect can be paid to a spectacle which is not likely soon to be repeated, and whatever character the arrangements on the oc• casion may assume, it is obvious that the Great Exhibition cannot be allowed to go out like a spent candle, It was inaugurated by a State procession and the solemn offices of religion. It cannot be allowed to expire without some marks of public sympathy, and some manifestations of gratitude for the mission which it has fulfilled and the objects which it has served. These need not be of a very formal or pretentious kind, and the less they aspire to, the more likely are they to be effected. By the middle of October we shall be in a winner deserted by foreigners and left to ourselves. Even provincial curiosity will by that time, to a great extent, have died away, and it is probable that the great rush of visitors which may be anticipated will be supplied by London and its vicinity. Already we begin to have a foretaste of this. On Monday and Tuesday the numbers were upwards of 60,000, whereas yesterday they dropped down to 52,000. Under all the circumstances a homely, unaffected ceremony at the close would be the most effective, and would satisfy every expectation and all the proprieties of the case. It is for those who have hitherto managed the business of the Exhibition so successfully to celebrate its obsequies with decent and becoming pomp. It is worthy of mention that the Council of the Society of Arts have announced their intention to give a great medal to the person who shall produce a box having the greatest number of the best colours for general use and brushes, to be sold retail for ls. They also announce a reward for the best and cheapest set of drawing instruments, and in both cases they are actuated by the:desire to encourage and develops design in our art-manufactures. GALVANIC PRINTING PRESS.—A patent is being taken by a Mr. Foreman for a printing press, moved and regulated by galvanic magnets. His paper works upon a reel, and is continuous, like the telegraphic coil. The paper passes over the type on a cylinder, and when one side is worked the paper is reversed, and the other side printed with a perfect register, and the sheets are clipped apart as they come from the press by an ingenious contrivance. According to American authorities, " there is no limit hardly to the speed at which the press will work; its exactness is beyond anything known in this line of machinery, and what is better than all, Mr. Foreman says he can put up the largest sized press at a cost of not more than 500 dollars. Mr. Foreman is practical printer, and at present a citizen of New Boston, Illinois. It has been reserved for the last week of the Exhibition, to show bow many persons the building actually could contain with only comparatively inconvenient pressure or diminution of the facilities for seeing its attractive contents. When the numbers on a former occasion amounted to 74,000, it was believed that the maximum had been reached; but the experience of the present week has shown how infinitely below the mark were all the calculations made on the subject. Monday was the first real test, and on that day the exact number of persons admitted was 107,815. It will add to the interest occasioned by so vast a crowd, to show at what hours and in what gradation the building was filled. The numbers were at ten o'clock, 10,090; at eleven, 35,404; at twelve, 64,157; at one, 84,701; at two, 97,887; at three, 104,263; at four, 107,058. Soon after ten o'clock the crowd around the eastern entrance was so great that the usual turntables were dispensed with, and the visitors were allowed to enter without that ?? Belshaw, the superintendent, and the various money collectors, taking the money as fast as it could be poured in; and for the space of two hours they had to endure a silver shower such as had seldom been witnessed, theamount received during the dayamounting to 5,1751.16g. Shortly after three o'clock, and when upwards of 100,000 persons were in the building, the Duke of Wellington entered at the east end, and was loudly cheered by those who recognised him. The intelligence soon spread in the eastern half of the edifice, and the rush and crowding which ensued to catch a glimpse of the Dake was such as to produce a momentry sensation of apprehension as to the fate of the building. Thousands ran along the galleries, and each court and avenue poured its torrent into the nave, while large numbers in the transept, hearing the distant noise, and seeing the confusion, but ignorant of its cause, rushed out of the building under the appre- hension that some casualty had occurred. By dint of pure physical force, Inspector O'Brien, and several other police-officers, succeeded in opening a narrow pathway for the Duke. A constable supported him under each arm, and six men behind, under the direction of Mr Pearcc, kept the crowd back by main force, until at last exit was obtained at the south transept. His grace was exceedingly discomposed by the tussle, and seemed to think that even popularity and public gratitude might run into excess. It is most satisfactory to state that not a single accident occurred; and those who have on former occasions favoured the public with their opinions as to the destructive effect of the rapid and irregular movement of an immense crowd upon the building, will be surprised to hear that not a single girder or II snag " has given way; and we may add that, although upwards of 100,000 persons were present in the building, there were many portions of it which were comparatively unoccupied by the masses, the nave and transept being of course the most crowded portions of the building. The hourly returns of the numbers formed during the day the subject of intense interest; betting was carried on to an enormous extent, and we are informed that upwards of 100,0001. was entered in various books as to the result. Yor some time past, we believe, 5 to 1 has been very generally offered, and taken, that a number of visitors would in no one day exceed 100,000. The services of the electric telegraph were in constant requisition throughout the day. -In spite, however, of the above enormous influx, Tuesday displayed its accustomed excess over its great holiday rival. The rush began at the earliest possible hour. All the entrances were besieged, and it required all the practised celerity of the money takers to receive the silver shower that poured in upon them without ceasing. By eleven o'clock nearly 60,000 persons had obtained admission, and by twelve the outward stream was nearly as incessant, as if people con- sidered the fact of passing through such a crowd quite enough for one day's amusement. The only precautions taken to preserve re- gularity were the placing of placards directing the visitors to the principal means of exit, and the presence of one or two of the executive committee at the most crowded entrance, to regulate the admissions. A rumour was spread that orders had been received to limit the admission to 100,000, but there was no evidence of its existence in the conduct of the officials. All music was prohibited as tending to congestion, and the guardian of the Queen of Spain's diamonds thought it wiser to withdraw them from the pressure, but in every other respect the internal arrangements were unaltered. Nothing could exceed the good conduct and good temper of the people. There was no pushing, no striving, no ill humour. When the crowd became too dense for transit, they stood still, and tranquilly ate their sandwiches ; and when passage was again attain- able, they went on leisurely, taking time to pause, with a spontaneous and instinctive discipline, before every object worthy of observation. The result was that, although the throng looked almost impervious about the crystal-fountain, where four streams of people were con- stantly meeting, there was facility of passage through every other part of the building, and some places, such as the back settlements of America, and the western gallery behind the great organ, were almost empty. A large body, tired with their struggling pro- snenade, took possession of all the seats in the various refresh. ment rooms, to the great interruption of trade, and consequent chagrin of the proprietors. But the sovereign people were there in all their might, and remonstrance or removal was out of the question. The only thing that tended materially to disturb the general harmony was the frequent disruption of domestic ties by the sweeping away of children from their parents by the billows of the great human torrent. The police station was filled several times during the, day with squalling innocents; and a large detatchbient of the force might be constantly seen doing the duty of careful nursemaids in carrying the little " strays " to the harbour of refuge. The cloak and umbrella stands were piled mountains high, and great delay and inconvenience was experienced in identifying and recovering the deposited articles. It may be repetition again to notice the deportment of these vast masses of human beings, but their orderliness and good conduct, without any restraining power other than their own innate sense of propriety, is really so irk. pressive that it appears to us to be more deserving of record than all the artificial wonders of the Exhibition. It is a great fact for the politician, and one full of future results, that, day by day, 100,000 people can congregate under one roof, can remain in almost crushing contiguity to each other during an entire day, can calmly examline the most wonderful collection of attractive objects that was ever col- lected together, and in the evening can retire at the tinkling of a bell, as calmly as the tide, without a single violation of the rules by which men are enabled to live together in communities. A class of machinists who have derived no inconsiderable advantage from the Exhibition are the locksmiths, being incessantly called into requisi- tion through the carelessness of ladies in forgetting their bunches Of keys in the interior or losing them on the road. On Saturday, the Great Exhibition closed its wonder- d ful career, and the publio took their last farewell of its d splendours. After being open for five months and eleven days, and concentrating ini that time a larger amount of t admiration than has probably ever been given within the P same period to the works of man, the pageant terminates, the doors of the Crystal Palace no longer yield to the open sesame of money, and in a few days hence thousands of hands will be busily engaged in removing all those trinmphs of human skill,- and those evidences of natural wealth which the world was assembled to behold. The a " Amazon," Van der Veu's " Eve," Strazza's " Ishmael," the two French bronzes, and many other contributions of the highest artistic merit were, for the last time, to be gazed at by the admiring multitude. All who had won- a dered over the chefis-d'h eere of Sevres and the Gobelins;s who, in Tunis had spent pleasant hours in examining everything, from the richly-brocaded dresses to the tent d hung with wild beasts' skins; or who in India had feasted their eyes on the splendid evidences of an ancient clvili- V sation-all had to take a final farewell of what had in- r terested and moved them so strongly. The mechanical wonders of the place were about to be withdrawn from n public view. The card-making machine, the circular t wool-comb, Appold's pump, and Whitworth's tools, were V to be seen no longer. The gratuitous distribution of en. velopes and soda water was to cease, and the alarml bed- steads were to do duty before admiring groups of cham- bermaids and cooks no longer. Even the time of that king of diamonds, the Koh-i-noor, was up; and, after having attracted more curiosity and inflicted more disap- pointment than anything of its size ever did since the world was created, the period had arrived when it mustc cease to shine its best before the public. Under such circumstances, and with the mingled feelings which they I could not help suggesting, the crowds of half-crown vi- I sitors bent their way to the Crystal Palace on Saturday. I The weather was splendid, and the sun looked down s warmly upon the only great building in the world, which does not inhospitably exclude his rays. At nine o'clock visitors began to arrive, and they continued to pour in steadily almost until the closing bells had com- menced to ring. All who came remained to the last, t and, although the numbers present were not so great as some had anticipated, they rose higher than on any pre- vious half-crown day, and were amply suficient to make the death scene of the Exhibition worthy of its unpre- cedented popularity. There were 53,061 visitors alto- gether, and, as might have been expected, they busied themselves during the entire day in examining once more all the objects which on former occasions had chiefly at- tracted their interest. Some few were strangers taking at one view their first and last look of a spectacle which in grandeur they may not hope soon to see equalled. There was also a slight sprinkling of the humbler orders present, and among them a band of hop-pickers with wreaths of the plant around their hats. In the main, however, the assemblage belonged to the middle and wealthier classes, and consisted of habitues of the Exhi- bition, or, at least, of people who had been there several times before. Faces that had not been seen in the in- terior since the first month after the opening were recog- nised among the crowd, and it was evident that every rank and grade of society was fairly represented upon an occasion interesting alike to all. An eager desire was manifested, especially in the French department, to pur- chase mementos of the great display, and, in conse- quence everything but an open sale was in progress. As the day wore on, a remarkable concentration of people in the nave began to be discernible. The side avenues and courts were deserted, and from end to end of the build- lig nothing was to be seen but a great sea of human beings filling up the centre, and agitated by a thousand different currents of curiosity, which kept the mass in motion without progress. Time passed, and the circula- tion in the transept became rather impeded. The people seemed to be taking up their position there, and the gal- leries, as far as the eye could reach, were occupied by spectators, who, as they gazed on the vast assemblage be- neath, evidently appeared to expect that some public demonstration was about to be made. The organs, which had been played constantly during the early part of the i day, were now silent; and even that wonderful man, Herr Sommer, with his still more wonderful instrument, sent forth Do longer those astonishing volumes of sound which have rendered him, par excellence, the trumpeter of the Great Exhibition. Nothing was to be heard but that strange and mysterious hum of voices which, rising from all large assemblages, is imposing, but which, in the Crystal Palace, swelling upwards from more than OT,000 people, leaves an impression on the mind not soon to be forgotten. It was drawing near five o'clock. From the top of Keith and Co.'s Spitalfields silk trophy, the whole nave, east and west, the area of the transept, and the galleries, might be seen packed with a dense mass of black hats, through which at intervals a struggling female bonnet emerged here and there into light. The vast' multitude had now become stationary, and were evidently awaiting, in silent but intense excitement, the last act of a great event, immortal in the annals of the 19th century. It was a most solemn and affecting scene, such Rs has rarely been witnessed, and for which an opportunity can- not soon arise. Not only the days, but the minutes of the Great Exhibition were numbered, and the first sign of its dissolution was given by Osler's crystal fountain. Just before five o'clock struck, the feathery jet of water from its summit suddenly ceased, and the silence of the vast assemblage became deeper and more intense. The mo- ment at last came. Mr. Belshaw appeared at the west corner of the transept-gallery on the south side, bearing a large red flag in his hand. This he displayed as the clock struck, and instantly all the organs in the building were hurling into the air the well-known notes of the na- tional anthem. At the same moment the assembled mul- titudes uncovered; and those who witnessed this act of loyalty from an advantageous position will long remember the effect which it produced upon their minds. Where just before nothing was visible but a mass of black hats stretching away until lost in the distance, immediately there appeared a great sea of upturned animated faces, and to the solemn silence of expectancy succeeded a vo- lume of sound in which the people joined. The Crystal Pa- lace is not adapted for organ music, and, notwithstanding the number of them exhibited, they cannot, from the size of the building, be played in concert. The consequence was that, as a musical performance,-there being no proper organisation in the matter,-the singing of "God save the Queen" was a very discordant demonstration of loyalty. Herr Sommer did everything in his power and in that of his instrument to keep the people in tune, but he was only partially Buccessful. Some professional singers also gave their aid upon the occasion, and inspired the assemblage with courage to follow. On the whole, however, foreigners would have managed this matter better; and, though it is useless now to express regrets, it does seem a pity that prower steps were not taken to make the performance of the National Anthem as effective as it might have been. About the feeling which accompanied it there could be no mistake, for as soon as it had closed there. arose such cheers as Euglishmen alone know how to give. These were continued for several minutes, and when the last of them died away there passed over the entire building, and with an effect truly sublime, a tremendous rolling sound, like that of thunder, caused by thousands of feet stamping their loyalty upon the boardedfloors. Under this demon- stration every part. of the edifice trembled, and, as it swept from west to east, many an eye was raised with anxiety to the girders and pillars, which in long perspec- tive were stretched out before them. And now the time had arrived for the death peal of the Exhibition to be rung out. Some one hung out from the gallery of the transept a piece of calico, on which was inscribed the well-known passage from Shakspere's Tempest, &c. "Our revels now are ended: these our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits, and Are melted into air, into thin air; And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, The cloud-capped towers, the gorgeous palaces, The solemn temples, the great lobe itself,- Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolves And, like this unsubstantial pageant faded,. Leave not a sack behind." IA minute or two was allowed to elapse before the fatal, signal wras given, and during this brief interval the assem- blage remained silent and motionless. At last it came, r and a perfect storm of bell peals broke over the building. China had to come to the rescue with her gongs, and India to strike up som'e fine savage notes from her tom-toms, before the signs of an intention to depart were unmis- > takeably manifested. The concourse of people for a long time remained massed together, as if no power could sep- arate or fuse them;'but at last small currents and ripples V of human beings might be seen setting towards the exit- t doors, and these gradually increased in volume and rapi- dity as the shades of evening fell. One by one the gas D lamps were lighted, and the building, divided between the empire of day and night, assumed an aspect curiously in t harmony with its defunct character. The crowds flowed l out faster every minute, and first the western, and then 3 the eastern portions of the nave, began to show vacant spaces. In the meantime, the ringing of bells was a occasionally suspended, and in the intervals hearty cheers Yi were given for Prince Albert, foi the Prince of Wales, for Mr. Paxton, for Mr. Fox, for the exhibitors and upon various other grounds. An attempt, too, was made by some vocalists to get upsa musical performance, but their efforts awere instantly drowned by the revived energies of the rin- t Kgems Some one proposed a cheer for Kossuth, but it met D with no response except some derisive laughter. The galleries and the eastern and western naves had now been completely cleared, but a dense body still clung round the crystal fountain, many filling bottles with' water from it as a memento, and others struggling in vain to approach it l for hat purpose. The police and the Sappers appeared on he cee, irt in small knots, and then, when they i, lied moved the people on'a little, in extended line. By geitprsing on them they at last induced them togo f but it was dark, and half-past six o'cloclr, biefore the build- in lg was completely cleared, and the bells finally ceased' f~tolling. The executive committee, and the chief members of their staff, met in the transept when it was all over, and many and hearty were the congratulatigas which they exchanged on the happy termination of their brilliant 1a- bours. Even the Sappers participated in the gratification which the event of Saturday inspired, and before the building was left to silence nsld solitude, they made Its dim and shadowy interior ring with three hearty cheers for the Queen.-Tines. On Monday, there was a numerous attendance of exhi- bitors and those introduced by them in the building. Re- lieved from the pressure of public curiosity, they examined leisurely and enjoyably every object of interest, nor could one help acknowledging the propriety of an arrauge- ment by which the last view of so many wonders has been reserved.for those who created them. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty paid another visit to the Crystal Palace on Monday, and remained a considerable time examining the agricultural implements and machinery and the collection of ores and minerals. Among the many curious and valuable specimens exhibited by Mr. Tennant is the large emerald, the property of his Grace the Duke of Devonshire, and which is said to be the third most valuable jewel in this country; the Koh-i-Noor being the first, Mr. Hope's great diamond the second, and the duke's large emerald the third. The story runs that when his grace was examining Mr. Tennant's collection of gems, he said, " I suppose you would like to have my emerald to exhibit V' Mr. Tennant replied that he would be delighted to have an opportunity of doing so, but he was afraid of the risk. " Then," said his grace, " I shall take the risk ;" and the emerald was sent to Mr. Tennant. The number of visitors on Monday was not quite so large as on Saturday, the afternoon having turned out unfavourable, but the diminution could only be perceived by those who are in the habit of frequenting the building daily, and, indeed, the weather has little effect upon the class of visitors to whom it is as yet confined, and who are to some extent independent of atmospheric inconveniences. The average daily receipts since the opening have been little short of 20001., and if the income continues to maintain the sense high figure for the ensuing fortnight, the whole expenses of the building will have been paid off before the price falls to a shilling and the general public are admitted. The frequent visits of her Majesty and the Royal Family have added cansiderably to the popularity of the Exhibition —all minds are occupied with it, and all tongues are loud in praises; one of its peculiarities is its vast extent, which cannot be fully comprehended on the first visit, and it is only when an attempt is made to methodise and arrange the process of investigation and inspection, that the stupendous scale upon which the whole has been planned can be fully comprehended- The efforts of a long day sink into insignificance when a trial is made to explore the illimitable mazes of the aisles and avenues vanishing in the remote perspective, or the sweeping extent of the galleries, to traverse which alone would be considered a reasonable promenade for a day. The pedestrian feats which delicate ladies accomplish within the building are marvellous, and it is only the sustaining power of continued excitement and novelty, the desire to pass from one object of interest to another, the swallowing of everything with the eyes and retaining little in the mind, the anxiety te see everything at once, and the utter impossibility of seeing anything well, that carries them through a rather fatiguing movement of four or five hours employed in advancing, turning back, stooping, straining, darting into this compartment, and gliding out of that, crawling slowly up staircases and skipping lightly down; and thus the movements of the visitors themselves are among the most curious and interesting features of the Exhibition. Certainly one of its many characteristics—apart from the architectural beauty of the lofty transept, the grand sweep of the naves, and the interminable looking aisles and passages, in which the illusion of remoteness and distance is still further heightened by the airines s and transparency of the encasing material, and the presence of the majestic monarchs of the park, that spread their branches overhead—is the fact that there is no one individual article, nor no particular collection, that monopolises attention to the comparative neglect of others. Apart from the attractions of the Koh-i-Noor—which, although one of the first objects sought for, never receives a second look, the feeling of most of the visitors being that of diappointment at its comparatively small size and want of that peculiar brilliancy which is conventionally attached to the diamond—the crystal fountain, which is continually receiving fresh accessions of admirers, and tho costly display of gems belonging to the Queen of Spain—setting these aside, which always captivate the attention of fresh arrivals—the four great classes into which the Exhibition is divided appear to have equal attractions for all. We believe, however, that those who wish to obtain a fair idea of the contents of the Crystal Palace, will do well to adopt our suggestion of taking each country in detail, and then having gone through the foreign departments, with their corresponding galleries, proceed in like manner through the western portion of the building. The foreign departments are now making rapid progress in the completion of their decorations, and before the end of the present week we have no doubt all the defects and deficiencies will be made good. Proceeding on our tour of inspection down the foreign nave, we now approach the more southern states of Europe, which bask under the bright—we cannot say warm—sun of the transept. The bay to the west of Italy is devoted to Spain and Portugal. The works of art are few, therefore the attention of the spectator is turned almost solely to the natural products of these countries, of which there is a very instructive and interesting selection. The minerals of Spain are well known to be of the most varied description, and there can be no doubt whatever that with enterprise and capital they might become the sources of vast national wealth. The recent move that has been made by English capitalists in mining speculation has partially extended to this richly-endowed country, and the specimens of native ores which the Exhibition supplies will consequently be examined with great and earnest attention. The directors and inspectors of the leading mines have submitted a great variety of specimens. Granada sends samples of the lead which has hitherto been the staple of its commerce in this particular department. Then, again, there are specimens of the quicksilver of La Mancha, a district long celebrated for its mineral riches. It has been stated that Spain was to the ancient what its American possessions have been to the modern world—that is, it was the principal source of the supply of the precious metals. But it is, on the other hand, doubted whether the Carthaginians or Romans ever discovered any mines of this description in Spain. It is presumed that the gold was obtained simply from washings, and that the silver, by far the most abundant, was chiefly obtained Irons the lead, which, as we have intimated, has always been raised in large quantities. There are numerous specimens of argentiferous ores, while the samples of tin, copper, antimony, iron, &c., are most abundant. The Royal Library of Madrid exhibits a curious collection of various marbles, in the production of which Spain ' we need hardly remark, enjoys an eminent distinction ; and in the neighbourhood of ibis display, also enriched by a series from Cordoba there are some fine specimens of rock and o th er salts. The agricultural produce of Spain is liberally represented. Of the wheat of this country, said to be among the finest in the world, there are many samples, besides maize, rice, barley, beans, chestnuts, &c. Dried fruits of all kinds are exhibited; likewise houses, oils, flax, and other produce. The wools and silks are extremely beautiful. Hanging upon the entrance of the bay is a fine specimen of the plant lagetta lottearia, showing the textile substance of the interior bark, as well as the cord made from the same. In this section there are also a variety of ropes, mattings, and the like, made from the fibres of the palm and majagur; as well as an extensive collection of the rushes, or grasses, used in manufactures. The domestic trades do not figure very conspicuously, for notwithstanding the opportunities which Spain has, not only from her abundance of wool and silk at home, but for the extent of her colonial produce, her manufacturing development has ever been in a poor and unthriving condition. Such industry as the country possesses is, however, shown in its silks, dewasks, velvets, laces, musline, woollen cloths, veils, &c., from Velentia, valiadolid, Seville, Andalueia, and other places ; while the blonde mantillas of Barcelone and elsewhere are of too national and distinctive a character not to be put prominently forward. Specimens of the taaning, which is carried on very extensively in the northern provinces of Spain ; of the soaps, &c., of Malaga ; of the saddlery, ironmongery, and bronzes of Madrid; of the pavement tiles of Segovia; of the straw manufactures of Valencia, &c., are numerous, and detain the visitor a few minutes, but they more or less exemplify the national inferiority, and challenge but little compliment, excepting, however, the finely-tempered sword-blades of Toledo, which no one cognisant of their reputation will pass by without examining. The first thing that strikes the spectator among the miscellaneous articles is the tabernacle of F. Moratilla, e: Madrid, standing at the entrance of this compartment. This has been described as one of the grandest things in the Exhibition—at all events, it is one of the most costly; for it is valued at no less a ruin than 23,000/. It is a " custodia," made for the Cathedral of Lima. It is about five feet high, and measures about two feet square at the base. Four angels, worked in silver, are kneeling at the corners of the pedestal, which is made of polished brass exquisitely ornamented. The shaft, of the same material, contains figures of Moses, David, St. Peter, and St. Paul, above which, standing under canopies on the entablature, are the four Evangelists, the whole being surmounted with a golden star of the most lustrous beauty. The cross which forms the centre is composed of precious stones—rubies, emeralds, and diamondsglittering brilliantly, and farming an ensemble certainly as magnificent as any combination of a like kind could possibly be. The general effect of this superb ecclesiastical emblem is very striking, though the beauties of the design and the intrinsic worth of the embellishments cannot be fully estimated until the spectator has scrutinised them with some degree of minuteness. The octagonal inlaid table from Barcelona, in the immediate rear of the " custodia," is also an object of great curiosity. It is divided into large medallion compartments, thickly bordered with arabesques and other ornaments. the centre containing the shield of England, which, although set in a space of three inches by two, is composed of some 53,000 separate pieces, and so minute are the points of wood that a magnifying glass is provided to determine the process by which the pieture is formed. Although it is described to be an "inlaid " table, we presume it to be but a very superior piece of Tunbridge work, and thet when the pattern was once formed, the ()refinery multiplications by the circular saw were made. This, however, dues not detract from its individual beauty, however much it may depreciate its pecuniary worth. A model of one half of the bull-fighting circus of Madrid, With 4000 Lilliputian wooden figures, gives the Englieli spectator an accurate idea of the notorious public sport of Spain, together with the species of building in which it is perpetrated. You survey the outside of thG circus, the gored horse that, brought out, ig 'Lying bleeding on the stones, and the cart that is driving up to carry off the dying brute. On the other side you see the vast range of spectators overlooking the area in which the matadors are exciting the infuriated bulls, while horsemen are engaged in the attack. The model is not very neatly executed, but it portrays a national amusement, and that with all the painful and repugnant circumstances with which it is so cruelly associated. A secretaire, with inlaid work, is almost the only article of household furniture which Spain produces; but there is a small group of antiquities which are interesting, among them an original piece of the Alhambra Palace at Granada. Let us add that the Agronomical Cabinet of the Botanical Garden of Madrid have sent 225 specimens of the woods of Cuba, and the Economical Society of Manilla 213 different spec:es of the woods of the Philippine Islands, together with a collection of the different qualities of the tobacco leaf employed in the government factories in Manilla and other places. Havannah cigars, too, assail you at every point. Passing into the eastern half of the same bay, we find ourselves in the midst of the contributions from Portugal, which also consist principally of natural productions—the manufacturing and industrial genius of this country, like that of Spain, being at a very low ebb. Indeed, it is well known, that most of the hardware, earthenware, linens, &c. used by the Portuguese are imported into Portugal by England and otter nations; and Baillie in his book on "Lisbon" affirms that "a very superficial knowledge of the commonest arts exists. A carpenter is the most awkward and clumsy artisan, and the way in which the doors and wood work belonging to the good houses are finished would have suited the rudest ages. The Portuguese carriages of all kinds, more particularly their waggons and carts, their agricultural implements and management, their cutlery, locks and keys, are ludicrously bad." These assertions are not practically disproved as far as the exposition is concerned. There are a few specimens of printed cottons, cloths, drills, leathers, cutlery, stationery, jewellery, &c., but none of them denote any particular amount of manipulative skill, or any very superior order of finish. A pretentious bouquet of artificial -flowers faces the spectator as he enters the Portuguese department from the nave, but, the French ardsans are too formidable in this ornamental work, and too profuse in their illustrations "over the way" to give it a chance of admiration. The dealers in snuffs come out strongly, and there are numerous varieties of this pungent preparation—palpable and impalpable, common and uncommon, dry, scented, and mixed—from Lisbon. The best show, however—wines being excluded by official behest —is that of the dried fruits. Preserved pears, figs, peaches, apricots, and the like, prettily arranged in fancy boxes, line the north-eastern side of th e b a y. Th e or di nar y vegetable products are also liberally paraded, such as wheat, rice, &c., precisely similar, as a matter of course, to the neighbouring display from Spain, with which Portugal necessatily has nearly everything of the sort in common. The works of art are lamentably scarce. A few lithographs, a pen and-ink drawing or two, and some wood and ivory carvings, none of them of any intellectual merit whatever, are all that we see. In the same compartment as that occupied by Portugal, the productions and manufactures of Madeira and the Western Islands are deposited. This collection is inconsiderable, but it contains samples of the opal and lime stone of Porto Santo, and the lignite of Madeira ; while a curious specimen of the porous stone peculiar to the Island of Terceira, formed into a large cauldron-shaped cistern, and practically exemplifying its filtering properties in a vessel below, is an interesting object in the centre of the area. The vegetable . kingdom of Madeira, singularly prolific in all useful growths, is well illustrated in the specimens which are here provided, one of the most prominent features being a tableau of ferns very picturesquely arranged under a glass frame. The manufactures consist of linens and shawls, mingled with such light arts as hair and flower workings, small cabinet toys, and a series of wax models delineating the flowers and fruits indigenous to the island. As the hour of closing approaches, the great bell sounds forth its note of preparation, and then the bulk of the visitors commence pouring out of the aisles and.compartments, scampering down the staircases, and collecting in the transept and eastern and western entrances. Carriages are called up in rapid succession, and meantime the exhibitors commence the work of cleaning and making snug for the night; feather brooms and brushes are called into requisition, and a prodigious dust is soon kicked up, which haslens the departure of those who have not yet drunk in their fill of the marvels of the Exhibition. Linea and calico cases and sheets are laid over the more precious articles, and the scantily. attired Venuses, Junos, and Hebes, who have all day unblushingly braved the gaze of the many thousand connoisseurs and critics, are clothed in night-gowns or ezemisee, while Power's Greek slave girl, who has been performing at fresco pirouettes all day to a crowd of admirers on her revolving pedestal, blushes to the ancles in a full snit of crimson drapery. The organs peal forth a final voluntary, although they are chary enough of their music throughout the day, and other indications of the shutting up of the great bazaar are shown in the appearance on the scene of watchmen, firemen, watermeu, and lamplighters; in addition to this numerous and efficient band of organised assistants, the opening of the water mains throughout the building are exposed, from whence start up huge brass-n zzled tubes, surrounded by buckets of water, leaving the spectator of these numerous precautions to infer that the whole building was as safe from fire as if it were enveloped in a wet blanket. A general scrutiny of the whole establishment succeeds—as the shades of night begin to fall, the great eastern star, the diamond mountain, sinks into its impenetrable safe, "the watch is set," and the frail crystalline fabric is as safe from intrusion as if it were encompassed I by walls of adamant. It having been determined that on and after the 2Oth of this month the charge for admission into the Exhibition shall be reduced to Is. for four days in the week, her Majesty's Commissioners have again had under their consideration the question of making arrangements for the accommodation of the working classes who may be expected to arrive from the country for the purpose of visiting it. This subject has engaged the attention of the commission from a very early period; and when, in July last, Mr. Alexander Redgrave, of the Home Office, was appointed for the special purpose of co-operating with Colonel Reid in obtaining such information and making such arrangements as might facilitate the visits of the labouring population to the Exhibition, he was particularly desired to consider the advisability of instituting a register of lodging and lodging-houses, for the information of visitors arriving from the country. The general result of the inquiries which the commissioners have made is, that it will be better for them to leave this matter to the exertions of visitors themselves, and to abstain from atbempting to organise a system for their accommodation, as it appears that by doing so they would interfere with many praiseworthy undertakings of private individuals, by means of which it is now probable that their object will be more fully accomplished than it could be by any system of centralisation. The commissioners have learnt with much satisfaction, that in many cases very liberal arrangements have been made for the reception of persons coming from particular districts. Where this is not the case, they recommend that mechanics about to visit the Exhibition should endeavour, by mutual co-operation, and by arrangements made before leaving their homes, to obviate the inconvenience which might arise from their coming together in large numbers without previously preparing for their accommodation. The preparations already made for their amusement are of a varied and continuous character; the daily promenade concerts, for which the German band has been re-engaged, with additional strength, from Cologne, will commence on the 19th instant, when a pyrotechnical fete will form an agreeble conclusion to the musical attractions of the evening. FATAL BOAT ACCIDENT AT GREENOCK.—A melancholy accident, by which two men lost their lives, occurred on Saturday evening, a little before six o'clock, opposite the Greenock Steam-boat Quay. The afternoon had been very fine, with a pretty fresh breeze of easterly wind, and a number of small sailing-boats darting backwards and attracted a considerable number of spectators to witness their evolutions. By•and-bye, however, the wind increased to such an extent, with a nasty cross sea, as to give cause for alarm for the safety of the crews, particularly that of the largest boat, which was observed to snip several seas. The men, two us number, were observed to put her about and make for the shore, running with the wind, when all at once, while still at a considerable distance from the harbour, she was observed to go down head foremost, and was never afterwards seen, though the mast was found. Several boats at once made for the spot, to reuder assistance to the men, but without avail, for they, too, had disappeared, and though the search was prolonged till dark, the bodies were not recovered. The unfortunate men,whose names were Charles King, foreman carpenter in Messrs. Steele's shipbuilding yard, and John M`Gilp, a working carpenter, in the same employ, were married. King has left a wife and three young children to lament his loss.
