THE GREAT EXHIBITION. ?? -- ,- Now that a large proportion of the conmmlissioners of foreign countries have arrived in England and taken ossession of the different spaces allotted to them in the Crystal Palace, the public will be curious to know how, they are satisfied with the arrangements made for their reception, and to what extent they are preparing them- selves for the opening in May. Is a former notice we alluded to differences which bad arisen between one or two of them and the'executive committee. These differ- ences have happily been adjusted, but others have arisen which give rise to great delay and inconvenience with- out any possible good result from them. It is very na- tural that the commissioners of foreign countries who find themselves encumbered by a host of exhibitors whom they cannot accommodate should desire to swell out as much as possible the exhibiting surface of the gross areas allotted to them; but it must be obvious also that the general arrangements made for the circulation of visitors and for the orderly conduct of the Exhibition cannot, and ought not, to be departed from. The good sense of the gentlemen who have been intrusted with the contri- butions of their respective nations will enable them, we trust, to see that no desire can exist on the part of any one connected with the Exhibition to act otherwise to- wards them than in the most liberal spirit, and that all the restrictions and conditions which are laid on them art equally binding upon our native contributors. In nearly all the- foreign consignments that have as yet been examiised by the Custom-house officers, numbers of packages have been found containing pure articles of general merchandise, apparently with no specific claim for a corner in the Great Exhibition. There appears to be considerable delay and reluctance on the part of the commissioners from abroad to have the goods under their care inspected by the Custom- house officers. This arises partly from the strong ob- jection which is entertained to unpacking so long before the Exhibition opens; and, undoubtedly, it is an incon- venience in many instances, but not so great, we fear, as that which must arise if the mass of the work is put off to the last moment, and the Custon-hiouse officers have to discharge their duties in the midst of all the hurry and confusion which must precede the opening in May. To many people it seems an unnecessary exercise of official ?? that an examiination of the goods for the Exhibition should at present take place for revenue purposes, it being contended that the Crystal Palace being declared a bonded warehouse, and every precau- tion taken to prevent any irregular or smuggling pro- ceedings, the Custom- house people usight quite as well perforni their duties after theexhibition has terminated as now. It appears, however, that they have no alterna- tive, being compelled by statute to act at once. We are even told, that to afford the necessary facilities for foreign and colonial contributions to the World's Fair, they have stretched the stringent lalws which bind them as far as they possibly or safely could, and that they are most anxious by all the means in their power to avoid proving stumbling blocks on so interesting an oc- casion, There are twelve landing waiters engaged within the building, under the superintendence of SIr. Rolt, and, as soon as they cani obtain the attendance of the agents, they pursue the examination of the packages in tre different compartments simultaneously. Mostpro- gress has, as yet, been made with the contributions from - Switzerland, which, as may be remembered, were brought in at a very early date. This part of the Exhilition premises, we hear, to be very interesting, and comprises a great variety of very beautiful articles. Among the objects in the Swiss collection which are most highly spoken of, are a gold peaholder with a di- minutive watch at the top of it, indicating not only the hours, minutes, and seconds, but even the days of ithe month, and a lady's escritaire of very elegant design, and elaborately carved. DEPARTURE OF THE DUKE or Baunswicx BY THE "NASSAU" BALLOON FOR GERMANY.-On Tuesday, one of the most peculiar feats in aerostation took place from the gardens of the " royal property," Vauxhall, by the- departure of the Duke of Brunswick, accompanied by Mr. Charles Green, the well-known aeronaut, in his bal- loon. Preparation beingmadeon the Waterloo-ground, oal Sunday evening a number of men were employed, under the direction of Mr. Lumm, the principal engineer of the London Gas Company, in laying down a nine- inch pipe from the works to inflate the machine, and at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning everything was in readiness for the inflation, and by eleven o'clock the bal- - loen was in a fit state for the ascent. The Duke of Brunswick, accompanied by a few friends, arrived on the ground with a laige quantity of provisions and viands necessary for a lengthened voyage, consisting of hams, fowls, pheasants partridges, breadstufis. chocolate, coffee, &c., with Soyer's apparatus for cooking. The ascent being strictly private, the event was a surprise to the in- habitants of the vicinity. Thirteen tried carrier pigeons, belonging to Mr. Henry Evans, of Kennington-lane, were placed in the car for the purpose of communicating with those interested in the fact; and precisely at twelve o'clock his highness, accompanied by Mr. Charles Green, stepped into the car. Mr. Green pulled the liberating- iron, and the machine arose. At the time of the ascent the wind was blowing'- -om-NzW..by W. The ballast carried was thirteen cwt., with air vessels, water-drags, and gutta percha lines. The balloon, on arriving at a sufficient altitude, took a south-easterly direction, pass- lug over the counties of Surrey and Kent in the direction of the Continent, and from the favourable nature of the ascent it was fully believed the attempt would be suc- cessful. But information has since been received that the balloon, with its voyagers, descended safely at Graves- end about two hours after leaving Vauxhall-gardeas, the duke having found the wind suddenl become adverse to the particular course which, in his aerial journey, lie mean to take. From 177I until his death, in 1822, Canova laboured in- cessantly; producing in the intervening period no less than 176 capital productions. The maxim which in his later years it was his wont to impress, forcibly and emphatically, upon his numerous pupils, was to the effect that sculpture could only be successfully prosecuted by those who gave all their studies to nature, constantly correcting the impressions gathered in those studies by compari- son with the peculiar conventionalities and refine- ments of ancient art. The advice he thus gave appears, throughout his long and arduous life, to have guided him in a successful endeavour to sub- stitute truth and beauty for the mannerism and exaggeration fashionable at the commencement of his career. Ilis various works were sought for by the rich and noble of every country in Europe. In his earlier years, English patronage was showered upon him with no sparing hand. In the climax of his fameE, Napoleon was successful in obtaining for France some of his noblest productions. In Ger- many his works were much admired, and many younn artists of great abilities were honoured by his instruction and kindly sympathy while re- ceivila their education (gratuitously) in his studio. It was, however, in Italy that the strongest impres- sion was made by the vigour of his opposition to antecedent prejudices. 13y Can ova principally, and by his friend Vis- conti (in his excellent critiques on the great monu- inents of antiquity) in an inferior degree, those laws of form and composition were given, in accordance with which the most beautiful specimens of Italian sculpture in the Great Exhibition appear to have beel conscientiously modelled. The " Wounded Achilles " of Fraccaroli will at once recall the pe- culiar manner of Cauova. The immortal Thorwaldsen drived from Canova the most nobly-rendered assistance in his art, and had the honour in return, in his later years, of raising into majestic dignity the aspirations of Callova after the beautiful. The greatest living ?? and Gibson-had both the satis- faction of working under the immediate eve of these two distinguished men; and the pupils of ?? and Rietschel-still hand en to us umiquenched the fire that was lit by Cauova. To France, Claudet imported the spirit of Canova and the study of the antique, so successfully prosecuted by David, and isiav so admirably exemplified to us in the beautiful `'lihryne" and other statues of Pradier, and in the severe monuments of Etex. From the influence of Canova and his studio have prvceeded all the most beautiful of those produc- ibns w hich, without departing from the strict limits of physical individuality of form, recall the bean-ideal of the Greeks. The natural and the romantic in sculpture must be traced in a great degree to other sources. The "Si woral" was mainly revived in Germauy, and pro- ceeded from that phase of mind which started to life in the independent philosophy of Goethe, Schil- In-, Kant, &c. Gottfried Schadow (born in 1764) turned his attention to portrait sculpture, and his productions may be regarded as having materially inilueisced many works of the great Rauch, Dan- necker, Tiock, and other subordinate artists. The spirit of romantic sculpture may scarcely ever be said to have been extinct in France, from the period of the lt6naissauce to the present day. That peculiar fanciful naiaet6 of treatment-some- times pleasing from its graceful conventionality, ?? annoying from its caricature-crept into the composition of works of all ages in France. From the rustic " figulines" of Bernard de Palissy, throughl the charming little groups of figures of the ,Kvres manufactory, tinged by the rosy fancy of Bouch6rr and Wutteau, down to the portrait statues and Joans of Arc which swarm in the galleries of V ersailles, we may readily trace an adhesion to the rowantio in art. Within our present limits it is scarcely possible to follow inl detail the analogies and dependencies which exist between works the production of living artists, and those of predecessors whose influence is by no means the less certain because not immediately pal- pable. We trust, however, that our rapid sketch of i the past may enable our readers in some degree more justly to apprehend the peculiarities of the present. These we propose to examine by nations, and we trust that in carrying out our purpose we may arrive at some conclusions not altogether without interest in the future. With that egotism for which, whether justly or unjustly, Englishmen are celebrated throughout the world, we shall proceed first to an examination of those specimens of the sculptor's art which have been contributed to the Great Exhibition by the artists of our native country. ; The leading impression which such an examina- tion must, as we conceive, impart to a foreigner, viewing it unaffected by strongly formed antece- dent impressions, would be that the English, as a nation, possessed oonsiderable affection for, and a ready appreciation of, physical beauty-but that r they were unendorsed either with a strong sym- pathy for the higher aims of art, or with any very accurate knowledge of its legitimate application,. In English sculpture it is comparatively rare to encounter a group in which anything like an at- tempt at the combined action of several figures is made. Nymphs bathing, Cupids, Psyches, athletes, and character-statues, we have in abundance; but seldom do we meet with any embodiments of scenes derived from sacred or national history, or from the highest order of epic or lyric poetry. Basso-relievo, in which the artists of ancient Greece, of cinque- i canto Italy, and of modern Germany, delighted and I delight to personify the traditions of their faith, in English art find little correspondent expression. , With the exception of a few picturesque and alle- ; gorical subjects, including a few figures-of two r large, religious, but not very beautiful composi- . tions, by Mr. Carew-aud of Gibson's admirable i work, the " Hours bringing out the Horses of the I Sun"-the British Sculpture Gallery exhibits i neither any specimen of dramatic embodiment in F basso-relievo, nor any indication of the connection N which, in the best ages of the art, has invariably k existed between sculptured representation and k mural or architectonic embellishment. r In that gallery, and dispersed throughout the I nave and transept of the building, are many statues of great power of conception, so far as composition of line and justness of expression are concerned, and of admirable refinement of execution. But there is, about the majority of them, a character of I indifference to the unities of the particular locality, if any, which they may be destined to occupy. The custom of modelling statues in the studio, composed So as to admit of being turned round 3 upon the "banker" of the sculptor, and to display a reasonably good form when viewed from every side- and the frequent practice of subduing emotion into I comparatively unmeaning prettiness of expression- while tending to increase the probabilities of the sale of such works of art, detract greatly from their real value in the eyes of the connoisseur. In all the periods during which, in any country, 1 sculpture has reached its most successful develop- ment, buildings have been planned to minister to a purpose-to express an intention-and to affect some peculiar series of sympathies. To carry out these objects clearly and emphatically, sculpture was indispensable. As Mr. Fergusson admirably says, in his " Beauty in Art," sculpture is but the voice of architecture, speaking so that the most uninitiated may read her aims, and the meaning of her conventionalities. With us, unfortunately, now-a-days, the case is very different. Houses of Parliament, pa- laces, churches, private mansions are planned, built, all but finished, and the architect often dismissed, before the founders awake to the consciousness that but half the work is done. " Committees of Taste" are formed, studios are ransacked, and whatever can be picked up to fill the vacant niches, or cover the blank walls, are pressed into the service, without special regard to propriety, and are placed in situations which, neither by conception nor execution, they can be legitimately qualified to occupy. It is for this reason that the walls of the Royal Academy are hung from I year to year with numbers of pretty but meaningless sketches and studies, suited, from their negative qualities rather than from their intrinsic excel- lences, to furnish any dining-room, or accommodate themselves to almost any taste. This is why it is that the condemned cell in which the worksX of British sculptors have for so many years been exhi-l bited in London has every year teemed with pro- ductions, nicely felt, well modelled, and very fairly finished, in plaster and in marble, well calculated to be stuck in any hall, or at the foot of any stair- case. The effect of this production of isolated specimens of art becomes singularly perceptible when any nobleman or gentleman attempts to form what is called a gallery of sculpture. The majority of such collections in England consist of one or two classic groups, half a dozen Nymphs, two or three Wrest- lers, and one or two Cupids or other fat children. One figure is naked, another draped; one is an- L tique, another is romantic; one is good, and three f or four are bad-not so much from being defective either in form, composition, or execution, but sim- ply because placed in an improper situation, and connected with uncomfortable or inconsistent asso- i ciations. It is, therefore, as we conceive, rather in its aim than in its form that English sculpture will, with some few bright exceptions, be found defec- tive. As compared with corresponding productions of other nations, the majority of the English single figures may successfully stand the test of compari- son In Mr. Gibson's " Hunter," exhibited by Lord Yarborough, one of the finest types of manly beauty , displayed in the Exhibition may be unquestionably recognized. Although every muscle is bound in tense excitement, the figure displays no affectation of anatomical development. Life and activity ani- mate alike the hoand and the man. In that group the artist has displayed the profoundest knowledge of the conditions of his art. Carefully avoiding that form of action under which the hound would 1 drag the man forward, or the pulling of the man would disturb the natural action of the hound; the moment has been seized in which the forces of each L are held in momentary equipoise. It certainly 1 would have been well for the reputation of the Eug lish school, if more of Mr. Gibson's works haid r adorned the Great Exhibition. With these general remarks on the character of English sculpture, we shall return to the subject in our next article, reviewing with some care the many F choice works exhibited. The people in their thousands” still flock to the Crystal Palace, although there is now little more for the journalist to do besides the duty of registering for public information the numbers admitted, and amounts paid in at the doors. Thursday the attendance of visitors at the building was greater than it had been for some days, the police returns giving 55,(138 as the total, and the receipts at the doors amounting to £2,662 9s. The cool agreeable weather has permitted people to move about without discomfort, and the increased ventilation ol the interior has been carried out very successlully. Among the gatherings of spectators there is now an extraordinary number of children, many schools in and around the metropolis contributing their quota of boys and girls almost every day of the shilling admission. Friday (says the Times) is now, perhaps, the most attractive day of the week at the Crystal Palace. The half-crown admission fee insures certain degree of selectness on the one hand, while it prevents the interior wearing too deserted or exclusive look upon the other. The baskets filled with provisions for luncheon and the odours of gin and oranges arc no longer perceptible; nor docs the visitor feel himself perplexed by the movements of a motley assemblage agitated like a beehive summer, and from which a humming sound is ceaselessly ascending. has leisure to observe everything without distraction, and when his curiosity about the inanimate objects around him satisfied, he can find relief in watching the company, in admiring the varied display of beauty, and even in enjoying the refreshing coolness of the air which by the system of ventilation adopted and the change in the weather has now been efiectually secured. Upwards of people entered the building last Fridav, and the receipts were £2,611 3s. The attendance at the Crystal Palace on Saturday exceeded that of the preceding five-shilling day. During the first hour 3,728 visitors were admitted, number which was augmented to 11,743 in the course of the afternoon. The receipts at the doors amounted to £1,565 155., and the sale of season tickets produced £l6 16s. Gigantic Locomotive. —ln the machinery department is a locomotive engine a gigantic scale, called the Liverpool,” constructed by Messrs, Bury & Co., for the North-Western Railway Company. This vast machine is constructed on the principle of the Crampton patent, the peculiarity of which is, that the driving wheels are placed at the rear of the engine immediately under the fire box. This immense machine is supported on eight wheels, the driving wheels being eight feet, and the supporting wheels four feet diameter. The cylinders arc eighteen inches diameter and twenty-four inches stroke. The evaporating power of the boiler must be enormous, since the heating surface exposed to the direct action of the fire is 156 square feet, and the total surface of the tubes which traverse longitudinally the boiler, and which the gaseous products of combustion are conducted from the fire box to the chimney and strained of their heat en route, have a total surface of not less than 2,090 square feet. Thus there is a total heating surface of 2,400 square feet. The weight of the machine when supplied with its full complement of coke and water is 37 tons. The Times on Asiatic Art. —While the subject of prizes is still under the consideration of the jurors, and before their awards have been finally made, we are anxious to press upon their consideration the claims of such contributions as those of the Indian Government, of the Hey of Tunis, and of the Sultan. nquestionably we have as much if not more to learn from those compartments than from any others in the Exhibition. We may look down with contempt upon industrial systems incompatible with our utilitarian standards, supplying only the luxuries and caprices of greatness, and careless the comforts and w&r.ts of the masses. Vet in another point of view these remarkable and characteristic collections have a value that can hardly overrated. By their suggestiveness the vulgarisms art manufactures, not only England, but of Christendom, may corrected ; and from the carpets, the shawls, the muslins, and the brocades of Asia, and from much of its metallic and earthenware products, can clearly traced those invaluable rules of art, a proper definition and recognition of which form the great desiderata qf our more civilized industrial systems. It would, therefore, be scandalous oversight on the part of the jurors they did not keep steadily in view’, when making their awards, these immense prospective benefits which are certain to derive from the manner in which the Governments referred to have supported the Exhibition. With them individual contributors have no existence, and therefore it may be imagined that the gratification of bearing off prizes need not he studied. But juries should close their eyes to persons and think only of tilings. Their business is not with the people who exhibit, but the articles exhibited, and if they find in India a carpet, or Tunis a prayer rug worthy of distinction, they should make their award accordingly. Exhibition Prizes : the principle on theij should be distributed —The dissensions among: the juries, and the struggles for first-class medals, continue subjects of serious uneasiness and annoyance. Were these ditfirences caused by the conflicting claims of native contributors, should be silent upon them, confident that in the hands of judges carefully selected merit would, on the whole, fairly and impartially rewarded. When, however, the question of rivalry between countries is raised and discussed by some with energy which savours of an undue organization for the purpose, it is time to call attention to those principles which were laid down at the outset for guiding the awards, and to remind all British jurors that on those principles they must stand firmly and fearlessly, doing justice to all, and yielding nothing to the clamour or exigent vanity of any single country. the first place, then, it has been clearly enunciated by the commission, that excellence in kind, and not in degree, was to made the rule for discrimination between first and secondclass prizes. The reason of this was obvious, for otherwise the bitterest individual rivalries would have been engendered, and not only so, but it would have been found impossible to render the highest awards as select in number it is so desirable they should be. From this it follows, therefore, that first-class medals should reserved entirely for qualities in contributions of a very’ marked and distinctive character; that there must be about such contributions something which clearly entitles them to the pre-eminence thus assigned to them. Again, to inventions, it is obvious that great discoveries, which have been long in use. and the benefits of which have been extensively realised by the public, are clearly put by time beyond the pale of competition. one would think now of awarding medal for the steam-engine as first introduced, or for Jacquard's loom, or Arkwright's spinning-jenny. The law of this country fixes 11 years as the term of patent-right, and claims to distinction which reach beyond that date are manifestly inadmissible. If the system of prizes is to carried out at all, it must not be suffered to degenerate entirely into a medium for puffing the manufactures of any nation or firm. It must be rescued from the evil influence of jurors banded together to obtain for their country preponderance of rewards without reference to the question of merit. Such combination, though strictly forbidden by the rules of the commission, which enjoin secrecy in each jury, are sorry to say exists ; and it can only defeated by firm resolution and unwavering impartiality. Every country whose industrial character is involved in the Exhibition is, equally with ourselves, interested in frustrating the objects of such organization.— Time*. Exhibition Prizes : the best period fur their distribution : The best period for distributing the prizes, and the proper ceremonial accompanying it, are now under discussion, and have been at some pains to ascertain what opinions are entertained these points those who are most qualified to come to sound conclusion with regard to them. It seems, for a variety of reasons, extremely desirable that the awards should not published, nor the distribution of prizes made, until the Exhibition has closed. If any other arrangement is adopted, difficulties of an almost insurmountable character present themselves. It is, in the first place, very necessary that while the building remains open to the public bias should he given to their inspection of its contents beyond that which each visitor's tastes suggest. Then we should tremble for the peaceful influences of the display and the harmony and concord among nations which it is expected to promote, if torrent of individual disappointments and jealousies were let loose upon the scene. Again, the present state of the interior woidd preclude the possib ilit) of any large number of persons witnessing ceremony which must immensely attractive, and in which the Queen will perhaps take part. Lastly, there is every reason to believe that as the time arrives for closing the Exhibition even - body that can will be desirous t.» take a farewell survey of its varied wonders. That interest will sufficient for the hour without being complicated by other excitements. When the play is ended, and the curtain lias fallen, the actors can most appropriately come forward to receive their respective tributes applause from the public, and to have their merits fairly recognised. It is only after death that the world can enter impartially upon the question of worth, and. when the Great Exhibition has* ceased to be, its honours and rewards will have posthumous character which will much do disarm animosities and soften disappointments. The spectacle too for distributing the prizes can thus made a grand one. The nave and transept, cleared of even- obstruction to the vision, may be occupied thousands of spectators, and in the centre of the vast building, and in the sight of assembled multitudes, successful exhibitors may receive from the hand of royalty those rewards which their industrial triumphs have won for them. I have hitherto said nothing of the fancied or pretended illegality of the diocesan synods. These synods are almost as old as the Church itself, older than the union of the Church with the State. But it is most remarkable, in connection with the question of the legality of such synods, that at no time and in no country has the temporal law interfered with them by any enactment whatever. This is especielle the case in our own country. Even the statute of Henry VIII., c. 19, which forbade the holding of national or prosirchil synods without the consent of the Crorp, did yet not forbid the holding of diocesan synods, which were, and always had been, called by the bishops on their sale authority. Thp account he gives of the opening-day cannot fail to interest our readers : "This day we have been present at the true pomps and ceremonies of ancient Royalty. This day and but a short while since we understood —we, the men of this rebellious age, and who are reaping the storms and discord sown by our fathers—we sceptics, who blush to obey the laws, and who bend our dishonoured heads beneath the iron yoke of necessity—we have contemplated, and closely, too, that with us nameless thing, a throne—that forgotten greatness, majesty—that all-powerful force, respect. From the first hour of morning we have seen a whole people, from every quarter of this immense city, rush to the rendezvous given to it by its Queen, and with unanimous eagerness patiently await her on her passage simply for the delight, the joy, of presenting her its homage, of testifying its respect. A strange people is that of England ! It is always calm ; it makes haste, but always within certain limits; it knows that every one must pass, and will pass, in its turn ; not wishing to be governed it governs itself, and whoever disobeys the order of things which has been marked out, the policeman finds ready assistance from the first man that passes. The appointed hour is respected here too ; people do not say eleven o'clock for twelve, but eleven for eleven, and both the people and the Queen possess equally the politeness of punctuality. At eleven o'clock, then, Her Majesty started. The cortege started from Buckingham Palace, drove up Constitution-hill, and passing through the triumphal arch laden with the equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington, arrived in Hyde Park, and proceeded to the north gate of the Crystal Palace. The cortege consisted of nine coaches, escorted by a detachment of Life Guards in full uniform; the Queen's coach came last. (The Queen's servants are easily recognised by their velvet caps.) This coach was drawn by two cream-coloured horses; these two horses form part of the famous set which figured at the coronation of the late King. Opposite to the Queen were her children, the Prince of Wales and the young Princess, his eldest sister, wearing a wreath of white roses. On the left of Her Majesty was seated Prince Albert. Vivas, hurrahs, from stentorian voices resounded in all directions, backed up by the booming of cannon and an immense flourish of silver trumpets, ornamented with heraldic banners. To hear these warlike flourishes made us recal the solemn entrance of those old kings in Shakspere's dramas. Thus did the Queen make her entrance, bringing with her her month of May and her sun, the two gold sticks being borne before her by two nobles of the Court in about the same manner as the manager of a theatre used formerly to walk before our King with his two wax candles in his hands. I imagine these two gold sticks must have found this backward promenade of theirs rather a long one, and that they had never such a journey in their lives. Then the Queen, bowing to the right and to the left to several personages of her acquaintance and of her Court, ascended that brilliant throne—itself one of the marvels of the world of art. In this place, on which was erketed a dais, the Queen took up her position; at theliame instant the Gentlemenat-Arms, or Civic Guard of Honour—who are on service only on ceremonial days and in the interior of the Palace-- placed themselves at the foot of the Throne. On this occasion these Gentlemen-at-Arms left their halberds at the door. In the cortege was also to be seen the Guard of Beefeaters, drest after the fashion of the soldiers of Henry VIII., with frills round their necks, red stockings, tricoloured rosettes on their gloves, and caps trimmed with riband. It was regretted that the high dignitaries of the city of London, and all the ancient magnificence of the Court of Alderman were absent. The Queen remained standing in the midst of this assembly of men and women.-- the ornaments of her Court. The national hymn was commenced, hundreds of voices led by Sir George Smart, the musical director of the Court, intonated 'God, save the Queen.' It is impossible to describe the effect of this chant, sung by all the voices and all the choirs of London—St. Paul's, Windsor, Westminster, combined with the singers of the Royal Academy and the Sacr e d Harmonic Society, who were joined by a great number of French and Italian • artists invited to the festival. "The hymn over, the Archbishop of Canterbury, dressed in a surplice, read a prayer, and, the prayer over, the famous Hallelujah chorus of Handel resounded beneath that vaulted roof. The baton of director was in the hands of another ennobled musician, Sir Henry Bishop. The most profound silence and the most sympathetic admiration circulated like a cold shiver through that assembly, met together in that place from every quarter of the habitable globe. "You will read, S ir, in the En g l ish papers, the addresses rod the answers to them which were pronounced at the foot of this throne, sur rounded by so many ben e di ctions and so much blimage ju y task is to tell you I saw and what I heard. I saw during the whole time ccupied by this grand spectacle an earnest and attentive people. Not a cry but harmonised with your frame of mind, not a gesture but was from the heart. We Frenchmen especially, wonderstruck at a spectacle such as we have been so long deprived of, could hardly contain ourselves with admiration, and we looked at each other with an expression of astonishment impossible to describe. When the Queen descended from her throne the shouts and hurrahs commenced afresh with renewed vigour, and the Queen and her cortege walked around the Crystal Palace, which gazed down upon them from its lofty summits. " The greatest order reigned at this festival, which can be compared to no other, and, for my part, to follow another order of associations, I have never seen a similar since that day of glory and of regret when the King Louis Philippe threw open to the elite of the nation the Palace of Versailles, which he had just saved and redeemed at the cost of a part of his fortune. To the filling of the Palace at Versailles France sufficed—of itself sufficed; to the tilling of the palace in Hyde-park all Europe even was not sufficient, and it was necessary to call in every generation of man now present under the sun. Such, however, is our passion for the mother country, and so great is our ambition for its glory and its labours that we are annoyed and hurt to think that France is not by iherself beneath those daring arches, and there is something murmuring and stirring within our astonished minds which tells us that all that is done around her she had been equal to do it herself. Once this moment of egotistical sadnesshas passed, we meet France again with joy, and we recognise her again in the efforts she has made, in her intelligence, in her courage, in that royal fashion of hers of preferring glory to money, and honour to success. Yes, and to her glory be it said, out of this industrial rencontre with England, accepted by us in these lamentable times, at a moment when not a Frenchman can say, tomorrow is mine,' will comei what will redound to our honour. In this battle of the 30,000, we had against us the place, the time, closed lists, and necessity. England fought on her own ground, with all her forces, with the peculiar genius of the nation, in the eyes of her compatriots, in full lustre, in the height of credit, under the august shadow of a throne hedged round with unanimous respect, under the shelter of a regularly-established authority, and of two legislative bodies, which vie with each other in national spirit and liberality of motive. In favour of England were enlisted the Past, the Present, and the Future; she walked upon solid ground; she obeyed laws framed loyally and accepted with sincerity; she reaped advantage from everything, even from the tumult, the agitation, the restlessness, and the revolutions of neighbouring people. "France, on the contrary, came to the lists with the strength merely of the passing moment, of the hour but Just expired. She gave to this glory of invention and useful art the last minute of that factitious existence which she has derived from the last revolution ; she performed her work in the midst of agitation, inquietude, and sinister forebodings ; every blow of the hammer was struck in vacancy, and she asked for herself, Who will profit by these labours of mine? Who will inherit the fruits of these vain efforts? What hands will reap the harvests of the summer of 1851 ? ' This last throw of the dice of her genius was thrown by France with a bold Sand generous hand, and come what will, whatever judgment she may herself pronounce on the results of this enterprise, and even taking into account the combatants who failed on the day of battle, she may do herself this justice that she did not retreat from the narrow pass in which the fight was pitched, abandoned as she was to her own resources, and calling in vain the gods to her assistance." At a quarter to sevea 'the bell rang, 'and in an inonceivably Ishort spaemof time the building was left to the tranquil pos- session of its nightly guardians. This process of clearing out is not the least remarkable feature of the Exhi- bition. Great military authorities have said that it was easy to collect 60,000 people in Hyde-park, but not so easy to get' them out again; but at the Crystal Palace the problem is solved every day without any coercive means save the inherent orderliness andgood feeling of the people. There is no rushing, no noise, no confusion. The tide recedes as ?? as it had advanced, and the only trouble the police have is to con- trol the curiosity of the ladies about the diamonds, and to make abstruse arithmetical calculations touching the ingress and egress. Some slight disturbances to the harmony of the proceedings was occasioned by an accident which oc- curred in the machinery in motion room aboutthree o'clock. A man, who was engaged in showing the working of the tile-making machine, by some means got his arm entangled in the works, and was severely hurt, the flesh being much lacerated and the hone broken. He was immediately re- moved to St. George's Hospital. Among the improvements which every day's experience suggests to the executive committee, a large coloured ground plan of the build- ing was yesterday posted up at the southern en- trance, with every department indicated in large letters, so that a few moments' reference would enable a visitor to proceed straight to any desired section. This will be a much better arrangement than the guide system, which has been in operation for a day or two, but has re- ceived little or no encouragement from the public. To-day, the whole of the honorary staff of the Exhibition are to pro- ceed by special train to Birmingham, on a visit to the mayor, who proposes a progress through the more impor- tant manufactures of the town. On Thursday the Dutchesses of Orleans and of Nemours, with the young Comte de Paris and the Due de Chartres, arrived at the Exhibition in the afternoon, and were occupied some hours in an examination of part of its contents. What if this vast collection was destroyed by fire? Many cities might be burnt to the ground without causing such a sensation as that would. Yet to that risk the Crystal Palace was for a moment exposed on Thursday morning. The flue attached to a gas stove in one of the offices of the contractors became heated, and ignited a piece of wood with bunting which rested upon or touched it. A piece of the burning cloth fell into a small open cask of Indian corn, which stood, as the Irish say, "convenient." All this mischief was brewing in secret in the southern part of the colonial collection on the east side. The drapery of the counter concealed what had happened, and it was only when the smoke began to break forth that an alarm was raised. Fortunately such casualties have been foreseen and amply provided for. There are no less than a dozen large fireengines within the building, besides an ample supply of water easily obtainable, and a thoroughly organized force ready to act at a moment's notice. The fire was extinguished before it had time to do more than slightly char one plank of wood, and no anxiety need be caused by an occurrence so trifling. The fineness of the day on Saturday, and the anticipation of the presence of Her Majesty, caused the Crystal Palace to fill better than on any day since the opening. Her Majesty's visit however, was a private one, the public not being admitted until after her departure. A general topic of conversation was Her Majesty's acquaintance with the continental languages. She might be heard at one moment speaking French, then Italian, and afterwards in German, with idiomatic correctness. The Duke of Wellington was also a visiter, and was an object of considerable curiosity in many of the visiters. The police computed the numbers at 40,000; and, judging by the rule of proportion, have formed wonderful anticipations of the influx when the shilling admission commences. It is stated that It is intended to limit the daily admissions to 60,000. A gloomy overcast sky acts upon the exchequer of the Royal Commission as sinister rumours, however groundless, do upon 'Change. Thursday was bright and cloudless, and the receipts from ss. visiters rose to upwards of 2,000/. On Friday the sun did not deign to shine, and the money taken fell to between 1,700/. and 1,800/.—a very respectable amount, however. In the course of Saturday afternoon more than 1,800/. was taken at the doors. The Duke of Wellington was there on Saturday, with Mrs. Fox, the wife of the contractor, on his arm. Where His Grace makes his appearance, a space is immediately cleared for him, and, except the Queen herself, no Royal personage could be treated with more distinction. Monday morning the Queen, accompanied by Prince Albert, again visited the Exhibition. The Crystal Palace knows no difference between Jew and Greek, Frank and Saxon. In that arena, for the first time In the annals of mankind, the Negro and the Malay, the Sclave and the American, will stand together on equal terms ; and merit of its kind will carry away the honours of genius and industry without reference to questions of blood, type, or colour. The preparations for the opening are carried on with in- creased activity, and every day shows a great step made in advance. One after another the different departments and sections are rapidly approaching Uie stage at which their arrangements may be considered complete. Wherever the eye turns an imposing spectacle of industrial activity presents itself, and nothing can well be conceived mere interesting than to watch how, from the general system of superintendence down to the very minutest details of labour, Uie evidences of control and design are discernible. Nearly 20,000 packages have been re- ceived from different parts of the globe, and deposited in their places according to a plan which does not violate nationalities, but nevertheless adheres to an orderly classification ; which will give the most ample opportunities for pictorial effect, and yet enable the philosophic miud to carry out without obstruction the labours of comparison and observation. With respect to the measures for the accommodation and circulation of spectators, these bave not yet been finally de- termined on, and of course no conclusive opinion can be pro- nounced upon them until they have been reduced into practice. Wide passages, staircases, aud doorways, conveniently disposed, have been pieserved for the accommodation of visitors, and the precautions which have thus been taken will, we be- lieve, be found satisfactory. Finally, if these ordinary resources do not satisfy thepublic, among the articles exhibited is Phillips' patent fire annihilator, which would thus, should the occasion unfortunately arise, have a decisive and memora- ble opportunity for demonstrating its practical utility. As the Exhibition bas from the outset been announced in the character of a self-supporting scheme.it is gratifying to announce Uie almost certainty which exists that this financial idea will be fully realized. "Notwithstanding the novelty of Uie undertaking and its world-wide comprehensiveness, all Uie details have hitherto been executed with extraordinary econo- my. Wheu the proper time arrives the information on this subject will, of course, be laid before the public, and Uiey will be enabled to judge the cost of the Crystal Palace as contrasted with ordinary buildings. It is believed that they will find tbe expenditure surprisingly small, and if half the results which are anticipated from the Great Exhibition are realized the people of this country will look contentedly at an outlay wbich advertises their industry to every portion of the globe. The £60,000 aud upwards collected by subscriptions, added to the vast and still iucreasiug sale of season tickets, and to the sums of money stipulated for in contrnets, leave at the present mo- ment a deficiency in Uie total liabilities of Uie concern which the entrance charges for the masses will no doubt amply supply ; and it certainly is gratifying to think that a scheme of such magnitude, and involving in die promotion of it such serious liabilities, should he carried out successfully upon what, by a new application of tbe term, M. Guizot has called " the volun- tary principle." It is curious, while glancing at die building itself, to observe Uie economy of labour which increased civilization and the development of mechanical ?? enable us to effect. The Crystal Palace covers a larger area tiian any other building in Uie world. It has been erected with a speed which substitutes weeks for years in all analogous cases. Yet the number of bauds employed by Fox and Henderson in Uie actual labour of construction has seldom exceeded 2,000 at a time. What would the architects of the Pyramids say to Uiis, which re- quired nations to build them up ? or of St. Peter's at Rome, which took 300 years to finish ? But Uie most remarkable fact remains to be mentioned— only two lives have been lost in Uie progress of the works. When the novelty of the undertaking is considered, and Uie risk of casualties (infinitely greater than in ordinary constructions), this certainly is a result as gratifying as it is surprising. We predict for Uie mechanical department of tbe Exhibition a success, as far as England is concerned, more complete and decisive than in any other part of Uie display ; Foreign nations bave slowly and reluctantly availed themselves of the facilities which Uiis department affords. There was space reserved for such of Uiem as were at all likely to become competitors, but France and America are the only countries tbat have entered the arena. But it turns out that it is tbe section of all others, perhaps, foremost in its prepara- tions, and a large proportion of tbe machines produced are now completely fitted up and ready for exhibition. We will not attempt to anticipate Uie interest which must attach to the motive portion of this department. Thousands of our practical hard-handed countrymen will turn aside from the more capti- vating parts of the general display to see those great iron frameworks, instinct with a life and energy beyond mat of human hands, and, obedient to tbe impulses of the steam en- gine, yielding results which set competition at defiance. In the fine arts' department we have ?? a very up-hill game to play against Uie overwhelming opposition of the Con- tinent. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Notwithstanding the heavy rain that fell yesterday in the forenoon, the building was densely crowded and the heat equally unpleasant and oppressive. The interest and excitement which the view of so large and varied a collection of objects of art, science, and industry, brought together from all parts of the earth, is calculated to produce, enables the visitors to undergo almost any extent of inconvenience and endure any amount of heat and pressure to which they may be subjected in the building. Not so the police officers en duty, or the attendants employed in the various departments of the building. They have certainly had, during the last two months, a great deal of extra duty and labour, under circumstances occasionally of great difficulty and embarrassment, and we believe the public generally will agree with us that they have acquitted themselves most creditably and discreetly. If the public have been orderly and wellconducted to an unusual degree, the police, both within and without the building, have been patient and judicious in the enforcement of their orders; and we have no doubt their services will receive due consideration from the authorities. The attendants employed by the Royal Commissioners have also had very responsible duties to discharge, and their hours of attendance have been unusually long, averaging from nine in the morning till seven or eight at night with very little intermission. The pay of these men is miserably law and inadequate, considering the respectable class of persons employed. It may have been necessary when the Exhibition was merely an experiment as to its proving remunerative to fix the Seale of salaries as low as possible, but this plea no longer exists, and we trust their case will receive some further consideration at the hands of the executive committee, who, as practical men, must know that the pay of the attendants, messengers, doorkeepers, clerks, &c., is much less than they would be entitled to in any private establishment. The perilous work of painting and repairing the glass roof of the transept still goes on, and we should be heartily glad if it were finished. Occasionally a piece of timber or a sheet of glass slips through and comes with a tremendous crash upon the floor of the building. There is the risk of inflicting serious injury upon some of the vast crowd below, and there is ever in one's mind, looking up at the men cr twling over the glass like flies, :the feeling that one of them by making a false step may be precipitated to the bottom, killing himself and whoever he may strike in his descent. We hear a good deal of the number of chevaliers d'induslrie who are plying their vocations in the building, but we believe few losses from this source have yet been recorded, and the two or three trifling articles abstracted from some of the stalls in the course of two months, and after the building has been visited by at least two millions of people, is in itself a proof of the integrity and propriety with which the heterogenous assemblages, including persons of all grades and classes of society,who have passed through, have conducted themselves. The establishment over the way, its great rival in attractiveness, has not been so fortunate. A thy or two since some thieves managed to effect an entrance into the grounds at the back of Soyer'e Symposium, and cut off about 25 yards of the enormous and unique table cloth, which measures 320 feet long, and cost the enterplising proprietor nearly 70/. It was spread out in the Encampment of al Nations, in the Pre, d' Orsay, and was safe at a late hour of the night. This dishonest attempt to "cut of the supplies" cannot be too severely reprobated, and as the cloth was of a peculiar texture and pattern there is every hope that the rogues may yet be detected and brought to punishment. GREAT EXHIBITION. Under the head of Foreign Conference and Evangelization Committee for 1851, will be found a very interesting Advertisement, exhibiting the names of a large body of gentlemen, clerical and lay, of the first respectability, and setting forth the objects of the confederation, which are of a nature to command the attention of the wise and the good of every community. This great idea we incline to consider as emanating from a higher source than the human mind; it is worthy of the British people, and seems indispensable to complete this great, and we might almost say, in some respects, mysterious movement. If it should turn out as some individuals, perhaps many, suppose, that six or seven millions of human beings, from first to last, will visit the metropolis in connexion with the Exhibition, it will be an event unique in itself, and such as has had no parallel in the history of nations. There seems reason to believe, from the nature of man and of human society, that the political effects will be great, as tending to promote friendship, peace, and civilization—matters in themselves far from unimportant—but we deem it neither superstitious nor fanatical to entertain the hope, that it will materially tend to contribute to objects higher than the highest of those which appertain to this sublunary scene. Such movements as that contemplated in the Advertisement referred to, would seem to indicate that this is destined to be one of the great projects whereby hidden springs are set in motion, and grand results, unlooked for by the best and the wisest of mere mortals are effected. The project seems to possess every element of success. It is generous and catholic, to the utter exclusion of everything low, little, and sectarian. Indeed, it is divested in some respects of the stamp of nationality, forasmuch as the speaking, generally, will be carried on, not by Englishmen, but by Foreigners. While much importance attaches to the living voice, this alone is not sufficient; and hence subordinate—but still, in themselves considered, important—means are to be used. The provision and the diffusion of the Scriptures in all the principal languages, whose representatives are expected to be present, with books and tracts in these divers ',tongues and dialects, and the procuring of missionaries, who shall devote themselves, morning, noon, and night, to the holding of intercourse, in such ways and in such seasons as prudence and counsel may dictate, and the opening of reading-rooms, where men of all nations may meet, and Englishmen with them, where mutual intercourse may be held, plans discussed, and friendships formed—all these we consider as things rational, practicable, and necessary, in order to efficiency. Nor let men, whose experience has been limited to their own stately home, conjure up difficulties, as standing in the way of such movements as this—an act of easy performance, and which will be capable of paralysing all rational effort. Let it be remembered, that Continental peoples differ in this respect exceedingly from us English, who are characteristically reflecting, cold, reserved,— for such is the character we universally bear upon the Continent, especially amongst Frenchmen, who, full of vivacity, are given to endless converse, which renders them favourable to the success of the enterprise. The other Continental nations, if less conversible, are yet frank and open, and of easy access. We, therefore, consider that there will be no difficulty in the way of gathering large numbers which may not be overcome—we say large numbers—something which will many times over more than compensate for the expense which the effort will require; and to accomplish this will be to accomplish something very great, something as great, we regret to say, as is accomplished among our own people. All that we are bringing, Sabbatically, under Divine instruction in London is but a small minority of the whole population, and we conceive it will be possible to collect as large a proportion as this of intelligent and respectable strangers, compared with the aggregate of foreign visiters. The project is every way not only feasible, but, as we view the matter, full of promise. At any rate it is worth the trying. It is such as it becomes the Christian portion of a so-called Christian nation. Even if it fail, they will have a good conscience in not having neglected the opportunity. We commend to our readers the careful perusal of the Appeal.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The erection of the stalls and fittings in the building has, {luring the past week, been proceeding with almost marvellous rapidity. Two or three days at the utmost will see the whole of the ground-floor on the east side of the building furnished with the permanent stalls, and within a week probably the main fittings of the whole ot the ground-floor of the building will be completed. The minor fittings, such as glass cases, shelves, steps, &c., fashioned according to the almost infinite variety of tastes of the exhibitors, and such as they conceive best suited for the display of their particular goods, is a work of enormous magnitude, and which, if left in other hands than those which had constructed within an almost incredible space of time the vast building itself, might well cause some apprehension as to the possibility of their completion by the required time. There can be no doubt whatever but that every fitting of this kind will be completed in ample time for the reception of the goods which they are intended to display. The number of men employed last week, the great majority of whom were carpenters, was upwards of 1,700, and it is intended to take on this week 500 painters, for the purpose of pushing on more rapidly the painting. The gradual completion of the fittings will afford opportunities for carrying on this kind of work more rapidly than hitherto. Nearly the whole of the painting of the south gallery is completed. The appearance which it presents is universally admired, and many of those who a short time since were loudest in their censures of the plan of decoration proposed by Mr. 0. Jones, or who expressed grave doubts as to its success, have admitted that their censures were hastily formed, and that their misgivings have been fully and completely removed. Now that the arrangements and fittings of the building and its decorations are being carried on, the obstruction to the view and waste of ground which the numerous trees in the building caused are very generally • felt and complained of, and there can be no doubt but ultimately the whole of them will be allowed to be removed. No really good purpose whatever can be served by allowing them to remain; several of them are extremely old and worthless, except for firewood, and the smaller ones might be easily replaced should the contingency arise of their being required as ornaments to the park. It is absurd to talk of public feeling being in favour of their retention in the building; for among the thousands who have visited the building, we would venture to assert that there has scarcely been an opinion expressed on the subject which was not in favour of the removal of every tree which was calculated in the slightest degree to interfere either with the harmony and completeness of the beautiful structure, or with the comfort and convenience of exhibitors and visitors. We have invited foreign countries to compete with us in a great national undertaking, and to meet us in an edifice which is confessedly the wonder of the age, and we may imagine the feeling of surprise with which visitors of taste will gaze upon a number of stunted and worthless trees in such a position, and the astonishment with which foreigners who have heard of us as a great, a powerful, and an enlightemd nation, will learn that they are allowed to remain as monuments of a petty and miserable hostility to an undertaking so vast and so noble as that of an Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations. We trust that the Executive will not fail to impress the importance of this subject upon whoever may chance to possess the required authority in the office of Woods and Forests. The present noble lord at the head of that department, if we are to lose his services, could not, we conceive, as his last act, perform one of greater service, or one which would render the memory of his official services more cherished, than giving his consent to the removal of these trees ; or, should he refuse, no successor of the noble lord could give a more favourable augury to the country of the mode in which he would perform his functions, than, as his first official act, allowing the Commissioners, or Messrs. Fox and Henderson, to order the removal of any or all of the trees which were found to interfere with the complete success of the Great Exhibition. . _ _ . _ . . _ A number of the foundations for the heavier articles of machinery are laid, and we were glad to observe that several arrivals of that description of goods had taken place. A large basin has been formed in the transept, from which it is intended to supply a very large and handsome fountain. Considerable progress has been made in the marking out and preparation of the fittings for the refreshment-rooms, waitingrooms, and other accommodations. It is intended to paint the iron railings round the galle a ries a light blue, and to have a background of Turkey red calico. The hand-rail on the top will be formed of the same wood as that of which the steps of the staircases are formed, savacca, a Brazilian wood of great hardness and durability, and of a colour similar to Honduras mahogany. The greatest precautions are taken to prevent any accident from fire in the building. The mains are always kept charged with water, and a number of the men of the fire brigade are present during day and night. Twenty engines, the property of the Board of Ordnance, a large number of leather buckets, and a quantity of hose, have been placid at the disposal of the Commissioners, and are kept ready for immediate use, should they be required, to extinguish any fire that might occur. The goods both from foreign and English exhibitors con tinue to arrive in great numbers, and the immense piles of bales and packages of all shapes and sizes give to the building the appearance of a vast warehouse. The total number of packages received from foreign countries by the end of last week was—from Bavaria, 45 ; Saxony, 135; Prussia, 597; Belgium, 257; France, 202; Spain, 24; Mexico, 4; Sweden, 19; Peru, 1 ; Switzerland, 140; United States, 18; China, 43; Holland, 56; and Russia upwards of 200. The sale of season tickets progresses rapidly ; up to Saturday night nearly 4,000 had been sold. Messrs. Spicer and Clowes are preparing four distinct catalogues of the Exhibition—two in English, one in French, and one in German. The English Official Catalogue will be sold in the building for Is., and will contain the name and address of each exhibitor, as well as a short description of his productions, in the precise order in which they will appear in the building, and with a system of reference by letters and numbers that will enable visitors to find any exhibitor's position without difficulty. The Illustrated Catalogue will be a work of considerable extent, arranged precisely in the same manner as the former, but containing much more detailed notice of the articles exhibited, and the various classes of articles will be annotated by gentlemen of scientific eminence. In this work exhibitors may have illustrations of their productions inserted, provided immediate application be made to the contractors. The French and German catalogues will be similar to the English Official Catalogue, and will be sold at 2s. 6d. The name and address of each exhibitor, as well as the description of the articles which he exhibits, will be inserted in all the four catalogues, without any charge whatever to the exhibitor, who is only required to furnish the description of his article in duplicate The great majority of these descriptions have been received, and many of them are already in type. Those exhibitors who have not already complied with this should, for their own interest, not lose a day in sending in their lists in as concise terms as possible. Those exhibitors who decide upon having engravings of their productions in the Illustrated Catalogue, will, of course, defray the expense of such engravings themselves, as the adoption of any other plan would have materially enhanced the price of the work, and consequently affected the purchasers. This catalogue will extend to upwards of 1,000 pages large octavo. The whole of the catalogues will appear on the Ist of May. We have noticed at different times the dissatisfaction which has been expressed by the representatives of some foreign countries with reference to the amount of space allotted to their exhibitors. Except in the case of France, these differences had almost entirely disappeared; but the commissioner of our continental neighbours—M. Salandrouze de Lamornaix—continued still to struggle fur increased accommodation. Happily the ExecutiveCommittea have been able to settle In an agreeable and friendly manner their differences with this gentleman, who will now direct all his energy to the preparation and arrangement of the large area which his countrymen possess in the building. It appears that from two causes 12 bays have been placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee in the eastern or foreign half of the Exhibition. In the first place Norway and Sweden and the States of Northern Germany had not supplied a sufficient quantity of articles to cover their allotments. They therefore willingly resigned their surplus space. America, again, wished to exchange a portion of the ground area assigned her for increased room in the galleries. Her agent has acted, we understand, with great liberality in the course of theme new arrangements, and hiss readily and cordially co-operated with the Executive Committee in securing a satisfactory settlement with our other visitors from abroad. All parties are now, we hear, perfectly well pleased with reference to the point of space; and it is sincerely to be hoped that no fresh disagreement may arise to destroy that spirit of harmonious and combined action the establishment of which becomes every day of gae3 ter impertance.France,Belgium, Austria, and the Z , Alvercin have all been especially benefittod by the additional accommodation placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee, and we take it for granted that the difficulties arising from the disappointments of intending exhibitors whose contributions, after inviting, we might be obliged to shut out, have now boon overcome. We have again, however, to warn our friends fr-m abroad the; their arrangements are still in a very back ward state, and that they must without delay put forth their best efforts to have every thing in order by the Ist of May. Their things come in slowly, and the Custom-house examinations necessarily occupy a great deal of time. Besides M. du Seigneur's specimen of sculpture a splendid organ will be placed in the nave as one of the most striking articles in the French collection. This is the fourth organ we have heard of as intended for exhibition, and it is quite clear that the Crystal Palace may be made available for the pleasures of sound as well of sight, if the Royal Commissioners think fit that it should be so. Over the vast expanse the sublime music of the Creation may be made to circulate, and while thousands of spectators assemble to admire the chief wonders of human industry the swelling notes may be sounded in their ears which so fitly recall the greatness of that Power by whom are all things. The American contributions brought over by the packet St. Lawrence are now rapidly arriving at the building, and although the quantity is not so great as was at one time expected, the quality will, it is believed, be not unwworthy of the great nation which acknowledges this to be its mother country. The colhction includes splendid specimens of copper, iron, and zinc ore, to illustrate the mineral we ilth of the United States; machinery to show the mechanical ingenuity of the people; and a most varied display of raw produce and manufactured articles, including an air-exhausted metal coffin, in which a human body could, it is said, be preserved for ages without decay, and which contains, we hear, a bouquet of flowers as fresh as when it was first placed there. The Commissioner from Tunis has been the first foreign agent to unpack. Judging from what we saw, this small section of the Exhibition will not be the least interesting portion of it ; and the fair sex especially will flock to a compartment where they may have an opportunity cf comparing their own style of apparel with that of the Moorish ladies. Among the entries in the catalogue of articles which the Bey has sent over is oleo which runs thus, " The beauty's dress on leaving the bath." The display is rich in specimens of male attire, also in mule trappings blankets, and stilettos. Turning to our own part of the Exhibition, there are several matters of importance to communicate since our last notice. With reference to the amount of work to be accomplished before the Ist of May, it now appears certain that the chief difficulty to be overcome lies in the completion of the building itself. As if the arrears of work already existing were not sufficient, new labours arise of a serious, but, we trust, not insurmountable character. The ridge and valley roof during wet weather has always leaked a little at different points, but it was believed that when the Paxton gutters had been well pitched and the interior of the sash bars painted no inconvenience on this score could be experienced. The late heavy rains have dissipated this idea, and water has penetrated in so many places that serious fears are entertained by some as to the practtcabilty of securing that exemption from drip or damp which is indispeusable iu such a building. We believe that the desired objected can still be accomplished by administering a thick coat of paint to the sash bars on the outside; but this constitutes a formidable addition to the work which the contractors have now scarcely six weeks to finish. Messrs. Fox and Henderson have done wonders, and we have no doubt will complete this great undertaking in a manner creditable to themselves, to their profession, and to their country. Their reputation is indissolubly bound up with the satisfactory manner in which the Crystal Palace fulfils the objects for which it has been created. If its gigantic roof cannot be made water-tight, Mr. Paxton's design, and their execution, will be equally condemned as failures. Not only so, but we shonld be exposed as a people, to just complaint from the countries whose industrial products we have invited to an imperfeet shelter from our damp and showery skies. Fancy the exhibitor of costly brocaded silks from Lyons, or of rich velvets from Genoa, watching the effects of a summer storm of rain oozing through the great window frames above his head, and drop after drop irretrievably tarnishing the rarest products of his taste and skill. The first day of the last week of the Exhibition has passed off in a manner at once gratifying and surprising. Everybody was prepared for a great accession of numbers to the usual average of shilling visitors, but the most extravagant expectations could hardly have anticipated anything so remarkable as the actual reality. Yesterday 107,815 people entered the building, and the sum of 5,175/. 165:was taken at the door;. Facts so astounding speak for themselves, and derive no additional force from expatiating upon them. Were it not so, we should despair of describing the scene which the interior presented. Popular demonstrations are always grand. Taking place in such an arena they exercise a transcendent and overpowering influence. In the presence of such an assemblage as yesterday was collected together the highest triumphs of industry and art are forgotten, and the mind has only time to think of that great mass of humanity tendering its homage at the shrine of Labour, and vindicating the nobility of toil. If any lingering doubts have been entertained that the Crystal Palace has not been popular among the masses, its closing hours will set them completely at rest. Great as the influx of visitors was yesterday, it will most probably rise still higher to-day ; but it is satisfactory to think that however vast the numbers that present themselves the building will be found capable of accomodating them all. The dreaded limit of 100,000 spectators has now been exceeded, and without any extraordinary inconvenience. In the Crystal Palace, as elsewhere, the people are their own best police, and from hour to hour crowds l eave t o ma k e room for the gathering tide that enters. Yesterday they began to ooze away as early as 11 o'clock, and so well balanced were the departures and arrivals that until the doors closed it was possible, without much effort, to make a systematic and effectual survey of all the principal objects and departments. We have no doubt that with considerably increased numbers this will continue to be the case, and a sanguine hope is entertained that no pressure will arise so great and inconvenient as to render it necessary to check the flow of visitors. That nearly 108,000 people should within one day and under one roof have enjoyed the grandest spectacle that the world has ever witnessed is of itself a sufficient marvel, but that they should have done so without a single known casualty to life or property is almost incredible. So, however, it is, and we leave to revolutionary and discontented minds the study of facts which place in so clear and unquestionable a light the love of order and the genuine kindliness of spirit which pervade all classes of our population. Yet, while we dwell with a natural complacency on those evidences of a happy and prosperous people, circumstances are constantly occurring to warn us of possible disaster. Such an event took place yesterday. Shortly after three o'clock, and when upwards of 100,000 persons were in the building, the Duke of Wellington entered at the east end, and was loudly cheered by those who recognised him. The intelligence soon spread in the eastern half of the edifice, and the crush and crowding which ensued to catch a glimpse of the veteran, was such as to produce a momentary sensation of apprehension as to the fate of the building. Thousands ran along the galleries, and each court and avenue poured its torrent into the nave, while numbers in the transept hearing the distant noise, and seeing the confusion, but ignorant of its cause, rushed out of the building, under the apprehension that some casualty had occurred. By dint of pure physical force Superintendent Pearce, and several other police-officers, succeeded in opening a narrow pathway for the bake—who, after having passed through the eastern half of the building, left at the southern entrance, where he mounted his horse and departed, amid the cheers of thousands outside the building. It is most satisfactory to state that not a single accident occurred; and those who have on former occasions favoured the public with their opinions as to the destructive effect of the rapid and irregular movement of an immense crowd upon the building, will be surprised to hear that not a single girder or " snag" has given way ; and we may add that, although upwards of 100,000 persons were present in the building, there were many portions of it which were comparatively unoccupied by the masses, the nave and transept being, of course, the most crowded portions of the building. A chart, showing by diagrams the fluctuations in the number of visitors during the time that the Exhibition has been opened, was yesterday completed by the Sappers and placed in the transept. It is a production of great merit and of much public interest, resembling those scales of mountain elevations which are usually prefixed to atlases. The shilling days form themselves into the Himlayas and Andes of this return ; the half-crown and five shilling days being represented by heights of much lower altitude. The loftiest peak, rising to a maximum of more than 70,000, will now be far eclipsed by the results of yesterday, and it is probable that within the next five days still greater and more astounding figures will be reached. Of the two half-crown days, Friday seems to be that which brings with it the largest amount of popularity at the Crystal Palace.
