THE CAPTURE OF A GANG OF WHOLESALE SWINDLERS. On Saturday last the Police-court at Plymouth was crowded by persons anxious to listen to one of the most extraordinary investigations (adjourned from the previous Wednesday) which has engaged the attention of the bench for some years, and which exposes an attempt at swindling upon a very large scale. It appears that early in the month of September there arrived in Plymouth two men of middle age and respectably attired, who forthwith took premises for the ostensible purpose of carrying on business as general outfitters and army and navy contractors. having engaged a store on Sutton-wharf, in the possession of Mr. Hicks, wine -merchant, a painter was employed to announce to those resorting to that locality that Rudwell's Stores were there situated, and a plentiful supply of letter-paper was procured, each sheet bearing the printed heading of " Sutton-wharf, Plymouth. Ship Stores Warehouses, General Outfitter, Army and Navy Contractors &c." As the business to be transacted was intended to be of the most extensive description, a counting-house became necessary, and for this purpose a room in Tin -street was hired, at the moderate sum of half-a-crown a week, and here, during the hours of business, Mr. Rudwell and his more retiring partner, Mr. Palmer, were generally to be found, each seated at a desk, conducting a voluminous correspondence with most of the principal contributors to the Great Exhibition, the Official Catalogue supplying them with the names and addresses of the various exhibitors. As the trade to be carried on was to be large, of course the orders were liberal, and assistance being deemed necessary the principals in the busine s s were j o i ne d a b out a week after their arrival by a younger man, of smart appearance, calling himself William James Widdicombe. He acted as clerk, and James Maddick, a labourer, whom the principals met with on the quay, was employed as storekeeper and porter. The firstfruits of the extensive correspondence carried on by the firm was the arrival of a large parcel, consigned to their address, on the 20th of September, and every succeeding day witnessed the advent of other goods, of a most miscellaneous description. There was an odd commingling of copperas and broadcloths, locks, and blankets, lamps and trouserings, hides and chicory, tweeds and iodine, canvas and saddles, twines and cooking apparatus, velveteens and ship's sheathing, cotton twist and oatmeal, compound levers and a lifting jack. But numerous as were the arrivals of goods, equally brisk appeared to be the sale, for not a single parcel remained in the store more than a couple of hours ere it was disposed of in some way or other, and it would seem in certain instances at prices which:would have enabled Rudwell to assert with greater truth than is the case sometimes with traders, that he was indeed making an alarming sacrifice. For example, the lifting jack above mentioned, the invoice price of which was 81., was no sooner delivered at the store than it was entrusted to the respectable agency of Messrs. Skardon and Sons, who were instructed to sell it fur 2/., if a purchaser could be procured at that sum. Oil-cake, too, the trade price for which is 121. 10s. per ton, was offered for sale to Mr. Parrott, of Buckwell-street, through the instrumentality of Mr. Nahum Cornbloom, for 71. 10s. per ton. Other goods were pledged at the office of Mr. Toms, pawnbroker, by Widdicombe. Such was the state of things until Tuesday last, when Superintendent Gibbons proceeded, in company with Inspector Thomas and Sergeant Hicks, to arrest Palmer and his clerk Widdicombe (who was discovered to have been living here under the assumed name of Matthews), as they were walking together from the railway station towards George-place, the charge being, that they had, in conjunction with Rudwell, obtained large quantities of goods under false pretences. Palmer, who described himself as a labourer, said " very well," and Widdicombe, alias Matthews, stated himself to be a clerk in the service of Rudwell, and was altogether innocent of the offence charged against him. Rudwell was also apprehended the same evening, and on Wednesday morning the trio appeared before the magistrate, in custody of the officers, charged as above stated. The sitting magistrates were the mayor and Messrs. Coryndon and Hawker : Mr. Lavers attendi ng on th e part o f t h e Trades' Protection Society, and applying for a remand in order to give the police time to institute the necessary inquiries. After hearing the whole of the evidence then forthcoming against the prisoners, and by which the foregoing statement was fully supported, the prisoners were remanded to Saturday. Mr. Nahum Cornbloom, who had left, came back after the case had been heard, and was advised by the mayor to give up the goods he had received of Rudwell into the possession of a third party. In a very independent manner he refused to do anything of the kind, told the mayor he would rather take his money than his advice, asked Mr. Phillips what was the price of a brief, said he defied them to do anything to him; he had not bought stolen goods ; he was "too deep" for that, and would never give up the goods till they were paid for. From the evidence produced on Saturday it appeared that on 'Wednesday evening upwards of two tons of goods arrived by railway for Rudwell and Co., which is in possession of the police, and that a letter, badly spelt and badly written, from the wife of Rudwell, has fallen into the hauls of the superintendent, but it contains no information of which use can be made. It was dated " London," and bore the signature of "Ann." Another letter dated from Manchester, which came to hand on Thursday, charges Rudwell with being an impostor, and threatens him with exposure, the writer alleging that he (Rudwell) had carried on his fraudulent practices in a great number of towns, assuming the name of " Cox," whe n at Wolverhampton, then as " Smith," of. Birmingham, as " Mill," of Liverpool, afterwards as " Edwards," of Manchester, and more frequently as " Darlington," of Portsmouth. A large quantity of goods arrived to the address of the firm, on Thursday, and are now detained in charge of Pickford and Co., railway-contractors. About two tons of oil cake also came by steamer, for which Cornbloom was found to be on the look out. The police accordingly waited until he had paid the freight, when they then stepped in and seized the lot, much to the chagrin of the hard-mouthed money-lender, who threatens to cite Superintendent Gibbons and his men in the high court of Westminster. It was also stated that a fresh lot of goods and s un d r y i nvo i ces came to hand on Friday morning, and that the police at the same time obtained information which was deemed sufficiently important to justify the immediate departure of Inspector Thomas per mail train for the metropolis. The nature of the evidence was such as to induce the bench, after a lengthened examination of witnesses, to further remand the prisoners to Wednesday next. Mr. Rudwell, on being asked what he had to say against being remanded, contended that as he had his name over the door of the wharf, and was nowhere in debt in Plymouth, zs he had not been applied to for money for the goods, but should be ready to pay on in to custody. ha ought not to have been even taken custody. As to Palmer, he was his (Rudwell's) friend, while Widdicombe was his clerk. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. - The following notice has been issued by the Executive Committee to exhibitors. It aims, as will be perceived, at a complete clearance of the building before the Ist of next month:— "SURRENDER THE BUILDING TO THE CONTRACTORS. " 1. The Executive Commitee have received the instructions of Her Majesty's Commissioners to announce that the possession of the building will be given up to Messrs. Fox, Henderson, and Co., the contractors, on the l at of December next. " 2. The Executive Committee have, therefore, to recommend that any exhibitors who may not yet have removed their goods or fittings do so without further delay, as it will not be in the power of the Executive Committee to afford any assistance to exhibitors after that date. On the Ist of December the stuff of the Executive Committee will be withdrawn, and the cranes, platforms, and various appliances for assisting the exhibitors removed. " 3. Any exhibitors who permit their articles, after the let of December, to remain in the building, must apply to the contractors, and make their own arrangements as to the hours, Sze., for admittance, &c. " 4. It must be distinctly understood that, like Her Majesty's Commissioners, the contractors, during any period they may suffer the exhibitors' goods to remain in the building, will not be responsible for any loss or datnege, or for accidents which may arise from the necessity of removing the goods from one pert of the building to another, and collecting the remaining articles into one spot. " By order of the Exectative Committee, "M. WYATT, Secretary." The following farewell letter has been addressed to the Executive Committee by Mr. Riddle, the United States' Commissioner : " United States Office, London, Nov. " Gentlemen,—As my official duties in the Crystal Palace have now ceased, I shall now take my departure for America on the 12th inst. I cannot allow mysclf to go hence without tendering you my sincere and heartfelt acknowledgments for the many acts of kindness, courtesy, and attention I have received at your bands, and for the uniform promptness with which you have responded to all communications emanating from this commission. Indeed, in my humble opinion, the of the Great Exhibition may be mainly attributable to the admirable and indefatigable management of your Committee, and the limited number of gentlemen of which it was composed, thereby preventing collisions„ which would inevitably have occurred had the whole responsibility been entrusted to a larger body of directors. While I have received every assistance from officers under your directions, there is one who has been high in authority, and of whom I cannot speak in too high terms of praise. I allude to Captain Owen, of the Royal Engineers. The even temper, and calm, dignified demeanour be has observed on all trying and pressing occasions, are worthy of the highest commendation, and, for one, I am proud to bear witness to the energetic and impartial manner in which he has discharged his arduous duties. "Wishing each and all of you, gentlemen, that continued success to which your brilliant talents so justly entitle you, "I have the honour to subscribe myself very respect • fully, your obedient servant, "EDWARD RIDDLE, United States' Commissioner to the Industrial Exhibition." Her Majesty and Prince Albert paid a short and somewhat unexpected visit to the Exhibition on Tuesday ; having, we believe, come up from Windsor expressly for the purpose. The Royal party arrived at the Crystal Palace shortly after 12 o'clock, and were received by Mr. Dilke and Mr. Cole, of the executive committee, who accompanied Her Majesty and the Prince through the building. Her Majesty passed down the foreign nave, where the dispersed workmen of Babel would seem to have re-assembled. In this once brilliant promenade, there remains but little to engage the attention, and Her Majesty gave but a cursory glance at the relics as she passed by. Her Majesty then ascended the southern gallery, and returned towards the British aide, where still less remains than in the foreign section. What seemed to engage most of Her Majesty's notice, was the building itself, which she had now a better opportunity lof observing than on the occasion of former visits, when her attention must have been unavoidably distracted by the gorgeous accessories displayed on every side, and the living panorama moving within. We mentioned some time since, that as the hoarding which shut in the full view of the interior was being removed, the building was revealing itself as a marvel of beauty. Her Majesty was evidently much struck with the view which the interior of the building even now presents, and was heard to express herself in warm terms of approbation at the prospect. MR. THE GREAT EXHIBITION Some misapprehension having arisen tending to lead exhibitors to suppose that the period for opening 'the Great Exhibition will be postponed, the Executive Committee have announced, that the Exhibition will be open on the Ist of May. The Building. —The construction of the building in Hyde Park has been pushed forward with much rapidity during the last few days. The glazing of the transept roof is now finished, and very little of this branch of the works remains incomplete in any part of the building. The east and west ends of the building are covered in, and viewed from the outside, they present a very pleasing appearance. The ground floors are in a state of forwardness, and there is scarcely anything to be clone in the galleries but completing the setting up of the hand railing which they will be protected. The ornamental painting of the exterior of the building has been commenced. The colours used are a pale blue and white, which, however suitable they may be for internal decoration, are, we fear, little calculated to withstand the skyey influences” of a London atmosphere. The face boarding of the outermost tier of the building will, however, stained in dark colours. It is hoped that the close of the week will witness the termination of the contractors’ labours as regards construction, and the completion of subordinate details will, of course, speedily follow. Terms of Admission to the Exhibition. —We understand that the arrangement of the prices of admission to the Great Exhibition of all Nations will be graduated to suit the means of all classes. It is probable that one day in the week will be set apart for the necessary cleaning and re-arrangement of the interior of the building. On one of the remaining five days the price will be eight shillings; on two other days five shillings ; and on the two remaining days, one shilling for each admission. This scale is not absolutely fixed until it shall receive the sanction of the general body of Royal Commissioners, but we believe something very like it will be finally adopted.— Observer. Use of Intoxicating Drinks at the Great Exhibition —Mr. Charles Gilpin, and other advocates of the temperance movement, have addressed a letter to Prince Albert, complimenting him upon the exclusion of intoxicating drinks from the Exhibition refreshment rooms; and hoping that his Royal Highness did not sanction the late distribution of beer among the workmen engaged upon the building, during a late visit to the works. Water the Exhibition Building. —For the supply of water, the Chelsea Water Works Company are laying a 9-inch main, with a column of 70 feet constantly on it, and a 6-inch pipe running across the building. A 6-inch pipe will run round the whole of the outside of the building, with sixteen branches into the interior, by which, with one length of hose, and without the aid of a fire-engine, they consider they will be able to control the whole area. A special arrangement has been made with the Chelsea Water Works Company for the water to be always on ; and the Company have been at the expense of an additional auxiliary engine, for the purpose of insuring a constant supply; whilst in ordinary cases they are bound to supply 300,000 gallons per day. “Lost Friends” Department. —lt has been suggested that a place should be set apart in the Crystal Palace or its vicinity where “ lost friends may and wait “till called for,” by those who are in search of them. This will be a great convenience to the numerous “country cousins” and others who are very likely indeed to lose themselves in the bewildering crowds attending the World’s Great Fair. The Crystal Palace. —At a meeting of the Society of Arts, Mr. Fox attended to give some information respecting various points connected with the Crystal Palace, of great interest to intending exhibitors and others. With respect to dryness, he believed it to be the driest building ever raised, because it will be constantly acting on the principle of a still. The exhalation from the ground, and any water which may get in from above, will be carried away, by capillary attraction, into the grooves, and thence flow off through the sewer. As to wind, he believed no wind could effect it It was calculated to resist a force of 6360 tons, whereas the greatest wind striking against the whole side of the building at once, would be only from 1400 to 1500 tons. As to expansion and contraction, he said, the greatest amount of contraction or expansion that could take place, owing to changes of weather, was a quarter of an inch ; whereas the building would be safe, even were the amount two inches. The girders had all been tested to at least fifteen tons, and they would not break with less than thirty ; whereas, it was calculated that they could not possibly be subjected to a weight of more than five and a half tons. As to the vibration of machinery, so confident was he of its capability, that he should be happy to see a locomotive run along the gallery. Unbleached calico was used for the lighting —giving an exceedingly beautiful, subdued light, greatly to the admiration of Prince Albert. As to the strength of the glass, it was at the rate of sixteen ounces to the foot, which was considerably above that used by them in all the thirty acres of glass which, by their firm, had been spread over all the kingdom. And as to provision against fire, no building could be better constructed (according to Mr. Braidwood, superintendent of the metropolitan fre brigade), than one of glass, in such a one the immediate seat of the fire could be instantly detected, and water could be poured in to extinguish it. Water pipes of adequate bore were being laid down, and the doors were so arranged as to facilitate Entrance and exit with the greatest readiness. The whole of the interior of this huge structure may be taken within the scope of a single glance, at several points, and from those points fire, should one occur, may be detected and commanded. The Police Arrangements. —Last week, the Commissioners of the Metropolitan police intimated their intention to augment the force by adding 900 men, who will be employed for twelve months only. , / France and the Exhibition. —Last week, the French Minister of Agriculture and Commerce gave notice to the central jury that they would have to proceed immediately to the examination aud choice of the productions of French industry destined for the Exhibition of London. M. C. Dupin is the president of the jury, which held its first meeting on the Ist of February. Accident at the Crystal Palace. —On Thursday evening, a singular accident took place at the Crystal Palace, which has not yet been satisfactorily accounted for. The wind at nightfall began to blow heavily from the south-west, but was not nearly so high as it has been from about the same quarter since the work commenced. All of a sudden the glazing of about 1,000 square feet gave way, but not in the usual way when glass is blowm in, for it rather seemed to be the effect of an eddy than of a direct current of air. The extent of breakage, though it seems large when stated in figures, is not so when examined with the eye. The cause of it is under investigation ; and the meantime it will be satisfactory to the public to hear that the columns, girders, and other important parts of the structure at the spot where the accident took place were not in the least affected. Insurance Companies and the Exhibition Building. —The principal insurance companies of the metropolis have come to the conclusion that the Crystal Palace is a very combustible edifice, upon the insurance of which a high premium must be paid. The calico coverng in which it is to be wrapped —the proximity of the fixed steam engine for the machinerythe proposed plan of lighting the interior by lamps fixed in the external wall—all these matters have impressed the companies with such a sense of danger that they refuse to insure at a lower rate than 21s. per cent for nine months, with a premium at the rate of about ,£2,000 per annum for the building, and with proportionate rates on the enormous amount of valuable property collected within it; the Great Exhibition of 1851 will prove profitable concern for these companies. France alone wishes to insure £BOO,OOO worth of goods for the occasion. Corn Trade.—Towards the close of the past, and in the early part of the week now about totenninate, there were slight symptoms of an improvement in the Wheat trade ; but having since had a return of wet weather, and the supplies of foreign breadstuffs having meanwhile increased, holders have lost confidence, and the anticipation of a small advance in prices has not been realized; nor is there anything in the present position of affairs to lead to the belief that any immediate amendment w'ill take place.— Mark Lane Express. Loss of Two British Ships and partial Murder of the Crew.—Advices have been received from Valparaiso, communicating the total loss of two British vessels, the Gloucester and Prirce Albert, both of 300 tons burthen, the property of Mr. Glendening, of Stamford Hill. The Glocester was overtaken by a storm near San Francisco, was driven ashore, and became a total wreck. The Prince Albert arrived at Magellan’s Straits on the 2nd of October, and was driven ashore by a violent gale. The ship being left high and dry upon the beach, some of the crew left her to procure fresh water. During their absence, the wreck was surrounded by the natives (Patagonians) who made an attack upon the captain and crew’. Two of them were murdered, The loss of the vessels, which, it is said, exceeded £20,000, is understood to be covered by insurance.—Times. A Hint to Quick Writers.—Locke siys that the faster a man writes the slower others read what written. Napoleon could write fourteen pages in minute ; unfortunately, however, each page consists of a blot and asj atter. Some of his lines to Maria Louisa appear to have he» n scattered over the paper by the explosion of bomb-shell, thc\ arc so knocked into cocked hats and smashed cockroaches.

THE GRSAT EXHIBITION. The numbers admitted on Saturday week were 17,866, and the total receipts at the doors 1,6041. l3s. On Monday the total number of visitors, according to the police returns, was 69,384- Of these, the number who paid upon admission was 67,266; the amount received being 2,8631. There was a large attendance of children connected with various schools-among others, twenty-three from a school in Shenley, thirty from Ashton (sent by the Hon. Mrs. Howard), twenty-six from the British School at Ebley in Gloucestershire, 113 from Willesden, sixty-eight from St. Dunstan's parish, and forty-one from Brighton. On Tuesday the number of visitors, as returned by the police, was 60,382, of whom 57,187 were admitted upon pay- ment.. The total receipts were 2,85lL 7is. The number of visitors on Wednesday was 84,540, the total receipts at the doors, amounting to 2,5721. 12e. Placards were posted up, by order of the Com- mittee, announcing that the Exhibition will close on Satur- day the 11th of October-that the building will be open upon that day at nine instead of twelve o'clock, as upon other Saturdays-and that no Bath chairs will be admitted. This announcement will, of course, set at rest any doubts which may have existed on the subject of the dual closing of the Exhibition upon the 11th of October. It has been dif- ficalt to make many of the foreigners believe that it was really intended to close the Exhibition upon the day originally named, and it was not till they saw the fact actually posted up in black and white, that they appearedto be convinced of it. With respect to the closing ceremony on the 15th of October, we have no reason for believing that any deviation will take glase from the plan already decided upon. The details of the arrangement are not yet finally completed, but it is probable that seats will be provided, upon a raised stage in the centre of the transept, for the accommodation of Prince Albert and the other Royal Commissioners, and in the immediate neigh. bourhood for those invited to be present. t'he principal por- tion of the business transacted will consist in onetof the mem- bers of the Council of Chairmen-probably the chairman, Viscount Canning - announcing to the Commissioners the awards of the prizes which the jurors have made, and stating the grounds upon which they have been given. Prince klbert, as President of the Commtission, will then, in all probability, on behalf of the Royal Commissioners, thank the jurors for the attention which they have bestowed upon the subjeat; and he will, no doubt, take that opportunity of alluding to the great success of the undertaking-the assistance which it has received from all classes of the community-the benefits to art, manufactures, and commerce, which is expected to flow from the lessons which it has taught -and the services of the foreign, metropolitan, and local commissioners and commit- tees; and last, but not least, the cordial support and assist- ance rendered by the exhibitors will be duly acknowledged. It is sot intended to admit the public upon this occasion, as accommodation for witnessing the ceremony and hearing the addresses, could not be provided for a greater number of per- sons than the exhibitors, jarers, foreign and local conmmis- sioners, and members of local committees, whose presence it is intended to request. The holders of seasoa-tickets will not possess any right to be present by virtue of their holding tickets, as the Exhibition will have closed to the public on the previous Saturday. The distribution of the medals will be a matter of after consideration, as comnparatively'few of those requiring the names of the owners to be stamped upon them wiU be ready for delivery by the 15th of October.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. AN ExPaCxANT PoET.-A difference of opinion has arisen be- tween Mr Wallis, the able secretary to the juries of the Great Exhibition, and Mr Ellis, one of the exhibitors in Class 17, as to what ought properly to form the elements of the verdicts of the juries in certain cases. This difference of opinion, and the reasons adduced by the respective parties, are set out in the correspondence betveen Mir Ellis and Mr Wallis, which has already appeared in the public papers. It appears from this correspondence that Mr Ellis deposited in Class 17 of the Exhibition a large volume of original poetry. At the time when this volume was thus deposited, it was expressly stated to the proper officer that it was exhibited as a specimen of ori- ginal pottry, and not as a specimen of typography or binding: and no objection was made at the time on account of this de- claration of the depositor. Mr Ellis now urges, that inasmuch as this volume was thus received as a specimen of original poetry the juries are bound to consider its poetic merit, and to award himt a prize for excellence in that department of the fine arts if his work should be found deserving of such reward. To this request of Mr Ellis, the Secretary of the Juries re- plies, that in estimating the value of books the juries can only consider the typography and binding, and their eves must be altogether closed to literary merit of every kind. To this answer of the Secretary, Mlr Ellis replies that his demand is supported by a strict analogy with other cases. That in other similar cases the juries have pursued a different mode of pro- ceeding, and he cites the article of Sevres china as one in the valuing of which a different rule has been adopted by the juries. On Tuesday L.2773, 16'. 'was taken at the doors, and the number of visitors was 57,059. Tie building nowv opens to the public at Dine o'clock in the morning, aid closes at six in the evening. An important meeting of the Royal Commission, which was very fully attended, took place on Tuesday in the Crvstal Palace, and was presided over by Prince Albert, who was na- turally anxious to see certain questions satisfactorily solved which pressed for a deci-ion before his departure for the Hitgh- lands. All matters that could stand over, such as the fate of the building, and the appropriation of the surplus funds, are still in reserve; but the following is a summary of the points finally settled:- "The Royal Commissioners have fixed Saturday, the I Ith of October, as the day for closing the Exhibition to the public. It is their intention to hold a meeting in the building on Wed- nesday, the 1 5th of October, at 12 o'clock, to receive the re- ports of the several juries, and to take leave of the foreign commissioners. (Jn this occasion they intenld to request the presence of the exhibitors, the jurors, the foreign and local commissioners, and the members of the local commit- tees. Immediately aiter the close of their proceedings permission vill be given to the exhibitors to remove their goods, subject to such regulations as may be made by the executive committee. The reports of the juries and the names of the persons to whom prizes shall have been awarded will afterwards be published in the London GCoceue. It is the desire of rite Roval Commissioners not only to present medals to the individuals towhom the juriesmay harelawarded them, but to mark their sense of the great exertions of alli the exhibitors, and also of the jurors, the foreign and local committecs, the chairmen, treasurers, and secretaries of local committees, and other persons who have rendered services in I promoting the Exhibition, and to present them with a perisa- cent memorial of the undertaking by distributing medals to l each, accompanied by a certificate and Ea copy of the reports of the jines. IThe three medals of which the designs were originally ap- proved are intended to be applied as follows :-That by Mr Leonard Wvon will be distributed to the prizenmen selected by the juries, that by M. Boneardel will be given in certain cases recommended by the Council of Chairmen, not as a mark of excellence in degree on the part of those who receive it, but for reasons which the Council of Chairmen have been re- quested to state specially in their reports. The medal de- signed by Mr Adams will be given to the jurors. In addition to these medals the Commissioners propose to cause two other mnedals to be struck, which will be presented respectively to the Exhibitors, and to those who bave rendered other services to the Exhibition. l The great number of the medals, books, and certificates, which will thus be presented obviously renders the distribu- tion of them on a single occasion a physical impossibility. " On the other band, the Commiissioners feel that it would be invidious to select acy persons to receive their medals at one time, and to omit others. And further it is clearly desirable that the medals, the certificates, and the reports should be presented simultaneous- ly, and the length of time *which must necessarily elapse bec fore the whole of them can be prepared makes it diflicult to fix any precise day oil which the distribution could be ef- fected. "U Under these circumstances the Royal Commissioners have come to the conclusion that it will be most desirable to fix a limited period wvitbin which each individual may make such arrarnements for receiving medals, books, and certificates from the Commission as may best suit his personal conveni- ence. DOe jIotice will be given on this point as soon as the Commissioners are able to fix a time for the distribution to commence.l From this it will he seen that it is not at present eon- teraplated to close the Exhibition with any pomp or cere- mony; that the Commissioners desire, so far as medals, cer- tificates, and jarors repurts can do so, to please everybody; that they cannot render the closing and the distribution of rewards and honours as they ought to be simultaneous acts; that the official announcements of prizes will be postponed, and other steps taken to avoid as far as possible individual jealousies and " make things pleasant ;` finally, as we some days ago hinted, that the Great Exhibition may he wellnigh forgotten, and the youngest contributor at an advanced period of life, before the honorary distinctions connected with it have reached their proper recipients.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION The Royal Commission have issued the follow- ing programme of the manner in which the State opening by Her Majesty, already announced to the public, is to be conducted : — "Exhibition of 1851. " Her Majesty having signified her Royal pleasure that arrangements should be made to enable Her Majesty to gratify a wish very ge- nerally expressed on the part of the public to be present at a ceremony by which Her Majesty should epen the Exhibition of the Works of In- dustry of all nations on the Ist of May, Her Majesty's Commissioners hereby give notice that the programme of this ceremony, and the regula- tions under which the holders of season tickets will be admitted, aie as follows : — " Exhibitors' attendants who have been sanc- tioned by the Executive Committee will be ad- mitted between the hours of 8 and 9 o'clock at doors specified on their cards, and will immediate- ly take their places by the counters or objects ex- hibited by their employers. " Holders of season tickets will be admitted at all doors on the east, south, and west of the building between the hours of 9 and half-past 11 o'clock, and will be allowed to take their places, subject to police regulations, in the lower part of the building and in the galleries, except the parts railed off in the nave and transept, " A platform will be raised to tbe north of the centre of the transept, on which a chair of State will be placed. " Her Majesty's Commissioners will assemble at half-past 11 o'clock in tbe transept, opposite the platform, together with their Executive Com- mittee and the Foreign Acting Commissioners, in full dress or in plain evening dress. The Royal Commissioners held a meeting on Thursday, at the Crystal Palace, his Royal Highness Prince Albert being present as President of the Commission, at which a report to the Queen was adopted, in which, after setting forth the details of certain facts which are already publicly known, they state that after all the accounts of the Exhibition are wound up, they have reason to believe that the surplus will not be less than 150,0001. They then say: Of the entrance fees, a portion has been paid by foreign visitors, and it was owing to the fact that the contributions of all nations Were there dis- played, that the number of visits made by persons attracted to the Exhi. bition amounted to upwards 6,000,000. The subscriptions were derived, with few exceptions, solely from your Majesty's subjects, and were made after a public announcement that they must be " absolute and definite," but that should any surplus remain it was the intention of your Majesty's Commissioners to apply the same to purposes strictly in connexion with the ends of the Exhibition, or for the establishment of similar exhibitions for the future. We humbly beg to represent to your Majesty that we are of opinion that it is not advisable to apply the surplus to the last named pur- pose. Considering that the Exhibition which has just closed has afforded ample proof that an undertaking of this kind can be made self-supporting, and that it may safely be left to the public again to provide, when required, the means of meeting the preliminary expenses,-considering also the im- possibility of fixing long beforehand any definite period for the repetition of such an exhibition, which requires for its success so many concurrent circumstances,-we are of opinion, that greater benefit may be derived by the public from a judicious application in the interval of the means at our disposal to the furtherance of the general objects for which the Exhibition was designed, and in such a manner that the advantages which may be obtained should not be confined solely to your Majesty's subjects. but should be shared, as far as it may be possible, by other countries. These objects your Majesty's Commissioners conceive to have been the further- ance of every branch of human industry, by the comparison of the pro- cesses employed, and of the results obtained by all the nations of the earth, and by the promotion of kindly international feelings, by the practical illustration of the advantages which may be derived by each country from what has been done by others. Your Majesty's Commissioners have the satisfaction to be able to express to your Majesty their conviction that the Exhibition has, to a great extent, attained these objects, and that in its consequences the most beneficial results may yet be expected. Already many requirements on the part of the public have become apparent during the course of the Exhibition, and have found expression in various sugges- tions made to us for the application of the surplus; many of them, however, were for objects quite inconsistent with the pledges above alluded to, whilst others, though for purposes in accordance with them, were of a limited, partial, or local character. Your Majesty's Commissioners are of opinion that no measures could be so strictly in accordance with the ends of the Exhibition as those which may increase the means of industrial education, and exten'd, the influence of science and art upon productive in- dustry. We are fully aware of the difficulty of devising a comprehensive plan to meet these objects; should the view, however, which we have taken as to the manner of fulfilling our pledges meet with your Majesty's approbation, we beg to assure your Majesty that we shall give our fullest and most careful consideration to this important subject, and we would suggest that full time should be afforded us to consider and mature such a plan as we should feel warranted in laying before your Majesty, the more so as from the disproportion between the end proposed and the means at present applicable to it, much will depend on the extent of co-operation we mav receive from the public. We are advised, however, that our powers under your Majesty's royal charter will ceose when all the expenses inci- dental to the Exhibition shall have been discharged and notice thereof given to your Majesty's Secretary of State, and that we have not thepower of deciding upon the disposal of the surplus. If, therefore, it be your Majesty's pleasure that we should act further in this matter it will be necessary, before we can take even any preliminary step, that your Majesty should grant to us by royal charter such further powers as your Majesty may deem necessary, to enable us to lay before your Majesty a scheme for the application of the surplus in accordance with the expectations held out to the public, and with the sanction and approval of your Majesty to adopt such measures as may be necessary for such purpose.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. COMPREHENSIVE VIEW OF THE CONTENTS OF THE CRYSTAL PALACE. A comprehensive view of the vast collection of objects in Hyde-park is what the public stand most in need of. When they have thoroughly mastered the disposition and arrangement of the building, when they know in which direction to go in search of Austrian or American products, and where the different branches of our native industry are represented, they will still find themselves at sea in endeavouring to form a just conception of the whole display, in distinguishing the characteristic features of each part, and storing their minds with definite ideas of the industrial attributes developed at this gathering of nations. When a man is introduced to a number of strangers, his first instinctive tendency, after examining their respective appearances so as to distinguish them again, is to ask himself and study attentively what tendencies of the intellect or what traits of the heart he can gather from the expression of each countenance. Now, this process is exactly what the public are at present endeavouring to go through within the transparent walls of the building in Hyde-park. They have been presented there to the industries of all nations. They find each country preserving the individuality of her own collection. They can go to one portion of the building and see France, to another and see Germany, and so on round this family circle of the globe for the first time in man's history formed. Well, then, the question arises, what are they all like? In no fairer or truer mirror can national characters be represented than in their industrial products. Other pictures may deceive, but this must tell the truth. The course of events, guided as it is by a higher power than man's, does not always illustrate the moral and social attributes of communities. Not so the fruits of labour—the quality and description of material which engross the toil, supply the demand, and engage the tastes and predilections of a people. These tell their story as faithfully as the actions or the physiognomy of an individual indicate his nature, and by them, thus considered, we hope to help the public by a new path and under a fresh light through the marvels of the Great Exhibition. THE BILITISII BIDE. Let us commence at home, and see what appearance this island of ours puts on at the peaceful reunion of nations. Is it Britannia, with her trident and plumed helmet and the lion recumbent at her feet, or John Bull's portly form, carrying weight in every limb, and determination, not unmingled with prejudice, from the crown of his broad-brimmed hat to the soles of his top-helots P Far, otherwise. Some traces of those popular types of our nationality may indeed be traced, but England has greatly changed. Her genius is mechanism, her master spirit the civil engineer, her tendencies to relieve labour from its drudgery, and delegate to iron, to steam, and to the other powers of the inanimate world, as much as possible of the burden of toil. If you doubt this, go and look at the great department of machinery in the Crystal Palace; watch that vast collection of interesting objects, every portion of which lightens immeasurably the burden of life and releases hundreds of hands from the most irksome forms of industry. You will there see how mechanism is extending her dominion over the whole empire of labour; how she rises in textile fabrics to the manufacture of the most delicate and intricate lace; how from wood she aspires to fashion iron into the most exact proportions; how, with steam as her handmaid, she works the printing press and navigates the ocean, and outruns the swiftest animal in her course. Turn into the agricultural implement department, and you will find everyt lung now done by machinery. By it the farmer not only sows and reaps ' but he manures and hoes. By it he thra s he s out and grinds his corn and prepares the food for his cattle. He can even drain by machinery, and it is difficult now to find a ilranch of his business into which it does not largely enter. In our manufactures the mechanical genius of the country reigns supreme. Those beautiful fabrics are nearly all the evidences of its power. Soft goods and hard ware are e q ually indebted to it, and in its presence the un a id e d e ff or t s of handicraftsmen appear small and insignificant indeed. It travels everywhere and invades every compartment, even that of the fine arts, in the court dedicated to which 801320 of the most conspicuous contributions are specimens of printing in oil, and attempts to reproduce by mechanical means the sea. timent and inspiration of the painter. Yet we are not altogether abandoned to thispower—this Frankenstein which we i created, and which s dragging us we know not whither. The medireval court and its crowds of visitors, and its gaudy embellishments, still draw us back to days when ornament was not inseparably wedded to usefulness, or when at least, if that pact was completed, she was not acknowledged to be the "weaker vessel.' We have some specimens of sculpture, such as those from the hands of Gibson,ll`Dowall, and others, , not unworthy of "art." The two colossal statues of the Scots have about thorn a certain solemn and massive grandeur which some minds will not unnaturally associate with the characteristics of the national intellect. These and other points will press upon the mind of an attentive observer • yet our main hope for the creation of the beautiful rests still in the adaptability of that power by' which as a nation we labour and produce. Through multiplied evidences of neglected taste, and violations of harmony in colour and design that must shock many of our visitors, the traces of a better and purer style of national industry begin to be discernible. Even our mechanical tendencies are yielding to the higher inspirations of tho fancy, or perhaps we should say, are subjecting the admiration to their stupendous efforts. Witness, in illustration of this, the great interior of the Crystal Palace itself, that surprising and splendid piece of mechanism, wherein the civil engineer has displaced the architect and iron and glass been substituted for bricks and mortar. Of our colonial possessions visitors will gather at the Exhibition an interesting but imperfect impression. They will see in that preponderance of raw produce the evidences of infant societies still struggling forward to a larger industrial development. The philosophic mind will be attracted by the advantages which the rising communities that have swarmed from our shores to settle in distant scenes possess—how science and education help them to investigate the natural resources of the new regions which they occupy—how, having tilled the virgin soils of Australia or Canada with the agricultural knowledge of the mother country, they at length send home the fruits of their labour to be absorbed by our markets. We enter the Indian collection, and examine thoughtfully the products of our empire in the East. What do they tell usp Those jewels, that rich display of mineral and vegetable produce s. those shawl s an d carpets in which the harmony of colours is so admirably represented ; filigree work in silver and gold, brocaded stuffs, curiously executed carvings, rude mode a of machinery, musical instruments, arms, elephant trappings, naval architecture —how suggestive they all are and what stories they tell. H ere are gathered .together the trophies of ancient civilization and arts, marvelously carried d own to our own time. Here may be studied the industrial habits of nations preserved through centuries without change or progress, yet still wonderful and magnificent in the eyes of modern labour. Look at those alabastar chairs, how regal they appear, how fitly they repres en t a country where many dynasties conquered and flourished and were overcome before the British away was established over its dusky p opu l at i ons. Nearly everything in that collection which is the work of man's hands indicates a vast expenditure of time for its production and a great display of taste. Yet it is nearly all ornamental, rather than useful, in its character. Whenever the really useful arts appear, rudeness of material and design are visible. A warlike weapon will be finished off in the most elaborate style, yet a pair of scissors be manufactured in a manner worthy of the South Sea Islanders. The East India Company begin their rule of India as if it were a new country. The evidences of barbaric pomp, the state umbrellas, the cloth of gold, and robes decorated with pearls and diamonds, concern not them. These belong to the natives, to the traditions of the past, and to industries which have been bequeathed from age to age as an heirloom, Our part of the collection is the raw produce—the mineral, vegetable, and animal trealities and unused till our commerce and the wants of oar manufactures sought them out. Resting upon them, we strive to build on substantial and permanent foundations the structure of empire and government i ‘ n India; at least, that is the lesson which the Exhibition seems to teach, and the question which each visitor asks himself as he surveys that most interesting collection is, "Shall we succeed m our attempt ? " Such is a brief outline of what we conceive to be the character and inward meaning of the vast mass Of objects which have been collected within the British half of the Crystal Palace. Each reader will fill up the sketch according to his peculiar bent of mind, and from the ideas thus formed may be gathered a succinct conception of the whole, tending to relieve the mind from those vague, unsatisfactory, and distracting impressions of astonishment and admiration which, with the great majority of visitors, are, we doubt not, in the ascendant.

Whitsun holidays have come and gone, and the Crystal Palace still stands a marvel for the multitude, for the tens of thousands who have already seen it, and for the hundreds of thousands who are yet to rejoice in the sight. But Whitsuntide has not produced the overwhelming numbers whose arrival was looked for, and for whose reception such ample preparation was made by the officials in charge of the building. It was settled that if too great a number of visitors presented themselves for admission, the entrances to the building should be shut, that a signal should be ex- hibited on the highest point of the roof, and that limits should be put to the swelling tide of popular curiosity. The course of events, however, in this instance, as in many others, disappointed calculations. Whit-Monday passed away without any unusual crush, and in a manner the most satisfactory. Whether fear held them back, or the in- auspicious character of the weather, or some other influence equally potent but less understood, we are unable to say, but, nevertheless, it is a remarkable fact that the numbers who visited the Exhibition on that day were not so great at one time as they have been on more than one former occa- sion, that no inconvenience was felt, and that it was not even found necessary to alter the usual arrangements for a free and uninterrupted circulation of spectators. The morn- ing was cloudy and threatening, and from the high winds which prevailed on Sunday many believed that the canvas covering of the roof would have been completely swept away. It stood well, however, the test to which it was ex- posed, and not a yard of it yielded to the violence of the blast. At nine o'clock, or thereabouts, omnibuses, cabs, and caravans filled with holyday folk might be seen passing in dense columns along all the leading thoroughfares to- wards Hyde park; the streets gave indications of an im- mense influx of visitors, and even the precarious elevation of the ' knife boards " was fully occupied. Between the hours of ten and eleven o'clock 21,526 persons were ad- mitted, and appearances promised a day of unusual bustle and excitement. From one of the galleries of the transept Mr Mayne, the Commissioner of Police, might have been observed watching with anxiety the seemingly inexhaustible tide of restless humanity poured into the interior. The task of counting so enormous an influx became one of great difficulty, and already an assemblage unprecedented in number was anticipated. Rain began to fall, all the indi- cations of a damp, disagreeable day were realized. Along the approaches to the building bands of sturdy pedestrians might, nevertheless, be seen pressing forward, sometimes seeking shelter and then starting afresh. Another hour passed away, and it became evident that the rush of visitors was checked. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The Royal Commissioners held a meeting on Thursday, at the Crystal Palace, his Royal Highness Prince Albert being present as President of the Commission, at which a report to the Queen was adopted, in which, after setting forth the details of certain facts which are already publicly known, they state that after all the accounts of the Exhibition are wound up, they have reason to believe that the surplus will not be less than £150,000. They then say : " Of the entrance fees, a portion has been paid by foreign visitors, and it was owing to the fact that the contributions of all nations were there displayed, that the number of visits madeby persons attracted to the Exhibition amounted to upwards 6,000,000. The subscriptions were derived, with few exceptions, solely from your Majesty's subjects, and were made after a public announcement that they must be " absolute and definite," but that should anysurplus remain it was the intention of your Majesty's Commissioners to apply the same to purposes strictly in connexion with the ends of the Exhibition, or for the establishment of similar exhibitions for the future. We humbly beg to represent to your Majesty that we are of opinion thst it is not advisable to apply the surplus to the last named purpose. Considering that the Exhibition which has just closed has afforded ample proof that an undertaking of this kind can be made self-supporting, and that it may safely be left to the public again to provide, when required, the means of meeting the preliminary expenses,— considering also the impossibility of fixing long beforehand any definite period for the repetition of such an exhibition, which requires for its success so many concurreut circumstances,—we are of opinion that greater benefit may be derived by the public from a judicious application in the interval of the means at our disposal to the furtherance of the general objects for which the Exhibition was designed, and in such a manner that the advantages which may be obtained should not be con fined solely to your Majesty's subjects, but should be shared, as far as may be possible by other countries. These objects your Majesty's Commissioners conceive to have been the furtherance of every branch of human industry, by the comparison of the processes employed, and of the results obtained by all the nations of the earth, and by the promotion of kindly international feelings, by the practical illustration of the advantages which may be derived by each country from what has been done by others. Your Majesty's Commissioners have the satisfaction to be able to express to your Majesty their conviction that the exhibition has, to a great extent, attained these objects, and that in its consequences the most beneficial results may yet be expected. Already many requirements on the part of the public have become apparent during the course of the exhibition, and have found expression in various suggestions made to us for the application of the stir. plus; many of them, however, were for objects quite inconsistent with the pledges above alluded to, whilst others, though for purposes in accordance with them, were of a limited, partial, or local character. Your Majesty's Commissioners are of opinion that no measures could be so strictly in accordance with the ends of the exhibition as those which may increase the means of industrial education, and extend the influence of science and art upon productive industry. We are fully aware of the difficulty of devising a comprehensive plan to meet these objects; should the view, however, which we have taken as to the manner of fulfilling our pledges meet with your Majesty's approbation, we beg to assure your Majesty, that we shall give our fullest and most careful consideration to this important subject, and we would suggest that full time should be afforded us to consider and mature such a plan as we should feel warranted in laying before your Majesty, the more so as from the disproportion between the end proposed and the means at present applicable to it, much will depend on the extent of co-operation we may receive from the public. We are advised, however, that our powers under your Majesty's royal charter will cease when all the ex pen ses Incidental to the Exhibition shall have been discharged and notice thereof given to your Majesty's Secretary of State, and that we have not the power of deciding upon the disposal of the surplus. If, therefore, it be your Majesty's pleasure that we should act further in this matter it will be necessary, before we can take even any preliminary step, that your Majesty should grant to us by royal charter such further powers as your Majesty may deem necessary, to enable us to lay before your Majesty a scheme for I the application of the surplus in accordance with the expectations held out to the public, and with the sanction and approval of your Majesty to adopt such measures as may be necessary for such purpose.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday there was a numerous attendance of exhibitors and those introduced by them into the building. Earliest and most conspicuous among the arrivals during 0:e day came the Queen herself. Her Majesty's visit was a lengthened one, and the department of the United States was that to which at the outset she directed her attention. She examined with great ' interest the service of plate made from Californian gold, the lustre of which is very surprising. She adtnired in passing the magnificent porphyry vase exhibited by the King of Sweden, and placed in the nave during her stay in the north. Ptoceeding to the display of French jewellery, she paid special attention to the stall of Fro went Meurice, which is well worthy even of Royal in.. spection. Probably influenced by agreeable recollections of Manchester, Her Majesty spent some time in examining the trophy which represents the staple. manufactures of that town. She also looked carefully over the sketches of artistic objects shown by Mr. Digby Wyatt in the nave, and over Mr. Lloyd's views of the building. Her visit terminated shortly before twelve o'clock. Her Majesty, accompanied by the Prince, came again to the building on Tuesday morning, and made the round of the galleries. There they were preqented by Mr. Henry Spicer and Mr. George Clowes with handsomely-bound copies of that valuable work, the Official' Illustrated Catalogue, which has at length been coinpleted. The Queen then visited portions of the United States, Russian, and Belgian displays, anti, in taking her departure shortly before twelve o'clock, with her usual kindness and condescension, took notice of the old Cornish pedestrian fisherwoman, who had been placed in her way, and, with hearty emphasis, said, "God bless your Majesty." The attendance of exhibitors and their friends was much more numerous than on Monday, but the interior was by no means inconveniently crowded. The preparations for the final ceremonial were in rapid progress, and among the visiters a painful sensation was experienced in finding that the Crystal Fountain, that favourite rendezvous, that central attraction of the building, had been entirely removed during the preceding .night, This was a necessary step, and Mr. Osier submitted to it with a cheerfulness worthy of the highest praise. Mr. Paxton was Jess resigned, naturally regarding the clearing away of the fountain as the first of a series of de.. structive acts which might terminate in the entire demolition of his fairy design. The following liberal and highly praiseworthy Circular to British exhibitors has just been issued by the Royal Commission : "Many of the foreign Acting Commissioners having represented that international advantages would be likely to arise if their countries possessed a collection of specimens of raw materials and produce, and patterns of some classes of manufactures shown by British exhibitors, together with the wholesale prices of them, and having expressed a desire that such collections should be formed, Her Majesty's Commisloners have authorised the Executive Committee to assist in forming them. "British exhibitors who may be willing to present specimens and patterns for this purpose are requested to immediately with Lieutenant Tyler; but in those cases , where they may not consider such presentation to be a sufficient commercial advantage to themselves, the Executive Committee are authorized to treat for the purchase of the necessary quantities, and exhibitors are requested to forward their terms for the purchase to Lieutenant Tyler Lefore removing their articles from the building. RESULTS OF GREAT FOREIGN INVASION —OUP foreign visiters have neither burnt our 'houses about our ears, nor endeavoured to overturn OirTloveenment, nor run away with our daughters. They have behaved themselves peaceably and good-naturedly, and have borne with our little peculiarities amiably. Moreover, they have paid for what they have had, like honest men. May I be permitted to surmise that from this mutual sight-seeing and metropolis-visiting, this international f&e-giving and hand-shaking, some little, some trifling good may arise? Is it too wild a thought to hope that our children will not quite believe that the French necessarily eat frogs and are all dancing-masters—that every Italian gentleman carries a stiletto in his bosom, and a bowl of poison in his left-hand pocket—that German babies are weaned on saner-kraut —that revenge is the one inevitable passion with which all Spaniards are possessed—and that the unvarying fate of all Turkish ladies is to be sown up in sacks and cast into the Bosphorus ? Is it really impossible that our grandchildren may discard those legemls altogether? On the other hand, it strikes me that our continental neighbours will not henceforward be quite so decided as heretofore in their notions and impressions respecting us. I don't think we shall be called "perfidious Albion" quite so frequently. lam of opinion that the editors of foreign newspapers will no longer declare that we live on raw beefsteaks, and occasionally eat the winners of our Derbies; that every nobleman takes his " bouledogue " to court with him ; that we are in the daily habit of selling our wives in Smithfieldmarket; and that during the month of November threefourths of the population of London committ suicide. Altogether, I think a little peace, and a little goodwill, and a little brotherhood among nations, will result from the foreign invasion ; and that it will, in future, be no longer a matter of course, that because 50,000 Frenchmen in blue coats and red trousers meet 50,000 Englishmen in blue trousers and red coats, they must all fall to, and cut and blow each other to atoms.—Dickens's Household Words. THE EGYPTIAN RAILWAY.—A large and influential meeting of merchants and others interested in the improvement of the communication with India arid China, via Egypt, was held on Tuesday at the London Tavern; Mr. Samuel Gregson in the chair. Upwards of two hundred gentlemen, including several Members of Parliament, were present. Mr. Briggs moved the first resolution, which affirmed a safe, speedy, commodious, and economical communication to be essential to the good Government of India, to the extension of commercial intercourse between Europe and the east, and to the industrial and social improvement of Egypt ; declaring it also to be opposed neither to the interests nor the legitimate ambition of any nation on earth. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. A. Anderson, M.P., moved the second resolution, which censured the conduct of the Sublime Porte, as calculated to injure British interests, and called for the prompt and active interposition of the Government. Mr. Anderson also moved the adoption of a memorial to Lord John Russell. The motion was put and carried unanimously. Mr. Foster, a Member of the Council of Port Phillip, moved that a Committee be appointed to procure signatures to the Memorial, to present it, to communicate personally or otherwise with the Government, to endeavour to procure the cooperation of parties in other parts ot the kingdom, and to call another meeting to receive a report of the proceedings. The resolution was carried unanimously. The following gentlemen were nominated Committeemen :—Mr. Gregson, Mr. A. Anderson, M.P.; Mr. Briggs, Mr. Lindesay, Mr. Larking,. Mr. Matheson, M P., Mr. Raikes Currie, M.P.; Mr. Macgregor, M.P.; Mr. J. D. Foster, and Mr. G. S. Barton. Mr. Macgregor, M.P., proposed a resolution thanking the - Viceroy of Egypt for his exertions to improve the route. General Briggs seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Our attention has been directed to a very useful and well constructed model of a farm-yard and building, in which steam-power is used to do all the work usually done by manual labour. The model is designed by Mr. Isaac Tyson, of Selby, in Yorkshire, and is upon a scale of two inches to the foot. The object of this model is to show to farmers and landed proprietors that a much more economical system may be pursued than has hitherto been adopted in the arrangement of farmsteads and the carrying on of every-day business. The plan proposed by Mr. Tyson will, it is said, effect a very considerable saving in the annual outlay of a farm. The model is designed for a farm of 500 acres, and is so arranged that the highest buildings are placed on the north side, and the various offices open into each other where necessary. The repository for fodder is placed as near as possible to where it is to be consumed, and, by tramways leading direct to the stables, as much can be conveyed on a truck at once as will supply the whole of the cattle for the day. In the same way the turnips, as they are cut, fall at once into the track, and are carried off to their destination. The stack-yards are also economically arranged, and the carriage, stacking, and conveying to market are managed without the intervention of manual or horse labour. The whole of the buildings are supplied with water by the engine, which is a fixed ome of six-horse power, of the simplest construction, and which besides performs all the operations of threshing, grinding, straw-catting, cakebreaking, and bean-grinding. The engine can also be made to crush bones, or saã, or perform any other work required on the premises; and thus, by means of this valuable servant of man, time and money and labour are saved to a considerable amount. The model is worthy the inspection of all interested in the promotion of the prosperity of English agriculture.

Among the incalculable number of articles in the Scottish department there is an unpretending piece of cabinet work, in Class 26, schedule 110, described in the catalogue as having been carved with a penknife by John Barrie, a ploughman in Peebleshire, by candlelight. The history of this unique specimen of untaught genius is highly interesting. Mr. Charles Mackie, author of the "Castles and Palaces of Mary of Scotland," being on a visit last year to a friend at Eddlestone, was introduced into Barrie's cottage while engaged, over a flickering candle, in engraving with the stump of a penknife a piece of ornamental cabinet work, without model or design. Mr. Mackie, struck with such a rare specimen of natural ingenuity and labour, at once recommended Barrie to prepare some similar specimen for the Exhibition, when he set to work and finished a curious book-tray, profusely carved on sycamore wood. On the ends of the tray are two Scotch thistles, so ingeniously disposed as to serve for handles; the centre engraving is one complete piece of intricate carving similar to some of the minute efforts of the Chinese. The moldings are beautifully executed, and must have been the work of much labour. We are happy to learn that her Majesty, having become acquainted with the above facts, has been most graciously pleased to purchase this curious piece of furniture, the only article of any sort which has been displayed from the whole county of Peebles. It is useless to say that the honest ploughman is deeply sensible of the high honour. "Fortune favours valiant men," and thus the executive had the thermometer all their own way throughout the month of May and for half the month of June. On this day things took a desperate, turn, and Mr. Bennett, who had fixed 20 of his standard thermometers at different points of the building, above and below, found a sudden rise in the mean temperature of the day, amounting to 10 deg.; the 13th showing 61.8 deg., and the 19th, 74.8 deg. This was a shilling-day, with 63,863 visitors. If this weather continued, it was clear something must be done, and finding matters grow worse till the 26th, when the thermometer rose to 2 deg. above summer heatviz., 78.6 (20 deg. " Reaumur," 10 deg. being "temperate"), the climax was reached. On this day the mean was the highest that has been felt during the Exhibition. At four p.m. the thermometer No. 5, placed on the north-east corner of the gallery, among the wax flowers, registered 97 deg. The public could not stand this, even to witness the grandest sight that man could produce. " The force of nature could no further go," for the air was not only hot but vitiated. Women fainted right out, and men declared the heat intolerable. Mr. Bennett recorded the exact state of the case, and after serious consultation the glass ends of the building at the entrance were removed on the 2d of July, upon which down came the thermometer from 79.4 deg. to 66.6 deg. Since this alteration 73.4 deg. has been the maximum, with one solitary exception. Still a difficulty of breathing was felt in the upper regions. The rarified air caused by the exhalations of the mob below rushed up throughlthe galleries, where the heat averaged 4 degrees above that of the main avenue, and frequently higher still during the crowded hours of the day. Even the policemen began to suffer in health and the Sappers on duty above felt the atmospheric tax •on their lungs. Accordingly on Monday, July 7, glazed arches at various parts in the galleries were removed. After this the temperatures in the galleries and the ground floor became more uniform, and were found to be under the control of the authorities. Fifty thousand pairs of lungs enjoyed daily the constant current of fresh air. This kept the multitude below the grumbling point till the 19th July, when Saturday with its ss. admission brought a thin attendance (9326). The first sudden transition from heat to cold was instantly felt throughout the building. Down went Fahrenheit to 59 deg. and, therefore, called for measures in an opposite direction, and accordingly up went the louvres and ventilators till the temperature was again adjusted. Thus man has made nature to a great extent obedient to his will in the very difficult matter of ventilation in an unwieldy building 1350 feet long. And thus, by th 3 strict observance of the indications of a very sensitive and delicate intrnment, hitherto much undervalued, an amount of comfort has been preserved under trying and extraordinary circumstances.

PROPOSED CENTRAL COLLF.OE or ARTS AND MANEFA-1: TuttEs.-Tho Hull Advertiser has the following remarks on the proposed appropriation of the surplus to the esta- blishinent of an institution in this country similar to the Conservatoire and Ecole Centrale at Paris, an account of which appeared a few days since in our columns:-" The time is last drawing to an end when the greatest wonder of the civilized world, the Great Exhibition of 1851, will be closed; and that realized fairy-dream of genius, the Crystal Palace and its marvellous contents, will become matter of history. Sensible of the moral grandeur of this display of the world's industry-impressed with profound gratitude to the illustrious Prince witl whom the design originated, and who has toiled so unceasingly in the accomplish- ment of its astonishing success-and desirous that those Royal Commissioners who, in conjunction with Prince Albert, perfected this wonderful work should leave behind them some suitable monument of their wisdom and enterprise in an institution destined to commemorate their past labours-we have for some time felt anxious to know to what purpose it would be deemed best to devote the surplus which the Commissioners would have in hand after defraying all the expenses of the Exhibition. At first, when Mr. Pax- ton proposed converting the Crystal Palace into a winter garden, we were in favour of that proposal, believing that it would result in the wonderful extension of horticultural science in this country. Nor do we now see the least ob- jection to that measure, provided the citizens of London, wrho would more immediately benefit by the use of such winter garden, and who have abundance of wealth at their disposal, would themselves purchase the palace for that purpose. But Since Mr. Paxtos's scheme of a winrter garden has been developed, it has been proposed to de- vote the surplus funds of the Exhibition, amounting to upwards of £200,000, to the establishment of a Central College of Arts and Manifactures, for the future education, in the more necessary branchsea of useful knewledge, of the youth of the United Kingdom. Connected with this college would be schools of design in all the large towns of the kingdom, by means of which every description of local talent would be fostered, and, if pecu- liarly striking or remarkable, at once brought into general notice. We have already-thanks to the philantsropy of the Government-several excellent schools of design established in various towns in the United Kingdom, suds as Leeds, Manchester, Newcastle, Glasgow, and so on i but we sadly want some grand central institution in which the more dis- tinguished pupils might graduate in certain departments of arts and manufactures, and thus become known to the whole kingdom. What we Wvant at present in this country is not talent of the highest order in every department of human knowledge and industry, but some established and certain mode of making it so known as to enable those in want of its assistance to call forth its de- velopment. It, the obtaining the services of scholarship we are never at a loss, because the fact of having obtained cer- tain honours at one or other of our universities is ample proof of competency in certain branches of knowledge; but where is the man largely engaged in business requiring exact knowledge in arts and manufactures, who has not had to lament the want of any test of fitness but such as is often purchased by the costly experience of a personal trial ? Those who doubt this need only put the question to Mr. Henry Blundell in relation to his colour-werks, or to any other extensive manufacturer requiring more than mere mechanical skill in his immediate neighbourhood, We admit that there are many thousands of excellent work- men in their respective trades in this country who know no- thing whatever of the theory of the businesses in which they are engaged. They work, and work well, by the old ' rule of thumb.' But such workmen can only move in one parti- cular track. They can never adopt improvements, nor com- prehend principles showing the desirableness of a change in the instrumentality by which their work is done. They invent nothing themselves, and detest all' short cuts,' as they call them, to an improved method of producing on the part of others. Not so the workmen who are educated to compre- hend fully the theory of their business-who are competent to philosophise upon the operation of certain causes upon the effects produced, and the extent to which such effects might have been modified by causes slightly or greatly al- tered. The uneducated tradesman is a human machine, capable of regular or irregularaction, whereasa carefully edu- cated and rightly trained tradesman is both a beautiful ma- chine and a creative intelligence, manifesting in new disco- veries the unlimited extent of the beneficence ?? to man. We hope that the memorial submitted to the supporters of the Great Exhibition in Hull by our estimable chief magis- trate vill not only be extensively signed, but cordially ap- proved of by the whole of the inhabitants. Its object being to dignify intelligent industry, and to elevate scientific skill, the mass of the people are particularly called upon to give to its prayer the meed of their most cordial approbation. If the memuorialists are only fortunate enough to enlist Prince Albert ol the side of this magnificent and permanently beneficial undeitaking. its success is certain. And well does it com- mend itself to the patronage of his Royal Highness by its national importance, and by its total disconnection with all questions of political, or sectarian, or party policy, for while it offers the widest field for the enlisting of good men of all creeds and all parties in the earnest and hearty prosecution of a common object, itadmits of no room for doubt, dis- quietude, or discrepancy of aim or object."

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The attendance yesterday, which considerably exceeded 20,000, was pronounced by the officials to be one of the best Friday's " companies " they bad seen for some week•. The visitors were evidently of the higher classes of society, especially the foreiguas. The building was delightfully cool and pleasant, and being much less crowded than on the shilling days, formed one of the most delightful promenades in the world. Mr. Hobbs lectured to numerous and distinguished audiences on the virtues of his lock, and the great Swedish gun was an object of much curiosity to the military vision. The general opinion is, that the breech would not stand repeated discharges. Two additions have recently been made in the Milan sculpture room, which from the homely and easily understood nature of their subjects and beautiful execution, attract continuous crowds, especially of the female visitors. One is the Italian maypole, with its circle of prizes round the top, and a group of children round the base, all stru4gling to ascend. The attitudes of these latter are so natural, and depicted with so much humour, that the ladies constantly surround the group, and sympathise with the li.tle girls who are pushed away from the prize by the more vigorous male candidates. The other novelty is a statuette: representing a little girl selling Cupids out of a basket. The figure of the girl is full of ease and nature, and the details of costume are worked out with much delicacy of handling. This figure, although placed in a corner, is much admired and inquired after. A good deal of entertainment was provided for the visitors, yesterday, in the musical department, of which it is refreshing to add the great organs took no share. We believe we may add to our list of medal-holden Prince Albert for his conception and patronage of the Exhibition. Mr. Paxton receives a similar reward for his design of the Crystal Palace, and Messrs. Fox and Henderson, fot the efficient manner in which they carried that design into execution. Messrs. Hibbert and Platt get a great medal for their beautiful display of the whole process of the cotton manufacture, and one each has been awarded to Grey and Davison for the English, and to Ducroquet for the French, organ. We trust that the ambition of these exhibitors will be now satisfied, and that they will permit their huge instruments to sleep for the remainder of the season. We believe it was proposed to grant one to the East India Company, for their magnificent display of Oriental luxuries ; but the proposal was resisted by souse of the jurors, on the grounds that th•r Company are neither manufacturers nor dealers but obtained their rarities either as tribute, or by conquest.
