After the customary devotional exercises, The SECRETARY read the annual Report, which detailed the operations of the Society during the past year, in London and in other maritime ports of the kingdom. It stated that the directors were very desirous to establish model lodginghouses for sailors, and that one gentleman had promised, as soon as fitting premises could be secured, to give towards the expenses, and another friend would supply the earthenware required in the building. The Committee of the Nautical College had been hindered by many obstacles, and principally by recent legal enactments respecting sailors, which, however, they believe would prove ultimately conducive to the cause of nautical education. A Secretary had been elected, and the Committee, it was hoped, would be able now to make permanent progress, and report the same at the next annual meeting. The evangelical labours of the Society had been carried on with increasing efficiency and success both in London and the provincial ports. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. A most elaborate and detailed classification of all the articles to be exhibited in the thirty different classes into which the productions of the United Kingdom will be divided is in course of preparation by Professor Playfair, which will, when completed, form one of thie most valuable of the many interest- ing and useful classifications yet published by the Comniissioners. Such a complete classification is required, not less for assisting in the arrangement of the articles in the building, than for the ap- pointment of jurors in each of the parti- cular classes of objects exhibited, in which their knowledge may be made more completely applicable. The exertions which have been made by Professor Playfair and the other members of the Commission, in order to obtain as full and as complete a representation as possible of our mineral treasures and raw productions, will, we believe, be eminently successful. By many persons these may no doubt be considered as the least attractive articles in the Exhibition. They form, however, the basis of our national wealth and greatness, and there will not be wanting thousands of visitors who will gladly leave the more showy and elegant productions of genius and industry to ponder over and study the products of our mines aud quarries, and the various substances used in manufactures or in the works of art. England, Scotland, and Wales will, it appears, have representatives of their colliery wealth. A few days since we stated that a huge block of coal will be sent from Staffordshire. Referring to this huge block the Atlas has the fol- 3owing remarks:- 1 Dark and solid in outward semblance, but animate with a spirit uf intense activity, Passive to the weakest hand, and yet possessed of energies which, like faith, can remove noon- taius, cheap in cost and priceless in worth, exhibited where itself is the exhibitor, nay, creator of the Exhibition-type of types, and monument of monuments, amidst the count. less stores of all things typical and monumental of human industry-one black sombre-looking mass will hold a chief place within the walls of the Crystal Palace in the department appropriated to ' raw materials.' " A fes- days since we heard how the I Exhibition block of coal' wias hewn out of a seam 30 feet thick in a Staffordshire colliery ; how it was fashioned into a cylinder, of size just sufficient to pass up the shaft into daylight, and of weight barely within the strength of the lifting tackles to support without breaking. Now it lies at the mouth of the mine, expectant of the time when it may be transferred to its destination beneath the transept. What otier among the million glittering articles around will have a better right to that post of honour 9 si osne ?? qIttltiS, cbttCtinssicC. In the multitudinous contents of those vast arcades-in the glass and iron edifice whieh contaihs thieni-in the means whereby the former were brought and the latter built-and, extending our range of vision, in the wide country around, with its incessant, prosperous, and iworld-defying industry- we see but the outcome and essence of the force that lies latent in that carbonised block. It needs no inscription. In onmely giuise it contains the summary of all virtues, the foun- tnin of aI power. Everything within reach of sight or thought pays silent homage to its beneficent attributes." The important coal-fields of Swansea will also be represented by an oblong piece of about 7 feet by 3 feet, and weighing about four tons. The ?? in'wau states that this block is now on its way to the Exhibition, and that "considering that it is ex- tracted from a vein onlyfour feet thick,of the hardest coal known, will, we think, prove an interesting and not unworthy rival of the piece which we noticed in a former number as about to be sent from the Ten-yard seam in the neighbourhood of Tipton, which is comparatively soft. This coal was extracted at a distance under ground of about half a mile from the bottom of the pit, to which, and up which-a depth of lo( yards-it was conveyed without any addition to the ordinary means in use for the daily working of the pit, which is a balance pit. The colliers, with that good spirit which we have seldom found wanting in Welsh workmen, willinely gave up to the purpose nearly three days, the only pay they asked for being some ' ewrw da,' to celebrate the safe landing of the monster. This fuel, which has some most valuable properties, is used throughout the district whence it comes for steamn boilers, and ought to be used for such purposes in all localities where smoke, soot, and dust are injurious, as it produces in burn- ing neither the one nor the other; and we have heard that it is probable that Messrs. James and Aubrey's offer to supply gratuitously a sufficient quantity for the use of one boiler fire during the period that the Exhibition will remain open will be accepted by the Cometnissioners."' We are to lave also from Scotland manufactures and articles of furniture sculptured from coal. AVe have already noticed a sofa and some other articles of furniture which wvere to be sent from lVemyss, carved out of solid blocks of coal ; and we under- stand that an elegant snuff-box, made from a par- ticular species of carbonic coal in its natural state will be sent to the great depot of all that is rich and rare of the productions of the world. A correspondent informs us that the carbonic mineral takes a polish so very trans- parent and beautiful as to vie with that of the richest and finest alabaster and marble. It has been ascertained that it can be fitted into fine lobby or bed-room tables of a deep and rich polish. It will also be of great utility in forming finely polished picture-frames, flower urns. watch-seals, pillars for mantelpieces, public monuments, and for other purposes, and at an expense so trivial as to be almost wvithin the reach of all. My Lord,—l take the liberty of addressing the present letter to your Lordship, feeling confident you will be glad to receive any information likely to correct the misapprehensions under which you appear to labour respecting the construction, stability, and suitableness of the Crystal Palace to be retained as a permanent building. From your Lordship's reported speech in the House of Peers on Friday last, it appears you had founded your principal objections to the building remaining as a winterpark and garden upon information derived from an anonymous pamphlet, very much calculated to mislead you, and which, if true, would furnish grave otjections to the continuance of the structure for the purposes I have suggested. The errors to which I allude are these—That the building as at present constructed is not stable enough to be put to any permanent use, being both frail and transient ; and that the only way to preserve it would be to take the whole of it down and rebuild it. That two-thirds of the columns of support are made of wood, which will in a short time perish, and the girders being of the same, are only calculated to endure for one season. That the sashes and other portions of wood-work would endure only for a very limited period, and would then have to be replaced at a great cost. In adding my corrections to these mistakes, I might just 459 mention that, from the very commencement, when preparing my original plans of the building, my views were to make it in every way suitable to be appropriated to a permanent use, which fact I mentioned to Lord Brougham, and many others; the entire framework and strength of the structure, as it now stands, is, therefore, composed of wrought and cast iron, fixed securely together, and firmly bedded in a concrete foundation, and with ordinary attention to painting this, the most important part of the edifice will last for ages to come, with but little repairs of any kind being necessary. _ Every column on which the house rests is made bf iron; the intermediate ones in the exterior row are merely placed there for effect, and to divide the sashes, but have nothing to do with the support or stability of the building. All the girders, which form part of the frame-work and security of its structure, are composed of wrought and cast iron. There are some wooden girders, but they are only introduced for effect. Of the permanence of wooden sashes and other woodwork, if kept properly painted and attended to, we have sufficient experience to be able to form a good opinion ; there are some hothouse lights at Chatsworth which have at least been in constant use for upwards of one hundred years, and appear likely to endure for a long time to come. My estimate of duration for the sash and glass work of the Crystal Palace is fifty years, but in my statement of the expenditure provision was made for a renewal every twentyfive years. However, with care and attention, my belief is that one hundred years would be nearer the reality. The duration of woodwork depends very much upon its position and the attention paid to it. We must not forget that many of our most enduring public buildings have wooden roofs for instance, Westminster-hall, Lincoln's-inn-hall, and the dome of St. Paul's, all of which are still in excellent preservation. In order to render the building as it now stands fit for a winter garden considerable expenses must be incurred, an estimate of which I shall shortly be able to lay before the public; but without at this time entering into financial particulars, I am convinced that when once formed the after expense for maintenance could be easily sustained without a public grant, and that the terms of admission could be made such as to suit the position and wants of all classes of individuals.

THE NEW PARK TOR FINSBURY.—In reference to this long-coveted boon for the borough of Finsbury, it is believed that the Government has at is Igth resolved on making the park. Mr. Lloyd, its projector, and to whose energy in promoting it its adoption by the Government is mainly due, -has been recently engaged at the office of the Woods and Forests in drawing up a report, embracing every important featur , of the plan, at the request of Lord John Russell. This report was forwarded by Lord Seymour to the Premier, by whom it was subsequently communicated to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It has since been returned, and full instructions given to the authorities at the office of the Woods and Forests to proceed forthwith in preparing plans and making the necessary surveys, it being intended that the project shall be carried wit without further delay. On Friday morning, Mr. Lloyd, accompanied by Mr. Penuethorne, and another gentleman from the office of Woods end Forests, with Mr. Burnett, the surveyor, went over the ground intended to form the site of the park, which they unanimously admitted to be the finest that could have beets chosen for that purpose. The spot selected is equidistant from Regent and Victoria Parks. It is proposed that one entrance shall be at Highbury-place, and that the park shall commence at Highbury crescent, passing along the right side of Holloway and Hornsey roads to the Seven Sisters-road, and (taking an easterly direction along this road until it joius the Green Lanes, and then proceeding south of these lanes) including all the space of fields to the west of Newington Green; afterwards inclining towards the New River, which it is proposed to cross north of the Horse Shoe, excluding the Birmingham Junction Railway, and extending to the bottom of Highbury-grove, where a second entrance may be formed, completing the enclosure; thus the park will be bounded by four roads without a public roal passing through it. An esplanade, fifteen feet wide, commencing at the bridge at the top of Portland place, New North-road, and continued until it reaches the Green Lanes, and through the park, is also one feature of the project, which includes numerous details of a character to render the park not merely a highly attractive resort, but an ornament to the metropolis and an honour to the borough. The park will cover an area of about 150 acres, and the estimated cost for the purchase of the freehold is 150,000/. It is stated that the new park will bear the name of Prince Albert.—Observer. THE PERSIAN AMBASSADOR is staying at Crawley'e Hotel, Albemarle-street, until a proper residence is selected and fitted up for the Persian embassy. Instructions were sent to Southampton from the Foreign Office, the Treasury, and the Board of Customs, to pay the Persian Ambassada all honours in that port, as soon as his arrival there was known in London. His Excellency, when he embarked on board the Euxine, at Constantinople, was escorted to the ship by all the most distinguished Persian merchants re4deEt In the Turkish capital. Previous to his embarkation the Persian flag-was sent on board the Euxine, a beautiful green embroidered one, the emblem on which was a lion with a sword in its mouth. This magnificent standard was flying on board the Euxine when she entered Southampton Water. His Excellency is a Mussulman, belonging to the great Mohammedan sect of All. He is remarkably strict in his religious observances. Every evening while on board the Euxine he prostrated himself and said prayers for about two hours. He had a number of ornaments in his possession adorned with jewels and precious stones. One of these ornaments contained an emerald as large as a small plumb. Most of these had been presented to him by the Shah of Persia to mark the favour and esteem of his Sovereign for him. Amongst the treasures he has brought to this country are some beautiful rugs and carpets. He has also presents for the Queen of England. Amongst his baggage were two immense trunks, filled with treasure, which he would not suffer to be placed with the ordinary baggage, He was three months travelling from Persia to England. He made a prolonged stay at Constantinople. About four years ago it appears an in came to this country as the representative, in some degree, of the Persian nation, but for some cause or other Le was not received, The political relations between this country and Persia have always been managed hitherto by Indirect means. Their arrangement and the settlement of commercial relations between England and Persia, on the part of the latter, by a duly accredited ambassador high in his Sovereign's favour, can scarcely fail to be of advantage to this country. Roallet d'Heric, , urt. the distinguished traveller, has brought from Abyssinia the root of the Cucumis Abyssinica, said to be possessed of the valuable property of curing hydrophobia in dogs. In presenting it to the Academy of Sciences. M. d'Hericourt stated that he had himself seen, in Abyssinia, several dogs in different stages of madness completely cured by having the powder of the root mixed with food. The communication was received with the liveliest interest, and experiments were ordered to be made. In the last sitting of the Academy, a Report was presented by the Director of the Veterinary School at Alfort, stating that he had tried the remedy on four mad dogs, but without the slightest success. He added, that fearing the roots might have lost their virtue, he procured one of a living plant from the Jardin des Plantes, but that it, too, was inefficacious. Further expr ments are, however, to be made, and more roots to be g.t from Abyssinia. There seems no reason why what it a remedy for a dreadful malady in Africa should not be a remedy for the same malady in Europe also.— Literarg Gazette. MOVABLE BRIDGE.—A very ingenious and simple mode of constructing bridges over wide ditches in marshy grazing lands, by which cattle and sheep from the common cannot cross and invade enclosed farms, has been invented by Mr. Mathew, of Wern, Carmarthenshire. They consist of poles, five inches square, and then sawn from corner to corner, ferming two triangular pieces. These are joined by a number of common iron butt hinges, according to their length, and a handle at each end to open them; thus, when open, one of these forme a safe and easy foot bridge, about fourteen inches wide, but when shut presents an angular projection, over which neither cattle nor sheep can pass; and, when shut, one rail forme a protection to the other from the effects of weather. Such a suggestion must prove valuable, particularly to fen farmers, and their evidently small cost mil probably cause their extensive introduction They can, of course, be a fixture, or easily removed. —Mining Journal,

Though three weeke only have elapsed since the Exhibition was first opened to the public on Saturdays at the reduced charge of half-a-crown, already the attendance that day has fallen nearly to the level at which it was during the latter period of the crown days. The number of vieieers on Saturday :ast was 14 903 only, as compared with 16,407 on the previous Saturday, and with 13,340 on the first day that the new tariff came into operation. A stroll through the Crystal Palace on Saturdays is now become a pelt:nee, acccnepati'd by very many agremens, and no longer the "toil of a pleasure" which it still continues to be on the shilling days. Go into the machine-rooms; navigate your way thence through the United States of America, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, France, and the colonies—prosecute your researches through the rich and varied productions of our own manufacturing industry, and the predominant feeling with which you are impressed is one of loneliness, though you are in the midst of the results of a refined and exalted state of civilisation and progress. Upon this body was to devolve the duties of framinig the rules for the guidance of the juries, to define the general prin- ciples upon which it would be advisable to conform in the award of the prizes, to see that the awards of the juries wvere made in accordance with the rules laid down, and to confirm such awards. article_text: THE ,GREAT EXHIBITION, Her 3lajesty the Queen visited the Exhibition on Wednesday morning shortly after 9 o'clock, and remained in the building for more than an hour. Her attention was chiefly confined to the Tunisian, Chinese, and Indian collections. From the improvement in the weather there was a large increase in the number of spectators during the day, and no less a sum than £l,BOO was taken at the different entrances. There must therefore have been, in addition to the vast number of season tickets, 7,200 persons who paid their ss. admission fee, It is estimated that the total amount netted was not much under 02,500. The proposed attempt to develope educational uses from the Exhibition is beginning to attract great attention, and already Professor Cowper, of King's College, has commenced a series of lectures to his class on the buildinc , and its contents, with a view to a systematic inspection of the whole display. The apartment for the display of products from the national manufactories of Sevres, the Gobelins, Aubusson, and Beauvais, is nearly completed, and will well repay a visit. Near it are a pair of bronze gates reduced from the original at the cathedral at Florence, and which, with a sideboard and bookcase on either side, must attract great attention. On the south side of the nave a splendid specimen of gold and silver work was for the first time uncovered. The design is a toilet-table and mirror, with basin, ewer, and dressing-room service complete, all executed in the precious metals, and finished in the highest style of art. The following incident is related as having occurred before her Majesty's arrival :—" Two persons, whose appearance indicated that they were not exactly of the class of three-guinea ticket-holders, were observed in the middle of the crowd in the transept, carefully scrutinising every one about them ; their conduct had so much that was suspicious about it that an active detective of the Birmingham police, who was present, and who had been watching them for nearly an hour, seeing that they took apparently little interest in the magnificent spectacle that was passing in their immediate neighbourhood, and that they looked harder than, in his opinion, honest men ought, at the watches and other trinkets so profusely displayed, advanced and took them into custody. The strangers turned out to be Frenchmen, but their explanations, whatever they were, being perfectly unintelligible to the Birmingham officer, he conducted them into one of the private offices of the building and searched them. It was satisfactorily ascertained, by documents found on them, that they were French police-officers, and a series of mutual explanations, if they may be so termed where neither understood the other, ensued. The strangers were readily satisfied, and the Birmingham detective got a practical lesson in the old Scotch proverb, that ' Hawks munna pick out hawks' een.' " The influx of visitors to the Exhibition, on Thursday, was greater than ever, and the sum taken at the doors could not have been much short of £2,000. This is of course entirely the proceeds of the ss. entrance fee, and does not include the large amount still accruing from the sale of season tickets. All connected with the undertaking are very naturally overjoyed with the success, in a financial point of view, which thus attends it, and which is manifested more and more decisively every day. The improvement in the weather has acted with magical effect upon the flow of visitors, and brought out the beauty and fashion of London into Hyde-park just as sunshine developes butterflies. They take possession of the Crystal Palace in a manner which must make the Royal Commission have sundry misgivings about their power to keep it in their own hands now, or to have it removed a few months hence. The Executive Committee continue to receive all kinds of applications front the country with reference to the terms of admission when the low prices commence. Among others, several clergymen have written to them offering to bring up with them all their parishioners in a body. Fox and Henderson are contemplating a grand entertainment of roast beef and plumpudding to be given by their foremen and chief workmen to the workmen of foreign countries in the building. A desire seems felt that every facility should be given to the industrial classes to see and enjoy the magnificent spectacle which their labour has created. The contractors for the catalogue are selling about 10,000 copies of the small catalogue per day—an enormous number when the bulk of the volume is remembered. As yet only one part of the larger work has appeared. A week has now passed since the opening, yet France is still far behindhand, and has many days more of preparation before her. In our own division of the building a few things are creeping into spots left unoccupied, or which at the last moment it was found impossible to complete in time. Among these was brought in and placed in the nave to-day a beautiful model, executed• by Mr. Deighton, of Great Collegestreet, Westminster, of the interior of her Majesty's Theatre. The decorations are all carefully represented, and to the multitudes who throng the centre of the Crystal Palace the work will convey a very accurate and pleasing idea of the extremely light and elegant yet rich style in which " Her Majesty" is fitted up. On Thursday a communication by the electric telegraph was completed between the Exhibition Building and Buckingham Palace, the Admiralty, and the Chief Police Station at Scotland-yard. The Crystal Palace was for a moment exposed to destruction by fire on Thursday. The flue attached to a gas stove in one of the offices of the contractors became heated, and ignited a piece of wood with bunting which rested upon or touched it. A piece of the burning cloth fell into a small open cask of Indian corn, which stood, as the Irish say, " convenient." All this mischief was brewing in secret in the southern part of the colonial collection on the east side. The drapery of the counter concealed what had happened, and it was only when the smoke began to break forth that an alarm was raised. Fortunately such casualties have been foreseen and amply provided for. There are no less than a dozen large fire-engines within the building, besides an ample supply of water easily obtainable, and a thoroughly organized force ready to act at a moment's notice. The fire was extinguished before it had time to do more than slightly char one plank of wood, and no anxiety need be caused by an occurrence so trifling. On Monday the building was thronged with visitors from the honr of opening till the gongs sounded at halfpast six in the evening. Some additional attractions were displayed to public view in the southern galleries, including a splendid counter of printed fabrics of all kinds, artistically grouped. Towards the eastern end of this gallery a huge stand, modestly veiled with green cloth, hiding painfully-accurate anotomical specimens in wax, excited general curiosity. Near this, the figure of a man, with a broken leg, scientifically strapped, was remarkable ; and a little further on, a man was busily employed throughout the day blowing a pair of bellows, to fill the sails of some model vessels, rigged with revolving masts. Late in the afternoon, Prince Albert, attended by three or four gentlemen, inspected some of the British compartments. In the British machinery department, crouds surrounded Applegarth's printing machine, which was working vigorously, and with 'great noise. Visitors should bear in mind that there is one entrance to the building exclusively devoted to pedestrians, and that by entering at this end they may avoid the unpleasant excitement of scrambling between rows of carriages. The public may also be reminded that on Saturdays the building is not accessible to visitors. On Saturday morning the Queen and Prince Albert, accompanied by their Royal guests, visited the Exhibition, and remained for nearly two hours. The illustrious party examined carefully the jewels belonging to the Queen of Spain, exhibited on the south side of the nave, in the French division. They also inspected the Swiss collection, and admired the fine display of artificial flowers contributed by Constantin. They paid a visit to the Sheffield Court, and minutely inspected Hoole's and Stewart and Smith's grates. In the section of woollen fabrics their attention was attracted to the specimens shown there of Huddersfield, Bradford, and Leeds manufactures. The collection of cottons and linens were also examined, and the Royal party took particular notice of Mercer's new patent method far increasing the brilliancy of colours, of Lydiard's chintzes, and of the contributions of Black, of Glasgow. During their stay they passed through the agricultural implement department, in which her Majesty seemed to be most interested by the display of churns and beehives. The royal party appeared highly delighted with their visit. At twelve o'clock the public were admitted to the building, and flowed in with such eagarness that in the course of the afternoon more than £l,BOO was taken at the d-nrs. The Duke of Wellington is a frequent visitor at the Exhibition. He was there on Saturday, and with Mrs. Fox, the wife of the contractor, on his AM, examined several of the departments. However crowded the spot may be where his grace makes his appearance, a space is immediately cleared for hlm, and, except the Queen herself, no royal personage could be treated with more distinction. The report of the King of Prussia being likely to visit the Exhibition, in London, is without foundation. The directors of the Atlas Insurance Compeny have given four days leave of absence to each of their officers, to enable them to see the Great Exhibition ; and the company will pay the cost of admission. Twelve thousand sparrows, a French paper gravely stated the other day, had been caught in Mr. Paxton's glass cag e ; and the water, added the editor, wag oozing throughthe . roof to such an extent that the workmen were obliged to pursue their labour in small boats. Several of the Glasgow teetotal bodies intend to charter a steamer, and keep it running all the summer, so that the passengers in each trip to the exhibition may use it as a sleeping place during their London visits, and sally forth every morning, like giants refreshed, after a night's repose on the bosom of the Thames. It is now stated that the " Chinese mandarin," who paid such special saluhtion to her Majesty at the opening of the Exhibition, and was so courteously received by all, was none other than the cook of the Chinese junk lying in the Thames, who had dressed himself up for the occasion 1 On Monday, the price of admission to the Crystal Palace fell from £1 to 55., and, in consequence, the receipts at the doors rose from £5OO to about £1,500 or £1,600. The sale of season tickets also, to use the language of the Stock Exchange, " continues active," and tb., total receipts of the Commission during the day considerably exceeded £2,000. Amongst the novelties in costume at the Exhibition, is a shoe which can be instantaneously converted from white to black satin; and also, in the same manner, a morning shoe of prunella or kid can be changed into a satin shoe for evening wear. There is also a lady's boot of peculiar construction, which, by naPlns of an artificial instep, gives grace to an ill-formed foot. It was noticed that in the " God save the Queen," as in the " Hallelujah Chorus," the tones of Lablache's voice were easily to be distinguished, as easily, indeed, in the vast structure of the Crystal Palace as in the smaller limits of the Opera House. It is likewise worthy of remark that the tones of the great organ were made sensible at a distance of 1,800 feet, or thrice the length of the longest cathedral. London out of doors exhibits many symptoms of expecting illustrious strangers. One of these symptoms i s the vastly increased prevalence in shop windows of the ' notification, "Id on parle Francais." Also on the outside and on the signs of eating houses, taverns, and other places of refection, the kind of cheer supplied within is frequently announced in French or other foreign language. " X X" has, in some instances, given place to " Double Biere." In the Crystal Palace foreign exhibitors have been equally complaisant in endeavouring to make the explanations inscribed on their productions intelligible to English readers, and not always with more success, as to accuracy, than the sign painters out of doors. Some portable steps for a library, made to shut up into a compact form, is explained in this style :—" One begs to exhibit this staircase after this manner. shut this staircase, One draws the rail A over downwards. One draws the arm B over upwards," &c. It must be observed, however, that although these directions are phrased in rather queer English, they are perfectly intelligible, which is more than can always be said of instructions in a purer idiom. It is an impression common with many persons familiar with the metropolis, that London is less thronged with busy crowds in its principal thoroughfares, and less enlivened with aristocratic and gay equipages in its fashionable squares and streets, than is usually the case at this season of the year. It may be that the regular habi. tues of the London season have, in a considerable proportion, deferred their coming till after the opening of the Exhibition ; and this supposition is confirmed by the very general prevalence of painters at work on houses at the West End, implying the expected advent of occupiers. It is also certain that the parliamentary business of the session has not been of such a nature as to bring up crowds of railway representatives, with i their numerous professional assistants, witnesses, &c., n the overwhelming rush of previous years. Then, as regards the influx of visitors to the Exhibition, the time has not yet arrived for the advent of The Million, who prudently wait for finer weather and for the period of the shilling admission to the Crystal Palace, which will commence on and after the close of next week.

The General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, has elicited an important declaration from Lord PALMERSTON, whom, at its yearly meeting in July, it memorialised on behalf of religious liberty in Roman Catholic countries abroad, especially the Papal States, Naples, and Austria. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The advent of the let of December, when the superintendence and control of the Crystal Palace is to revert to the contractors, seems to have a moat salutary effect in stimulating the muscular capabilities of the workmen employed in the remo'al of the goods. The exhibitors are informed in bills liberally posted through the building, that the aids heretofore so kindly provided by the commissioners fur the purpose of expediting the dissolving process can no longer be relied upon, as far as they are concerned; and that those whose goods continue iu the building after that date, must make their arrangements with the new autho• rities. It is felt, no doubt, by the foreign exhibitors that there would be great inconvenience and perhaps some uncertainty in having to act under an untried government. They have accordingly made great exertions within the last two days, and a larger area has been cleared during that time than on any previous occasion. The colossal cast of the hero of the crusades was yesterday taken to pieces. Some of the other artistic treasures in the foreign nave have been more kindly treated, but the preparations for their exile are quite at far advanced. The beautiful and spirited bronze statue of Libussa, the famous sorceress and queen of Bohemia, modelled by Schwanthalcr, has been considerately and emblematically covered over with the purest of white. Each day uow subtracts one or more well known work of art from the longing vision, that we should not be at all surprised if we had to record even before the let of December that not a vestige remained of this once glorious gallery of art. CESSATION OP MARRIAGES AT PARISH CHURCH OP LEloll.—Most of our readers are aware that some time ago the Vicar of Leigh instituted a number of obstacles in the hitherto smooth course of matrimony in Leigh. He will not marry any one who cannot say the catechism off very well, or who has not been confirmed, or become a re' ohm sammanicant. The result is, that marriages have Mina be solemnised at the ancient parish church. Them difficulties in the road to matrimony have turned antra to other channels. At the last meeting of the Maid of guardians the usual returns were read over, from which it appeared that not a single marriage had taken place at Leigh church during the quarter (June to Sept.)— an unparalleled circumstance in the history of Leigh. It appears that the marriages formerly solemnised at church are now taking place before the registrars, and at the various dissenting chapels licensed for the purpose. Belem the vicar's new arrangement nearly , 200 mamagea per am• num were solemnised at the parish church. l times now driven away to other places. Before the new tration Act a still greater number were solemnised at the parish church. At the last meeting of guardians no less than eighteen " askings" were read before the meeting by the superintendent registrar. TILE CANTERBURY ASSOCIATION.—Yesterday meeting of members and friends of this association took place at the offices, Adelphi-terrace, for the purpose of receiving information upon the subject of the settlement, and discussing such matters relative thereto as might be brought forward on the occasion. Mr. Selfe, one of the committee of management, occupied the chair, and observed that they were not in a position to communicate any particular news,but a large packet of documents had been received, which were now in the possession of a member of the committee, and would be brought forward on a future occasion. In answer to a question, the chairman said it was almost certain that Dr. Jackson would not return to New Zealand ; but he might observe, that no time would be lost in applying to the ecclesiastical authorities to appoint a new bishop, possessing those qualifications which were so much admired in Dr. Jeckson. The chairman then read the following extract from a letter which had been received from Dr. Jackson on the subject of the coleny : " I find that an impression has gained currency at ellington that I am, un the whole, disappointed with New Zealand. The origin of such a notion I am utterly at • loss to guess. On the contrary, I am daily more and more convinced that our j adopted country must become one of the most valuable dependencies of the British crown. I have now travelled some distance into the interior of this part of the country, in two directions ; while one cannot help being enchanted with its MagnifiCeat scenery of woodland, mountain, harbour, lake, and valley, one feels at every step its inferiority to the Canterbury plains in the agricultural and pastoral reserves, which are so necessary to the foundation of a great settlement. My communications with the best informed. persona lead me to expect a similar condition of the soil in New South Wales. I return to England with the most thorough conviction that Canterbury must become to New Zealand what New Zealand is to the Australasian Colonies. I shall feel obliged if you will kindly convey these my sentiments to the Society of Land Purchamrs." Some conversation having taken place, the business terminated. GREAT EXHIBITION. The Executive Committee have published the following directions for the removal of British articles not liable to Customs duties : 1. The removal of the articles will commence on Thursday the 16th of October, and the following are the rules which the Executive Committee have laid down with a view of promoting the security of goods, and affording the greatest convenience to the exhibitors. 2. The doors will be opened at 8 o'clock in the morning, when preparations for removal may be commenced. But in order that articles may not be improperly removed until it may be convenieut to the majority of Exhibitors to be present, no goods will be permitted to be taken out of the Building before 9 a.m., or after sunset, when the bells will be rung. 3. A permit to remove articles will be issued to every Exhibitor. This will admit himself or his agent and the requisite number of workmen, for which he must make arrangements with the district superintendent. It will be absolutely necessary that the Exhibitor or his agent attend irs person to admit his workmen. The permit will be dated, and the articles must be removed within the period entered on the permit, and through that exit door only which is marked on the permit. If owing to its bulk any article cannot be taken out by the exit door appointed, then the Exhibitor must obtain from the _district superintendent a special pass for the west door. 4. Every exhibitor, or his authorised agent, in taking out articles must fill up a receipt, and deliver the same to the officer on duty at the exit door. Forms of receipt will be given by the district superintendents. The permit must also be given up when the Exhibitor has removed his goods. - - ' 5. In order to provide as far as may be possible against confusion and accidents in the removal, in some cases a rotation will be established for the removal of each exhibitor's articles, and the permits to remove articles will be dated accordingly. If an exhibitor fail to remove his goods within the period assigned to him, his articles must remain until the turn for their removal again arrives. 6. Whatever aid the Executive Committee may be able to afford, is to be considered as auxiliary only to the arrangements made by the exhibitors themselves for the removal of their own articles, and the exhibitors or their agents should. therefore bring with them force sufficient to insure the security and safe and speedy removal of their goods. 7. Among so many thousand exhibitors, and so great a variety of articles, it will obviously be impossible to identify every labourer employed by exhibitors with the articles which he may claim to be employed in packing; and, although every care will be taken to prevent errors and losses, still it must be clearly understood that no responsibility for losses rests with the Royal Commissioners or Executive Committee; but that it rests entirely with the exhibitors themselves. The Executive Committee particularly recommend every exhibitor or his agent to attend as early as possible, and make due arrangements to insure the proper security and removal of his articles; and it is suggested that it will be prudent that at every important stall the exhibitor should appoint a trustworthy person always to remain in charge of his articles until they are finally removed. 8. The Executive Committee think it right to repeat, for the information of the exhibitors, the following decisions of Her Majesty's Commissioners (dated May, 1850) :- 13. " The Commissioners are prepared to take the greatest care in their power of all objects sent, but they are not prepared to incur a degree of responsibility unusual with regard to public exhibitions. For this reason it has been already stated, that exhibitors must be at the charge of insuring their own goods, and that the Commissioners cannot be responsible for losses which may be occasioned by fire, or anY other accident. They will spare no pains in making such police and other arrangements as may appear adequate for the protection of the Exhibition, and the security of the articles exhibited. They will, of course, give all the aid in their power for the legal prosecution of all persons guilty of robbery or wilful injury of any of the articles in the Exhibition, should such unfortunately occur in spite of the precautions which will be taken." 21. " Packing-cases in which articles are brought to the building must be removed at the cost of the agent or exhibitor, as soon as the goods are examined and deposited in the charge of the Commissioners." " All packing-cases, &c., must be removed by the Exhibitors, &c., as soon as they receive orders from the Executive Committee to do so. Packing-cases not removed within three days after notice by the Exhibitors or agents, will be sold by the Executive Committee, and the proceeds applied to the funds of the Exhibition." Due notice was accordingly given respecting all packing' cases which the Exhibitors neglected to take away before the opening, and consequently the Executive Committee did not undertake the charge of any packing-cases whatever. 9. The conveniences for packing in the building are limited, and can only be provided in certain parts of it, and if performed in the building, must entail delay, and all those casualties consequent on delay. Exhibitors are, therefore, particularly recommended in all cases, where it may be possible, to remove light and valuable articles without repacking them in the building. It is desirable , to prevent accidents, that all small glass-cases should be removed within the three first days, namely, 16th, 17th, and 18th October. 10. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Fears have been entertained by exhibitors that it will not be possible to keep the building of the Exhibition wvater-tight, in consequence ox its having been found that the rain comes through many parts of the roof. Such appre- bension we believe to be entirely without foundation ; and the roof is now being carefully gone over, the brolcen glass replaced, and any deficiencies in the glazing work made good. This was being proceeded with rapidly pre- vious to the commencement of the heavy rains, about a fortnight since, ekeus it was of necessity suspended. Those parts of the floorhig upon which the wet falls have been carefully marked, so that no difficulty what- ever weill exist, upon the cessation of the rain, in discovering the faulty parts of the building. Upwards of 8,000 packages have already been sent in ; and already. on the British side, the visitor may form a fair notion of the exceeding value and variety of the articles to be exhibited, The foreign countries still continue backward in their preparations, but the representatives of France and several other countries state that they are perfectly confident of being ready by the 1st of May. No intention what- ever is entertained by the Commissioners of postponing the opening beyond the 1st of May, and notices have been posted up in various portions of the building calling the attention of exhibitors to tise decision of the Commis- sioners that the Exhibition would open upon that day. A meeting of " American Contributors, Agents, and others, from the United States of America," was held on Wednesday at the Chapter Coffee-house, Paternoster row, in pursuance of an advertisement, in which it was stated that they were convened " on important business connected with the Exhibition ;" Mr St John, of New York, in the chair. Previous to the commencement of the business, an application was made by some reporters to be present. A discussion took place as to the pro- priety of their admission, when a resolution was agreed to that they would be allowed in the room on condition that their report should be subject to revision. This was, of course, refused, upon which some of the repre- sentatives of the daily press wvent away. At a subsequent period another reporter entered the room, but he was not allowed to take notes. The meeting proceeded to discuss a series of resolutions which had been pre pared at a previous meeting, held at the same place, on Saturday last, the purport of which was that they strongly opposed the appointment of the jurors to decide on the relative merits of the foreign contributions, also to the adjudication of the bronze medals as prizes by the royal commis- sioners, when awards of much greater value had been promised, which they considered not keeping faith with contributors; they also objected to the price of admission of three guineas for a season ticket. Strong observations were made in consequence of contributors being at the ex- pense of erecting their own " fittings." It was stated that English con- tributors were at the expense; but in answer, it was observed that the original understanding was that contributors should be at no expense. Another ground of complaint was in reference to the delay in affording protection to articles which required a patent, and upon this subject a resolution was agreed to, that a deputation be appointed to wait on Sir G. Grey, intimating to him that until some security be given to such contri- butions, no packages should be opened. It was alleged that the object of the delay in obtaining a law was a covenant not to take advantage of any new invention or original design. At the close of the proceediigs the reporter asked to look at the resolutions, but on a show of hands this was refused. The meeting then separated.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. EXHIBITION HONOURS AND REWARDS. Last Thursday the Queen held a Court and Privy Council at Windsor Castle. The chief business done was of a singu- larly holiday diameter, being a general interchange of civilities and honours on the close of the Great Exhibition. Lord Sey- mour, the First Commissioner of Woodsaud Forests, and Lord Granville, Vice-President of the Board of Trade, took their seats at the Privy Council, and are now members of her Majesty's .Cabinet— the fo-f»er, pc presume, for the nse of Hyde Park, for the iron rating, the 'carriageways, the slip of Rotten Row, the new lodges at Prince's Gate, vie temporary entrance near Hyde Park Corner, and the other conveniences so stingily pro- vided by the Woods and Forests during this wonderful season; and the latter for having been the chief working man among the Royal Commissioners, unwearied, decisive, affable, and wise. Her Majesty had the next turn, being presented by the East India Company, for her part m the Exhibiton, with the largest of the splendid pearl necklaces exhibited anions tbe Lahore jewels, and with a very choice and valuable selection from the other objects exhibited by the Company, embracing Dacca muslins, furniture, jewellery, silver lii agree work, jewelled agate caps, carpets, shawls, brocades — a meet offering to the Empress of Inde. Considering the grace which Her Majesty gave to the Exhibition by opening it in person, and the indefatigable attention she has given to it.haviug almost completed her daily inspection before many of her subjects were out of their bed- rooms, a few trinkets, the spoils of old Runjeet Siugh's Palace, and other trifles more peacefully acquired, were no extravagant reward. Then the two new Vice-chancellors received tlie houour of Knighthood. When Sir Richard Kindersley and Sir James Parker had stept aside, the designer, the consulting engineer, and die contractor of the Crystal Palace were presented to the Queen, and were severally made Sir Joseph Paxton, Sir William Cubitt, and Sir Charles Fox— names that will long be remembered in the annals of industry and peace. When the Court was over the Royal Commissioners for tho Exhibition held a meeting iv the Castle, when, as we are told, one of the subjects under discussion was the pecuniary rewards due to some of Uie Executive and the staff. Considering the brilliancy of the success and the greatness of the surplus, and considering how much the zeal and ability of a dozen picked men have contributed to that success and that surplus, we are sure that the public will not grudge " a good slice" in return for the time, tlie days and uights, the wear aud teur, the anxiety aud tlie an- noyances, suffered by the men who have done the work of the Exhibition. Sir Joseph Paxton, it is said, is to have £5,000 somewhere about 21 per cent, on the cost of the building as it stands— certainly not too much for oue of the newest and brightest ideas ever imagined by self-taught or professional architect. Ihe actiug members of the Executive Committee two of whom had a large share iv originating the Exhibition' will also be remunerated on a somewhat more moderate scale Thus ended the distribution of prizes at Windsor Castle which was never more worthily or gracefully employed. In about two months hence the Crystal Palace will be left alone in its glory, and wheu the public nre once more admitted within its spacious precincts, and have time to admire in its unadorned grandeur the gigantic shell of the Great Exhibition, we shall be surprised indeed if they allow it to be pulled down. The full effect of 18 acres of grouud under one roof, without v single partition wall, with the light of heaven penetrating every corner of it, unu the whole seeu at a glance, has never yet been thoroughly realized. If to that attraction the contractors add those of balls and promenades, the success that must be achieved thereby would tell powerfully upon the fate of tiie building when discussed in Parliament.— Times. Sr. PANCRAS, NIARYLEBONE, AND PADDINUTON FIDEEHOLD LAND ETY.—A crowded meeting of the friends and supporters of the freehold land movement assembled on Wednesday evening at the Temperance Hall, Somers-town, for the purpose of considering the enfranchisement of the working classes, and of explaining the working of the freehold laud societies, It. F. Brettingliam, Esq., in the chair. The chairman, in opening the business, remarked that the time had now arrived for the people to possess themselves of those rights and privileges to which they . were legitimately entitled. Every man ought to have a voice in returning members to parliament, but since, as a ' matter of fact, the law required a certain property qualification, the Freehol I Land Society, at a cost of ono shilling weekly, secured to the subscribers the neci.eisery possession to entitle its members to a county vote. Mr. Spong, the secretary, entered into a statistical account of the working of the above society since its formation up to the present time. It appeared that upwards of 1,600 members had been enrolled, and that 2,200 shares had been taken ; five purchases of land had been made, two of which had been allotted, and the society were about concluding another purchase, which would be divided into 600 more allotments. Thus the benefit of cooperation was clearly shown, and the ultimate success of the society was established beyond doubt.—Mr. Mortimore 'f impson moved a resolution, affirming that the St. Pancras, Marylebone, and Paddington Freehold Land Society offers advantages moral, political, and pecuniary. —Mr. Howley, in seconding the resolution, entered into some interesting details of the movement generally. One of the primary objects of this society was to help men to help themselves The rules were drawn up by working men to suit the of those in their own class, and the whole management was open to the inspection of every member. The demonstrative year of 1851 was a proud one for the working classes, who had shown themselves not only a credit to themselves, but an ornament to society. The resolution was unanimously agreed to.—Mr. Whyman moved a resolution to the effect that the principles of the Freehold Land Society wero the :most efficient for extending the franchise, and for improving the social and domestic comfort of the working classes, and enabling them to become county electors. As a mere pecuniary investment these societies were superior to say other, they yielded seven per cent. upon the best possible security. A subscribed caoital of 800,0001. would give in ten years four millions of allotments, and as man_ county votes ; supposing these allotments to be let at 21. per annum each this would yield a net annual rental of 8,000,0001. ; this would produce labour to the benefit of the community.—Mr. Deane seconded the resolutien, and urged Om necessity of an immediate reform in the representative system. It was monstrous that in Hampshire eight out of every nine adult men were disfranchised; iu Berkshire the proportion was seven out of eight; and in Surrey, out of a population of 154,000 there were only 9,000 electors, thus fifteen-sixteenths of the men of Surrey were deprived of the franchise.—The resolution having been unanimously carried, several new members were enrolled, and, after the usual compliment to the chairman, the meeting broke up. The success of last week's experiment has encouraged the managers of the Literary Institution, in John-street, Fitzroy-square, to afford their subscribers and the public another intellectual treat. Mrs. Dexter last night re-appeared upon their boards in trowsers, to advocate the universal abolition of petticoats—in her own words, "to deliver an address to the women of London in favour of the Reformed Dress movement." The attendance was numerous, as might have been expected, and this time there was no escaping the twopences. Men were placed inside and outside the door to regulate the admittance, and, thanks to this double sentry insisting on the fee, A great sum must have been collected for the advancement of science before the pioneer of female progress commenced her exhortation to the fair sex. By that time the hall and galleries were crowded, principally of course, with men ; on the platform, however, were a party of women, almost persuaded perhaps, but still adhering to the costume of their mothers ; and even amongst the general audience not a few females were to be seen. Bloomerism bad evidently excited curiosity if it had not made converts. Mrs. Dexter, of course, illustrated her doctrines by presenting herself to her audience in the apparel, which, if she accomplishes her mission, all ladies are henceforth to wear. We have already done our bast to describe it. The material is black satin ; the peculiarity, trowsers ; the general effect, something between the popular notion of Turkish and the minortheatrical conception of a page clothed as these young gentlemen were et an indefinite period during tho middle or " dark" ages. As to the lecture, it " well alone," being simply a repetition of that given last week, with a few amplifications and additions arising out of subsequent events. Lord Shaftesbury, toe, who at Mrs. Chisholm'a group meeting of colonists did unfortunately introduce the topic of Bloomerism, in pursuit of a new figure of speech, was copiously quoted ; and, in a parenthesis, female emigrants were especially recommended not to import the error of drapery into the countries they intended to colonise. There remained still one subject to be treated—the opinions of the press. Upon what Thackeray calls " The Corporation of the Goosequill" Mrs. Dexter was rather severe. She did not complain of its reports,which, though necessarily abbreviated, were, on the whole, fair, whilst as to its praise or censures she was Equally indifferent. She had defined the secret of editorial silence—wise oblivion. " The conductors of the press did not yet know what might be the feeling of the British public ; therefore they were afraid of committing themselves." It is only candid to state that this solution was perfectly satisfactory to the audience, they could conceive no reason why, when the author of " Sartor Resortus" is treated so respectfully, a more practical exponent of the philosophy of clothes should not, as soon as recognized, become the common topio of leading articles. Literature, we confess, is convicted of neglect of Mrs. Dexter. Her condemnation of temporising journalism waiting for the suffrage oe the people was received by an enlightened audience, members of a scientific institution, with roars of approbation. Ought we to apologise ? Like all practised orators, Mrs. Dexter drew up at a climax. Placing upon her head a hat similar in style to those usually worn by the Adelphi haymakers, with just enough veil upon it to hide no part of her face, she bowed gracefully to the public, and retired in the very midst of the thunders of applause which a respectful but determined defiance of everybody, coupled with a promise of consistency in the advocacy and perseverance in the wearing of trowsers, had been the very natural and efficient means of producing.—Morning Paper. I THE GREAT EXHIBITION. I Her Majesty arrived' for her almost daily visit to the Crystal Palace, at a quarter past nine yesterday morn- ing. The royal party consisted of the Queen, Prince Albert, the King of the Belgians, and the Princess Char- lotte, attended by the usual suite. Mr. Wentworth Dilke, Col. Reid, and Mr. Cole accompanied the illustrious visitors through the building. The Austrian sculpture- room was first inspected, after which her Majesty and friends proceeded to' the collection of English marbles, which were subjected to a lengthened examination; Bell's ",Babes in the Wood," and Gibson's "Hunter" receiving warm commendation. The party thenpromenadedthrough the fine arts room, and after a glance at the Mexican figures, went on to the foreign nave, where the beautiful Mosaic, newly placed there by Lord Foley, was eagerly examined and much admired. This picture, which is a very large specimen of the art, representing the ruins of Poestum, has all the variety of light and shade which one would expect in a finished oil painting, with the brilliancy of colour which is peculiar to the material employed. It was surrounded by crowds of visitors during the day, and much admired. Her Majesty's next visit was to the Eng- lish glass and china, after which the royal party descended to the nave; where the company were drawn up as on her Majesty's previous visit, in double file, and greeted their Sovereign'with loyal respect andcourtesy as she passed out of the building. AU cheering wa s suppressed from feelings of respect, but her Majesty's gracious acknowledgments of the loyalty of her reception were universally and deeply appreciated. The number of visitors was not much greater than on the previous day, and consequently there was free circulation throughout the building. Among the novelties, all of which, by the way, make their appearance in the foreign nave, are' some sets of china of 'novel pattern from Dresden. They consist of tea services with elaborate pat- terns in high rplief, birds, flowers, some beautiful flower- baskets, &e.,and have great originalitytorecommend them. There is also a handsome b Ureau in tortoiseshell, inlaid in brass, whith shows great skill and delicacy of workmanship. There were a great many foreigners among the company, among whom were several German peasants. The resem- blance of these elder Saxons 19 our own people was very striking, indeed so close was it, that until they spoke one would have guessed them for Rent or Sussex folk. A great number of these homely guests collected round the apiaries at the extreme end of the gallery, and took much interest in the movements of the inmates. The bees are now in fill work, the young ones building the combs and the old ones istoring the honey, for which detachments rush out into the park. every five minutes. The whole operation may be seen through the glass case, and forms certainly not the least interesting of the innumerable wonders of the Exhibition. There are two or three exhibitors of these very curious little palaces of industry whose names are very legibly painted over each hive. They have been frequently visited by her Majesty and Prince Albert. The various fountains were in active requi- sition, and, towards the close of the day, exhibited a peculi- arity which would be well worthy of investigation by the commissioners of water supply. Any one mingling at that hour-with the crowds by which they are surrounded, could not fail to detect a strong odour of brandy, and seeing that spirits are so strictly prohibited in the Crystal Palace, there must be some extraordinary quality in the sources of supply to give rise to so curious a delusion. The number of petty thefts in the Crystal Palace seem rather on the increase, and demand increased vigilance on. the part of the police. Another amateur collector was detected yesterday pocket- ing cigars in the Zollverein section. On his apprehension he stated himself to be a gentleman's servant in Bedford- shire, and urged a curious taste in his smoking as his ex- cuse. He was immediately despatehed to reason the matter over with the magistrate. Besides watching the thieves the police have also a good deal of trouble with lost articles. Upwards of a hundred articles have already accumu- lated at the station, for which no owners can be found, and people are constantly coming, in with parasols, brace- lets, and other articles (chiefly female property), which they have found in the course of their perambulations. It is noticed that very little is lost or found on Friday or Satur- day. One of the most extraordinary metamorphoses is the change that has come over the Koh-i-noor diamond. The doubts that have been thrown upon its value and its authenticity, and the difficulty of fully appreciating its brilliancy in the broad glare of day, have led to the enveloping of the cage and its contents in massive folds of crimson drapery, and showing its splendour by artificial light. The diamond has stood the test wonderfully, and has fully redeemed its character. Like other beauties who show best by candle light, the sparkling prismatic hues of the gem are now fully displayed, and even connoisseurs are ready to admit that the Koh-i-noor is no humbug. The difficulty of obtaining access to the cavern in which it is enshrined is little less than those encountered by Aladdin in his visit to the garden of diamonds, and has revived all the attractions and fascinations of this famous gem. People who have seen it a hundred times now stand patiently in the crowd assembled round the dark narrow entrance. You pass in singly—the cage, with the exception of about an eighth of its circumference, is enveloped in thick folds of cloth; half a dezen jets of gas are arranged behind it, and the light from these is again reflected by more than a dozen small mirrors upon the diamond. After all the trouble the arrangers of this theatrical display have taken, we would suggest to them to go one step further, and conceal the light of the gas from the eye of the spectator. The effect will then be perfect. With regard to this gem, which public report had magnified into some most extraordinary dimensions previously to its exhibition, it is said that its original value was estimated at 3,500,0001., but in consequence of the unskilfulness with which it was cut by the Venetian lapidary, Hortensee Borghese, in whose hands it was placed, it was reduced in weight from 800 carats to 279. It is at present unshapely, and to give it a perfect form it would require still further reduction. The history of the Koh-i-noor has been traced back to a vary remote period. It passed, through the treachery of the minister of one of the last of the Mogul princes, into the hands of the Persian conqueror, Nadir Shah, who was invited to Delhi, and who, in consequence of some real or pretended opposition received by his troops, gave orders for the plunder of the city of Delhi, which had then an immense population, and was said to be the richest city in the world, and to contain 2000 palaces. The work of plunder lasted 20 days, and the great Koh-i-noor, among other treasures, amounting to upwards of 40,000,000/. sterling, fell into the hands of the conqueror. Although he was adored by his army, Nadir Shah was asseesinated by one of his followers, and the great diamond disappeared for some time, until Ahmed Shah united the whole of Afighanistan into one kingdom, made incursions into Persia, and, becoming possessed of the great diamond, again restored it to India. Shah Soojah, one of the descendants of this monarch, had for his vizier one of the brothers Barakzye, of whom becoming jealous, he put out his eyes. The other brothers took up arms, and expelled him from the throne, and compelled him to take refuge at a frontier station of the British, 12 miles from the Sutlej. He carried a part of his treasures with him, and ultimately accepted the invitation of Runjeet Singh, who promised to aid him in the recovery of his dominions, and proceeded to his c eurt ; and that astute prince, working partly on his fears and partly on his hopes, obtained possession of the wonderful gem. Shah Soojah was il:timately restored by the British arms, contrary to the advice of Captain Burnes, who recommended that the pretensions of Dost Mahomed, as being the most popular and the next lineal descendant, should be supported. This was Shah Soojah's fourth restoration, but it was ineffectual, The army was excited, and rose against him because his restoration had been effected through the hated agency of the Christians, and he was murdered. Ihe last scene in the strange eventful history of the great Indian diamond was enacted at Lahore, where, amongst other treasures, it fell into the hands of the British, and was considered a fitting gift from the wealthiest and mast powerful company in the world to the greatest monarch of modern times. It will require some such convulsion as was conceived in the addled brain of the New York editor to effect a change in its future and, we trust, more peaceful destinies. The two golden hands that slightly clasp its extreme points, and present it in gorgeous relief on the deep purple velvet ground, are indicative of the graceful and delicate fingers which now hold it, while the massive and impenetrable safe by which it i surrounded illustrates the moral and material power which defies the assaults of all enemies, and secures it more effectually than the triple ramparts of Lahore. One of the peculiarities of Mr. - Chubb's wonderful safe is said to be that the moment the surrounding glass shade is touched, the diamond, like a sensitive plant, shrinks from the too near approach of a profane hand, and descends into its adamantine fastness. The conventional value of these gems is well illustrated by a story told, if we remember aright, by Clapperton, who in one of his exploratory journeys into the interior of Africa was informed by a native king of a diamond of immense value which he possessed, and which he, after much solicitation, was induced to allow the traveller to behold. The diamond was brought out in due state on a magnificent velvet cushion with embroidered canopy and cover, as the vulgar eye was not permitted to look upon it; and all the usual formalities and ceremonies having been, gorse through the cover was taken off, and Captain Clapperton saw what turned out to be the common glass pendant of a chandelier, with the hole through which the brass wire had been Passed! Now the Mollalis or priests having denounced the Europeans as being enemies of the state, Clapperton had the tact to perceive at once the danger of undeceiving the King, so he looked reverently on while the pseudo diamond was restored to the safe custody of a king's guard, leaving the monarch in the blissful state of ignorance that made him as happy as if he possessed the real "mountain of light." The model house for the labouring classes erected by his Royal Highness Prince Albert at the Cavalry Barracks, Hyde park, has often been referred to in connection with the Exhibition. The sub- iect is one of great importance, and a visit to the building, which is new completed, will be found very instructive. It is a good workcing model,; not a mere prettiness expensively got up and inapplicable to practice, but a sincere, honest, and sensible attempt to supply a design for the style of architecture suitable to the labouring classes and within their means to command and pay for. It is adapted for the occupation of four fialllilies of the class of manufacturing or mecia- nical operatives residing in town or near it. Each tenement is arranged on precisely the same plan, having a well-lighted lobby or porch, a living room, a scullery, a wvater-closet, and three sleeping apartments, all simply but effectually provided with convenient fittings for domes- tic comfort. The separation of the sexes and of parent and child is complete. Closets, dust-bins, sinks, safes, shelves, &c. are included in the plan. The ventilation is carefully attended to, and, above all, the water-supply is not neglected. Let any one who wishes to understand, in its true significance, the importance of that movement for improv- ing the condition of the labouring classes over which Prince Albert so appropriately presides, after paying a visit to the model houses at the Knightsbridge barracks, go direct to Carrier street, or Church lanie, or Kennedy court, St Giles's, and lie will learn an instructive lesson from the contrast thus presented to him. He vill be moved with compassion at the spectacle of such squalid misery, and wvith gratitude that at the Great Exhibition of the world's industry the hard lot of those who toil in the lowest grades of labour is not forgotten.
