I' THE CREAT.. .EXHIBITION | Another week has passed, during which, with the ex- ception of Monday afternoon, we heve had glorious weather for sight-seeers, and still the' exhibition is not 'finished, the workmen being as! actively engaged in the Freech, Russian, Persian, and one or two other depart- ments, as ever. Not that we would hfave it understood that no progress has been wade during the past week in filling up the .Wrld's Show; far from it, there is scarcely a department belonging to every.country, that does not appear to have added to its treasures since we last came before the public. The East India Company have, in addition to the Lahore jeivels, unveiled to view the " Durria-i Noor," or sea of light diamond; set in an armiet, with ten smaller stones around it -an attraction which fairly divides attention with the " Kor-i-Noor"- in addition to an immense collection of other goods. The French exhibitors appear to have' doubled their stores ; the Russians begin to show that their collection, when completed, will, for beauty and taste, vie with that of many of their neighbours, and the riches of Persia can be somewhat indistinctly seen, although as yet they wait arrangement. Yet time passes on, and the " shil- ling" days will be here before the exhibition can be said to be completed, and then we may expeft to see the in- dustrioas artisan; with his family, thronging those courts and avenues which have hitherto presented an almost.ex'. clusively aristocratic appearance, the Fridays 'and Shtur- days being set apart for those who, eschewing crowds, wish to examine the exhibition with greater attention, and in more select society. We are glad to obseive that the interest in the exhi ?? tion appears to increase, rather than diminish, something, like 14,000 having been taken at ?? for single admissions during the week, in addition tq some 2,000 or 3,000 for season tickets, the demaud- foi which still continues. 'Daring the week the Royal Commissioners have conceded an extra hour to the public 'to view the collection, the exhioition being now open until seven o'clock in the evening, and'we doubt not that, as the season advances, a still later hour will even be fixed upon. The continued interest which her Majesty and his Royal Highness Prince Albert take in the Exhibitionis shown by the fact that they have again visited it three times, accom- panied by their Royal visitors. First, on Saturday, when they principally directed their attention to the beautiful jetwels of the Queen of Spain, exhibited in the French department; the artificial flowers of' Constantine, in the Swiss department; and the products of Sheffield, Hud- dersfield', Bradford, Leeds, Glasgow; in the British department. Secondly, on Wednesday, Iarriving as early as nine o'clock in the morning, when they con- fined their attention almost exclusively to the British portion of the Exhibition in inspecting the leather and paper goods, and in promenaditig the fine arts court; and thirdly, on Friday, when she also visited the British department. Her Majesty, with her visitors, remained upon each occasion about two hours, being compelled to leave on Friday, we regret to say, from the pressure of the company. upon her steps. Perhaps the most noticeable feature of the week, however, is -the supposed robbery from the American department, notwithstanding all the vigilance, Iwhich appears ,to be observed, of a detached'breecher rifle pistol, with stock to form a gun, exhibited by the inventor, Mr.D.W. Wisson, of Hertford, Connecticut. lI e' have used the term sup- posed robbery,'because'nobody appears to know when the pistol could have disappeared, the last time any one can recollect, positively'to have. seeu it being the day on which her Majesty opeied the Exhibition,' and, therefore, we are in hopes'that it is only mislaid, not lost. Having thus briefly adverted to the general events of the week, we will now ask our readers to take our arm, and accompany us in our Walks through thei E daibition, in which'we will briefly remark, upon the more striking objects which -meet our view, confining-our attention upon the present occasion to, ' WaMk inthe tTranlsept. which w e will enterthrough the South, ?? door. p11pbh'payp iig our -money a nd passing the turn. stile, the first thing that meets our;view~ s ia park-gate6, bronzed and.. gilt, from the minufactory of M essrs.Cot- tam and Hallen of Winsloow-street,:Oxford-street, ight, elegant, and tasteful. -Passing this gate, we enter the transept, and find ourselves in the trarisept;' houbded on the right by Tunis and China, and on the left by the agricultural avenue, and India, which for the present we pass unnoticed. Here it is that the collection of statues, fountains, shrubs, evergreens,' &c., first meet the astonished view of the beholder, and make him almost fancy that he is in fairyland-an idea which is somewhat strengthened by the number of "dark-eyed houris," "children of earth with golden hair," and other beau- teous forms flitting before him, or taking their rest amidst the treasures of art by which they are surrounded; this being the principal " trysting" place in the exhi- bition, and the seats for those who are tired being more plentifully disposed here than in any other part of the building. Having somewhat recovered from our surprise, we will, kind reader, look around us ; and now let us call your attention to a tastefully arranged parterre by Messrs. Knight and Perry, exotic nurserymen, of Chelsea, in which you will find beautifully arranged the sweet bay, from the North of Africa; the long.leaved hereptuastus, from Domingo; the variegated croton, from the East Indies, with a variety of rhododendrons, azalias, &C., too numerous to mention, though they never fail to attract a large share of attention from our female com- panions, among whom we reckon a considerable portion of our readers. Well, kind reader, having passed this parterre, we will, with your permission, refer to the other contents of the transept. We wonder not that your attention has been excited by Thorneycroft's statue of her Majesty, on her favourite charger, Hammon, for a more wretched caricature of the human form divine, or the equine animal, it has not been our lot for a long time to witness. Her Majesty's-we beg pardon, this mis- representative of her Majesty's-figure is bad in the ex- treme-her attitude unnatural-and her horse one of the sorriest we have seen' for a long time. Well, it is your wish before we examine the other objects in the transept we should first dispose of the statuary. Be it so. We need not spare much time upon the equestrian statues of her Majesty and Prince Albert you see before you, by Wyatt, designed, we are told, to be executed in bronze. We trust to Heaven they never will, for they give us no other idea than that of her Majesty and her Royal Con- sort seated upon two of Batty's horses, and decorated in meretricious tawdry to take part in an Astley's pageant, unless we caa be brought to suppose, which no stretch of imagination can yet lead us to, that it is her Majesty's intention hereafter to go down, to open' Parliament in state, similar to that of Margaret of Valois, or some such theatrical Princess, on horseback always wearing a crown or tiara on her head, and carrying her sceptre in her hand to encumber' her in her movements. Thorneycroft's idea is better, if his execution is worse. We do not wish it to be understood, however, that the transeet does not present us with some beautiful specimens of sculpture, and those of a high order. If you have formed that opinion, kind reader, you have mistaken us, and we will disabuse it, by pointing your attention to a colossal group of Virginius and his daughter, in marble, by M'Dowall; where the Roman father has just killed his daughter to save her honour. The expression of Virginius is noble-manly; and that of the dead girl, almost falling from her father's arms, touchingly pathetic. This is, indeed, a gem of price, and makes us feel with pride that genius is not dead among Britons. Then, again, the Eve of the same artist is touchingly simple and innocent in expiession. The only other specimens of statuary in the iransept to which we will call attention is a model of Jacob and Rachael, by Earle, in which the expression of confiding love in the girl's face, irrespective. of the other merits of the composition, is deserving of all' praise; a manly statue of flampden, whose memory all Englishmen must revere, by Foley; Prometheus, beauti- 'fully executed in 'marble, by Theed; a marble group of an episode' in the wars between the Argonaiuts and- the mazons; a statue of Lord Falkiind, by Bell-a fit cornpanion to the Hampden of Foley; and Alfred the Great, encouraged to iearnidg byhismother, by Thorney- craft, which shows that this artst can do something better than his equestrian statues. . Having done with the statuary, ee need not trouble ourselves with tbe collection of palms, azalias, and other plants, with which the transeptisliberallyenriched;'albeit, they add much to the beauty of the scene. But we will request our readers to look at, and we are sure they will admire, the large fountain in 'cut'crystal glass, exhibited by the Messrs. Osler, of Oxford street.- Situated. in the very centre of the transept, this fountain is visible from every part of the exhibition, and forms one of the most prominent features in it, being twenty-seven feet high, and said to contain nearly four tons of glass, A short distancebehind this fountain, we find an hydraulic ram, exhibited by Freeman, Rowe, and Hanson, of the Strand, which throws the water through a small pipe, no bigger than a gas pipe, some thirty feet high, and which is in connexion with a fountain emitting innumerable jets of water 'from flowers, &c., well suited. to a gentleman's garden. Thereis also a fountain, exhibited by the Coal- brook-dale Iron Company, of cast iron, bronzed, which is seven feet wide, and stands eight feet high, of Cupid and the Swan. The jet issues from the mouth of the Swan, which, in the arms of Cupid, forms the centre of a tazza, decorated by white and yellow water lilies. This fountain' well deserves attention, and but for its proximity to the chef d'uevre of the Messrs. Osler, would doubtless command it. There is nothing more, dear reader, in the transept to which we need direct your attention, except- ing some exquisite cases of stuffed birds, from Newcastle, in which the hooded falcon, and the struggle with 'the Iquarry, cannot fail 'to interest all who have heard of the ancient English sport called falconry; and another set of gates, somewhat'similar, though upon the whole more 'elaborate than those' at the south end of the transept, we having now arrived at the north end, by the Coal- dbrook/dale Iron'Company. They 'consist of two principal gates. and 'to''sidet gates, hung on iron pillars of a peculiarly light construction,.. surmounted with lamps, and which would form an' ornament to any park or court yard. RAILWAYS AND TlHE EXwrar3TioN.-One of the most wonderful facts of the Exhibition is the mode in which its visitors came to it. How did they all get there 1 The total number of visits was 0,201,856, and supposing that on the average each person went twice, there were more -than three million visitors. The arrivals from the con- tinent during the whole period of the Exhibition did not exceed, it is said, 70,000; and it is also said that there were not more than 4,000 names entered on the American visitors' book; but of our own people a very fair propor.. tion came from the manufacturing districts in the midland and northern counties, and other still more distant parts of the empire. Now, how did they come ? Had it been proposed thirty years ago, or even twenty-five years ago, to get up an Exhibition in London, on the speculation that three million persons would come up to it, and half a million of money would be taken at the doors, the most practical men of the day would have laughed the propo- sition to scorn. It is evident then, that the Exhibition *ould have been impossible in those days; and Prince Albert, Mr. Cole, Mr. Paxton, and Messrs. Fox and Hen- dersen would have been thought very proper subjects for Bedlam.-Next to the Exhibition itself, and the numbers brought to it by the railways, the most striking fact of the year is the extraordinary profit that has flowed into their exhausted exchequers. Prior to the opening of the Exhibition the increase in the traffic of the eight metro- politan lines over the corresponding period of last year amounted to £166,037, ori 05 per cent. The increase in the other lines of railway in the United Kingdom up to that date amounted to £305,904, or 14 39 per cent. During the 23 weeks of the Exhibition a very great change tools place in these proportions, for, instead of the traffic on the metropolitan lines being only 9 per cent., as at the com- inencement of the Exhibition, it gradually rose to 28 per cent., while the traffic on the other lines of the United Kingdom, which was 14.39 at the commencement, gradu- ally receded to 8.42 per cent. The total increase on the railways of the United Kingdom for the 17 weeks ending May 3, amounted to £461,041, and for the 23 weeks end- ing October 11, to £1,107,180; of which £821,863 was the increase on the metropolitan lines, leaving but £285,317 for the increase on the other lines. Had the rate of increase during the first 17 weeks of the year con- tinued during the 23 weeks of the Exhibition, the increase for that period would have been £264,380, which, deducted from £821,863, the actual increase, as above stated, leaves £557,483 as the extra receipts from the Exhibition as compared with those of the corresponding period of 1850. It thus appears that immense as have been the receipts of the Exhibition itself, the receipts of the eight metropolitan lines from the same source have been greater. Nay, it is evident that it would have answered their purpose to de- fray all the expenses of the Exhibition, and band over the whole of the £505,000 received for admission, &c., to the Royal Commissioners, to be applied as they please. If this suggestion is too late for this year, it is in tood tirme for another, and for many more yet to come. Notwithstand- ing the great reduction of fares made by all the railways to meet the general class of visitors, that reduction may be carried still further, or rather the accommodation given for the same fares may be greatly increased, and yet have a handsome profit to the companies. Further, we beg to suggest, whether it will not answer the purpose of the me- tropolitan railways to contribrte towards maintaining periodical and even permanent attractions of some sort; such, forexample, as would beimplied in the notion of awin- tergarden used occasionally forentertahiments and exhibi- tions. Of course it would be ridiculous to expect that so great an occasion as that we have witnessed could besustain- ed; but something on a less scale, and varying from year to year, might answel the purpose. The total increase of £821,863 for the twenty-three weeks ending October 11 is divided among the metropolitan lines in the following ?? Eastern Counties, £18,150; Great Western, £162,723; Great Northern, £176.537; London and North-Western, £259,010; London and Blacliwall, £7,249; London, Brighton, and South-Coast, £29,631; South-Western, £87,068; S. Eastern, £81,596. Though a considerable part of this increase has been absorbed in additional expenses, still there can he no doubt that the railways have received the lion's share of the profits. Nor has the Exhibition traffic been accompanied with a positive loss of traffic in other directions, except in a few special instances. The aggregate traffic of all the rail- ways of the United Kingdom, from January 1 to October 11, is greater than that for the same period of last year by no less an amount than £1,581,604, and nearly three millions greater than that for the same period of 1849. l To what extent the expenditure of the Exhibition visitors has been withdrawn from other objects it is difficult to say; but it is certain, from the returns of the Board of Traile and the Revenue Tables, that the general con- sunmption. of imports and exciseable articles has beeit greater than usual this year. It is also satisfactory to Know, as we are informed from various quarters, that the money spent on the Exhibition by its provincial visitors has been generally rather saved beforehand than borrowed at the time, so that we need not apprehend a reaction such as usually follows an improvident expenditure.- Times.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday there was a very considerable falling off in the numbers that visited the building, the police returns giving 52,879 as the total, while the receipts at the doors amounted to 2,4691. I6s. The excessive heat of the weather is probably the cause, for there is no reason to believe that the Crystal Palace is as yet losing its attraetiveness with the masses. By a constant use of hand watering•carts and cans, and by removing the glass partitions at the eastern and western ends, the interior was kept pretty cool throughout the day, and the temperature must have been considerably lower than it was outside. A good deal, however, still remains to be done in the way of ventilation, and it is satisfactory to find that the Management are 'taking vigorous steps to insure the comfort of their visiters during these veritable dog-days. They intend to open up large spaces for the admission of fresh air both below and in the galleries. The inte riot was exceedingly cool and agreeable during the day, and there would no doubt have been a larger attendance but for the showers that fell during the morning and the afternoon. A accident occurred near the east entrance of the building. The heavy rain which fell in the morn. ing caused a branch of one of the large trees there to give way, and descending upon a boy who had taken refuge beneath it for shelter, it killed him on the spot. Every day the assemblage wears a more countryfied aspect, and is more popular in its character, so that the falling off in the attendance is less easy to account for. Until now the weather might have been pointed to as the eause, , but the decline is so steady that even this explanation ceases to be satisfactory. Perhaps, after all, the multitude have found out that there are limits to the numbers which the Crystal Palace can accommodate with comfort, so as to see properly its varied wonders. The presence of charity children still continues to form an agreeable feature of each day's incidents. The girls of St. Olave's school were enabled to 4o there by the liberality of Mr. Ex-Sheriff Pitcher, and the trustees of the Broad-street Ward School also treated their scholars to an inspection of the interior. THE GREAT EXHIBITION AND THE SYMPOSIUM. A grand banquet and file , to do honour to the exhibitors of all nations, took place last evening at the Symposium. The arrangements were carried out in Soyer's best style, which is saying for it all that language could say. Nearly 300 sat down to a most recherche dinner, in that gorgeous salon, the Baronial-hall. G. Thompson, Esq., M.P., presided. The vice-chair was filled, in the absence of Mr. Scholefield, by Hercules Ellis, Esq , barrister. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were proposed by the Hon. Chairman with his usual eloquence and good taste, and enthusiastically responded to by the meeting. " The exhibitors at the National Exhibition," the great toast of the evening, drew forth thunders of applause ; as well as the toast which followed, proposed in very appropriate and eloquent terms by the vice-chairman—" The Artisans by whose skill the object of the exhibition was carried out." Mr. Miller, to whom the company were much indebted, in a most happy and well-merited strain of eulogy proposed " The Chairman's " health. We understand the beautiful card of admission, which attracted so much attention and admiration, was designed by Mr. Miller. After some other toasts, amongst which was that of " The Vice. Chairman," the company left the brilliant hall for a more brilliant scene still—a display of fireworks in the beautiful grounds, of unequalled magnificence. The Prince of Epicureans excelled himself on this great occasion, and well merits the thanks of the committee and the support of the public. We believe this is a practice not hitherto adopted at these establishments. FATAL Accinvir.—An accident attended with the loss of seven lives, occurred on Monday last on the river Tyne. A steam-boat from Newcastle to Marsden Rock, on a pleasure trip, stopped at Howden to take in passengers. A sculler boat put off with seventeen or eighteen passengers on board, and had scarcely got twenty yards from the shore when it was driven by the tide athwart two vessels lying in the stream of the ebbing tide, when it was upset, and the whole of the passengers immersed in the water. Assistance was difficult to render, and seven perished, the others having been rescued with great difficulty. The boat was overcrowded, but great want of management and precaution is attributed to the boatmen. The seven drowned were all young women, f r om twelve to twenty-one years of age. Immediately after the accident the steam-boat, which had before been sailing down the stream with banners flying, lowered its colours and did not proceed further. Only one body had been recovered up to Monday evening. EASY COMMUNICATION QITII ENGLAND. The Chester and Holyhead Railway Company is increasing, we perceive, the facilities of communication between Ireland and England. The booking though and return-ticket system now extends not only to Dublin, but many of our most important towns have been brought within its operation. Among these are Cork, Limerick, Kilkenny, Ballinasloe, Athlone, Mullingar, Belfast, Newry, and Dundalk. Passengers can book, by one payment, either for the single or double journey, between any of these towns and London, Birmingham, 111anchester, Liverpool, or Chester. Return tickets to or from London and any other station are available for fourteen days; between stations, for seven days. It is difficult to over-estimate the convenience which this system confers on the travelling public.—Dublin Daily Express. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Friday, August 15, the receipts amounted to 20511. 7sN, and the number of visitors was 20,859. Among them came a party of four Iroquois Indians, who, besides inspecting the interior of the Building, had a " palaver" with the Executive Committee, and were less reserved and more sensible than from American romance might have been expected. They expressed great astonishment, not at the Koh-i-ncor itself, but at its value, and the whoop which they raised when Mr. Catlin, their guide, told them this, for a moment suggested misgivings for the safety of the policemen who guards the treasure. The machinery in motion also produced a strong impression upon these wild men of the woods, and when one of the selfaoting " mules" was suddenly arrested in its course, " the maniton" or " great spirit" was the cause. Their " palaver" with the Executive related, we hear, to some things which they had brought over with them from the other side of "the Salt Lake," and which they wished admitted into the Exhibition. FINAL CLOSING OF THE EXHIBITION. A full meeting of the Royal Commissioners, at which Prince Albert, Lord John Russell, and Lord Granville were present, was held at the Building on Tuesday, when it was decided to close the Exhibition to the public on Saturday the 11th of October. It is the intention of the Commissioners to hold a meeting in the building on Wednesday the 15th of October, at twelve o'clock, to receive the report of the several juries, and to take leave of the foreign commissioners. On this occasion they intend to request the presence of the exhibitors, the jurors, the foreign and local commissioners, and the members of the local committees. Immediately after the close of their pro- ceedings, permission will be given to the exhibitors to remove their goods, subject to such regulations as may be made by the Executive Committee. The reports of the juries, and the names of the persons to whom prizes shall have been awarded, will afterwards be published in the London Gazette. It is the desire of the Royal Commissioners not only to present medals to the individuals to whom the juries may have awarded them, but to mark their sense of the great exertions of all the exhibitors, and also of the jurors, the foreign and local commissioners, the chairmen, treasurers, and secretaries of local committees, and other persons who have rendered ser- vices in promoting the Exhibition, and to present them with a permanent memorial of the undertaking, by distributing medals to each, accompanied by a certificate and a copy of the reports of the juries. The three medals, of which the designs were originally approved, are intended to be applied as follows :-That by Mr. Leonard Wyon will be distributed to the prizemen selected by the juries; that by M. Bonnardel will be given in certain cases recommended by the council of chairmen, not as a mark of excellence in degree on the part of those who receive it, but for reasons which the council of chairmen have been requested to state specially in their reports ; the medal designed by Mr. Adams will be given to the jurors. In addition to these medals the Commissioners propose to cause two other medals to be struck, which will be presented respectively to the exhibitors, and to those who have rendered other services to the Exhibition. The great number of the medals, books, and certificates which will thus be presented, obviously renders the distri- bution of them on a single occasion a physical impossibility. On the other hand, the Commissioners feel that it would be invidious to select any persons to receive their medals at one time, and to omit others. And further, it is clearly desirable that the medals, the certificates, and the reports, should be presented simultaneously, and the length of time which must necessarily elapse before the whole of them can be prepared makes it difficult to fix any precise day on which the distri- bution could be effected. Under these circumstances the Royal Commissioners have come to the conclusion that it will be most desirable to fix a limited period within which each individual may make such arrangements for receiving medals, books, and certificates from the Commission, as may best suit his personal convenience. Due notice will be given on this point as soon as the Commissioners are able to fix a time for the distribution to commence. Following up our notice of the display of English and foreign crystal in the Exhibition, we may appropriately refer to the varied and beautiful collection of porcelain under its numerous types of Pekin, China, Dresden, and Sevres porcelain, English table and ornamental china, pottery and cameo ware. The great elegance and variety which distinguishes the English collection in the north-west gallery near the transept, has been achieved during the last 10 or 12 years, and the progress must be c onsi d ere d li t tl e l ess t h an met - venous to teose who recollect the enormous prices paid for the quaint and inelegant but rare and highly pr zed specimens of Oriental china paraded in hign festivals and state occasions by our thrifty ancestors. When we take into consideration the high antiquity of the potter's art, we have certainly no right to pride ourselves upon the advances that had been made in this departmenteof manufacture up to the beginning of the present century. The first attempts at the finer descriptions of pottery are ascribed to the Arabians, who introduced the art the south of Spain in the ninth century. From thenem it passed into the island of Majorca, and in the fourteenth century Majolica ware , as it was termed by the Italians, was highly prized, and sold at enormous prices. The first specimens of Eastern china were brought to Europe by the Portuguese, and were then only to be found in the cabinets of the curious or on the tables of princes. Most of them were drinking cups or vases, and from that circumstance arose the name "porcelain," from porcellana, the Portuguese for a cup. In the early history of many of our manufactures we are met by constantly recurring evidences of the real antiquity of what are set down as modern di.coveries. Little figures, covered with a fine deep blue glaze, found deposited in the Eg3ptian mummies, prove that the making of porcelain was known to these singular people some thousauds of }ears ago, end a chemical analysis of the colouring matter leaves no doubt that it is oxyde of cebalt, one of the most recent and important of the discoveries of modern times, and which has given a wonderful impetus to the manufacture of the finer , descriptions of porcelain. The establishment of this maeufacture in Saxony was the result of accident. Baron de Botticher, a German alchemist, while prosecuting experiments in search of the philosopher's stone, observed that some of his crucibles assumed, by being subjected to intense heat, all the characteristics of Oriental porcelain. The importance of the discovery became at once apparent to him, and he established a manufactory, but with the usual jealousy of the times the processes employed in these Dresden works were veiled in impenetrable mystery, while the profit to the fortunate discoverer rendered porcelain making the true philosopher's stone. In the middle of the sixteenth century we meet with the first mention of the white faience, or earthenware, as having been introduced into France by Bernhard de Palizzy, and from that country it was hareduced into Holland, but the manufacture there was only a rude and coarse imitation. In the French department there is a large-sized statue of this Bernhard de ralizzy, who, in the face of incredible difficulties and privations, persevered with his experiments, burning even the timber of his garden and the wood work of his house to feed his furnaces until he succeeded. In the seventeenth century, Burslem, in Staffordshire, became the nucleus of the large industrial community now engaged in the manufacture of pottery and porcelain in the district to which it has given a name. A space of six miles broad, by eight miles long, is completely covered with the pottery works, and between 60,000 and 70,000 persons are constantly employed. Even in the time of Queen Elizabeth, the only articles manufactured in earthenware were beer mugs and drinking cups of coarse material, covered with a brown glaze. Some specimens of thee which were exhibited in the medimval collection of the Society of Arts attracted mach attention, and there are one or two of these curiosities of manufacture to be found in the collection in Hyde Park. The first improvements introduced in the manufacture of poitery were by two brothers named Elers, irons Nuremberg, who, in 1690, effected a kind of glazing by means of salt. They were persecuted and actuilly driven from the country oo the absurd plea that the fumes of the works were injurious to the public health, and the prosecutor was the very individual who availed himself of their discovery and carried it out. The shapes of the vessels manufactured by these artists were also a decided improvement upon the more ancient specimens, and might in some instances be said to be almost graceful and classic. They also shod traces of moulding, and, in one instance, probably the result of accident, a vitrified colour is observable. The specimens still preserved resemble the ordinary terracotta, but somewhat better fired. The history of the early manufacture in this country contains the usual proportions of prejudice and accident. The discovery of another improvement in the firing of the vessels V. as surreptitiously filched from the inventor, an individual named Astbury having feigned himself to be of weak intellect, and in that way obtained a Knowledge of their secret. Astbury then introduced flint es a component part of porcelain, thus alike improving its appearance and sul:stance, and its use was also the result of accident. He saw an ostler at a country inn calcine flint and reduce it to a fine powder, to blow into the eye ot a horse labouring under a disease of that organ, and he conceived the idea of using it in the manufactu e of earthenware. Little more than a century ago, the PCre Eutre- Icolles, a Fiench Jesuit missionary, contrived to procure the two ingredients used in China in the manufectuse of the porcelain of thet country, and sent them over to Europe. In 1754, the first porcelain manufactory was established in this country at Derby, by Mr. Duesbury, and a dozen years later Wedgwood, introduced it into Staffordshire, where his fertile and scientific mind speedily effected the most marked and decided improvements in the art. To him we are certainly indebted for infusing into it some portion of the artistic spirit so prominent in the labours of the ancient potter, and in this menufactory was first developed in its full power and vigour the geeius of John fo,axman, whose resplendent light may still be traced animating the living sculptors of our land. Wedgwood was undoubtedly the true orisinator of ceramic art manufacture—the man of taste and the man of science are alike his debtors, and the chief excellencies of the advanced and matured specimens of the present day are his. Until the time of Wedgwood it was impossible to produce a hard, dense, durable material, with a brilliant and permanent glaze, capable of sustaining sudden transitions of temperature. To him may also be attributed the terracotta, which could be made to resemble porphyry, granite, or Egyptian pebble; a black porcelain, bard and vitrified, with the property of taking a high polish, and of sustaining a degree of heat equal to the natural basalt; the white porcelain biscuit, applied by him to the making of ornaments and statuettesf and jasper ware, a hardened substance, capable of being readily coloured by the admixture of metallic oxidee. This peculiar property, which it shares with no other p rcelain or earthenware body of ancient or modern composition, renders it applicable in a pleasing manner to the production of cameos, portraits, &c. Of this singular material are formed copies of the Barberini Vase, and other fac-similes of ancient art, which have received no small share of public , admiration, these unique and costly articles being thus multiplied through his instrumentality. Mr. Wedgwood paid 400/. to the workmen who modelled the Barberiui Vase. Another of his wonderful discoveries was what is known to chemists and scientific men under the name of " 'Wedgwood ware," from its power of resisting acids and corrosive substances generally, and although it bears only a remote reference to a sketch of porcelain and china ware, it is one of his most interesting and valuable discoveries, and formed an 1 important era in the history of the progress of a manufacture now become of so rouch commercial as well as domestic importance, while the who:e of his long and useful career has been a stimulus and a guide to those who have succeeded him. It was, however, many years after the time of Wedg-1 wood, before the knowledge of chemistry, and the discovery of the colouring properties of metallic oxidi s, enabled the manufacturers of Staffordshire and Worcestershiee to produce those beautiful specimens in burnished gold and brilliant colours which now enable them to compete with the wondrous prielucts of the manufactories of Sevree, Dresden, &c. In this disposition there is one great fault-viz. that those stops which, in our English organs, are three and two feet in pitch-or otherwise called " twelfth" and " fifteentth"-are omitted as single stops, and put into the furniture of five ranks, all of which must be drawn together. By this injudicious arrangement it is impossible to produce that agreeable sparkle which can only he derived from a two-feet stop, in conjunction with all the various pitches below-ntamely, four, eight, and sixteen ; neither can there be any augmentation of power above the principal without drawing the far- niture, which, as we have before said, is equal to five stops. Next to this we must draw the reeds, which, by being "1 voiced" upon a heavy pressure of air, are peculiarly loud-so loud, indeed, that they completely change the essential character of the organ to an vchostra composed of trombones and trumpets, nor one with plenty of strings and a proper amount of wind. Thus, in our opinion, the French taste (if this in- strument really represents it) in the construction of the tone of an organ is highly injudicious. More power is required than diapasons of eight feet and principals of four feet to cope with such power- fal reed work, and one-half the amsount of furni- ture would be sufficient for an organ twice the size. The flute work in this instrument, though of small scale, is well-finished; and looking at this organ in another point of view-namely, in its workmanship and materials-it presents a striking contrast to the generality of English organs. There is much oak used in its machinery, and a general neatness prevails in its arrangement. Some of the attachments are, iow- ever, upon an old-and we hope, now in England, obsolete-plan. We refer to the bent wire passing through a hole, used in place of a tapped wire, with what is technically called a button screwed on. The quality of metal used for the front pipes is, we should think, tin alloyed with about six or eight lbs. of lead to the cwt., and these pipes are excellently made; the internal pipes are apparently made of metal of about the same quality as that used by our own builders. The pneumatic lever- a machine for lightening the touch, invented in 1832 by Barker, a native of Northampton-is also used in this instrument for the great organ macsual. M. Ducroquet states that this power is but little known in England. We wvill, therefore, describe it as clearly and intelligibly as we are able-though at the same time we must, in justice to our own builders, state that M. Ducroquet is evidently wrong in his opinion, as we find the machine in question more extensively applied in the great organ by Willis than it has ever been in France ; and as it was brought to perfection in England by an English- man, we cannot see how M. Ducroquet can main- tain his position, The pneumatic lever is an intermediate power between the keys and the valves, necessary to over- come the resistance offered by the pressure of air upon the surface of the valve, or rather the aper- ture which it covers. i As no great inconvenience i3 ever felt by the opening of a small valve, the key is made to act upon one of sufficient size to admit compressed air into a small bellows, which thereby becomes infleted ; and if the superficial surface of this bellows is greater than that of the valves, with sufficient addition to overcome the resistance offered by friction, the action of the pallets is the immediate and inevitable consequence. There is, therefore, no difficulty in opening any number of valves by the action of one small pallet, but there is difficulty in exhausting the air contained in the small bellowsathat performs the work; this is, how- ever, accomplished in two ways-either by opening a still smaller valve than the one which admitted the air, or by the closing or returning of the move- menc. This valve may be either outside or within the machine. Mr. Barker, in the French organ, adopts the former plan, which requires a spring of sufficient strength to keep it sound while the bellows remains inflated. Mr. Willis, in the construction of his levers, we believe, adopts the latter plan for the swell. We think, however, that it is bad, in con- sequence of the rising key having to overcome the resistance of the pressure of air upon this cmall valve, ' thereby producing an unpleasant and difficult touch. In order to overcome this difficulty, Mr. Willis has made an improvement in the exhausting valve which appears to us of the greatest importance, in- asmuch as a more ample valve for the purpose of exhausting the bellows is contrived, and the resist- ance offered by the pressure of air is entirely over- come. The end is simply attained by opposing one surface to another; the valve (which is extremely light) opens with the greatest conceivable facility; thus a complete reiteration is produced, and, at the same time, that agreeable resistance offered to the finger in a small organ with a good touch, is re- tained. The effect of this improvement may be seen in Willis's great organ, which instrument is easily entered ; and we are much indebted to the ' acilities offeted us by Mr. Willis for obtaining the necessary information upon this remarkable power, which, like the hydraulic press, appears capable of producing almost any amount of effect. The mechanical arrangement of placing the couplers upon the pneumatic lever, as in the French organ, is very neat, as the player thereby feels no augmentation of weight on the touch. All octave couplers, either above or below, are decidedly bad, because the effect in either case must fall an octave short of the real compass. Besides, the grave octave coupler for the bass will continually be producing such effects as the following :-Suppose the chord of A to be held, and if, dating from the first space in the bass, as is most likely, a fifth or third above is held with it, the lowest note heard will be either Csharp orE, and thus the music becomes altered to a chord of the sixth, or one of the fourth and sixth, In the acute octave coupler we continuallylose the effeet, in consequence of the passages running into the apper octave, though it is not so likely to be felt in an organ that goes up to C ; but as there is no great advantage derived from putting such couplers into the organ, why make the instrument imper- feet by doing so ? All this is, however, done in the French organ. IUpon the whole, we do not consider the mecha- nical skill displayed in this organ, and its musical construction, well brought together. As this instrument is devoid of all mechanical novelty, except the concave surface of its pedal board-which would be a fault rather than an im- provement, if applied to an organ possessing a swell, or composition pedals-we have but little to say with respect to it. The organist will find, upon referring to Bach and Mendelssohn, that their works are expressly written for instrumenti of this design, though the compass of the pedals is not sufficiently extensive. There are some good points in the tone of this organ, which will, no doubt, be appreciated; but, as a whole, it is very harsh, noisy, and chippy, and that peculiar effect is observed which is derived from over-blowing a pipe, particularly in its gamba. In respect of quality of workmanship and mechanical design, this organ shows no attempt at excellence. The simplicity of its machinery is obtained at the expense of its tuneable capabilities. It is well known to organ-builders that pipes below a certain note have a sympathy with each other (unless re- moved to intervals of a whole tone), producing what are technically called " drawings." The plan of blowing first into a reservoir from the feeders is decidedly good, but the conistruction of the whole instrument, and particularly as regards its movements and attachments, appears exceed- ingly toy-like. In every possible way cheapness is the mark aimed at, but not judiciously. In the Italian department there is a very com- pact, and somewhat ingenious, little charnber-organ. It consists of one row of keys, and an octave of pedals. Its stops are a claribella, with closed hass, mixture, and trumpet, and one pedal pipe, formed in the stool upon which the player sits to perform. This pipe is made to speak the whole oc- tave by opening valves like flute-keys, and which produce the saine effect. In tone the organ has no claim to excellence, as may be supposed from the stops that it contains, though in appearance it is very elegant. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty and Prince A:bort visited the model cottages erected by his Royal Highness in Hyde Park, at an early hour on Saturday morning. They arrived at the cottages at a quarter before nine o'clock, and the Queen spent upwards of half an hour in examining the various ingenious exhibited for economising space and fuel, and for securing efficient ventilation. The Earl of Shaftesbury, whose benevolent and philanthropic 'exertions in behalf of the humbler classes is well known, was in attendauce to explain the principles upon which the buildings were constructed. Mr. Roberts was also present, and Mr. Wentworth Diike represented the Royal commissioners. Her Majesty and the Prince then crossed the carriage drive and entered the Crystal Palacenby one of the exit doors opposite the model cottages, and proceeded up the nave to the Spitalfields gallery, in which the satins, silks, velvets, and other costly fabrics are exhibited. All the exhibitors had been previously warned of the intends d honour, and were present to afford any explanations that might be required. Mr. J. Lavanchy had the honour of submitting to her Majesty and the Prince specimens of Spitalfields silks made upwards of one hundred years ago, in the year 1745. The silk was manufactured by James Lemun, of the city of London, and designed by John Van Sommer, a Dutch artist. Amongst the specimens were a pattern of the silk made for Queen Caroline, wife of George 11., and some for court dresses, worked in gold and silver, the whole of which are of the most perfect make, of beautiful colour, and elegant designs. The Royal visitors then passed on to the lace department, examining the peculiarities of the iloniten, point, and other hand-made laces, and also the machine made lace of bobbin net, the coarser descriptions of which are now manufactured so cheaply as to be extee sively used for window curtains and hangings. The mode of manufacture was explaiued to her Majesty by the Mayor of Nottingham and other exhibitors present. The Queen then passed through the jewellery and gold and silver plate department, all the exhibitors being here also in attendance. The extensive purchases recently made in gold and silver plate by Prince Henry of the Netherlands, Prince Demidoff, the Pacha of Egypt, and other distinguished penonages, were pointed out to the Queen, who has been a very extensive purchaser herself in various parts of the Exhibition rince its opening. Some jealousy, however, having been created by the ticketing of articles marked as sold to her Majssty the executive committee have directed the removal of all the labels. We understand that public entertainments in connection with the exhibition are in contemplation in Norwich, Nottingham, and others of our large manufacturing towns. Mr. Paxton will be honoured with a public entertainment at Derby on the 4th of next month, and a fete upon a magnificent scale, to which all the foreign exhibitors ' &c., will he invited, is in contemplation by the Botanical Seciety. The building was by no means crowded on Saturday, and the visitors had ample space for promenading, although the heat in the afternoou was rather oppressive, the thermometer reaching close to 80 degrees. Continuing our notice of the agricultural implements, we find that meny of the steam-engines have received prizes from the Agricultural Society, and from local societies. Some of them exhibit great economy of space and power. The moveable engines are all mounted on travelling wheels, and are nearly all different in construction. The principal points to be sought for in a steam-engine are, that its effective power shall bear as high a relation as possible to its absolute power; (simplicity of construction by reducing unnecessary friction gives this); that the fullest effect shall be given to the combustion of the fuel used, so that the largest amount of power may be obtained, the largest quantity of water evaporated: this is none by surrounding the fire with the boiler, by increasing the heating surface by means of placing tubes through the boiler, and by coating its exterior with felt or wood to prevent loss of heat by radiation; that the strength of all its parts should harmonise; that they should be easily accessible for the purpose of cleaning or repairing, and that the engine should be made as light as possible consistent with a due regard to 'strength and durability. These engines are all on the non-condensing or highpressure syttem. The boilers are tubular, similar to the railway locomotives, mounted on four wheels, and not too heevy for the draught of two horses. In the threshing-machines exhibited the principle of ; action is nearly the same in all—the grain is brought into contact with a drum which is driven by multiplying wheels at a high velocity. A pair of feeding rollers are attached between which the corn passes to the drum. Straw-shakers are attached to most, as a considerable per-centage of grain gets mixed with the straw and is carried away. Clayton, Sentrieseortla and ia an caceilont spec:rnen of tho threshieg-tnechine in its most improved form. The great quantity of pulse, or colder, which drops through the bars of the straw-shaker, has long been considered very objectionable, inasmuch as it increases considerably the amount of labour in the barn, both at the time of threshing and also when going through the dreeting-machiue. On Saturday morning, pursuant to invitation, the Royal Commissioners and Executive Committee of the Great Exhibition of 1851, with many distinguished foreigners, arrived in Liverpool, on the invitation of William Brown, Esq., the popular member for South Lancashire, for the purpose of accepting that gentleman 's hospitality on board the magnificent steam-ship Atlantic,—a floating palace of the New World, most appropriately selected by Mr. Brown to receive as guests the assembled elite of the Old World. Besides the noblemen and gentlemen more immediately connected with the Exhibition, including the representatives of all nations, all the distinguished foreigners in England holding official situations were invited, together with the Lord Lieutenant and High Sheriff, the Mayors of the various towns of Lancashire, and select personal friends. The London and North- Western Railway Company placed a special train, free of charge to the foreign visitors, at the disposal of the invited guests, the Royal Commissiomers and other English gentlemen paying excursion fares; but it was stated that even the fares of the foreign visitors Mr. Brown had himself agreed to defray. At ten o'clock a numerous company assembled on the landing-stage at St. George's Pier, where a steamer, specially engaged for the occasion, received the guests for an excursion on the Mersey. After some little delay the company were taken on board the America (Captain Neil Shannon), British and North American Royal Mail steamer, which had just before left her moorings to proceed en her outward voyage to New York. Here they were received with the utmost cordiality by Charles M'lver, Eq., the agent for the British line of mails, assisted by Mr. Fowler, the respected manager of that house. After minutely inspecting the transhipment of the mails from the Satellite tender to the America, the distinguished company returned on board their excursion boat, when a parting salute was fired from the America, and he stood out gallantly to sea. The commissioners were next conducted to Birkenhead and Woodside, and had an opportunity of viewing the evolutions of many of the splendid yachts engaged in tee race of the Royal Mersey Yacht Club. The wind blew almost a gale, yet the weather overhead wee remarkably fine, and nothing could exceed the delightful trip that this excursion afforded. Alboni, after a two years' absence in Madrid and France, made her re • entree on Saturday night. What better character could be selected for this interesting occasion than the Cenerentola, in which this fascinating syren has been in former seasons so triumphantly successful! She was received with the applause commensurate with her reputation, and no one ever enjoyed the puV.ic favour more unequivocally than herself. It will gratify her admirers to be told that she has lost none of her personal characteristics; her figure being as comfortably round as it ever was, and her countenance as declaratory of simplicity and goodness. Best of all her voice retains all its original beauty; and it was a delight not easily to be measured to hear once again those pearly notes, which can scarcely le said to have their equal in ringing sympathetic loveliness. Every one remembers the exquisite way in which this gifted vocalist executes the pretty melodies of the Cenerentola. Indeed, how can such things be forgotten? Alboni never sang them more ravishingly than on Saturday night, and when we say this, we exhaust all ordinary terms of praise. In the highest graces of style and finish this accomplished artist may, with but an exception or two, be pronounced unrivalled. We have taste the most delicate, as well as that supreme condition of art when all apparent effort is thoroughly and completely subdued. Although she perform exploits which few besides herself would be capable of achieving, the hearer is less astonished than pleased, less impressed with the precision of the mechanism than with the voluptuous and playful lightness of the expression. Were we called upon to point to any public singer in whom vocal elegance was strongly and instructively visible, would be to Alboni, who betrays the utmost excellence of practical cultivation, and who, without the slightest tincture of affectation "enchants the ear" simply by the purity and amiability of her method. It is not unworthy of remark, as being a singular feature in the maritime history of Great Britain, thatwhilst during a period of war vast improvements were being made in its military service, very little was effected for its navy Until after the Treaty of Peace. It was not until a general pacification in 1814 bad freed Europe from a severe and terrible military struggle, that Sir Robert Seppings, then Surveyor of the Navy, brought forward his improved method of naval construction The lower parts of the frames of ships of war were then for the first time filled in, and no longer afforded interstices for the accumulation of dirt and putrid water; and the frame timbefs of the bottom presented a compact mass of wood from the keel up to about the light water-line. Besides this great improvement, the whole fabric was further strengthened by means of a system of diagonal trussing, which, together with the solid bottom, opposed such resist- ance to the forces due to the weight of the hull and its con- tents acting downward, and to the forces due to the displace- ?? or pressure of the water acting upward, as effectually to prevent the keel from shortening, and consequently the ship from hogging or breaking down in the direction of her length, as it was liable to (1o formerly, or otherwise yield- ing to the forces of pressure under sail, or those of pitching and rolling in a tempestuous sea. In addition to these first great steps in the progress of ship-l;uilding, the upper parts of men-of-war were much improved in form and strength; the :stern, instead of re- maining open to the fire of an enemy, has been more strongly built, in a semicircular or rather elliptical shape, better fitted for defence in every direction. The upper decks have also been enlarged, andpace gained for work- ing the guns. Tho building of ships of war has been further improved in many ways which cannot be explained here. More so- lidity has been obtained by greater precision in joining the various masses of wood constituting the ship. By such means the working of the timbers in a heavy sea is greatly prevented; and both solidity and greater durability are obtained. Instead of firing the great guns by the same mechanism as old muskets, caps and hammers have been adapted to them. Advantages of still higher importancehave been ob- tained by the introduction of guns of very large calibre, mainly due to General Paixhans, which were introduced nearly twenty years ago, and called canons d la Paikkans. At first very few such guns were placed in each ship; but now we find complete batteries of 68-pounders, the effect of which cannot fail to be tremendous. The combination of large masts have been tendered more economical, easy, and solid, by the employment of coaks or cylinders of hard wood, inserted one-half of their length into each of the pieces of the masts, brought into contact. Sir W. Symonds, who succeeded Sir Robert Seppings in 1832, as surveyor of the navy, turned his attention toward an improved form for ships of war, and designed them of such figure and dimensions as to require very little ballast; this he in great measure accomplished by a considerable increase of the breadth. This system had many advan- tages; it gave greater stability, and in sharp ships more space below for stowage, besides a larger field or deck for working the guns; and although many talented naval constructors and officers considered this form uufa- vourable to an easy motion at sea, and liable to distress the spars; we have, nevertheless, great cause to be thank- ful to this talented and meritorious officer for his laudable and unwearied endeavours to improve the construction of ships of war.. We are further indebted to Mr. J. Scott Russell, the dis- tinguished Secretary of the Royal Commission, for a series of valuable experiments and researches on the form of least resistance at high velocity; this form being determined by examining the form of waves produced by drawing vessels through a canal at different degrees of speed. Further ex- periments are being made by this gentleman in the applioa- tion of his deductions to sea-going ships, and he has our best wishes for their ultimate success. The theory of stability, so important to the navy, and which we considered in a geometrical point of view, has been examined, both successfully and in 'niousy, by the Rev. H. Mosely, the Pre?sident of Jury e u y The stowage of ships has been much improved of late years, both in the form and disposal of stores; thus water- casks are replaced, at the suggestion of General Bentham, by iron tanks. The cubic or prismatie form of these tanks insures a great economy of space ns compared with the cylindrical form of casks; they also preserve the water perfectly pure, during long voyages; casks, on the con- trary, have the soluble part of their wood dissolved by the water, causing putridity, which produces various diseases, especially in hot climates. Equally important with the improvements in keeping water free from taint, must be considered the modes in- vented by M. Appert for preserving all kinds of meat. The preservation of gunpowder free from humidity, so necessary for ships of war, is now rendered perfect by the employment of hermetically sealed metallic eases, or wood cases with metallic lining; an improvement due to the Bri. tish navy. In the French navy great improvements have been made by separating passages for the conveyance of cartridges from the magazine up to the various batteries of the ship. These arrangements were particularly remarked by the English during the visit to the French fleet at Cherbourg in 1850. We now come to a series of improvements of the highest importance to the safety of ships. The hemp cables formerly employed were very objectionable, being liable to rapid de- cay, particularly in hot climates. When the anchor was east on a rocky bottom, the cable was frequently cut by the rocks, and very often parted, so that the ship was greatly endangered. A captain of the British navy (Sir Samuel Brown), in- troduced cables made of iron links, so arranged as to be easily worked. These chaia-cables are now in general use, not only in ships of war, but also in the commercial ship- ping 01 every maritime nation. We should have been happy if so vast an improvement had been recent enough to have received the highest of our awards, as being one of the greatest effected for the shipping interests and the preservation of life and property. The first method for stopping iron cables is due to the English; the last and best belongs to the captain of the French frigate Legof A high encomium is due to M. Barbotin, capitaine de refreec in the French service, for lhaving devised the means by which the chain-cable can be worked on the capstan. The various links as they succeed each other fall into grooves, on the periphery of a large polygonal prism forming the body of the capstan. When the capstan is put in motion, the links of the chain- cable have in succession half their thickness lodged in these grooves, and successively disengage themselves with mathe- matical precision. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The building was by no means so crowded or so hot on Tuesday as it was on Monday. This was so far fortunate, as the supply of water was rather limited, the glass fountain in the transept, Forster's patent filter fountain, and the Acis and Galatea fountain being hors de combat; and hundreds who were not aware of the taps laid on in the side avenues wandered disconsolately up and down gin and brandy having lost their attractions in the dearth of the purer element. The visitors who have lately formed the main body of the sight-seers in the Crystal Palace have apparently come armed at all points, and prepared to stand a siege in the way of provisions, and the receipts in the refreshment departments during the last fortnight have fallen off materially. The speculations as to the closing of the Exhibition are now beginning to assume something of form, and we believe if the votes of the exhibitors were taken 19 out of 20 would vote for its being closed at the end of the present month. It is quite pitiable to see some of those who have been condemned to dark corners and back slums sit moping and sighing day after day in the most melancholy mood, bearing all the brunt while others reap all the profit. The foreign exhibitors, when a balance is struck, will, we have no doubt, be found to have the best of it. Orders have been given to an enormous amount for foreign goods, articles of vertu, and works of fine art, which would never have been given but for the Exhibition • while, on the other hand, the cheap rate at which articles of ordinary use can be manufactured abroad —as, for instance, wine glasses at 6d. and 9d. a dozen; broad cloth at ss. and 6s. a yard; and gentlemen's Wellington boots at 6s. a pair, will lead to wholesale orders to a considerable extent being also given. GREAT PEDESTRIAN FEAT.—We are informed that the great pedestrian feat of 1,000 half-miles in 1,000 successive half hours concludes to-night at six o'clock. Throughout the first fourteen days the weather was most unpropitious, Coates having to change his attire thirty-three times. Still undaunted, he persevered against all difficulties. Up till twelve o'clock on Friday he had accomplished 852 half miles. The weather having now taken a more favourable change, leaves little doubt of his accomplishing the feat. His bodily health appears very little affected, further than pains in the limbs, caused by the wet weather, and blistered feet.—North British Mail. JENNY LIND AT NIAGARA FALLS.—A party writing from the Clifton Hotel states :—The society here is decidedly aristocratic. Sir Hugh Dalrymple, of the 71st Regiment, and suite, are here, and several other military characters. Jenny Lind arrived yesterday from New York, by way of Oswego. THE CRYSTAL PALACE —Upon the walls of the Fine Arts Court, slightly to the west, on the north side, will be found several specimens of typo-chromatic printing; a process which is deservedly obtaining much attention both from artists and connoiseurs by reason of the great advance marked by it in imitative art. These specimens are exhibited by Messrs. George Rowney and Co., the well-known artists' colourmen of Rathbone-place, and will doubtless startle the casual observer by their remarkable fidelity to water-colour drawing. The rustic figures, the more particularly " The Fishing Girl " and " The Gleaners," are especially good, that breadth and truth of touch so agreeable in the spirited sketches of our eminent artists being here secured. The landscapes are likewise noticeable for their correctly embracing the most salient features of Avater-colour execution. As it would appear that this really novel and captivating process renders similes of the most costly masterpieces easy of access to a more extended circle of art-worshippers, we cheerfully direct especial attention to these elegant evidences of its usefulness. CoNTENTION OF FILER NEGROES IN INDIANA.—A. convention of free people of colour is now in session at Indianapolis, and is occupied in deliberating upon various natters relating to the interests of its constituents as a class. There is said to exist among its members a strong inclination to remove out of the state of Indiana to some othercountry, where they hope to enjoy greater social advantages. Atter much debate a resolution was adopted, by a large majority, providing that should the laws of the state become so oppressive as to be intolerable, they would recommend their people to emigrate to Canada, Jamaica, or elsewhere, in preference to Liberia, against which there appears to be a violent prejudice in the convention. Among the countries spoken of for the purpose of emigration, besides those mentioned, are Mexico, New Granada, and Central America; but Canada is generally regarded as most eligible, on account of its accessibility. At last accounts the convention had under discussion a resolution somewhat contradictory to that which had just been passed, as mentioned above. It asserts, in substance, that the free negroes have a right to remain, if they choose, in the United States, the land of their nativity, and it accordingly recommends them to stay hare, and strive for their moral, social, political, and intellectual elevation. It was expected that the resolution would, be defeated.—New York Herald. We have this week had an opportunity of inspect. ing the estuary works. Our readers are doubtless aware that Messrs. Peto and Betts have contracted to excavate a new channel from West Lynn into the wash of Lincoln, for a distance of four miles. The terms of the contract are for the first two miles through the land, 143,0001. ; and for the two through the sand, 20,0001. The average depth of the excavation for the first two miles will be 30 feet ; the width at the bottom, 265 feet; and at the top, 518 feet. At the extreme end of the land cutting, the width will be 280 feet. This part of the excavation commences at West Lynn, near Fisher-street, and is continued in a straight line across North Lynn St. Edmund, as far as the dry land extends. The excavation will be further continued for two miles through the sands of the Wash, and thence it is expected that the new direction of the ebb and flow of a vast body of . water will force a straight channel for many miles through the wash to the sea. The old circuitous channel, full of shifting sands, will be closed up, and thousands of acres will be laid dry, and be made available for agricultural purposes. Since December last about 1,200 men have been employed in the excavation work ; and more than a million and a half of cubic yards of earth have been removed. The soil is clay at the top, and below silth and strong loam ; so that the cutting through and removing such a vast quantity will require an enormous amount of labour. It is, however, expected that the first two miles of the new channel will be completed within a year, and then large vessels may be brought into this port. Whatever may be the benefit accruing to the trade of this town, there can be no question as to the advantage of reclaiming 30,000 acres of land; adding in fact, so much to the territorial extent of the country ; and from this beginning we may anticipate that in time a large part of the land now under the waters of the Wash will be gradually laid dry. Multiplication by Division. —An experiment on the fertility of wheat has, during the past year, been carried out in the garden of Mr. Stowe, a surgeon at Buckingham, of which the following is a correct account. On the 13th of July, 1850, a single grain of wheat was sown in the garden; the plant came up in 10 days, and grew luxuriantly till the loth of September; it was then taken up and divided into slips, and replanted. The plants lived, and flourished till the of November, w hen they were again raised, divided, and replanted, and suffered to remain till the 16th of April of the present year. The weather then becoming favourably wet, they were all taken up again and divided into no less than 114 plants; these being planted, were permitted to stand till the present month of August, when they were productive of the amazing number of 520 ears of wheat, many of them of full size, containing more than grains of com. The crop was gathered before it was fully ripened, as the birds attacked it in spite of revolving feathers and a protecting net. Whether the result of this trial will strengthen the opinion of those who contend for the thin sowing of wheat in ordinary field cultivation, must be left to the judgment of more practical agriculturists, but of the amazing productiveness of the wheat plant, under such treatment, any one may easily satisfy himself repeating the experiment. The Fatal Explosion at Washington. The inquest on the bodies of the miners who perished by the explosion in the Washington colliery, has been brought to a conclusion. The further evidence was of very similar tenor to that given last week; a number of miners testifying that the pit had been for some weeks in a state which caused them alarm. They had often mentioned their fears to William Hall, the overlooker, and to Thomas Todds, the deputy—both of whom are among the dead ; but they had both considered the pit safe; and it seems that others of the miners, some who have perished, and some who have escaped, although they considered the pit was foul, yet believed it would not fire. All the new witnesses concurred also with the preceding ones in giving to Hall the character of a careful man. Mr. Matthias Dunn, the government Inspector, stated his opinion that the pit certainly did not come under the denomination of a fiery pit’*; but if the men had acquainted him with the facts they have stated at the inquest, he should have felt it his duty to inspect the pit. A leading article in the Times of Thursday heralded the existence of an engineering scheme for bringing London and Calcutta within teveu days’ journey of each other ! Referring to an article about two years ago, in which the journalist surprised his readers with the original prospectus of the Direct Calais and Moollan,” he now follows up that announcement with the statement, that since then the scheme has been actually extended in its scope, discussed in its details, approved in much of its purport, and so far advanced that of the four great divisions of the route two have been positively decided on, and are in present course of completion.” It is to be accomplished by stages. A coutinuous line of railway from Ostend to Orsova on the frontier of the Turkish empire is already decided on.” From Constantinople it is proposed to step over to Asia Minor, and, skirting the Mediterranean coast with the line till you come to the mouth of the Orontes, to carry it up the banks of that river till the head waters of Euphrates are reached, and then to lead it down the valley of the Euphrates to Bussorah at the head of the Persian Gulf. The Euphrates Railway would be but nine hundred miles long; and yet it \wuld, by cutting off the immense detour round Arabia, shorten the time to Calcutta twenty days out of the thirty-nine.” These portions of the scheme are to be accomplished 1860. From Bussorah, the railway is to be carried along the Persian Gulf, and by the coast of Beloochistan, to Hyderabad on the Indus ; whence the several branches of Indian lines would soon whisk the traveller to Bombay, Lahore, or Calcutta, according to his wants.” From Gracechurch Street to Calcutta, by the perfected route, would be about 6500 miles of railway; seven days’ journey “without stoppages;” and the whole scheme might be completed in years from the present time. Suicide of Mrs. Colonel Crowther. At Cheltenham, yesterday week, Mrs. Crowther, the widow of the late Colonel Crowther, of the 27th Fusiliers, committed suicide by precipitating herself from the bedroom window, and the day of the fatal act was the thirteenth anniversary of her husband’s death. Her mind had become affected through an attack of bronchitis, and during her visit strict orders had been given by her medical attendant that she should be constantly watched, but she eluded the vigilance of her nurse, and threw herself out of the window. It was third floor. She was found lying in the yard, having fallen from a height of fifty feet. She breathed heavily twice, and then expired. Her skull was frightfully fractured, her right ann broken, and other severe injuries were also discovered, although her face was not disfigured. She was upwards of sixty years of age, and very corpulent. Her fashionable reunions were the life of the Cheltenham season, and her death will be greatly regretted. Nov. 8, 1851. ATROCIOUS MURDER OP A WOMAN BY lIER BUSBAND, IN MARYLEBONE. Yesterday considerable excitement prevailed in the neigh.- bourhood of North-street, Manchester-square, in consequence of a report that a female of the name of Bare, who occupied a back room on the first floor at the house No. 33, in that street, had been brutally murdered by her husband, and that he had, soon after the perpetration of the horrid deed, given himself into custody. The report, upon inquiry, was found to be unfortunately too true, and it is supposed that the motive for the act had its origin in jealousy, and differs so far from those which recently took place in Bermondsey and Camberwell. From information received by our informant, it appears that the unfortunate woman had been living separate from her husband about three weeks, that being the period of time that she has had apartments in North-street. She took a room there in her maiden name, her object, it is supposed, being to avoid discovery by her husband; and she was also employed at a feather menufacturer's,in Wigmore-street, esvendish-square. On Saturday night last her husband was at the Bedford Arms, the corner of North-street and South street. He had a little boy with him, who is supposed to be his son. He had a pint of porter, and while he was drinking it the boy went out. Having traced out her residence, and having ascertained that his wife was not at home, he remained in the street until her arrival. Upon seeing her he spoke to her, and followed her into the house, and then into her room, soon after which the landlady, Mrs. Dinning, who was in the front parlour, was alarmed by hearing them in angry conversation with each other. He then called the boy, who was with him, who is supposed to be his son, and directed him to take some of the boxes out of the room. His wife resisted, when a scuffle between them ensued, in the course of which his wife was heard to utter a faint moan. He subsequently left the room and went away, letting himself out at the street door. Mrs. Lanning, suspecting from the disturbance . that the unfortunate woman might have received pme injury, proceeded to her room, when she found her lying upon the floor in a state of insensibility, and was bleeding ' from several stabs in her face and neck. She rushed out of the house and gave the alarm. She at the same time sent to Mr. Davidson, surgeon, South-street. He promptly attended, but the woman was then dead. She had a punctured wound in her left eye, which is supposed to have penetrated the brain, and to have caused death. Her husband went to the Bedford Arms, where he had previously been, and where he ordered a glass of gin. He was in great agitation while he drank it, and his hand was observed to be smeared with blood. A policeman of the G division came to the door, when on the mFderer seeing him, he gave himself into his custody, observing, "I have stabbed my wife." Upon a policeman ruching the room of the murdered woman, it w as found in gird disorder, and a file, upon which there was blood, and with which the injuries were inflicted, was observed on the ground. This was taken possession of by the polies. The husband, who gave the name of Wm. Bare, and is a labourer, was taken to the station-house of the G division in Maryleboneelane. The parties have been married Twiny years, as they have a son about ten, and a daughter about twenty years of age. On Thursday the Dutchesses of Orleans and of Nemours, with the young Comte de Paris and the Due de Chartres, arrived at the Exhibition in the afternoon, and were occupied some hours in an examination of part of its contents. What if this vast collection was destroyed by fire? Many cities might be burnt to the ground without causing such a sensation as that would. Yet to that risk the Crystal Palace was for a moment exposed on Thursday morning. The flue attached to a gas stove in one of the offices of the contractors became heated, and ignited a piece of wood with bunting which rested upon or touched it. A piece of the burning cloth fell into a small open cask of Indian corn, which stood, as the Irish say, " convenient." All this mischief was brewing in secret in the southern part of the colonial collection on the east side. The drapery of the counter concealed what had happened, and it was only when the smoke began to break forth that an alarm was raised. Fortunately such casualties have been foreseen and amply provided for. There are no less than a dozen large fireengines within the building, besides an ample supply of water easily obtainable, and a thoroughly organized force ready to act at a moment's notice. The fire was extinguished before it had time to do more than slightly char one plank of wood, and no anxiety need be caused by an occurrence so trifling.
