THE LATE EARL OF BRIDGEWATER'S WILL. ( From the Times.) Lord Cranworth delivered judgment in the Vice- Chancellor's Court, on Wednesday, in a very singular case, connected with the will of the late Earl of Bridgewater, who died in 1823. The story deserves a transitory notice from the evidence it affOrda of the keen zest with which our great aristocratic houses pursue the phantom of increased rank. One should have supposed that men who by their birth are placed in so high a social position as the late Earl of Bridgewater, could afford to look with complacency and inlifference at the struggle for rank and station. Our dramatists and novel-writers have drawn many amusing sketches of vulgar parvenus, who, in the midst of the wealth they may have acquired in vulgar ways, or by a mere freak of fortune, think their felicity incomplete because they are not provided with what sailors call "handles" to their names. No doubt the spectacle ofia pompous and under-bred man, who is endeavouring through a thousand humiliations to work his way into a class to which he does not belong, is ludicrous enough. Still, to a certain degree, such an effort is excusable. It is natural that he should deceive himself as to the happiness which results from an unaccustomed salutation. The House of Peers, contemplated from behind a counter in Cornhill, may appear an enchanted region to the eye of the observer. But it would seem well-nigh impossible for those who have lived behind the scenes—nay, who have been actually born in the green-room, to deceive themselves materially as to the real splendour of theatrical properties, or the purity of the diamonds in Queen Huncatnunca's crown. Let us not be misunderstood. When elevation to an upper class in the social scale, or an increase of rank where rank has been once achieved, follows as the natural consequence of heroic actions, or of an eminent civil career, ridicule and animadversion are out of the question. Let those who have earned the laurel by their great deeds wear it amidst the general applause. In such cases the mere outward mark of social elevation is the accident of a great man's position; it was not the prospect of a peerage, or of a " step," which nerved his energies through forty years of struggle within the walls of Parliament, or the sad vicissitudes of a protracted campaign. Titles and honours fall naturally on a great man's head ; he does not propose them to himself as the ultimate object of his ambition. " Victory or Westminster Abbey," said England's noblest seaman, in an age of naval paladins, on the eve of one of those fearful contests which have immortalized his name in his country's annals. Compare for a moment such a spring of action as this with the motives which operate upon the minds of paltry intriguers for rank—and more rank. We have great men, and we have make-believe great men. We have heroes who win our battles by sea and land, who extend their countrYs power and maintain its security; we have had statesmen who have successfully guided the fortunes of the empire through many a dark day of trial and adversity. On the other hand, we have had gentlemen of England " who have lived at home at ease," who have done nothing but amass money and carry on intrigues, and who have yet contrived to wriggle their names into a higher position in the Redbook than those who have borne the brunt of the day. The explanation of such a phenomenon is no mystery to those acquainted with the secret traditions of our great families. Money, land, electioneering, and, consequently, Parliamentary influence, are the engines by which such notable results have been obtained. It is not often, however, that we have the opportunity of following up the contortions of vulgar ambition. A steeplechase for a dukedom over boggy ground is not an everyday spectacle. The late Earl of Bridgewater has been bountiful to his countrymen in this respect. He made his will in 1823, and in it he devised his estates to the late Viscount Alford and his issue; but upon one condition. If Lord Alford should die without having acquired the title of a Marquess or Earl of Bridgewater, then the limitation of the estate to himself and his heirs was to eease, and the estate was to pass to other parties named. So with regard to the Earldom of Brownlow. The Earl of Bridgewater—poor man! —in the year 1823 passed away to regions where an English marquisate or dukedom is a matter of small account. Lord Alford, however, did not succeed to the estates until 1849, and in January of the present year he too died, without having accomplished the requisite juggle with the decorations of his coronet. Then the case came before Lord Cranworth. On the one hand, the guardians of the late Lord Alford's infant son prayed that the will—or at least the certain portion of it affecting the estates named—might be declared invalid. The child's uncle, the Earl of Brownlow, asked that its validity might be affirmed. Passing over the mere legal hair-splitting of " conditions subsequent" and " conditions precedent," as interesting only to the more dili gent inquirers into contingent remainders and executory devises, we find this broad position stated and denied by the advocates on either side A limitation over, with such a condition attached as in the will of the late Earl of Bridgewater, was void in equity, as contrary to public policy. Lord Cranworth, however, decided this matter against the nephew, on the ground " that it could not, in his opinion, be said that the will induced the devisee to resort to corrupt means for the purpose of obtaining the title; on the contrary such a condition would tend rather to produce good than dishonourable conduct." Had the late Lord Alford lived long enough to carry the necessary steps into effect, it would have been worth his while to unite with his heir for the purpose of sacrificing three-fourths of the estates, that they might hold secure possession of the remaining fraction. We are not interested in discussing the doctrines of equity as propounded by Lord Cranworth, but to a man of plain understanding it would scarcely appear possible to propose a greater inducement to rascality and corruption. The whole transaction reads more like a chapter in the Duc de St. Simon's Memoirs than as a history oc curriug in our own time. Bend your thoughts day and night upon the noble art of money-getting, said the Roman father to his son in Rome's degenerate days— Rem ; Si possis, mote ; si non, quocurnque modo rem." i Such is the language of the late Earl of Bridgewater to his heirs :—" Get a step n the peerage at any price. Here is boundless wealth—hoard it up for all purposes save one, then lavish it with unsparing hand. Rank, rank, hunger and thirst, and lust for rank. Let the strawberry leaves which encircle the ducal coronet never be absent from your waking nor your sleeping thoughts. I indeed cannot hope to wear them. Life is too short for the attainment of so noble an end. But at least I have the satisfaction of foreknowing, that when my bones are mouldering in the grave, my descendants — my devisees, if you will—will one day bear that glorious cap for which my heart has yearned in vain." Compare for a moment this will of the Earl of Bridgewater with the testamentary dispositions of Sir Robert Peel. The late Premier had played at skittles with coronets, but would none of them. Not only would he not accept them for himself—but, should his heir ever feel his veins tingle with the expectation of a " step" in the peerage, there is a warning finger -ever raised from beyond the grave, which bids him spurn from him so unworthy, so paltry a thought. And yet Sir Robert had done and said things in his time which would have entitled him to place his family in the highest position British subjects may attain. A comparison between the will of the mere Lord and the great Statesman is not devoid of interest or instruction. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The building was on Saturday as quiet, and cool, and aristocratic as the most exclusive season-ticket-holder could wish for. Tee fashionable visitors came and went in large numbers certainly between twelve and eix o'clock, but there were not at any time of the day more than 10,000 or 12,000 persoes present, and this is saying that the attendance web very limited. Her Majesty, the Prince Albert, the Priucess Royal, the Princess Alice, and the Princess HAena again visited building, arriving at their usual early hour of half-past nine o'clock. The portion visited by the Royal party to-day was the north and north central galleries, extending along the entire length of the British half of the building, and including animal and vegetable substances, mathematical and surgical instruments, and cutlery, civil engineering, philosophical and musical instruments, and glass. Commencing with the brilliant display of glass at the head of the gallery, the , Queen examined with 831112 interest the model of the Koh-i-noor, with its two attendant satellites, which has just been placed in front of Mr. Apsley Pellatt's collection. 'rue velvet cushion, the gold stems and wires on which the diamond is supported, the glass shade, and a miniature iron cage, surmounted by a crown, have all been successfully imitated; and we believe many persons, after lookieg at the original and the copy, wculd be puzzled to tell which is the ' great Indian diamond, valued at 2,000,000/. sterling, and which the piece of British crystal glass, value—say one shilling. The glass is of the purest colourless crystal, and the size, shape, cutting of the facets, &c., have all been most accurately reproduced. Her INlajesty then passed to the specimees of glass silvering by Mr. Hale Thomson's patent process, in which a variety of plateaux, mirror globes mounted on eagles, atlases, and ornamental stands, vases, salvers, chess-hoards, &c., are displayed in every variety of colour. The great feature of the collection, sent expressly on account of her Majesty's visit, consisted of a pair of vases, which, although only 30 inches high, are valued by the proprietors at 500 guineas. The ground is an ambercoloured glass, which by the silvering process is heightened to a rich golden hue. The vases are symmetrically proportioned, and exhibit a specimen of the finest and most minute glass engraving ever produced. Although cut in the deepest intaglio so perfect is the art displayed that they present the illusion of standing out in alto relieve. On the body of the vases are shields, one representing a drove of wild horses surprised in a forest by a panther, which is in the act of springing from a tree. The pendant represents a gri•tly bear capturing and overpowering a horse. The details of the forest vegetation are made out with the most microscopic minuteness, and the grouping and attitudes of the various animals wonderfully correct and artisle. The cutting of these vases is by a Bohemian artist, and they were executed at St. Louis, in France, the silvering enrichment being added since their arrival in this country. In the centre of the compartment, on a table of lapis lezuli glass with arabesque patterns in silver, is a pink topaz-coloured drinking cup, being a duplicate of the one presented to his Royal Highness Prince Albert at the York banquet, and containing an exquisitely engraved medallion portrait of the Prince. The original is now at Windsor Castle. IN e understand that a similar cup, containing a medallion copy of Wyon's last medal portrait of her Majesty, will be presented to the Queen at the grand civic entertainment to-morrow (Wednesday). The Royal party spent some time in examining these unique and beautiful articles, which include also some of a more utilitarian character, such as silvered reflectors, applicable to railways, lighthouses, and other purposes of artificial illumination. In the adjoining compartment of Cogan and Co. are some wonderful imitations of lace, wood, and marble in glass for the decorations of summer arbours, &e., to which her Majesty's attention was directed by the Prince. The model of the Crystal Palace, by the i same exhibitors, was also much admired , and it s understood that a copy has been ordered to be constructed for the Prince. Messrs. Richardson's (of Stourbridge) display of fine crystal was also inspected, and the Royal party then proceeded through the long and varied d is p la y of pianofortes and harps, which extend through the greater portion of the gallery, and in which are exhibited specimens of the peculiar improvements and construction of all our most eminent manufacturers. The remainder of the articles were looked over more cursorily, it being intimated that her Majesty in her next visit would again pass through the north gallery. THE QUEEN . 1N DANGER. We have received the following communication, on which the utmost reliance may be placed, from a gentleman who travelled by the royal train. The journey of her Majesty to the north was nearly being attended with consequences fearful to contemplate, owing to the velocity with which the royal train was driven over the Newcastle and arwick portion of the route. As those will rembember who have approached the town of Newcastle over the stupendous bridge and viaduct which crosses the Tyne, there is a curve of very small radius at the southern entrance, which is continued so far as to form the quarter circumference of a circle. Of course great caution should be observed in traversing this portion of the line on all occasions, but with such a responsibility as that which devolved on the driver in charge of the royal train, no care and attention, as regards not only the safety, but the feelings of the illustrious passengers, could have been excessive or overcharged. The situation is quite enough to excite one'e nervous sensibilities when passing the bridge with all leisure, looking down on the dark waters of the Tyne, with the shipping and housetops far underneath. What must have been the sensations of the Royal party when the whole train dashed at great speed upon this narrow curve, and immediately received three successive shocks, which were felt distinctly from ono end of the train to the other? The shocks were caused by the impetus of the trai❑ running against the sides of the rails in going so rapidly along the curve. The consequences of a carriage getting off the line are too horrible to think of. Surely it should be enough to make :an enginedriver careful, even if he were as rigid as the engine he drove, to reflect that to him were entrusted the lives of the Queen of England, of the Prince, of the heir to the Throne, of the Princess Royal, of her brother, and of the Prime Minister, and that ho was the guardian for the time of the present happiness and of the hopes of the nation.— Glasgow Constitutional. JONES.—On the 30th ultimo, died, in his 73d year, Mr. Richard Jones, for many years an actor of some repute at Covent -garden Theatre. He commenced his career in the histrionic profession, as other comedians have done before him, by enacting tragedy at different provincial theatres, until the accidental illness of a brother performer led to his impersonation of Gossamer in Laugh when you Can. From this time his attention was directed to comedy, and ho made his first appearance on the London stage at Coventgarden in 1807, as Goldfinch in The Road to Ruin. He will, however, be chiefly remembered by his gentlemanly end lively performance of Puff in The Critic. Mr. Jones, always careful of his purse and person, was long known among his professional brethren by the soubriquet of "Gentleman Jones." He was the author of two amusing pieces, The Green plan and Too Late for Dinner, and since his retirement from the stage has frequently employed himself in giving lessons of elocution. —Literary Gazette. The ascent took place about seven o'clock. The wind was rather strong at the time and blowing south-west, and the moment the machine was r, leased from its moorings it rose very heavily, and barely cleared the circus iuclosure. Madame Garneron immediately emptied a bag of ballast among a large crowd who were watching it in Victoria-road, but before she was able to discharge another the car of the balloon struck the projecting garret window of No. 1, Madeley-villas, which is just on the opposite side of Victoria-road to the Circus, and is an instant the poor lady was seen with her feet entangled in the netting at the side of the half inverted car, and hanging right out of it with her head downwards. I PaicE or ARTICLES.-It has been erroneously stated that the Royal Commissioners have abandoned their original idea of refusing to allow the prices to be affixed to the articles exhibited. No alteration whatever has been made on this point. It is well understood, how- ever, that exhibitors will be at perfect liberty to distribute in the building, by means of handbills, catalogues, or otherwise, any amount of information they may please pon this subject, it being of course understood that the Commissioners do not in the slightest degree hold them- selves responsible for any of the statements which may be thus circulated, nor by thus consentig to their dis- tribution give that official character or sanction to them which would of necessity be attached to prices affixed on the articles exhibited. COMPLETION OF THE FLOORING OF THE BUILDING.-' It is most important that exhibitors should know that it las been decided that the whole of the flooring of the building must be laid down by the 2d of April, and that, consequently no waggons or other vehicles will be allowed in the building after that date. All packages or articles which cannot be conveyed into the building by band must, therefore, be practically excluded. Goods will of course continue to be received up to the period for which an extension of time has been granted, but they will be received at the eastern or western ends of the building, and not, as is the case at present, in the building itself. Except in cases where extension of time has been granted beyond the 2d of April, all articles which cannot be conveyed by hand to their respective places in the building will be excluded. THE GREAT EXHIBITION CATALOGUES -We are lad to hear that both the small and large catalogues will be ready by the 1st of May, and that they are likely to be more accurate than the general belief would lead one to expect. Every exhibitors before his contributions are received at Hyde Park, must show that a description of them has been forwarded to Messrs. Spicer and Clowes, and thus, whatever other imperfections the hurry of compilation may render unavoidable, there will be no omissions. The arrangement of matter will follow strictly the order of allotments, and thus all confusion will be avoided. In order to rectify as soon as possible any defects in the larger work, the first edition will be limited in its issue. Our own exhibitors who have not already sentin their illustrations or descriptions of articles should do so without delay, and the agents of foreign countries who have not forwarded their lists, drawings, orn engravings, should lose no time in that respect. Messrs. Spicer and Clowes appear to have had some difficulty in making the French exhibitors especially understand that the descriptions of their contributions were to be inserted in the illustrated catalogue gratuitously -subject, of course, to the revision of the editorial staff employed in the compilation. This revision is indispen- sable to the practical usefulness of the catalogues, for inventors are notoriously fond of blowing their own trumpets, and it is quite amusing to see the extent to which the agricultural implement makers especially can spin out the specifications of their machines. It is calculated that there will be altogether about 15,000 exhibitors, and if they were allowed to run riot in descrip- tion, not only would it be quite impossible to keep the catalogues within a reasonable size, but things of no importance would probably occupy the greatest space, while things that are really worth a full notice would frequently be disposed of in a few lines. Among other curious facts connected with the preparation of these works we may mention that Messrs. Spicer and Clowes have had tendered to them an epic poem for bodily inser tion. Whether it is that they have no love of the muse, or that they believe their catalogues too prosaic in charactertoinclude such acontribution, or that theycon- sider the public taste for poetry dying out, certain it is that they have not accepted this advantageous offer, which we understand came from abroad. WE have heard of fewer eccentric contributions to the Exhibition, either from native or foreign contributors, than might have been expected. M. Soyer, however, must look well after his culinary honours, for a pie of immense size, 4 feet long, 2J wide, and 1 foot deep, has arrived at the Crystal Palace from Holland, which is represented as a gastronomic wonder. THE TAUNTON CABINET, MANUFACTURED BY MR. JOHN STEEVENS, FOR THE ExHIBITIoN.-This cabinet is made of fine walnut wood grown in the neighbourhood of Taunton, elaborately carved, representing youth, man- hood, maturity, and old age; also the seasons of the year, in carving and needlework, the passions, &c., crowned with a figure of Peace extending over the globe. The figure of youth, at twenty years of age, whose countenance bespeaks the innocency and candour of his heart, wears in his hair the emblems of the season,-the violet, prim- rose, cowslip, &c.,-holding in his right hand a portion of a festoon of flowers which connects the whole four figures, and extending his left hand to the figure of man- hood, at the age of forty years, a fine manly form, with candour and open countenance bespeaking "the noblest work of God," and wearing in his hair the emblems of summer (that being his time of life),-the rose, the lily, and pinks; carnations, strawberries, gooseberries, &c., surround his brow; his right hand is receiving the festoon of flowers from youth, and with his left he is supporting the frame of cabinet, the festoon of flowers continuing and extending to the figure of maturity,-a figure of sixty years of age,-whose right hand supports the frame of cabinet, and his left hand extends to old age. Over the head of youth is a basket of strawberries, cherries, rasp- berries, and early fruit, surrounded with leaf work, en. closing a pannel of needlework, covered with bent plate glass, and motto. At the extreme top of this glass dome stands a beautiful figure of Peace, with extended wings, bending over the globe, holding in one hand the olive branch, and the other pointing to the Diety. Having thus given a escription of the, carvings of this magnificent cabinet, it is necessary to point out the enrichuents in needlework, worked on black velvet from nature by Miss Kingsbury, who previously receivedamedal fromhis Royal Highness hi'XLcO Albert for diwii -pPeVlJ , It is impossible to give a description or do justice to the talent and good etaste which are displayed-nature being so beautifully imitated as to require the most minute inspection to discriminate the difference. The attention of chemists and others interested in the subject has been much arrested by a new preparation, called amorphous phosphorus, and by which all the difficulty encountered in the transport and use of phosphorus for manufacturing purposes, as in the making of lucifer matches, is removed. This, the third and last fete of the Horticultural Society, took place on Saturday, and the visitors were, as usual on such occasions, favoured with about as moist an afternoon as one often meets with in the month of July. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. All doubts as to the punctual opening of the Exhibition on the Ist of May now seem to be set at rest. Executive Committee, the contractors, and all classes of exhibitors, to have combined their efforts to overcome the difficulties in the way of arranging, in all its completeness, the extensive area of the building. Vast as must be the labour, yet the activity of the last week, and the resolutions which have been published by the committee as to the limits of the time for receiving goods, have dispelled all uncertainty on this point. The contributors have responded to the urgency of the committee, and for several days past an enormous quan. tity of goods has been poured into the building. Waggons laden with every species of commodity have deposited their burthens in the interior, and though the operation of unloading has been carried on with remarkable despatch, the string of conveyances in waiting often extended down the Kensington-road as far as the end of Sloane-street. Such a spectacle was probably never witnessed in any thoroughfare of the metropolis before, and passers-by stopped to gaze at that long procession of industrial products, more wonderful in its character than even the rows of splendid equipages assembled in the adjoining park during the height of the season. On Monday GOO ,waggon-loads were received; yet the'whole of this vast consignment was deposited with the utmost regularity, and without any inconvenience to the ordinary traffic of the thoroughfare. Such are the advantages of judicious arrangements. As Saturday, the 29th ult., was the last day allowed for receiving agricultural implements, Wednesday was fixed as the limit of time within which large and heavy articles could be sent in. The arrivals in the machinery department may now, therefore, be considered as nearly completed, and an approximation may be made to a correct estimate of the leading features of that great section of our native industry. T.At authorities at the Crystal - Palace express themselves entirely satisfied with the prospect before them in this portion of the Exhibition. In every other part of the British side of the Exhibition, the preparations are far advanced. Nothing farther has transpired, with regard to the "vexed question" of the leakage of the building; and it may therefore be fairly assumed that this difficulty has been satisfactorily disposed of. On Wednesday her Majesty and Prince Albert visited the building, and examined attentively the immense preparations in progress for the opening next month. They inspected the machinery and agricultural implements departments, the sculpture and fine arts courts, and the great organ in process of construction on - the western gallery. Crossing the transept, they passed into the foreign division of the Exhibition, and entered the Austrian, Spanish, and several other allotments. The exhibitors and their work- , men in the different sections received them with every mark of loyalty and respect, and they were repeatedly cheered in their progress. , It may fitly be added here, that her Majesty has consented to the exhibition of the great diamond, the "Koh-i-Noor," which will occupy a prominent position, 'although great precautions will be taken to ensure its safety. THE BEL GIAN FINE ARTS EXHIBITION F OR 1851. | During the last two months there has been at Brussels a grand Exhibition of the Fine Arts, which has attracted an immense number of re- sidents and travellers, and which merits a few words of notice. Triennially, there is anexhibition of the kind, mainly for the purpose of grouping the works of Belgian artists, but to which foreign artists also send their works. As the triennial oq- casion fell in the present year, ,M. Rogier, the Belgian Prime Minister, proposed to the King to extend the range of, the exhibition, to invite more largely foreign contributors, through the agency of the Belgian envoys abroad, and, in every respect, to make the triennial festival of art a worthy pendant, or companion, to our own Great Ex- hibition. This idea received immediately .the sanction of the King, and a commission was at once appointed, consisting of the Burgo- master of Brussels and some of the principal civic authorities, M. Van Eycken (Professor of Painting at the Royal Academy of Brussels), M. de Keyser (the well-known historical painter, of Aptwerp)l M. Leys (one of the best of the modern Belgian artists), M. Madou (a painter who blends happily the style of Teniers and Wilkie with an original man- ner quite his own), M. Simonis (the distinguished sculptor), M. Romberg (the able chef de division in the Ministry of the Interior), M. Van der Beleu (also a chef de division in the Ministry of the Inte- rior), M. Navez (director of the Royal Academy at Brussels), and M. Materne (secretary-general to the Foreign Ministry of Belgium). These gentlemen immediately proceeded, aided by the Minister for Fo- reign Affairs, to invite, through the various foreign embassies-of Belgium, the co-operation of the artists of various countries. A spacious and commodious building was erected in the square opposite the Museum, one of the most accessible points in Brus- sels; and on the 15th of August the exhibition was ready for the public. The extent to which the in-, vitations of the commission were responded to is best testified by the fact that very nearly fifteen huu- dred pictures were to be found in these extensive saloons. These were contributed by painters from every country having the slightest pretension to eminence in the arts ; and it will at once be seen that the collection of so large a number of pictures on so short a notice-for the proposal of M. Rogier dates only from the 16th March-is no slight tri- umph for a country like Belgium, so snmall, and so limited in its resources, while, at the same time,: it exhibited an alacrity and responsiveness on the part l of the artists of various countries very cheering to all those who regard the advance of the fine arts as a vital element in civilization. Of course we do not pretend to giveany detailed account of a collection so numerous, nor does the occasion serve for any comparison of the relative merits of different modern schools; because, although each country, and most of the schools, I are represented, it was not to be expected that the different artists could, or would, send their chefs d'Xexres. We simply propose to name a few of the I pictures most worthy of noting, with a view to recording and signalising the claims of some artists, whose names even are not generally known in Eng- land. Yielding precedence to the Belgian artists, we will first mention a few of their most notable pic- tures. There has been a marked revival in Bel- gian art during the last twenty years. It cannot te said that the modern artists of Belgium have created any distinctly marked school, but they have arrived at a very high degree of excellence, both in the conception and in the execution of their works. The influence of the old Dutch and Flemish masters manifests itself in even their most finished works, while the examples of the school of Dussel- dorf on the one hand and of the modern French historical school on the other are more or less traceable in the works of even their most distinguished artists. The na- tional history of Belgium during the middle ages furnishes a fine field for the histo- rical painter; the quaint middle-age aspect of the old cities, the still picturesque costumes in many districts, and the ease and freedom of man- ners, inspire with very marked characteristics the class of artists coming under the general designa- tion of painters de genre; and the strong religious feeling pervading society in many parts of the country has led to the adoption of sacred subjects by a class of artists who work with the devotional spirit, and sometimes with not a little of the power, of the best Italian masters. M. Gallait is recognised, and deservedly so, as the principal historical painter of modern Bel- gium. His picture of the abdication of Charles V., which may be seen in the Cour de Jus- tice at Brussels, for composition, drawing, colour, and, above all, for the grand senti- ment pervading it, is a chef-d'ewre. The interest centres in the chief figure-that of Charles himself, who is blessing his son, kneeling at the foot of a throne, whereon is seated a lady of venerable aspect. On the left of Charles is the Prince of Orange, the same who subsequently deprived Philip of so rich a portion of his dominions. All the minor groups, of eoolesiastics, nobles, ladies of the court, &c., are admirably disposed, depending naturally on the chief figures, and illustrating the sentiment of the piece, without affectation in the attitudes. The colour of this picture is very fue, almost Vene- tian in richness of tone. The same characteristic of coloar is to be found in the sole historical work exhibited by Gallait in this exposition. Its subject is national, representing the last honours paid by the Flemings to the Counts Egmont and De Horn, after their execution by the order of the Duke of Alba. This work, which is recog- nised as at least the most striking picture in the exhibition, is highly creditable to its author, in so far as relates to the excellent drawing, the fine colour, and the careful execution in all details,; but to those who have not seen other pictures by this artist, it will not convey an adequate idea of his powers. It wants impressiveness and invention; nor is the sentiment likely to be inspired by an oc- casion so solemn, and one so identified with Flemish independence, sufficiently conveyed. Another pic- ture by M. Gallait, entitled " Art and Liberty "-a poor student of music enjoying his instrument, though evidently steeped in poverty-conveys a fine sentiment with vigour and power; and a portrait by the same artist is another evidence that portrait painting can be elevated to the highest rank in the hands of a man of genius. Van Eyoken is a painter who deservedly enjoys a very high reputation in his own country, which has extended amongst connoisseurs- elsewhere. Her Majesty Queen Victoria was the purchaser of a very beautiful picture of his, entitled " L'Abondance." One of his pictures gained the prize gold medal in Paris in 1840. He also is the painter of the four- teen pictures, illustrating the life of our Saviour, which adorn the Church de la dhapelle de Notre Dame at Brussels. He has been the means of in- troducing into Belgium the practiceof open air fresco painting, to study which he went to Germany in 1850, where he was in communicatioawith Cornelius Kaulbach and other chiefs of the German art world. He brought back with him to Belgium the new mode of fresco painting on stone. Van Eycken devotes himself to historical, religious, and mythi- cal subjects, and is distinguished by the reverential spirit with which he regards his art. In the col- lection of pictures by living painters exhibited this season at Lichifield House, St. James's-square, three of this artist's productions, in his chosen style, are to be seen. His contributions to the exposition at Brussels consist of three works, each characteristic of his high-art tendencies. The subjects chosen are respectively, " Ossian and Malvina," " A Vision of the Prophet Jeremiah," and " Hope and Faith." These works, the more they are examined, the more they establish that Mons. Van Eycken is an artist who thoroughly feels the high responsibility of his mission, while they are distinguished by that careful and laborious attention to details which, in an artist, is the seal of his faith. At the same time, it. is just to this painter to say that, as in the case of Gallait and some others, the works ex- hibited on this occasion are not the best represen- tatives we have seen of his talent. De Keyser, as also the Baron Wappers, has long enjoyed a high reputation among modern Bel- gian historical painters. In the Eglise des Augus- tins, at Brussels, there is a large picture by this artist, representing a battle famous in Flemish history. It certainly does not 'sustain the reputa- tion deservedly attained by ?? de Keyser; but the curious in modern art will find in it many significant hints as to the position of its professors in Belgium. In this exhibition De Keyser has four pictures, of which the most striking is that entitled S"t. Elizabeth of Hungary distributing Alms to the Poor." A formality of. style is the chief draw- back on the, enjoyment derivable from this artist's works. Au artist but little known in England, although sonieof his works are exhibited in Lichfield House, is M. A. Chauvin, of Liege. This gentleman studied at Dusseldorf under Schadow. From the Dusseldorf school he imbibed a combined spirituality in con- ception and severity in execution ; but in his works there is a grace and au originality quite his own. His- two works in the collection exhibited at Lichfield House evince originality in an eminent degree. In the Hotel de Ville at Liege there is a fine picture by this artist, embodying an incident I is the life of Beckmann, a. celebrated burgomaster and leader of the Liegeois, who is dying while ad- ministering his functions, from the effects of a slow poison administered by his adversaries. There is iin the principal figure great dignity, and'iu the whole work a fine historical tone. In the Epis- copal Palace at Liege there is also a very fine portrait, by Chauvin, of the celebrated priest orator of Notre Dame at Paris, the 'Abb4 Lacordaire. . The only contribution of this spiritual and accomplished artist to be seen in the Brussels exhibition is a por- trait of the Baron de Schiervel, painted by order of the Government for a national collection. Verboeckhoven, as an animal painter, is known in Englami'd. Except for a remarkable fidelity in imi- tation, his works are not remarkable, nor will they bear comparison for one moment with those of our' own artists in this branch.' He might rank with' Herring, but could not bear competition even with :Ansdell. He has three pictures in the exhibition distinguished by his accustomed care and fidelity in detail,' but, wanting the sentiment and character which elevate the worksof Laudseer high above their subjects, and which add so graceful a charm to the works of Madame Rosa Bonheur. Pictures by Madou, Leys, Mathysen, and many other Belgian artists serve to assert the excellence 'of the modern. Belgians;' and if we do not name .all the artists whose works confer honour on their 'country, it is that our space and the cursory oha- racter of thisnotice forbid our en &ering into details. We must signalise, however, the admirable pictures of the two Messrs. Stevens, and one or two works by M. Van Moer, indicating much executive ability. France has contributed some ' very 'charming works in a school but little known in this country, one which combines with delicate and unexagge- rated sentiment a freshness, freedom, and vigour of execution which impart to the works of these artists a distinguishing characteristic, promising great future fame and eminence. The cattle and landscape pieces of Rosa Bonheur are re- presented, though imperfectly, in" some small pictures, which however display, in a man- ner not to be mistaken, the extraordinary perfection attained by the fair artist. Her chef- d'rFore-now, we believe, at Amsterdam-ought to grace one of our princely collections. A very fine specimen, of her powers is to -be seen at Liohfield House. Pictures, small, but exquisitely drawn, coloured,.and finished, from the pencil of Plassanu and Fauveletn attest the originality and perfection of this, the most rising school in modern French art. Diax contributes two or three small works, indi- cating powerfully his classical taste and originality, both of style and execution. Perhaps the gems of the whole collection are to be found in two ex- *quisite little works by Ernest Meissonier, the one re- presenting a soldier choosing his favourite sword, a marvel of-free yet delicate execution, having all the minuteness of ?? schoolwithout its man- nerism; the other a very small, but finely executed figure of a man smoking-a still more remarkable instance of the same qualities. Germany contributes a few works. The only contributor whose name is known in this country is Hasenclever. Two scenes from his well-known Jobsiade exhibit his characteristic, vigorous humour and coarseness.' As an artist, he is inferior to our own Webster. An Hungarian painter, named Cermak, con- tributes a fine picture, full of nationality, and highly artistic in treatment, representing the emi- gration of an Hungarian family. M. Beranger ex- hibits a very pretty and graceful work, entitled " La Gonvernante d'un Savant." Tony Johannot has a little picture, remarkable for glowing and brilliant colour, representing the halt of a party of falconers. M. Constant Troyon exhibits some of his beautiful landscapes, with sheep; and a young Dutch artist, M. Weisenbouch, has two scenes in Dutch towns, remarkable for an originality of treat- ment and an extraordinary transparency of atmo- sphere We have only culled a few of the most striking works from a collection which would justify us in a more extended notice. It is to be hoped that the success attending this attempt to make art cosmopolitan will lead to future efforts in the same direction; and that Brussels, which is so well situated as the centre of communication, may also become permanently, or at least periodically, a metropolis of the fine arts.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Monday mon:ling, at nine o'clock, or thereabouts, omnibuses, cabs, and caravans filled with happy holy_ day folk might be seen passing in dense columns along all the leading thoroughfares towards Hyde park; the streets gave indications of an immense influx of visiters, and even the precarious elevation of the "knife-boards" was fully occupied. Between the hours of ten and eleven o'clock 21,526 persons were admitted, and appearances promised a day of unusual bustle and excitement. From one of the galleries of the transept Mr. Mayne, the Commissioner of Police, might have been observed watching with anxiety the seemingly inexhaustible tide of restless human ty poured into the interior. The task of counting so enormous an influx became one of great difficulty, and already an assemblage unprecedented in number was anticipated. Rain began to fall—all the indications of a damp, disagreable day were realized. Along the approaches to the building bands of sturdy pedestrians might, nevertheless, be seen pressing forward, sometimes seeking shelter, and then starting afresh. Another hour passed away, and it became evident that the rush of visiters was checked. From 11 to 12 o'clock the numbers admitted fell to 12,785; from 12 to 1, they were 8,064 ; from 1 to 2, 4,832; from 2 to 3, 3,312; from 3 to 4, 1,666; and the total, according to the police returns up to the hour of closing, was 54,104. At the doors 2,436/. 4s. was taken, and we find this amount increased by the sum of two guineas for the sale of a lady's season-ticket. There were a great many people, evidently from the agricultural districts and the provincial towns, who arrived in parties, and whose astonishrnont on first entering the building it was exceedingly interesting to watch; some were accompanied by their wives and children. When they separated at the crystal fountain, they took leave of each other as if they never hoped to meet again ; yet you might overbear the appointment made for a rendezvous at four o'clock, in order to be in time for the return train. Mechanics and artisans on entering the building generally started off at once for the machinery department, and on no former occasion have we seen the marvels of that section so thoroughly and intelligently explored. Each contribution appeared to have throughout the day a circle of experienced critics around it. who scrutinized every detail, and frequently subjected the exhibitors to a searching crossexamination. Other portions of the interior which seemed to attract particular attention were the northwest galleries, containing the electric telegraphs and the civil engineering models. In the former division Henley's new magneto-electric machine, which supersedes the use of the galvanic battery, and opens up a new field of experiment and practical application in this department of science, was specially noticed. Among the mass of spectators we observed a large proportion of women with young children, some of whom squalled so lustily as to be heard at a considerable distance, notwithstanding the extent to which the Crystal Palace absorbs sound. Shortly after twelve the country folk, who had brought baskets with thetn well stored with provisions, proceeded to recruit their exhausted strength therefrom, and homely unpretending luncheons were despatched with great gusto, and washed down afterwards by copious draughts of water from the nearest fountain. With vast energy the labours of inspection were pursued as the hours crept onward, and, when the number of visiters reached the highest point, it was a curious and a touching sight which the interior of that great storehouse of human industry presented. There were collected thousands of the labouring classes eagerly admiring the triumphs of their own handiwork, and appreciating most fully the effects which skilful combination produces. Nothing could be more orderly and decorous than their conduct, and still there arose from them that peculiar hum of satisfaction which forms so remarkable a. feature of vast assemblages while their interest is excited and their tastes are gratified. The Americans, who are always coming out with something extraordinary, treated the visiters with some strange music on an incomprehensible instrument, which they call a " piano-vioiono," in the front of which are the ordinary piano keys, but within which ere, seen through glass, two violins, painfully stretched upon the rack, across which bows scraped incessantly with all the vigour of a steam engine. The sound is very much like what one might expect from a saw-mill in a high state of excitement. This machine was constantly surrounded by a crowd of wondering rustics. In the immediate neighbourhood there have been placed, with very questionable taste, two hideous figures of Esquimaux from Mr. Catlin's collection, which look all the more horrible from being placed in the neighbourhood of the beautiful Flemish and Italian marbles, with which the foreign nave is studded. These two monstrosities also attracted a considerable share ot notice. The diamonds and pearls, the gold and silver fancy work, which on the gala days so monopolise the public attention, were almost neglected by the visiters. They speedily turned away from the Koh-i-noor in evident disappointment, and stopped but a moment before the rare collections of the East India Company. The galleries received their full share of attention, even the comparatively neglected aisle devoted to stained glass. Here we could perceive that the groups invariably stopped before the good things, turning away from those outrageous contrasts of reds and blues with which some of the windows are disfigured. The charming female face from Milan was universally admired, as were' also some curious little glass portraits, in which the outline is produced by inequalities in the glass. The spectators quickly found out the mode in which the effect was produced, and this discovery only increased their admiration. There was not a single accident throughout the day. An incident occurred which will perhaps not be without useful results. A gentleman visiting the foreign departments a little after five found them, as usual, closed and covered up, although the official time of closing i. 3even o'clock. On entering the south side of the French department, the attendants had begun operations in covering up, and on the visiter inquiring whether the Exhibition shut up at that hour, the man told him it was quite time enough to keep it open from ten till half-past five. The visiter remonstrated, and observed, that, under such circumstances, it became impossible to make use of the remaining time. " Well! you'll see precious little now, I can tell you. We'll take care of that." The visiter then inquired where was the office of the French Commissioner, but the attendant asserted he did not know of any, and the policeman, who was inclined to abet him, said there were two, without pointing out where they were. At length, by inquiring elsewhere, the gentleman found the office, and applied to M. Triscak, the Inspector-General in charge of the French department, who accompanied him forthwith to the scene of complaint. M. Triscak inquired why the goods were covered up, and required the removal of the wrappers; but the attendant showed himself insolent and insubordinate, and the official immediately tore sway the wrappers with his own hands, informing the attendant that he had no right to close before seven o'clock. At the same time, he explained to the visiter that the fault lay with the attendants who had been provided by some of the exhibitors, and who, to shirk work, closed before the time. The covering up is carried out by the efficient attendants in five or ten minutes. There were honest fellows in fustian and corduroys, agricultural labourers in smock-frocks, and rural swains in their full dress of velveteen, with their sweethearts in bright- coloured shawls of scarlet or green, and operatives and artisans of every class, dressed in their best. It was amusing to observe the amazement of these good folks as they entered, and the betsildered look of their "upturned, wondering eyes," gazing up at the roof of the transept, during their brief pause of stunned and staggered astonishment, ere they plunged into the vast compartments opening on either side of it, with exclamations such as one we overheard—" Well, I suppose we can go where we like ?" One fine old farmer looking yeoman was heard to exclaim, very idiomatically, "Dang my buttons! it be a mighty fine place! I be bound this is something grand, now !" The "something grand" was the Amazon group of Kiss. Many of the humbler visiters came from considerable distances; we know of one instance in which they came from St. Albans (walking to the railway station at Hat': field, and from the station at Shoreditch), and went back the same way in the evening. In reference to the expected number of strangers this year in London, it should be remembered that on the Continent there is one great holiday-time in the year, and one only. The vacances of all the courts of law, colleges, schools, and generally of every in. stitution or body that can ever have a holiday, commence about the 12th August, and terminate on the 30th September. At no other part of the year can professional men absent themselves from their lnomes without injury to their affairs; and the same reason applies to that very large portion of the middle classes who live by their in- dustry. Then, and not sooner, may we expect the great mass of Con. tinental visitors to the Exhibition; particularly of those who bring with them wives and children. Among the many acts of cordial liberality on the part of employers towards their worksnenn in connection with the Exhibition, a very in- teresting one is that which we understand is about to be given by Messrs Garratt and Son, the agricultural engineers, of Leiston Works, Suffolk. A most valuable and inter- esting addition wasmade on Thursday to the department of gems and precious stones in the Exhibition, by Mr A. J. B. Hope, M.P., who has there deposited a portion of his valuable collection, placing it, in memory of the collector, the late Mr H. P. Hope, in the Holland compartment. They are placed upon a pedestal firmly secured to the floor, and covered with a circular iron frame made by Mr Chubb, similar in form to that which contains the priceless Koh-i-noor. In the collection of Mr Hope is the largest known pearl in the world. It is of great be'auty; its length is two inches, its circumference 44 inches, and it weighs three ounces, or 1,800 grains. Near this splendid specimen is placed a beautiful Hungarian opal, 1 15-16 inch in length by 1 5.16 in breadth. A third specimen, which will not fail to be regarded with great interest, on account of its historic as- sociations, as well as of its extreme beauty, is the handle of Murat's sword, the hilt of which is formed of a single beryl or aqua- marine. A rough beryl deposited near it shows its original condition. "Le Saphir Merveillcux"--a sapphire of an amethystine colour by candle-light-will be viewed with interest by every admirer of the delightful productions of Madame Genlis, one of whose most charming tales is founded upon this very stone, which was formerly in the pos- session of Philippe Egalit6. By the side of this remarkable gem is a specimen of a very scarce variety of amethyst from Transylvania, with two emeralds, one of very considerable dimensions, engraved and arranged as a vinaigrette, their joint weight being 193 grains. There is another very large emerald in the collection. There is also an extremely beautiful asterias sapphire, showing a six-rayed star, and weighing 234 grains; and a gold-coloured cat's eye and an engraved jacynth after the antique. The largest known cat's eye, taken from the King of Kandy, is a stone of remarkable interest and great beauty. A crystal containing a drop of water, is a remarkable and interesting curiosity. Other specimens of interest are a Mexican opal, engraved with the face of the sun, and an engraved jacynth ring of Popes Gre- gory XIII and Pius VII. A carbuncle or garnet hooped into a cup, is remarkable for its size and rich colour, as is also a diamond cut against the grain as a cross. An engraved Oriental ruby of Cinque Cento date, is a very remarkable object; it represents the head of Jupiter. The remaining specimens, all of which possess more or less of interest and beauty, are a rich colou red turquoise with Persian writing, an emerald in the matrix, three beryls or aquamarines, an Irish beryl, and an engraved dichroite, after the antique. There are several specimens of pearls, one of which is quite black, another en- graved. of a pink colour; also a beautifully engraved emerald and cat's-eye, an enamelled garnet, a curious two-coloured topaz, showing pink and yellow in the same stone, and an asterias ruby. In ad- dition to these there are eight other opals, a white topaz, several green diamonds arranged as a cross, a turquoise in the matrix, a mina nova, four fine sun-stones. a very rare gem, a tourmaline of two colours, a ring set with five different stones, and jacynths. THE PUonTr HEALTE1-The mortality of London has been greater than usual during the four weeks of May. In the first three returns of the month the deaths numbered respectively 1,041, 1,002, 1,000. In the week ending last Saturday a decrease occurred, but not of con- siderable amount, the number having fallen to 990. Taking the weeks corresponding to last week of the ten years ) 841-50, it will be seen that the mortality, which in one instance fell so low as 736 (namely, in the fourth week of May last year), did not in any case exceed 960, and that the average was 855. If this average be raised in proportion to the supposed rate of increase in the population, it will amount to 933; compared with which the 990 deaths of last week exhibit an increase of 57. The zymotic or epidemic class of diseases produced last week 220 fatal cases, and of these 169 occurred among children under fifteen years. Small-pox had fatal termination to twenty-three persons, six of whom were twenty years of age and upwards; measles carried off 39 children, scarlatina 10, hooping-cough 64, and croup 5. Of these complaints, almost exclusively confined to young persons, hooping-cough much exceeds the usual contingent, and scarlatina falls still more below it. To diarrhoea 16 deaths are ascribed, to dysentery 6, to erysipelas 11, and under typhus, which shows about the usual amount of fatality for the present time, 32 are enumerated. The above class of diseases exhibits an increase on the preceding week, but those which affect the organs of respiration show a diminution. Laryngitis numbers 5 cases, bronchitis 51, pleurisy 6. pneumonia 64, and asthma 7; these, with other undefined diseases of the lungs, numbering in the aggregate 136 deaths, which is rather more than the corrected average of corresponding weeks. Four dis- eases are comprised in the tubercular class: scrofula, from which five deaths are enumerated last week ; tabes mesenterica, which counts ten, hydrocephalus 85, and phtbisis, or consumption, 150. In the ten corresponding weeks of 1841-50 the lowest number ascribed to consumption is 103, and the highest 166. The births of 764 boys and 769 girls, in all 1,533 children, were registered last week. The ave- rage number of six corresponding weeks in 1845-50 was 1,336. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Thursday the morning was chilly and wet; yet, as will be seen, the number of visiters was as great asindeed rather more than—it had been on the day before. The numbers were as follow : First hour, 10 to 11 o'clock 11.400 Second hour, 11 to 12 „ Third hour, 12 to 1 (about) Fourth hour, 1 to 2 Fifth hour, 2 to 3 4,300 Sixth hour, 3 to 4 47,000 Total up to 5 o'clock Between twelve and one o'clock a very striking and gratifying incident occurred—the entrance of a body of nearly 800 yeomen and agricultural labourers, all looking clean and comfortable, must of them in smock frocks, each bearing on his breast a small rosette of coloured ribbon ; and evidently in some degree organized and under regular guidance. Upon inquiry, we found that these good folks (many of whom were accompanied by their wives and children) had come up from three parishes—Crowhurst in Kent, and Linchfield and Lingford in Surrey (near East Grinstead, in Sussex); and that they had for some months been subscribing for the trip, under the auspices of the clergy, one of whom originated the idea, which was warmly espoused by the farmers and gentry. The arrangements bad been made with such admirable economy that the total charge per head—including not only the conveyance per rail, and a boat to Westminster bridge, but the shilling for admission—was only 3s. 2d.; that is to say, only 2s. 2d. for the expenses of travelling, for which the railway company only charged Is. Od. per head. The honest fellows appeared delighted,though somewhatconfounded, by the vastness of the Crystal Palace and the strange collection of objects among which they found them selves. It was amusing to observe how they seemed almost to stand in awe of the building; its greatness paralyzed them; they hardly liked to penetrate into the huge compartments which opened on each side, but stuck close to the crystal fountain; or if they moved forward, kept close together in small parties—the young ones held by the hand lest they should be lost, and even the adults seemed apprehensive of a similar disaster. To guard against this, the rosettes had been provided, and even other precautions taken ; the men were regularly divided, like the contents of the Exhibition itself, into classes or sections ; each division had a leader; and these leaders had prepared sticks on which were fixed cards with their names, which they held up, in order the better to "rally their men," as the hour appointed for their muster—four o'clock—approached. Before they had been in the building ten minutes the cry was raised—`‘ The boy Saunders is lost !"—but the good people were assured that the boy Saunders would not be in any peril. By degrees the leaders of divisions —each of them provided with a map of the buildingcontrived to draw off their people to the different corn • partineuts, and they and their eight hundred were soon merged in the thirty-five thousand who by that time were in the Exhibition. Occasionally they might be seen, one or two at a time, scattered through the building, looking amazed and astounded. At four o'clock they all mustered in the transept— at least as many as could find their way there—and went off in tolerable order, to return that evening, per railway, to the borders of Sussex. A cloudy morning, symptomatic of rain, ushered in the great holiday, Whit-Monday; but it could not damp or de- press, in the minds of the people, the pleasure-seeking spirit of the day. The great western road gave sign,' from an early hour, that the Crystal Palace had a rival in the one at Hamp- ton, for huge and well-filled vans were seen proceeding to the latter, early in the day. The Executive of the Crystal Palace had ordered the door-keepers and check-takers to be at their posts at nine o'clock; so that if there should be a great pres- sure of people waiting round the doors, they might be opened at that hour. This precaution, however, like so many others that have been taken, proved superfluous; for no one was there at nines, probably because it was not known that there was auy chance of the doors being opened at that hour. Soon after nine, however, the people began to pour into the Park from all quarters; and before the usual hour of opening, each porch of the building was encircled by a considerable crowd. Hlow rapidly and continuously they arrived, may be seen from the simple fact, that within the first hour-that is, by eleven o'clock-there were upwards of 21,000 persons in the building; nearly four times as many as on days when the place has been fairly filled, and twice as many as on eome of the heaviest days known; and nearly 4,000 more than on the very heaviest day before experienced. The stream of visitors still seemed to come up rapidly during the next hour, though it perceptibly slackened in the course of the third. Through- out these three hours there had been rain, at first gentle, but by this time becoming more rapid; and the arrivals dimi- nished in a corresponding ratio. Between two and three the fall of rain was steady and settled, and the diminution in the number of visitors was very rapid. The total amount re- ceived at the doors was 2,4368. 4s., and from sale of a season ticket, 21, 2s.-making a total of 2,43S1, os. From this statement it will be seen that there was no great crowding; and, in fact, as the visitors on this, as on every other shilling day, were distributed throughout the building, examining everything with attention, there did not appear to be so many present as there really were; and there was less crowding than is seen (in many parts of the Exhibition) on some five-shilling days. For example, the Russian compart- ment, which on Saturday week was like the Opera crnsh-room; was on Monday comparatively clear, although it was certainly occupied by a considerable number of delighted visitors-and the same remark applies to the place occupied by Mr. Hope's jewels, The presence of the shilling visitors seems equalised, ubiquitous, and impartial, and there is no particular pressure anywhere. The stream appears, like that of water, to find'its level: and circulating freely, to be at about the same height everywhere. There were, on Monday, honest fellows in fos- tian and corduroys, agricultural labourers in smockfrocks, and rural swains in their full dress of velveteen, with their sweet- hearts in bright-coloured shawls of scarlet or green, and operatives and artisans of every class, dressed in their best. It was amusing to observe the amazement of these good folks as they entered, and the bewildered look of their " upturned, wondering eyes," gazing up at the roof of the transept, during their brief pause of stunned and staggered astonishment, ere they plunged into the vast compartments opening on either side of it, with exclamations. such as one we overheard- Well, I suppose we can go where we like ?" Many of the humbler visitors came from considerable dis- tances; we know of one instance in which they came from St. Albans (walking to the railway-station at Hatfield, and from the station at Shoreditch), and went back the same way in the'evening. As the people entered, and were amazed by the magnitude of the edifice, they seemed in many eases sud- denly seized with a nervous dread of being lost in it, and such cries were heard as "Now, mind, let us keep together !" "Oh, where's Jim ?" And in the course of the day persons might be heard lustily calling out to each other, after the fashion of the " gods " of a minor theatre. Among the visitors we ob- served the Duke of Wellington and the Duchess of Sutherland. More than once in the course of the day, expresses were sent to Buckingham Palace to inform how things were going on. The weather was yet more unfavourable to holiday takers on Tuesday than on Whit-Monday. From the first the sky was cloudy and overcast, and rain soon set in, which con- tianed more or less all day. The entire number of arrivals on Tuesday was about 50,000; the money received, 2,2 811 li. Between five and six o'clock, when the visitors were rapidly departing, the aspect of affairs was about as miserable as it could be-more like an evening in November than in June- dull, chilly, wet, and dirty; but, happily, the multitude were of a sturdy class, so that they went away in good spirits and good humour. The bulk of the visitors were, as on Monday, of the hum- bler orders-many almost of the very humblest-downright day-labourers of every class, in every species of working- men's dress, smock frock, or jacket, or " shirt ;" plough- maen from the country, and porters from town; soldiers, and sailors, and tillers of the soil; workmen in every trade, and operatives in every kind of manufacture. These sons of toll often seemed rather confounded than enchanted by the works of art-the sculptures, or the statues-the figures, metaphorical or mythological-the Satyr or the Pan, the Amazon or the Venus, the Flora or the Lesbia. Dim ideas of the beautiful or the sublime were, no doubt, floating in their minds, but the hard crust formed by a whole life- of labour could not be all at once softened and illumined. At such eights they scarcely stopped-but wondered, and passed on. They found their feelings and their sympathies, however, more worked upon and laid hold of by some of those familiar images of loveliness which are scattered about-the children of Belzeni, or the infants of Urekin and Simonis, or such groups as those of the two orphans, by Miller, or the two pieces representing the child defended from a serpent by a dog. Works of art like these, breathing the warm affections and domestic associations of thecommon human heart, seemed to attract more attention than loftier creations of genius. And, again, it is to be ob- served that this class of visitors were more attentive to works of industry than of art; and, with the natural sympathies of their order, looked perhaps with even more interest at trophies of labour than at triumphs of science-at the speci- mens of indomitable industrial energy than at the most mar- vellous monuments of genius-at the works of the hammer or forge than at the achievements of the pencil or the burine. Hence they were found, for instance, carefully examining the specimens of brass work exhibited in one of the French stands (passed over by most of the five-shiling visitors), such as the brass pans, which won the gold medal of France in 1848 and 18 08, four feet in diameter, and weighing upwards of 1O0lba., all Brought by the hammer out of a single solid sheet of brass; or the coil of brass wire, 11,000 yards in length ; or circular bar of brass, 8 feet long by 5 inches thick; or the sheet of brass, 4 'feet by 4, and two inches thick, weighing 1t,-6olbs. So, again, in the Sheffield compartment they were to be seen intently inspecting the specimens of minute brass wire-wire so fine that hundreds of yards weigh only an ounce or so; or again, they would pause at the huge block of cast steel recently exhibited in " Erusaia"-aid so of many simi. I lar articles usually escaping the observation of more educated spectators. The visitors of Tuesday were not, however, at all indiffer- ent to the more magnificent objects exhibited, though they were attentive to the more homely ones. Thus the Russian compartment, although not at all inconveniently crowded, was evidently a great attraction, and was all through the day frequented by large numbers. Several additional objects *have been exhibited since the compartment was opened. In the plate-stand there are two superb pieces of frosted silver on a ground of gold, sculptured in relief, with repre- sentations, the oneof the " Passion," the other of the "' Taking down from the Cross." On the other of the two central stands are three large lumps of native platina, a precious metal, heavier and more valuable than gold, weighing respec- tively 211bs., 22lbs., and 25ibs,, all from the mines of Prince Demidoff; and two lumps of native gold, from the same mines, one weighing gibs. asd the other 6ibs. loz. On the stand against the American side is a carious pillar about eighteen inches high, of a dimly transparent substance, which the visitor will never conceive to be salt. The strange speci- men Comes from some celebrated salt manufacture in Russia. The great addition, however, consists in another casket of Jewellery, if possible, more brilliant and costly than the one before exhibited. The contents are:-1. A bouquet of roses, composed of diamonds. Value, 8001. 2. A bouquet of turquoises and diamonds. The turquoises are large, and five in number. Value, es5L. 3. A berths of diamonds and rubies, fully. eighteen inches long, comprising five clusters; the vine leaves (the size of nature) composed of diamonds, and the grapes of rubies, each cluster placed between pen- dants of the same gems. The value of this is about 3,0001. 4. A diadem, or tiara, composed of diamonds and emeralds- the emeralds thirteen in number, and exceedingly large and brilliant, some of them about an inch long. . The value of this is about 5,0001. It should be stated that these are said to be the values in Russia, where precious stones are far more cheaper than in this country. The berthe belongs to the Princess Woronzoff. Nothing can describe the beauty and brilliancy of the diamonds, which are so thickly spread on the' delicate silver filagree work which forms the setting as quite' to obscure it. Opposite this compartment the visitor will have seen two enormous pedestals, nearly three yards long,; by about two yards broad. These are designed. for two co- lossal statues in bronze, which form the two principal of the expected contributions, and which are of the same design asi the two spirited equestrian statuettes to be seen among the gilt bronze works on one of the two central stands. A superb. suit of Caucasian mail armour is likewise expected, with a splendid shawl worth 1,sOOl I I On Wednesday the weather became again auspicious to the Crystal Palace. The sun once more shone upon its trans-. parent roof, sparkled in the lustrous fountains, and shed the usual air of splendour on the scene. For nearly an hour be- fore the doors were opened, multitudes were wending their way towards the Exhibition. The Queen and Prince Albert were present inspecting the machinery. Among the machines which the. party more particularly inspected, may be men- tioned Messrs. Maudslay's models of steam-engines and ma- chines for hammering and stamping iron and other metals. At the stamping machine Messrs. 31audelay struck off a num- ber of medals, bearing on one side the image of Prince Albert, and on the other the royal arms, with the inscription,: "I Great Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations, London, 1851," and presented the Queen and the Prince, aun their visitors, with copies. The Queen next examined the printing, machinery, particularly MIr. Applegurth's vertical machine. This machine was shown in action. The party next pro- ceeded to some comman printing machines. Subsequently they examined the mechanism employed in lithographic printing, and the machine for cutting out and making. enve- lopes, and departed shortly afterwards, about a quarter to twelve. Generals ?larvaez and Messaros were present amongst the visitors. The concourse of early visitors was steady and constant, although not so rapid as on the day before; and only twenty- five thousand persons were present at mid-day. It will be seen that the total number of visitors was less by some thou- sands than on Tuesday. The day, though fine, as compared with the preceding one, was farlfrom warm or brilliant, and there were symptoms of wet in the afternoon. The Whit- suntide holidays, too, had passed away, so far as the working classes, at least, were concerned. The visitors, consequently were,ias on ordinary shilling days, of the middle class-small traders or farmers, yeomen rather than ploughmen, the higher sort of artisans, clerks, and so forth. Corduroys had been displaced by ierseymeres, and the jacket and the smock by the coat; -and not more than a mere sprinkling was to be seen ef persons of the humbler class. At ten o'clock Professor Tennant, F.GS., commenced a series of lectures on mineralogy. At two o'clock Professor Cowper lectured upon cotton-spinning. There are two lecture- rooms esected at the back of "' Turkey;" one of which is quite completed, the other nearly so, and which can hold from .200 to 250 persons each. 'There was a very good attendance at Professor Cowper's room, and he was listened to with great interest. At the back of the lecturer, upon a screen of green baize, were arranged coloured drawings and diagrams, repre- senting the flowers, stalks, and pods of vegetables of the fibrous order; and also exhibiting cotton wool in its various stages-as just gathered from the shrub, as imported, as woven, as spun into yarn, and as finally spun into, thread. To illus- trate and explain tie successive processes was the object of the lecturer, who had also before him a variety of models to be put into action, in order still further to elucidate the subject. Altogether, there were about 48S,01 visitors on Wednesday, being 2,000 less than on Tuesday. After three o'clock the day. was overcast, and the departures were very rapid, axd the arrivals proportionately few. The money taken amounted to 2,1651. 3I. SIR,—I shall feel much gratified by the insertion of the following recommendation relative to the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park in your paper, premising that I sent a letter embodying the greater Fart of the present with other observations, to a leading journalist. Whether it was received or not I am unable to say; at all events, it has not, as far as I am aware, appeared in the columns of that journal. . a atort period the Exhibition at the Crystal Palace will I assume be closed, and it will then be for consideration and determination in what way, after all expenses shall have been defrayed, the balance in hand shall be disposed of. I consider the Exhibition in its intention essentially artisan; and viewing it in that light I would, under the fullest consideration, respectfully suggest that the balance be appropriated to the erection of an asylum for the euppert of as large a number of decayed artisans as the fund would provide for, under such regulatioes and restrictions as shall seem judicious. By this disposal of the money the comfort end happiness probably of a considerable number of meritorious individuals would he iasured; and I kuo , ,v of no class whose claims for the benefit of such an asylum rank higher than those whose efforts have contributed so essentially to the success of this undertaking, and to whose labours we are indebted for the gratification so universally evinced.
