Hamid came to England in charge of the cases of Turkish goods for the Exhibition. From Stockholm news has reached to the effect that a pleasure excursion from that city to Paris and London, has just been organised for the beginning of June, and that 500 persons have taken tickets. From Vienna we have news to the effect, that the Emperor of Austria intends to exhibit a magnificent carved book-case (containing a quantity of unpublished national music ofthe 15th century), which he will after- wards present to the Queen. The Koh-i-Noor Diamond.— Mr. Chubb, of St. Paul's Churchyard, has been commissioned by the executive committee to manufacture an apparatus, according to a design submitted to him, for the safety of the Koh-i- Noor diamond. The plan adopted, whilst providing for the complete security of the gem, will allow a perfect view of its beauty. — Morning Chronicle. The Trees in the Building.- -Exhibitors, intending visitors, and the friends of the Exhibition generally, will be pleased to learn that the long-delayed order for the removal of the trees in the building, which have given so much annoyance to all parties concerned has arrived and preparations were immediately made for their removal. — Morning Chronicle. The Shoe-black. — On Saturday a number of young men, dressed in red uniform, and furnished with appa- ratus for cleaning clothes and shoes, were stationed in the vicinity of the Exhibition building and west-end thoroughfares. They are all lettered, and wear badges inscribed " The Shoeblack Society." They have been selected to these offices from the London ragged schools, previous to being assisted to emigrate. Progress of the Building. — The Executive Com- mittee have issued another red-lettered handbill, warn- ing exhibitors, native and foreign, that the Exhibition will positively and undoubtedly open on the Ist of May. We also learn that the contractors have entered into a positive arrangement with the Executive Com- mittee to have every foot of scaffolding removed from the interior by Saturday (this day) the 12th, and, as it is a matter of extreme importance that the building should be handed over at the earliest possible moment to the exhibitors, in order that they may push forward their preparations uninterruptedly, we do trust thai, this time at least, the promise made may be fulfilled to the letter. It is also reported that her Majesty has inti- mated it as her intention to open this great world's industrial triumph on the Ist of May. It is stated to be the determination of the Russian government to carry out a great extension of their railway system, which will, it is understood, embrace the great sections between Moscow and War >aw, and thus place St Petersburg in communication with Berlin, Vienna, Trieste, Paris, Lyons, Orleans, Brussels, and Amsterdam. The loan for this purpose is to bear a guarantee of five per cent, and is to be under the joint management of Baron Stieglitz and an eminent firm in this city. Suicide from London Bridge. — On Tuesday, an inquest was hold on the body of Mr. Charles Mayo, nineteen years of age, who resided with his father in Bedford-place, Rotherhithe, and had formed a strong attachment to a young lady living at Rotherhithe, but it seems some words had taken place between them, and she had sent him a note desiring that their correspondence should cease. This had a great effect on his mind, and, on the morning of Thursday, the 20th of March, he left a letter for the lady with her servant, and about three on the same after- noon the mate of the Citizen D steamer saw a body falling from the parapet of London Bridge, and the hat falling off, it was at once identified as the deceased's. His body was not found, however, till Monday last, when it was disco vered floating down by Horsleydown. He had a gold watch in his pocket, and a locket round his neck, which had been presented to him by the lady. Verdict — " Tem- porary insanity." The Socialists of Paris. — On Sunday afternoon a workman caused a crowd to assemble on the Boulevard St. Martin by addressing gross insults to every well dressed lady who passed. "Wives of aristos," he cried, "your laces and velvets shall be burnt; your husbands shall be hanged, and you shall be sent to the guillotine." Shortly after, seeing a carriage come up containing several ladies splendidly dressed, he cried, "Yon see that lady in that magnificent velvet cloak; I will bum it, " and at the same time he rushed to the carriage, clung to the door, and threw a bottle of vitrol on to the lady's dress. Fortunately her clothes only were burnt. The spectators, indignant at this act of fury, arrested him. When questioned by the Com- missary of Police, he said that he had long been tormented by the fixed idea of destroying the splendid toilette of some lady, and had purchased vitrol to effect his design. It is supposed that he is mad, and was sent to the Prefecture of Police. Scene in a Wild-beast Show. — On Saturday evening week, a scene took place in Wombwell's menagerie, at Rochdale, which produced a powerful impression on the minds of those who witnessed it. There were about 150 persons in the exhibition, and while one ofthe keepers was showing the hon cubs at one end ofthe place, there was a dreadful crash heard at the other end, which attracted the attention of the visitors. A huge and savage-looking ani- mal, called a South American tapir, of the hippopotamus species, had broken loose from its den, and walked majes- tically forth into the space assigned for the visitors. The people were terribly alarmed, and ran about in all direc- tions, jostling one another by the rapidity of their motions. The other animals were much excited by the noise and consternation produced, and the whole place appeared to shake in consequence of the sounds which issued forth from bipeds and quadrupeds combined. The keepers at length succeeded in restoring order, by assuring the people that the animal was quite harmless, and might be approached with safety. The keepers, assisted by others, were about twenty minutes in replacing the animal in his den. No accident occurred, and the people seemed no worse for the excitement which their fears had created. Wholesale Swindlers —Richard Douglas, otherwise Sir Richard Douglas, otherwise Captain Douglas, of Orpington House, Kent, Ascot Villa, Ascot, and No. 6, Belgrave-terrace, and his two sons, Charles and Arthur Douglas, were brought before Mr. Hard wick, at the Marl- borough Police-office, on Saturday, for final examination, charged with having, for a length of time, carried on a most successful system of obtaining goods from various tradesmen without the least means of paying for them, and in many instances by fraudulent pretences. It appeared from statements made in court that within two years the father and sons have succeeded in getting from between forty five and fifty tradesman £3,702 worth of property. On the elder prisoner a diary was found which revealed a system of living by the wits unexampled for success, auda- city, and extent. The diary for the year 1851 was kept in a business- like manner. It opened with a list ofthe names of gentlemen and ladies to whom begging applications for money had been made, the names of the parties who had not replied to the applications being brought forward and posted in quite a mercantile way. The first day of the year was opened by a prayer to Providence, to bless the exertions of the writer and his son, and make them more prosperous and productive than the last year. The three prisoners were committed on five charges; two for con- spiracy, and three for obtaining goods under false pre- tences. Charge of Adultery against a Clergyman.—Gais- ford v. Karr, clerk. — This was a case tried at the Glou- cester Assizes on Friday and Saturday last. The plaintiff was an attorney and solicitor at Berkeley, and had practised there since 1835, and the defendant was the vicar of that town, having been presented by Lord Fitzhardinge in 1839. Mrs. Gaisford was the daughter of a Mr. Ulph, a respectable timber-merchant at Lowestoft, in Suffolk, and had been adopted from infancy by the family of the late Rev. John Amyas, rector of Theustead, in that county. On the death of the rev. gentleman, his family removed to Bath, and Miss Ulph came with them, together with a maiden aunt, Miss Clarke, who was governess to the family. Miss Clarke died soon afterwards In 1835 the plaintiff was introduced to Miss Ulph, and became so en amoured, that, against the wishes of his family, who remon strated on account of his youth and her want of fortune, he married her in the September of that year. They lived most happily for several years. He was a fond and doating husband, and she was a most affectionate wife and mother. They had four children, all sons. The. eldest was. now thirteen, and the youngest seven. Unluckily for then- peace and happiness, the plaintiff was employed by the defendant, in 1840, to collect his tithes and manage his professional business. This led to an acquaintance and intimacy, which resulted in the ruin oi the plaintiff's hap- piness, and the blighting of all Ms fondest hopes. The evidence was very voluminous, and the case ultimately turned upon the point whether it was proved that the defendant and Mrs. Gaisford want to % disorderly house together. The jury, unable to agree, were looked up from five till half-past ten o'clock, when his lordship sent for them to his lodgings, and, on their saying that there was no chance of their agreeing if looked up for a month, dis- charged them without agreeing to a verdict..

HOBBS'S OF LOCKS.—His mode of working, as we are told, is this :—He applies a lever to press the bolt in a backward direction, and then proceeds, by means of instruments previously manufactured, to lift the tumblers of the lock one by one, and retain them in their right places. When the last tumbler is lifted the bolt flies back. Thirty days were given to Mr. Hobbs for his attack on the Brame'', and to make his instruments he was allowed to take impressions of the key and the tops of the wards. Day after day he was shut up alone with the lock, none being permitted to enter the room while he was at work ; and, with the aid of " thieves' wax" a hinged mirror in the key-hole, a strong light, all sorts of odd instruments, and his own great cleverness, he has succeeded in the task. For our own part we did-not think that any lock could be found, 'made at a cost which would admit of sale, to resist such appliances, and are astonished thatMessrs.Bramah consented to submit it to such practices for so long a period. Whether, after all, Messrs. Bramales challenge, as written on the lock, has been met by Mr. Hobbs, is a question: we think not, spite of the arbitrators' award. The challenge was, " The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas reward the moment it is produced." Where is the ins.ttrnment ? As to the American's own lock, the " Parantoptic," it is a wonderful piece of mechanism, put by its price quite out of the list of commercial locks; but whether even this is impregnable remains to be seen, and will, we hope, be tried. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The appearance of the building yesterday, when the admission was confined to the exhibitors and their friends, — when the receipt of custom was stopped, and the surveillance of the Executive Committee in its various branches and departments at an end, was decidedly unfavourable, and satisfied us at once that its usefulness had terminated, and that a wise discretion had been exercised in not adopting the suggestions and recommendations thrown out in vaiious quarters to keep it open for a still further period, and under altered circumstances. The Exhibition was evidently closed, and there appeared in its stead a huge bazaar, in which the buyers and sellers were doing a brisk trade, and the articles were apparently changing hands in both the British and foreign departments with an alacrity that must have been highly satisfactory. We do not suppose that the purchasers are permitted to remove the goods, but they are being rapidly stowed away, now that the object of the exhibitors has been so far accomplished; and in every quarter eye miss many rare and attractive specimens of art and art-manufacture; the counters and compartments here and there showing unmistakeable evidence of a clearance probably at what may be considered " enormous sacrifices." The London shopkeepers will certainly find the market pretty well glutted for the next month or two; and although the public were assured that all the foreign articles in the Exhibition were in bond for re-exportation, we were not deceived; and the inevitable result of such an immense accumulation of goods, thrown suddenly, as nine-tenths of them necessarily will be, upon the market, must be to depress trade, and inflict grievous injury and loss the home dealer. This, however, is one of the results of the Exhibition which we foretold some months ago; and the announcements pat forward in every quarter for the last few days of the unreserved sale of goods exhibited therein, is only what might have been anticipated. The expense of repacking, reshipping, and undergoing all the perils of a long sea and land transport, is so serious, that a sale in England upon any terms would be more advantageous. In front of the southern entrance a solid platform is being constructed for the;purpose of conveying out the larger and heavier packages. Many of the departments of machinery have already ceased working—a greater activity is observable among the Sappers and Miners, who have enjoyed a long respite from their labours, and significant notes of preparation for the final removal of the goods are observable in various quarters. The great Indian diamond, the Koh-i-noor, has been finally withdrawn from its iron prison, after having excited the wonder and the sneers of so many hundred thousand visitors, and to the great relief of the policeman who has been on duty beside the cage since the Ist of May. At present no preparations are being made for the ceremoni,l of to-morrow ; but as it will merely consist in the presentation of an address from the Chairman of the Juries, Viscount Canning, to his Royal Highness, and a brief reply from the Prince, in presence of the exhibitors, jurors, and foreign commissioners, little previous arrangement beyond the placing of benches and the erection of a temporary platform in the transept will be required. The Commissioners of the Exhibition have re- ported to the Queen on the general objects to which they consider it desirable to devote the Surplus Funds. The future results of the Exhibition admit of being made more important even than those already attained, while its character as an historical event cannot but be affected by the nature of the monument which shall record its existence and purpose. As its main object was to give a healthy progress to industry, its sequel must have reference to this end, or the name of the Exhibition will de- generate into the remembrance of a gigantic show. The intellectual Prince, to whom both its origin aud success are mainly due, doubtless contemplated results of a directly practical character; for the public were from the first apprised that, in consi- deration of their subscriptions being "absolute and definite," any surplus funds arising out of them would be devoted to objects strictly in accordance swith the ends of the Exhibition, or for the establishment of like exhibitions in future." We publish to-day the report to her Majesty on the destination of that surplus, which, it may be ob- served, falls legally, like the fortune of a man dying intestate, to the absolute disposal of the Queen. The Commissioners, under these circum- etauces, solicit her Majesty to renew the expres- sion of her confidence by granting a Royal charter, empowering them to recommend a scheme for the disposal of the surplus. They state that they do not consider it expedient to keep it as a reserve for future exhibitions, because the success of the one that is past gives ample guarantee that a future one will be self-supporting. They there- fore proceed to consider what is meant by the term used in their pledge-" the ends of the Exhi- " bition." These obviously mean the advancement of industry, and the promotion of a kindly feeling among nations. Let us examine, then, in what manner the industry of a country may be most ad- vanced at the present time. Iua manufactures, four elements are involved- viz., the raw material, the science or intellect en- gaged in adapting it to the purposes of industry, the capital employed in the purchase of the two previous elements, and the skilled labour put at the disposal of the superintending science. The raw material is a most important element of manufa* ture, but constantly diminishes in importance with the advance of civilization, while the science used in adapting it to industrial uses as constantly augments in value. Local advantages for a time do much for a nation ; they stamp its manufactures with a peculiar character, and even continue to give it a precedence as a manufacturing country over all other nations less liberally endowed by nature, until the natural superiority becomes levelled by science. England, annually producing 35,000,000 tons of fuel, was destined to advance foremost in the ranks of manufacturing nations, and she must continue in advance until some powerful transition reduces the value of this powerful auxiliary to industry. But as science pro- gresses, the transport by land and by sea is so much improved that the fuel and raw material of England, and of other producing countries, are spread over Europe, if not at equal prices, at least at a cost so little augmented by the transport, that any supe- riority in the science applied to its adaptation more than counterbalances the local advantages of the country which produced the raw material. The time therefore arrives when an industrial must be con- verted into an intellectual competition, and when two nations can only compete according as they equal or excel each other in the intellectual training of their industrial classes. The Exhibition gave powerful evidences, of this position, for nearly all the great nations were seen competing in the staple manufactures which, a few years since, were almost monopolized by England. Our woollen cloths were certainly not superior to those shown by Belgium or Russia, and were nearly equalled by those of the Zollverein. Our glass, both plate and flint, was usquestionably inferior to that of France and Bel- giuu, and, in purity of colour, to that of America. Our edge tools and agricultural tools, such as spades and dung-forks, were intensely clumsy, and invariably inferior to those of the latter country,even though the steel of which they were made was sent fronm England. Our calico printing was neither equal in colour nor design to that exhibited by our French neighbours; and, where it was equal, it was obviously designed by French artists. In some departmnts of manufactures, luckily for us, we did excel ; but even then English producers were startled by finding that foreign nations were rapidly approaching. In spite of our national vanity, it vas quite obvious that foreign countries were ad- varcing in industry with steps much more rapid than our own. The cause of this obviously was, that foreign nations had been compelled to com- pensate for their less and fewer local advantages by infusing into their manufactures a greater amount of science and of industrial skill. This intellec- tual superiority rises in importance at every onward step in civilisation, while mere local advantages of cheap fuel and raw material daily become of less value. But will our capital not save us from this don~ward progress ^ Is it not all powerful and all sufficient to buy foreign talent, and infuse it into our home manufactures, and thus compensate for Our past neglect ia not having fostered the scientific training of our industrial population ? Capital, no doubt, suffices to act as a temporary drag to our downward progress-only to slip away, however, aad allowv us to descend with accelerated velocitv afterwards. The Commissioners to the Exhibition, in announcing their desire toilevote the Surplus to the purposes of indus- l education, evidently regard their funds as quite insufficient to meet wants of such acknow- ledged imagnitude. They view the sum in their hands rather as a lever to move the public mind in this direction, and rely on its sympathy and mate- rial support for the means adequate to carry out the end in view. At the same time, when we recollect that the Prime Minister and other men of high political influence form part of the Commission, and that it is presided over by the Consort of the Queen, its decision cannot but be regarded as the authentic acknowledgment of a State necessity. Any system of industrial education must be pro- vincial as well as metropolitan. The chief manu- facturing towns have already pressed this view strongly on the Commission. Manchester, Bir- mingham, Sheffield, Hull, Sunderland, Leeds, Bristol, Nottingham, Leicester, and other towns have, by memorials from their leading manufac- turers, expressed their strong conviction of the necessity of an industrial education, not only pro- viucial, but metropolitan. It is not a mere ele- mentary scientific education which is required. The scientific alphabet being learned, further les- sons must be given how to use it in reading manu- factures. These towns do not, in their memorials, suppose that men can be made actual mauufac- turers in such institutions, but only that they can there learn the principles on which their industries depend, and thus be enabled to apply them advan- tageously in practice. There can be no doubt that provincial schools are necessary-that, in fact, they are indispensable as feeders to a large central collegeof manufacturers. They are essential to the development of the peculiar branches of industry carried on in the towns where they severally exist. The establish- ment of Schools of Design has been a faint expres- sion of this necessity. They have, it is true, been useful, on the whole, but much less so than they ought to be. Little more than drawing schools in most instances, they frequently turn out indifferent artists, and always bad manufacturers. It is, in- deed, obvious that they are radically wrong in principle, since it is hopeless for an artist to be useful to manufactures, of the wants and re- sources of which he is ignorant. A School of Design should certainly be only an integral part of a School of Industry. It is thus on the Continent, where the alliance between art and technical know- ledge produces such excellent effects. To ad- vauce in our industrial training, it is essential that Government should proceed to render more efficient their Schools of Design. The country has now decidedly expressed itself in favour of indus- trial education, and it will not submit to leave, in their present inefficient state, those Schools of Design, which, as the first expression of the want, would naturally appear to be the institutions upon which might be engrafted a more extended scheme of practical education. It would, of course, have been premature for the Commission to an- nounce, whether they look in this direction, or what is their detailed scheme for carrying out the industrial education which they announce their in- tention to promote. But we may venture to suggest the necesajy of including in their plan an adequate development of provincial schools, in full con- fidence that ?? wise considerations which have led them to decide upon the general objects to which their surplus is to be devoted, will also conduct them to an enlarged view of a general system of education, giving to the provinces and to the metro- polis equal benefits. In conclusion we may observe, that the necessity of engrafting upon the scheme of Education am international character is acknow- ledged in the Report of the Commissioners, who do not, however, explain by what means they intend to effect this desirable object. "May it please your Majesty, " We, the Commissioners appointed by your Ma- jesty's Royal Warrant of the 3d January, 1850, for the promotion of the Exhibition of the Works of Industry of all Nations, and subsequently incorpo- rated by your Majesty's Royal Charter of the 15th August, 1850, humbly beg to submit to your Ma- jesty the following report. " The Exhibition for the promotion of which we were appointed by your Majesty, was finally closed on the 16th of October of this year, and we humbly beg to report to your Majesty that the medals and prizes have been awarded to the successful exhibi- tors by the juries appointed to judge on the merits of their productions, and are in course of distribu- tion. The full reports of the juries will be laid before your Majesty when completed, together with the list of the successful competitors. We are now engaged in bringing to a close all the business connected with the Exhibition, and in defraying the various expenses incurred during its progress. Most of the claims on the funds at our disposal, how- ever, are already discharged, and after all shall have been satisfied, a considerable surplus will remain, the precise amount of which cannot be ascertained until the accounts are finally wound up, when they will be duly laid before your Majesty, but, which surplus we have reason to believe will not be less than £150,000. "This surplus will consist in the balance that may remain in our hands after deducting all ex- penditure from the sum of (in round numbers) £505,000, which has been derived from the follow- ing sources:- Subscriptions ?? £67,400 Entrance fees ?? 424,400 Casual receipts ?? 13,200 Total .£50.0... 0, " Of the entrance fees, a portion has been paid by foreign visitors, and it was owing to the fact that the contributions of all nations were there displayed, that the number of visits made by per- sons attracted to the Exhibition amounted to up- wards of 6,000,(00. " The subscriptions were derived, with few ex- ceptions, solely from your Majesty's subjects, and were made after a public announcement that they must be ' absolute and definite,' but that should any surplus remain, it was the intention of your Majesty's Commissioners 'to apply the same to purposes strictly in connection with the ends of the Exhibition, or for the establishment of similar ex- hibitions for the future.' " We humbly beg to represent to your Majesty that we are of opinion that it is not advisable to apply the surplus to the last-named purpose. Considering that the Exhibition which has just closed has afforded ample proof that an under- taking of this kind can be made self-supporting, and that it may safely be left to the public again to provide, when required, the means of meet- ing the preliminary exponses-conuidering also the impossibility of fixing long beforehand any definite period for the repetition of such an Exhibi- tion, which requires for its success so many concur- rent circumstances-we are of opinion, that greater benefit may be derived by the public from a ju- dicious application in the interval of the means at our disposal to the furtherance of the general ob- jects for which the Exhibition was designed, and in such a manner that the advantages which may ! be obtained should not be confined solely to your Majesty's subjects, but should be shared, as far as it may be possible, by other countries. " These objects, your Majesty's Commissioners conceive to have been the furtherance of every branch of human industry, by the comparison of the processes employed, and of the results obtained by all the nations of the earth-and the promotion of kindly international feelings, by the practical illustration of the advantages which may be derived by each country from what has been done by others. Your Majesty's Commissioners have the satisfaction to be able to express to your Majesty their conViO- tion that the Exhibition has, to a great extent, at- tained these objects, and that in its consequences the most beneficial results may yet be expected. " Already many requirements on the part of the public have become apparent during the course of the Exhibition, and have found expression in various suggestions made to us for the application of the surplus; many of them, however, were for objects quite inconsistent with the pledges above alluded to, whilst others, though for purposes in accordance with them, were of a limited, partial, or local character. " Your Majesty's Commissioners are of opinion that no measures could be so strictly in accordance with the ends of the Exhibition as those which may increase the means of industrial education, and ex-- tend the influence of science and art upon pro- ductive industry. We are fully aware of the diffi- culty of devising a comprehensive plan to meet these objects; should the view, however, which we have taken as to the manner of fulfilling our pledges, meet with your Majesty's approbation, we beg to assure your Majesty that we shall give our fullest and most careful consideration to this im- portant, subject, and we would suggest that full time should be afforded us to consider and mature such a plan, as we should feel warranted in lay- ing before your Majesty, the more so as from the disproportion between the end proposed and the means at present applicable to it, much will depend on the extent of, and co-operation we may receive I from the public. " We are advised, however, that our powers under your Majesty's Royal Charter will cease when all the expenses incidental to the Exhibition shall have been discharged, and notice thereof given to your Majesty's Secretary of State, and that we have not the power of deciding upon the disposal of the sur- plus. " If, therefore, it be your Majesty's pleasure that we should act further in this matter, it will be neces- sary, before we can take even any preliminary step, that your Majesty should grant to us by royal charter such further powers as your Majesty may deem necessary, to enable us to lay before your Majesty a scheme for the application of the surplus in accordance with the expectations held out to the public, and with the sanction and approval of your Majesty, to adopt such measures as may be neces- sary for such purpose. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. -•--- Resuming our tour in the French section, and entering the bay opposite the great organ in the nave, we meet with a large display of dressing-cases, pocket-books, work-boxes, and various other articles of a similar kind, not exhibiting any particular feature either of pattern or manufacture. In fact, in the latter respect, most of the things of this class found in the French depots are vastly inferior to those shown in the English district. The statuettes, vases, flagons, &c e lla porcelain, on the opposite side:of the bay, executed by M. Gille, are very beautiful specimens of a pretty species of domestic ornament, and the chimney-piece, painted elaborately with figures & la Watteau, exhibits the very perfection of a branch of pictorial art no less dainty than graceful. The liqueur-cases, portfolios, flower-stands, and two or three ' specimens of tulip-wood cabinet work, merit no more praise than that bestowed upon the other articles of the same kind to which we have before alluded. They are all delicate and fanciful to look at, but examination of the work is apt to spoil the charm. The next parallel bay is filled with a large collectioe of china, earthenware, and stoneware—also some superb lustres, and statues by Valin. The enamellings of Boudin and of Colville are well worthy of examination; the portraits—including the Queen and the Prince, being remarkable for their brilliancy and finish. Passing the stand of "artistic cabinet work," and seine farther samples of enamelled pottery, we tarn into the next bay, in which there are a variety of stone carvings for sepulchral and other uses. The earthenware here is particularly fine, and so also is the biscuit china,—the shapes evincing grace and novelty of design, and the execution sharpness and decision. The funereal vases, and other symbols of like import, are well modelled, and suggest the sentiment intended to be enforced in good and appropriate taste. The French bay adjoining Switzerland, on the east side, is partly filled with specimens of carving and gilding, some lookingglasses and picture-frames by M. Lombard, at once seizing the attention by the depth and beauty of their ornaments. A door in the style of the period of Louis X IV., a pilaster of a figured frieze in the Renaissance style, and some smaller works, are prominent illustrations of the skill of M. Huber; while the carvings of M. Hardouin are equally good as instances of decorative art. The visitor on turning to the opposite side of this vestibule will be struck with the pictures in relief of M. Bourgery. These comprise several sorts of subjects, such as fruit, fish, &c., carved we presume in wood, and then painted richly after nature; the effect is certainly very forcible and graphic, and the bright natural colours, combined with the tangibility of detail, give them an air of positive reality. There are several other specimens of the same kind of mimetic art in the French department. They are curious only because they are so real; they make no pretensions to ideality of any kind; on the contrary, a hard literal resemblance is all that is aimed at, and this is accomplished with excellent effect. As specimens of carving they are perfect. Some of the subjects we may mention are pathological, and here we have a recurrence, as far as appearance goes, of the old form of modelling certain surgical autopsies in wax. In the immediate vicinity of these models are some articles in cartonpierre by M. Leschesne, together with some small carvings in oak, and other fancy articles, which are of merit. The short aisle going south contains some varied displays of woollens, satins, merinos, kerseymeres, waistcoat pieces, twills, linen tissues, ticks, and the like; but the principal show of articles of this kind is confined to the long aisle which runs at right angles, and the spectator finds nothing here to interest him either as regards purity and brilliancy of colour or superiority of texture. Returning into the nave, and entering into the next bay, we find ourselves in a charming little store-house of the fine arts. The ivory carvings of M. Tellier are extremely beautiful, the ship fully rigged which stands in the centre of his contributions being a noticeable instance of careful and industrious labour. Then there are some paintings of porcelain by different artists more or less delicate and skilful, some bronzes—particularly a battle-piece of minute and multitudinous detailan ivory vase exquisitely embossed with the same sort of subject, some wood carvings, some dagurreotypes good, bad, and indifferent, and several pastel drawings. A gallery of works by this process was opened a year or two ago at the West-end of the town, at which were exhibited a variety of fine and effective specimens, well illustratieg the soft and eligible character of this medium for portraiture in preference to the harder and less manageable vehicle of oil. But crayon painting is no novelty in this country. Years ago it was in considerable vogue, and several of our native artists were distinguished for their adroitness in the art; but it has fallen into disuse,partly through the capriciousness of fashion, and partly, probably,through the decline of manipulative shill. The exhibition to which we have alluded has in a measure restored the taste, and the French artist who originated it is reaping a large harvest in the higher circles by the dexterity he evinces in this particular application of coloured crayons. The portraits by this process at the Crystal Palace are striking proofs of its excellence as a medium for the representation of female heads; the copies of fancy pictures are not so good, the gaiety of the colours bordering on the vulgar, suggesting the idea of a common and cheap style of brightness. The specimens of fictile ivory, though wanting in the sharpness incident to the ordinary cutting, are very good. The remainder of the contents of the bay comprise a variety of miscellaneous articles, such as gelatine figures, a porcelain plate, upon which are excellent portraits of her Majesty and Prince Albert, some capital carvings, the most noticeable of which are a holy water basin in pear-tree wood, an oval frame encircling a composition of the Virgin and Child, and a series of medallions, executed by different artists, illustrative of religious subjects. There is also a mosaic of the head of Christ, curious on account of its obvious antiquity. The parallelogram apartment,into which the foregoing bays lead, is of inferior interest to that which contains the bronzes and silver work. We here meet with nothing but a collection of small shops, devoted to sundry gay but unimportant displays. We successively pass cases of buttons, imitation gems, jewellery, steel pens, head dresses, painted fans, steel purses, cutlery, door-knobs, hair plaitings, cornelian ornaments, and an infinity of articles of like insignificance, though making up a very pretty and glittering ensemble. The centre tables are loaded with the same kind of matters, demonstrating many of the small handicrafts in which our lively French neighbours excel—such as bijouterie, bracelets, masonic decorations, smelling-bottles, beads, tortoiseshell snuff-boxes, coiffures, cigar-cases, portmonnaies, watch-keys, souvenir tablets, and hundreds of other things, quo nunc prescribere, &c. The fire-place and mantel-piece, by M. Luce, at the west end of the chamber, is, perhaps, the object that the most decisively arrests the attention. Covered with mirrors, tastefully let into light panellings, and beautifully embossed with arabesques and floral emblems, the general effect is exceedingly good, and when associated with the gay furniture of a drawing-room, and illuminated with the reflection of numerous candelabra, nothing, no doubt, would be more pleasing. There are some electro-platings in the neighbourhood of this fire-place which seem to be, as far as outward appearances go, successful applications of the Elkington process. But the ladies are most amused with the mechanical birds, which, by an iegenious combination of clock-work, hop about from branch to branch, spread open their wings, and chirrup a roulade of little delicate notes. The naturalness with which all this is accomplished is curious; and the toy, we apprehend, is covetted every hour of the day. The baskets made of feathers and the bouquets made of glass are also suggestive illustrations of the skill of the Parisians in turning trifles to account. The bay leading into the nave contains a superb show of Hadrot's moderator lamp, which burns by means of a spring wound i up periodically like a clock. This lamp s well known in the metropolis, and the display at the Exhibition simply exhibits it in a variety of patterns in bronze, marble, and porcelain, many of thorn exceedingly beautiful, and encrusted with ornaments of the most elegant and recherché design. There is likewise an extensive assortment of giraudoles and suspension lamps. The figured silks, lampas, and damasks of Lemire, the great manufacturer of Lyons, make a magnificent tableau at the entrance of the bay; and this effectively contrasts with the group of consoles, cabinets, and other specimens of decorative upholstery, at the opposite corner. The articles in question partake of the ordinary characteristic of Parisian furniture, the outside show being remarkably indicative of taste; the inside work only of clumsiness and negligence. The long sweeping folds of curtains and table•covers which descend from the gallery into the nave at the next projecting point, convey a sentiment of the extremest costliness. The gigantic dimensions of the patterns, and the exquisite beauty of the manufacture, well merit all the encomiums that the spectators unite in bestowing. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Friday, May 30. — T0-day the price of admission, as settled by the Royal Commission, was half-a-crown. It was not anticipated that tiie number of visitors would be great, nor was it so, but the result exceeded the cal- culations made, and the receipts at the doors were £2,839 Bs. The police returns represent that 30,345 persons entered the building during the day. Her Majesty and the Royal family continued their inspec- tion during a great portion of the morning, the people mside conducting themselves with marked propriety. During her last two visits the Queen has taken parti- cular notice of several branches of national industry, the contributors to which will feel flattered by such attention. She examined closely the specimens of Paisley shawls and the needlework of the Scotch and Irish peasantry. Some embroidered vests from Belfast exhibited by Mr. M'Gee, especially attracted her ; and the collection of embroideries by Salomons and Sons was also much admired by her. Her Majesty looked over with great care and interest the display of Lyons silks, and the muslins and printed fabrics of Mul- hausen. Saturday, May 31.— Today the charge for admission to the building was ss. Owing to the attractions of the drawing-room, of a review at Woolwich, and of the other festivities connected with the celebration of her Majesty's birthday, there was a smaller attendance of visitors than usual, the number being only between 15,000 and 16,000, and the receipts being £1,771 125. 6d. A considerable sensation was created in the building by the appearance among the visitors of a Spanish family, dressed in their picturesque national costume. They were accompanied round the interior by Lord Rane- lagh, and were stared at and crowded round with a per- severance and impudence which, considering the charge for admission, and the presumed presence, in conse- quence, of a rather select assemblage, said very little for its good breeding. Greeks, Persians, Egyptians, Indians, Turks, and Armenians, have all been allowed to exhibit their finery since the Exhibition opened without let pr hindrance, but the appearance of a Spanish sen ora in the dross of her country offered too great an attrac- tion to be resisted in deference to the ordinary rules of politeness. Monday, June 2. — The receipts at the doors yesterday amounted to £2,129, and the number of spectators who entered the building was 45,000 to 50,000. The ex- treme beauty of the weather was in favour of a great concourse of people, and the evidences of an extensive importation from the country were more conspicuous than they have hitherto been. It was particularly re- markable in the large number of Quakers present, pro- bably attracted to town by the religious meetings of the season. There was also a very considerable influx of people evidently from the rural districts, and not much above the condition of labourers. They were respectably clad, and had brought their families with them. The crowds who thronged the Exhibition to-day approached nearer the ideal upon which the scale of shil- ling admissions was fixed than anything that we have yet witnessed. The mass was well leavened with the unmis- takeable traces of a labouring population ; it was at once interesting and gratifying to observe how, after a short time spent in simple wonder and astonishment each seemed by a natural instinct to betake himself to those departments upon which he could bring his own prac- tical knowledge most distinctly and intelligibly to bear. Every portion of the interior was well examined, and, though crowds still collect round the more curious and attractive objects, there is evidently a singular instinct at work among the body of the community to which our upper classes were not subject. . While they re- tained possession of the building, the eastern, or foreign half, Was more favoured and frequented. Now the western division comes in for the largest amount of admiration. Altogether, the conduct of the visitors to the Exhibition, now that the price of admission is lowered to Is., is beyond praise, and amply vindi- cates the confidences reposed in their good behaviour. Her Majesty and the royal visitors came to the Crystal Palace at nine o'clock, and, as some 400 or 500 exhibi- tors had been formally requested to be present, more than usual interest attached to the occasion. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. LOCOMOTIVE ENGINES. The collection of machinery under this head embraces e consideraMe variety of forms of construction and poner. We may here see the gradual development of railway traffic illustrated by the improvement in the mode by which that traffic is now worked or proposed to be worked. The practical advocates or theoretic admirers of the light engine system, can ii.spect the best and most beautiful specimens of tank-engines of nine or ten tons weight, admirably adapted for the traffic of most of our branch lines, but which several of our ingenious engineers and manufacturers desire to have applied to the working of the passenger trains of main lines, such even as the Great Western and London and North-Western; while the practical and experienced railway man will perhaps have his attention confined chiefly to the specimens of those immense locomotives, the power of which is equal to the heaviest of our passenger trains at high speeds, in all states of the weather. Of the smaller class of locomotives, we may mention those by Messrs. England and Co., of Ilatcharn Works, near Deptford, of Mr. W. B. Adams, of Bow; of Messrs, Kitson and Co., of Leeds, and Messrs. Fairlyern, of Manchester. In the engines of Messrs. England 4U:i Co., and Mr. Adams, we have a return to the weight of the "old Rocket" of Robert Stephenson, the lozomotive which carried away the prize in the trial of speed and power on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1330, but with such engines we have, in the details of construction, the improvements that have since that time been introduced by various engineers. There are intermediate sizes of locomotives, until we arrive at the engines to which we have already alluded—viz the " Liverpool," constructed on Mr. Crampton's principle, with the driving-wheel placed behind the fire-box, so as to lower the centre of gravity, and which engine was constructed. during the war of the gauges for the purpose of demonstrating that a narrow gauge locomotive could be made equally as pcvverful, for the conveyance of passenger trains at high speeds, and as safe, as those of the broad gauge light-wheel locomotives, one of which, " The Lord of the Isles," is to be found in the exhibition. Tne weights of these engines are about equal, viz. , 31 tons Each, with) water or co'ee. The commercial question which presses itself upon the public writer in noticing the small and large classes of locomotive engines, is the economy, efficiency, or safety of their application in working the traffic for which they are designed. Experience, in the working of our principal railways' has proved that economy, i n re f erence to heavy traffic, is to be effected only by the introduction of powerful engines equal to the maximum traffic, rather than by increasing the number of trains, and increasing, consequently, the number of servants employed, or by placing two or three engines upon one train. The use of light engines rendered the arrangements for working a large goods traffic on the same rails used by the passenger trains a very difficult matter, on account of the great difference in the speed of the two classes of traffic, and the liability to delays, and, therefore, the chances of accident. The use of two engines to a train is also disadvantageous, not only from the augmentation of expense which is involved in a multiplication of servants, but in repairs also, as the wear and tear of one large engine is in but a slight degree more expensive than the wear and tear of a small engine per mile run. Another objection to the use of two engines to a train is the difficulty of managing the former so as to start,. stop, and work the latter without considerable jerking and destruction to the stock. To work passenger trains at the high speeds which the public now require, it is necessary, if economy is to be studied, to have large driving-wheels. These ' large wheels can have the requisite power supplied to then only by the use of large cylinders, which in their turn must be supplied by a largaboiler. This principle has bEea carried out, both in Mr. Crampton's "Liverpool" and its Mr. Gooch's "Lord of the Isles," both of which haveeight-feet driving-wheels, eighteen-inch cylinders, and an enormous amount of heating surface. As an element of economy in the wear and tear of the permanent way, both these engines have eight wheels. This enables the engineer to distribute over four wheels the large amount of weight which is usually thrown upon the single pair of leading wheels in uncoupled six-wheeled engines, and at the same time gives as we have found in practice, considerable steadiness to the engine when running at high speeds. Another element of considerable importance ia the use of very powerful engines is the ability which they afford of meeting the demand for low rates, which it is now imperative on railway companies to charge, if they desire, under the present system of competition, to obtain a fair proportion, for instance, of coal traffic. Indeed, to carry this traffic at all with anything like profit, the companies must charge not only a low rate per ton per mile, but they must so economise their stock and fuel that every teen shall take the largest possible amount of net weight. This can be done over variable gradients only by the use of engines of very great power. For instance, the Great Western Company are now constructing broad gauge waggons, weighing under four tons, for the purposes of carrying each 10 tons of coal, and it is estimated that by using this class of waggon, their large engines will be enabled to draw about 300 tons net over the various gradients of their lines. By no other means will railway companies find themselves able to carry coal a long distance at the low rates competition has induced. This principle of economy appears to be fully recognised in the construction of several of the engines, as well as in that of some of the rolling stock exhibited, several of the passenger carriages being constructed for the express purpose of taking a large number of persons with the smallest possible amount of dead weight. And here we may observe that some of those practical men who in 1845 and 1346 were the strenuous advocates of small vehicles for the accommodation of railway traffic, now appear to be among the foremost in the admiration of engines of the greatest power and carriages of the largest possible dimensions. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. "The cry is still, they come !" Every day adds to the number of visitors; and we have some doubts whether, when the price falls to a shilling, there will be any possibility of examining the contents of the building with either satisfaction or advantage. The season ticket-holders will therefore do well to avail themselves of their present comparative freedom from interruption, as the number even of this class is daily increasing, those who have paid ss. for a day discover , that they have been unable, in the course of a ramble of some hours, to do more than glance hurriedly over the general arrangements and plan, and that the best economy is 1 to purchase a season admission. If we may judge from the g-neral sprinkle of rain that fell through the transept a day or two since, we should say that the labours of the contractors are not yet terminated. We were sorry to observe that in the galleries, also, some water had penetrated, and in one or two of the foreign departments costly goods that had been exposed have been again covered up. We have no doubt, however, that a little time and patience will set all this to rights. Outside, matters are still in great confusion; although some progress has been made in clearing away the accumulations of rubbish—the east end is comparatively free, but along the north side and around the west entrance, the heaps of timber and debris of materials that encumber the ground is extraordinary. Outside the wesern entrance there appears to be growing up another exhibition, the reflux or overflowing of the crowded compartments within, and when these singular and somewhat heterogeneous materials are placed in some sort of order, and where the visitors can obtain access to them, we have no doubt they will be found to have a merit of their own which the selected articles within do not invariably display. The timber employed in constructing the state entrance for her Majesty on the opening day is still piled up to a great height at the back of the building, and here hundreds of men, women, and children, are all day long scrambling up and down to obtain a peep at the g:ories of the transept, and of the happy promenaders inside. A sawing and carpentry establishment on a large scale is carried on in the same neighbourhood, to complete the second and third refreshment courts, which are not yet finished, although by no means impracticable, If we may judge from the numbers who frequent them. Still nearer the eastern end, and opening into the French department, is a small door, at which are stationed two sentinels and two or three policemen. This is the private entrance by which her Majesty and the Prince arrive at and take their departure from the Exhibition in their early morning visits, which are now become almost matters of course. They evince the deep interest taken by the Royal pair in the success of the undertaking, and we doubt not the personal desire of both to examine, as far as practicable, the many curious and wonderful productions displayed therein. The Serpentine looks somewhat animated in the back-ground with its fairy yachts and the miniature frigate, which of late has swung lazily at her anchors, " her gellant crew," in all probability, playing at marbles on the main-deck instead of "long bowls" with the enemy. The mere outside spectators have dwindled away to a few hundreds—the police arrengemeets compel them to remain on the opposite aide of the carriage drive—and few stay longer than just to gratify their curiosity with a look at the building. We shall commence our notice of to-day with a look at the compact and well-arranged stalls and counters of Belgium. Her contributions may be divided into three great heads; laces and embroideries, cloths and stuffs, and metalliferous productions, with the usual variety of miscellaneous matters, such as leather—raw and manufactured—carriages, paper. hangings, musical instruments, &c. The whole is typical of the industrial energies of the country, and of the vast progress she has made during the last 20 years. Fortunately for her, the revolutionary storm of 1848 swept over Europe without crossing her frontiers, and left her free to proceed with the development of her mining and manufacturing resources; and the number and character of her contributions are a sufficient proof of the advance she has made in these departments. We shall pass over, for the present, these more solid and permanent characteristics of the nation, and address ourselves in the first instance to a manufacture which has rendered her capital famous for centuries; we mean lace, although, by the way, little is now manufactured in the city of Brussels. In the north central gallery there is a very interesting and artistic display of the varioes descriptions manufactured in Belgium, in ladies' berthes, frills flounces, lappets, veils, skirts, robes, &c., in Brussels, Valenciennes, tulle, application, point, guipure, and all the other varieties, including Pompadour. The value of the manufactured articles may be estimated when we state, that the flax thread used in the net costs from 100 to 140 guineas per lb. weight—this is owing to its exquisite fineness, evenness, and strength. Vanderkelea-Bressen exhibits, among other specimens, a handkerchief with the arms of England, and emblematical figures of Justice, Glory, and Industry, surrounded by wreaths of fruit and flowers, shaded with the needle. This is one of the most elaborate of the many gossamer-like tissues we have seen—a perfect toile d'araignee, just enough to pinch between a fair lady's finger and thumb, and press to her lips as something very dear to her, and precious it is, the price being somewhere about 1000 francs. Notwithstanding its delicacy, its beauty, and its costliness, there is one stage further necessary to render the handkerchief complete. Having secured it, the fortunate possessor must proceed along the gallery to the north of the transept, and there will be found, as the fairy tales say, a fountain of ever gushing golden water, guarded by a very civil dragon in the shape of a police official, who permits you to dip your handkerchief in the golden stream, and you have then arrived at the acme of mouch.oir perfectibility. We thank the Messrs. Rowland and Son for this courteous and delicate attention to the fashionable visitors at the Exhibition, which they are apparently not slow to avail themselves of. The perfume is a new and delicious one, and its fregrance is retained for a long period. There is another handkerc'nief of guipure, point de Venise, which is also of exquisite fineness, and some Mechlin lace lappets the pattern and finish novel and tasteful. Adjoining the lace department is the gold and silver embroidery, which is employed in Belgium chiefly in the ornamentation of clerical robes, and for other church purposes. The work is gorgeous and almost heavy, but the introduction of gold tissues of different tints gives it some variety. For the purpose of illustrating the extent to which this style of decoration is carried, there are exhibited, in large glass cases, life-size figures of Affre, Archbishop of Paris, who was killed in the streets during the last revolutionary outbreak in 1843, St. Ca.rlo Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, and St. Thomas A'Beckct, Archbishop of Canterbury,all attired in their archiepiscopal robes,with mitre, crozier, &c., and all overloaded with embroidery and lace to an extent the taste of which appears to us questionable. A new art, which we recommend to the study of blue-nosed young ladies during the prevalence of the east winds, is called Xylopyrography, and consists in the making designs on wood with a red-hot iron—the effect is that of a sepia drawing. A Monsieur Henricq, who announces himself as printer to "the Holy See, the Sacred Congregation of the Propaganda, and the Archbishop of Maliees," exhibits a large bock-case full of rituals, missals, &e., in gorgeous bindings, and close at hand is one of those large figures of the Virgin and Child so common in the Belgian churches—the whole party dpparently very much out of place in an exhibition of practictil industry. The bijouteria, medals, medallions, glass, and china, which are also placed in the gallery, possess no peculiar excellence. Descending to the nave, we find several casts in plaster to illustrate the progress of Belgian modelling. A large group of the "Lion in Love," with the inscription "Amour, Amour, quand none liens, on pent bien dire, adieu prudence !" is remarkable for the expression of confiding:affection in the recumbent figure of the lion, over whom a female figure is bending with a look of arch triumph while she clips his talons. It is a well-conceived and pleasing group designed by Geefs, of Bruszels. Jeholte exhibits a large marble figure of "The Virgin and Child," the expression of which is admirable, and the draperies graceful. The "Indian Mother," by Cuyper, is an adecting subject touchingly treated, but not well adaptel for statuary. "A Girl feek/ing a Bird" is a pretty and graceful conception. Ch. Geerts, of Louvain, has some very elaborate specimens of wood-carving for church decoration. One is a figure of the Virgin and Child surrounded by angels; the grouping and expression of the faces are good; but the grain of the wood is much too coarse for the delicate carving. Designs for pulpits, &c., by the same artist, are also exhibited. The display of carpeting and tapestry from the Royal manufactory at Tourney is large and highly cred itable; there are specimens of velvet pile, Brussels, hand-worked carpets, imitations of Smyrna, Wilton, &c.; they are well covered, and the patterns rich and in good taste. A Wilton carpet, representing the ancient coat of arms of the Netherlands, and various allegories, is a model of patient industry and ingenuity. The central compartments south of the nave contain a very extensiveand neatly-arranged show of woollen manufactures, flannels, plain, cross-barred, and coloured; mixed fabrics, pure cotton printed calicoes, linen, sail cloths, thread, towels, damasks, and other textile fabrics. The whole is highly creditable to the looms of Verviers, Tourney, Courtray, Alcst, and the other manufacturing districts by which they are contributed. The cloths generally are strong and durable, but they want the finish and delicacy of surface of our English manufactures. Behind these come the iron and other metallurgical productions. The Royal cannon foundry at Liege sends specimens of cast-iron cannon, prepared with coke and wood; a light Netherlands piece, short Belgian piece, howitzers, mortars, bombs, shells, shot, and all the other military materiel for which this foundry is famous. There is a large display of fowling-pieces, muskets, pistols, and blunderbasees, from the manufactory of Ancion and Co., of Liege, arranged round a circular stand. The light pieces are well finished, and the stocks beautifully polished and inlaid with gold, silver, steel, &c. The adjustment of the stock to the shoulder appears to be well considered. We have only room to notice the specimens of crude iron and ores and the leather department, which is extensive

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The fluctuations in the daily attendance at the buildirg are extrsmely puzzlirg, and it is as difficult to account for the jump from 50,000 on one shilling day to the 74,000 on another, as to explain the occasional collapse that takes place, of which Saturday was a remarkable instance, follow. lug closely upon the plethora of the previous days. The building presented a very deserted look, and at any time one might have counted all the persons in the trausept. The only places where we observed anything like a crowd were the neighbourhood of the tent in which the Koh -i-noor is displayed, and the nave near the French organ, on which M. Adolphe Hess, Doctor of Music in the College of Prussia, and organist of the church of St. Bernard, Breslaw, a proftssor of some eminence, played for upwards of an hour a selection from Bach's and his own compositions. The thinness of the attendance may have been occasioned partly by the threatening appearance of the weather, the rain having fallen at intervals during the morning, and the attractions of the Chiswick flower show, which, as being the last this season. was sure to be numerously attended. The Duchess of Kent and suite visited the building in the morning, and spent an hour and a half in exsmining some portion of its contents. The Duke of Cambridge was likewise present, but rather later in the day, and in passing through the central gallery held out his hand for a spoonful of Jean Maria Farina's de Cologne, which was supplied to him by the attendant. The quantity consumed at the various fountains on Friday averages three to four spars each, and on the Saturdays about half that quantity. In the north end of she trausept a carpet loom has been erected by Messrs. Jackson and Graham, and two females are now constantly employed in working an Axminster carpet of very handsome design. The value of this costly fabric may be inferred from the fact that it takes two workwonien three weeks to make a singlet yard, and this is of course exclusive of the value of the materials employed. At three o'clock in the afternoon a performance of classical music took place upon Willis's great organ, which was never heard to better advantage, in consequence of the absence of the usual noise and bustle. The ies , rumentalist was Mr. G. W. Morgan, and the performance appeared to give much satisfaction. With resard to the safety of the building as a depository of valuable property, about which we have heard some doubts expressed, we believe that there need not be the slightest apprehension entertained. There is a body of 60 policemen constantly on duty during the night, and these are assisted by 24 Sappers and Miners, half of whom are always on foot. In addition to these, there is a numerous and efficient fire brigade, and cisterns of water opened in various places, stirrounded by buckets full of water. A strong military force ift also stationed in the immediate neighbourhood, whcse services could be rendered available in a few minutes, and the electric telegreph enables the parties in charge to communicate instantaneously with the most remote parts of the metropolis. Very few lights are permitted, but sufficient to enable the watchers, with ordinary vigilance, to detect any persons lurking about, should any such have escaped the strict scrutiny and examination the whole building undergoes every evening. In the foreign displays of bronzes the most striking and prominent are the colossal lion of Muller of Bavaria, and his two heroic statues. The lion is 14 feet long by Bin height, and was cast in one piece. It is modelled from a design by Halbig, and forms one of four intended to be yoked to a triumphal car to crown one of the city gates of Munich. The equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington on the triumphal arch at Constitution-hill, gigantic as are its proportions, sinks into insignificance before such a monument. The cast of the Bavarian lion has never, it is said, been touched by the chisel, and if so it is highly creditable to the Munich foundry. The bronze statues, which are each seven feet high, are Libusa, Queen of the Bohemians A.D. 700, and George of Padiebad, King of the Bohemians; both are modelled by Schwanthaler, and form part of an extensive cyclns of bronze statues in the possession of a Prague connoisseur. There is much dignity in the attitude, and simplicity in the drapery, of Libusa and the details of the King's armour are elaborately chiselled. Kiss's celebrated group of the Amazon, although often referred to, cannot be passed without a word. The muscles of the horse are rigid as iron, agony and fear are fineiy expressed in the expanded nostrils, the swollen veins, the eyes starting from their sockets, and the ears thrown back. Firmly seated almost on the hips of the horse, the Amazon, grasping the mane with one hand and poising the spear in the other, is about to fracture the tiger's skull. The body is finely poised, the face is the concentration of sublime and assured power, the forehead intellectual vigour, and the whole figure courage and determination in its most refined yet potent form. The composition is grand beyond all description, and comparable with no work of art we know of, for the higher qualities of dramatic action. It is of Silesian zinc and bronzed. The original, in bronze, was purchased by a society of amateurs of Berlin, and presented to the King of Prussia, by whom it was placed at the foot of the flight of stairs in front of the Museum of Berlin. Next to these in point of graindeur of design and beauty of execution are the bag and alto relieves of Barbedienne of Paris. The chef d'auvre of his collection is a reduced copy of the famous gate of Cehiherti in the baptistry of the Church of St. John at Florence, with its marvellous frieze and boldly relieved pictures in the panels. It will be remembered that it was of these gates Michael Angelo said that they were worthy to form the entrance gates to Paradise. The door of the one exhibited (for there is we regret to say only one) is onefourth the siz t of the original, the reduction being made by a mechanical process that secures the utmost accuracy. Those who are familiar with the gates, or their copies, will recollect the many figures, especially in the panels, so beldly relieved as be almost detached from the background, necessitating the utmost delicacy of moulding and skill in casting. These, as well as the bas-reliefs, are expressed with a beauty and precision that exact the praise of the initiated, and excite the surprise of the amateur. The colour of the bronze is exceedingly rich, and is said to owe its excellence to the admixture of gold. Close beside this is a bookcase of ebony and bronze by the same artist. The panels of the lower part of the case are from the Ghiberti gates, ann consist of the choicest scriptural pictures; the frieze is , also from that great work. The figures in the pediment are ! the far-famed Night and Morning of Clesinger, and the I mailed figure seated on the apex, with his head resting upon his hand, is the celebrated Thinker of Michael Angelo, found in the Sorenti Chapel. The frames of the glass doors are formed of bronze columns, and the details of the casting will bear the most rigorous investigation. The dark wood and bronze harmonise well, and the subjects selected for illustration give to the work an elevation and a dignity, the result not the less of its beauty than of the associations connected with Ghiberti's master-piece. The single figures of Barbedienne are not less worthy of note. Among the best are the Apollo Belvedere, the Gladiator, the Euterpe. and the Leocoon. It may add to the interest of this unique collection to say that they are placed in a remote corner, where none but a professional explorer who has been cloyed with the more prominent and brilliant displays of the naves and transept could discover them. When they are found, we feel assured that there is no visitor of taste who will not return to them again. In the gallery over the eastern entrance was exhibited yesterday for the first time his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales's rowing skiff, which is constructed upon a peculiar principle, under the superintendence of Captain Light, and presented to his Royal Highness in the year 1849 by Light's Patent Marine Buoyancy Company. She is 20 feet long, and 3 feet 2i inches broad across the main thwart, 3 feet 7 inches at the rowlock, and about a foot deep. She was built by Messrs. George Searle and Sons, of Lambeth, boat-builders to her Majesty, and is constructed of bird'reeye maple, the linings, egaboards, and thwarts being of Spanish mahogany; her keel band, stem band, and rudder hangings are of bronze, the rudder of maple, with a carved yoke, gilt, and silk lines and tassels of crimson and ' gold colour. She is also fitted with an elegantly-carved chair, the seat of which is covered with crimson satin damask, with an elaborate pattern in raised velvet of the same colour, the back being supported by the Prince of Walee's feathers, carved in maple and heightened with gold. The rowing mat is of the same material as the cushion of the chair, and there is a small foot ottoman of Utrecht velvet. The sculls are of mahogany end very light. The boat, which is a "single scalling skiff," is lined throughout between the timbers with Captain Light's patent material, which gives to her all the buoyancy and other properties of a life-boat. In some trials of this principle on the boats for the Preventive Srvice at Deal, it was found to render them extremely buoyant, and at the same time to stiffen them very much under canvass ; and as the hazardous services on which these boats are employed are such as to place them continually in imminent danger of being swamped, the adoption of this system, both for them and for the boats of her Majesty's service generally, would be of great value, and would tend to prevent loss of life and sacrifice of property. The experiments showed that boats lined with Light's buoyancy material were capable of carrying a full complemeat of hands with much more dead weight than usual, and yet, when filled gunwale deep with water, they could not be submerged. The same prir.ciple has been extensively used in the construction of swimming belts, life buoys, &c., and for the stuffing of yacht cushions, mattresses, &c.; and as the material used is merely light tough rushes properly prepared, and only three. fifths the weight of cork, no injury can ensue from puncture or cutting, as with air cushions, or the destruction of the elasticity, as in the case of cork shavings. Two beautiful specimens of swimming belts mid small lifebuoys were presented with the boat, for thence of his Royal Highness.
